59.q: Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by
59.e: Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by exosome. Exosomes are derived from Multivesicular bodies (MVB). These extracellular vesicles are mediators of cell to cell communication in eukaryotes. Other options: Option A: Lysosomes are membrane-bound spherical organelles which contain a variety of hydrolytic enzymes meant for intracytoplasmic digestion. Lysosomes remove intracellular products of metabolism from the cell. Option B: Peroxisomes are small spherical organelles that contain oxidases which promote oxidation of lipids and catalases that liberate oxygen from H2O2. They protect the tissue from oxidative stress. Option C: The genetic information stored in chromosomes of a cell is known as the genome. The human genome contains about 3 billion nucleotide pairs and in diploid cells they are organized into 23 pairs of chromosome

59.e: Microfilaments Are mainly actin and myosin concerned with muscle contraction and cell motility Some types of cell motility occur solely as the result of actin polymerization and do not involve the activity of myosin Reference: Ganong, 25th edition page no.38

59.e: Body surface area is the most important factor that affects basal metabolic rate "Rubner's law" states that BMR should be related to surface area rather than body mass. This law is also called as "surface law of metabolism" Reference: Ganong, 25 th edition page no.488

59.e: Ohm's Law which deals with relationship between potential difference, current and resistance V =I * R In vascular physiology, current flow is equated with the blood flow (F) and the voltage difference is equated with the pressure difference (P) across the vessel wall. So, the modified Ohm's Law is, P =F * R Reference: Ganong, 25th edition page no.572

60.q: Which of the following hormones have an intracellular receptor?
60.e: Thyroxine hormones have intracellular receptors. Steroid and thyroid hormones bind to the intracellular receptors which regulate gene transcription. The hormone diffuses through the cell membrane into the cytoplasm and combines with the receptor which is present either in cytoplasm or in nucleus. o: Removal of CSF during dural tap causes intense intracranial headache
Formed by arachnoid villi within the ventricles
pH is less than that of plasma
63.e: The CSF is formed in the choroid plexuses and the remainder is formed around blood vessels and along ventricular walls. CSF fills the ventricles and subarachnoid space. In humans, the volume of CSF is about 150 mL and the rate of CSF production is about 550 mL/d. Thus the CSF turns over about 3.7 times a day. The composition of CSF is essentially the same as that of brain extracellular fluid (ECF), which in living humans makes up 15% of the brain volume. pH (7.31 - 7.34) slightly less than plasma (7.35 - 7.45). CSF contain no neutrophils. Its differential count is: Lymphocyte - 60-70%, Monocytes - 30-50%, Neutrophils - None. Ref: Barrett K.E., Barman S.M., Boitano S., Brooks H.L. (2012). Chapter 33. 65.q: In skeletal muscle DHPR & RYR receptors are coupled by?
65.e: In skeletal muscle DHPR & RYR receptors are coupled mechanically. The membrane of T-tubules contains voltage-gated Ca2+ channels called dihydropyridine (DHP) receptors. When the action potential reaches the tip of Ttubule, it activates the DHP receptors. Activated DHP receptors in turn trigger the opening of Ca2+ release channels located on the terminal cisterns known as ryanodine receptors (RYR). This is possible as the lateral cisterns are located very close to the tips of T-tubules and the protein channels of the cisterns i.e DHP and RYR are mechanically interlocked.

66.q: Which one of the following is the CORRECT statement regarding coronary blood flow?
o: Coronary blood flow is directly related to perfusion pressure and inversely related to resistance
Coronary blood flow is inversely related to perfusion pressure and directly related to resistance
Coronary blood flow is directly related to perfusion pressure and also to resistance
Coronary blood flow is inversely related to both pressure and resistance
66.e: Coronary blood flow is directly related to the perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic pressure) and the duration of diastole. Because coronary flow drops to negligible values during systole, the duration of diastole becomes a limiting factor for myocardial perfusion during tachycardia. Coronary blood flow is inversely proportional to coronary vascular resistance. Resistance is determined mainly by intrinsic factors—including metabolic products and autonomic activity—and by various pharmacologic agents. Damage to the endothelium of coronary vessels has been shown to alter their ability to dilate and to increase coronary vascular resistance. Ref: Katzung B.G. (2012). Chapter 12. Vasodilators & the Treatment of Angina Pectoris. In B.G. Katzung, S.B. Masters, A.J. Trevor (Eds), Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 12e.

69.e: Gate control theory is the mechanism behind Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibers in the vicinity of the injury. 73.q: Shivering is controlled by: September 2012, March 2013
73.e: Ans. B i.e. Posterior hypothalamus Shivering/Shuddering It is a bodily function in response to early hypothermia in warm- blooded animals. When the core body temperature drops, the shivering reflex is triggered to maintain homeostasis. Muscle groups around the vital organs begin to shake in small movements in an attempt to create warmth by expending energy. Shivering can also be a response to a fever, as a person may feel cold, though their core temperature is already elevated. Located in the posterior hypothalamus near the wall of the third ventricle is an area called the primary motor center for shivering. This area is normally inhibited by signals from the heat center in the anterior hypothalamic-preoptic area but is excited by cold signals from the skin and spinal cord.

76.q: Airway resistance is lowest in which of the following?
76.e: Airway resistance decreases as lung volume increases because the increasingly subatmospheric intrapleural pressure increases the radial traction on the airways, thereby increasing airway diameter and decreasing airway resistance. During a forced expiration or at the residual volume, the intrathoracic pressure is positive, compressing the airways and increasing their resistance. The vagus nerve constricts airway smooth muscle. Resistances in parallel add as reciprocals. Thus, the large number of small, peripheral airways increases the number of airways arranged in parallel, and lowers the total resistance of the peripheral airways compared to the total cross-section of the central airways. 79.q: A 57-year-old female presents with dyspnea on exertion. Pulmonary function studies with plethysmography demonstrate an increase in the work of breathing, and the oxygen consumption is higher-than-normal at rest. Which of the following will decrease the oxygen consumption of the respiratory muscles?
o: A decrease in the diffusing capacity of the lung
An increase in the rate of respiration
79.e: Respiratory muscles consume oxygen in proportion to the work of breathing. The work of breathing is equal to the product of the change in volume for each breath and the change in pressure necessary to overcome the resistive work of breathing and the elastic work of breathing. Resistive work includes work to overcome tissue as well as airway resistance; thus a decreased airway resistance will decrease the work of breathing and the oxygen consumption of the respiratory muscles. A decreased lung compliance would increase the elastic work of breathing. An increase in respiratory rate or tidal volume increases the work of breathing. Reference: Ganong, pp 657-658. It increases when there is a deficiency of surfactant
79.e: Lung compliance is an index of lung distensibility or the ease with which the lungs are expanded; thus, compliance is the inverse of elastic recoil. Compliance is defined as the ratio of change of lung volume to the change in pressure required to inflate the lung (Δ V /Δ P ). Compliance decreases in patients with pulmonary edema or surfactant deficiency and increases when there is a loss of elastic fibers in the lungs, such as occurs in patients with emphysema and with aging. 82.e: Increasing cardiac output or pulmonary artery pressure causes pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) to passively decrease due to two mechanisms-distention of the perfused vessels, and recruitment of more parallel vascular beds. At high lung volumes, the pulmonary capillaries ("alveolar" vessels) are stretched and compressed causing an increased PVR. At low lung volumes, the "extraalveolar" blood vessels are compressed, increasing PVR. The lowest PVR occurs near FRC. Decreasing PO2 or increasing PCO2 or H+ concentration causes PVR to rise. The sympathetic nervous system has little effect on PVR under physiologic conditions, but experimentally, stimulation of sympathetic nerves will constrict the pulmonary vessels, causing increased PVR. Five of the six vascular channels functionally close at birth, but the ductus arteriosus remains open normally for ~48 hours (though ductal flow is reversed from that in fetal life). 91.e: Explanation: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone that regulates red blood cell (RBC) production. Approximately 90% of erythropoietin is synthesized in the kidneys , while the remaining 10% is produced in the liver . In the kidneys, fibroblast-like interstitial cells in the cortex and outer medulla are the main sites of production, responding to tissue hypoxia. The liver contributes mainly during the fetal stage , serving as the predominant site of erythropoietin synthesis before birth. When hypoxia occurs, the hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) activates the erythropoietin gene , increasing hormone synthesis to stimulate erythropoiesis in the bone marrow. 107.q: Which one of the following choices does not represent a function of glucagon?

111.q: In a 90-kg man, follows a high carbohydrate meal diet plan, which metabolic pathway is predominantly active and contributes to weight gain? 1. Malonyl-CoA 2. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 3. Mitochondrial carnitine transporter 4. Tricarboxylate transporter (citrate)

(statement 4) Mitochondrial carnitine transporter (CPT-I) is involved in fatty acid oxidation. It helps transport fatty acids into mitochondira for breakdown. 112.q: Thermogenin protein is mainly found in:

UCP1 acts as a proton channel, allowing protons to leak back into the mitochondrial matrix without passing through ATP synthase. This uncouples oxidative phosphorylation from ATP synthesis, dissipating the proton gradient energy as heat to maintain body temperature, especially in newborns and hibernating mammals. Key Takeaways: Thermogenin (UCP1) is an uncoupling protein found in the mitochondria of brown adipose tissue. It generates heat by uncoupling electron transport from ATP production.

113.q: A diabetic patient presents with elevated VLDL levels due to which combination of the following enzyme activities?
113.e: Explanation: Hormone-Sensitive Lipase (HSL): HSL breaks down stored triglycerides in adipose tissue into free fatty acids and glycerol. In diabetes, HSL activity is increased , releasing more free fatty acids into circulation, which the liver uses to synthesize VLDL (Very Low-Density Lipoprotein). Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL): LPL hydrolyzes triglycerides in VLDL and chylomicrons into free fatty acids for tissue uptake. In diabetes, LPL activity is reduced , impairing the clearance of VLDL from the bloodstream. Combined Effect: High HSL → more substrate for hepatic VLDL production. Low LPL → reduced VLDL clearance. 114.q: Bilirubin in serum can be measured by:

An assay conducted in the absence of added methanol measures "direct bilirubin," which is bilirubin glucuronide. An assay conducted in the presence of added methanol measures total bilirubin. The difference between total bilirubin and direct bilirubin is known as "indirect bilirubin," and is unconjugated bilirubin. Option B: Ehrlich's Reaction is used to detect urobilinogen in urine. Option C: Schlesinger's Reaction is used to detect urobilin. Option D: Fouchet's Reaction is used to detect bile pigment like bilirubin in urine.

ALAS1 is ubiquitously expressed throughout the body, whereas ALAS2 is expressed in erythrocyte precursor cells. 117.q: Following is false regarding Vitamin D?

117.e: Vitamin D is not strictly a vitamin since it can be synthesised in the skin, and in most conditions, this is the major source of the vitamin. Only when sunlight exposure is inadequate, a dietary source is required. Its main function is in the regulation of calcium absorption and homeostasis most of its actions are mediated by way of nuclear receptors that regulate gene expression. It also has a role in regulating cell proliferation and differentiation. There is evidence that intakes considerably higher than are required to maintain calcium homeostasis reduce the risk of insulin resistance, obesity, and the metabolic syndrome, as well as various cancers. Deficiency, leading to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, is a problem in northern latitudes, where sunlight exposure is inadequate Reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd Edition, Page Number- 1297.

117.e: A number of other proteins undergo the same vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of glutamate to y-carboxyglutamate which include: Osteocalcin Protein C and S Matrix Gla protein in bone Nephrocalcin in kidney and Growth arrest specific gene Gas6, which is involved in both the regulation of differentiation and development in the nervous system, and control of apoptosis in other tissues. All of these y-carboxyglutamate containing proteins bind calcium, which causes a conformational change so that they interact with membrane phospholipids. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition; page 390, Lippincott illustrated reviews 8 th edition biochemistry page 1305

117.q: Haemolytic anemia is due to the deficiency of which vitamin?
117.e: The lack of Vit. E causes the membrane of the RBC to be abnormally fragile and as a result of lipid peroxidation, there is membrane lysis causing haemolytic anemia Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 1302

117.q: Patient with Abetalipoproteinemia frequently manifests with delayed blood clotting. This is due to inability to:
117.e: Fat soluble vitamins are absorbed in Chylomicrons Most clinical manifestations of abetalipoproteinemia result from defects in the absorption and transport of fat-soluble vitamins. Vitamin E and retinyl esters are normally transported from enterocytes to the liver by chylomicrons. Vitamin E is dependent on VLDL for transport out of the liver and into the circulation. As apo B containing lipoproteins are not formed these patients, there is, marked deficiency of Vitamin E, mild to moderate deficiency of Vitamin A and K. Bleeding manifestation due to defective absorption of fat and hence fat-soluble vitamins. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 275

117.q: All of the following are conjugating agent, except:
117.e: In phase 1 reactions, xenobiotics are converted to more polar, hydroxylated derivatives. In phase 2 reactions, these derivatives are conjugated with molecules such as glucuronic acid (Option A), sulfate, glutathione (Option B), Glycine (Option D), Acetyl Co A, Methyl group etc. This renders them even more water-soluble, and they are eventually excreted in the urine or bile. But glucose is directly not used as conjugating agent. So, Option C is correct. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 47 PN 558

117.q: Metabolism of following compounds will involve enzyme cytochrome P450, except:
117.e: The main reaction involved in phase 1 detoxification metabolism is hydroxylation, catalyzed by a family of enzymes known as monooxygenases or cytochromes P450. Option A: At least half of the common drugs that we ingest are metabolized by isoforms of cytochrome P450. Option B: They also act on steroid hormones, carcinogens, and pollutants. Option C: Cytochromes P450 are important in the metabolism of a number of physiological compounds-for example, the synthesis of steroid hormones and the conversion of vitamin D to its active metabolite, calcitriol. Option D: Vitamin E metabolism do not involve role of cytochrome P450. A conversion of vitamin D to its active metabolite, calcitriol required cytochrome P450 enzyme. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 47 PN 557

117.q: False regarding Vit. D toxicity is?
o: Excess dietary Vit. D causes toxicity
Prolonged exposure to sunlight can cause formation of excess active compounds
Excess Vit. D can cause contracture of blood vessels causing high blood pressure
117.e: Excess Vit. D is the most toxic vitamin when taken in excess as it causes abnormal calcification of soft tissues. Excess Vit. Dcan lead to contraction of blood vessels, high blood pressure, and calcinosis-the calcification of soft tissues. In at least a few cases, hypercalcemia in response to low intakes of vitamin D is due to genetic defects of calcidiol 24-hydroxylase, the enzyme that leads to inactivation of the vitamin. Although excess dietary vitamin D is toxic, excessive exposure to sunlight does not lead to vitamin D poisoning, because there is a limited capacity to form the precursor, 7-dehydrocholesterol, and prolonged exposure of previtamin D to sunlight leads to formation of inactive compounds. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition, page 1300

117.q: Compounds that have the biological activity of Vit k are all except?
117.e: Three compounds have the biological activity of vitamin K Phylloquinone, the normal dietary source, found in green vegetables Menaquinones, synthesized by intestinal bacteria with differing lengths of side chain, Menaquinones are absorbed to some extent, but it is not clear to what extent they are biologically active Menadione and menadiol diacetate, synthetic compounds that can be metabolized to phylloquinone. Quinolone is an antibiotic and has no relation to Vit. K Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 1302

118.q: How many ATPs are produced by the oxidation of one molecule NADPH in oxidative phosphorylation?
118.e: Option A: NADPH is never used to produce ATP in oxidative phosphorylation, instead it is used for reductive biosynthesis of many compounds. Option B: The oxidation of one molecule FADH2 in oxidative phosphorylation produces 1.5 ATPs. Option C: The oxidation of one molecule NADH in oxidative phosphorylation produces 2.5 ATPs. Option D: It was believed that the oxidation of one molecule NADH in oxidative phosphorylation produces 3 ATPs earlier, but recently it is corrected to 2.5. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 11 PN 108

118.q: Which coenzyme act as reducing agent in anabolic reaction cholesterol?
118.e: Many steps in fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol synthesis and steroid hormone required NADPH. NADPH helps in the reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids, Cholesterol and steroid hormones. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 269
Ans. is 'a' i.e., NADP [Rep Harper 29t5/e p. 201-204] Gulonate dehydrogenase is an enzyme in glucuronic acid pathway (uronic acid pathway) that requires NADP'.

118.q: In TCA Cycle, conversion of pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A and carbon dioxide:
o: Involves the participation of lipoic acid.
Is activated when pyruvate decarboxylase of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHC) is phosphorylated by PDH kinase in the presence of ATP.
118.e: The PDH Complex contains five coenzymes that act as carriers or oxidants for the intermediates of the reactions. E1 requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), E2 requires lipoic acid and CoA, and E3 requires FAD and NAD+. [Note: TPP, lipoic acid, and FAD are tightly bound to the enzymes and function as coenzymes–prosthetic groups][Note: Lipoic acid linked to a lysine residue in E2 functions as a “swinging arm” that allows interaction with E1 and E3.] The PDHC catalyzes an irreversible reaction that is inhibited when the decarboxylase component (E1) is phosphorylated. The PDHC is located in the mitochondrial matrix. Biotin is utilized by carboxylases, not decarboxylases. Reference: Lippincott SAE, page no. 207-208 Reference: Harper's 32 nd edition, chapter - 17

Option B: The main clinical manifestation of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy is generalized seizures, which usually occur in the first days of life and are unresponsive to conventional anticonvulsant therapies. Some mothers of affected fetuses report abnormal intrauterine fluttering movements. The seizures are usually tonic-clonic in nature but can be almost any type. Other manifestations such as dystonia, respiratory distress, and abdominal distention with vomiting, hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia and hypothermia may be present. Learning problems and speech delay are common sequelae. Late-onset forms of the condition (as late as 5 years of age) have been reported. Consequently, a trial with vitamin B6 is recommended in any infant with intractable convulsions Option A, Option C & Option D: Thiamine, Riboflavin & Pantothenic acid deficiency not reported to cause neonatal seizures.

118.q: Vitamin B1 is required for which reaction
118.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e.,Oxidative decarboxylation [Ref Harper 29th/e p. 534] * Active form (coenzyme form) of thiamine is thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), also called thiamine diphosphate (TDP). * TPP acts as coenzyme for - Oxidative decarboxylation:- Pyruvate dehydrogenase, a- ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, brached-chain keto acid dehydrogenase. - Transketolase in PPP.

Ans. is 'c' i.e., 0.03 mg/kg [Ref. Park 22"d/e p. 572] Vitamin A→ 600 mcg retinol Vitamin B7 (Thiamine)--> 0.5 mg per 1000 Kcal of energy intake Vitamin B, (Riboflavin) → 0.6 mg per 1000 Kcal of energy intake Vitamin B, (Niacin) → 6.0 mg per 1000 Kcal of energy intake Vitamin 135 (Pantothenic Acid) → 10 mg Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) →2 mg Vitamin B, (Folic Acid) →200 mcg Vitamin B12(Cobalamin) →1 mcg Vitamin D 100 IU (2.5 mcg calciferol) Vitamin E (Tocopherol) ⇒ → 0.8 mg per gm of essential fatty acids Vitamin K → 0.03 mg per kg

119.q: Catabolism of H2O2 is carried out by:
119.e: Peroxisomes (or) microbodies are concerned with three vital functions in a cell namely: Generation and degradation of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) Oxidation of very long chain fatty acids (ag, C20 C22) Detoxification of harmful chemicals Reference: Ganong, 25th edition page no.38

119.q: How many atoms of copper are incorporated in Erythrocuprein?
119.e: Explanation: Erythrocuprein, also known as ceruloplasmin, is a copper-carrying protein in the blood. Each molecule of ceruloplasmin contains one atom of copper that is essential for its enzymatic activity, which includes oxidising iron and functioning in iron metabolism.

119.q: Which of the following sentence is true regarding chemical modification of LDL (Low density lipoprotein) by free radicals?
o: Easily recognized by liver LDL receptor
Not taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors
119.e: Chemical modification of the proteins or lipids in plasma low-density lipoprotein (LDL) leads to abnormal LDL. Option A & Option B: Such modified LDL is not recognized by the liver LDL receptors, and so is not cleared by the liver. Option C: Such modified LDL is highly atherogenic. Option D: The modified LDL is taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors. Lipid-engorged macrophages infiltrate under blood vessel endothelium (especially when there is already some damage to the endothelium), and are killed by the high content of unesterified cholesterol they have accumulated. This occurs in the development of atherosclerotic plaques. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 45 PN 542

119.q: Which of the following molecule is present in glutathione peroxidase as prosthetic group?
119.e: In erythrocytes and other tissues, the enzyme glutathione peroxidase, containing selenium as a prosthetic group, catalyzes the destruction of H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides through the conversion of reduced glutathione to its oxidized form, protecting membrane lipids and haemoglobin against oxidation by peroxides. So, Option C is correct. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 12 PN 114

119.q: Following metal is present in Glutathione peroxidase for their catalytic action
119.e: In erythrocytes and other tissues, the enzyme glutathione peroxidase, containing selenium as a prosthetic group, catalyzes the destruction of H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides through the conversion of reduced glutathione to its oxidized form, protecting membrane lipids and hemoglobin against oxidation by peroxides Selenium is present in various enzymes as part of the 21 st amino acid, Selenocysteine. Selenocysteine containing enzymes include: Glutathione Peroxidase (1-8) Iodothyronine Deiodinase (1-3) Thioredoxin reductase (1-3) Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase Exportin-1 LRP-2, LRP-8 eIF-4A3 eEFsec Selenoprotein H, I, K, M, N, O, P, R (1,2,3), S, T, U, V, W Selenocysteine Lyase & Synthase Selenophosphate synthetase 1 & 2 Tocopherol alpha transfer proteins Reference: Harper's 32 nd edition, page 122

119.q: The co-factor for glutathione peroxidase is:
119.e: Explanation: Glutathione peroxidase (GPx) is a key antioxidant enzyme that reduces hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides to water and alcohols, respectively, using glutathione as a reducing agent. Selenium is an essential co-factor for this enzyme, as it is incorporated into its active site as the amino acid selenocysteine , which is critical for its catalytic activity. Explanation of other options: Manganese (Option A): Manganese is a co-factor for enzymes like manganese superoxide dismutase and arginase . Copper (Option C): Copper is a co-factor for copper-zinc superoxide dismutase and cytochrome c oxidase. Magnesium (Option D): Magnesium is a co-factor for many ATP-dependent enzymes like kinases and polymerases. Key Takeaways: Selenium is the crucial co-factor for the antioxidant enzyme glutathione peroxidase. A deficiency can impair the body's ability to neutralize peroxides.

119.q: Which mineral serves as a cofactor for the enzyme glutathione peroxidase?
119.e: Explanation: The enzyme glutathione peroxidase is an important antioxidant enzyme that helps protect cells from oxidative damage by reducing hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides. Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes and plays a crucial role in cellular metabolism, immune function, and protein synthesis. It is also involved in the activity of several antioxidant enzymes, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), which helps neutralize free radicals. However, it is not the primary cofactor for glutathione peroxidase.

119.q: In humans, ascorbic acid cannot be synthesized because of ?
119.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Deficiency of L-gulonolactone oxidase In man, other primates and guinea pigs, ascorbic acid can be synthesized due to absence of L-glucanolactone oxidase, an enzyme used in lower animals to synthesise ascorbic acid as a byproduct of uronic acid pathway (glucuronic acid cycle).

120.q: In the metabolism of cytosine, what is one of the final products?
120.e: Explanation: Cytosine is a pyrimidine base, and during its catabolism, it is first deaminated to uracil, which is then further broken down via the pyrimidine degradation pathway. One of the final products of uracil (and thus cytosine) metabolism is β-alanine. This distinguishes pyrimidine breakdown from purine metabolism, where the final product is uric acid, and from muscle metabolism, where creatinine is formed

120.q: Allantoin is a more water soluble product of purine catabolism compared to uric acid. But in human, uric acid is not further converted into allantoin due to lack of enzyme:
120.e: Option A: Xanthine oxidase enzyme convert Hypoxanthine into Xanthine and Xanthine into Uric acid. This enzyme presents in mammals and humans both, so both breakdown purines up to uric acid. Option B: HGPRTase is an enzyme involved in the salvage pathway. It converts Guanine & Hypoxanthine into GMP & IMP. Its deficiency can lead to Lesch Nyhan syndrome. Option C: Urease catalyzes the hydrolysis of Urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. It is also not present in humans, so human urea is excreted in urine. Option D: Uricase enzyme convert uric acid into allantoin. Allantoin is more water soluble than uric acid. But in human uricase enzyme is absent, so the end product of purine catabolism is uric acid. Uricase is present in mammals, so they convert uric acid into allantoin. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 33 PN 334

120.q: Which enzyme catalyses the conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides?
120.e: Explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase is the key enzyme that converts ribonucleotides (RNA precursors) into deoxyribonucleotides (DNA precursors), making it essential for DNA synthesis and repair. Ribonucleotide phosphorylase is involved in the breakdown of ribonucleosides during nucleotide metabolism. Nucleoside phosphorylase functions mainly in the salvage pathway by converting nucleosides into nitrogenous bases and sugar phosphates, helping recycle nucleotides. Nucleotidase simply removes phosphate groups from nucleotides to convert them into nucleosides and is mainly involved in nucleotide degradation and regulation.

120.q: All of the following deoxynucleotides are present in DNA except
120.e: The chemical nature of the monomeric deoxynucleotide units of DNA are deoxyadenylate, deoxyguanylate (Option C), deoxycytidylate (Option D), and thymidylate (Option B). But it does not contain deoxyuridylate (Option A). These monomeric units of DNA are held in polymeric form by 3′,5′-phosphodiester bonds constituting a single strand of DNA. So Option A is the correct answer, rest Option B, Option C and Option D are not correct. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 34 PN 338

120.q: Which of the following is not involved in synthesis of pyrimidines?
120.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Glycine [Ref Harper 29th/e p. 336-337] Amino acids involved in purine synthesis → Glycine, aspartate, glutamine. Amino acids involved in pyrimidine synthesis → Glutamine, aspartic acid (aspartate)

120.q: What condition is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT)?
120.e: Explanation: HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch Nyhan syndrome , an X-linked recessive disorder in which failure of the purine salvage pathway leads to excess uric acid production and neurological symptoms like developmental delay and self-mutilation. Gout involves hyperuricemia and is primarily linked to purine metabolism and the overproduction or underexcretion of uric acid. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is a urea cycle disorder leading to hyperammonemia and Adenosine deaminase deficiency is purine metabolism disorder but results in severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).

Ans. is 'c' i.e., Fatty acid [Ref Harper's 28"/e p. 286] Nucleotides are monomeric units of nucleic acids. They are required for synthesis of nucleic acid. Each nucleotide is made up of : (i) A nitrogenous base, (ii) A sugar (pentose sugar) and (iii) A phosphate group (phosphoric acid). Nitrogenous base combines with a sugar to form nucleosides. The nucleoside combines with phosphoric acid to form a nucleotide.

120.q: How does methotrexate affect nucleotide metabolism?
o: It reduces the availability of thymidine and purines
It has no effect on nucleotide metabolism
120.e: Explanation: Option wise explanation Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, an enzyme required to convert dihydrofolate(DHF) into tetrahydrofolate(THF). THF is essential for one-carbon transfer reactions involved in the synthesis of purines and thymidine. By blocking DHFR, methotrexate depletes THF, leading to reduced availability of both purines and thymidine, which impairs DNA synthesis and cell division. This is why it's effective in rapidly dividing cells like cancer and in autoimmune disorders.

121.q: A 42 yr old patient with symptoms of premature aging and is diagnosed as Werner syndrome. The most likely mechanism?
o: Short telomere with damaged DNA and loss of helicase
121.e: Werner syndrome is characterized by the dramatic, rapid appearance of features associated with normal aging. Individuals with this disorder typically grow and develop normally until they reach puberty Werner syndrome is characterised by the defective DNA Helicase Enzym, which causes short telomere and damage DNA

121.q: What is the function of DNA ligase ?
o: Unwinding (denaturation) of dsDNA to provide an ssDNA template
Seals the single strand nick between the nascent chain and Okazaki fragments on lagging strand
Initiation of DNA synthesis and elongation
121.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Seals the single strand nick between the nascent chain and Okazaki fragments on lagging strand [Ref Harper 2501e p. 367]

121.q: Radiant damage can lead to following types of DNA damages which leading to cancer, except:
121.e: Some Types of DNA Damage Caused by Radiation Option A: Formation Pyrimidine Dimer (Thymine dimer) - condensation of adjacent thymine Option B: Formation of purine dimer not seen commonly. Option C: Formation of apurinic or apyrimidinic sites by elimination of corresponding bases, Hydrolysis of N glycosidic bond which connect N base with deoxyribose sugar Option D: Formation of strand (chain) breaks or cross-linking of DNA strands Chain break - Disintegration of backbone element, can be single strand or double strand Cross linkage - Between bases in same or opposite strands, also between DNA and protein molecules (eg, histones) Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 56 PN 683

121.q: Which of the following is true regarding reverse transcriptase enzymes?
o: RNA polymerase having reverse transcriptase activity
121.e: Option A: RNA polymerase does not have reverse transcriptase activity, it has only transcriptase activity. Telomerase enzymes have reverse transcriptase activity. Option B: Reverse transcriptase enzyme is RNA dependent DNA polymerase, not DNA dependent RNA polymerase. Option C: Reverse transcriptase enzyme is RNA dependent DNA polymerase Option D: Present in RNA virus. There exists in one species of animal viruses (retroviruses) a class of enzymes capable of synthesizing a single-stranded and then a dsDNA molecule from a single-stranded RNA template. This polymerase, termed RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, or "reverse transcriptase," first synthesizes a DNA - RNA hybrid molecule utilizing the RNA genome as a template. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 31 st edition CH 35 PN 367

121.q: Which mineral is essential for the function of the enzyme DNA polymerase?
121.e: Explanation: DNA Polymerase is an essential enzyme responsible for DNA replication and repair. It reads the DNA template strand and synthesises a complementary strand by adding nucleotides in a 5' to 3' direction, ensuring the fidelity of DNA replication. Magnesium ions (Mg²+) act as crucial cofactors for DNA polymerase. Magnesium stabilises the structure of nucleotides and the active site of the enzyme, facilitating the formation of phosphodiester bonds between nucleotides. This ion is essential for both the catalytic activity and the accuracy of DNA polymerase during DNA synthesis.

121.q: What is the role of the 3' to 5' exonuclease activity of DNA polymerase?
121.e: Explanation: The 3′ to 5′ exonuclease activity of DNA polymerase functions in proofreading by removing incorrectly paired nucleotides from the 3′ end of the growing DNA strand and replacing them with the correct ones, thereby maintaining high fidelity of DNA replication. DNA unwinding is done by helicase, RNA synthesis by RNA polymerase, and primer removal occurs through 5′ to 3′ exonuclease activity (in prokaryotes) or RNase H and DNA polymerase δ (in eukaryotes).

121.q: Which of the following is a true sentence about linker DNA?
o: Short DNA consisting of roughly only 30 bp
121.e: In chromatin, core nucleosome particles are separated by DNA termed "linker DNA" Option A: It is a Short DNA consisting of roughly 30-bp regions. Option B: It links two nucleosomes, not present inside the nucleosome core. Option C: Contain histone H1; H2A & H2B are present in the nucleosome core. Option D: Two strands of DNA is linked by hydrogen bond, not linker DNA Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 35 PN 353

DNA polymerases only synthesize DNA in the 5' to 3' direction. Because the DNA strands are antiparallel, the polymerase functions asymmetrically. On the leading (forward) strand, the DNA is synthesized continuously. On the lagging (retrograde) strand, the DNA is synthesized in short (1-5 kb) fragments, the so-called Okazaki fragments, so named after the scientist who discovered them. Several Okazaki fragments (up to 1000) must be sequentially synthesized for each replication fork. Option A: On the lagging (retrograde) strand, the DNA is synthesized in short fragments, called Okazaki fragments. Option B: On the leading (forward) strand, the DNA is synthesized continuously. Option C & D: Any RNA does not contain Okazaki fragments. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 35 PN 363

122.q: Which RNA is used in RNA splicing ?
122.e: Ans. is 'B' i.e., Small nuclear RNA [Ref Harper 29th/e p. 378, 390] Splicesome Splicesome is an assembly made up of small nuclear RNA (snRNA), some proteins and hnRNA. snRNA combines with proteins to form small nuclear ribnonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs or snurps) that mediate splicing. It is snRNA component of snurps that catalyzes splicing°. Snurps are U,,U,,U3,U4, U5 and U6

122.q: Which of the following pharmacological agents inhibit protein synthesis due its structural similarity with tyrosyl-tRNA?
122.e: Option A: Tetracycline prevents the binding of aminoacyl-tRNAs to the bacterial ribosome A site. Option B: Chloramphenicol works by binding to 23S rRNA, which is interesting in view of the newly appreciated role of rRNA in peptide bond formation through its peptidyl transferase activity. Option C: Puromycin is a structural analogue of tyrosyl-tRNA. Puromycin is incorporated via the A site on the ribosome into the carboxyl terminal position of a peptide but causes the premature release of the polypeptide. Puromycin, as a tyrosyl-tRNA analog, effectively inhibits protein synthesis in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Option D: Cycloheximide inhibits peptidyl transferase in the 60S ribosomal subunit in eukaryotes, presumably by binding to an rRNA component. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 37 PN 407

122.q: Menke's disease is due to a defect of which enzyme?
122.e: Option A: Menkes syndrome, characterized by kinky hair and growth retardation, results from a dietary deficiency of copper, an essential cofactor for the enzyme lysyl oxidase that functions in formation of the covalent cross-links that strengthen collagen fiber. Option B & Option D: Lysyl and Prolyl hydroxylases are required for the postsynthetic modification of procollagen to collagen. Both this enzyme requires vitamin C. In vitamin C deficiency(scurvy), leading to skin changes, fragility of blood capillaries, gum decay, tooth loss and bone fracture, which can be attributed to impaired collagen synthesis(leading to delayed wound healing). Option C: Prolyl oxidase does not exist.

122.q: Ascorbic acid is required for synthesis of ?
122.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Hydroxylysine [Ref Harper's 29th/e p. 540] Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residue takes place during post- translational modification in rough ER. The enzyme catalyzing the reactions are prolyl hydroxylase (for proline) and lysyl hydroxylase (for lysine). Both these enzymes are dioxygenases° using molecular oxygen (02) and cofactor for both these enzymes is vitamin C (ascorbic acid)°. a- Ketoglutatrate is a coreductant, which is oxidized to succinate.

122.q: Which antibiotic is used primarily to treat tuberculosis by inhibiting transcription?
122.e: Explanation: Rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA synthesis by binding to the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, effectively stopping transcription. This antibiotic is a critical component of tuberculosis (TB) treatment and is often combined with other drugs to prevent resistance. Its unique mechanism and effectiveness against Mycobacterium tuberculosis make it a first-line drug for TB therapy.

Ans. is 'a' i.e., RNA dependent DNA synthesis [Ref Harper 29thle p. 348] Synthesis of RNA from DNA is called transcription. In transcription, RNA is synthesized by RNA polymerase. RNA polymerase is also called DNA dependent RNA polymerase because it is dependent on DNA (non-coding strand) for RNA synthesis. Reverse transcription, as the name suggests, is the reverse of transcription i.e. synthesis of DNA form RNA. In reverse transcription DNA is synthesized by reverse transcriptase. Reverse transcriptase is also called RNA dependent DNA polymerase because it is dependent on RNA for DNA synthesis.

122.q: The process of formation of Apo-B48 from Apo-B is by?
122.e: The process of formation of apo B-48 from apo B is by RNA editing. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 950

122.q: Rifampicin is widely used in the treatment of tuberculosis and leprosy. It inhibits transcription at which of the following steps?
122.e: Rifampicin inhibits the initiation of transcription by binding to the beta subunit of prokaryotic RNA polymerase, thus interfering with the formation of the first phosphodiester bond So Option A is correct, rest are incorrect options. Reference: Harper’s illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 36 PN 376 & Lippincott’s Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7 th edition (SAE) PN 627.

123.e: Explanation: The anticodon is a sequence of three nucleotides in tRNA that is complementary to a specific mRNA codon. This sequence allows the tRNA to recognize and bind to the corresponding codon on mRNA during translation, ensuring that the correct amino acid is added to the growing polypeptide chain. The anticodon is what primarily determines the tRNA's binding specificity to mRNA.

123.q: In sickle cell anemia, translocation on codon 6 is due to substitution of ?
123.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Valine for glutamate [Ref Harper's 29th/e p. 444] Sickle cell disease, is caused by mutation of a single base out of the 3 x 109 in the genome, a T-to-A DNA substitution, which in turn results in an A-to-U change in the mRNA corresponding to the sixth codon of the 13-globin gene. The altered codon specifies a different amino acid (valine rather than glutamic acid), and this causes a structural abnormality of the p-globin molecule.

123.q: Stickler Syndrome is due to deficiency of which type of collagen?
123.e: Chondrodysplasias are a mixed group of hereditary disorders affecting cartilage. They are manifested by short-limbed dwarfism and numerous skeletal deformities. A number of them are due to a variety of mutations in the COL2A1 gene, leading to abnormal forms of type II collagen. One example is Stickler syndrome (may also be due to mutations in the COL11A1, COL11A2), manifested by degeneration of the joint cartilage and of the vitreous body of the eye. Reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 32 nd Edition, Page Number-643.

123.q: Shine dalgarno sequence is related to ?
123.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Translation Shine dalgarno sequence in prokaryotes and Kozak consensus sequences in eukaryotes helps in initiation of protein synthesis (Translation) In prokaryotes, a sequence of nucleotide bases on mRNA known as Shine-Dalgarno sequence (SD sequence) facilitates the binding of mRNA to the preinitiation complex. SD sequence is a purine-rich sequence of nucleotide bases, which is located -6 to -10 bp from AUG codon°. In Eukaryotes, 'Kozak consensus' sequence surrounds AUG (initiation codon) and determines the initiating codon of mRNA.

123.q: All of the following are features of constitutive gene expression, except:
o: Often referred to as housekeeping genes
Mutation can convert inducible gene to become constitutively expressed
123.e: Option A: The expression of some genes is constitutive, meaning that they are expressed at a reasonably constant rate. Option B: A constitutive gene expression is not known to be subject to regulation. Option C: A constitutive gene is often referred to as housekeeping genes. Option D: As a result of mutation, some inducible gene products become constitutively expressed. A mutation resulting in constitutive expression of what was formerly a regulated gene is called a constitutive mutation. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 38 PN 411

123.q: What effect does glucose have on the lac operon?
o: It enhances the expression of the operon
It inhibits the expression of the operon through catabolite repression
It has no effect on the operon
It directly activates the lac repressor
123.e: Explanation: Glucose inhibits the expression of the lac operon through catabolite repression. When glucose is present in high amounts, intracellular cAMP levels fall. cAMP is necessary to activate CRP (cAMP receptor protein), which binds near the promoter and helps RNA polymerase strongly attach and transcribe the lac operon.

123.q: Which of the following is a condition that gene therapy has been used to treat?
123.e: Explanation: Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, leading to thick mucus production that affects the lungs and digestive system. Gene therapy has been actively explored for treating cystic fibrosis. Approaches include introducing a functional copy of the CFTR gene to correct the defect. Some clinical trials have shown promise .

124.q: In FITC the color emitted after blue light absorption? \
124.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Yellow green Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) is a derivative of fluorescein used in wide-ranging applications including flow cytometry. FITC is the original fluorescein molecule functionalized with an isothiocyanate reactive group (-N=C=S), replacing a hydrogen atom on the bottom ring of the structure. This derivative is reactive towards nucleophiles including amine and sulfhydryl groups on proteins. FITC (fluorescein isothiocyanate) is a fluorochrome dye that absorbs ultraviolet or blue light causing molecules to become excited and emit a visible yellow green light. This emission ceases upon removal of the light causing the excitation.

124.q: Which of the following statements regarding mature cytoplasmic messenger RNA is true ?
o: Has Thiamine in place of Uracil
Its molecular weight is more than hn-RNA
124.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Transcribed from Nuclear DNA [Ref: Lippincott's Biochemistry 5thp.428;Fundamentals of Cytogenetics & Genetics (2010) p. 444] Mesenger RNA (mRNA) is formed by the process of 'transcription' from one of the strands of double stranded nuclear DNA and carries genetic information from the nuclear DNA to the cytosol where it is used as a template for protein synthesis. mRNA comprises only 5-10% of total cellular RNA. It carries the information (massage) from the nucleus to the ribosome. mRNA is synthesized in the nucleus as lieterogenous RNA (hn RNA)', which is processed into functional m RNA.

124.q: Which of the following is the most powerful technique used in transcription factor research which allows identifying genome wide DNA binding sites for transcription factors?
124.e: Option A: Systematic deletion mapping is genetic mapping technique that enables to determine the location of specific genes on chromosomes. Option B: DNAse I sensitivity assay used for discovering regulatory domains. This method maps discrete sites in the genome where the conformation of chromatin renders its DNA hypersensitive to cleavage by endonuclease DNAse I. Option C: Chromatin immunoprecipitation-sequencing (ChIP-seq) is used for simultaneous identification of all of the genomic sites bound by a given transcription factor under a given set of physiologic conditions Option D: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a molecular cytogenetic technique that uses fluorescent probes that bind to only particular parts of a nucleic acid sequence with high degree of sequence complementarity. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 39 PN 447

124.q: If a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification is run for 26 cycles, how many cycles would yield exactly half the number of DNA copies produced at 26 cycles?
124.e: Explanation: At 25 cycles the yield will be exactly half of that after 26 th as PCR amplification is exponential , following the formula: Number of copies = 2 n , where n is the number of cycles. Copies after 26 cycles = 2 26 Half of this amount = 2 26 / 2 = 2 26 x 2 -1 = 2 25 Therefore, the number of cycles needed to get half the copies is 25 cycles . Key Takeaways: Each PCR cycle doubles the number of DNA molecules. Therefore, one cycle less gives half the amount.

124.q: Which of the following techniques is primarily used to determine DNA sequences?
124.e: Explanation: Polymerase Chain Reaction ( PCR ) is a widely used molecular technique that amplifies specific DNA sequences. Once amplified, these DNA fragments can be sequenced accurately using methods such as Sanger sequencing or next-generation sequencing (NGS). Hence, PCR is central to determining DNA sequences. Explanation of Other Options: Flow cytometry (Option A): Used for cell sorting, counting, and analysis of cellular characteristics; not for sequencing DNA. FISH (Option B): Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization detects and localizes specific DNA sequences on chromosomes but does not determine nucleotide sequences. RFLP (Option C): Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism identifies genetic variations based on fragment length differences after restriction enzyme digestion but is not a sequencing method. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3883366/

124.q: Which of the following is NOT a method for introducing recombinant DNA into host cells?
124.e: Explanation: Natural selection is a process by which organisms better adapt to their environment and tend to survive and produce more offsprings. It is not a method for introducing recombinant DNA into a cell. Electroporation, microinjection and liposome-mediated delivery are all direct methods of introducing recombinant DNA into host cells by physically or chemically helping DNA enter the cell (electric pores, needle injection, or lipid fusion).

124.q: What role do telomeres play in genetic stability?
o: They prevent chromosomal fusion and maintain integrity
They are not involved in genetic stability
124.e: Explanation: Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences located at the ends of linear chromosomes. Their primary role is to prevent the ends of chromosomes from being recognized as DNA breaks, thereby avoiding chromosomal fusion and ensuring the integrity and stability of the genome. Telomeres protect chromosomes from degradation and help maintain genomic stability during cell division.

124.q: The megaloblastic anemia that results from vitamin B12 deficiency is due to inadequate supplies of which of the following?
124.e: Deficiency of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) leads to a deficiency in tetrahydrofolate and subsequently a deficiency of the dTMP required for DNA synthesis. Homocysteine and N5-methyltetrahydrofolate accumulate. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 844

125.e: Types of Collagen Major Collagen present in Bone-Type I (90%) Major Collagen present in Dermis, ligaments and tendons-Type I (80%) Major Collagen present in Cartilage-Type II (40-50%) Major Collagen present in Hypertrophic Cartilage- Type X Major Collagen present in Aorta-Type I and Type III (20-40% each) Major Collagen present in Basement Membrane Type IV Most abundant Collagen-Type I Major Collagen in Keloid is Type 3 >> Type 1 Collagen in Wound Healing At first a provisional matrix containing fibrin, plasma fibronectin, and type III collagen is formed, but this is replaced by a matrix composed primarily of type I collagen Reference: Harper's 32 nd edition, page 628

125.q: Which of the following is not a part of the classic triad to diagnose primary hemochromatosis?
o: Micronodular cirrhosis with marked brown pigmentation.
125.e: Explanation: The classic triad for diagnosing primary hemochromatosis consists of: Micronodular cirrhosis with marked brown pigmentation Diabetes mellitus Skin pigmentation Glomerulopathy is not part of the classic triad for diagnosing primary hemochromatosis. While kidney involvement can occur in advanced hemochromatosis, it is not considered a hallmark feature for diagnosis.

125.q: If the RNA sequence is CAAGGU, what would be the corresponding sequence of the DNA template strand?
125.e: Explanation: Given RNA sequence: CAAGGU Relationship between RNA and DNA: RNA is transcribed from the DNA template strand. The DNA template strand is complementary to the RNA sequence. Base pairing rules: Cytosine (C) pairs with Guanine (G) Adenine (A) pairs with Thymine (T) Uracil (U) in RNA pairs with Adenine (A) in DNA Step-by-step conversion: RNA: CAAGGU Complementary DNA template strand (3' → 5'): C pairs with G A pairs with T A pairs with T G pairs with C G pairs with C U pairs with A Resulting template strand: GTTCCA Since DNA sequences are usually written in the 5' → 3' direction, reverse the above sequence: 5' → 3' template strand: ACCTTG

126.q: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with Jaundice. His laboratory reports show increase in AST, ALT and Serum Bilirubin. Which of the following correlates the condition?
126.e: The condition suggests liver cellular injury. All options other than cell membrane rupture are reversible cell injury. Irreversible injury like cell membrane injury shows elevated serum levels due to leakage of intracellular enzymes. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:37

126.q: Which of the following is/are effect(s) of irreversible cell injury caused by reactive oxygen species?
o: Lesions in DNA, loss of phospholipids
126.e: The production of ROS is increased by many injurious stimuli. These free radicals are removed by spontaneous decay and by specialized enzymatic systems. Excessive production or inadequate removal leads to accumulation of free radicals in cells, which may damage lipids(by peroxidation), proteins and DNA, resulting in cell injury. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 44

126.q: Which of the following conditions is an example of disuse atrophy?
o: Skeletal muscle in patients with limb immobilization
Cardiac muscles in patients with Brown atrophy of the heart
126.e: Causes of atrophy include a decreased workload(e.g., immobilization of a limb to permit healing of a fracture), loss of innervation, diminished blood supply, inadequate nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation and aging(senile atrophy). Although some of these stimuli are physiologic(e.g., the loss of hormone stimulation in menopause) and others are pathologic (e.g., denervation), the fundamental cellular changes are similar. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 50

126.q: Which of the following is/are example(s) of pathological hyperplasia? i. Endometrial hyperplasia ii. Organogenesis iii. Benign prostatic hyperplasia iv. Increase in size of uterus during pregnancy
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
126.e: Endometrial hyperplasia is an example of abnormal hormone induced hyperplasia and benign prostatic hyperplasia is in the response to hormone stimulation by androgens. Pathological hyperplasia is seen in these two conditions. Whereas, organogenesis and increase in size of uterus during pregnancy refers to increase in the size of cells, resulting increase in size of the affected organ. These are physiological conditions. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 9 th ed Pg:34

126.q: All the following conditions are examples of hypertrophy EXCEPT:
o: Skeletal muscle changes in weight lifters
126.e: Prostatic changes in elderly males is an example of hyperplasia. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 49

126.q: Which of the following is the example of coexistence of hyperplasia and hypertrophy?
o: Premature breakdown of red blood cells
126.e: The massive physiologic enlargement of the uterus during pregnancy occurs as a consequence of estrogen stimulated smooth muscle hypertrophy and smooth muscle hyperplasia. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:48

126.q: During muscle hypertrophy, the myosin switches from:
o: Beta heavy chain to Alpha heavy chain
Beta light chain to Alpha light chain
Alpha heavy chain to Beta heavy chain
Alpha light chain to Beta light chain
126.e: During hypertrophy, there may occur a switch of contractile proteins from the adult isoforms to the fetal or infantile isoforms. In muscle hypertrophy, the alpha isoform of myosin heavy chain is replaced by the beta isoform of the myosin heavy chain , which produces slower and more energetically economic contraction. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 57

126.q: Deficiency or excess of which of the following vitamins induce squamous metaplasia in the respiratory epithelium?
126.e: Vitamin A is essential for normal epithelial differentiation. Its deficiency also may induce squamous metaplasia in the respiratory epithelium. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:51

127.q: Which of the following gives moth eaten appearance in the cytoplasm of necrotic cell?
127.e: Necrosis is characterized by changes in the cytoplasm and nuclei of the injured cells. Necrotic cells show increased eosinophilia(i.e., they are stained red by the dye eosin), attributable partly to increased binding of eosin to denatured cytoplasmic proteins and partly to loss of basophilic ribonucleic acid(RNA) in the cytoplasm(basophilia stems from binding of the blue dye hematoxylin). Compared with viable cells, the cell may have a glassy, homogeneous appearance, mostly because of the loss of lighter staining glycogen particles. Myelin figures are more prominent in necrotic cells than in cells with reversible injury. When enzymes have digested cytoplasmic organelles, the cytoplasm becomes vacuolated and appears "moth-eaten." Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:35

Anti-apoptotic. BCL2, BCL-XL, and MCL1 are the principal members of this group; they possess four BH domains (called BH1-4). These proteins reside in the outer mitochondrial membrane as well as in the cytosol and ER membranes. Regulated apoptosis initiators or sensors. Members of this group, including BAD, BIM, BID, Puma, and Noxa, contain only one BH domain, the third of the four BH domains, and hence are sometimes called BH3-only proteins. The activity of BH3-only proteins is modulated by sensors of cellular stress and damage; when upregulated and activated, they can initiate apoptosis. Reference: Robbins& Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 44

127.q: Which of the following changes are seen in infarction microscopically?
127.e: In most tissues, the main histologic finding associated with infarcts is ischemic coagulative necrosis. Coagulative necrosis is a type of cell death that occurs when blood flow to cells stops or slows (ischemia). It can occur anywhere in the body except the brain. Many conditions can cause ischemia, including atherosclerosis. Treatment and prognosis depend on the extent of the damage to the cells and tissues. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:115

127.q: Which of the following is also known as chicken fat clot?
127.e: At autopsy, postmortem clots can sometimes be mistaken for venous thrombi. However, the former are gelatinous and because of red cell settling they have a dark red dependent portion and a yellow "chicken fat" upper portion; they also are usually not attached to the underlying vessel wall. By contrast, red thrombi typically are firm, focally attached to vessel walls, and they contain gray strands of deposited fibrin. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:110

127.q: Cell to cell permeability occurs through:
127.e: Communicating junctions (Gap junctions) mediate the passage of chemical or electrical signals from one cell to another. Consists of pores called connexions and formed by hexamers of transmembrane proteins called connexins. Reference: Robbins 9th/pg 11

127.q: All of the following are intermediate filaments, except:
127.e: Intermediate filaments are 10-nm diameter fibrils which provide tensile strength to a cell. Cadherins are cell-cell desmosomal junctions that are formed by homotypic association of transmembrane glycoproteins. Reference: Robbins 9th/pg 21-24

127.q: In sickle cell trait, number of bands found in Hb-
127.e: In heterozygotes approximately 40% of Hb is HbS and the remainder is HbA, which interacts only weakly with deoxygenated HbS. Because HbA greatly retards HbS polymerization, the red cells of HbS heterozygotes have little tendency to sickle in vivo. Such persons are said to have sickle cell trait. On electrophoresis, 2 bands are produced. In homozygous state, most of all hemoglobins are HbS. So, single band is produced. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number - 445

127.q: Fibrinoid necrosis with neutrophilic infiltration is seen in:
127.e: PAN is characterized by segmental transmural necrotizing inflammationQ frequently accompanied by fibrinoid necrosis.Q OPTION B, C, D are granulomotous vasculitis. Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 509; 8th/pg 511

Interstitial fibrosis of the lung parenchyma
Prominent bronchial smooth muscle cell hyperplasia

128.e: B and c are realetd to neoplasia and d is related to quality control Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 42

128.q: Which pathological process is the reason of release of cardiac specific enzymes in blood?
128.e: The biochemical mechanisms of necrosis vary with different injurious stimuli. These mechanisms include: Failure of energy generation in the form of ATP because of reduced oxygen supply or mitochondrial damage Damage to cellular membranes, including the plasma membrane and lysosomal membranes, which results in leakage of cellular contents including enzymes Irreversible damage to cellular lipids, proteins and nucleic acids, which may be caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS); and others. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:35

128.q: Assertion: Dystrophic calcification is associated with necrosis Reason: Serum calcium level is high in Dystrophic calcification
o: Both statements are true and causally related
Both statements are true but not causally related
The first statement is true and second is false
The first statement is false and second is true
128.e: Dystrophic calcification: In this form, calcium metabolism is normal but it deposits in injured or dead tissue, such as areas of necrosis of any type. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:53

o: Both statements are true and causally related
Both statements are true but not causally related

The first statement is false and second is true
128.e: Pigments are colored substances that are either exogenous, coming from outside the body, such as carbon or are endogenous, synthesized within the body itself, such as lipofuscin, melanin and certain derivatives of hemoglobin. 128.e: Lipofuscin pigment is called as the "wear and tear" pigment Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:52

o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
128.e: Melanin is an endogenous, brown-black pigment that is synthesized by melanocytes located in the epidermis and acts as a screen against harmful UV radiation. Although melanocytes are the only source of melanin. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:52

129.q: A 42-year-old man has had increasing progressive muscle weakness in both arms and legs along with dysarthria and difficulty in swallowing for the past 2 years. He is now wheelchair-bound. Physical examination shows 3/5 motor strength in all extremities. He has no muscle pain on palpation, no deformities or loss of joint mobility, and no tremor. A biopsy specimen of the quadriceps muscle is obtained, and microscopic examination shows no inflammation, but only atrophy of the myofibers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
129.e: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is also known as Lou Gehrig disease, named for the famous New York Yankee first baseman affected with the disorder. Lower and upper motor neurons can be affected, resulting in a denervation type of pattern of muscular atrophy. This occurs because an individual neuron innervates a group of muscle fibers. Bulbar (cranial nerve) involvement denotes a more rapid course. Werdnig-Hoffmann disease also is a neuropathic disease with grouped atrophy, but onset is in infancy. The other listed options are not associated with denervation.

Inflammation is never associated with apoptosis and this is one of the major differences between necrosis and apoptosis. Reference: Robbins& Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 44

129.q: Which of the following is/are the morphological feature(s) of acute pancreatitis? i. Microvascular injury and edema ii. Fat necrosis and acute inflammation iii. Destruction of pancreatic parenchyma and blood vessels iv. Infiltration by eosinophils
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
129.e: Acute pancreatitis, is sudden inflammation of pancreas that may be mild or life threatening. The basic alterations in acute pancreatitis are microvascular leakage causing oedema. necrosis of fat by lipases, an acute inflammatory reaction, proteolytic destruction of pancreatic parenchyma, and destruction of blood vessels leading to interstitial haemorrhage. Mild cases are usually successfully treated with conservative measures. Severe cases often require admission in intensive care unit to monitor and manage complications of the disease. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-681

129.q: Assertion: In liquefactive necrosis there is transformation of tissue to a liquid creamy yellow viscous mass. Reason: In liquefactive necrosis there is enzymatic digestion of cells by accumulated leukocytes.
o: Both statements are true and causally related
Both statements are true but not causally related
First statement is true and second is false
First statement is false and second is true
129.e: Liquefactive necrosis is seen in focal bacterial and occasionally, fungal infections because microbes stimulate rapid accumulation of inflammatory cells and the enzymes of leukocytes digest ("liquefy") the tissue. Whatever the pathogenesis, the dead cells are completely digested, transforming the tissue into a viscous liquid that is eventually removed by phagocytes. If the process is initiated by acute inflammation, as in a bacterial infection, the material is frequently creamy yellow and is called pus. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th Edition, Page Number-36.

129.q: Clearance of apoptotic cells by professional and nonprofessional phagocytes is called
129.e: Apoptotic bodies may also become coated with natural antibodies and proteins of the complement system, notably C1q, which are recognized by phagocytes. Thus, numerous ligands induced on apoptotic cells serve as “eat me” signals and are recognized by receptors on phagocytes that bind and engulf these cells. This process of apoptotic cell phagocytosis is called efferocytosis; it is so efficient that dead cells disappear, often within minutes, without leaving a trace. Reference: Robbins 10 th ed pg 46

129.q: This process of apoptotic cell phagocytosis is called
129.e: Numerous ligands induced on apoptotic cells serve as "eat me" signals and are recognized by receptors on phagocytes that bind and engulf these cells. This process of apoptotic cell phagocytosis is called efferocytosis ; it is so efficient that dead cells disappear, often within minutes, without leaving a trace. In addition, production of pro-inflammatory cytokines is reduced in macrophages that have ingested apoptotic cells. Together with rapid clearance, this limits inflammatory reactions, even in the face of extensive apoptosis. Reference: Robbins& Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 42-44

129.q: Phagocytosis of apoptotic cell occur due to following changes except:
o: Coating of apoptotic body by thrombospondin
Coating of apoptotic body by C3
129.e: In apoptotic cells this phospholipid "flips" out and is expressed on the outer layer of the membrane. Apoptotic bodies may also become coated with natural antibodies and proteins of the complement system, notably C1q, which are recognized by phagocytes. Some apoptotic bodies are coated by thrombospondin, an adhesive glycoprotein that is recognized by phagocytes. Reference: Robbins& Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 2 pg 42
They make both p selectin which glues wbc with endothelium and vwf which glues platelets. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 72

130.q: Which is the first site of scar deposition in liver biopsy under the microscope?
130.e: Scar formation may follow very severe acute injury, but occurs more often as a reaction to chronic injury. The principal cell type involved in scar deposition is the peri-sinusoidal hepatic stellate cell. Following liver injury, stellate cells may become activated and convert into highly fibro genic my fibroblasts, which produce the fibrous scar. Stellate cell activation involves complex interactions between Kupffer cells, hepatocytes, and inflammatory cells. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-639

130.q: Complement complex that attacks cell membrane is:
130.e: The complement complex attacking the cell membrane is membrane attack complex having a composition of C56789. Action of this complex leads to entry of fluid and ions inside the cells leading to cell lysis. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 85

130.q: Lewis triple response is caused by:
130.e: Histamine is vasoactive amine that is located in most body tissues but is highly concentrated in the lungs, skin and gastrointestinal tract. It is stored in mast cell and basophils. When it is injected intradermally, it causes the triple response: Red spot: due to dilatation Wheal: due to exudation of fluid from capillaries Flare: Redness in surrounding area due to arterial dilatation Reference: Goodman and Gilman, 10 th ed, Pg: 650.

130.q: All of the followings are the promoter of inflammation EXCEPT:
130.e: Arachidonic acid metabolites(prostaglandins and leukotrienes), platelet activating factors are involved in vascular reactions, leukocyte chemotaxis and other reactions of inflammation; antagonized by lipoxins. Lipoxins also are generated from arachidonic acid by the lipoxygenase pathway, but unlike prostaglandins and leukotrienes, the lipoxins suppress inflammation by inhibiting the recruitment of leukocytes. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 78.

130.q: Pro inflammatory Cytokines include all of the following except:
130.e: The following are the anti inflammatory cytokines: IL-10, TGF-B, IL-4, IL-13. Reference: Robbins 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 85

130.q: In hepatitis B 'Ground glass' hepatocytes are seen. BECAUSE In hepatitis B endoplasmic reticulum is swollen by HBsAg.
o: If both statements are true and causally related
If both statements are true but not causally related
If the first statement is true and second is false
If the first statement is false and second is true
130.e: In chronic hepatitis B, 'ground-glass' hepatocytes (cells with endoplasmic reticulum swollen by HBsAg) are a diagnostic hallmark, and the presence of viral antigen in these cells can be confirmed by immunostaining. 'ground-glass' hepatocytes are liver cells which have eosinophilic granular, glassy cytoplasm on light microscopy. This appearance corresponds to a proliferated smooth endoplasmic reticulum ultrastructure. These changes may be drug-induced or associated with hepatitis b antigenaemia, particularly in carriers. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-649

Ans. is 'c' i.e., Bridging necrosis . Portal tracts show severe chronic inflammation with inflammatory cells extending into the liver lobules disrupting the limiting plate of hepatocytes. - Piecemeal necrosis - Portal fibrosis . Bridging necrosis - Interface hepatitis

130.q: A 58-year-old male patient presented with weakness, hematuria and other vague symptoms. Proper clinical examination shows presence of palpable purpura. Laboratory investigations performed show presence of proteinuria (2+) and MPO-ANCA positivity. Histopathological examination of the vessel shows fibrinoid necrosis without granuloma as shown below. Based on the above histopathological findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
130.e: Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that generally affects capillaries as well as small arterioles and venules. Unlike PAN, all lesions of microscopic polyangiitis tend to be of the same age in any given patient, suggesting a single episode of antibody or immune complex deposition. It is also called hypersensitivity vasculitis or leukocytoclastic vasculitis. The skin, mucous membranes, lungs, brain, heart, gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and muscle all can be involved. Most cases are associated with MPO-ANCA positivity. Microscopic polyangiitis is characterized by segmental fibrinoid necrosis of the media with focal transmural necrotizing lesions; granulomatous inflammation is absent. Reference : Robbins 10th Ed pg 514

131.q: Maximum collagen in wound healing is seen at -
131.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., End of second week During second week there is continued accumulation of collagen and proliferation of fibroblast. Maximum collagen is seen in second week.

131.q: Which of the following contains PDGF?
131.e: Platelets are disc-shaped anucleate cell fragments that are shed from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow into the bloodstream. Their function depends on several glycoprotein receptors, a contractile cytoskeleton, and two types of cytoplasmic granules. α-Granules have the adhesion molecule P-selectin on their membranes and contain proteins involved in coagulation, such as fibrinogen, coagulation factor V, and vWF, as well as protein factors that may be involved in wound healing, such as fibronectin, platelet factor 4 (a heparin-binding chemokine), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and transforming growth factor-β. Dense (or δ) granules contain adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate, ionized calcium, serotonin, and epinephrine. Reference :Robbins, 10th edition, page number - 102

131.q: Which of the following is derived from fibroblast cell?
131.e: Interstitial matrix is produced by mesenchymal cells like fibroblasts and is mainly composed of fibrillar and non-fibrillar collagen. TGF-beta is chemotactic for leukocytes and fibroblasts. It induces proliferation of fibroblasts. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 85

131.q: Which of the following is absolutely essential for wound healing?
131.e: Healing is modified by a number of influences(including both systemic and local host factors) frequently impairing the quality and adequacy of both inflammation and repair. Ascorbic acid deficiency causes reduced cross linking of tropocollagen to collagen So, the patient has increased bleeding tendencies and poor wound healing. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 108

131.q: Find the false statement about wound healing
o: 3 phases in sequence are: Inflammation, proliferation and maturation
In healing by second intention, initially first matrix containing fibrin, plasma fibrin, plasma fibronectin and type III collagen is formed
70-80% tensile strength of unwounded skin is obtained in 3 months
After 2 months of wound healing, the increase in tensile strength is due to excess collagen synthesis
131.e: Option a-true-Three phases of wound healing-Inflammation(early & late), Granulation tissue formation & re-epithelialization and Wound contraction, ECM deposition & remodelling Strength never reaches 100% Q Option d - The recovery of tensile strength results from the excess of collagen Synthesis over collagen degradation during the first 2 months of healing and at later times, from structural modifications of collagen fibers(cross-linking, increased fiber size) option D. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 108

131.q: Which cell is principally responsible for repair and scar formation in brain?
131.e: Astrocyte Injury and Repair. Astrocytes are the principal cells responsible for repair and scar formation in the brain, a process termed gliosis. In response to injury, astrocytes undergo both hypertrophy and hyperplasia. The nucleus enlarges and becomes vesicular, and the nucleolus becomes prominent. The cytoplasm expands and takes on a bright pink hue, and the cell extends multiple stout, ramifying processes called gemistocytic astrocyte. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Page: 850

131.q: Tensile strength of wound after laparoscopic cholecystectomy in a 30 year old woman depends upon:
131.e: Fibrillar collagens(mostly type I collagen) form a major portion of the connective tissue in repair sites and are essential for the development of strength in healing wounds. Net collagen accumulation, however, depends not only on increased collagen synthesis but also on decreased degradation. The recovery of tensile strength results from the excess of collagen synthesis over collagen degradation during the first 2 months of healing and at later times, from structural modifications of collagen fibers(cross-linking, increased fiber size) after collagen synthesis ceases. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 107

131.q: WHICH of the following is not true about healing
o: Predominant collagen in adult skin is type I whereas in early granulation tissue, it is type III and I
Permanent wound contraction requires the action of myofibroblasts
Fetal cutaneous wounds heal with scar formation
131.e: FETAL WOUNDS DO NOT FORM SCAR REPAIR Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 103

132.q: Assertion: Septic infarctions occur when infected cardiac valve vegetations embolize Reason: Septic infarct gets converted into a granuloma.
o: Both statements are true and causally related
Both statements are true but not causally related
The first statement is true and second is false
The first statement is false and second is true
132.e: Septic infarcts occur when infected cardiac valve vegetations embolize, or when microbes seed necrotic tissue.
