In these cases, the infarct is converted into an abscess, with a correspondingly greater inflammatory response and healing by organization and fibrosis. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:115

132.q: Elevated D-dimer levels are specific for:
132.e: Levels of fibrin degradation products, including crosslinked fibrin degradation products (D-dimer), are usually increased in the presence of acute venous thromboembolism. Absence of an elevated level of D-dimer in patients undergoing an evaluation for acute DVT or PE has an excellent negative predictive value for thrombosis. Reference : Wintrobe's 12th/pg 1437

132.q: Which is the commonest site of thrombosis?
132.e: Venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis) are almost invariably occlusive; they frequently propagate some distance toward the heart, forming a long cast within the vessel lumen that is prone to give rise to emboli. Because these thrombi form in the sluggish venous circulation, they tend to contain more enmeshed red cells, leading to stasis or thrombi. The veins of the lower extremities are most commonly affected (90% of venous thromboses); however, venous thrombi also can occur in the upper extremities, periprostatic plexus, or ovarian and periuterine veins, and under special circumstances they may be found in the dural sinuses, portal vein, or hepatic vein. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:110

Causes of splenic infarcts are as follow: Haematological disorders: sickle cell anemia, Polycythemia vera, Hypercoagulable state, CML, Leukemia, Lymphoma, Myelofibrosis, Erythropoietin therapy Embolic disorders: Arterial fibrillation, Endocarditis, HIV associated mycobacterial infections Collagen vascular disorders: SLE, Kawasaki disease, Wegner’s granulomatosis, PAN Infections: Infectious mononucleosis, Kala-azar, Meningococcemia, Clostridium perfringes, Salmonellosis, P. vivax, Falciparum, Leptospirosis Trauma Miscellaneous: Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, ARDS, Splenic vein thrombosis, Liver transplant Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 8 th edition, page number -634

132.q: Assertion: Hyperaemia is an active process resulting from arteriolar dilation and increased blood inflow. Reason: Erythema occurs in affected tissue because of increased delivery of oxygenated blood.
o: Both statements are true and are casually related.
Both statements are true but not casually related.
The first statement is true and second is false.
132.e: Erythema is redness of skin or mucous membrane caused by hyperemia (increased blood flow). Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:97

132.q: Assertion: Lung and small intestine show red infarcts Reason: Lung and small intestine have dual circulation which allows blood to flow from an unobstructed parallel supply into the necrotic zone.
o: If both statements are true and causally related
If both statements are true but not causally related
If the first statement is true and second is false
If the first statement is false and second is true
132.e: Red infarcts occur (1) as a result of venous occlusions (such as in ovarian torsion); (2) in loose tissues (e.g., lung) where blood can collect in infarcted zones;(3) in tissues with dual circulations such as lung and small intestine, where partial, albeit inadequate perfusion by collateral arterial supplies is typical; (4) in previously congested tissues (as a consequence of sluggish venous outflow); and (5) when flow is reestablished after infarction has occurred (e.g., after angioplasty of an arterial obstruction). Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-114-115

132.q: Which of the following conditions occur due to increased blood volume to any organ: i Hyperemia ii Necrosis iii Congestion iv Odema
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
132.e: Hyperaemia and congestion both refer to an increase in blood volume within a tissue, but have different underlying mechanisms. Hyperemia is due to increased blood flow, congestion is due to decreased outflow Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:97

132.q: An 18-year-old man suffers massive trauma in a motorcycle accident. A CT scan shows multiple intracerebral hemorrhages. The patient expires after 6 months in a coma. At autopsy, there are cystic cavities within the frontal and temporal lobes, corresponding to the areas of prior hemorrhage. These cavities were formed in large measure due to the phagocytic activity of which of the following cell types?
132.e: Microglia are phagocytic macrophage-derived cells of the CNS, accounting for 5% of all glial cells. In response to necrosis, macroglia become phagocytic, accumulate lipids and other cellular debris, and are designated gitter cells. Some reactive microglia exhibit a prominent elongated nucleus, in which case they are referred to as rod cells. After microglial phagocytosis, astrocytosis (choice a) then leads to local scar formation, which persists as telltale evidence of a prior injury. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter – 28 pg 1243

133.q: Why do all mitochondria DNA of the embryo come from the mother?
o: Head and tail of sperm degrade upon fertilization
Cell division process leaves out mitochondria DNA from sperm
Mitochondrial DNA of sperm is degraded upon entering egg
133.e: During fertilization, the sperm penetrates the outer layer of the egg and fuses with the plasma membrane. Upon fusion, the sperm releases its contents inside the egg and the head and tail are degraded. Mitochondria are heavy in the tail so DNA does not get transferred from the sperm. Reference - Textbook of Langman's, 12th Edition, General Embryology Page number - 29

133.q: All of the following features are true pertaining to autosomal recessive disorders EXCEPT:
o: Onset is frequently early in life.
The expression of the defect tends to be uniform
50% reduction in the normal gene product is associated with clinical signs and symptoms.
133.e: 50% reduction in the normal gene product is associated with clinical signs and symptoms is a feature of autosomal dominant disorder. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 246

133.q: ABO blood group is an example of ?
133.e: WHEN BOTH ALLELES EXPRESS THEMSELVES, ITS CALLED CO-DOMINANCE Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 9 th Edition page No.141
In some autosomal dominant disorders, like osteogenesis Imperfecta, phenotypically normal parents have more than one affected child. This is due to germline mosaicism. Reference: Robbins 9th/pg 160

133.q: Which of the following kidney disease is autosomal dominant inheritance?
133.e: Adult polycystic kidney disease is characterized by multiple expanding cysts affecting both kidneys that ultimately destroy the intervening parenchyma. In 85% to 90% of families, PKD1, on the short arm of chromosome 16, is the defective gene. This gene encodes a large (460-kDa) and complex cell membrane-associated protein called polycystin-1. Polycystic kidney disease in adults usually does not produce symptoms until the fourth decade of life, by which time the kidneys are quite large. The most common presenting complaint is flank pain or a heavy, dragging sensation. Acute distention of a cyst, either by intracystic hemorrhage or by obstruction, may cause excruciating pain. Sometimes attention is first drawn to the lesion on palpation of an abdominal mass. Intermittent gross hematuria commonly occurs. Reference :Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page- 574

133.q: A 3-year-old boy has a history of progressive developmental delay, ataxia, seizures, and inappropriate laughter since infancy. The child has a normal karyotype of 46,XY, but DNA analysis shows that he has inherited both of his number 15 chromosomes from his father. These findings are most likely to be indicative of which of the following genetic mechanisms?
133.e: This child has features of Angelman syndrome, and the DNA analysis shows uniparental disomy. The Angelman gene encoded on chromosome 15 is subject to genomic imprinting. It is silenced on the paternal chromosome 15, but is active on the maternal chromosome 15. If the child lacks maternal chromosome 15, there is no active Angelman gene in the somatic cells. This gives rise to the abnormalities typical of this disorder. The same effect occurs when there is a deletion of the Angelman gene from the maternal chromosome 15. The other listed options do not occur in uniparental disomy. Reference: Robins Basic Pathology 10th ed/ pg 271

133.q: Which of the following is not an Inherited cancer syndromes?
133.e: Inherited cancer syndrome: Familial retinoblastoma Familial adenomatous polyps of the colon Multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes Neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2 Von Hippel- Lindau syndrome Familial cancers Breast cancer Ovarian cancer Colonic cancer other than familial adenomatous polyps Autosomal Recessive syndromes of Defective DNA Repair: Xeroderma pigmentosum Ataxia telangiectasia Bloom syndrome Fanconi anemia Reference: Robins basic pathology, 10th ed, Page: 201.

134.q: A 10 year old child complaining of abdominal pain and weakness. On examination hepatosplenomegaly noted. In blood investigation pancytopenia was found. Bone marrow shows 'crumbled tissue paper appearance'. This disorder is occur because of accumulation of which of the following molecule.
134.e: Gaucher’s Disease Most common Lysosomal Storage Disorder Enzyme Defect:- Glucocerebrosidase defect Lysosomes filled with Glucocerebroside No cherry red spot in the macula Hematological features: Pancytopenia, bleeding manifestation Hepatosplenomegaly Bone Pain and Pathological Fractures of long bones X-ray Femur Erlenmeyer Flask Deformity Bone Marrow Biopsy Gaucher cell with Wrinkled paper appearance/crumbled tissue paper appearance. Elevated seruml levls of chitotriosidase, ACE & TRAP, also CCL-18/PARC Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 251

134.q: Accumulation of sphingomyelin in phagocytic cells is feature of:
134.e: Niemann-Pick Disease Autosomal Recessive Biochemical defect Deficient activity of acid sphingomyelinase, a lysosomal enzyme encoded by a gene on chromosome 11 Accumulation of sphingomyelin and other lipids in the monocyte-macrophage system. Clinical features Failure to thrive Hepatosplenomegaly Rapidly progressive neurodegenerative course. Treatment Orthotopic liver transplantation Amniotic cell transplantation Bone marrow transplantation Miglustat A phase I trial of enzyme replacement therapy for type B NPD. Reference: Harper's 32nd edition, page 250-251

134.q: Lysosomal enzymes are tagged with which residue in Golgi apparatus to direct them to lysosome?
134.e: Mannose 6- phosphate is marker for delivering lysosomal enzymes Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing roughly 40 different acid hydrolases (i.e., enzymes that function best in acidic pH - 5). These hydrolases include proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases, phosphatases, and sulfatases. Lysosomal enzymes are initially synthesized in the ER lumen and then tagged with a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) residue within the Golgi apparatus. Such M6P-modified proteins are subsequently delivered to lysosomes through trans-Golgi vesicles that express M6P receptors. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 1 pg 13

134.q: A 48-year-old lady presented with hepatosplenomegaly with pancytopenia. On bone marrow examination, a tissue paper crumpled appearance is seen. Which is the most likely product to have accumulated?
134.e: The clinical feature and bone marrow feature is typical of Gauchers disease. This results due to accumulation of cerebrosideQ inside mononuclear phagocytic cells due to deficiency of ß-glucocerebrosidase. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 9 th Edition page No.151

o: Accumulation of short chain fatty acids
Accumulation of very long chain fatty acids
Accumulation of medium chain fatty acids
135.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Accumulation of very long chain fatty acids [Ref Harper 29m/e p. 554; Chatterjea 6th le p. 412] Zellweger Syndrome is a rare inborn error of peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation° due to absence of functional peroxisomes in all tissues. As a result, the long chain fatty acids are not oxidized in peroxisomes and accumulate in tissues particularly in brain, liver, kidney and muscle and usually result in death by age six.

135.q: A patient was diagnosed with isolated increase in LDL. His father and brother had the same disease with increased cholesterol. The likely diagnosis is:
135.e: Disease:- Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa) Defect:- Defective LDL receptors or mutation in ligand region of apo B-100. Remarks:- Elevated LDL levels and hypercholesterolemia, resulting in atherosclerosis and coronary disease. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, page 275

135.q: A child presents with micrognathia and low-set ears. These clinical features are commonly associated with which type of genetic abnormality?
135.e: Explanation: Micrognathia (small jaw) and low-set ears are classic dysmorphic features seen in several chromosomal deletion syndromes, such as: Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) Wolf -Hirschhorn syndrome (4p deletion) 2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome) 13q deletion syndrome T Translocations, inversions, or amplifications may also cause genetic disorders, but specific features like micrognathia and low-set ears are most characteristically seen with deletions. (option B, C, D) Key Takeaways: Deletions consistently produce the distinct facial dysmorphisms (micrognathia, low-set ears) due to loss of developmental genes. References: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4736720/ https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1523/?utm_source=chatgpt.com https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1183/

Answer- D. Cytogenetic abnormalities Most common cause of female pseudohermaphroditism - CAH due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency. Most common cause of male pseudohermaphroditism - Gonadal dysgenesis and defect in androgen action.

135.q: Fragile X syndrome is characterized by all Except:
135.e: Fragile X syndrome is the prototype of diseases in which the causative mutation occurs in a long repeating sequence of three nucleotides. Fragile X syndrome results from a mutation in the FMR1 gene, which maps to Xq27.3 and is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation, after Down syndrome. The typical physical phenotype includes a long face with a large mandible, large everted ears and large testicles(macroorchidism). Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 269

135.q: In fragile X syndrome, the clinical features worsen with each successive generation, this phenomenon is called?
135.e: Anticipation refers to the phenomenon whereby clinical features of fragile X syndrome worsen with each successive generation, as if the mutation becomes increasingly deleterious as it is transmitted from a man to his grandsons and great-grandsons. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 269

135.q: A disease with Mitochondrial disease inheritance is inherited from which of the following family members?
135.e: Explanation: Mitochondrial diseases follow maternal inheritance , meaning they are exclusively passed down from the mother to all of her children . This is because mitochondria are inherited only from the oocyte (egg) , as sperm mitochondria are typically degraded after fertilisation. (Option B, C and D ruled out) Thus, individuals inherit mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) exclusively from their mother , and mutations in mtDNA result in mitochondrial disorders. Key Features of Mitochondrial Inheritance: Only mothers pass the disease to offspring. Both males and females can be affected , but only females transmit it. Affected males do not pass the condition to their children. Key Takeaway: Mitochondrial diseases are inherited exclusively from the mother , meaning both males and females can be affected , but only females pass the disease to the next generation .

135.q: A 15-year-old girl has developed multiple nodules on her skin over the past 10 years. On physical examination, there are 20 scattered, 0.3-1 cm, firm nodules on the patient's trunk and extremities. There are 12 light brown macules averaging 2-5 cm in diameter on the skin of the trunk. Slit-lamp examination shows pigmented nodules in the iris. A sibling and a parent are similarly affected. Genetic analysis shows a loss-of-function mutation. Which of the following inheritance patterns is most likely to be present in this family?
135.e: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1) is characterized by the development of multiple neurofibromas and pigmented skin lesions. Neurofibromas are most numerous in the dermis but also may occur in visceral organs. Patients with NF-1 also may develop a type of sarcomatous neoplasm known as a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST). NF-1 is a tumor suppressor that appears with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, though some cases result from spontaneous new mutations (no prior family members with the mutation). NF-1 exhibits variable expressivity, because the manifestations (location and types of neoplasms) are not the same in all patients. The other forms of inheritance listed are not associated with tumor suppressor genes. Reference: Robins Basic Pathology 10th ed/pg 245

136.q: Which of the following statement is NOT TRUE for invasion and metastasis?
o: Cell-cell contacts are lost by inactivation of E-cadherin
Some tumour show organ tropism due to expression of adhesion or chemokine receptors whose ligands are expressed by endothelial cells at the metastatic site
Sarcomas preferably metastasize through the lymphatic route
SNAIL and TWIST are metastasis oncogenes
136.e: Lymphatic spread is more typical of carcinomas , whereas haematogenous spread is favoured by sarcomas . Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 196.

136.q: Which of the following is MOST suitable definition for Differentiation in context to Neoplasia?
o: The extent to which tumour cells resemble their normal mature tissues in structure
The extent to which tumour cells resemble primitive tissue of the fetus in function
The extent to which tumour cells resemble their normal mature tissue in structure and function
The extent to which tumour cells resemble primitive tissue of the fetus in structure and function
136.e: Differentiation refers to the extent to which neoplasms resemble their parenchymal cells of origin, both morphologically and functionally; lack of differentiation is called anaplasia. In general, benign neoplasms are composed of well-differentiated cells that closely resemble their normal counterparts. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 192.

136.q: Which of the following is an unequivocal sign of malignancy?
136.e: Metastasis is defined as the spread of a tumour to sites that are physically discontinuous with the primary tumour, an event that unequivocally marks a tumour as malignant. The spread of cancer cells from the place where they first formed to another part of the body. In metastasis, cancer cells break away from the original(primary) tumor, travel through the blood or lymph system, and form a new tumor in other organs or tissues of the body. Metastasis is a pathogenic agent's spread from an initial or primary site to a different or secondary site within the host's body; the term is typically used when referring to metastasis by a cancerous tumor. The newly pathological sites, then are metastases. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 272-273.

136.q: Which of the following is/are true in the context of stage of a tumour? i. The degree to which the tumour has spread locally ii. The level of lymph node involvement if any iii. Presence or absence of metastasis iv. The degree of differentiation or Anaplasia
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
136.e: The staging of solid cancers is based on the size of the primary lesion, its extent of spread to regional lymph nodes and the presence or absence of blood borne metastases. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 236.

136.q: A study is performed to analyse characteristics of malignant neoplasm in biopsy specimens. The biopsies were performed on patients who had palpable mass lesions on digital rectal examination. Which of the following microscopic finding is most likely to indicate that the neoplasm is malignant?
136.e: Invasion, and metastasis, the major causes of cancerrelated morbidity and mortality, result from complex interactions involving cancer cells, stromal cells and the extracellular matrix(ECM). These interactions can be broken down into a series of steps consisting of local invasion, intravasation into blood and lymph vessels, transit through the vasculature, extravasation from the vessels, formation of micrometastases and growth of micrometastases into macroscopic tumors. Predictably, this sequence of steps may be interrupted at any stage by either host-related or tumor-related factors. For the purpose of discussion, the metastatic cascade can be subdivided into two phases: (1) invasion of ECM and (2) vascular dissemination and homing of tumor cells. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 220.

136.q: Which of the following is most reliable feature of malignant transformation of pheochromocytoma ?
136.e: Ans. is None "Because benign and malignant pheochromocytomas may have an identical histological appearance, the only absolute criterion of malignancy is metastasis." "The diagnosis of malignant pheochromocytoma is made only when metastasis is demonstrated."

137.q: Cancer cell survival is enhanced by which of the following events? i. Overexpression of p53 gene ii. Suppression of p53 protein iii. BAX iv. BCL-2
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
137.e: Activation of p53 leads to cell cycle arrest and it also directs the transcription of several pro-apoptotic genes such as BAX and PUMA which are believed to tip the balance in favour of cell death via intrinsic pathway. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 295.

137.q: Which of the following gene is the Governor of proliferation of the cells in neoplasia?
137.e: RB , a key negative regulator of the cell cycle, is directly or indirectly inactivated in most human cancers. The function of the RB protein is to regulate the G1/S checkpoint , the portal through which cells must pass before DNA replication commences. RB exerts anti-proliferative effects by controlling the G1-to-S transition of the cell cycle. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 208-211.

137.q: Which of the following is/are true statement's about p53 i. It regulates the genes involved in cell cycle progression ii. Its increased levels can induce apoptosis iii. Mutations of p53 gene are common genetic alteration seen in variety of human cancers. iv. UV radiation decreases its activity and causes cell cycle stimulation.
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
137.e: UV radiation decreases its activity and causes cell cycle arrest. p53, also known as Tumor protein P53, cellular tumor antigen p53 or transformation-related protein 53 is a regulatory protein that is often mutated in human cancers. The p53 proteins are crucial in vertebrates, where they prevent cancer formation. Activated p53 promotes cell cycle arrest to allow DNA repair and/or apoptosis to prevent the propagation of cells with serious DNA damage through the transactivation of its target genes implicated in the induction of cell cycle arrest and/or apoptosis. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 211.

137.q: Which of the following mechanism's is/are used by cancer cells to evade Apoptosis? i. Reduced CD95 level ii. Inactivation of death-induced signaling complex, FADD, FAS-associated via death domain iii. Loss of p53, leading to reduced function of pro-apoptotic factors such as BAX iv. Increased transport of cytochrome c from mitochondria as a result of up regulation of anti-apoptotic factors such as BCL-2, BCL-XL and MCL-1
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
137.e: All are correct except(iv). Increased transport of cyt c will cause apoptosis and killing cells thus preventing cancer. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 217.

137.q: The tumour suppressor gene p53 induces to inhibit cell cycle at which phase?
137.e: The tumour suppressor gene that is most commonly affected by point mutations in cancer is TP53, a prototypical "guardian" type tumour suppressor gene. DNA damage leads to activation of p53 by phosphorylation. Activated p53 drives transcription of CDKN1A(p21), which prevents RB phosphorylation, thereby causing a G1-S block in the cell cycle. This pause allows the cells to repair the DNA damage. If the DNA can be repaired, p53 activates other genes to fix the damage. If the DNA cannot be repaired, this protein prevents the cell from dividing and signals it to undergo apoptosis. By stopping cells with mutated or damaged DNA from dividing, p53 helps prevent the development of tumors. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th Edition, Page Number 212 & 213.

137.q: All are cyclin dependent kinase(CDK) inhibitor except?
137.e: Cyclin and cyclin - Dependent Kinases in regulation of cell cycle. Cyclin D/CDK4, cyclin D/CDK6 and cyclin E/CDK2 regulate G1-S transition by phosphorylation of the Rb protein. Cyclin B/CDK 1 help in G2 - M transition CDK Inhibitors ­ LNK4 inhibitors composed of p16, p15, p19 and p18 act on cyclin D/CDK 4 and cyclin D/CDK 6 p21, p27, p57, can inhibit all CDKs Reference: Robins basic pathology, 10th ed, Page: 205.

137.q: Which of the following statement is NOT TRUE for Telomerase enzyme?
o: Present in less amounts in stem cells
Immortalizes cancer cells by maintaining the telomere length
137.e: Unregulated proliferation in incipient tumours leads to telomere shortening, followed by chromosomal instability and the accumulation of mutations. If telomerase is then reactivated in these cells, telomeres are extended and these mutations become fixed, contributing to tumour growth. The telomere acts as a buffer to ensure the important genetic information coded for on the chromosome is completely copied for each new cell and protected from damage. Over time, this results in fewer and fewer DNA repeats making up the telomeres after each cell division i.e., gradually the telomeres shorten. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 219.
This DNA repair defect increases the risk of both SCC and basal cell carcinoma Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1135

138.q: Carcinoma of lung, breast marker is -
138.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., CEA Carcinoembryonic antigen is a marker in cancer of colon, pancreas, lung, breast, and ovary.

138.q: All the following are associated with obesity EXCEPT?
138.e: Explanation: Cancers with increased incidence in obesity due to: Hyperinsulinemia, increased IGF-1 , Chronic inflammation , Increased estrogen (from aromatization in adipose tissue) . Cancers associated with obesity include : Adenocarcinomas of the esophagus, gastric(Option C ruled out), colon , rectum , liver , gallbladder , pancreas(Option D ruled out) , kidney , thyroid . In women: endometrium, ovary, breast (postmenopausal) . In men: prostate . Meningioma (Option A ruled out)

138.q: Which of the following growth factors is associated with cancer cachexia? i. PDGF ii. EGF iii. VEGF iv. TNF
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
138.e: It is suspected that TNF and other cytokines produced by macrophages in response to tumour cells or by the tumour cells themselves mediate cachexia. TNF suppresses appetite and inhibits the action of lipoprotein lipase, preventing the release of free fatty acids from lipoproteins. TNF-α is chiefly secreted by macrophages in response to stimuli for the induction of systemic inflammation. The binding of the ligand TNF-α to the TNF receptor(TNFR1) initiates the pro-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic signaling cascades. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 236.

138.q: Acanthosis nigricans is not associated with
138.e: Acanthosis nigricans can occur as paraneoplastic syndrome caused by growth factors released from tumors. RCC is rarely associated with acanthosis nigricans. Most common associations are with obesity and diabetes. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1143

Hypoglycemia as Paraneoplastic syndrome in some tumors: Mesenchymal tumors, sarcomas, adrenal, hepatic, gastrointestinal, kidney, prostate, Cervix (small-cell carcinoma) The first association of hyperglycemia was made by Glicksman and Rawson who noted a 25% incidence of "diabetes" in patients with sarcomas of bone. Marcove and Francis found hyperglycemia in 85% of their chondrosarcoma patient and Turner and Horne reported similar abnormalities associated with fibrosarcoma Reference: Cancer 42:603-610, 1978;

138.q: Patient with mediastinal mass was diagnosed with red cell aplasia. What is the most probable cause of aplasia?(Recent Question 2021)
138.e: Pure red cell aplasia can either be inherited or acquired. Congenital PRCA Diamond-Blackfan or Blackfan-Diamond syndrome Acquired PRCA Autoimmune/Collagen disorders - systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease. Leukemias Lymphoproliferative disorders Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (common) Large granular lymphocytic leukemia (LGL)(common) ABO-incompatible stem cell transplant Solid tumors Thymoma is strongly associated Virus Parvovirus B19 (most common) - can lead to transient aplastic crises Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) T-cell leukemia-lymphoma virus, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) Hepatitis A, B, C, and E Cytomegalovirus Bacterial infections - group C streptococcus, tuberculosis, bacterial sepsis Drugs - recombinant erythropoietin (rhEPO) is most common. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number 384

138.q: Which of the following are AIDS defining cancers?
o: Primary lymphoma of brain e. Invasive cancer of uterine cervix
138.e: The neoplastic diseases considered to be AIDS-defining conditions are Kaposi's sarcoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and invasive cervical carcinoma. In addition, there is also an increase in the incidence of a variety of non- AIDS-defining malignancies: Hodgkin's disease; Multiple myeloma; Leukemia; Melanoma; and Cervical, brain, testicular, oral, lung, gastric, liver, renal and anal cancers. Reference: Robbins, 9th ed, Pg: 253.

138.q: Which of the following initiation-promotion sequence's can cause tumour formation? i. Only initiator, no promoter ii. Only promoter, no initiator iii. Multiple doses of promoters applied at wider duration iv. Promoter following initiator
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
138.e: Both initiators and promotors are required for cancer to occur. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 321.

139.q: Which of the following is toxic to parasite -
139.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Peroxidase Neutrophils and monocytes contain a peroxidase (myeloperoxidase), that has been implicated in antiparasitic activity. However, monocytes lose this enzyme when they mature into macrophages. Eosinophils also contain peroxidase that differs from myeloperoxidase of neutrophils. However, like myeloperoxidase, eosinophil peroxidase combines with H20, and a halide to form an antiparasite system. Parasite Egg size 1) Fasciola gigantica 190 X 100 m 2) Echinostoma iliocanum 100 X 70 m 3) Gastrodiscoides hominis 150 X 70-100 m 4) Opisthorcis viverni <30 X 15 m

139.q: Which cell produce antibodies required for humoral immunity?
139.e: There are two types of adaptive immunity. Humoral immunity is mediated by soluble proteins called antibodies that are produced by B lymphocytes(also called B cells). Cell-mediated(or cellular) immunity is mediated by T lymphocytes(also called T cells). Humoral immunity is the aspect of immunity that is mediated by macromolecules - including secreted antibodies, complement proteins and certain antimicrobial peptides - located in extracellular fluids. Humoral immunity is named so because it involves substances found in the humors or body fluids. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 124.

139.q: Gene for major histocompatibility complex is located on which chromosome?
139.e: The human major histocompatibility complex(MHC) commonly called as human leukocyte antigen(HLA) complex is a 4 megabase region on chromosome 6p. The major histocompatibility complex(mhc) is a group of genes that encode proteins on the cell surface that have an important role in immune response. Their main role is in antigen presentation where mhc molecules display peptide fragments for recognition by appropriate t-cells. Reference: Harrison, 17 th ed, Pg: 2045

139.q: An example of antigen presenting cells is:
139.e: ANTIGEN PRESENTING CELLS ARE B CELLS, DENDRITIC CELLS AND MACROPHAGES Dendritic cells(DCs) are the most important antigen presenting cells for initiating T-cell responses against protein antigens. A special type of immune cell that is found in tissues, such as the skin and boosts immune responses by showing antigens on its surface to other cells of the immune system. A dendritic cell is a type of phagocyte and a type of antigen-presenting cell(APC). Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 128.

139.q: HIV mainly infects cells bearing the which cell surface antigen.
139.e: HIV infects cells by using the CD4 molecule as a receptor and various chemokine receptors as coreceptors. Binding of HIV gp120 to CD4 is essential for infection and accounts for the tropism of the virus for CD4+T cells and for CD4+monocytes/macrophages and DCs. In molecular biology, CD4 is a glycoprotein that serves as a co-receptor for the T-cell receptor. CD4 is found on the surface of immune cells such as T helper cells, monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 175.

139.q: Pattern recognition receptors are located in all the cellular compartments where pathogens may be present. Which amongst followings is not receptor for innate immunity?
139.e: The major classes of innate immune receptors are TLRs, NOD-like receptors in the cytosol(NLRs), C-type lectin receptors, RIG-like receptors for viral RNA, named after the founding member RIG-I and cytosolic DNA sensors. Caspases are a family of protease enzymes playing essential roles in programmed cell death. They are named caspases due to their specific cysteine protease activity - a cysteine in its active site nucleophilically attacks and cleaves a target protein only after an aspartic acid residue. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 122.

139.q: About Natural killer cells, all are true; except:
139.e: True, because of its morphology False, T lymphocytes need thymus for development True, CD16 is FcR of IgG true, NK cells kill viruses & tumor infected cells Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 6, pg 192

139.q: Which of the following patterns of immune complex deposition is seen by immunofluorescent microscopy in good pasture syndrome?
139.e: Immunofluorescence studies reveal the characteristic strong linear staining with IgG and C3 along the GBM in anti-GBM antibody-mediated disease, a granular pattern of glomerular staining in immune complex-mediated GN, while in pauci-immune GN the stains are negative. Electron microscopy shows electron dense immune complex deposits within the glomeruli in immune complex-mediated GN, but not in biopsies from those with anti-GBM and pauci-immune crescentic GN. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Page- 563

140.q: Which of the following is not an autoimmune disorder?
140.e: Influenza is caused by virus - Myxovirus Influenzae. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 145.

140.q: Which of the following type of lymphocyte is activated exaggeratedly in type 1 hypersensitivity?
140.e: Th2 cells mediate the activation and maintenance of the humoral or antibody-mediated, immune response against extracellular parasites, bacteria, allergens and toxins. Th2 cells mediate these functions by producing various cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-9, IL-13 and IL-17E(IL-25). In immediate(type I) hypersensitivity, often called allergy, the injury is caused by TH2 cells, IgE antibodies and mast cells and other leukocytes. Mast cells release mediators that act on blood vessels and smooth muscle as well as cytokines that recruit and activate inflammatory cells. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 136.

140.q: Schwartzman reaction is an example of:
140.e: Schwartzman reaction is a non-immunologic phenomenon in which endotoxin(lipopolysaccharide) induces local & systemic reactions; It can either be local or systemic type. Reference: Robbins, 9th ed, Pg: 208.

140.q: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis is classically described as which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
140.e: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immunologically mediated inflammatory lung disease that primarily affects the alveoli and is therefore often called allergic alveolitis. Most often it is an occupational disease that results from heightened sensitivity to inhaled antigens such as those found in moldy hay. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-514

140.q: Which organ is most commonly affected in systemic sclerosis?
140.e: Systemic sclerosis is an immunologic disorder characterized by excessive fibrosis in multiple tissues, obliterative vascular disease and evidence of autoimmunity, mainly the production of multiple autoantibodies. Although the term scleroderma is ingrained in clinical medicine, the name systemic sclerosis is preferred because excessive fibrosis is seen in multiple organs. Cutaneous involvement is the usual presenting manifestation and eventually appears in approximately 95% of cases. Systemic sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disease of still not fully understood pathogenesis. Fibrosis, vascular wall damage and disturbances of innate and acquired immune responses with autoantibody production are prominent features. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 159.

140.q: Dry eyes(keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth(xerostomia) are features of which of the following?
140.e: Sjogren syndrome is a chronic disease characterized by dry eyes(keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth(xerostomia) resulting from immunologically mediated destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands. It occurs as an isolated disorder(primary form), also known as the sicca syndrome or more often in association with another autoimmune disease(secondary form). Lacrimal and salivary glands are the major targets of the disease, but other exocrine glands, including those lining the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts and the vagina, also may be involved. The earliest histologic finding in both the major and the minor salivary glands is periductal and perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. Later there is atrophy of the acini, fibrosis and hyalinization; still later in the course, the atrophic parenchyma may be replaced with fat. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 158.

141.q: Graft vs Host reaction can be reduced by?
141.e: Irradiation with a dose of 2,500 cGy at the center of the irradiation field, with a minimum dose of 1,500 cGy at any point in the field inhibits proliferation of donor lymphocytes but has no significant adverse effect on red cell, platelet or granulocyte function. It should be noted that though the other options are also effective in reducing the leukocytes but they do not completely deplete the lymphocytes and so can cause GVHD. Reference: Wintrobes, 13th ed, Pg: 704-705.

141.q: Which histological staining reaction/s stains amyloid? i. Reticulin ii. Congo-red iii. Methenamine silver iv. Thioflavin T
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
141.e: Different stains for amyloid are: Congo Red shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light Methyl or cresyl violet Thioflavin T with examination using fluorescence microscopy Reference: Hamodat M. Amyloidosis. Pathology Outlines.com

141.q: Dialysis-associated amyloidosis is a serious complication in a patient undergoing chronic dialysis. Because Plasma beta2-M level is elevated in chronic renal failure.
o: Both statements are true and causally related
Both statements are true but not causally related
The first statement is true and second is false
The first statement is false and second is true
141.e: Patients on long-term hemodialysis for renal failure can develop amyloid deposits derived from β2-microglobulin. This protein is present in high concentrations in the serum of individuals with renal disease and in the past it was retained in the circulation because it could not be filtered through dialysis membranes. With new dialysis filters, the incidence of this complication has decreased substantially. The classical features of this form of amyloidosis are the triad of scapulohumeral periarthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome and flexor tenosynovitis of the hand. Renal involvement gives rise to proteinuria that may be severe enough to cause the nephrotic syndrome. Progressive obliteration of glomeruli in advanced cases ultimately leads to renal failure and uremia. Renal failure is a common cause of death. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 185-186.

141.q: Following conditions must be fulfilled in a person before taking him as a kidney donor except:
o: Presence of two normally functioning kidneys
141.e: Donor for kidney transplantation: Donors can be deceased or volunteer living donors. Living donors are usually family members who have at least partial compatibility for HLA antigens. At least 50% HLA match (3/6) is a must requirement for kidney transplant Living volunteer donors should be normal on physical examination Should have the same major ABO blood group, because crossing major blood group barriers prejudices survival of the allograft. Should have two normally functioning kidneys Donor should be free of malignant neoplastic disease, hepatitis and HIV. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 6, pg 234

141.q: Which of the following infection is common within 1-4 months post transplant?
141.e: Transplant patients are among those most vulnerable to CMV infection, especially in the critical few months after the transplant. Between 20% and 60% of people with a solid organ transplant develops a symptomatic CMV infection. These symptoms are similar to the flu - fever, body aches, sore throat and may be difficult to control. The disease caused by post-transplant CMV (PT-CMV) occurs due to: Transmission from the transplanted organ, Due to reactivation of latent infection, or After a primary infection in seronegative transplant patients. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 20, pg 896

141.q: A patient requires liver transplant. He plans to receive it from his brother. They are not twins. On HLA typing, HLA is matched at the A, B and DRB1 loci. Siblings are:
141.e: Important terminologies for Donors in transplant im-munology: Matched Donor: HLA allelic identity at HLA A, B, C and DRB1 loci which is referred as 8/8match. (These 4 HLA antigens have 2 alleles each that makes it 8). Related Donor: Siblings from same parents who is HLA matched for HLA A, B, DRB1 minimum at the antigen level. So obviously, the answer here is matched related donor. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 6, pg 234

142.q: Which of these is not involved in iron metabolism?
142.e: Ceruloplasmin acts as an oxidase for a variety of substrates, one of which is ferrous iron. There is evidence that ceruloplasmin is required for the optimal mobilization of iron from cells to plasma. Reference: Wintrobes 14th/p 813

142.q: Thalassemia is/are more common in which community of India? i. Lohanas and Sindhis ii. Hindus iii. Punjab is from Western and Northern India iv. Parsi
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
142.e: Thalasemias are inherited disorders caused by mutations in globin genes that decrease the synthesis of α- or β-globin. Decreased synthesis of one globin results not only in a deficiency of Hb, but also in red cell damage that is caused by precipitates formed from excess unpaired "normal" globin chains. The mutations that cause thalassemia are particularly common in Mediterranean, African, and Asian regions in which malaria is endemic. As with HbS, it is hypothesized that globin mutations associated with thalassemia protect against falciparum malaria. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition page number - 447

Screening tests for Thalassemia trait: NESTROFT (Naked Eye Single Tube Red cell Osmotic Fragility Test) assesses osmotic fragility of red cells at a single concentration of buffered saline (0.36% in single tube) Reference: Robbins 9th/pg 638; 8th/pg 648

142.q: A two-year-old male child presented to the paediatric OPD with complaints of lethargy, weakness and delayed milestones. On examination, the patient had pale yellowish skin, yellowish sclera, frontal bossing and a protruded jaw. There was moderate splenomegaly on palpation. Peripheral smear revealed a severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia with low reticulocyte count. Further confirmatory and genetic studies revealed that there is premature termination of DNA transcription of the beta-globin chain which causes little to no haemoglobin A production. What kind of mutation is seen in this patient?
142.e: A two-year-old child is suffering from beta-thalessemia. Replacement of amino acid by a stop codon illustrates nonsense mutation. The presence of this premature stop codon results in the production of shortened and likely non-functional protein. The example of disease in which nonsense mutations are known to be among the causes that includes: Cystic fibrosis, Beta thalassemia, hurler syndrome. Reference: Robbins basic pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 244

142.q: The following are all hemoglobin adducts except:
142.e: Hemoglobin adducts are post- translational modifications of hemoglobin molecules. When glucose is added to hemoglobin A, it is known as HbA1c. Similarly individuals with HbS and HbC will have HbS1c and HbC1c, respectively. When the hemoglobin molecule is aged, glutathione becomes bound to cysteine at the 93rd position of the β chain. When this occurs to HbA, this is known as HbA1d or HbAIII. Similarly, patients can have HbS1d and HbC1d, if they have HbS and HbC respectively. Hemoglobin Constant Spring is not a hemoglobin adduct. It is an abnormal hemoglobin that may be seen in individuals with α thalassemia. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 72

142.q: Which of the following is the best indicator to assess iron deficiency anemia? (AIIMS Nov 2019)
o: TIBC increased, Ferritin increased, Transferrin saturation increased, Serum transferrin receptors increased
TIBC reduced, Ferritin reduced, Transferrin saturation reduced, Serum transferrin receptors decreased
TIBC increased, Ferritin reduced, Transferrin saturation reduced, Serum transferrin receptors decreased
TIBC increased, Ferritin reduced, Transferrin saturation reduced, Serum transferrin receptors increased
142.e: In iron deficiency anemia, TIBC (Total iron-binding capacity) is increased, transferrin saturation is decreased, and ferritin is decreased. The diagnosis of IDA ultimately rests on laboratory studies Serum Fe and ferritin are low and the total plasma Fe binding capacity is high. Low serum Fe with increased Fe binding capacity results in a reduction of transferring saturation to below 15%. Reference: Robbins 9th/pg 659

142.q: Which of the following is used in the treatment of sideroblastic anemia?
142.e: Causes of acquired sideroblastic anemia are Excessive alcohol use Vitamin B6 or copper deficiency Lead poisoning or zinc overdose Cancer or myelodysplastic syndrome Certain medications, such as antibiotics, chemotherapeutics, and chelators Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number - 364

142.q: All decrease in iron deficiency anemia; except:
142.e: Transferrin is quantified in terms of the amount of iron it will bind, a measure called the total iron-binding capacity (TIBC; In the average subject, the plasma iron concentration is ∼(100 μg/dL), and the TIBC is ∼(300 μg/dL). Serum iron concentration is reduced in iron deficiency, and the TIBC is often increased. Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases, 10 th edition Chapter 14, pg 655

143.q: Criteria for severe aplastic anemia are all; except:
143.e: A bone marrow cellularity of Reference: Wintrobes 13/p 1189

143.q: Blood examination shows pancytopenia WITH HYPOCELLULAR MARROW a, which can be correct?
143.e: FANCONI ANEMIA IS INHERITED BONE MARROW FAILURE SYNDROME CAUSING APLASTIC ANEMIA Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 622

143.q: A 23-year-old male presented to the clinic with history of Fatigue and tiredness. On investigation he was found to have Hb values of 9 gm%, MCV of 101fl. Peripheral smear examination showed macrocytic hematology (RBCs) and hypersegmented neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?
143.e: MCV - 101fl is suggestive of macrocytosis Most commonly (especially when the increase in size is mild, and just above normal range) the cause is bone marrow dysplasia secondary to alcohol abuse and chronic alcoholism, Poor absorption of vitamin B12 in the digestive tract can also cause macrocytosis. Macrocytosis is frequently linked to alcoholism, with or without liver disease. In fact, it is purported to be one of the most common causes of non megaloblastic macrocytosis. In cases of macrocytosis related to alcoholism the elevated MCV may be due to the direct effect of the alcohol, liver disease and/or folate deficiency. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 18, pg 841

143.q: In which of the following conditions is macrocytic anaemia seen?
143.e: Explanation: Macrocytic anaemia in liver disease arises due to: Altered lipid metabolism: Excess cholesterol deposition on RBC membranes increases their surface area, leading to macrocytosis. Nutritional deficiencies: Liver disease is associated with vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, impairing DNA synthesis and causing megaloblastic anaemia. Bone marrow suppression: Chronic liver dysfunction can affect erythropoiesis, contributing to macrocytosis. Explanation of other options: Thalassemia (Option A): Associated with microcytic anaemia due to defective haemoglobin synthesis; MCV is decreased. Anaemia of Chronic Disease (Option B): Typically, normocytic or microcytic due to inflammation-mediated iron dysregulation; MCV is normal or low. Sideroblastic Anaemia (Option C): Usually microcytic due to defective heme incorporation into globin chains; MCV is low or normal.

143.q: Parvovirus preferentially involves in which of the following cells:
143.e: A special form of red cell aplasia occurs in individuals infected with parvovirus B19, which preferentially infects and destroys red cell progenitors. Normal individuals clear parvovirus infections within 1 to 2 weeks; as a result, the aplasia is transient and clinically unimportant. However, in persons with moderate to severe hemolytic anemias, even a brief cessation of erythropoiesis results in rapid worsening of the anemia, producing an aplastic crisis. Reference: Robbins 9th ed p 655

143.q: Which one of the following is not associated with a high reticulocyte count?
o: Response to treatment in 'nutrition - deficiency' anemia
143.e: Megaloblastic anemia has a low normal Retic % as it is a nutritional anemia. Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases, 10 th edition Chapter 14, pg 651

143.q: Bone marrow failure with neutropenia and exocrine pancreatic deficiency is a feature of:
143.e: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and persistent or intermittent neutropenia and an increased susceptibility to infections. Hematologic problems also can include anemia, thrombocytopenia, and pancytopenia. Reference: Wintrobes 13/p 1523-1533

144.q: All of the followings are the features of intravascular hemolysis except?
144.e: In intravascular hemolysis, destruction of RBC leads to hemoglobinemia. Excess of haemoglobin may be excreted by kidney called hemoglobinuria. Some of the haemoglobin is reabsorbed in kidney and is converted to hemosiderin which is then excreted as hemosiderinuria. Free haemoglobin in plasma bound to haptoglobin, and this complex is rapidly cleared by mononuclear phagocytic system - Decreased haptoglobin When haptoglobin is depleted, free haemoglobin is oxidized to methemoglobin - methemoglobinemia Excess heme groups are catabolized to bilirubin within the mononuclear phagocytic system - Increased indirect bilirubin and jaundice LDH is stored in blood. During hemolysis this enzyme is released in the blood - Increased serum LDH. Reference: Robbins, 8 th edition, page number - 642

144.q: What is the cause of intracorpuscular defects in hemolysis? (Recent Question 2019)
144.e: Acquired mutation of phosphatidyl inositol Glycan complement group A gene (PIGA) Deficient in CD55, CD59, C8 binding protein CD59 prevents activation of alternate pathway Chronic hemolysis without hemoglobinuria is typical Intravascular hemolysis Loss of heme iron can cause IDA Thrombosis is the leading cause of disease related death in individuals with PNH. 5% develop AML. Diagnosis: Flow cytometry Treatment: Immunosuppressant and bone marrow transplant Hemolytic Anemia Hemolysis could be: Intracorpuscular Hereditary Defects Defects in RBC membrane Enzyme defects Hemoglobinopathies Thalassemia Syndromes Acquired Defects PNH Extracorpuscular (areas of sluggish circulation or hypo-oxygenation) Immunohemolytic anemia, infections, microangiopathic Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases, 10 th edition Chapter 14, pg 648

144.q: Which of the following statements are true about Factor H
o: Inhibits alternative pathway of complement activation
Inherited defects in Factor H can cause an atypical form of HUS
Polymorphisms in Factor H gene have been linked to ARMD
144.e: Factor H inhibits alternative complement pathway by promoting destruction of C3b and C3 convertases. Polymorphisms in Factor H gene have been linked to Age related Macular Degeneration, an important cause of vision loss in elder population. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 87

144.q: Which of the following tests is gold standard to diagnose a case of PNH? (Recent exam 2018)
144.e: PNH is diagnosed by flow cytometry, which provides a sensitive means for detecting red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59 and CD55. Reference: Robbins 9th/pg 643

145.q: Which is/are the factors affect rate and degree of sickling in sickle cell disease? i Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration ii Haemoglobin S level iii Haemoglobin F level iv Mean corpuscular hemoglobin
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
145.e: Following factors determine the rate at which the polymerization of HbS and consequent sickling take place: Presence of non HbS hemoglobin Intracellular concentration of HbS Total hemoglobin concentration Extent of deoxygenation Acidosis and dehydration Increased concentration of 2, 3 BPG in the red cells Reference: Harsh mohan, 6 th edition, page number-319

145.q: In a patient suffering with sickle cell anemia, eletrophoretic mobility of HbS in relation to HbA will be?
o: Will depend upon concentration of HbS
145.e: Pathogenesis of Sickle cell anemia: Sequence of codon 6 of the Beta-chain changed from GAG in the normal gene to GTG in the sickle cell gene, resulting in substitution of valine for glutamic acid Concept: So if you see, the charge of amino acid is changing from charged (glutamic acid, more negative) to neutral amino acid (valine), so when we do an electrophoresis, the mobility of HbS will be lesser than HbA towards Anode (i.e retarded) (which is positively charged). Reference: Complete review of Pathology 1st/343

145.q: Which of the following test guide us to the hereditary spherocytosis?
o: Measurement of folate and B12 concentration
145.e: This disorder stems from inherited (intrinsic) defects in the red cell membrane that lead to the formation of spherocytes, nondeformable cells that are highly vulnerable to sequestration and destruction in the spleen. Hereditary spherocytosis is usually transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait; a more severe, autosomal recessive form of the disease affects a small minority of patients. The characteristic features are anemia, splenomegaly, and jaundice. The anemia is variable in severity, ranging from subclinical to profound; most commonly it is moderate in degree. Because of their spherical shape, red cells in hereditary spherocytosis show increased osmotic fragility when placed in hypotonic salt solutions, a characteristic that can help establish the diagnosis. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number445

145.q: Which of the following are causes of increased reticulocyte count
145.e: Hereditary spherocytosis is hemolytic anemia so high reticulocyte count. All others have normal to low reticulocyte count Reference: Wintrobe 1165

145.q: All of the following statement is true regarding hemolytic anemia except:
145.e: Hemolytic anemias have high retic counts. Autosplenectomy can be seen in sickle cell anemia. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition page number - 111, 117, 488

145.q: Decreased ESR is seen in: (Recent Question 2016)
145.e: A decreased Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) can be caused by several factors. Here are some of the common causes: Polycythemia Vera: This is a condition characterized by an increased number of red blood cells Sickle Cell Disease: This is a genetic disorder that affects the shape and functionality of the red blood cells Hyperviscosity Syndrome: This is a group of symptoms triggered by an increase in the viscosity of the blood Hereditary Spherocytosis: This is a condition that leads to an abnormality in the red blood cell membrane, causing the cells to take on a spherical shape Abetalipoproteinemia and Acanthocytosis: These are rare inherited disorders affecting fat absorption and red blood cell shape Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases, 10 th edition Chapter 14, pg 641

145.q: 1-day old baby has developed severe jaundice on the neonatal ward. The mother is rhesus negative and had one previous pregnancy but she was not administered prophylactic anti D in first pregnancy. What is most probable diagnosis in given case history?
145.e: Hemolytic disease of new born results from the passage of IgG antibodies from maternal circulation across the placenta into the circulation of the foetal red cells. Besides pregnancy, sensitization of the mother may result from previous abortions and previous blood transfusions. It occurs from incompatibilities of ABO or RH blood group. Rh incompatibilities results in severe hemolytic disease of new borns. It results in intrauterine death from hydrops fetalis. Moderate disease produce baby born with severe anemia and jaundice due to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. When the level of unconjugated bilirubin exceeds 20 mg/dl, it results in deposition of bile pigments in the basal ganglia of CNS called kernicterus and gives permanent brain damage. Reference: Harsh mohan, 6 th edition, page number - 341

145.q: Assertion: The mutation in sickle cell anaemia is an example of nonsense mutation Reason: The mutation in sickle cell anaemia causes replacement of glutamic acid with Valine in beta chain of haemoglobin
o: Both statements are true and causally related
Both statements are true but not causally related
The first statement is true and second is false
The first statement is false and second is true
145.e: The mutation in sickle cell anaemia is an example of missense mutation. Sickle cell disease(scd) is a genetic disorder caused by a mutation in both copies of a person's hbb gene. This gene encodes a component of hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. The mutation causes hemoglobin molecules to stick together, creating sickle-shaped red blood cells. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 244

146.q: Direct Coomb's test positive is seen in all; except:
146.e: Coomb's test is positive in Immune hemolytic anemia They can be of two types: Direct Coomb's test: Detects Antibody on RBC Surface Indirect Coomb's test: Detects Antibody in Serum Out of the given options: Aplastic anemia is not a hemolytic anemia and so is automatically the answer here. Reference: Wintrobe 13th ed/Page 576

146.q: What does the red cell distribution width (RDW) deal with?
146.e: Red Cell Distribution Width The RDW is an index of the variation in cell size and volume within the red cell population. Normal Value RDW-SD 39-46 fL, RDW-CV 11.6-14.6% in adult Condition with Increased RDW Iron deficiency anemia Folate/vit B12 deficiency anemia Reference: Wintrobe textbook, pg 1432

146.q: A 30-year-old woman came with complaints of easy fatigability, exertion dyspnea and weight loss. She also complaints of frequent fall. Physical Examination revealed there was bilateral decrease in vibration sense. Her hemoglobin levels were 8.2 gm%. She was treated with folate. Her anemia improved but neurological symptoms worsened. Which of the following is the most probable reason for her condition?(Recent Question 2020)
o: Deficiency of folate reductase in CNS
Folate therapy caused rapid use of B12 stores aggravating symptoms
146.e: Vitamin B12 Major role in providing cofactors that are required to form myelin. Required for the production of methionine (precursor for S-adenosyl methionine), which is required for methylation reaction. Myelin maintenance and nerve function. Demyelination occurs from vitamin B12 deficiency. Neurological problems occur in most people who are deficient in vitamin B12. Folic acid can usually correct the anemia. Thus it could mask the underlying disease, and allow the development or progression of neurological deterioration, if diagnosis depended on the presence of anaemic symptoms. Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases, 10 th edition Chapter 14, pg 651

147.q: A 4-year-old boy with sudden onset of petechial rashes. History of viral illness 2 weeks ago present. Investigations reveal thrombocytopenia and antiplatelets antibodies. What is your diagnosis?
147.e: Thrombocytopenia and anti-platelets antibodies in a child presenting with purpura after 2 weeks of viral illness is characteristic of ITP Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 659; 8th/pg 669

147.q: A 9-year-old boy has developed prominent bruises on his extremities over the past week. On physical examination, he has ecchymoses and petechiae on his arms and legs. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin, 13.8 g/dL; hematocrit, 41.9%; MCV, 93 μm3; platelet count, 11,300/mm3; and WBC count, 7720/mm3. He had respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia 3 weeks ago. His condition improves with corticosteroid therapy. Which of the following abnormalities is most likely to cause his hemorrhagic diathesis?
147.e: Acute immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and chronic ITP are caused by antiplatelet autoantibodies, but the acute form is typically seen in children after a viral disease. If the bone marrow was aplastic, all cell lines should be reduced. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa dysfunction/ deficiency can be seen with Glanzmann thrombasthenia and chronic ITP. Scurvy caused by vitamin C deficiency leads to increased capillary fragility with ecchymoses, but not to thrombocytopenia. Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases 10 th edition, Chapter 4, pg 118

147.q: Which of the following is true regarding BernardSoulier syndrome?
o: It is due to defect in platelet adhesion
It is due to defect in platelet aggregation
It is due to defect in platelet receptor GpIb-IX
147.e: Bernard-Soulier syndrome illustrates the consequences of defective adhesion of platelets to subendothelial matrix. Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by an inherited deficiency of the platelet membrane glyco protein complex Ib-IX. This glycoprotein is a receptor for vWF and is essential for normal platelet adhesion to the subendothelial extracellular matrix Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 660

147.q: Which of the following hormone secreted from the liver regulates platelet production?
147.e: Thrombopoietin (TPO) is the principal physiologic regulator of platelet production. In vitro, TPO induces the growth of colony-forming units-megakaryocyte (CFU-MK) and the generation of mature polyploid megakaryocytes, which subsequently form extended cytoplasmic processes, termed proplatelets. The liver secrets thrombopoietin at a constant rate into the circulation, where it bind to c-mpl ligands on both platelets and megakaryocytes. Thrombopoietin bound to platelets are internalized and degraded and thrombopoietin bound to platelets stimulates platelet production. Reference: Mitchell, Oscar et al. 'The pathophysiology of thrombocytopenia in chronic liver disease. 'Hepatic medicine: evidence and research vol. 8 39-50. 15 Apr. 2016, doi:10.2147/HMER.S74612

147.q: The von Willebrand factor play a central role in primary haemostasis. It forms bridge between platelet surface glycoprotein receptor and collagen on damaged endothelium. Which of the following is that glycoprotein receptor?
147.e: VWF has a central role in primary haemostasis where it mediates platelet adhesion to damaged vascular subendothelium and subsequently platelet aggregation. Following a vascular injury, VWF binds specifically to fibrillar collagen type I and III. The below figure explains Structure and function of factor VIII-von Willebrand factor (vWF) complex. Factor VIII and vWF circulate as a complex. vWF also is present in the subendothelial matrix of normal blood vessels. Factor VIII takes part in the coagulation cascade by activating factor X by means of factor IX (not shown). vWF causes adhesion of platelets to subendothelial collagen, primarily through the glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) platelet receptor. Reference : Robbins, 10th edition, page number - 489

147.q: Which of the following is the correct statement regarding Glanzmann thrombasthenia?
147.e: Glanzmann's thrombasthenia is an abnormality of the platelets. It is an extremely rare coagulopathy (bleeding disorder due to a blood abnormality), in which the platelets contain defective or low levels of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GpIIb/IIIa), which is a receptor for fibrinogen. As a result, no fibrinogen bridging of platelets to other platelets can occur, and the bleeding time is significantly prolonged. Characteristically, there is increased mucosal bleeding Heavy menstrual bleeding Easy bruising Nosebleeds Bleeding from the gums Gastrointestinal bleeding Postpartum bleeding Increased postoperative bleeding. Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Glanzmann%27s_thrombasthenia&oldid=1075482842

147.q: Which of the following is not the component of dense granules of platelets?
147.e: Platelets are disc-shaped anucleate cell fragments that are shed from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow into the bloodstream. Their function depends on several glycoprotein receptors, a contractile cytoskeleton, and two types of cytoplasmic granules. α-Granules have the adhesion molecule P-selectin on their membranes and contain proteins involved in coagulation, such as fibrinogen, coagulation factor V, and vWF, as well as protein factors that may be involved in wound healing, such as fibronectin, platelet factor 4 (a heparin-binding chemokine), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and transforming growth factor-β. Dense (or δ) granules contain adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate, ionized calcium, serotonin, and epinephrine. Reference : Robbins, 10th edition, page number - 102

Platelets attach to exposed surface of endothelium following injury; this adhesion is mediated by vWF, which binds to GpIb receptors on platelets. This intiates activation of platelets, which change shape of platelets from a disc to sphere and release their contents to the exterior. These are mainly adenosine diphosphate (ADP), serotonin and thromboxane A2. Platelet aggregation (sticking of platelets to each other) is mediated by thromboxane A2, collagen, ADP and thrombin. Binding of ADP to platelets causes exposure of GpIIb/IIIa receptors which bind fibrinogen. Fibrinogen binding to multiple platelets causes formation of large platelets aggregates. Reference :Essentials of clinical pathology, 2nd edition, page number - 320

148.q: Which of the following regulates warfarin oral anticoagulant therapy?
148.e: PT is the standard test for monitoring treatment with oral anticoagulant (warfarin) inhibit carboxylation of vitamin K dependent factors (Factor II, VII, IX and X) and make these factors inactive. In a patients receiving oral anticoagulants, PT should be reported as a ratio of PT of patient to PT of control; it should not be reported as percentage. Various types of thromboplastin reagents obtained from different sources (like ox brain, rabbit brain, rabbit lung) are available commercially for PT test. Reference : Essentials of clinical pathology, 2nd edition ,page number - 332

148.q: Which of the following enzyme is involved in ubiquitin proteosome pathway of atrophy?
148.e: The degradation of cellular proteins occurs mainly by ubiquitin proteosome pathway. Nutrient deficiency and disuse may activate ubiquitin ligases, which attach the small peptide ubiquitin to cellular proteins for degradation in proteasomes. This pathway is thought to be responsible for various catabolic conditions. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 19 th ed Pg:37

148.q: Which of the following is true regarding Factor V Leiden mutation?
o: Increased risk of deep vein thrombosis
Factor V becomes resistant to cleavage by protein C
148.e: Factor V Leiden mutation results in glutamine to arginine substitution at amino acid residue 506 that renders factor V resistant to cleavage and inactivation by protein C. As a result, an important antithrombotic counterregulatory pathway is lost and chances of thrombosis are highly raised Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 123

148.q: An 8-year-old girl experiences sudden severe dyspnea. On examination, she has upper airway obstruction from soft tissue swelling in her neck. A radiograph shows a hematoma compressing the trachea. She was then diagnosed to have hemophilia A. Both parents and two female siblings are unaffected by this problem, but a male sibling has experienced a similar episode. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most likely to account for the findings in this girl?
148.e: This girl has features of hemophilia A. This X-linked recessive condition is expected to occur in males who inherit the one maternal X chromosome with the genetic mutation, and they do not have another X chromosome with a normal functional allele, as is the case in her brother. Hemophilia in a female can be explained by the Lyon hypothesis, which states that only one X chromosome in a female is active (the “turned off” X chromosome is the Barr body) for most genes, but this inactivation is a random event. Some unlucky females are out on the tail end of the Poisson distribution of random events and have few active X chromosomes with the normal allele, leading to markedly diminished factor VIII activity. The other choices do not explain this phenomenon. Reference: Robins Basic Pathology 10th ed/pg 267

148.q: Which among the following laboratory investigation is best to reveal about bleeding in Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)?
148.e: Two types of DIC are acute (decompensated and chronic compensated). In acute DIC, there is rapid activation of coagulation leading to bleeding from consumption of coagulation factors. Findings in acute DIC are low platelet, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, and increased FDP and D-dimer. In chronic DIC, there is slow activation of coagulation with slow consumption of coagulation factors. Findings are normal platelet count, normal PT and APTT. However, FDP and D-dimer are increased. So in acute DIC, all the four options are correct, while if we consider the question as chronic DIC, then best possible answer is increased FDP. Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases 10 th edition, Chapter 14, pg 667

148.q: The following is not a contraindication for heparin in DIC
o: If the platelet count cannot be maintained at >50,000/ mcL
In cases of central nervous system/gastrointestinal bleeding
148.e: About use of Heparin in DIC: Low doses of continuous infusion heparin (5-10 U/ kg per h) may be effective in patients with low-grade DIC associated with solid tumor, acute promyelocytic leukemia, or in a setting with recognized thrombosis. Heparin is also indicated for the treatment of purpura fulminans during the surgical resection of giant hemangiomas and during removal of a dead fetus. In acute DIC, the use of heparin is likely to aggravate bleeding. To date, the use of heparin in patients with severe DIC has no proven survival benefit. Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 662; 8th/pg 672

148.q: Which clotting factor deficiency will not affect clotting in vivo?
148.e: Deficiency of factor 12 doesnot cause bleeding Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10 th edition, 120

148.q: A 10-day infant presented with large cephalohematoma. His parents gave no history of trauma but severe umbilical bleed during his childbirth. What is the most likely factor deficiency associated?
148.e: Abnormal bleeding manifests shortly after birth, when bleeding from the healthy umbilical cord remnant occurs. Umbilical stump bleeding is an uncommon presentation for other congenital bleeding disorders. Rebleeding at circumcision is also common. The most life-threatening complication of factor XIII deficiency is spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage. Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 662

149.q: CBC done on a patient who had come for blood transfusion revealed MCV 56fl, Hb 13 gm%, MCHC 32 gm/dl & RDW 14, RBC count 6million/ul
149.e: This patient has a normal Hb but low MCV. So if you calculate the Mentzer index = MCV/RBC count, it comes to 9.3, which is less than 13 which is indicative of Thalassemia trait. Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases, 10 th edition Chapter 14, pg 644

149.q: Direct coombs test is positive in all except
149.e: Direct Coombs test (DAT) : This test checks for antibodies attached directly to the surface of your red blood cells. The DAT POSITIVE IN : Abo in compatibility Screening for blood compatibility before transfusions. Hemolytic disease of newborn Testing for transfusion reactions. Prenatal blood testing. Drug induced autoimmune hemolytic anaemia Pre-transfusion blood typing. Reference :Robin's basic pathology, 10 th edition, pg: 492

149.q: All except following is true for Apheresis Platelet Collections
o: The minimum platelet count required to donate apheresis platelets is 150,000/μL.
AABB Standards limits apheresis platelet donations to no more than twice in a 7-day period and no more than 24 times per year.
149.e: Platelet apheresis Effects of Anticoagulant : Excess anticoagulant goes into patient body during plateletpheresis to prevent clotting The anticoagulant can affect the donor's calcium levels causing hypocalcemia which is rather common after apheresis One common side effect is a tingling sensation in the lips , which can be counteracted by administering calcium-containing antacid tablets. Reference: AABB manual of blood banking, pg 1140

149.q: All of the following are histology features of psoriasis except
o: Regular downward elongation of rete ridges
149.e: Characteristic histological findings are increased epidermal cell proliferation results in marked epidermal thickening (acanthosis), with regular downward elongation of the rete ridges sometimes described as appearing like test tubes in a Mitotic figures are easily identified well above the basal cell layer, where mitotic activity is confined in normal skin. The stratum granulosum is thinned or absent, and extensive overlying parakeratotic scale is seen. Typical of psoriatic plaques is thinning of the portion of the epidermal cell layer that overlies the tips of dermal papillae (suprapapillary plates) and dilated, tortuous blood vessels within these papillae. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1157

149.q: Which of the following types of aberrant immune reactions may be diagnosed by a Coomb's test?
149.e: Antibody-mediated (type II) hypersensitivity disorders are caused by antibodies directed against target antigens on the surface of cells or other tissue components. The antigens may be normal molecules intrinsic to cell membranes or in the extracellular matrix or they may be adsorbed exogenous antigens (e.g., a drug metabolite). A Coombs test, also known as an antiglobulin test, is of two blood tests used in immunohematology. They are the direct and indirect Coombs tests. The direct Coombs test detects antibodies that are stuck to the surface of the red blood cells. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th Edition, Page Number-139.

149.q: What is used in irradiation of blood products before transplant surgery?
149.e: It is done to prevent transfusion associated graft versus host disease in immunocompromised host Uses: the recommended dose for the irradiation is 2,500 cGy at the center of the irradiation field, with a minimum dose of 1,500 cGy at any point in the field Reference: Robin's basic pathology, 10 th edition, pg:491

149.q: Which of the following blood components has the shortest shelf life?
149.e: Shelf life for various components Red blood cells 35-42 days. Platelets 5-7 days. Fresh frozen plasma 1 year. Cryoprecipitate 1 year. Reference: Wintrobe's Clinical Hematology, 12th Edition, Page Number-677.

149.q: ABO is located on which chromosome?
149.e: The ABO gene , which determines the ABO blood group, resides on chromosome 9 at the band 9q34.2. This gene contains 7 exons Reference: Dacie - pg 486

150.q: How will you differentiate mediastinal mass from thymoma differentiating it from ALL?
150.e: A mediastenal mass has a differential of thymoma and T cell ALL. T –ALL will have the markers TDT (Lymphoblast), CD 1a and CD3. Thymoma has two components: epithelial and lymphoid component.
