So is positive for EMA, cytokeratin 7 and 20, CD57 CD5, bcl-2, calretinin, vimentin, CD3, CD1a, CD20, CD99 and Ki67 and TdT. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 594-596

150.q: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room by his family. Over the past two weeks, he has developed marked fatigue, and his parents have noted pinpoint hemorrhages in his eyelids. On examination, the patient appears ill. His vital signs are temperature of 99.6°F, blood pressure of 100/65 mm Hg, and pulse rate of 102 bpm. The white blood cell count is 87,000 cells/μL, with 92% blasts, hemoglobin of 8.6 g/dL, and platelet count of 68,000 cells/ μL. Of the following, which would genetic testing most likely reveal?
150.e: The patient has acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The symptoms and signs are consistent with an infiltrative process in the bone marrow, and the differential indicates an acute leukemia. In children, the majority (around 75%) of the acute leukemias are acute lymphoblastic leukemia, so, although other forms of leukemia are possible, the most common would be ALL. t(12;21), which translocates the TEL1 and AML1 genes, is characteristic of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. t(9;22) can be found in ALL, but most commonly in adult ALL. Of the translocations, t(11;14) is found in mantle cell lymphoma, t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, and t(15;17) in acute myeloid leukemia. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, page number - 465

150.q: All of the following are seen in the development of T lymphocyte at a point; except:
150.e: PAX-5 is a B Cell marker Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 594

150.q: Which type of leukemia shows block positivity on PAS (periodic acid schiff) stain?
150.e: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphomas (ALLs) are neoplasms composed of immature B (pre-B) or T (pre-T) cells, which are referred to as lymphoblasts. Histochemical stains are also helpful, in that (in contrast to myeloblasts) lymphoblasts are myeloperoxidase-negative and often contain periodic acid-Schiff–positive glycogen granules. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, page number-465

151.q: The anaemia associated with leukaemia is ?
151.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Myelophthisis type Myelophthisic anemia Space - occupying lesions that destroy significant amount of bone marrow or disturb the marrow architecture, depress its productive capacity. This form of anemia is referred to as myelophthisic anemia. Characteristically, immature erythroid and myeloid progenitors appears in the peripheral blood —> Leukoerythroblastosis. Causes are Metastatic cancer (M.C. cause) Granulomatous disease infiltrating bone marrow. Myeloproliferative disorders (such as myeloid leukemia) Myelofibrosis

151.q: Child with chloromas. Next step in evaluation.
151.e: In chloroma, there is extramedullary proliferation of blasts so its necessary to do a bone marrow evaluation to rule out concomitant leukemia. since bone marrow is not in option, peripheral smear is the next best answer. Since if the blasts are present in peripheral smear, it is suggestive of leukemia Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 592

151.q: All Trans' retinoic acid is used in the treatment of tumor associated with:
151.e: All trans retinoic acid is used in the treatment of Acute promyelocytic leukemia Acute promyelocytic leukemia (M3) with t(15;17) (q22;q12); PML/RAR-a Therapy with the retinoic acid analogue all trans retinoic acid can result in maturation of these leukemic cells and clinical remission Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 588-590

151.q: A patient presented with painless b/l proptosis. What is the next investigation to diagnose it as chloroma?
151.e: Myeloid (granulocytic) sarcoma, or myeloblastoma are extramedullary blast proliferation.These tumors are called chloromas because some appear green or turn green in dilute acid secondary to expression of MPO. The tumors are usually localized; they often involve bone, periosteum, soft tissues, lymph nodes, or skin. Common sites are the orbit and the paranasal sinuses. The diagnosis can be made, if Auer rods are detected on blasts in peripheral smear or if myeloid origin is confirmed by cytochemical or immunohistochemical methods. The diagnosis should be suspected, if eosinophilic myelocytes are present in hematoxylin and eosin–stained biopsy sections. Imprint preparations can be helpful. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 601

152.q: A 20-year-old male presented with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histology of lymph node shows RS cell with vague nodule formation and background T reactive lymphocytes. The cells were positive for CD20, LCA, EMA and negative for CD 15 and CD30. Diagnosis is:
o: T cell rich B cell lymphoma
152.e: This is classical description of NLPHL. (Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma) Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 9 th Edition page No.606

152.q: Ebstein Barr positivity is found in which of the following types of Hodgkin's disease? i) Lymphocyte depleted ii) Mixed Cellularity iii) Lymphocyte Rich iv) Nodular Sclerosis
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
152.e: HL can be classified into two clinicopathological entities: the nodular lymphocyte predominant type (NLPHL) which represents 5% of cases and are virtually never associated with EBV, and the classical HL, which can be further subdivided in four morphological subtypes: nodular sclerosis (NSHL) which accounts for the majority of cases, mixed cellularity (MCHL), lymphocyte-rich (LRHL) and lymphocyte-depleted (LDHL). Reference: Massini, G., Siemer, D., & Hohaus, S. (2009). EBV in Hodgkin Lymphoma. Mediterranean journal of hematology and infectious diseases, 1(2), e2009013. https://doi.org/10.4084/MJHID.2009.013

152.q: Lymphohistocytic variant of Reed Sternberg seen in which subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma?
152.e: Lymphohistiocytic variants (L and H cells) with polypoid nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and moderately abundant cytoplasm are characteristic of the lymphocyte predominance subtype Hodgkin lymphoma. Reference: Robbins 9th ed p 608

152.q: Lacunar cells is seen in which type of Hodgkins Lymphoma: September 2010
152.e: Ans. C: Nodular Sclerosis Type Reed-Sternberg cells (also known as lacunar histiocytes for certain types) are different giant cells found on light microscopy in biopsies from individuals with Hodgkin's lymphoma (aka Hodgkin's disease; a type of lymphoma), and certain other disorders. They are usually derived from B lymphocytes.

152.q: PAX-5 is a STRONGLY POSITIVE marker for:
152.e: PAX-5 is a B-cell differentiation including lymphoblasts (used as a novel pan B-cell marker); also seen in R-S cells in NLPHL (+) vs. classic HL (weak). Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 594

152.q: All of the following are true about NLPHL except
o: Poor prognosis compared to classical Hl
152.e: NLPHL is now considered to be a distinct entity from HL. The neoplastic cells in NLPHL are called the HRS like cells or L&H cells or popcorn cells. They lack CD15 and CD 30 unlike RS cells. They are positive for CD19, 20, 45, 79a and BCL2. They run a chronic indolent course. EBV is implicated in HL and not NLPHL.

153.q: Which of the following shows BCL-2 positive marker?
153.e: Greater than 85% of follicular lymphomas have a characteristic (14;18) translocation that fuses the BCL2 gene on chromosome 18 to the IgH locus on chromosome 14. This chromosomal rearrangement results in the inappropriate 'overexpression' of BCL2 protein, which you will recall is an inhibitor of apoptosis that contributes to cell survival. Immunophenotype. These tumors express B cell markers such as CD20 and the germinal center B cell markers CD10 and BCL6; of note, BCL6 is a transcription factor that is required for the generation of germinal center B cells. Reference : Robbins, 10 th edition, page number - 468

153.q: Which of the following is the most common extranodal site for non- hodgkin's lymphoma?
153.e: Two thirds of hodgkin’s and non hodgkin’s lymphoma presents with nontender nodal enlargement. Two thirds of non hodgkin’s lymphoma are at extranodal sites which are Skin, stomach and brain. Reference:- Robbins, 7 th edition page number - 668

At least one quarter of non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas (NHL) arise from tissue other than lymph nodes and even from sites which normally contain no lymphoid tissue. These forms are referred to as primary extranodal lymphomas. Gastrointestinal localizations, CNS, skin (Mycosis fungoidosis), thyroid, testis. Primary nodal NHL have presentation in lymph node, Waldeyer’s ring, spleen or bone marrow Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 602

153.q: Which of the following lymphoma is triggered by autoimmune disorders?
153.e: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma is an example of a cancer that arises within and is sustained by chronic inflammation. It tends to develop within tissues that are involved by chronic inflammation triggered by autoimmune disorders (such as the salivary gland in Sjogren syndrome and the thyroid gland in Hashimoto thyroiditis) or that are the sites of chronic infection (such as H. pylori gastritis). In the case of H. pylori–associated gastric marginal zone lymphoma, eradication of H. pylori with antibiotic therapy often leads to regression of the tumor cells, which depend on inflammatory cytokines secreted by H. pylori–specific T cells for their growth and survival. Reference : Robbins, 10 th edition, page number - 469

153.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of abdominal discomfort. Physical examination demonstrates splenomegaly but no lymphadenopathy. A CBC shows pancytopenia. Examination of a peripheral blood smear reveals atypical lymphoid cells that exhibit tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase activity. Which of the following is the appropriate diagnosis?
153.e: Hairy cell leukemia Hairy cell leukemia is a clonal B cell proliferation of smallto medium-sized lymphocytes that display abundant cytoplasm and hair-like protrusions of the cell membrane. The disease involves primarily the monocyte/macrophage system of the bone marrow, spleen, and liver. Hairy cell leukemia is rare and affects mainly middle-aged to elderly persons, with a markedly increased male-to-female ratio of 5:1. Unlike the other choices, hairy cell leukemia expresses tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 13, pg 603 - 605

153.q: Which of the following Immunohisto chemistry marker is used in Cyclin D1 negative Mantle cell lymphoma?
153.e: WHO 2016 Hematolymphoid textbook. Mantle Zone Lymphoma Positive stains - CD5, CD19 (strong), CD20 (strong), cyclin D1/BCL1 (variable nuclear staining since cells are at different stages of cell cycle) also CD22, CD43, CD79a, FMC7, surface IgM or IgD, kappa or lambda, BCL2 SOX 11 positive in cyclin D1 negative mantle lymphoma. Negative stains - CD23, usually CD10; also BCL6, CD11c, TdT, T cell antigens Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 598

153.q: Mantle cell lymphoma is positive for all except?
153.e: Mantle cell lymphoma is composed of cells resembling the naive B cells found in the mantle zones of normal lymphoid follicles. It constitutes approximately 6% of all NHLs and occurs mainly in men older than 50 years of age. Almost all tumors have an (11;14) translocation that fuses the cyclin D1 gene to the IgH locus. The tumor cells express surface IgM and IgD, the B cell antigen CD20, and CD5, and they contain high levels of cyclin D1 protein. Another marker, CD23, is a low affinity receptor for ige. It is located at the surface of B cells and binds ige/antigen complexes to be presented to specific CD4+ cells. Thus, CD23 enhances the antibody response, promotes the production of ige in its soluble form and inhibits the production of membrane ige Reference : Robbins, 10 th edition, page number - 469

154.q: Most common type of testicular lymphoma
o: EBV positive extra-nodal NK/T cell lymphoma
154.e: Testicular lymphoma is most common testicular neoplasm in men >60yrs age and have a propensity for CNS metastasis. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 969

154.q: A 7-year-old Nigerian child is treated at a regional medical center for a facial tumor. The mass is located within the mandible itself. Biopsy reveals sheets of medium-sized neoplastic cells that stain deep blue on Giemsa stain with numerous vacuoles in the cytoplasm, interspersed with macrophages. Which of the following is true regarding this patient's disease?
o: Most of the cases in HIV-positive patients are associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection.
This disease is caused by up-regulation of the c-myc oncogene
Tumor lysis syndrome is uncommon in this disease
The disease is usually unresponsive to chemotherapy
154.e: Translocation between the c-myc gene and immunoglobulin genes is the defining feature of a Burkitt lymphoma. In 80% of cases the translocation, t(8;14), is between c-myc and the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene. The remainder of the cases involve translocation of c-myc with immunoglobulin light chain genes. Epstein-Barr virus is involved in almost all cases of African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma, but fewer than 30% of sporadic or immunodeficiency related cases. This malignancy has one of the highest turnover rates known, making it extremely fast growing but also very chemo sensitive. Because of this fact, the risk of tumor lysis syndrome is very high. The neoplastic cells in Burkitt lymphoma do not express terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), distinguishing it from acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Reference : Robbins, 10 th edition, page number - 471

155.q: A 55-year-old man complains of pain in his back, fatigue and occasional confusion. He admits to polyuria and polydipsia. An X-ray examination reveals numerous lytic lesions in the lumbar vertebral bodies. Laboratory studies disclose hypoalbuminemia, mild anemia, and thrombocytopenia. A monoclonal Igk peak is demonstrated by serum electrophoresis. Urinalysis shows 4+ proteinuria. A bone marrow biopsy discloses foci of plasma cells, which account for 18% of all hematopoietic cells. What is the appropriate diagnosis?
155.e: Plasma cell myeloma (multiple myeloma) is characterized by a multifocal infiltration of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow. There are typically multiple destructive lytic lesions or diffuse demineralization of bone. Major diagnostic criteria for plasma cell myeloma include marrow plasmacytosis (>10%), plasmacytoma on biopsy, and immunoglobulin paraprotein (M-component). Neoplastic cells typically secrete a homogeneous complete or partial immunoglobulin chain, which can be seen in serum or urine electrophoresis. In this patient, the neoplastic clone secretes excess kappa light chains. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter 13, pg 616-618

155.q: Which of the following is the most common immunologic type of multiple myeloma?
155.e: The most frequent M protein produced by myeloma cells is IgG (60%), followed by IgA (20% - 25%); only rarely are IgM, IgD, or IgE M proteins observed. The plasma cells produce only κ or λ light chains. Because free light chains are small in size, they are also excreted in the urine, where they are referred to as Bence Jones proteins. Bence Jones proteins in the urine can be a diagnostic marker for multiple myeloma and are often used in laboratory tests to detect and monitor the disease. Reference :Robbins, 10th edition, page number - 472

155.q: Which is the commonest site for the lytic lesion to occur in a case of multiple myeloma?
155.e: Bony lesions are most common in vertebral column. The following is the ascending order of lesion to occur: Vertebral column> Ribs> Pelvis> Femur> Clavicle> Skull Reference:- Harrison, 16 th edition, page number - 659

155.q: Russel bodies, Mott bodies and Dutcher bodies seen in?
155.e: Russel bodies, Mott bodies and Dutcher bodies are seen in Plasma cells and plasma cell associated disorder is Amyloidosis. Reference: Wintrobe 8th edition, page 789

155.q: A 70-year-old man presents with chronic lower back pain, fatigue, and headaches for several weeks. Examination reveals pallor and bony tenderness, and lab investigations show elevated ESR. Skull radiographs demonstrate punched-out lytic lesions. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
155.e: Explanation: Serum electrophoresis showing IgG is the best diagnostic test for multiple myeloma . Detects monoclonal immunoglobulins (M-protein) produced by malignant plasma cells. Confirms clonality and quantifies abnormal proteins, aiding in diagnosis and monitoring. Multiple myeloma typically presents with: CRAB features: Hypercalcemia, Renal failure, Anaemia, Bone lesions Lytic bone lesions (punched-out lesions on skull X-ray) Elevated ESR and fatigue Explanation of Other Options: Serum CA 15-3 (Option B): Tumor marker primarily for breast cancer monitoring ; not diagnostic for myeloma. Whole-body scan (Option C): Useful to assess disease extent but not for initial diagnosis of multiple myeloma. CT head with contrast (Option D): Not indicated as first-line investigation Lytic lesions are better evaluated by X-ray or MRI if needed.

155.q: Russell's bodies are round eosinophilic inclusions found in plasma cells in multiple myeloma are due to accumulation of which substance?
155.e: Cells may accumulate abnormal amounts of various substances, which may be harmless or may cause varying degrees of injury. The substance may be located in the cytoplasm, within organelles(typically lysosomes) or in the nucleus and it may be synthesized by the affected cells or it may be produced elsewhere. In multiple myeloma, the marked accumulation of newly synthesized immunoglobulins that may occur in the RER of some plasma cells, forming rounded, eosinophilic Russell bodies. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg:51

156.q: True about BCR-ABL 'traits' are all except:
o: P190 is a bad prognostic factor
P230 is positive in chronic neutrophilic leukemia
156.e: CML can have 3 types of transcripts. P190–Poor prognosis Seen in ALL P210–Seen in CML P230–Seen in CNL good prognosis Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 633

156.q: 50-year-old male complained of fatigability persistent for one year. Mild anemia massive splenomegaly. Hb 10 gm%, TLC of 1.2 lakhs, platelets 5 lakhs/ul, Neutrophils 60, Basophil 4, Eosinophil 6, Lymph 15, Myeloblast 3. Rest were myelocyte and bands. M:E ratio of 18:1, Most specific further investigation:
156.e: FISH or PCR to document BCR-ABL translocation.

156.q: A 60-year-old male living in hilly area has Hb of 16 gm%, TC 21000/mL. DLC showed metamyelocytes and myelocytes 40%, N25% L40%, E5%. Platelet count 3.25 lakh/u. He presented with hypertension and on examination, spleen was just palpable below costal margin. What is the next step?
156.e: In this case, the clinical features are suggestive of polycythemia. Since, he is from hilly area, it may be due to secondary causes. To rule out primary (low epo) vs secondary cause (high epo), erythropoietin must be the next logical step. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 13, pg 624

156.q: A 53-year-old man has had increasing fatigue for the past 6 months. On physical examination he has a palpable spleen tip. Laboratory studies show a WBC count of 189,000/microliter. The peripheral blood smear shows many mature and immature myeloid cells present. Cytogenetic analysis of cells obtained via bone marrow aspiration reveals a t(9:22) translocation. This translocation leads to formation of a hybrid gene that greatly increases tyrosine kinase activity. Which of the following genes is most likely translocated to cause these findings?
156.e: The above history shows organomegaly with increased WBC counts. Peripheral smear with mature, immature myeloid cells and t(9:22) translocation is case of chronic myeloid leukemia. BCR-ABL fusion gene formation is an early, perhaps initiating, event that drives leukemogenesis. The crucial role of BCR-ABL in cancer has been confirmed by the dramatic clinical response of patients with chronic myeloid leukemia to BCR-ABL kinase inhibitors. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 207.

156.q: A 3 year old child presents with scattered lesions in the skull. Biopsy revealed Langerhans giant cells. The most commonly associated marker with this condition-
156.e: Langerhans cell proliferations take on different clinical forms, but all are believed to be variations of the same basic disorder. The proliferating Langerhans cells express MHC class II antigens, CD1a, and langerin. Langerin is a transmembrane protein found in Birbeck granules, cytoplasmic penta laminar rodlike tubular structures that in electron micrographs have a characteristic periodicity and sometimes a dilated terminal end ('tennis racket' appearance). Under the light microscope, the proliferating Langerhans cells do not resemble their normal dendritic counterparts. Instead, they have abundant, often vacuolated cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei, an appearance more akin to that of tissue macrophages (called histiocytes by morphologists) hence the term Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Reference : Robbins, 10 th edition, page number - 484

156.q: A 24 - year - old woman who presented with aquagenic pruritic had a Hb level of 20g/dL . Her lab investigations are given below, Which of the following is not seen in this condition ? Hb - 19g/dl Hematocrit - 52% S. erythropoietin - decreased JAK2 mutation - positive
156.e: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of polycythemia vera. It is a myeloproliferative neoplasm, presents with history of hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd Chiari syndrome ) and can progress to Myelofibrosis. It can also undergo clonal evolution to AML. Hepatic failure is not seen in this condition. Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2. In this condition, clonal erythrocytosis is taking place autonomously i.e, independent of erythropoietin. Clinical features of polycythemia vera : Headache Hypertension Dizziness

156.q: In Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis, the characteristic abnormality seen is
156.e: Birbeck granules Also known as Langerhans bodies or X granules Seen on Electron microscopy Rod-shaped organelles with a central striation and terminal vesicular dilation, giving them a 'tennis racket' appearance. Reference: Robbins 9th/pg 531

156.q: Delayed dentition is seen in all/except ?
156.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., All of above Causes of delay in tooth eruption : 1) Impacted teeth 4) Cong hypothyroidsm 2) Down syndrome 5) Gaucher Cleidocranial dysplasia 6) Osteo petrosis

157.q: A patient presented to the pathology lab with following TLC 2000 cells /ul, DLC Stab03 P10 L80M5E2. What is the ANC of the patient
157.e: Stabs are precursors to neutrophils so added together Wbc x neutrophils/100 : 2000x 13 /100 : 260 Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 72

157.q: A 20-year-old carpenter with a wound infection on his left thumb presents with an enlarged and tender lymph node in the axilla. A lymph node biopsy shows follicular enlargement and hyperemia. The sinuses are filled with neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
157.e: Acute suppurative lymphadenitis occurs in the lymph nodes that drain a site of acute bacterial infection. Suppurative lymph nodes enlarge rapidly because of edema and hyperemia and are tender due to distention of the capsule. Microscopically, infiltration of the lymph node sinuses and stroma by polymorphonuclear leukocytes and prominent follicular hyperplasia are noted. Neutrophils are not a morphologic feature of the other choices. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter 13, pg 598

157.q: A 21-year-old female college student develops fatigue and a low-grade fever after a visit by her boyfriend, who goes to a different college in another state. During a massage given to her by a friend, her friend notes small swellings on the back of her neck. The next day, she goes horseback riding with her friends and falls from a horse onto a large pile of hay. Several minutes after the fall, she becomes unresponsive, and ultimately dies. At autopsy, of the following, which is most likely to be identified by the forensic pathologist?
157.e: The patient has signs and symptoms consistent with infectious mononucleosis, with the swellings noted by her friend being posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Many people with infectious mononucleosis develop splenomegaly, and the spleen is more fragile and can rupture after minor trauma. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-460-461

158.q: All is true about Giant cell arteritis except ?
o: Involves large to small sized areteries
Most commonly involved artery is abdominal aorta
158.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Most commonly involved artery is abdominal aorta It is the most common form of systemic vasculitis in adults, is an acute and chronic, often granulomatous, inflammation of arteries of large to small size. It affects principally the arteries in the head-especially the temporal arteries— but also the vertebral and ophthalmic arteries and the aorta, where it may cause thoracic aortic aneurysm

158.q: Atherosclerosis causes fibroblast plaque formation by injury to:
158.e: Pathogenesis of atherosclerosis best explained by the ‘Response to Injury hypothesis to endothelium Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 498-499; 8th/pg 505; Harrison 18th/pg 1503

158.q: Which of following gross features is/are seen in specimen of benign nephrosclerosis? i. Flea-bitten appearance ii. U shape scar on cortical surface iii. Pale yellow abscess formation iv. Grain leather appearance
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
158.e: Nephrosclerosis refers to sclerosis of small renal arteries and arterioles that is strongly associated with hypertension. The characteristic morphologic alterations of the small arterioles are called hyaline arteriolosclerosis, while the arteries show fibrous intimal and medial thickening often resulting in luminal narrowing. The vascular changes cause ischemia, which leads to various combinations of interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, and focal global glomerulosclerosis. Grossly, the kidneys are symmetrically atrophic. Typically the renal surface shows diffuse, fine granularity that resembles grain leather. Others are the features of malignant nephrosclerosis. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page- 570

158.q: A 60yr old male presented with urinary frequency and painful micturition, his pelvic USG shows an enlarged prostate, his clinician makes a diagnosis of BPH, true statements regarding BPH
o: BPH affects transitional zone of prostate
Glands are lined by two layers of cells, inner columnar and outer layer of cuboidal or flat basal epithelium
Prostatic infarcts with areas of squamous metaplasia may be seen
158.e: In marked enlarge glands, compromise of vascular supply may produce prostatic infarcts. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 976

158.q: A 7-year-old male patient having 3-year history of coughing and intermittent respiratory distress. He now presented in casualty with respiratory distress, he also feels chest tightness, cough with sputum and wheezing. He uses accessory muscle during distress. Laboratory findings revealed an elevated serum IgE level and peripheral blood eosinophilia. A sputum sample examined microscopically shows increased numbers of eosinophils. Which of the following histologic features is most likely to characterize the disease he is suffering?
o: Dilation of respiratory bronchioles with loss of elastic fibers
Interstitial and alveolar edema with hyaline membrane formation
Remodeling of airways with smooth muscle hyperplasia and increased submucosal glands
158.e: (d) Patients long history and classic symptoms of chest tightness, cough with sputum and wheezing along with elevated serum IgE level, peripheral blood eosinophilia and eosinophils in sputum are suggestive of asthma. Characteristic histopathological findings in asthma are: Thickening of airway wall Sub-basement membrane fibrosis (due to deposition of type I and III collagens) Increased vascularity Increase in the size of the submucosal glands and number of airway goblet cells Hypertrophy and/or hyperplasia of the bronchial wall muscle with increased extracellular matrix Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 686

158.q: Which of the following is seen in kidney in malignant hypertension?
158.e: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis. This lesion occurs in severe hypertension; vessels exhibit concentric, laminated ("onionskin") thickening of the walls with luminal narrowing The laminations consist of SMCs with thickened, reduplicated basement membrane; in malignant hypertension, they are accompanied by fibrinoid deposits and vessel wall necrosis (necrotizing arteriolitis) , particularly in the kidney Reference : Robbins 10th/pg 493

158.q: Jaw tightness is typically seen in:
158.e: Answer is C (Giant Cell Arteritis): Jaw Claudication (law Tightness) is a typical manifestation of Temporal arteritis or Giant cell arteritis.

158.q: A 12-year-old boy develops fever, accompanied by occasional headaches, malaise, fatigue, and nausea a month after being bitten by a dog. One day later, he experiences episodes of rigidity, hallucinations, breath holding, and difficulty swallowing because of uncontrollable oral secretions. Neurologist were consulted and immediately treatment started with some injectable medicines. Which of the pathological findings is the hallmark of the disease?
158.e: The child had rabies, an infectious disease in which the virus travels from the site of an infected animal bite up nerves to the CNS. Pathognomonic Negri bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions found in the hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 28 pg 1266

159.q: In Marfan's syndrome, Aortic aneurysm occurs most commonly in:
159.e: The answer is A (Ascending Aorta) Aortic aneurysms in Marfan's syndrome occur most frequently in the ascending aorta. Cardiovascular lesions in Marfan's syndrome Cardiovascular lesions are the most life-threatening features of Marfan's syndrome. Mitral valve prolapse(MVP) Loss of connective tissue support in mitral valves leaflets makes them soft and blowy creating the so-called 'floppy valve'. Mitral regurgitation frequently results. Dilatation of Ascending Aortae The media undergoes cystic necrosis (cystic medionecrosis). Loss of medial support results in progressive dilatation of aortic valve ring and root of the aorta Severe aortic incompetence Aortic dissections

159.q: A 59-year-old male patient presents with abdominal pain, history taking revealed he has hypertension since long duration and also smokes since very long time. Radiological investigations were performed which show pulsating mid line mass possibly aneurysm. Which of the following statements are true regarding its generation?
o: Abnormal transforming growth factor beta signaling
Inflammation leading to collagen degradation and alteration
Weakening of vascular wall due to loss of smooth muscle cell or generation of noncollagen extracellular matrix
159.e: (a) Abnormal transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling: Excessive TGF-β activity alters vascular wall remodeling, primarily of the ascending aorta, leading ultimately to diminished ECM content and integrity with aneurysmal dilation. (b) The balance of collagen degradation and synthesis is altered by inflammation and associated proteases. Inflammatory cells in the setting of an aortitis or associated with atherosclerosis can be found throughout the aortic wall. The vascular wall is weakened through loss of SMCs or the inappropriate synthesis of noncollagenous or nonelastic ECM. Ischemia of the inner media occurs when there is atherosclerotic thickening of the intima, increasing the distance that oxygen and nutrients must diffuse. Reference : Robbins 10th Ed. pg 505

159.q: A 65-year-old patient diagnosed as having hyperlipidemia on screening tests or a routine physical and laboratory investigations. Laboratory studies show total serum cholesterol of 350 mg/dL, LDL of 280 mg/dL, HDL of 37 mg/dL, and triglycerides of 380 mg/dL. This patient is symptomatic, however, is most at risk of developing an aneurysm in which of the following anatomic locations?
159.e: The two most important causes of aortic aneurysms are atherosclerosis and hypertension; atherosclerosis is a greater factor in abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), while hypertension is the most common etiology associated with ascending aortic aneurysms. Reference : Robbins 10th Ed pg 506

159.q: Which of the following is not a cause of aneurysm?
159.e: Monckeberg medial sclerosis is characterized by calcifications of the medial walls of muscular arteries, typically starting along the internal elastic membrane. Adults older than age 50 are most commonly affected. The calcifications do not encroach on the vessel lumen and are usually not clinically significant Reference : Robbins 10th/pg 493

159.q: Syphilitic aneurysm is seen most commonly in:
159.e: Syphilis usually affects proximal ascending aorta (esp aortic ring) > aortic arch. Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 503

159.q: Visceral aneurysm is most commonly seen in:
159.e: Visceral artery aneurysms (VAAs) and visceral artery pseudoaneurysms (VAPAs) frequently present as lifethreatening emergencies Splenic artery aneurysms- most common VAA Hepatic artery aneurysms (HAAs)- second most common VAA Clinically, the patients with VAPAs, typically present with an antecedent history of arterial trauma or surgical manipulation Reference: Semin Intervent Radiol. 2009 Sep; 26(3): 196 - 206

159.q: Most common cause of dissecting hematoma is because of:
159.e: MC cause of dissection is hypertension, seen in men between 40 and 60 years of age. 2nd MC cause of dissection is cystic medial necrosis. (option b) Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 504; 8th/pg 509

160.q: Kaposi sarcoma true is: a. Causative agent HHV 8 b. Can be Seen in depressed cell mediated immunity c. Treatment is chemotherapy and surgery d. Vascular tumor
160.e: KAPOSI SARCOMA It is caused by KS Herpes virus or Human herpes virus 8 (HHV8)-option a is true Characterized by proliferation of spindle cellsQ which are of vascular originQ (Option d is correct) Transplant and HIV associated Kaposi usually occur in immunosupressed individuals. (Option b is correct) Treatment - (Option c is correct) HAART is the best way to treat HIV associated Kaposi’s sarcoma Topical retinoid treatment Cryosurgery (cryotherapy) Surgery; Radiation therapy Intralesional chemotherapy Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 518.; 8th/pg 523

160.q: Fish hook pattern of capillaries is seen in:
160.e: Hemangiopericytoma Tumor derived from pericytes- perivascular cells that wrap around blood capillaries These tumors most commonly arise from pelvic retroperitoneum or the limbs (particularly thighs). Capillaries are arranged in 'fish-hook pattern;' seen best with silver stains Reference : Sternberg's Diagnostic Surgical Pathology, 5th Edition, table 5 11

160.q: HHV-8 is related to all; except:
160.e: HHV 8 is associated with Castleman disease Primary effusion lymphoma Kaposi sarcoma Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 10 th Edition Chapter 13, page No.603-605

160.q: Most common benign tumours during infancy is-
160.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Hemangioma o Hemangiomas, the most common benign tumors of infancy, occur in 10% of term infants.

160.q: Antidote for overdose of fibrinolytic drugs is?
160.e: Fibrinolytics are drugs used to lyse a fibrin clot. Examples are Streptokinase, Urokinase, Alteplase, Tenecteplase etc. So the drugs that are used for treating fibrinolytic overdose should be antifibrinolytics. Both tranexamic acid and EACA are anti fibrinolytics. The antidote for fibrinolytic over dose is EACA. EACA should not be given unless the bleeding is life threatening, as EACA can cause widespread thrombosis and ischemia and can worsen DIC or HIT.

160.q: Which of the following is true regarding the action of clopidogrel?
o: It is a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor
It is a hydroxymethyl coenzyme A inhibitor
It is an ADP receptor antagonist
160.e: Clopidogrel prevents platelet aggregation through antagonism of the adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor. It has been shown to reduce mortality from stroke and ischaemic heart disease (IHD) in primary prevention studies. Vorapaxar is an anti-platelet agent that reduces platelet aggregation through reversible antagonism of Protease Activated Receptor-1 (PAR 1), also known as thrombin receptor. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2060

161.q: A 65-year-old man dies due to a myocardial infarction. Which stains can be used to see the infarct in the heart while conducting an autopsy?
161.e: Explanation: Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) is a histochemical stain frequently used in autopsies to detect myocardial infarction (MI) . Within the first 4 hours of MI, gross examination may not reveal any visible infarct. However, when tissue slices are immersed in TTC solution, the stain differentiates viable from necrotic myocardium: viable myocardial tissue with intact lactate dehydrogenase activity stains brick-red , while infarcted areas remain pale due to leakage of dehydrogenases from damaged cell membranes.

161.q: A patient is suspected of having a myocardial infarction. A triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) stain is used to identify myocardial ischemic damage. When is the best time to use TTC staining for optimal visualisation of myocardial necrosis?
161.e: Explanation: Myocardial infarcts that are less than 12 hours old are typically not grossly visible. However, those older than 3 hours (Option A ruled out) can be identified using vital stains like triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC), which is a substrate for lactate dehydrogenase. Infarcts can be grossly visualised as red-blue areas due to trapped blood by 12 to 24 hours (Option C and D ruled out) .

161.q: A 46-year-old male presented in the emergency room with sudden onset of chest pain. The ECG done shows normal wave pattern. Analysis of which pair of serum markers given below would be most helpful in excluding a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction in this patient?
161.e: The laboratory evaluation of MI is based on measuring the blood levels of proteins that leak out of irreversibly damaged myocytes; previously, this involved measurement of the MB fraction of creatine kinase (CK- MB). Currently, the most clinically useful biomarkers of myocardial damage are cardiac-specific troponins T and I (cTnT and cTnI), proteins that normally regulate calcium- mediated contraction of cardiac muscle. Reference : Robbins 10th Ed pg 550

161.q: All the following are microscopic features of acute pulmonary congestion EXCEPT:
161.e: Cut surfaces of hyperemic or congested tissues feel wet and typically ooze blood. On microscopic examination, acute pulmonary congestion is marked by blood-engorged alveolar capillaries and variable degrees of alveolar septal edema and intraalveolar hemorrhage. In chronic pulmonary congestion, the septa become thickened and fibrotic, and the alveolar spaces contain numerous macrophages laden with hemosiderin (“heart failure cells”) derived from phagocytosed red cells. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:97

161.q: Heart failure cells are seen in which of the following condition?
161.e: In chronic pulmonary congestion, the septa become thickened and fibrotic, and the alveolar spaces contain numerous macrophages laden with hemosiderin (“heart failure cells”) derived from phagocytosed red cells. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:97

161.q: Which of the following is not true regarding Ranolazine?
o: Useful in patients with refractory chronic angina
Inhibitor of If current in the SA node cells
Administered at a dose of 500-1000 mg/day
Contraindicated in patients with QTc prolongation
161.e: Ranolazine inhibits the late sodium current in myocardial cells. It is contraindicated in patients with liver dysfunction and QTc prolongation. Ivabradine helps control the heart rate by inhibiting the funny current (If) in the SA node cells. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition

161.q: A man who is on antihypertensives has several symptoms and his medications require reviewing. Which one of the following is a complication of thiazide diuretic therapy?
161.e: Side effects of thiazide diuretics: Hypokalaemia(Blocking NaCl channels) Hyponatremia Hypercalcaemia Hyperglycemia hyperuricemia Hyperkalemia is caused by ACE inhibitors and potassium sparing diuretics Loop diuretics can also cause hyperuricemia and gout. Gynaecomastia is caused by spironolactone. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 277, Pg:20.

162.q: A patient had a quarrel with his brother with heightened emotion and falls suddenly and died. Most likely cause of death in this case is:
162.e: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is an entity characterized by left ventricular contractile dysfunction after extreme psychological stress (thus also called broken heart syndrome); affected myocardium may be stunned or show contraction band necrosis. For unclear reasons, the left ventricular apex is most often affected, leading to "apical ballooning" that resembles a takotsubo, Japanese for "fishing pot for trapping octopus" (hence, the name). The mechanism of catecholamine cardiotoxicity is uncertain but likely relates either to direct myocyte toxicity due to calcium overload or to focal vasoconstriction in the coronary arterial macro- or microcirculation in the face of an increased heart rate. Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10 th edition, 570

162.q: 55 year old male died on autopsy. He was found to have mass in atria. Most common primary tumor of heart is:
162.e: Myxomas are the most common primary tumor of the adult heart These are benign neoplasms arising from primitive multipotent mesenchymal cells. Although sporadic myxomas do not show consistent genetic alterations, familial syndromes associated with myxomas have activating mutations in the GNAS1 gene, (in association with McCune-Albright syndrome) or null mutations in PRKAR1A, encoding a regulatory subunit of a cyclic-AMP-dependent protein kinase (Carney complex). About 90% of myxomas arise in the atria, with a left-to-right ratio of approximately 4:1. Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10 th edition, 579

163.q: A 68-year-old female patient having long standing cardiac valvular disease of mitral stenosis. She is getting respiratory distress which is slowly increasing day by day. Mainly reason is due to engorgement of pulmonary capillaries leading to pulmonary edema. Which of the following statements are true regarding pulmonary edema?
o: It initiates from the basal region of the lower lobes
Fibrosis and thickening of the wall can cause brown induration
163.e: (a) Edema accumulates initially in the basal regions of the lower lobes because hydrostatic pressure is greatest in these sites (dependent edema). Histologically, the alveolar capillaries are engorged, and there is an intraalveolar transudates. (b) Alveolar microhemorrhages and hemosiderin-laden macrophages (HLMs) ("heart failure" cells) may be present. (c) In long-standing pulmonary congestion (e.g., as seen in mitral stenosis), hemosiderin-laden macrophages are abundant, and fibrosis and thickening of the alveolar walls cause the soggy lungs to become firm and brown (brown induration). Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 675

164.q: A 45-year-old male patient who had long duration smoking history and diagnosed as a case of small cell carcinoma of lung and on chemotherapy regimen develops a recently developed heart murmur. Undergoes some laboratory tests which revealed normal TLC and negative blood culture. No growth seen on urine culture examination. Possibly noninfective endocarditis was the reason for the heart murmur. All of the following statements are true regarding nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis; except:
o: Characteristic deposition of sterile Thrombi on the leaflet of cardiac valves
Histologically these are bland thrombi, loosely attached to the underlying valve
Vegetation are destructive and shows marked inflammatory response
These vegetation have trivial effect but can be a source of emboli
164.e: (a) NBTE is characterized by the deposition of small (1 - 5 mm) sterile thrombi on the leaflets of the cardiac valves (b) Histologically, these are bland thrombi, loosely attached to the underlying valve (c) The vegetations are nondestructive and do not elicit any inflammatory reaction. (d) The local effect of the vegetations is usually trivial, they can be the source of systemic emboli that produce significant infarcts in the brain, heart, or elsewhere. Reference : Robbins 10th Ed pg 564

164.q: A 9-year-old girl presented with subcutaneous nodules over the skin of her arms and torso 3 weeks after a bout of acute pharyngitis. She manifests some abnormal movements and begins to complain of pain in her knees and hips, particularly with movement. A friction rub is heard on auscultation of her chest. An abnormality detected by which of the following serum laboratory findings is most characteristic of the disease affecting this girl?
164.e: (a) Acute rheumatic fever can involve any or all layers of the heart. Because rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal infections, the antihyaluronidase, anti- DNase, and antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers are often elevated. (b) The ANA level could be elevated in systemic lupus erythematosus, which is most likely to produce a serous pericarditis. (c) The strains of group A streptococci that lead to acute rheumatic fever are less likely to cause glomerulonephritis, so an elevated creatinine level is unlikely. (d) Cardiac troponins are markers for ischemic myocardial injury. Although their levels may be elevated because of the acute myocarditis that occurs in rheumatic fever,this change is not a characteristic of rheumatic heart disease. Reference : Robbins 10th Ed pg 563

164.q: Vegetations of the following endocarditis has the maximum chances of embolization:
164.e: Vegetations on heart valves are the classic hallmark of IE; these are friable, bulky, potentially destructive lesions containing fibrin, inflammatory cells, and bacteria or other organisms. Vegetations are prone to embolization; because the embolic fragments often contain virulent organisms, abscesses frequently develop where they lodge, leading to sequelae such as septic infarcts or mycotic aneurysms. Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10 th edition, pg 564

165.q: A 35-year-old man complains of recurrent hematuria since his youth. The hematuria typically occurs following upper respiratory tract infections. Vital signs are normal. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, hematuria, and a few red blood cell casts. Laboratory studies disclose normal levels of BUN and creatinine. The ANA and ANCA tests are negative. Which of the characteristic findings that leads to diagnosis of disease is:
o: Predominantly deposition on IgG in mesangium
Predominantly deposition on IgG in Subendothelial
Predominantly deposition on IgA in Subendothelium
Predominantly deposition on IgA in mesangium
165.e: IgA nephropathy (Berger Disease)- IgA nephropathy, characterized by the presence of prominent IgA deposits in the mesangial regions and recurrent hematuria, is the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide. Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg 922

165.q: Which is the most common mechanism leads to edema in nephrotic syndrome?
165.e: Nephrotic syndrome is the most important cause of albumin loss from the blood. In diseases that are characterized by nephrotic syndrome, the glomerular capillaries become leaky, leading to the loss of albumin (and other plasma proteins) in the urine and the development of generalized edema. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:99

165.q: A 17-year-old female patient presented with facial puffiness. Physical examination revealed edema. Laboratory findings revealed creatinine of 3.8 mg/dL along with proteinuria. A differential diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome was made. All of these metabolic findings will be seen in this patient; except:
165.e: Nephrotic syndrome is caused by a derangement in glomerular capillary walls resulting in increased permeability to plasma proteins. The manifestations of the syndrome include, Massive proteinuria, Hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, lipiduria along with loss of anticoagulants. Due to low albumin levels, fibrinogen and vWD levels are raised. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 20, pg 909

165.q: Which of the following would immunofluorescence staining of the kidney with Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis most likely reveal?
o: IgG positivity with a granular pattern
IgG and IgM positivity with a granular pattern
IgG positivity with a linear pattern
165.e: FSGS has entrapped IgM and C3 noted by immunofluorescence staining. IgG positivity with a granular pattern is seen in membranous glomerulonephropathy, IgG and IgM positivity in postinfectious glomerulonephritis, and IgG positivity with a linear pattern in type I rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. IgM positivity with a linear pattern is not normally described in diseases of the kidney. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Page- 556

165.q: A patient presenting with haemoptysis and renal failure with anti-basement membrane antibodies positives on renal biopsy. What is your diagnosis?
165.e: Anti-GBM antibody-mediated crescentic GN (Goodpasture disease) is characterized by linear deposits of IgG and, in many cases, C3 in the GBM. In some patients, the anti-GBM antibodies also bind to pulmonary alveolar capillary basement membranes to produce the clinical picture of pulmonary hemorrhages associated with renal failure. These patients are said to have Goodpasture syndrome. Anti-GBM antibodies are present in the serum and are helpful in diagnosis. It is important to recognize anti-GBM antibody-mediated crescentic GN, because affected individuals benefit from plasmapheresis, which removes pathogenic antibodies from the circulation. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page- 562-563

165.q: 56 year old female presents with breast carcinoma, She started presenting with froathy urine. What is most common nephropathy in these cases
165.e: The most common nephropathy in malignancy is membranous nephropathy . Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Page- 558

166.q: Not true about chronic pyelonephritis in children -
o: Males are more affected than female
166.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Males are more affected than female o 3 basic forms of UTI - (1) Pyelonephritis (2) Cystitis (3) Asymptomatic bacteremia Chronic Pyelonephritis :- Characterised by renal inflammation & fibrosts induced by recurrent or persistent renal infection, vesicoureteric reflux or other causes of UTI. Progressive renal scarring which leads to end stage renal diseaes. In reflex nephropathy, Intrarenal reflex of infected urine induces renal injury which heals by renal scarring. Being - straight, short & wide urethra, recurrent UTI is more common in female, so CPN is also twice as common is female than male.

166.q: Which of the following area in a kidney is usually spared in early pyelonephritis?
166.e: The characteristic histologic feature of acute pyelonephritis is liquefactive necrosis and abscess formation within the renal parenchyma. In the early stages, pus formation (suppuration) is limited to the tubular lumina, but later abscesses rupture into the interstitial tissue. Large masses of intratubular neutrophils frequently extend within involved nephrons into the collecting ducts, giving rise to characteristic white blood cell casts in the urine.Typically, the glomeruli are not affected. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Page- 565

166.q: Tamm-Horsfall protein is a major component of which of the following?
166.e: Explanation: Tamm-Horsfall protein is synthesized in the ascending loop of Henle and is the most abundant protein in normal urine. It plays a role in tubular function and helps prevent urinary tract infections . It is the main constituent of hyaline casts , which are the most common type of urinary casts. Explanation of other options: Mural thrombi (Option A): Blood clots adhering to the vessel or heart walls; unrelated to Tamm-Horsfall protein. Curschmann spirals (Option B): Mucus plugs seen in sputum from asthma or other obstructive pulmonary diseases. Bence-Jones proteins (Option D): Free immunoglobulin light chains in urine, associated with multiple myeloma , not a normal renal protein.

167.q: Most important prognostic factor of wilms tumour -
167.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Histopathology Anaplastic nuclear change is the only criterion of "unfavourable" histology in Wilm's tumor and all Wilm's tumor lacking this feature are designated as having "favourable histology". Anaplastic nuclear change reflects extreme polypoidy & is usually apparent under low magnification. "Anaplastic histology remains a critical determinant of adverse prognosis. Even anaplasia restricted to kidney confers an increased risk of recurrence & death, underscoring the need for correctly identifying this histologic features."

167.q: Renal cell Carcinoma is associated with following genetic defects EXCEPT:
167.e: The familial variants of renal cell carcinomas are: Von Hipple landau (VHL) syndrome Hereditory leiomyomatosis Hereditary papillary carcinomas Birt hogg dube syndrome Hemihypertrophy, also referred to as hemihyperplasia, is a condition in which one side of the body or a part of one side of the body is larger than the other. hemihypertrophy is related to several congenital syndromes including beckwith-wiedemann syndrome and russell-silver syndrome. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 9 th edition, Page- 953

167.q: Which ONE of the following is a commonest childhood Renal tumour?
167.e: Wilms tumour, or nephroblastoma, is the most common primary tumour of the kidney in children, with most cases occurring in children between 2 and 5 years of age. Three groups of congenital malformations are associated with an increased risk for Wilms tumour. These are WAGR syndrome (i.e., Wilms tumour, aniridia, genital abnormalities, and mental retardation); Denys-Drash syndrome (DDS), and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS). On microscopic examination, Wilms tumours are characterized by recognizable attempts to recapitulate different stages of nephrogenesis.The classic triphasic combination of blastemal, stromal, and epithelial cell types is observed in most lesions, although the percentage of each component is variable. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page- 289-90

168.q: Transitional cell carcinomas can be caused by which of the following etiological factor(s)? i Naphthylamine ii Smoking iii Bilharziasis iv Betel nut
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
168.e: Environmental factors are important in the pathogenesis of urothelial carcinoma and include cigarette smoking, various occupational carcinogens, and prior cyclophosphamide or radiation therapy. A family history of bladder cancer is a known risk factor. Squamous cell carcinoma is related to Schistosoma haematobium infections in areas where it is endemic. Cancers occurring in the setting of schistosoma infections arise in a background of chronic inflammation, which you will recall provides the 'soil' for the development of a number of different cancers. Other risk factors are aromatic amines, chlorinated hydrocarbons and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons including benzidine. Some genetic predispositions are also included. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg- 702

168.q: A 37-year-old male presents to his family physician with complaints of blood in his urine. A urine analysis reveals 4+ blood, with microscopic clots identified. The patient returned home 4 months ago after a missionary trip to Africa. He does not smoke nor drink alcohol. He has no family history of hereditary disorders. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
Schistosoma haematobium infection of the bladder
168.e: Given the recent travel history to Africa and work as a missionary, followed by hematuria, a Schistosoma infection is the most likely of the choices, as this parasite is found in Africa, it infects the bladder, and can present with hematuria. Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder and renal cell carcinoma can cause hematuria with blood clots; however, he has no risk factors for either, and given his young age, they are unlikely. Membranous glomerulonephropathy does not cause hematuria, and postinfectious glomerulonephritis does cause hematuria, but the characteristic feature is red blood cell casts, and microscopic clots would not be formed. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Page- 702

168.q: Which of the following carcinogenic agent is associated with cancer of the urinary bladder?
168.e: The aromatic amines and azo dyes constitute another class of indirect-acting carcinogens. Before its carcinogenicity was recognized, β-naphthylamine and benzidine was responsible for a 50-fold increased incidence of bladder cancers in heavily exposed workers in the aniline dye and rubber industries. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 230.

168.q: Which ONE of the following is the commonest type of bladder tumour?
168.e: Two distinct precursor lesions of invasive urothelial carcinoma are recognized. The most common is a non invasive papillary tumour. The other precursor is carcinoma in situ (CIS), which is discussed later. In about one-half of patients with invasive bladder cancer, no precursor lesion is found; in such cases, it is presumed that the precursor lesion was overgrown by the high-grade invasive component. Adenocarcinomas of the bladder are rare. Carcinoma of the bladder is more common in men than in women, in industrialized than in developing nations, in urban than in rural dwellers. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Page- 702-703

169.q: Pap smear with hyperchromatic nuclei pleomorphism with low maturation index involving almost all thickness. What is this called?
169.e: Dysplasia is a term that literally means "disordered growth." It is encountered principally in epithelial cells and is recognized on the basis of several morphologic changes. Dysplastic cells may exhibit considerable pleomorphism and often contain large hyperchromatic nuclei with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Dysplastic epithelial surfaces also typically show architectural disarray and a loss of orderly differentiation Metaplasia is defined as the replacement of one type of cell with another type Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10 th edition, 272

169.q: Chromosome number of partial hydatidiform mole is:
169.e: A partial hydatidiform mole (PHM) arises due to the fertilization of an ovum by two sperm (dispermy), leading to a triploid karyotype (69 chromosomes) . The common chromosomal compositions observed in PHM are: 69,XXX (most common) 69,XXY 69,XYY (rare) Incorrect Choices Explanation Choice A: 46 XX A 46,XX karyotype is seen in complete hydatidiform moles , which occur due to fertilization of an empty ovum by a single sperm that duplicates its DNA. Choice B: 46 XY Similar to 46,XX, a 46,XY karyotype is also found in complete moles , not partial moles. Choice D: Any of the Above Only triploid (69) karyotypes are found in PHM , making this choice incorrect. Key takeaway: Partial Hydatidiform Mole: Triploidy (69 chromosomes) Fetal parts may be present Less trophoblastic proliferation than complete mole

169.q: Arrange the steps of PAP smear in correct sequence? A. Retract vagina B. Take smear C. Make smear on the slide D. Fixation
169.e: STEPS FOR PAP SMEAR ARE TO RETRACT WITH HELP OF LUBRICATED SPECULUM TAKE SAMPLE MAKE A SLIDE FIXATION WITH 95% ETHANOL Reference: Cytojournal. 2022; 19: 24.

170.q: Which is not a germ cell tumor derived from germ cell neoplasia in situ
170.e: Germ cell neoplasia in situ is a precursor lesion found in association with 90% of germ cell neoplasms and with every type of GCT except spermatocytic tumor and unusual types that arise in infancy. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 969

170.q: On IHC seminoma cell is positive for
170.e: Seminoma cells are negative for cytokeratin. Placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP) is also positive in seminoma Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 969

170.q: Teratoma with somatic type malignant transformation can lead to
170.e: Rarely malignant non-germ cell tumors arise in post-pubertal teratomas, a phenomenon referred to as teratoma with somatic type malignant transformation. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 969

170.q: Most common genetic alteration in prostate cancer
o: Chromosomal rearrangement that juxtaposes ETS next to TMPRSS2
170.e: All these alterations are seen in prostate cancer, but chromosomal rearrangement that juxtaposes coding sequence of ETS family transcriptor gene next to androgen-regulated TMPRSS2 promoter is the most common of these, such that ETS oncogene is overexpressed in an androgenic fashion. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 977

o: Pleomorphism is seen within tumor cells
Tumor cells are negative for OCT3/4
170.e: Tumor cells are positive for OCT3/4 and cytokeratin, and negative for KIT and podoplanin. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 969

170.q: Reduplication of which chromosome is found invariably in invasive GCTs regardless of histologic subtype
170.e: Isochromosome 12p, a cytogenetic alteration that is invariably in invasive GCTs regardless of histologic subtype. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 969

170.q: Gleason grade group 1 has a score of less than or equal to
170.e: Gleason system stratifies prostate cancer into 5 grades on basis of glandular patterns of growth. Grade 1 corresponds to well-differentiated tumors and grade 5 to poorly differentiated tumors. Most tumors contain more than one pattern, in these cases a primary grade is assigned to the dominant pattern, and a secondary grade is assigned to the second most frequent pattern. Gleason grade groups Group 1: score less than equal to 6 Group 2: 3 + 4 Group 3: 4 + 3 Group 4: 4 + 4/3 + 5/5 + 3 Group 5: 4 + 5/5 + 4/5 + 5 Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 977

170.q: Components of testicular dysgenesis syndrome are all except
170.e: Hypospadias is a component, not epispadias. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 969

171.q: A patient presented with cirrhosis. On liver biopsy showed eosinophilic material cytokeratin positive. This is most likely composed of:
171.e: Mallory hyaline are tangled skeins of intermediate filaments such as keratin 8 and keratin 18 that are partially degraded and ubiquitinated Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10 th edition, 842

171.q: Phenomenon of Quasi-species is seen in which viral hepatitis?
171.e: Because of the low fidelity of the HCV RNA polymerase, the viral genome is inherently unstable, giving rise to new genetic variants at a high pace. This has led to the appearance of six major HCV genotypes worldwide, each with one or more "subspecies." Infections in most individuals are due to a virus of a single genotype, but new genetic variants are generated in the host as long as viral replication persists. As a result, each patient usually comes to be infected with a population of divergent but closely related HCV variants known as quasi species. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-646

171.q: A 37-year-old male presents to an acute care clinic with complaints of abdominal pain, which began a few days ago. His vital signs are a temperature of 98.7°F, pulse of 101 bpm, respiratory rate of 19 breaths per minute, and blood pressure of 129/82 mm Hg. A physical examination reveals an enlarged and tender liver. Laboratory testing reveals an AST of 271 U/L, ALT of 46 U/L, GGT of 190 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase of 210 U/L. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?
171.e: The individual has laboratory evidence of liver damage, with elevated AST, ALT, GGT, and alkaline phosphatase. The AST: ALT ratio is around 6:1, which is most characteristic of an alcoholic hepatitis. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-652

171.q: A 42-year-old male labourer consulted a doctor because he noticed yellow discoloration of sclera and also gives history of passing yellow urine since few days. He was advised complete blood counts, liver function test and a liver biopsy was undertaken. The liver biopsy shows yellowish brown pigment on H & E stain. Which of the following is the most likely pigment?
171.e: The condition reflects Jaundice with Hyperbilirubinemia. Bilirubin is the normal non-iron containing pigment present in the bile. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 52-53

171.q: A healthcare worker is seropositive for HBsAg, HBeAg, and anti-HBc IgM, indicating acute HBV infection with high infectivity. Which liver biopsy feature is least likely to be seen?
171.e: Explanation: In acute hepatitis B, biopsy findings typically include ballooning degeneration, focal necrosis, and confluent necrosis in severe cases. Ground-glass hepatocytes, however, are absent in acute infection and instead signify chronic HBV infection. Explanation of other options: Ballooning change (Option A): Seen in acute hepatitis as hepatocyte swelling and degeneration. Focal or spotty necrosis (Option C): Common in acute HBV, involving scattered apoptotic hepatocytes. Confluent necrosis (Option D): Seen in severe acute hepatitis with widespread cell death. Key Takeaways: Acute HBV is marked by hepatocyte ballooning and necrosis, without ground-glass cells. Ground-glass hepatocytes are pathognomonic for chronic HBV infection. Serology differentiates acute from chronic HBV.

171.q: A 23-year-old pregnant female presents to the emergency room complaining of pain in the upper portion of the right side of her abdomen. Physical examination reveals a fluid wave and hepatomegaly, with her liver palpable 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory testing reveals an AST of 213 U/L, ALT of 178 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase of 52 mg/dL. A complete blood count reveals a hemoglobin of 13.4 mg/dL and a platelet count of 224 * 103 cells/μL. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?
171.e: Budd-Chiari syndrome is due to thrombosis of the hepatic veins or inferior vena cava. Risk factors include pregnancy, use of oral contraceptives, Factor V Leiden, and other coagulation disorders. Patients can develop ascites due to the acute increased pressure in the portal system. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-667

171.q: A 44-year-old female patient presented to the emergency department with history of abdominal pain which is associated frequently on and off vomiting. Ultrasound performed shows presence of gallstones and patient was planned for cholecystectomy. PAC examination shows HBsAg positivity with value of 4.42 IU by ELISA method. Further investigations revealed presence of HBeAg. If Liver biopsy performed at this time, it will show all the following features; except:
171.e: HBeAg, HBV DNA, and HBV DNA polymerase are detectable in the serum soon after HBsAg and signify active viral replication. (a & b) Microscopically, there is a portal and lobular inflammatory infiltrate comprised predominantly of lymphocytes and variably admixed with plasma cells and eosinophils. (c) In chronic hepatitis B, the swollen endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes are swollen and filled with HBsAg, leading to a "ground-glass" appearance. (d) The hepatocyte injury may result in necrosis or apoptosis. Necrosis of groups of hepatocytes (i.e., confluent necrosis) may be seen in severe cases and can progress to necrosis of the entire lobule (i.e., panlobular or panacinar necrosis) or connect vascular structures (i.e., bridging necrosis). Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 837

171.q: A 42-year-old male patient presented with complaints of nausea fatigability and yellowish discoloration sclera. He gave history that he is taking alcohol in large quantities since long time. On proper clinical evaluation, serum bilirubin level is raised. Liver biopsy was performed and diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis was made. Which of the following histological features can be seen in this diagnosis?
171.e: The morphologic findings in alcoholic hepatitis include the following: (a) Ballooned hepatocytes. These are injured, swollen hepatocytes with cleared-out cytoplasm and cytoskeletal damage, which when extensive, results in formation of Mallory hyaline. (b) Lobular lymphocytic infiltrates are common, and portal lymphocytic infiltrates also may occur. (c) Perivenular/pericellular fibrosis. Steatohepatitis is often accompanied by fibrosis. Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 844

172.q: All of the following autoantibodies are present in type 1 autoimmune hepatitis EXCEPT
o: Anti soluble liver antigen/liver pancreases antigen antibodies (anti- SLA/LP)
172.e: Type 1, more common in middle-age and older individuals, is characterized by the presence of antinuclear (ANA), anti-smooth muscle actin (SMA), anti-mitochondrial (AMA), and anti-soluble liver antigen/ liver-pancreas antigen (anti-SLA/LP) antibodies. Type 2 auto immune hepatitis, is more common in children and is characterized by anti- liver kidney microsome-1 (lkm-1)antibodies, which are directed against cyp2d6, and anti-liver cytosol-1 (acl-1) anti bodies. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-651

172.q: A 53-year-old male presents to his family physician with complaints of fever, chills, and abdominal pain. He reports that he has had past episodes of a similar nature, but has not chosen to seek treatment. He has a past medical history of ulcerative colitis and had a colectomy 5 years ago for Stage I colonic adenocarcinoma, which has been in remission. An ERCP reveals strictures in the extrahepatic bile ducts. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?
172.e: The signs, symptoms, and history, combined with the results of the ERCP, are most consistent with primary sclerosing cholangitis. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (psc) is a chronic liver disease in which the bile ducts inside and outside the liver become inflamed and scarred, and eventually narrowed or blocked. When this happens, bile builds up in the liver and causes further liver damage. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-664

172.q: A 41-year-old female has been followed by a physician for several years. Originally, she presented to her primary care physician with episodes of itching. Today she is being seen for fatigue. On physical examination, her physician notes that her conjunctivae are yellow. Other than mild hypothyroidism requiring hormone replacement, she has no other significant past medical history. She has no family history of liver disease. Of the following, what is her most likely diagnosis?
172.e: Primary biliary cirrhosis is most common in middle aged females, and patients will often present with pruritus due to cholestasis, which can evolve to cirrhosis of the liver (D). Jaundice is a sign of liver failure, and thus, among the choices, α-1-antitrypsin and Galactosemia could cause fatigue, but they are not commonly associated with pruritus; also, Galactosemia would affect younger ages (A, B). Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with ulcerative colitis (C). Primary biliary cholangitis, previously called primary biliary cirrhosis, is a chronic disease in which the bile ducts in your liver are slowly destroyed. Bile is a fluid made in your liver. It aids with digestion and helps you absorb certain vitamins. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-664

173.q: Central stellate scar is seen in
173.e: Answer- A. Focal nodular hyperplasia Focal nodular hyperplasia is a rare tumor-like condition predominantly found in women during to third to the fifth decade of life. Most commonly it is incidentally discovered as asymptomatic mass. The pathognomonic microscopic feature. A central stellate scar seen in liver imaging studies is a highly characteristic feature of focal nodular hyperplasia. It is also seen in Renal cell carcinoma(RCC).

173.q: A 52-year-old male presents to his family physician with complaints of vague abdominal pain and a sensation of fullness. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a mass in the right upper quadrant. The patient is scheduled for resection, and a pathologist examining the tumor identifies it as being derived from bile ducts. Of the following, which is a characteristic of this tumor?
o: It rarely occurs in association with cirrhosis.
It frequently produces an elevation of α-fetoprotein
One complication of ulcerative colitis is a significant risk factor for the tumor
173.e: The tumor derived from bile ducts is a cholangiocarcinoma, which commonly occurs in cirrhotic livers, often in combination with hepatocellular carcinoma (A). The tumor has a poor prognosis (B). Hepatocellular carcinomas are most frequently associated with an elevation of α-fetoproteins; in fact, patients with cirrhosis of the liver, a risk factor for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma, can be followed with serial α-fetoproteins to monitor for the possible development of the tumor (although ultrasound imaging is preferred) (C). Primary sclerosis cholangitis, which occurs in a large proportion of patients with ulcerative colitis, is a significant risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma, along with Opisthorchis sinensis infection (D). Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-669

174.q: A 45-year-old male patient who is chronic alcoholic drinker and also having uncontrolled diabetes since 5 years presented with sudden onset on pain abdomen and vomiting. Pain is intense and referred to back. Patient was sent for ultrasound, which revealed diagnosis of acute pancreatitis and conservative management was done. If biopsy was taken at this stage, what will be the histopathological findings you observe?
174.e: (a, b, c) Chronic pancreatitis is characterized by parenchymal fibrosis, acinar atrophy and dropout, and variable ductal dilation. (d) In acute necrotizing pancreatitis, acini, ducts, and even islets undergo necrosis. In the most severe form, hemorrhagic pancreatitis, extensive parenchymal necrosis is accompanied by intraparenchymal hemorrhage due to vascular injury. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 18, pg 882

174.q: A 40-year-old female have gall stones since 5 years. Now since 2 weeks she had intermittent pain abdomen. Now she presented in emergency with acute severe pain in the right upper quadrant associated with mild fever, nausea, vomiting and tachycardia. He underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and specimen sent for histopathological examination. What are the histological findings to be seen in chronic cholecystitis?
174.e: All of these are features of chronic cholecystitis.

174.q: Empyema of the gallbladder and Gangrenous cholecystitis are seen in-
174.e: In acute cholecystitis, the gallbladder usually is enlarged and tense, and has a bright red or blotchy, violaceous colour, the latter imparted by subserosal hemorrhages. The serosa frequently is covered by a fibrinous or, in severe cases, a fibrinopurulent exudate. In 90% of cases, stones are present, often obstructing the neck of the gallbladder or the cystic duct. The gallbladder lumen is filled with cloudy or turbid bile that may contain fibrin, blood, and pus. When the contained exudate is mostly pus, the condition is referred to as empyema of the gallbladder. In mild cases, the gallbladder wall is thickened, edematous, and hyperemic. In more severe cases, the gallbladder wall is green-black and necrotic-a condition termed gangrenous cholecystitis. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-674

174.q: Which of the following is/are true for the pancreatic pseudocyst? i. Lack of epithelial lining ii. Contains necrotic and haemorrhagic material iii. Requires surgical removal if more than 6.0 cm iv. It arises following a bout of acute pancreatitis
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
174.e: Pancreatic pseudocyst is a poorly defined cyst with a necrotic brownish wall. Histologically, the cyst lacks an epithelial lining and instead is lined by fibrin and granulation tissue, with typical changes of chronic inflammation. Signs and symptoms of pancreatic pseudocyst include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and bloating. Diagnosis of pancreatic pseudocyst can be based on cystic fluid analysis. Complications of pancreatic pseudocyst include infection, hemorrhage, obstruction and rupture. Pseudo cysts typically arise following a bout of acute pancreatitis, particularly one superimposed on chronic alcholic pancreatitis. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-684

174.q: Persons with pancreatic divisum and other genetic abnormalities are prone to develop chronic pancreatitis. BECAUSE In pancreatic divisum the bulk of pancreas drains into duodenum through minor papillae.
o: If both statements are true and causally related
If both statements are true but not causally related
If the first statement is true and second is false
If the first statement is false and second is true
174.e: Pancreas divisum is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas. More than 95% of individuals are asymptomatic. The remaining 5% develop acute or chronic pancreatitis, possibly related to inadequate drainage of pancreatic secretions through the minor papilla. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-680

174.q: Which of the following is/are TRUE for pancreatic carcinoma? i. 60-80 years of age ii. Associated with cigarette smoking iii. It is the infiltrating ductal carcinoma of pancreas iv. There is an activating mutation of CDKN2A
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
