174.e: The recent sequencing of the pancreatic cancer genome has confirmed that four genes are most commonly affected by somatic mutations in this neoplasm: KRAS, CDKN2A/ p16, SMAD4, and TP53: KRAS is the most frequently altered oncogene in pancreatic cancer; it is activated by a point mutation in greater than 90% of cases. Cdkn2a (chromosome 9p ) is inactivated in 30% of pancreatic cancers through point mutations or homozygous deletions Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-687

174.q: Which of the following is/are the characteristic(s) of pancreatic carcinoma? i. High invasiveness ii. Trousseau sign iii. Desmoplastic response iv. Murphy's sign
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
174.e: Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) occurs in about 10% of patients and is attributable to the elaboration of platelet-aggregating factors and pro-coagulants from the tumour or its necrotic products. Murphy's sign is elicited in patient with acute cholecystitis. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-686-689

174.q: Patient presented with pain in abdomen. His symptoms are relieved by steroids and diagnosis is autoimmune pancreatitis. Which of the following finding(s) is/are TRUE for the autoimmune pancreatitis? i. Ductocentric mixed inflammatory infiltrate ii. Increased IgG 4 related plasma cells iii. Presence of venulitis iv. Clinical presentation can mimic pancreatic carcinoma.
o: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
174.e: Autoimmune pancreatitis is a pathogenically distinct form of chronic pancreatitis that is associated with the presence of IgG4-secreting plasma cells in the pancreas. Autoimmune pancreatitis is one manifestation of IgG related disease, which may involve multiple tissues. It is important to recognize because it responds to steroid therapy. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-683-84

175.q: Which of the following change is seen in barrets esophagus?
o: Metaplasia from squamous to columnar epithelium
Metaplasia from columnar to squamous epithelium type
Metaplasia from columnar to transitional epithelium type
Metaplasia from transitional to columnar epithelium type
175.e: It is a reversible change in which one differentiated cell type(epithelial or mesenchymal) is replaced by another cell type. Metaplasia from squamous to columnar type occur in Barrett's oesophagus, in which the oesophageal squamous epithelium is replaced by intestinal-like columnar cells under the influence of refluxed gastric acid. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 9th ed Pg:38

o: Intestinal type is the most common type
175.e: Answer- B. Predisposes to SCC Barrett's esophagus is premalignant condition for adenocarcinma esophagus and not SCC.

175.q: Oxidised LDL is more athreogenic because ?
175.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Accumulates in macrophages [Ref Robbin's 8thle p. 837] Macrophages engulf LDL cholesterol and form foam cells formation of earliest lesion, i.e. fatty streak. Macrophages also form oxygen free radicals that cause oxidation of LDL to yield oxidized LDL (modified LDL).

176.q: A 54-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis complaints of weakness and fatigue. She states that her stools have recently become black after taking a new nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). Gastroscopy shows numerous superficial, bleeding mucosal defects. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
176.e: (a) Acute hemorrhagic gastritis is characterized by necrosis of the mucosa and is commonly associated with the intake of aspirin, other NSAIDs, alcohol, or ischemic injury. The factor common to all forms of acute hemorrhagic gastritis is thought to be the breakdown of the mucosal barrier, which permits acid induced injury. Mucosal injury causes bleeding from superficial erosions. Defects in the mucosa may extend into the deeper tissues to form an ulcer. The necrosis is accompanied by an acute inflammatory response and hemorrhage, which may be severe enough to result in exsanguination and hypovolemic shock. (b, c, d) The other choices are not associated with the use of NSAIDs. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter 17, pg759 - 761

177.q: Which of the following enzyme is required to activate digestive zymogens?
177.e: A majority of pancreatic enzymes are synthesized as inactive pro-enzymes and sequestered in membrane bound zymogen granules, as mentioned earlier. Activation of pro-enzymes requires conversion of trypsinogen to trypsin by duodenal entero peptidase. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th edition, Pg-679

177.q: From which of the cell does the carcinoid tumour develop? i. J cells ii. Neuroectoderm iii. Goblet cells iv. Enterochromaffin cells
o: Only i, ii and iii are correct
Only i and iii are correct
Only ii and iv are correct
177.e: Carcinoid tumors are malignant tumors composed of cells that contain dense-core neurosecretory granules in their cytoplasm and, rarely, may secrete hormonally active polypeptides. These are rare, slow growing neuroendocrine tumours arising from the enterochromaffin cells. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-543-44

177.q: Diagnosis of carcinoid tumour is done Urinary estimation of:
177.e: Answer is D (5HIAA): Carcinoid Tumors Carcinoid tumors are associated with elevated levels of metabolites of Tryptophan/ serotonin which include 5HIAA, 5HT and5HTP. Pheochromocytomas Pheochromocytomas are associated with elevated levels of catecholamines and their metabolites which include Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)and metanephrines The diagnosis of Typical carcinoid syndrome is suggested by elevated levels of 5HIAA The diagnosis of Atypical Carcinoid Syndrome is suggested by elevated levels of 5HTP. established by elevated levels of 5HIAA.

179.q: Which of the following agent causes atypical pneumonia?
179.e: Causes of atypical pneumonia: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia pneumonia, Influenza, Adenovirus, RSV, Legionella, Coxiella burnetti and Pneumocytis carnii. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 9 th ed, Pg-703-05

179.q: In primary tuberculosis, all of the following may be seen EXCEPT
179.e: Primary tuberculosis is the form of disease that develops in a previously unexposed and therefore unsensitized patient. Ghon focus, ghon complex and ranke complex are features of primary tuberculosis. Secondary tuberculosis is the pattern of disease that arises in a previously sensitized host. It may appear shortly after primary tuberculosis, but more commonly arises from reactivation of dormant primary lesion. The upper parts of both lungs are riddled with gray-white areas of caseation and multiple areas of softening and cavitation. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-528

179.q: Cotton candy exudates are characteristic of?
179.e: Involved areas of the lung contain a characteristic intraalveolar foamy, pink-staining exudate with hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) stain ("cotton candy" exudate). The septa are thickened by edema and a minimal mononuclear infiltrate. Special stains are required to visualize the organism. Silver stain of tissue sections reveals round- to cup-shaped cysts (4 to 10 µm in diameter) within the alveolar exudates. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-534

179.q: Reactivated TB is located most commonly in which anatomical part of lung.
179.e: Secondary pulmonary tuberculosis is classically localized to the apex of one or both upper lobes. The reason is obscure but may relate to high oxygen tension in the apices. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-529

179.q: A 70-year-old male dies of an acute ischemic stroke. During the autopsy an incidental lesion is found in the apex of the right upper lobe of the lung. Microscopy reveals abundant macrophages with indistinct cell boundaries, surrounded by a rim of lymphocytes and a central zone of necrotic debris. Of the following, which is the most likely cause of this patient's lung lesion?
179.e: Tb granuloma has characteristic feature of layering of lymphocytes outside. If no lymphocytes are present are on outside it is called naked granuloma seen in sarcoidosis. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 96

179.q: Which is the most common way of termination of Lobar pneumonia?
179.e: In the final stage of resolution, the exudate within the alveolar spaces is broken down by enzymatic digestion to produce granular, semifluid debris that is resorbed, ingested by macrophages, expectorated, or organized by fibroblasts growing into it. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-522

179.q: Gray hepatization of lungs lasts for how many days?
179.e: In lobar pneumonia, four stages of the inflammatory response have classically been described. The stage of gray hepatization that follows is marked by progressive disintegration of red cells and the persistence of a fibrinosuppurative exudate, resulting in a colour change to grayish-brown. In the final stage of resolution, the exudate within the alveolar spaces is broken down by enzymatic digestion to produce granular, semifluid debris that is resorbed, ingested by macrophages, expectorated, or organized by fibroblasts growing into it. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology,10 th ed. Pg-522

179.q: Which is not an inflammatory stage in pneumonia?
179.e: In lobar pneumonia, there are four inflammatory stages: Stage of congestion, Red hepatisation, Grey hepatisation stage of resolution. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-522

180.q: Which of the following microscopic features seen in sputum examination of an individual is NOT diagnostic of Bronchial asthma?
o: Crystalloids made up of membrane protein
180.e: Eosinophils are key inflammatory cells found in almost all subtypes of asthma; eosinophil products (such as major basic protein) are responsible for airway damage. An increase in size of the sub mucosal glands and goblet cell metaplasia of the airway epithelium Hypertrophy and/or hyperplasia of the bronchial muscle are seen. The most striking finding is occlusion of bronchi and bronchioles by thick, tenacious mucous plugs containing whorls of shed epithelium (Curschmann spirals). Numerous eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals (crystalloids made up of the eosinophil protein galectin-10) also are present. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-505

180.q: Which part of the lung are damaged by emphysema?
180.e: Emphysema is characterized by permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without significant fibrosis. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-498

180.q: A 58-year-old male with an 80-pack-per-year smoking history has developed over several years a non-productive cough and worsening dyspnea on exertion. A biopsy of the lung reveals essentially all alveolar airspaces to contain finely pigmented macrophages. What is the probable diagnosis?
180.e: Desquamative interstitial pneumonitis is one form of restrictive lung disease and can present with a slowly developing chronic cough and dyspnea on exertion. It is strongly associated with tobacco use, and the histologic feature is alveolar airspaces filled with pigment-laden macrophages (the pigment being carbonaceous material from the tobacco use). Respiratory bronchiolitis with interstitial lung disease occurs under a similar clinical scenario (i.e., a tobacco user presenting with dyspnea on exertion and chronic cough), but has patchy involvement of the pulmonary parenchyma and not diffuse involvement. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-507

180.q: Which of the following helps in generating reactive O2 intermediates in the neutrophils?
180.e: With in the phagocytes, the following reaction takes place: The initiating enzyme for this process is NADPH oxidase(also called respiratory burst oxidase). Glutathione peroxidase, glutathione reductase and superoxide dismutase are antioxidants. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 3, pg 78

180.q: Asbestos exposure can cause all EXCEPT
180.e: Asbestos is a family of crystalline hydrated silicates with a fibrous geometry. On the basis of epidemiologic studies, occupational exposure to asbestos is linked to parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis); localized fibrous plaques, or, rarely, diffuse fibrosis in the pleura; pleural effusions; lung carcinoma; malignant pleural and peritoneal mesothelioma; laryngeal carcinoma. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-511

180.q: A 28-year-old man with a history of recent occurrence of respiratory distress after some strenuous exercise. Physical examination reveals mild hypertension (blood pressure = 150/100 mm Hg), bilateral wheezing, and numerous purpuric skin lesions on the feet. Laboratory investigations performed show presence of raised TLC (15300/μL) and eosinophilia, serum creatinine is elevated to 3.5 mg/dL. The serum ANCA test is positive. Urinalysis shows 3+ proteinuria and RBCs. A renal biopsy demonstrates vasculitis accompanied by eosinophilia. Based on the above findings what is your probable diagnosis?
180.e: Churg-Strauss syndrome (also called allergic granulomatosis and angiitis) is a small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis classically associated with asthma, allergic rhinitis, lung infiltrates, peripheral eosinophilia, extravascular necrotizing granulomas, and a striking eosinophilic infiltration of vessels and tissues. (b, d) The vasculitis histologically resembles the lesions of polyarteritis nodosa (choice d) and Wegener granulomatosis (choice c), but these diseases do not typically present with an asthmatic syndrome. Reference : Robbins 10th Ed pg 515

180.q: Most common cause of chylothorax is?
180.e: Answer- B. Lymphoma Chylothorax is a pleural collection of a milky lymphatic fluid containing micro globules of lipid. It results from lymph formed in the digestive system called chyle accumulating in the pleural cavity due to either disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct. The total volume of fluid may not be large, but chylothorax is always significant because it implies obstruction of the major lymph ducts, usually by intrathoracic cancer like primary or secondary mediastinal neoplasm, such as lymphoma.

o: Knee joint effusion and lymphedema, associated with discolored nails
Pericardial and lymphedema, associated with discolored nails
Peritoneal effusion and lymphedema, associated with discolored nails
Pleural effusion and lymphedema, associated with discolored nails
180.e: Answer- D. Pleural effusion and lymphedema, associated with discolored nails Yellow nail syndrome is a rare disorder of the nail, which is usually accompanied by Lymphoedema It may also be associated with : Recurrent pleural effusions Bronchiectasis

181.q: A 62-year-old male patient presents with increasing chest pain, bloody sputum, and weight loss over the past 3 months. An HRCT scan reveals a mass, circumscribing the right main bronchus protruding into its lumen. Endobronchial lung biopsy was taken, based on the histopathological findings diagnosis of carcinoid tumor was given. All of the below mentioned IHC markers will shows, positivity in this tumor except:
181.e: Specific markers associated with adenocarcinoma (TTF-1, napsin A) or squamous cell carcinoma (p40, p63), neuroendocrine tumor (Synaptophysin, NSE, chromogranin). Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 719

181.q: A 63-year-old male patient having smoking history presented with shortness of breath and hemoptysis since 4 months. He is also complaining of productive cough and chest pain. Chest X-ray performed shows small mass in the right lung in the periphery. A transbronchial lung biopsy was performed and diagnosis of adenocarcinoma was made. Which IHC marker will be used to confirm the diagnosis?
181.e: Specific markers associated with adenocarcinoma (TTF1, napsin A) or squamous cell carcinoma (p40, p63), neuroendocrine tumor (Synaptophysin, NSE). Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 719

181.q: A 63-year-old female with an 80-pack-per year smoking history has been complaining of weakness and constipation. She also has abdominal pain and episodes of seizure. Laboratory testing reveals a total calcium of 13.0 mg/dL. On chest X-ray, she has a probable mass in the left upper lobe of the lung near the hilum. Of the following, what would a biopsy of the mass most likely reveal?
o: Small neoplastic cells with a high nuclear to cytoplasm ratio
181.e: The patient has symptoms consistent with hypercalcemia: weakness, constipation, abdominal pain, and psychiatric symptoms. Seizures can also occur. Squamous cell carcinoma, which has keratin pearls, can produce a parathyroid-hormone-like protein that will result in hypercalcemia (C). Adenocarcinoma (A) and small cell carcinoma (B) are not usually associated with PTH production. The mass is not a pulmonary sarcoidosis (D). Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-539

181.q: A patient is brought to the emergency room following a seizure. Serum Na+ level is 128 mEq/L. The urine osmolarity is higher than serum osmolarity. Chest X-Ray reveals a centrally located lung mass. On biopsy it shows salt and pepper appearance. Which tumour is most likely present in view of the clinicopathological profile?
181.e: Until recently, carcinomas of the lung were classified into two broad groups: small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the latter including adenocarcinoma, squamous and large cell carcinoma, and large cell neuroendocrine carcinomas. Small cell lung carcinomas (SCLCs) generally appear as pale gray, centrally located masses that extend into the lung parenchyma. These cancers are composed of relatively small tumor cells with a round to fusiform shape, scant cytoplasm, and finely granular chromatin with a salt and pepper appearance. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg-539-540

181.q: A 63-year-old male chronic smoker patient presented with respiratory difficulties these days which usually gradually increasing since 2 months. Chest X-ray and CT scan show a mass in the periphery of left lung. Transbronchial lung biopsy was performed and based the histopathological features diagnosis of small cell carcinoma was given. To confirm your diagnosis which IHC will show positive expression?
181.e: Specific markers associated with adenocarcinoma (TTF-1, napsin A) or squamous cell carcinoma (p40, p63), neuroendocrine tumor, small cell carcinoma (Synaptophysin, NSE). Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 719

181.q: Orphan annie eye nuclei appearance is characteristic of -
181.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Papillary carcinoma thyroid o The nuclei of papillary carcinoma cells contain finely dispersed chromatin, which imparts an optically clear or empty appearance, giving rise to the designation ground glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei.

182.q: What is most probable diagnosis of a patient who has prolactinoma, parathyroid hyperplasia and family history of renal stones?
182.e: MEN-I, or Wermer syndrome, characterized by abnormalities involving the parathyroid (Primary hyperparathyroidism resulting in renal stones), pancreas, and pituitary glands (prolactinoma) ; thus the mnemonic device, the 3Ps. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 9 th edition, pg 1136

182.q: A 25-year-old woman has noted breast secretions for the past month. She is not breastfeeding and has never been pregnant. She has not menstruated for the past 5 months. Physical examination yields no abnormal findings. MRI of the brain shows a 0.7 cm mass within the sella turcica. Histopathological examination of the lesion after removal shows dystrophic calcification. Which of the following additional complications is she most likely to have?
182.e: Prolactinomas are more common than other hormonesecreting pituitary adenomas. In addition to her galactorrhea and infertility, this patient also may have decreased libido, and her amenorrhea is secondary to the excessive prolactin secretion. Microadenomas might not have pressure effects on surrounding structures such as optic chiasm, but they can be discovered because of their hormonal effects. Acromegaly results from a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma in an adult. Cushing disease occurs when there is an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. A thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)-secreting pituitary adenoma is uncommon, but it could account for elevated levels of T4 and TSH in a hyper-thyroid patient. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 24, pg 1066

182.q: A 62-year-old man with a long-standing history of type 2 diabetes mellitus suffers a massive hemorrhagic stroke and expires. Examination of the pancreas shows hyalinization of many islets of Langerhans. Which of the following characterizes the material within the islets of Langerhans?
182.e: In T2DM, amyloid is often present within the islets of Langerhans, particularly in patients over 60 years of age. This type of amyloid derives from a polypeptide molecule known as amylin, which is secreted with insulin by the β-cell. As many as 20% of aged nondiabetic persons also have amyloid deposits in the pancreas, which is a finding that has been attributed to the aging process itself. None of the other choices show Congo red staining and apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 24, pg 1097

182.q: Zellballen pattern is found in histology of which of the following condition?
182.e: The histologic pattern in pheochromocytoma shows tumor cells composed of clusters of polygonal to spindle shaped chromaffin cells or chief cells that are surrounded by supporting sustentacular cells, creating small nests or alveoli called zellballen. These are supplied by a rich vascular network. Reference: Robbins 9th ed. Pg. 1135

182.q: A 38-year-old man complains of sudden attacks of dizziness, blurred vision, and excruciating headaches of 4 months in duration. During one of these attacks, his blood pressure was 180/120 mm Hg. The patient's father had been treated for thyroid cancer about 15 years ago. Laboratory studies show normal serum levels of aldosterone, renin, and angiotensin. A 24-hour urinalysis reveals increased metanephrines. Episodic hypertension in this patient is most likely caused by a tumor in which of the following endocrine organs?
182.e: Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor of chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla that secretes catecholamines. Such tumors also originate in extra-adrenal sites, in which case they are termed paragangliomas. The clinical features associated with pheochromocytoma are caused by the release of catecholamines. Patients with pheochromocytoma come to medical attention because of (1) asymptomatic hypertension discovered on a routine physical examination, (2) symptomatic hypertension that is resistant to antihypertensive therapy; (3) malignant hypertension (e.g., encephalopathy, papilledema, proteinuria), (4) myocardial infarction or aortic dissection, or (5) convulsions. The other choices do not include tumors that lead to episodic hypertension. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 24, pg 1127

183.q: Which of the following antibodies is most frequently seen in Antiphospholipid Syndrome?
183.e: Anti- beta 2 glycoprotein antibody is most frequently seen in Antiphospholipid Syndrome Reference : Robbins 9th/pg 124; 8th/pg 123

183.q: A patient presented with neck swelling. Cytology showed parafollicular cells along with clusters of plasmacytoid and scant amyloid. What investigation should be done to follow up the patient?
183.e: Parafollicular cells along with clusters of plasmacytoid and scant amyloid are suggestive of medullary carcinoma thyroid gland. Serum calcitonin levels are used as a tumor marker in this case. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 24, pg 1091

183.q: All the following condition can be diagnosed by FNAC; except:
183.e: The hallmark of all follicular adenomas is the presence of an intact, well-formed capsule encircling the tumor. Careful evaluation of the integrity of the capsule is therefore, critical in distinguishing follicular adenomas from follicular carcinomas, which demonstrate capsular and/or vascular invasion. This can be demonstrated by biopsy of the gland and not FNAC which will demonstrate only the morphology of the tumor cells and not the entire gland histology. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 9 th edition, pg631

183.q: Radiation exposure during infancy has been linked to which one of the following carcinoma -
183.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Thyroid "Differentiated thyroid carcinoma particularly papillary variety frequently follows accidental irradiation of thyroid in infancy and childhood" - Bailey Radiation induced cancers Radiation may induce some non-lethal changes in DNA sequences which may cause malignant transformation

184.q: A 59-year-old woman has a firm mass with irregular borders felt in her left breast on a routine physical examination. A fine needle aspiration is performed and microscopic examination shows an infiltrating ductal carcinoma. A left mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection is performed. A tissue sample of this neoplasm is submitted for analysis by flow cytometry. Which of the following does flow cytometric analysis most likely provide?
184.e: Aneuploidy is defined as a number of chromosomes that is not a multiple of the haploid state; for humans, that is a chromosome number that is not a multiple of 23. Aneuploidy is remarkably common in cancers, particularly carcinomas and was proposed as a cause of carcinogenesis over 100 years ago. Aneuploidy is the presence of one or more extra chromosomes or the absence of one or more chromosomes. The risk of fetal aneuploidy rises with increasing maternal age. Because fetal aneuploidy can affect any pregnancy, all pregnant women should be offered screening. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 203.
Ans. is 'd' i.e., Papilloma Examples include atypical ductal hyperplasia, atypical lobular hyperplasia, and intraductal papillomas.

184.q: A 52-year-old woman feels a lump in her right breast. Her physician palpates an irregular 3 cm mass that is not movable because it appears fixed to the overlying skin, which is retracted. A mastectomy is performed and the pathologist on sectioning the breast finds a 3 x 3.5 cm ovoid mass that does not have discrete borders, but appears to infiltrate into the surrounding fibrofatty breast stroma. The mass is firm, white and has a fibrous consistency. Which of the following features is most likely demonstrated by the gross appearance of this mass?
184.e: Malignant potential is revealed only by invasion into adjacent tissues or metastasis. The stroma carrying the blood supply is crucial to the growth of tumours but does not aid in the separation of benign from malignant ones. The amount of stromal connective tissue does, however, determine the consistency of a neoplasm. Certain cancers induce a dense, abundant fibrous stroma(desmoplasia), making them hard, so-called "scirrhous tumors". Desmoplasia is the result of increased synthesis of extracellular matrix proteins and collagen by stromal cells. It is considered to be a reaction and response of the host tissue against invasive cancer cells.[5] The biological relevance of the desmoplastic response to cancer is still unclear. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 193.

185.q: Most common site of bone metastasis in prostate cancer
185.e: Lumbar spine > Proximal femur > Pelvis > Thoracic spine > Ribs Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter - 21 pg 977

Answer- D. All Infection :- Osteomyelitis, Brodie's abscess, syphilis Neoplasms Benign : Osteoid osteoma Malignant : Ewing's sarcoma, osteosarcoma Eosinophilic granuloma Healed stress fracture Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy

185.q: GNAS mutation is associated with malignancy of which cells?
185.e: The mutation of guanine nucleotide-activating alpha subunit (GNAS) gene is the somatic mutation related to the McCune-Albright syndrome. GNAS mutation is also detected in about 30% to 40% of sporadic growth hormone (GH) secreting tumors.

185.q: "Sunray appearance" on X-rays is suggestive of:
o: A metastatic tumour in the bone
185.e: C i.e. Osteogenic Sarcoma Sunray appearance is classically seen in osteosarcoma. It may also occur in metastases, Ewings sarcoma, Haemang oma, Meningioma and tuberculosis.

185.q: A 50-year-old female on corticosteroids from a long duration presented with pain in the right hip region initially associated with activity and later on becomes constant. Fracture at neck along with irregular densities of the cancellous bone of femur is noticed in X-ray. The head of femur is replaced by artificial head. The histopathological examination of the head shows empty lacunae and necrotic adipocytes. What is the probable diagnosis based on histology?
185.e: Infarction of bone and marrow is relatively common. It can be limited to the medullary cavity or involve both the medulla and cortex. Fractures and corticosteroid administration are the two most common causes. Microscopically, dead bone is characterized by empty lacunae surrounded by necrotic adipocytes. The released fatty acids bind calcium and form insoluble calcium soaps. The remaining trabeculae act as scaffolding for deposition of new bone, while osteoclasts resorb necrotic trabeculae. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, chapter 26, pg 1185

185.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of left leg pain. His temperature is 38.7°C (103°F). He has a harsh systolic murmur and echocardiographic evidence of bacterial endocarditis. If this patient has developed hematogenous osteomyelitis, his bone infection would most likely be found in which of the following anatomic locations?
185.e: Hematogenous osteomyelitis primarily affects the metaphyseal area of the long bones (knee, ankle, hip) because of the unique vascular supply in this region. Normally, arterioles enter the calcified portion of the growth plate, form a loop, and then drain into the medullary cavity without establishing a capillary bed. This vascular loop permits slowing and sludging of blood flow, allowing bacteria time to penetrate the walls of the blood vessels and establish an infective focus within the bone marrow. Osteomyelitis may break into the periosteum (choice e) but does not originate there. Vascular loops do not reach the epiphysis (choice c). Choices a and b would be distinctly uncommon. Reference :Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition , chapter 26, pg 1171

186.q: Which of the following/s is/are seronegative arthritis?
186.e: SERONEGATIVE ARTHRITIS REFERS TO A GROUP OF FOUR CHRONIC DISEASES - ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS, PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS, REACTIVE ARTHRITIS, AND ENTEROPATHIC ARTHRITIS. ALL OF THEM ARE NEGATIVE FOR RHEUMATOID FACTOR, THEY'RE ALL POSITIVE FOR HLA-B27, AND THEY TYPICALLY ALL RUN IN FAMILIES. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number- 822

186.q: Which of the following is involved in the development of rheumatoid arthritis?
186.e: Explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks healthy joint tissues. In genetically susceptible individuals, exposure to specific antigens activates CD4+ T-cells. These T-cells release inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and interferon-γ, which in turn activate endothelial cells, B-cells, and macrophages. This immune cascade leads to persistent inflammation, joint damage, and the characteristic deformities of RA. Explanation of other options: IgE-mediated (Option A): Primarily seen in allergic reactions, not in RA. Defective cellular and humoral immunity (Option B): RA involves targeted autoimmunity rather than a general immune defect. Chronic microbial infections (Option D): May trigger or worsen autoimmune responses but are not the primary cause of RA.

186.q: Which of the following factor is not included in predisposing factors of Gout?
o: Age older than 60 years of age
186.e: Only about 10% of patients with hyperuricemia develop clinical gout. Other factors contribute symptomatic gout: Age of the individual and duration of the hyperuricemia. Gout usually appears after 20 to 30 years of hyperuricemia. Genetic predisposition. In addition to the well-defined X-linked abnormalities of HGPRT, polymorphisms in genes involved with urate or ion transport and possibly inflammation are also associated with gout. Alcohol consumption. • Obesity. • Drugs (e.g., thiazides) that reduce excretion of urate Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number- 824

186.q: Which of the following tumour is a benign skeletal muscle tumour?
186.e: Benign skeletal muscle tumor is rhabdomyoma. In heart, it is associated with tuberous sclerosis and show spider cells. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 192.

186.q: Which of the following is the most specific test for rheumatoid arthritis?
186.e: Ccp antibodies, also called anti-ccp antibodies, are a type of antibody called autoantibodies. Antibodies and autoantibodies are proteins made by the immune system. Antibodies protect you from disease by fighting foreign substances like viruses and bacteria. Reference: https://www.healthline.com/health/rheumatoid-arthritis/rheumatoid-arthritis-test#takeaway

186.q: A 5-year-old child was presenting with proptosis. Microscopic examination of the mass has revealed a round cell tumor positive for Desmin immunohistochemical marker. Most likely diagnosis would be:
186.e: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. In the four options provided, all four show morphology of a round cell tumor. However, Desmin positivity is seen only in cases of rhabdomyosarcoma. Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor with skeletal muscle differentiation. Three subtypes are alveolar (20%), embryonal (60%), and pleomorphic (20%). In embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, the tumor cells mimic skeletal muscle at various stages of embryogenesis and consist of sheets of both primitive round and spindled cells in a myxoid stroma. Immunohistochemistry for desmin and myogenin confirms the rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 26, pg 1212

186.q: Which of the following is Not a manifestation of Reactive arthritis?
186.e: REACTIVE ARTHRITIS, FORMERLY KNOWN AS REITER'S SYNDROME, IS A CONDITION THAT CAUSES INFLAMMATION (REDNESS AND SWELLING) IN VARIOUS PLACES IN THE BODY. IT USUALLY DEVELOPS FOLLOWING AN INFECTION, AND IN MOST CASES CLEARS UP IN A FEW MONTHS WITHOUT CAUSING LONG-TERM PROBLEMS. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition, page number - 822

186.q: Regarding desmoid tumour which is not correct ?
186.e: Ans. is `d' i.e., Highly radiosensitive Desmoid tumour is an aggressive fibromatosis or musculoaponeurotic fibromatosis is a monoclonal fibroblastic proliferation arising in musculoaponeurotic structures. Histologically these tumours are consist of spindle shaped cells in collagenous matrix and lack the pleomorphic, atypical or hyperchromatic nuclei of malignancy. A minority of desmoid tumours are associated with Gardener syndrome and mutations of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) gene. Most spontaneous desmoid tumours are associated with mutations of beta-catenin gene.

187.q: Basal cell layer dysplasia associated with hyper and parakeratosis is seen in
187.e: Actinic keratosis may show dysplastic changes that lead to cutaneous SCC. The stratum corneum is thickened (hyperkeratosis) and cells in this layer retain their nuclei (parakeratosis). Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1145

187.q: Regarding histology of dysplastic nevi, all are correct except
o: Linear fibrosis occurs around epidermal rete ridges involved by the nevus
Lymphocytic infiltrate may be seen in the epidermis
Presence of cytological atypia in form of irregular nuclear contours and hyperchromasia
187.e: Lymphocytic infiltrates may be seen in superficial dermis. Release of melanin from dead nevus cells into dermis may occur (melanin incontinence) and this is phagocytosed by dermal macrophages leading to a peculiar fibrosis surrounding epidermal rete ridges that are involved by nevus. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1137

o: These are benign neoplasms that have mutation leading to constitutive activation of RAS or BRAF
Earliest lesion is a junctional nevus
May become more prominent in pregnancy
Lack neurotization, a phenomenon present in melanoma
187.e: At the deepest extent of melanocytic nevi, nevus cells often acquire fusiform contours and grow in fascicles resembling neural tissue, this phenomenon is called neurotization and it is absent in melanoma. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1136

187.q: True statements about dysplastic nevus syndrome are
o: Also called familial atypical multiple mole and melanoma syndrome
187.e: FAMMM is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by multiple dysplastic nevi and melanomas and in 50% cases melanomas develop by the age of 60. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1137

187.q: Tumor depth of invasion is denoted by Breslow thickness and it is calculated from
o: Deepest margin of tumor cells to upper extent of tumor
Epidermal granular layer to deepest intraepidermal tumor cells
Stratum corneum to deepest intradermal tumor cells
Stratum Basale to deepest intradermal tumor cells
187.e: It is calculated from top of granular layer to deepest intradermal cells if overlying skin is intact, if ulcerated start from base of ulcer. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1135

o: Composed of fibroblasts arranged in storiform pattern
May extend to subcutis and rarely metastasizes
Imatinib can be used for unresectable tumors
187.e: There is overexpression of PDGF beta due to translocation involving genes encoding collagen 1A1 (COL1A1) and platelet-derived growth factor-beta (PDGFB), so tyrosine kinase inhibitors are used. Although they are locally aggressive and can recur, they rarely metastasize, metastasis is seen with tumors that exhibit greater cytologic atypia. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1150
Multiple small seborrheic keratosis on face are termed as dermatosis papulosa nigra. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition Chapter 25, pg 1158

187.q: Sezary syndrome is included in the category of?
187.e: Mycosis fungoides is the most common form of a type of blood cancer called cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas occur when certain white blood cells, called T cells , become cancerous; these cancers characteristically affect the skin, causing different types of skin lesions. Reference : Robbins Basic Pathology, 8 th edition, page number - 616

188.q: What is the most common site for Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma?
188.e: Pilocytic astrocytomas are relatively benign tumors that typically affect children and young adults. Most commonly located in the cerebellum , they also may involve the third ventricle, the optic pathways, the spinal cord, and occasionally the cerebral hemispheres. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 883

188.q: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency room 2 hours after being involved in an automobile accident. The patient denies striking his head, although his head was thrust forward and backward. His vital signs are normal, and he returns home. The following day, the patient's wife notices that he is lethargic. By the time the ambulance arrives at the emergency room, the patient is comatose. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the decline in mental status in this patient?
188.e: The consequences of traumatic brain injury may be internal and subtle. The parasagittal cortex is anchored to arachnoid villi, whereas the lateral aspects of the cerebrum move more freely. This anatomical feature, together with the differential density of gray and white matter, permits generation of shearing forces between different brain regions, leading to diffuse axonal shearing injuries, particularly in vehicular accidents. Shearing injuries can distort or disrupt axons, causing them to retract into "spheroids", as well as lose myelin. This type of injury typically occurs in parasagittal white matter and may be accompanied by multiple small hemorrhages. Duret hemorrhage (choice b) occurs in the uncus during transtentorial herniation. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter – 28 pg 1249

188.q: Which is the most common brain tumour?
188.e: Most common brain tumour is Metastatic tumour and the most common primary brain tumour is meningioma. Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10 th ed, Pg: 885

188.q: A 42-year-old man with AIDS dementia complex dies of respiratory insufficiency secondary to Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia. Examination of the brain at autopsy reveals mild cerebral atrophy, with dilation of the lateral ventricles. Which of the cells are the main culprit for the neuropathologic changes?
188.e: In most patients with AIDS encephalopathy, the disease is attributable to an active infection of the CNS by the virus itself. Macrophages and microglial cells in the CNS are productively infected by HIV-1. Although neurons and astrocytes may interact with the virus, they do not seem to be infected but are injured indirectly by cytokines or other neurotoxic factors released by macrophages. Also only microglia cells express both CD 4 co-receptor and chemokines receptor (CCR5 and CXCR4) that are required in combination for efficient infection by HIV. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter – 28 pg 1267

188.q: Pathological change in CNS of AIDS patient:
188.e: Like the lymphoid system, the nervous system is a target of HIV infection. Macrophages and microglia, cells in the CNS that belong to the macrophage lineage, are the predominant cell types in the brain that are infected with HIV. Microglial nodules are a well-known phenomenon in viral encephalitis, in which perineuronal aggregation of activated microglia/macrophages indicative of neuronal phagocytosis is often observed. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 177.

188.q: Which of the following morphology is included in WHO grade II classification for meningioma?
188.e: Atypical meningiomas (WHO grade II) are recognized by the presence of either an increased mitotic rate, or prominent nucleoli, increased cellularity, patternless growth, high nucleus-to cytoplasm ratio, or necrosis. These tumors demonstrate more aggressive local growth and a higher rate of recurrence and may require therapy in addition to surgery. Some histologic patterns-clear cell and chordoid-also correlate with more aggressive behavior, as does the presence of brain invasion. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed Pg: 885

188.q: In WHO classification, glioblastoma belongs to which grade of astrocytoma?
188.e: Explanation: Glioblastoma is designated as Grade IV astrocytoma in the WHO system, representing the most aggressive type. It is associated with necrosis, vascular proliferation, and marked pleomorphism and carries a poor prognosis. Explanation of other options: Grade I (Option A): Pilocytic astrocytoma, benign, common in children, slow-growing, favourable prognosis. Grade II (Option B): Diffuse astrocytoma, slow growing, lacks necrosis or high mitotic activity. Grade III (Option C): Anaplastic astrocytoma, with cellular pleomorphism and mitotic activity but no necrosis. Key Takeaways: WHO grading system classifies gliomas based on malignancy and prognosis. Glioblastoma (Grade IV) is the most malignant astrocytoma. Features include necrosis, vascular proliferation, and rapid progression.

188.q: In a study of hypoglycemic shock, cellular changes in the brain are analyzed. One cell type in the hippocampus is noted to exhibit intense cytoplasmic eosinophilia, central chromatolysis, spheroidal swellings, and nuclear pyknosis. These changes appear 12 hours after blood glucose levels drop below 20 mg/dL. What is this cell type most likely to be:
188.e: Hypoxic and hypoglycemic injury leads to "red" neurons as the initial reaction. The larger pyramidal neurons are the most sensitive, particularly in the hippocampus with hypoglycemia, as well as neocortical Betz cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells. Astrocytes proliferate in reaction to brain injury in the process called gliosis. Endothelial cells are most likely to proliferate in neoplasms. Microglia respond to brain injury with a macrophage-like function. Oligodendroglial cells provide myelination for brain neuronal axons. Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10 th edition, Chapter – 28 pg 1242

189.q: Flow cytometry is used to detect?
189.e: Flow cytometry helps in subtyping hematopoietic cells. Blood cell counters give differential leukocyte count Coagulometers give coagulation profile Antibody quantification is usually done by ELISA Reference: Pathology Outlines - Flow cytometry

189.q: Flow cytometry is routinely utilized for:
189.e: Flow cytometry is used routinely in the classification of leukemias and lymphomas. In this method, fluorescently labeled antibodies against cell surface molecules and differentiation antigens are used to obtain the phenotype of malignant cells. Flow cytometry is a technology that rapidly analyzes single cells or particles as they flow past single or multiple lasers while suspended in a buffered salt-based solution. Each particle is analyzed for visible light scatter and one or multiple fluorescence parameters. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 238.

189.q: What is/are use's of DNA Microarrays?
189.e: The most common method for large-scale analysis of RNA expression in use in research laboratories has been based on DNA microarrays. DNA microarray analysis helps as the bacterial genomic DNA often outlasts the viability of the bacteria and a diagnosis can be made using a small amount of DNA, as opposed to the large numbers of bacteria needed for culture. Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10 th ed, Pg: 240.
10% buffered neutral formalin is used in histopathology as fixative. Reference: Ackerman, 9th ed, Pg: 27

190.q: Resolution provided by light microscope is:
190.e: Resolution power: It is the ability to produce separate images of closely placed objects so that they can be distinguished as two separate entities. The resolution power of: Unaided human eye is about 0.2 mm (200 μm) Light microscope is about 0.2 μm Electron microscope is about 0.5 nm The best resolution for an optical microscope is about 0.2 microns = 200 nm. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 7-8

190.q: Resolution provided by electron microscope is:
190.e: Resolution power: It is the ability to produce separate images of closely placed objects so that they can be distinguished as two separate entities. The resolution power of: Unaided human eye is about 0.2 mm (200 μm) Light microscope is about 0.2 μm Electron microscope is about 0.5 nm Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 11

190.q: Resolution provided by unaided human eye is:
190.e: Resolution power: It is the ability to produce separate images of closely placed objects so that they can be distinguished as two separate entities. The resolution power of: Unaided human eye is about 0.2 mm (200 μm) Light microscope is about 0.2 μm Electron microscope is about 0.5 nm Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 2, Pg 10

190.q: Bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan layer is composed of all EXCEPT:
190.e: Each peptidoglycan layer is mucopeptide (murein) chain composed of alternate subunits of N-acetyl muramic acid (NAM) and N-acetyl glucosamine (NAG) molecules. Teichoic acid are polymers of ribitol or glycerol joined by phosphate groups. Cell wall teichoic acid: Covalently linked to NAM of cell wall. Lipoteichoic acid: attached to lipids of cell membrane Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 17

190.q: A surgeon wants your advice about rust found on surgical instruments that are required for an operational procedure this afternoon. He has no other sets available. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Wipe the rust off with a disinfectant and use
Return the complete set to sterile services for reprocessing and use a new set
190.e: Surgical instruments are made from high-grade stainless steel and are coated for protection against the aggressive nature of the decontamination process (passivation layer) and prevents the steel from rusting. If at any time rust is found on the surface of an instrument it indicates that either the passivation layer is compromised or there is weakness in the metal from which the instrument is made. When rusty instruments are found, the items need to be taken out of service so as not to compromise patient care. Loan equipment or alternative instruments need to be provided as replacement. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 3, Pg 28-29

190.q: Which of the following is true about Autoclave operation?
o: Dry air at 121°C and 15 lb/square inch pressure
190.e: Most commonly used Sterilization operating conditions for autoclave: 121°C for 15 min at pressure of 15 psi. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 126

190.q: Which of the following chemical is NOT sporicidal?
190.e: Sporicidal agents include: Aldehyde: Formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde Halogens: Sodium hypochlorite, iodine/iodophors Hydrogen peroxide Peracetic acid Ozone Peroxynitrite Gaseous or vapor-phase disinfectants like Ethylene oxide. Reference: Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities (2008) Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 3, Pg 28-29 Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 3, Pg 31-33

190.q: Gamma radiations are used for sterilization of:
190.e: Ionising radiations (X-rays, gamma rays from Cobalt 60, cosmic rays) Mechanism: It causes breakage of DNA without increasing surface temperature (cold sterilization). Spectrum: It destroys spores and vegetative cells, but not effective against viruses. Use: Disposable plastics, rubber or plastic syringes, infusion sets and catheters. Catgut sutures, bone and tissue grafts and adhesive dressings, antibiotics and hormones. Advantages: High penetrating power, Fast action and cold sterilization Sterilization control: Bacillus pumilus. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 3, Pg 31-33

191.q: Most potent stimulator of Naive T-cells -
191.e: Mature Dendritic cells Mature B-cells and T-cells before antigenic exposure are called naive-B and T cells respectively. Sequence of events in activation of naive T cells. Immature dendritic cells in the epidermis are called langerhans cell. These immature dendritic cells (langerhans cells) capture the antigen in the epidermis. After capturing the antigen these cells secrete cytokines. These cytokines cause loss of adhesiveness of langerhans cells. Langerhans cells separate from each other and migrate into lymphatic vessels. In lymphatic vessel, maturation of langerhans cells takes place. Then these mature langerhans dendritic cells reach to naive T cells in the lymph nodes and present antigen to these cells and activate them.

191.q: A 20-year-old female presents with history of recurrent episodes of swelling of the submucosal tissue of the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts from childhood. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates that her C1 inhibitor level is less than 6% of the reference value. The most likely diagnosis is:
191.e: Hereditary angioedema is caused by deficient levels of C1 inhibitor. This reduces the ability to control activation of the classical pathway. Autosomal-dominant inheritance Gene locus: SERPING1(C1 inhibitor) on chromosome 11 Excessive spontaneous activation of classical complement pathway (especially C2) causing local inflammation of gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts. Swelling of tracheal and bronchial passages can be life-threatening. Nutrition-based immunodeficiencies are not does not presents with severely reduced levels of specific cell types or related molecules. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is caused by a deficiency of CD59. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is caused by a deficiency of the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19, Pg 187-190

191.q: Lysozyme is found in significant quantities in all of the following bodily secretions, EXCEPT:
191.e: Lysozyme is present in tears, saliva, human breast milk and respiratory mucus secretions. It is also present in cytoplasmic granules of the macrophages and the polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs). Reduced lysozyme levels have been associated with bronchopulmonary dysplasia in newborns. In certain cancers (especially myelomonocytic leukemia) excessive production of lysozyme by cancer cells can lead to toxic levels of lysozyme in the blood. High lysozyme blood levels can lead to kidney failure and low blood potassium. It is used as a marker of sarcoidosis disease activity and is suitable for disease monitoring. (Sensitive but less specific) Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition Chapter 14, Page Number: 175

191.q: Half-life of C reactive protein is:
191.e: CRP is an acute-phase protein of hepatic origin that increases following interleukin-6 secretion by macrophages, adipocytes and T cells. Plasma half-life of CRP: It is 19 hours. This half-life is constant in all medical conditions. Therefore, the only factor that affects the level of CRP in blood is only its rate of production. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition Chapter 14, Pg 175

191.q: Gene components of HLA class I includes -
191.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., A, B, C . Class I HLA comprises A, B and C loci.

191.q: A 35-year-old patient presents with frequent bacterial infections and is found to have a genetic deficiency in complement component C3. Which aspect of innate immunity is most directly affected by this deficiency?
191.e: Complement component C3 is crucial for opsonization, a process where pathogens are tagged for easier recognition and engulfment by phagocytes like macrophages and neutrophils. A deficiency in C3 impairs this process, leading to increased susceptibility to bacterial infections. While C3 is important for opsonization, it does not directly affect interferon production, T cell activation, or the barrier function of the skin. Key Takeaway: Deficiency in complement component C3 primarily affects the phagocytosis of pathogens due to impaired opsonization. Tags: INICET 2022 | Clinical Tag Line: Hard / Clinical Reference: Shastri, A. (2023). Immunology: Chapter 13on Complement System, pp. 163-167.

191.q: Rajesh is a 32 year old man who has been worried about his weight loss. He was 70kgs 6 months ago and currently weighs 58kg. He has also been experiencing bouts of diarrhea, episodes of fever in the evening and generalized fatigue. Upon repeated questioning he revealed having illicit relations and unprotected intercourse with his partner. Unfortunately, he tested positive for both HIV AIDS and TB. You explain to him that he will have to undergo treatment for both. He asks you if he can just take his medications together . What will you counsel?
o: Prescribe ATT and advise him to begin with ART 8 weeks later
Prescribe ART and advise him to begin with ATT 8 weeks later
ATT is not recommended in HIV AIDS
191.e: The optimal timing to commence ART in HIV-infected patients with TB is relatively complex. It must balance the risk of morbidity and mortality in very advanced HIV disease with the potential occurrence of additive toxicities, drug-drug interactions, and TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). The current World Health Organization guidelines recommend that ART should be started as soon as possible "within the first 8 weeks" of starting anti-tubercular treatment and within the first 2 weeks for patients who have CD4 cell counts less than 50 cells/mm 3 Reference- https://aidsrestherapy.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12981-016-0106-y

191.q: Which innate immune component is responsible for recognizing and binding to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs)?
191.e: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are a type of pattern recognition receptor that recognizes and binds to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) on pathogens. This recognition helps initiate the immune response. B cells and T cells are part of the adaptive immune system, while NK cells are involved in killing infected or cancerous cells, not in recognizing PAMPs. Key Takeaway: TLRs play a critical role in the innate immune system by detecting and responding to pathogens through PAMP recognition. Tags: FMGE 2023 Tag Line: Moderate Reference: Shastri, A., & Bhatt, S. (2023). Essential Microbiology . Chapter 9: Immunity, pg.133.

192.e: T-independent antigens can stimulate B cells directly without the need for T-cell help. These antigens are typically polysaccharides or repetitive structures that can cross-link B cell receptors, leading to B cell activation and antibody production. Key Takeaway: T-independent antigens activate B cells directly, bypassing the need for T helper cells. Tag: FMGE 2023 Tag Line: Moderate Reference: Apurva Shastri, Review of Microbiology and Immunology , chapter 12 on antigens - antibody reaction.PP-152.

192.q: All of the following interactions occur between antigen-antibody reactions except:
192.e: Antigen-antibody interactions primarily involve ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, and Van der Waals forces. Covalent bonds are not typically involved in these interactions. Key Takeaway: Antigen-antibody interactions are primarily mediated by non-covalent forces. Tag: May know Tag Line: Moderate Reference Apurva Shastri, Review of Microbiology and Immunology , chapter 12 on antigens – antibody reaction.PP-160.

192.q: Which of the following is very difficult to induce antibody?
192.e: Following antigens have poor immunogenicity (difficult induction of antibody): Smaller size/molecular weight antigens Nucleic acid > Lipids > Carbohydrates (in decreasing order) Antigens not degradable by tissue enzyme self-antigen Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 15, Pg 148-150

192.q: The following constitutes approximately 75% of total immunoglobin in humans:
192.e: IgG is the major serum immunoglobulin 80% of total Mol wt - 150,000 (7S) Half-life - 23 days Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 197-198

192.q: The earliest immunoglobulin to be synthesized by the fetus is:
192.e: IgM is the first immunoglobulin developed during human fetal development at 20 weeks. Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 199-200

192.q: First immunoglobin to appear following infections:
192.e: IgM antibody appears first, followed by IgA on mucosal surfaces or IgG in the serum Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 199-200

192.q: When an antigen is administered for the first time to animal or a human being who has never been exposed to it, the first antibody to develop is:
192.e: IgM is the first antibody produced and secreted by B cells during the primary and secondary immune responses. Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 199-200

192.q: IgA secretion is mainly seen in:
192.e: IgA is concentrated in secretions and on mucus surfaces and Resistant to digestive enzymes. IgM is present in trace amounts in all secretions and does not vary considerably. IgA is the major immunoglobulin in colostrum, saliva and tears. Secretory IgA is found essentially in the superior genital tract. Reference: Jalanti R, Isliker H. Immunoglobulins in human cervico-vaginal secretions. Int Arch Allergy Appl Immunol. 1977;53(5):402-8. doi: 10.1159/000231778. PMID: 558170. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition Chapter 13, Pg 198-199

193.q: A 30-year-old male presents with headache, fatigue, light-headedness, dyspnea, and tachycardia. Laboratory investigations reveal decreased hemoglobin and a positive direct Coomb's test. The patient is presently on an antibiotic for symptoms of upper respiratory infection. These findings suggest which of the following?
o: Type I, mediated by IgG antibodies
Type II, mediated by IgG antibodies
Type III, mediated by IgG antibodies
Type III, mediated by IgG or IgM antibodies
193.e: Type II reactions involve antibodies directed against self-cells (erythrocytes) or membranes. Certain drugs react with erythrocytes to form neoantigens. Type I responses are against foreign antigens (e.g., allergens), cause IgE responses, and do not invoke a Coomb's reaction. Type III reactions involve soluble antigen-antibody complexes, and type IV reactions do not involve antibody. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

193.q: True regarding Histamine release from mast cell granules:
o: It requires the cells to have IgE of only one antigenic specificity per cell
It cannot occur in the absence of antigen-specific IgE
It occurs after IgE Fc receptor crosslinking
193.e: Basophils and mast cells bind IgE via high affinity Fc receptors, so each cell has IgE of many different specificities on its surface. Ca2+is required Many non-lgE triggers (C3a and C5a) can produce granule release. IgE Fc receptor crosslinking triggers release of granule content from mast cell. Referene: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

193.q: A young student immediately felt difficulty in breathing and tightness in his chest. Hestarted sweating and fainted. His friends found out that a bee had just stung him. The emergency school medical team attended him and within minutes he recovered. Which one of the following drugs was administered by the medical team?
193.e: This patient had a major anaphylactic reaction and his tracheal-bronchial smooth muscle has contracted. Epinephrine is the only treatment in this group to reverse this reaction. It will relax the smooth muscle of the respiratory tree and stimulate the heart to beat stronger to raise the blood pressure. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

193.q: A 6-month-old male infant presents with diarrhea, extensive fungal infections, skin rashes and failure to gain weight. He has deficient T and B cell function. The thymus is of normal size. The most likely way to permanent restoration of normal immunity is:
193.e: The patient has a defect in the lymphocytic lineage. This could be permanently restored by replacement of defective stem cells through bone marrow transplantation. Isolation is beneficial but is a severe imposition on the quality of life and constitutes protection rather than restoration of function. The remaining choices require constant repetitive application but not permanent restoration of function. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19, Pg 187-190

193.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with muscle weakness and a positive anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody test. Which autoimmune disease is most likely in this patient?
193.e: Myasthenia gravis: Characterized by the presence of anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, leading to muscle weakness due to impaired neuromuscular transmission. Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Involves autoantibodies against thyroid peroxidase and does not typically present with anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Grave's disease: Involves autoantibodies against the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor, not acetylcholine receptors. Addison's disease: Involves adrenal cortex autoantibodies, not anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Key Takeaway: Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are indicative of myasthenia gravis. Tags: FMGE2023 Tag Line: Easy Reference: Shastri, A., & Bhatt, S. (2023). Essential Microbiology . Chapter 17: Autoimmunity, pp. 203-207

193.q: Which genetic factor is commonly associated with an increased risk of developing autoimmune diseases?
o: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in non-coding regions
193.e: HLA gene variations (Human Leukocyte Antigen) are strongly associated with susceptibility to various autoimmune diseases due to their role in immune system regulation. Mitochondrial DNA mutations are related to mitochondrial disorders, not specifically autoimmune diseases. X-linked chromosomal abnormalities can affect various genetic conditions but are less directly linked to autoimmune diseases. SNPs in non-coding regions may play a role but are not as directly associated with autoimmune risk as HLA variations. Key Takeaway: HLA gene variations are significant genetic factors in autoimmune disease susceptibility. Tags: Clinical | integrated Tag Line: Genetic Insights Reference: Shastri, A., & Bhatt, S. (2023). Essential Microbiology . Chapter 17: Autoimmunity, pp. 203-207

193.q: Which MHC Class I molecule is associated with an increased risk of developing the autoimmune disease ankylosing spondylitis?
193.e: HLA-B27: This MHC Class I allele is strongly associated with an increased risk of developing ankylosing spondylitis, a type of inflammatory arthritis. HLA-B35 and C. HLA-A2 are not specifically linked to ankylosing spondylitis. HLA-Cw6 is associated with psoriasis, not ankylosing spondylitis. Key Takeaway: HLA-B27 is a key genetic marker for susceptibility to ankylosing spondylitis. Tags: FMGE 2020 | Good to know Tag Line: Hard Reference: Shastri, A., & Bhatt, S. (2023). Essential Microbiology . Chapter 14: Autoimmunity, pp. 170-183.

Ans. is 'c' i.e., Normal B cells Most patients with common variable immunodeficiency have normal or near-normal numbers of B cells in the blood and lymphoid tissues. These B cells, however, are not able to differentiate into plasma cells. The clinical manifestations are caused by antibody deficiency. The feature common to all patients is hypogammaglobulinemia, generally affecting all the antibody classes but sometimes only IgG.

194.q: Bence Jones protein are composed of:
194.e: Bence-Jones proteins: Multiple myeloma light chain immunoglobulin - kappa or lambda. Identified in urine by coagulation when heated to 50°C but redissolving at 70° In single patient - kappa/lambda, never both Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition Chapter 13, Pg 201

194.q: Most effective method to prevent transmission of MRSA in a ward is?
194.e: Single most effective method of prevention of hospital acquired infections is handwashing. DOC in the treatment of MRSA is vancomycin. Nasal carriers are treated with mupirocin. Reference: Essentials of medical microbiology by Apurba sastry 1 st edition Pg no.218

194.q: Treatment for nasal carriers of MRSA is by
194.e: Single most effective method of prevention of hospital acquired infections is handwashing. DOC in the treatment of MRSA is vancomycin. Nasal carriers are treated with mupirocin. Reference: Essentials of medical microbiology by Apurba sastry 1 st edition Pg no.218

194.q: VRSA and VISA are respectively due to:
o: vanA gene and cell wall thickness
Both due to cell wall thickness
vanA gene and there is no term like VISA
194.e: Erroneous and overuse of vancomycin has led to the emergence of resistance to vancomycin. It may be of low-grade resistance, known as VISA (vancomycin intermediate S. aureus) or high-grade resistance, known as VRSA (vancomycin-resistant S. aureus). VRSA is mediated by van A gene; whereas VISA is due to increase in cell wall thickness of S. aureus. The van A gene is believed to be acquired from a vancomycin-resistant strain of Enterococcus faecalis by horizontal conjugal transfer Treatment of VRSA should be based on an antimicrobial susceptibility report. Linezolid, telavancin, daptomycin and quinupristin/dalfopristin are the effective drugs. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 518

194.q: Which of the following is positive by Indian ink staining?
194.e: Negative staining: The background stains black whereas unstained bacteria stand out in contrast. It is used for the demonstration of capsules which do not take up simple stains. Example: India ink or nigrosine Capsulated bacteria: Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae), Meningococcus (Neisseriae meningitidis), Klebsiella pneumoniae Capulated fungus yeast: Cryptococcus neoformans Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 12

Capsule swelling (delineation) or Quellung reaction : It was described by Neufeld (1902) It was widely employed for the typing of pneumococci in the pre-sulphonamide days when lobar pneumonia used to be treated with specific anticapsular sera. Swollen, refractile and delineated capsules are seen on adding antisera mixed with methylene blue. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 20

195.q: Which of the following is not a step in Pathogenesis of listeriosis?
195.e: Pathogenesis of listeriosis: Intracellular survival : After entry into the intestinal epithelium, it survives inside the host cell, mainly due to lysis of phagosome by forming pores (mediated by listeriolysin O) Then it causes host cell actin polymerization , which helps the bacterium to reach near the cell membrane. Finally, it migrates to the adjacent epithelial cells/ macrophages by direct cell-to-cell spread, mediated by listeriopods . Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 698.

195.q: Periodontal disease form of actinomycosis is caused mainly by:
195.e: Dental caries and periodontal diseases: Mainly caused by naeslundii and A. odontolyticus. Oral-cervicofacial actinomycosis: This is the most common form, usually presented as a painless, slow growing, hard mass with cutaneous fistulas, a condition commonly known as lumpy jaw. Thoracic actinomycosis may present as cavitary lesions and pleural effusion. Abdominal form: It occurs due to spillage of intestinal flora secondary to bowel surgery or other conditions of bowel such as appendicitis. Pelvic form: It occurs following intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUCDs) insertion. Brain abscesses. Bone destruction and soft tissue infections. Disseminated form: It may occur due to hematogenous spread. Lungs and liver are the common sites; where multiple nodules are formed. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 543.

Diphtheria is disease of childhood, it can be of various types. Faucial, cutaneous etc. Faucial is most common. In his patient has white to grey membrane on tonsil which bleeds on touch. Treatment of Diphtheria is diphtheria antitoxin is to be given. It is made up of antibodies used in the treatment of diphtheria. Dose is as below. Less than 48 hrs duration Pharyngeal/laryngeal - 20000 to 40000 units. Nasopharyngeal - 40000 to 60000 units More than 72 hrs duration 80000 to 120000 units. So all the options given are not true. Key Takeaways: Diphtheria Antitoxin (DAT) neutralizes circulating toxin Given along with antibiotics (penicillin/erythromycin) Dose depends on severity and duration of symptoms

195.q: Which of the following corynebacterium species causes endocarditis in bone marrow transplant patients and to which drug it is sensitive to?
195.e: C.Jeikeium: It is a lipophilic species, colonizing the skin of hospitalised patients. It can cause bacteremia, endocarditis and meningitis. especially in immunocompromised hosts. It is usually multidrug resistant, responsive to only vancomycin. U.urealyticum: It is skin commensal, rarely causes urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis) and alkaline encrusted cystitis (struvite stones in alkaline urine) in immunocompromised and renal transplant patients Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 605

195.q: An elderly female patient with thyroid carcinoma metastasized to the lungs became seriously ill following the initiation of chemotherapy. The patient was admitted with symptoms of generalized convulsion and an altered level of consciousness and was treated empirically with meropenem, amikacin and linezolid injection. Cultures of blood and cerebrospinal fluid revealed Listeria monocytogenes on day 5 post-admission. Along With immune compression, which of the following is a major risk factor for this infection?
195.e: Listeriosis is caused by \Listeria monocytogenes, which is a food-borne pathogen that can cause serious infections, particularly in neonates, pregnant women and elderly people. It is also a ubiquitous saprophyte and known to cause epizootic disease in birds and animals. Listeriosis is common among extremes of age (neonate and old age). Use of proton pump inhibitors increases the risk by reducing the gastric acid mediated killing of Listeria. Other risk factors: Pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk. Due to its ability to survive refrigeration (4°C), it is commonly found in stored foods especially aged soft cheeses, packaged meats, milk and cold salads. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 698.

195.q: Intracellular survival of listeria monocytogenes is mediated by:
195.e: Pathogenesis of listeriosis: Intracellular survival: After entry into the intestinal epithelium, it survives inside the host cell, mainly due to lysis of phagosome by forming pores (mediated by listeriolysin O ) Then it causes host cell actin polymerization, which helps the bacterium to reach near the cell membrane. Finally, it migrates to the adjacent epithelial cells/ macrophages by direct cell-to-cell spread, mediated by listeriopods. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 698.

195.q: A farmer suffered a wound on the dorsum of his foot. It later involved the subcutaneous tissue and became a discharging ulcer. Microscopy reveals gram-positive branching filaments. Identify the organism.
195.e: Explanation: Sporothrix (Option B) Patients with sporotrichosis will usually present with a history of thorn prick followed by ulcers/pustules formation at the trauma site and lymphadenopathy. Histoplasma (Option C) is caused by bat or bird droppings and affects the reticuloendothelial system. Candida (Option D) on microscopy, candida will appear as both buds and pseudohyphae forms.

195.q: A butcher presented with seal finger. What is the drug of choice to treat seal finger?
195.e: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is a gram-positive bacillus that causes erysipeloid ; characterized by violaceous swelling with severe pain, but no pus; which differentiates it from staphylococcal and streptococcal erysipelas where pus is seen at the infection site. Most common site is fingers (called " seal finger" and "whale finger" ). Transmission: It usually infects animal handlers ( abattoir workers, butchers) and fishermen; transmitted by direct inoculation from animals or animal products. Treatment: Penicillin G is the drug of choice for severe infections. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 547.

196.q: Which cleaning agent is recommended for effectively eliminating Clostridium difficile spores from environmental surfaces?
196.e: C. Sodium hypochlorite (bleach): This agent is highly effective at killing C. difficile spores, making it the recommended choice for disinfection in environments where C. difficile is present. Why Not Others: A. Alcohol-based disinfectants: These are ineffective against C. difficile spores, as they do not have sporicidal properties. B. Hydrogen peroxide: While it has some antimicrobial activity, it is not as effective as sodium hypochlorite for specifically eliminating C. difficile spores. D. Quaternary ammonium compounds: These compounds lack efficacy against C. difficile spores, making them unsuitable for this purpose. Key Takeaway: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) is the recommended disinfectant for eliminating C. difficile spores from surfaces, ensuring effective infection control. Tags : good to know Reference: CDC guidelines on disinfection for C. difficile.

196.q: Which serotype of botulinum toxin is known for being the most severe in human disease?
196.e: Serotype A : This serotype is known for being the most severe and is the one most commonly associated with human botulism. Why Not Others : Serotype B does cause disease but lacks the severity associated with serotype A . Serotype E is less severe and not the primary concern in human botulism cases. Serotype G is not recognized for its severity in human infections, unlike serotype A . Key Takeaway : Serotype A of botulinum toxin is the most severe and is commonly linked to human disease . Tags : neet 2020 Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-40 Food poisoning pp-397.

Pseudomembranous colitis is caused by Clostridioides difficile which is an obligate anerobic gram positive spore forming bacilli. The important risk factors associated with it are Prolonged Antimicrobial use. Prolonged hospital stay Old age Intestinal surgery Antacid treatment Reference: Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 492-493

196.q: Chinese restaurant syndrome is associated with which of the following organism?
196.e: Bacillus cereus is a normal inhabitant of soil and can be isolated from vegetables, meat and poultry. Food poisoning with emetic toxin is associated with Chinese fried rice. It is a preformed toxin.The incubation period is 1-5 hours. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.494

196.q: What type of toxins does Clostridium difficile produce?
196.e: Pathogenic strains of clostridium difficile produces 2 distinct toxins.Toxin A is an enterotoxin and Toxin B is a cytotoxin.Both are high molecular weight capable of binding to specific receptors on the intestinal mucosal cells. Tags : neet 2020 Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-72 Miscellaneous Bacterial Infections of Gastrointestinal System pp-422-423.

196.q: Which clostridial species is most commonly associated with gas gangrene?
