196.e: Clostridium novyi : While this species can cause gas gangrene, it is less common compared to C. perfringens. Clostridium histolyticum : This species is rarely implicated in gas gangrene cases. Clostridium perfringens : This is the most common etiological agent of gas gangrene, accounting for about 60% of cases . Clostridium sordellii : Although associated with other infections, it is not the primary cause of gas gangrene. Why Not Others : Clostridium novyi and Clostridium histolyticum are less prevalent causes of gas gangrene. Clostridium sordellii is linked to different types of infections, not gas gangrene. Key Takeaway : Clostridium perfringens is the most common pathogen responsible for gas gangrene . Tags : neet 2020 Reference: Etiological agents of gas gangrene.

196.q: Which of the following is the primary mode of transmission for Clostridium difficile?
196.e: C. Fecal-oral route: This is the primary mode of transmission, as C. difficile spores can be ingested through contaminated surfaces, hands, or food, leading to infection. Why Not Others: A. Airborne droplets: This is not a primary transmission route for C. difficile; the spores are not spread through the air. B. Contaminated water: While water can harbor pathogens, it is not the main transmission pathway for C. difficile. D. Vector-borne transmission: This mode is not relevant to C. difficile, as it does not rely on vectors like insects for transmission. Key Takeaway: C. difficile is primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route, underscoring the need for stringent hand hygiene and effective surface disinfection to prevent infection. Tags : fmge 2021 Reference: CDC guidelines on Clostridium difficile infection control.

196.q: Gastrointestinal enteritis necroticans is caused by?
196.e: Enteritis necroticans/Nectrotising enteritis refers to gas gangrene of bowel, which is characterized by ischaemic necrosis of jejunum and gas in tissue plane. It is also referred to as Pigbel. It is caused by C.perfringens type C strains producing beta toxin. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.493-94

197.q: Primary pulmonary TB is defined as the initial exogenous infection with tubercle bacilli. What is the name of the complex when the primary complex gets calcified?
197.e: Ranke Complex is formed when the primary complex gets calcified. Ghon focus refers to the initial nodular cavitations. When these involve hilar lymph nodes, it is called primary complex. Simon focus is the hematogenous seeding of apex of the lung in post primary TB. reactivated Simon focus with central caseation is called Assman's focus. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 625

197.q: A patient presented to the urology department with urinary frequency, dysuria, nocturia and abdominal pain. The patient is afebrile at the moment but complains of low grade fever at night. Upon urinalysis,pus cells were found but no bacterial agent was isolated. Imaging revealed a thimble bladder. Which specimen should be collected next for establishing a diagnosis?
197.e: The given clinical features, along with sterile pyuria in urinalysis raises a suspicion of genitourinary TB. It is seen when tubercular bacilli are disseminated hematogenously. It is diagnosed by collecting 3 early morning urine samples and processing them via culture in MGIT or LJ media or Genexpert Radiology may show strictures or perinephric abscesses. It is treated well with ATT Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 752

197.q: Isoniazid is one of the first line drugs for the treatment of tuberculosis. Which of the following layers of the cell wall does it inhibit, that also gives Mycobacteria its acid fastness?
197.e: Mycolic acid layer is the principal constituent of the mycobacterial cell wall, made up of long chain fatty acids attached to arabinogalactan. It confers very low permeability to the cell wall and is responsible for acid fastness. Lipoarabinomannan facilitates the survival of tubercle bacilli within the macrophages. It is also used as a target antigen for the TB diagnosis. Peptidoglycan maintains the shape and rigidity of the cell. Lipopolysaccharide is found in gram negative bacteria. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 624

Ans. Pulmonary hamartoma Popcorn calcification o Popcorn calcification is a cluster of sharply defined, irregularly lobulated, calcification, usually in a pulmonary nodule. o Popcorn calcification is characteristic of hamartoma on chest X-ray examination. o It may also be seen in mediastinal lymph nodes of acute histoplasmosis. Egg-shell calcification o Egg-shell calcification means peripheral rim calcification of lymph nodes: o It is seen in: N Silicosis (most common cause) (vi) Histoplasmosis (vii) Tuberculosis (ii) Coal worker pneumoconiosis (v) Sarcoidosis (viii) Coccidiodomycosis (iii) Lymphoma following radiotherapy (vi) Progressive massive fibrosis

197.q: Which of the following mycobacteria is microaerophilic?
197.e: All mycobacteria are obligate aerobes except M Bovis, which is microaerophilic Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 23

197.q: Smear microscopy for the detection of Mycobacteria species is done by the Ziehl Neelsen staining method. One of its modifications is the Kinyoun's acid fast staining. Which of the following is not an advantage of this method over the ZN method?
o: Phenol concentration in carbol fuschin is decreased
Duration of carbol fuschin staining is more
197.e: The concentration of phenol in carbol fuschin is increased in the Kinyoun's method. It is also called the cold method as heating is not required. This method doesn't use fluorescent dyes. However, fluorescent staining with auramine rhodamine stains can also be done wherein the bacilli appear as brilliant yellow against a dark background. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 628

197.q: Which strain is used for vaccination against Tuberculosis in India?
197.e: In India, WHO recommended Danish 1331 strain of BCG is used. BCG is available in lyophilized form, and should be reconstituted before administration. This is done by using normal saline as diluent. Distilled water is never used as it is irritant. Once reconstituted; it has to be administered within 1 hour Administration of BCG:0.1 mL (0.1 mg TU) of BCG vaccine is administered above the insertion of left deltoid by intradermal route, using a 26 gauge tuberculin syringe. BCG is directly given to the newborn soon after birth. If not given at birth it can be given later, maximum up to 2 years. Edmonston Zagreb strain is used in measles vaccine Oka strain is used in chicken pox vaccine SA 14-14-4 is used in JE vaccine Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 635

197.q: A 25-year-old male presents with fever, cough, and night sweats. Further examination reveals increased respiratory rate, oral thrush and decreased breath sounds in the right middle lung field. Laboratory investigation report states a CD4 count of 60/L. The most likely underlying pathology is:
197.e: Normal CD4 count is 400/µL. Extremely low count of CD4+ T cells associated with Oral thrush is characteristic of HIV/AIDS. None of the other choices would be associated with this finding. Respiratory difficulties due to infection are frequently seen in HIV/AIDS patients. HIV weakens the immune system, increasing the risk of TB in people with HIV. HIV-TB coinfection is very common. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Chapter 19, Page Number 187-190.

198.q: Which of the following strains has been used for developing the leprosy vaccine?
198.e: The killed Mycobacterium indicus pranii vaccine has been developed in India in 2018. Trials have shown that if given in close contacts, cases can be brought down by 60% in 3 years Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 538

198.q: Which nerve is never involved in Leprosy?
198.e: The medial plantar nerve is never involved in leprosy. The most commonly involved nerve is ulnar followed by post auricular Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 535

198.q: Which is the earliest sensation lost in leprosy?
198.e: Since lepra bacilli grow in cooler areas, they invade cutaneous nerves first, hence thermal sensations are lost earlier. Reference- https://internationaltextbookofleprosy.org/chapter/neurological-manifestations-leprosy

198.q: 2 yrs duration in terms of leprosy is with regard to -
o: Post Rx surveillance of paucibacillary leprosy
Post Rx surveillance of multibacillary leprosy
198.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Post Rx surveillance of paucibacillary leprosy

198.q: Which of the following human pathogenic bacteria cannot be cultivated on artificial cell-free culture media?
198.e: Explanation: Mycobacterium leprae , the causative agent of leprosy (Hansen's disease) , is an obligate intracellular bacterium that cannot be grown on artificial culture media . It has never been consistently cultured in vitro. It is propagated in the footpads of mice or nine-banded armadillos for research purposes. Staphylococcus aureus, M. tuberculosis, S. pneumoniae a ll of these bacteria can be readily cultured on standard or enriched artificial laboratory media (e.g., blood agar, LJ medium, chocolate agar). (Options B, C and D ruled out) Key Takeaways: leprae is uncultivable on artificial media. Other notable uncultivable pathogens include Treponema pallidum and Rickettsia spp.

198.q: Which of the following is known as Johne's bacilli?
198.e: Mycobacterium paratuberculosis is known as Johne's bacilli Mycobacterium intracellulare is known as Battey's bacilli Mycobacterium leprae is known as Hansen's bacilli Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 34

198.q: How are live bacilli of Mycobacterium leprae typically characterized under the microscope?
o: Uniformly stained with parallel sides and round ends
Stained in clusters with irregular shapes
198.e: Uniformly stained with parallel sides and round ends : Correct ; live bacilli display a uniform stain with distinct parallel sides and round ends, appearing five times longer than wide. Why Not Others : Irregularly shaped with fragmented ends : Incorrect; this description is typical of dead bacilli rather than live ones. Stained in clusters with irregular shapes : Incorrect; live bacilli should be uniform and not clustered or irregularly shaped. Invisible in the smear : Incorrect; live bacilli are visible and identifiable using the Ziehl-Neelsen stain. Key Takeaway : Live M. leprae bacilli are characterized by being uniformly stained with parallel sides and round ends , facilitating their identification under the microscope. Tags : inicet 2020 Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-54-Leprosy , pp-536.

198.q: Which of the following Non-Tuberculous Mycobacteria species is commonly associated with pulmonary infections in immunocompetent individuals?
198.e: Mycobacterium avium complex : Correct ; this includes Mycobacterium avium and Mycobacterium intracellulare, which are associated with pulmonary infections in immunocompetent individuals. Why Not Others : Mycobacterium leprae : Misleading as it pertains only to leprosy, not respiratory issues. Mycobacterium tuberculosis : A known pathogen for tuberculosis, distinctly separate from NTM. Mycobacterium bovis : Primarily zoonotic and not typically linked to pulmonary disease in healthy individuals. Key Takeaway : The Mycobacterium avium complex is commonly linked to pulmonary infections in immunocompetent individuals, distinguishing it from other mycobacterial species. Tags : fmge 2021 Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-63, pp-623.

199.q: What is media used to differentiate EHEC from other E coli?
199.e: Sorbitol Mac Conkey agar is used to differentiate EHEC from other E.coli. It does not ferment sorbitol and produces pale colonies. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.482

199.q: Which of the following is a motile bacterium?
199.e: Proteus spp. are motile by peritrichous flagella. Clostridium perfringens is the only clostridium species that produces a capsule in animal tissues and it is non-motile. Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Bacillus anthracis are non-motile. Arrangement - example Monotrichous - V.cholerae Lophotrichous - Psuedomonas fluorescens Amphitrichous - Alcaligenes faecalis Amphilophotrichous - Spirillium minus Peritrichous - Salmonella typhi Referece: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 21

199.q: A patient is diagnosed with an infection caused by Enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC) O157:H7. In this serotype designation, what does the "H" denote?
199.e: Explanation: The "H" antigen in E. coli serotyping refers to the flagellar antigen, which determines the motility of the bacteria. O157:H7 is a strain of Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) known for producing Shiga toxin, leading to hemorrhagic colitis and Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS). Serotyping of E. coli: "O" antigen → Somatic (LPS) antigen (Option D) "H" antigen → Flagellar antigen (Option C) "K" antigen → Capsular antigen (Option A) Fimbriae (Option B) aid in bacterial adhesion , but they are not part of E. coli serotyping as the "H" antigen.

199.q: Which of the following E.coli species produces a toxin which acts by inhibiting 28s rRNA of the 60s subunit, thus inhibiting protein synthesis?
199.e: Enterohemorrhagic E.Coli commonly produces Shiga like toxin or verocytotoxin, which is the most common cause of HUS in the world. Its mechanism of action is similar to Shiga toxin ie, inhibition of protein synthesis by inhibiting 28s subunit of ribosomes. ETEC, which causes traveller's diarrhea produces Labile toxin,which increases cAMP and Stable toxin, which increases cGMP and causes watery diarrhea DAEC also causes watery diarrhea and shows slow adhesion on Hep-2 cell assay UPEC is implicated in E.coli associated UTI. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 400.

199.q: Which of the following is true about urease producing bacteria?
o: Urease acidifies the urine creating neutrophils inactive
Acidification of the urine can lead to precipitation of struvite stones
Morganella morganii is a urea-splitting bacteria
Are commensals that prevent hepatic encephalopathy
199.e: Bacterial urease alkalises urine, and urease-producing bacteria are implicated in the development of infection-induced urinary stones. The formation of struvite stones occurs when urine pH increases and ammonia production increases, decreasing the solubility of phosphate. Proteus spp., M. morganii and Klebsiella pneumoniae are urea-splitting bacteria E.coli is the most common cause of lower urinary tract infections, it is not associated with significant alkalinisation, nor is infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The production of excessive amounts of ammonia by bacterial urease, and its subsequent re-absorption into the systemic circulation, can result in hyperammonaemia, a condition associated with hepatic encephalopathy. Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition pg 33

199.q: What is by far the Most common site of Proteus infection?
199.e: Proteus species are part of the colonic flora P. mirabilis causes 90% of Proteus infections, which occur in the community, LTCFs, and hospitals. By contrast, Proteus vulgaris and Proteus penneri are associated primarily with infections acquired in hospitals. Adhesins, flagella, IgA protease, and urease representing the principal known urovirulence factors. Clinical spectrum of Proteus infections: Urinary tract infections (most common) Pneumonia Nosocomial sinusitis Intra abdominal abscesses Biliary tract infection Surgical site infection Soft tissue infection (especially decubitus and diabetic ulcers) Osteomyelitis Bacteremia Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 161 Pg: 1278

200.e: Heterophile antibodies are typically detected in the Weil-Felix test, which is used to identify certain types of rickettsial infections. The Widal test is used for typhoid fever, and standard agglutination tests are used for various bacterial infections. Key Takeaway: The Weil-Felix test is associated with the detection of heterophile antibodies. Tag: Good to know Tag Line: Easy Reference: Apurva Shastri, Review of Microbiology and Immunology , chapter 12 on antigens – antibody reaction.PP-152.

200.q: Investigation of choice in 2nd and 3rd week of enteric fever is?
200.e: Principle: It is an agglutination test where H and 0 antibodies against S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A and B are detected and measured in the patient's sera by using O and H antigens. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.300-301

200.q: Recommended transport medium for stool specimen in a case of bacillary dysentery is:
200.e: Recommended transport medium for stool specimen is: Sach’s Buffered glycerol saline medium (when Salmonella spp. or Shigella spp. are suspected) Venkatraman Ramkrisnan (VR) medium/ Carry Blair (CB) medium (when Vibrio cholerae is suspected). Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 4, Pg 40-45

Ekiri syndrome is a complication seen in Shigellosis. It is most commonly seen in children. It is also called toxic encephalopathy and manifests as altered sensorium, seizures, delirium etc. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.481

200.q: A patient has a 2-week history of gradually worsening fever (step-ladder pattern), abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, and malaise. Which test is most appropriate for diagnosis at this stage?
200.e: Explanation: The clinical presentation is classic for enteric fever (typhoid fever caused by Salmonella Typhi). The optimal diagnostic test depends on the duration of illness (mnemonic: BASU ): Week 1: Blood culture (highest yield) (Option C ruled out) Week 2: Antibody test (Widal test) . Antibodies (O and H agglutinins) become detectable. Week 3: Stool culture (organism is shed in feces) (Option B ruled out) Week 4: Urine culture (Option D ruled out) At 2 weeks , the Widal test (demonstrating a rising antibody titer) is the most appropriate serological test. Key Takeaways: Use the BASU mnemonic for diagnosing enteric fever based on week of illness. Blood culture is best early; Widal test is best in the second week.

200.q: Which of the following culture media is specifically used for the identification of Salmonella?
200.e: Explanation: Wilson & Blair medium is a selective agar designed to isolate and identify Salmonella species, particularly Salmonella typhi . The medium contains brilliant green , which suppresses the growth of most other bacteria while allowing Salmonella to grow. It also facilitates identification based on distinctive colony morphology . Explanation of Other Options: PLET medium (Option A): Used for the isolation of Listeria monocytogenes , not Salmonella. BCYE medium (Option B): Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar is intended for Legionella species isolation, not for Salmonella. Stuart's medium (Option D): A transport medium for maintaining pathogen viability during specimen transport; it is not used for Salmonella isolation . Reference: Oxoid - Product Detail

200.q: A HIV patient presents with the history of nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, fever 1 day after consumption of hamburger at a local bakery.As the fever spikes increased, blood cultures were sent and it flagged positive for Salmonella enteritidis. What would be the appropriate treatment of choice in the following case?
200.e: In uncomplicated NTS gastroenteritis, treatment is conservative with fluid replacement. Antibiotic use is associated with increased rates of carriers and relapse, hence is limited to invasive cases only. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.480

200.q: A 30 year old male developed arthritis type knee pain 7 months after an episode of dysentery with Shigella. A diagnosis of reactive arthritis was made. Which HLA is commonly associated with this syndrome?
200.e: Patients expressing HLAB27 typically develop autoimmune reactive arthritis after shigellosis. It typically occurs in males less than 40 years of age. The clinical features include early morning arthritis, ocular inflammation and urethritis, classically remembered as can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree. HLAB54 is associated with Behcet's disease and HLADR04 with Rheumatoid arthritis. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 434

201.q: Cholera is known to cause diarrhea through its interaction with specific receptors in the human body. Which of the following is known to make it easier for cholera toxin to enter the body through the intestinal mucosa?
201.e: Explanation: Cholera toxin is produced by Vibrio cholerae and is the main factor responsible for watery diarrhea in cholera. The toxin attaches to receptors on the intestinal epithelial surface and enters the cells. The specific receptor is GM1 ganglioside , a glycosphingolipid located in the intestinal cell membrane. Binding to GM1 initiates endocytosis of the toxin. Inside the cell, the toxin disrupts ion transport, causing massive fluid loss and diarrhea. Explanation of other options: GLUT1 (Option A): Facilitates glucose transport across membranes; not a receptor for cholera toxin. GM2 ganglioside (Option B): A glycosphingolipid, but not the binding site for cholera toxin. Cephalin (Option C): A membrane phospholipid, unrelated to cholera toxin entry. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3089049/

201.q: A 25 yr old man presents with history of diarrhea and fever since 5 days.There is a history of consumption of uncooked crabs and oysters on the trip to Bangkok. On culture ,it showed swarming on blood agar and the organism was found to be motile. Identify the culture media which is blood agar with high salt content which shows beta hemolysis
201.e: Halophilic vibrios can withstand higher salt concentration (>6%) in contrast to V. cholerae, which can tolerate upto 6%. They are widespread in marine environment. Kanagawa phenomenon: It causes hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar (a special type of high salt blood agar). Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.487

201.q: DOC for chemoprophylaxis of cholera is?
201.e: Tetracycline is the drug of choice and is indicated in household contacts during epidemic.
Ans. is 'd' i.e., Alkaline peptone water om

201.q: An 18-year girl was playing in a slowly moving stream when she cut her foot on a sharp object. Three days later, she was brought to the emergency room because of pain and swelling at the site of the wound and drainage of pus from it. The most likely cause of the infection is
201.e: Vibrio vulnificus: Cutaneous Infection Apart from sepsis, V. vulnificus can also cause primary wound infection (Vulnificus is Latin word for "wound maker" ). Characterized by painful erythematous swelling or cellulitis or even vesicular, bullous or necrotic lesions. It generally affects people without underlying disease, in contrast to sepsis, which is usually observed in patients with underlying disease such as liver disease, iron overload or immunosuppression. Wound infections can also be produced by Vibrio parahaemolyticus. Other options are less likely in comparison to vibrio vulnificus to cause wound infection. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 417

201.q: You are doing a presentation on Vibrio. You come across a species of vibrio which shows 'Kanagawa' phenomena and grows in a halophilic media of upto 8% salt solution. Which of the following vibrio species are you most likely referring to?
201.e: Parahemolyticus shows kanagawa phenomenon on Wagatsuma agar. It grows in upto 8% salt solution, shows swarming growth on blood agar. It is known to cause invasive diarrhea. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 417

201.q: You are studying biochemical reactions of bacteria. You perform the string test where a suspension of the organism in 0.5% sodium deoxycholate produces a viscous mucoid string when lifted with an inoculating loop. Which of the following reactions and cultural characteristics are shown by this bacterium (Vibrio cholerae)? i. Cholera red reaction ii. Kanagawa phenomenon iii. Black colonies on Tinsdale media iv. Yellow colonies on TCBS agar v. School of fish appearance on wet mount
201.e: The above image depicts string test, shown by Vibrio Cholerae. A suspension of the bacteria, along with bile salts gives a positive test. Along with this, Vibrio also shows a positive nitrate reduction test. On a wet mount, it gives a FISH IN STREAM appearance. It is a non- fastidious bacteria. Transport media include autoclaved sea water and VR media. Enrichment media includes Alkaline peptone water and Monsur's taurocholate tellurite agar. Selective media are TCBS, where V.cholerae show yellow colonies and Monsur's GTTA. they are late lactose fermenters. Other options- Kanagawa phenomena is shown by V. parahaemolyticus Black colonies on Tinsdale media are shown by C. diphtheria School of fish appearance is shown by H.ducreyi, while V.cholera shows Fish in stream Appearance Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 414

201.q: Which of the following conditions is required for growing microaerophilic bacteria like Campylobacter?
201.e: Campylobacter Growth Conditions Microaerophilic Environment: Campylobacter species thrive in a specific atmospheric condition of 5% O2, 85% N2, and 10% CO2 . Unsuitable Conditions: Other oxygen levels or gas compositions do not support the growth of microaerophilic bacteria like Campylobacter. KEY TAKE AWAY: Campylobacter, Helicobacter and Actinomyces Israeli - microaerophilic, require- 5% O2 , 85% N2 and 10% CO2 . Tags: inicet 2022 Reference: Shashtri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology . 3rd Edition. Chapter: (General Bacteriology), Page no. 25-51.

202.q: Organism most likely responsible for ventilation associated pneumonia is:
202.e: Baumannii causes widespread hospital infections such as: Ventilator associated pneumonia Central line associated bloodstream infection Post-neurosurgical meningitis Catheter- associated UTI Wound and soft tissue infections Infections in burn patients Acinetobacter can be grouped into several genomospecies. A. baumannii is the most pathogenic species. Most other species such as A.calcoaceticus and A. lwoffii are rarely pathogenic to man. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 646

202.q: In a Microbiology laboratory you were asked to differentiate Burkholderia pseudomallei and Burkholderia mallei on the basis of biochemical properties. Which of the following test would be used for the same?
202.e: Mallei differs from B. pseudomallei in being non-motile and oxidase negative. 203.q: Acellular pertussis vaccine is composed of: a) Pertussis toxoid b) FHA c) Pertactin d) IgA e) Adhesins f) cAMP
203.e: Acellular Pertussis Vaccine: It is composed of pertussis toxoid and 2 or more other bacterial components such as FHA, pertactin or fimbriae. Though the efficacy is same as the WC vaccine, it is associated with fewer side effects as compared with the latter and can be safely given after 5–6 years. It is available as DaPT (along with diphtheria and tetanus toxoid). It is recommended for older children who have missed their primary doses of DPT. 203.q: Which of the following special factors are required for Haemophilus? A. Hemin B. Christmas factor C. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide D. Fibrinogen E. Thrombin F. Ca2+ G. Fe2+
203.e: Haemophilus requires two accessory growth factors (factor X and V) in blood for their growth. Factor X is a hemin, present freely in blood. Factor V is nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD), which is present inside RBCs. It is also produced by some bacteria, such as Staphylococcus aureus. Growth surrounding X and XV disks only: Produced by species that require X factor, but not V factor; examples include H. ducreyi and A. aphrophilus. Growth surrounding V and XV disks only: Produced by species that require X factor, but not V factor; examples include H. parainfluenzae, H. parahaemolyticus and A. paraphrophilus. Growth surrounding combined XV disk only: Produced by species that require both X and V factors; examples include: H. influenzae, H. aegyptius and H. haemolyticus. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 612

203.q: Which growth factor is essential for the growth of Haemophilus influenzae in culture media?
203.e: Hemin (Factor X): Correct - Haemophilus influenzae specifically requires hemin (Factor X) for growth, which must be supplied in enriched culture media, as it cannot synthesize it. Why Not Others : Vitamin B12: Incorrect - While important for many bacteria, it is not necessary for the growth of Haemophilus influenzae . Folic acid: Incorrect - Although it may be involved in metabolic processes, it is not the primary growth factor required by Haemophilus influenza . Sodium chloride: Incorrect - Sodium chloride is used for osmotic balance but is not a specific growth factor for Haemophilus influenzae . Key Takeaway: Hemin (Factor X) is crucial for the growth of Haemophilus influenzae in culture media, as this organism cannot synthesize it. Tags: good to know Tag Line: EASY Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher, Chapter 61, pp 610.

203.q: A 3 year old boy came to Pediatric OPD with complaints of low-grade fever, cough and vomiting. His vitals are normal and growth is appropriate for his age. Which of the following media is used to isolate the given bacteria? i. PPLO agar ii. Bordet-Gengou agar iii. PLET media iv. Regan Lowe media v. Pike's media

204.q: Drug of choice for rabbit fever is:
204.e: Tularemia, also known as “rabbit fever,” is a disease caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis. Tularemia is typically found in animals, especially rodents, rabbits, and hares. Gentamicin is considered as the drug of choice,given 5mg/kg for 7-10 days. Doxycycline or ciprofloxacin can be given as alternatives. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 810

204.q: Which of the following subspecies of Francisella tularensis is most virulent for humans?
204.e: Tularensis has four subspecies: tularensis, holarctica, novicida, and mediasiatica. The first three subspecies are found in North America, whereas subspecies mediasiatica is found in central Asia. Subspecies tularensis is the most common and the most virulent among all. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 808

204.q: Which part of bacteria is most antigenic ?
204.e: Ans. is d i.e., Lipids Proteins are most immunogenic, while lipids & nucleic acids are least immunogenic. 204.q: A 29-year-old woman who worked as a research assistant in a veterinary microbiology laboratory complained of intermittent fever, anorexia, profuse sweating, malaise, headache, normo-tensive and muscle pain especially of the neck and shoulder, and arthralgia for 3 d. She was one of the 7 laboratory workers who were involved in a research on isolation of B. melitensis from goats for the past 6 months. Which of the following is not the mode of transmission of this organism?
204.e: B.melitensis is the most pathogenic species, followed by B. abortus and B. suis. Human infection with other species is extremely rare. Transmission: Brucellosis is zoonotic, transmitted from infected animals to man by various modes: Direct contact: The most common route is direct contact of abraded skin or mucosa with the infected animal tissue, blood, urine, vaginal discharge or placenta Food-borne: By ingestion of unpasteurized milk or dairy products or undercooked meat from infected animals or rarely vegetables or water contaminated with animal excreta Air-borne: By inhalation of dust or aerosols in the infected cowshed or slaughterhouses Person-to-person spread is extremely rare; through breast milk or by tissue transplantation or blood transfusions. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 316

204.q: Which of the following methods are not used for diagnosing brucellosis in animals?
204.e: Brucellosis is diagnosed in animals by various methods such as: Milk ring test and Rose Bengal card test; detecting antibodies in infected milk. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 318

204.q: What is the WHO regimen for Brucellosis?
204.e: Various regimens are recommended for the treatment of brucellosis. Standard regimen in adults: Gentamicin for 7 days plus doxycycline for 6 weeks. Streptomycin can be given alternative to gentamicin. WHO regimen in adults: Rifampicin for 6 weeks plus doxycycline for 6 weeks Relapse or treatment failure occurs in 5–10% of cases. For CNS involvement: Ceftriaxone is added to the regimen and treatment is prolonged for 3–6 months. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 319

205.q: Two girls in the same class are diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. Their 12-year-old close friend is in fear of contracting disease. What advice should be given to her-
o: No vaccine needed as exposure has already occurred.
205.e: Meningococcal meningitis can spread from one person to other. Because it stays in nasopharynx of person. Now in the given case 2 girls in the same class are already diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. Their friend must get two dose of conjugate vaccine to prevent getting infection. Incorrect options : Option A is wrong two dose of polysaccharide vaccine. Option C i s wrong Single dose of meningococcal vaccine. Because meningococcal vaccine has two dose not one. Option D is wrong, vaccine can help in spreading of infection. No matter exposure has occurred or not, vaccine can always help. Key Takeaways: Conjugate vaccines (MCV4) are preferred over polysaccharide vaccines (MPSV4). Close contacts of meningococcal meningitis cases require vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis. Meningococcal conjugate vaccine induces stronger, long-lasting immunity and reduces carriage.

205.q: Which of the following is not the content of the Modified New York city medium used for the culture of Neisseria?
o: Above all are the contents of modified new york city medium

205.q: Meningococcal vaccine is ineffective against which of the following serogroups?
205.e: Meningococcal polysaccharide vaccines are currently formulated as either bivalent (serogroups A and C) or quadrivalent (serogroups A, C, Y, and Wl35). Dose: 50 µg of each polysaccharide antigen per dose is used, administered as two doses, 2-3 months apart to children of 3-18 months of age or a single dose to older children or adults. No vaccine is available for serogroup B because: Capsule of serogroup B (made up of sialic acid) is less immunogenic. lt is also encephalitogenic due to expression of similar cross reactive antigens on neural cells. Not given below 3 years. Conjugated vaccines can be given below three years. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 697

205.q: Which of the following is a component uniquely found in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria?
205.e: Explanation: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) , also known as endotoxin , is a unique and defining component of the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria . It consists of lipid A (the toxic component), core polysaccharide, and O antigen. It is a major virulence factor and potent activator of the host innate immune system. Explanation of other options: Lipoproteins (Option A): Found in both gram-positive (e.g., Braun's lipoprotein) and gram-negative bacteria. Peptidoglycan (Option B): A core component of the cell wall in both gram-positive (thick layer) and gram-negative (thin layer) bacteria. Teichoic acid (Option D): A component found embedded in the thick peptidoglycan layer of gram-positive bacteria; it is absent in gram-negative bacteria. Key Takeaways: LPS (endotoxin) is specific to the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria. Teichoic acid is specific to gram-positive bacteria.

205.q: A 25-year-old woman has a history of repeated infections with Neisseria species, including Neisseria meningitidis. She reports several episodes of meningitis and septicemia. Complement testing reveals a deficiency in C5, C6, C7, C8, and C9. Which complement deficiency is most likely contributing to the patient’s recurrent Neisseria infections?
205.e: The deficiency of C5 through C9 components affects the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC), which is essential for the lysis of certain bacteria, including Neisseria species. This deficiency makes individuals highly susceptible to infections caused by Neisseria, as the MAC is crucial for killing these Gram-negative bacteria. Key Takeaway: Deficiency in C5 through C9 components results in an increased risk of Neisseria infections due to the impaired ability to form the membrane attack complex. Tags: INICET | must know Reference: Shastri, A. (2023). Immunology: Chapter 13on Complement System, pp. 163-167.

206.q: Identify the true statements for C. psittaci. 1. Is sensitive to sulfonamide. 2. man-to-man transmission present. 3. Causes psittacosis by inhalation route. 4. Exclusive human pathogen. 5. Forms diffuse vacuolated inclusions without glycogen matrix.

Disease caused by it: Psittacosis (Atypical interstitial pneumonia). Transmission is by inhalation route - pet birds (parrots) and poultry (turkeys and ducks) No man-to-man transmission. 206.q: What is used to promote contact between chlamydiae and the cells in cell lines, thus increasing the chance of isolation?
206.e: Pre-treatment of cell lines with diethylaminoethanol (DEAE) dextran or centrifugation after inoculation of specimen should be done to promote contact between chlamydiae and the cells, thus increasing the chance of isolation. 206.q: Cell wall structure is absent in:

206.q: All of the following indicates chlamydia to be a bacteria except:
o: Is susceptible to a wide range of antibacterial agents
206.e: Chlamydiae were once thought to be viruses because of possessing a few viral properties, such as: They are obligate intracellular. They cannot be grown in artificial media. Filterable - small enough to pass through bacterial filters. Produce intracytoplasmic inclusions. However, chlamydiae are now confirmed to be bacteria, because they have many other properties similar to that of bacteria, as follows: Possess both DNA and RNA. Their cell wall is similar to that of gram-negative bacteria (although they lack peptidoglycan layer). Multiply by binary fission. Susceptible to a wide range of antibacterial agents. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 766

207.q: A 20-year-old female with a history of penicillin allergy unknown to her treating doctor, was given a single injection of penicillin for the treatment of syphilis. Within minutes, she developed diffuse urticaria, tachycardia, and hypo-tension. This patient has experienced:
207.e: This patient displays the hallmarks of a classical anaphylactic reaction to penicillin. Anergy is the impairment of effector immune responsiveness. Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity is most often localized to tissues bearing epitopes to which the antibody binds. Contact sensitivity results from the epicutaneous application of a reactive antigen/hapten; in the present question, the antigen (penicillin) was administered intramuscularly. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

207.q: Painless genital ulcer in male with everted margin is seen in ?
207.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e.,Syphilis [Ref Harrison 18th/e p. 1382, Jawetz 22"/e p. 642] Painless indurated ulcer with everted margins, h/o of sexual exposure and lack of systemic symptoms favours the diagnosis of syphilis.

207.q: A 27-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant presents to the Obstetrics clinic for prenatal care. She has a history of treatment for syphilis 4 years previously. The results of serologic tests for syphilis are as follows: Non treponemal test RPR: Non-Reactive Treponemal test (TP-PA) reactive Which of the following statements is most correct?
o: The baby is at high risk for congenital syphilis
The mother needs a lumbar puncture and a VDRL test for her CSF for neurosyphilis
The mother needs to be treated again for syphilis
The mother's previous treatment for syphilis was effective
207.e: Non-treponemal tests, such as VDRL and RPR are preferred over treponemal tests for monitoring response to treatment. Antibody titers of treponemal tests remain elevated even after clinical improvement. VDRL has to be done at 3 month's intervals for at least 1 year. For primary and secondary syphilis: Following clinical improvement, there should be at least a fourfold decline in the titer by the third or fourth month and non-reactive by 12 months. For latent or late syphilis, or patients with multiple episodes of syphilis: It may show a gradual decline in titer, low titers may persist for years. Here, Non treponemal tests are negative hence the treatment to the mother was effective. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 761

207.q: Smith Noguchi's media is used for cultivation of:
207.e: Spirochetes are spiral shaped bacteria. Medically important spirochetes are Treponema, Borrelia and Leptospira. Smith Noguchi's medium is used for cultivation of non-pathogenic Treponemes (Pathogenic Treponemes cannot be grown in artificial culture medium) Reference : Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 4, Pg 40-45

207.q: An investigator studying patients with symptoms of arthritis detects a non-enveloped virus with a single-stranded DNA genome in the serum of a pregnant patient. Fetal infection with this pathogen is most likely to cause which of the following manifestations?
207.e: Parvovirus B19, can lead to the development of hydrops fetalis during pregnancy. Infection of RBCs by this virus induces apoptosis and massive destruction of erythroid lineage cells, causing severe anemia and heart failure in the fetus (secondary to excessive fluid accumulation within the fetal vascular compartments). This often-fatal condition can also be caused by chromosomal abnormalities, inborn errors of metabolism, Rh incompatibility, lymphatic dysplasia, and Treponema pallidum infection. Other Options: Chorioretinitis is seen with Toxoplasma gondii or CMV infection Sensorineural deafness is seen with CMV, Rubella or Syphilis Vesicular rash is seen with HSV2 infection Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

207.q: Which is the most likely presentation of leptospirosis?
207.e: High fever, myalgia, and headache are common clinical manifestations of leptospirosis. Leptospirosis can be associated with acute abdominal pain, sometimes mimicking acute cholecystitis; however, diarrhea rarely occurs. Localized seizure would be an atypical presentation of leptospirosis, which is generally not considered to be associated with focal neurologic findings. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 184 Pg: 1419 Goldman Cecil's Medicine 26th Ed. Chap 307 pg. 1999

208.q: Choose the correct statement with respect to nucleic acid replication in viruses
o: All DNA viruses replicate in Cytoplasm except Poxvirus
All DNA viruses replicate in nucleus except Poxvirus
All RNA viruses replicate in nucleus except Retrovirus
All RNA viruses replicate in cytoplasm except Papillomavirus
208.e: In DNA viruses, the DNA replication occurs in the nucleus except in poxviruses, which synthesize DNA in the cytoplasm. In RNA viruses, the RNA replication occurs in the cytoplasm except in retroviruses and orthomyxoviruses, which synthesize RNA in the nucleus. Option D is incorrect because Papilloma virus is not an RNA virus Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 83

208.q: Which of the following families includes non-enveloped RNA viruses that cause gastroenteritis?
208.e: Reoviridae is a family of non-enveloped RNA viruses that includes rotavirus, a major cause of gastroenteritis. The other options either include DNA viruses or non-gastroenteritis related RNA viruses. Key Takeaway: Identifying Reoviridae as a family of non-enveloped RNA viruses associated with gastroenteritis is essential for understanding and managing outbreaks of this illness, especially in children. Rotavirus vaccination is associated with intussusception. Tags: neet 2023 Difficulty Level: Medium CDC Reference: CDC - Rotavirus

208.q: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of a red, itchy, burning rash on her vulva. She has had three similar episodes over the last two years that have all self-resolved. Genitourinary examination shows a small area of erythema with an overlying cluster of vesicles on the inside surface of the vulva. Latent infection of which of the following is most likely responsible for this patient's recurrent symptoms?
208.e: This patient with acute onset of itchy, burning rash and grouped vesicles on genital examination has recurrent genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Latency and reactivation in the dorsal root ganglion of host sensory neurons is the mechanism underlying the recurrent symptoms seen in herpes simplex virus 1 and 2 infection. Under certain conditions (e.g., immunodeficiency, stress, trauma), HSV may reactivate and multiply in the dorsal root ganglia of the trigeminal (HSV-1) or sacral (HSV-2) nerves, producing recurrent flares, as are seen in this patient. Other Options: TB undergoes latency in Macrophages HIV goes into latency in Lymphocytes JC virus undergoes latency in Astrocytes Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

209.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Plaque assay Plaque assay and Pock assay are quantitative infective assays.

209.q: A 40-year-old female with hepatitis C viral infection presents with decreased renal function, hypertension, and anemia. Laboratory findings decreased serum C3 and urine sediment contains leukocytes, erythrocytes, and red blood cell casts. Her renal biopsy demonstrates changes consistent with glomerulonephritis. These findings suggest which type of hypersensitivity?
o: Type 1 hypersensitivity mediated by CD4+ T cells
Type 4 hypersensitivity mediated by IgG and sometimes IgM
209.e: Glomerulonephritis is often associated with immune complex deposition, a type III hypersensitivity. Red blood cell casts are indicative of glomerulonephritis, and reduced C3 levels indicate a high level of cleavage and activation of C3. Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE, not by CD4+ T cells. Type II hypersensitivity responses usually involve IgG. Type IV hypersensitivities do not involve antibodies. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

209.q: A 35-year-old male doctor presents after a needlestick exposure. Additional hepatitis tests are ordered upon patient's request. The patient's results are: HIV Ag/Ab: Negative/Negative HBsAg: Negative HBsAb: Positive Hepatitis C antibody: Negative HBc IgM: Negative HBc IgG: Positive What is the most likely explanation of the results above?
209.e: Hepatitis B serologies can reveal significant information about the status of hepatitis B in any given patient. Major components of the test include HBsAg (surface antigen), HBsAb (surface antibody), HBc IgM (core IgM antibody), and HBc IgG (core IgG antibody). Immunization from a previous infection indicates previous exposure to viral antigens and subsequent development of antibodies against both to the surface and core antigens. Patients who develop antibodies against the viral envelope antigen (HBeAb) are more likely to achieve long-term clearance of the virus. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.q: Ramya is a 20-year-old medical student who is attending her clinical postings in college. She is eager to draw blood samples. However, unfortunately she pricks her fingers with a used needle. It was later found that the needle which she had been injured with had been used to draw samples from an HBV infected patient. She was immediately started on post exposure prophylaxis for HBV. Later, her blood is sent for examination for serological markers for HBV infection. Had she been infected, which of the following antigens would not be seen in her blood?
209.e: Hepatitis B core antigen, or HBcAg is an intracellular core protein, hence it is not secreted in blood. However, it can be demonstrated in hepatocytes by immunofluorescence. HBeAg is a non-particulate soluble antigen and is present in circulation. HBsAg, also called Australia antigen is the first to be elevated following an infection. Anti HBC IgM is the first antibody to be elevated following an infection. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 479

209.q: Nila, a 2-month-old, is an infant born to an HBV infected mother. She was given her birth dose of HBV at 12 hours of birth. However, a month later, when she is tested for serological markers of HBV, she tests positive for HBV DNA, however, she is not HBsAg positive. What could be the reason for the same?
o: HbsAg is not secreted in infants
209.e: This case describes escape mutation seen in the HBV genome. The escape mutants of HBV have mutations in the S gene which leads to alteration of HBsAg. Escape mutants are observed in three situations: Infants born to HBeAg positive mothers liver transplant recipients who underwent the procedure for hepatitis B and who were treated with a high-potency human monoclonal anti-HBs preparation A small proportion of recipients of active and passive immunization, in whom antibody pressure may favor evolutionary change in gene coding an antigen. Patients infected with escape mutants lack HBsAg and therefore are often underdiagnosed by routine serological test for HBsAg Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 480

209.q: Ramu, a 35-year-old man complains of myalgia, fever, abdominal pain, and arthralgia. He also complains of testicular tenderness. The consultant diagnosed it to be a case of polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN). Which of the following active infections predispose one to this vasculitis?
209.e: PAN is a small/medium vessel vasculitis. It follows HBV/HCV infection. It is characterized by the presence of inflammatory reactions of medium or small-sized blood vessels with multiorgan involvement including skin, kidney, peripheral nerve, muscle, gastrointestinal tract and others. Reference : Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 17, Pg: 268

209.q: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of generalized malaise, yellowish discoloration of the eyes, and pruritus on the back of his hands that worsens when exposed to sunlight for the past several months. He has not seen a physician in 15 years. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and mild jaundice. There is a purpuric rash with several small vesicles and hyperpigmented lesions on the dorsum of both hands. The causal pathogen of this patient's underlying condition was most likely acquired in which of the following ways?
209.e: This patient's scleral icterus and jaundice should raise suspicion for liver disease. His pruritic rash that worsens upon exposure to sunlight is suggestive of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT), a condition that is associated with hepatitis C virus infection. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.q: Which of the following is known as Australia antigen?
209.e: HBsAg is also known as Australia antigen. It is the first to be elevated following an infection. HBsAg is a protein on the surface of HBV. Continuous presence of HBsAg indicates carrier state. Without HBsAg, Anti-HBs indicates immunity to HBV due to resolved infection or vaccination. Usually appears ∼ 1-3 months after infection or vaccination. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

210.q: Which of the following is true for IPV (Salk)?
o: Can be given in immunocompromised patient
210.e: Salk (Injectable Polio Vaccine) is prepared by Formalin killed strain. No local & herd immunity Zero chance of VAPP & VDPV Can be given to immunocompromised patient, pregnant and old aged patients Short duration of protection Relatively safer than OPV Sabin (Oral Polio Vaccine) is prepared from live attenuated strain. Provides both local & herd immunity More chances of VAPP & VDPV Cannot be given to immunocompromised patient, pregnant and old aged patients Longer duration of protection Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 711

210.q: Which of the following is the vector for yellow fever
210.e: Yellow fever is an acute febrile illness which is characterized by liver dysfunction which leads to jaundice. Humans get the infection by the bite of Aedes aegypti or tiger mosquito. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.530

210.q: Which antigenic type of polio is responsible for Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis?
210.e: Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) is due to an OPV-like isolated strain, which is slightly genetically divergent from parental OPV strain. VAPP is spread among recipient and its close contacts, and it cannot cause an outbreak. Vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPVs) show high level of genetic divergence from parental OPV strain at VP1 sequences. Most VDPV cases occur due to IPV type 2 strain. VDPVs can be classified into 3 types: Circulating VDPVs Immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs Ambiguous VDPVs Reference: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264410X98004095

210.q: Which of the following structure accurately describes Picornaviruses?
210.e: Picornaviruses are +ve sense ssRNA, non-enveloped and icosahedral in shape. Picornaviruses are classified into 2 main groups: Enteroviruses: transmitted by feco-oral route Poliovirus Coxsackie virus Echovirus Parechovirus Hep A virus Rhinovirus: transmitted by respiratory route and cause common cold Enteroviruses are the most common viruses that can cause meningo-encephalitis in children. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 82

210.q: By which phenomenon does the OPV vaccine prevent an outbreak of wild polio strains?
210.e: Viral interference is when two viruses infect a host line or a cell line and one of the viruses leads to an inhibition of the other. Genetic reassortment is seen in segmented viruses, such as influenza. Genetic recombination occurs between related viruses of the same family infecting a host cell simultaneously. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 86

210.q: Nitin, a 6-year old boy, presented to the Paediatric OPD, with complaints of weakness in his hips 5 days ago, followed by weakness in his feet 2 days ago. He was partly immunized. Which sample should be taken in order to diagnose it as Poliomyleitis paralysis?
210.e: Poliovirus may be detected from throat swabs (upto 1 week of illness) or from stool samples (upto 6-8 weeks of illness). However, longer excretion rates are observed in case of immunocompromised patients. Virus isolation from CSF or blood is very rare. Reverse cold chain (RCC) technique is used to transport stool samples from site of collection to laboratory. Other Options: d. Slit skin smear is used to detect M. leprae (Leprosy) Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 711

210.q: What is the site of action of poliovirus after entering human body?
210.e: Poliovirus is transmitted by feco-oral route. It multiplies locally in Peyer's patches in the intestines, tonsils and other lymphoid tissue. Entry into the host cell is via CD155 receptor. Spread to spinal cord is via hematogenous route or neural route. Final site of action is the Anterior Horn Cell of the spinal cord which leads to muscle weakness and flaccid paralysis. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 710

210.q: Which of the following viruses have segmented RNA? 1. Corona 2. Bunya 3. Arena 4. Filo 5. Rhabdo 6. Calici 7. Orthomyxovirus 8. Picorna 9. Reo 10.Toga
210.e: RNA viruses which have segmented RNA are: Arenavirus: 2 segments Bunyavirus: 3 segments Orthomyxovirus: 8 segments Reovirus: 10-11 segments Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 80

211.q: A 2-year-old girl, Aarti, presented with diarrhea, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and weakness. She suffered from chickenpox before 1 week, for which her mother gave her a tablet of Aspirin for fever. What is the girl suffering from?
211.e: Reye’s syndrome commonly occurs in children undergoing recovery phase of viral infections especially Chickenpox and Influenza, and are taking Aspirin. Symptoms in Reye’s syndrome occurs typically due to fatty degeneration of liver. There is no specific treatment, only supportive management is indicated. Hence, Aspirin is avoided as much as possible in infants and children. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

211.q: A 36-year-old male, Rahul, presented with severe fever, impaired awareness, headache and seizures. Neck rigidity was not seen. CSF PCR was conducted which was positive for HSV1. Which lobe is commonly affected in this condition?
211.e: Fever, impaired awareness, headache and seizures without nuchal rigidity and PCR positive for HSV is suggestive of Herpes Encephalitis. Herpes is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis, and it commonly affects Temporal lobe in adults. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

211.q: A 15-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of the sudden appearance of a rash on her trunk that started 6 hours ago and subsequently spread to her extremities. Four days ago, she was taken to the emergency department because of a high fever and vomiting. She was treated with acetaminophen and discharged the next day. The fever persisted for several days and abated just prior to appearance of the rash. Physical examination shows a rose-colored, blanching, maculopapular rash, and postauricular lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
211.e: Roseola infantum is a self-limited viral exanthem (usually due to HHV-6 and less commonly, HHV-7) that primarily affects infants and young children and is characterized by a high fever for 3–5 days that is immediately followed by a blanching, maculopapular, non-pruritic rash. The rash initially appears on the trunk but may spread to the face and extremities. It is commonly associated with cervical, postauricular, and/or occipital lymphadenopathy and may also cause febrile seizures. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

211.q: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain with defecation, anal itching, and blood in the stool. Over the past month, she has also had a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss. She has a history of irritable bowel syndrome, HIV infection, and human papillomavirus infection. Digital rectal examination shows a tender mass and bright red blood in the anal canal. Anoscopy shows an exophytic, ulcerated, 2.5-cm mass that is located just above the anocutaneous line and below the dentate line. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
211.e: A history of hematochezia, anal pruritus, painful defecation, and weight loss in a patient with an exophytic, friable, ulcerated mass above the anal verge is suggestive of anal canal cancer. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common histological type of anal canal cancer and typically arises below the dentate line. Patients must undergo a biopsy of the tumor to confirm the diagnosis. Women diagnosed with anal canal squamous cell carcinoma should also undergo a gynecological examination for cervical cancer screening. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

211.q: Which mode of transmission of HIV has the maximum risk of transmission?
211.e: Blood transfusion is the least common mode of transmission but it has the maximum risk. On the other hand, heterosexual intercourse is the most common mode of transmission but it has a minimal risk of transmission. Saliva contains inhibitory substances that prevent transmission of HIV. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 326

211.q: HIV enters human cells by binding to CD4 receptors. It also requires a second co-receptor. Maraviroc is an anti-HIV drug that binds to one such co-receptor, CCR5. On which of the following cells is this receptor present?
211.e: CCR5 receptor is present on macrophages and its lineage of cells. It acts as a second co receptor for fusion of HIV to gain entry into the host cells. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 327

211.q: To which genus does HIV-2 belong?
211.e: Retroviridae family consists of 2 genera, Lentivirus and Delta retrovirus. Lentivirus contains HIV 1 and 2, while Delta retrovirus contains HTLV-1 Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 325

211.q: Which is the main receptor for HIV to bind to CD4+ cells?
211.e: Gp120 is the main receptor for HIV to bind to CD4+ cells. Gp41 is the fusion protein P24 is a core antigen P18 is a matrix antigen Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 326

212.q: Which of the following is Fungi imperfecti
212.e: Taxonomical Classification - Based on the production of sexual spores, the Kingdom Fungi has been divided into four medically important phyla. They are as follows: Phylum zygomycota: They are lower fungi, produce sexual spores known as zygospores and possess aseptate hyphae, e.g. Rhizopus and Mucor Phylum ascomycota: They produce sexual spores known as ascospores and possess septate hyphae, e.g. Aspergillus Phylum basidiomycota: They produce sexual spores known as basidiospore e.g. Cryptococcus Phylum deuteromycota (Fungi imperfecti): In majority of the medically important fungi, the sexual state is either absent or unidentified yet. Hence, they are traditionally grouped as fungi imperfecti. Reference : Sastry 3rd ed pg. 116 Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 87

212.q: Which of the following agent is highly infectious requiring bio safety level 3?
212.e: Cultures of Coccidiodes are highly infectious; may lead to accidental inhalation of spores in laboratories and hence require biosafety level-3 precautions Reference : Sastry 3rd Ed pg. 382 Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 413

Ans. is 'd' i.e. T. mentagrophytes Zoophilic dermatophytes are the species which primarily infect animals and occasionally transmitted to humans. Zoophilic species of trichophyton are T. montegrophytes and T verrucosum. Other zoophilic species of dermatophytes is M. canis.

212.q: What is the pH of sabouraud dextrose medium?
212.e: SDA (Sabouraud dextrose agar): It is the most commonly used medium in diagnostic mycology. It contains peptone 1%, dextrose 4% and has a pH of 5.6. This may not support some pathogenic fungi. Neutral SDA (Emmons modification): It differs from the original SDA in having neo peptone 1% and dextrose 2% with a pH of 7.2. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number-117.

212.q: Which of the following is true about dimorphic fungi?
212.e: They exist as molds (hyphal form) in the environment at ambient temperature (25°C) and as yeasts in human tissues at body temperature (37°C). Examples Histoplasma capsulatum Blastomyces dermatitidis Coccidioides immitis Paracoccidioides brasiliensis Talaromyces marneffei Sporothrix schenckii. Reference : Sastry 3rd ed chapter 6 Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 86

212.q: At 34 weeks a pregnant lady had to undergo emergency C section. Premature baby delivered but due to hypoxia admitted in NICU. Intra uterine growth restriction noted and received Total parental nutrition following which baby developed Fungemia. Which of the following is suspected
212.e: Malassezia furfur is lipophilic, SDA with olive oil overlay is the ideal media for culture. Typical 'fried egg' colonies appear after incubating for 5-7 days at 32-35° C. Since it is lipophilic, patient receiving total parental nutrition are more susceptible. Reference : Sastry 3 rd edition pg. 575 Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 599

213.q: Latex agglutination study of the antigen in CSF helps in the diagnosis of
213.e: Cryptococcal antigens can be detected in CSF, serum and urine by latex agglutination test. Antigen titre in CSF stays for longer duration and is directly proportional to mortality of the patients. Reference : Jagdish Chander 3/e p306, Harrison 18/e p1651,17/e p1252 Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no. 473

Individuals at high risk for cryptococcosis include: Patients with hematologic malignancies, recipients of solid organ transplants with ongoing immunosuppressive therapy, Persons whose medical conditions necessitate glucocorticoid therapy. Patients with advanced HIV infection and CD4+T lymphocyte counts of Reference: Harrison 18/e p1650-51, 17/e p1251

213.q: Galactomannan antigen in patient's sera or urine (by ELISA) is used for
213.e: Detection of Aspergillus specific galactomannan antigen in patient's sera or urine (by ELISA) Reference : Sastry 3rd edition pg. 118

213.q: A known case of HIV comes to the OPD for follow up. His CD4 cell count is currently 350 cells/uL. Primary prophylaxis for which opportunistic infection should be started at this stage?
213.e: Cotrimoxazole preventive therapy for preventing PCP infection (CPT), at a dose of 800 mg/160 mg PO once daily may be initiated in the following scenarios: Primary prophylaxis: It is initiated in HIV patient in any of the conditions- If CD4 count There is no role for primary prophylaxis of cryptococcal meningitis. MAC infection occurs at CD4 count Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 334

213.q: A 34-year-old HIV positive patient presents with complaints of high-grade fever, frothy expectoration and cough for 2 days. Upon testing for different etiologies with a sample of lung fluid obtained from Broncho-Alveolar Lavage (BAL), the Gomori Methanamine Silver stain showed a CRUSHED PING PONG ball appearance, suggesting Pneumocystis Jirovecii infection. Which of the following morphological form is observed in the sample?
213.e: Like protozoa, Pneumocystis exists in cyst and trophozoite forms. The cysts are found in the environment, whereas in human tissues both cysts and trophozoites (containing 4-8 sporozoites) are found. Once inhaled, the cysts are carried to the lungs where they transform into the trophozoite stage. The trophozoites induce an inflammatory response, that leads to recruitment of plasma cells resulting in formation of frothy exudate filling the alveoli. Hence, this condition is also called plasma cell pneumonia. Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) staining is the method of choice to demonstrate the cysts of P. jirovecii. The cysts resemble black colored crushed ping-pong balls, against the green background. Treatment is with Cotrimoxazole. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 679

213.q: Which of the following is positive by India-ink staining on a CSF sample for demonstration of capsule of yeast?
213.e: Negative staining: The background stains black whereas unstained bacteria stand out in contrast. It is used for the demonstration of capsules which do not take up simple stains. Example: India ink or nigrosine Capsulated bacteria: Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae), Meningococcus (Neisseriae meningitidis), Klebsiella pneumoniae Capsulated fungus yeast: Cryptococcus neoformans Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 12

213.q: Which of the following is positive by Nigrosin staining?
213.e: Negative staining: The background stains black whereas unstained bacteria stand out in contrast. It is used for the demonstration of capsules which do not take up simple stains. Example: India ink or nigrosine Capsulated bacteria: Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae), Meningococcus (Neisseriae meningitidis), Klebsiella pneumoniae Capulated fungus yeast: Cryptococcus neoformans Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 12

213.q: A 1.5-month-old male infant presents with persistent diarrhea, Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, and an oral thrush with Candida albicans. HIV PCR is negative. The most likely cause of these findings is:
213.e: The fungal infection is highly suggestive of a T cell defect. Choices A and C do not of themselves imply a deficiency in T cell function. HLA genes are autosomal, not X-linked. Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19 , Pg 187-190

214.q: Which of the following statement is NOT accurate for Microsporidia species -
o: Reproduce in cell by spore formation
Demonstrated by hematoxylin and eosin stain
214.e: Option D - Microsporidia are unicellular obligate intracellular parasites. They reproduce in host cells by producing spores. 3 genera and 13 species are associated with human disease particularly, in HIV and other immuno-compromised patients. Infection is caused by an inhalation or ingestion of spores. Though commonly causes diarrhea, it may also lead to extra intestinal infections like sinusitis, cholangitis, bronchiolitis and kerato- conjunctivitis. Because of its intracellular locations, they are not routinely demonstrated by hematoxylin and eosin stain. Modified trichrome stain, gram stain and modified acid-fast stain are usually used to demonstrate them. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -106

214.q: An intermediate host whose presence may be required for the completion of a parasite's life cycle but in which no development of the parasite occurs is -
214.e: Paratenic host : An organism that harbors the sexually immature parasite (larva) but is not necessary for the parasite's developmental cycle to progress. Reservoir host : an organism that harbors a pathogen but suffers no ill effects, responsible for continued existence of parasite in area Accidental host : an organism that generally does not allow transmission to the definitive host, thereby preventing the parasite from completing its development. Definite host : An organism in which the parasite reaches the adult stage and reproduces sexually Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -1

214.q: A first-year pathology resident is given exercise to demonstrate various parasitic infections from peripheral blood smear (PBS). He should look for following parasites in PBS EXCEPT
214.e: Option A – L.donovani is present intracellularly in monocytes or macrophages in PBS as L-D body. Option B – T.brucei and T.cruzi are present extracellularly in plasma. Option D – Babesia are present in RBCs. Schistosomes though present in vesical and pelvic plexuses, it is never demonstrable in peripheral blood smear due to its location in capillaries of internal organs. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -7

214.q: Following statement about a thick smear for diagnosis of plasmodia is INCORRECT -
214.e: Option C - As the thick smear concentrates 20-30 layers of RBC in a small area, it is more sensitive and requires more blood. Fixation is not required. As the RBCS are destroyed due to the dehemoglobinaztion, the characteristics like RBC enlargement and stippling cannot be seen. So, species identification is difficult. Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -82

214.q: Toxoplasmosis in man is acquired by all EXCEPT :
214.e: Option C - There are many ways by which humans acquired Toxoplasma infection. Consumption of oocyst in cats faces through contaminated food or water is a common mode of infection. Ingesting contaminated pork or lamb containing tissue cyst can also lead to infection. As the parasite resides inside reticuloendothelial cells, humans can also acquire infection through blood transfusion & organ transplant. The parasite is also able to cross the placenta, producing congenital infection. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -93

214.q: Regarding E.granulosus, which of the following is most accurate?
o: Mode of infection for humans is ingestion of contaminated eggs along with food and water
214.e: Option C - Hydatid cyst in humans is due to ingestion of contaminated eggs excreted in dog feces, along with food and water. Thus, humans are intermediate hosts, while dogs are definitive hosts. E.granulosus is one of the smallest tapeworms. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 129-130

214.q: The larval stage of Schistosomes infective to human is -
214.e: Option D - Cercariae are infective forms to humans, which enter through skin penetration. Once inside the blood vessels, they lose their tails and convert into schistosomules. When they reach mesenteric venous plexuses, they convert into adult forms. Living in copula, females produce eggs, which passes along with feces or urine, and reach water. Eggs containing ciliated embryo (miracidium) hatch immediately and release miracidium. Miracidium enters snails and successively pass through stages of first and second generation sporocyst. Sporocyst convert into cercariae which escape from snails in water. Stage of redia is not found in Schistosomes. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 143

214.q: Consumption of pork can lead to
214.e: Option C – Trichinella spiralis is acquired due to consumption of pork. T.spiralis has a direct life cycle requiring only a single host to complete the life cycle. Pigs are the optimum host. Humans are accidentally infected due to consumption of pork, representing the dead end of life cycle. Option A – Consumption of pork which contains cysticercus cellulosae (larva of T.solium) can lead to taeniasis initially but not cysticercosis. However, later on due to autoinfection, the patient might get cysticercosis. Option D – Clonorchiasis is due to consumption of contaminated fish. Option B- Toxoplasmosis occurs due to consumption of oocyst which are excreted in cat feces. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -171

215.q: Regarding T.cruzi, which of the following is most accurate :
o: Exists as both amastigote and trypomastigote in humans
Complications of chronic diseases are common in children
215.e: Option C - Metacyclic trypomastigotes are infective forms of parasite which after entry through bug bite, enters R-E cells and convert into amastigote forms. Some of them, after converting through epimastigote form, convert to trypomastigote forms inside blood. Reduviid bug is a vector which when feeds on human blood, acquires infection. Option A - Tsetse fly is a vector which transmits T.brucei Option B - Armadillo, cat ,dog and pigs are major reservoir Option D - complications of chronic diseases are common in adults, while in children acute disease is common. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -48

215.q: Best way to differentiate amoebic dysentery stool from bacillary dysentery stool in microscopy is -
o: Presence of trophozoite with ingested RBC
215.e: Option D – the only confirmatory way to diagnose E.histolytica infection (amoebic dysentery) is presence of trophozoites with ingested RBCs. Macrophage can be present in amoebic as well as bacillary dysentery. Though characteristically present in clumps, RBC’s can be present discrete and it is very difficult to identify type of dysentery based on arrangement of RBCs as its not very specific. Charcot-Leyden crystals are present in amoebic dysentery but it is also present in other parasitic infection and allergic conditions. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -20

215.q: Conversion of uninucleate cyst into mature quadrinucleate cyst in E.histolytica is accompanied by all EXCEPT -
215.e: Option C – Uninucleate cyst is spherical about 10-20 µ in size. It has a single nucleus, large glycogen mass and 1-4 chromatoid bodies. With successive nuclear division, glycogen mass is reduced in size and the chromatoid body disappears and the cyst is surrounded by refractile cyst wall. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -16

Option A – Protozoa reproduce by asexual and sexual methods. Asexual method like binary fission, multiple fission and endodyogeny. E.histolytica, Leishmania and Trypanosomes multiplies asexually by binary fission. Plasmodia multiplies by multiple fission (Schizogony). Some protozoa like Toxoplasma multiply by internal budding (Endodyogeny). Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -16

215.q: Etiological agent of granulomatous amoebic encephalitis is :
215.e: Option B -Acanthamoeba causes primary amoebic granulomatous meningo-encephalitis. E.histolytica cause brain abscess secondary to infection in intestine. Naegleria causes acute suppurative inflammation.
