D.fragilis though classified as amoeboflagellate like Naegleria, causes gastro-intestinal symptoms like diarrhea, flatulence, abdominal pain, anorexia and fatigue. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -29

215.q: What is the infective stage of Entamoeba histolytica to man?
215.e: E.histolytica exists in three forms a)Trophozoite b)Precyst c)Cyst Mature quadrinucleate cyst is the infective form. It is passed in the feces of convalescents and carriers. The cysts remain viable under moist conditions for about 10 days. Reference: Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.503

215.q: Ingested RBC's in trophozoites is seen in
215.e: E.dispar, E.bangladeshi are amoeba which are morphologically similar to E.histolytica.They are differentiated by a)Absence of Lectin antigen b)No RBC's inside trophozoites c)PCR Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.504-505

Ans. is 'b' i.e., Balantidium coli [Ref Paniker p. 111] Largest protozoa Balantidum coli Smallest intestinal amoeba Dientamoeba fragilis Smallest tapeworm found in H. nana human intestine Largest helminth (largest T. saginata (beef tapeworm) worm) Largest liver fluke F. hepatica Largest trematode infecting man→ Fasciolopsis buski Largest Nematode Ascaris Smallest Nematode - Trichinella Only protozoan parasite found in Giardia lamblia small intestine of man Only ciliate protozoan parasite of Balantidum coli man - Parthenogenic worm (female is Strongyloides stercoralis. able to produce fertile eggs or larvae without fertilization)

216.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Laveran . The specific causative agent of malaria was discovered in the red blood cells of a patient in 1880 by Alophonse Laveran, a French army surgeon in Algeria. Remember . Romanowsky developed a method of staining malaria parasites in blood films.

216.q: Which of the following provide protection against malaria all except
216.e: Answer- D. PNH Red cell surface antigen that offer protection against malaria Duffy blood group system ABO (H) blood group system Glycophorins Gerbich antigen Complement receptor type I Knops blood group Abnormalities of the red cell cytoskeleton which may offer protection include South-east asia ovalocytosis Hereditary elliptocytosis Hereditary spherocytosis Sickle cell HbA/S

216.q: You are performing the ZN staining for your microbiology practicals. You notice that the decolourizer is 5% sulphuric acid. Which of the following will stain acid fast positive with this concentration of sulphuric acid? i. M.leprae ii. MAC iii. Legionella iv. M.tuberculosis v. Oocyst of cryptosporidium vi. Oocyst of tenia vii. Actinomyces
216.e: The above question describes the staining method of modified ZN staining , wherein 5% sulphuric acid is used instead of 20%. The former concentration shows positive with M. Leprae, whereas the latter shows acid fastness for M.TB and Atypical mycobacteria. Oocysts of Cyclospora, Isospora and Cryptosporidium are also acid fast with 5% H2SO4 Nocardia, Legionella and Tenia oocysts are acid fast with 0.5%-1% H2SO4. Actinomyces is not acid fast. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 29

216.q: Chronic carrier state is not seen in all except ?
216.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Malaria 792. Following are examples of human "dead end" disease except - a) Bubonic plague b) Japanies ecephalitis c) Hydatid disease d) Leishmaniasis Correct Answer - D Ans. is 'd' i.e., Leishmaniasis Dead and host o A dead end host is an infected person from which infectious agents are not transmitted to other susceptible host or from which a parasite cannot escape to continue its life cycle. o The diseases in which human acts as dead end host, i.e., dead and disease : ?

216.q: Malaria is not seen in patients with :
216.e: Option D - These are inherent, natural, non-immune mechanisms of host resistance against malarial parasites which have evolved as survival advantage under environmental stress induced by Plasmodia. Duffy negative RBC lacks glycoprotein receptors required by merozoite to attach and penetrate. Thus duffy negative blood group people are naturally protected from P.vivax. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -80

216.q: Schizont of P.falciparum are not found in peripheral blood because of :
o: Schizonts are absent in life cycle
Develop only in capillaries of internal organs
216.e: Option C - Merozoites released from liver cells infects RBS’s. Inside RBC, they convert into early trophozoite- late trophozoite and Schizont. Late trophozoite, early and mature schizonts are not found in peripheral blood as this stage occurs inside capillaries of internal organs like spleen, liver and kidney. Thus, only trophozoite (ring forms ) and gametocytes are diagnostic forms present in peripheral blood smear. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Page no : 73

216.q: Young RBCs are preferentially infected by :
216.e: Option B - P.vivax merozoites after entering into RBC convert into early trophozoite(ring form) about 2.5 -3 in diameter which remains in middle of RBC. This early ring form further convert to late trophozoite form having size of 6-7 . In order to accommodate such a large ring, RBC has to enlarge. RBCs infected with P.vivax became pale, enlarged, irregular and became mottled having Schuffner's dots. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -72

216.q: Which form of malarial parasite is present in the saliva of infective mosquitoes?
216.e: Option B - Sporozoite is an infective form developed in the female anopheles mosquitoes after external incubation period. It is formed when introduced inside the human body through mosquito bite. It undergoes asexual development inside liver cells (pre-erythrocytic schizogony). Merozoites released from pre-erythrocytic schizogony infects RBCs and undergoes a developmental cycle of trophozoite-schizont-merozoite. Reference : Paniker's Textbook of Parasitology, 8th Edition, Page Number-67.

217.q: An example of type I hypersensitivity is:
217.e: a) Lepromin test: Type 4 Hypersensitivity b) Tuberculin test: Type 4 Hypersensitivity c) Casoni's test: Type 1 Hypersensitivity d) Arthus reaction: Type 3 Hypersensitivity Examples of Type I Hypersensitivity: Experiments: P-K reaction Schultz Dale phenomenon Theobald smith phenomenon Systemic anaphylaxis Localized anaphylaxis (atopy) such as: Allergic rhinitis (or hay fever) Asthma Food allergy Atopic urticarial Atopic dermatitis (allergic eczema) Drug allergy Wheal and flare reaction. Parasitic diseases: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia (TPE) Loeffler's pneumonia (Ascaris) Ground itch (Hookworm) Leakage of hydatid fluid Cercarial dermatitis/swimmer's itch (Schistosoma). Parasitic tests: Casoni test (hydatid disease) Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

o: Patient is allowed to swallow a capsule containing coiled thread
Used for demonstration of giardia lamblia
Not used for obtaining eggs of Fasciola hepatica
217.e: Enterotest is a simple method of obtaining duodenal contents. Patient is allowed to swallow a gelatin capsule in which a thread of nylon yarn is coiled. The end of the yarn is affixed to the patient's face. Upon reaching the stomach, gelatin dissolves and a weighted string is carried to duodenum. Secretions are retrieved after 3-4 hours and content adhered to yarn is scraped off and examined under microscope. Traditionally used for Giardia lamblia, it is now used to collect eggs of F.hepatica, larva of S.stercoralis and oocyst of Isospora. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -35

217.q: Intestinal bilharziasis (Schistosomal dysentery) is commonly seen in infection with -
217.e: Option B - S.mansoni resides in venules of inferior mesenteric vein in sigmoido-rectal region. Because of the presence of characteristic eggs having lateral spine, eggs deposited in the intestinal wall leads to erosion, microabscesses, granuloma and dysentry. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 148

217.q: Which of the following parasite is associated with cholangiocarcinoma?
217.e: Clonorchis sinensis is called Chinese liver fluke. Morphology:- Adult worm-lives in biliary tract and sometimes in pancreatic duct. Eggs-eggs are flask shaped and operculated. Mode of infection-By eating undercooked freshwater fish carrying metacercariae larva. Chronic infection has also been linked to cholangiocarcinoma. Reference : Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition pg no.536

217.q: Autoinfection is seen in all of the following parasites EXCEPT -
217.e: Option B – Auto infection is a feature of Taenia solium but not of Taenia saginata. Due to unhygienic habits of not washing hands, a person having taeniasis due to T.solium can auto infect himself resulting in cysticercosis. Option A – In H.nana, internal and external autoinfection takes place. Internal infection is due to eggs in the intestine hatch, penetrate mucosa and develop into larval stage (cysticercoid). External autoinfection is due to faeco-oral contamination due to unhygienic habits. Option B – E.vermicularis has features of auto infection and retro infection. Option C – S.stercoralis can undergo auto infection (hyper infection syndrome) in persons with defective cellular immune response. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 137,183, 196

217.q: Water lily sign is seen in infection due to
217.e: Hydatid disease is caused by Echinococcus granulosus Definitive host-Dog Intermediate host and accidental host-MAN Waterlily sign is seen in ultrasound. This is due to collapsed cyst (floating membrane)floating in the abdomen. Reference: Essentials of medical Parasitology by Apurba sastry 2nd edition Pg no.181

217.q: Symmers pipestem fibrosis is associated with which of the following?
217.e: This is seen in chronic schistosomiasis, due to fibrosis and granuloma formation as a result of egg deposition in sites like liver which is called symmers pipestem fibrosis. Reference : Essentials of medical Parasitology by Apurba sastry 2nd edition Pg no.200

217.q: Regarding neurocysticercosis, which of the following is most accurate?
o: Caused due to eating of beef
Serological test for antibody detection is not available
Antigen can be detected in serum or CSF by ELISA
217.e: Neurocysticercosus is caused by eating pork. Option C - Antigen can be detected in CSF and serum by ELISA using monoclonal antibodies and indicate recent infection. Anticysticercus antibodies can be detected in CSF or serum by ELISA. Surgical excision is the best treatment wherever possible. Albendazole or praziquantel along with corticosteroids can be given. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 126-27

218.q: Intestinal re-infection (Hyper infection syndrome) is seen in -
218.e: Option B - in S.stercoralis infection, if patient has defective cellular response - AIDS patient, lepromatous leprosy, corticosteroid therapy or severe malnutrition, rhabditiform larva which are released in intestinal lumen instead of passing into feces develop into filariform larva in intestine which penetrate intestinal mucosa and lodge into lungs and various tissue and organs - condition called as intestinal re-infection or Hyper infection syndrome. Option A & D - intestinal re-infection usually does not occur in these parasites. Option C - auto-infection and retro-infection is a feature of E. vermicularis in which eggs deposited in perianal skin, autoinfects person due to itching and unhygienic habits or larva hatched in perianal skin moves retrograde through anus causing retrograde autoinfection. Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -184

218.q: Following statement is INCORRECT about Visceral larva migrans
o: Common mode of infection is ingestion
Larva develops into adults in ectopic sites
Can also be caused by larva of S.stercoralis and A.lumbricoides in ectopic sites
218.e: Option C - Visceral larva migrans (VLM) or toxocariasis is a zoonotic infection usually caused by dog or cat ascarids of the Toxocara genus. The eggs are ingested and then hatch into larvae, which penetrate the intestine and start migrating. These nematodes can infect but not mature in humans so larva is not developed into adults. It is also seen in human nematodes like S.stercoralis and A.lumbricoides, when larvae of these parasites are not able to complete their normal development and enter ectopic sites. Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -167

218.q: Unsegmented eggs are in which parasite?
218.e: Ans. a. Trichuris trichura 706. In malaria, sexual cycle is - a) Sporozoite to gametocytes b) Gametocytes to Sporozoite c) Occurs in human d) Responsible for relapse Correct Answer - B Ans. is 'b' i.e., Gametocytes to sporozoite LIFE CYCLE OF PLASMODIUM Plasmodium passes its life cycle in two different hosts ?

Ans. is `b' i.e., Strongyloides [Ref Panikar 6th/e p. 171] Rhabditiform larva is the first stage feeding larva found in some nematodes. It is non-infective. Filiform larva is the non feeding infective larva in some nematodes. Rhabditiform larva and filiform larva are found in following important nematodes

218.q: What is the Most common clinical manifestations of first-episode HSV-1 infection?
218.e: Gingivostomatitis and pharyngitis are the most common clinical manifestations of first-episode HSV-1 infection, while recurrent herpes labialis is the most common clinical manifestation of reactivation HSV-1 infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 192, Pg: 1473

218.q: A 22-year-old lady recently returned from a holiday in Malta was admitted with a 3 day history of fever, generalised lymphadenopathy and a macular rash over the trunk and legs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis.
218.e: Among the given options the most likely diagnosis is IMN, considering the age and the travel history. Familial Mediterranean fever should have recurrent history of fever. Tuberculosis is a chronic infection with a more prolonged course. There is nothing to suggest a sarcoidosis like mediatinal adenopathy and the duration is short. Infectious Mononucleosis occurs most commonly in adolescents and young adults. Clinical features occur after a 2-5 week incubation period and include fever, malaise, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 194, Pg: 1484

219.q: What is one example of a situation where routine environmental microbiological sampling is indicated?
o: Outbreak investigation of a new infection
Assessment of a new method for equipment sterilization
Monthly water surveillance in hemodialysis units
Evaluation of a new hospital construction
219.e: Monthly water surveillance in hemodialysis units: Correct , routine monitoring is critical to ensure safe water quality for dialysis patients. Why Not Others: A. Outbreak investigation: Focuses on targeted sampling, not routine checks. B. Equipment sterilization: Involves evaluative sampling after changes, not regular monitoring. D. New hospital construction: Involves specific sampling rather than ongoing routine checks. Key Takeaways: Routine environmental sampling is indicated for monthly water surveillance in hemodialysis units to ensure safe water quality . Other situations often require targeted or specific sampling rather than routine. Tags : good to know Reference: Guidelines on routine and targeted environmental microbiological sampling.

219.q: Hospital associated infection can be defined as all of the following except:
o: The infection should be incubating at the time of admission
The symptoms should appear at least after 48 hours or after admission
The patient should be admitted for a reason other than the infection in context
Infections acquired in hospital, but symptoms present after discharge
219.e: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) can be defined as- The infections acquired in the hospital by a patient admitted for a reason other than the infection in context , The infection should not be present or incubating at the time of admission , and The symptoms should appear at least after 48 hours of admission. This also include: Infections that are acquired in the hospital but symptoms appear after discharge. Occupational infections among staff of the healthcare facility (e.g. needle stick injury transmitted infections). Infection in a neonate that results while passage through the birth canal (in contrast to congenital infections due to transplacental transmission, which are not HAIs). Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 229

219.q: Patients with similar infections requiring contact precautions can be placed together if single isolation rooms aren't available. This is called Cohorting. What is the minimum distance for a spatial separation of two patients in a room?
219.e: For infection control: Single isolation room with a bathroom facility is preferred. If not available, then cohorting is recommended. Cohorting may be carried out in various ways Patients with similar infections requiring contact precautions can be placed together either in the same isolation room, or in the same cubicle or corner of a ward or Spatial separation of minimum of 3 feet distance between the beds with privacy curtains. Other measures for infection control are: Hand Hygiene should be maintained. Health care workers should wear PPE. Single-use patient-dedicated equipment. Patient movement should be limited only to medically-necessary purposes. Disinfection of rooms should be carried out frequently and adequately. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 236

219.q: Why is an indwelling catheter a risk for UTI?
o: Increased lateral urethral pressure leading to impaired mucosal blood flow and mucin secretion
219.e: Indwelling urinary catheterization is a risk for UTI because: The presence of a urinary catheter is the single most important risk factor. The risk of developing CAUTI is directly proportional to the duration of catheterization. Urethral pressure : an indwelling catheter exerts lateral urethral pressure causing decreased mucosal blood flow, urothelial mucosal disruption and impaired mucin secretion; All these factors together predispose to infection Incomplete emptying : In catheterized patients, bladder is often incompletely emptied because of pressure differentials created by patient movement or catheter manipulation. A small amount of urine always pools around the balloon which serves as a nidus for infection. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 242

219.q: Treatment of catheter associated asymptomatic bacteriuria is recommended in all the following cases except:
o: In a patient who was operated for cholecystectomy 4 days before due to persistent bacteriuria 24 hours after removal of catheter.
In a primigravida patient who came for an emergency labour at 38 weeks with asymptomatic bacteriuria.
A patient having bacteriuria planned for transurethral resection of prostate.
In a patient with persistent bacteriuria 4 days after catheter removal.
219.e: Management of CAUTI includes removal of catheter and institution of appropriate antimicrobial therapy based on the susceptibility pattern of the organism isolated. Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (Ca-aSB) is not recommended except when: Bacteriuria persists for >48 hours after removal of the catheter. In pregnancy , as there is 20–30 fold increased risk of developing pyelonephritis and risk of premature delivery with low birth weight. Prior to traumatic urological procedures such as transurethral resection of prostate where mucosal bleeding is anticipated which may cause bacteremia. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 242

219.q: An occupational exposure is defined as all of the following except:
o: Contact with mouth by splash of infected fluid
Contact with skin afflicted with dermatitis by splash of fluid
Contact with the intact skin when the duration is for few seconds
219.e: An occupational exposure is defined as: Percutaneous injury, . needle stick injury (NSI) or other sharp injury. Splash injury : Contact with the mucous membrane (e.g. eye or mouth). Contact with non-intact skin (abraded skin or afflicted with dermatitis). Contact with the intact skin when the duration is prolonged (e.g. several minutes or more). An occupational injury is often loosely termed as needle stick injury though it includes injury through needle or other sharps and splashes. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 267

219.q: CDC recommends targeted air surveillance, which should be carried out for which of the following indications: 1) Investigation of an outbreak 2) For research purposes 3) Before fogging 4) After reconstruction or newly constructed buildings 5) After fogging 6) For short-term evaluation of a change in infection control practice 7) Routinely at regular intervals
219.e: Routine air sampling (i.e. random or periodic sampling) is not recommended because HAI rates are not related with levels of general microbial contamination of air or environmental surfaces, There is no standard guidelines mentioning permissible levels of microbial contamination of environmental surfaces or air. CDC recommends targeted air surveillance, which should be carried out for the following indications: Investigation of an outbreak For research purpose After reconstruction or newly constructed buildings After fogging (to monitor the quality) For short-term evaluation of a change in infection control practice. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 281

219.q: Which is the correct method of framing antimicrobial policy by the Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) team?
o: AMS team discuss with each other and frame the policy based on the standard guidelines
AMS team discuss with each other and frame the policy based on the standard guideline as well as local AMR pattern
AMS team discuss with each other and frame the policy based on the standard guidelines as well as local AMR pattern, then discuss with each clinicians for their suggestions
AMS team just copy the guidelines from any other renowned institute of India
219.e: Framing Antimicrobial Policy: Every hospital should frame their own hospital antimicrobial policy which is usually a pocket handbook, consisting of system/syndrome wise indications for antimicrobial choice and their dosage. It should be prepared by the AMS team after discussing with all the clinicians, microbiologists and administrators. The policy must be compliant to the standard national and international antimicrobial guidelines and local antibiogram pattern. Common consensus between all clinicians must be arrived at, before framing the policy; which facilitates better adherence to policy. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 273

221.q: An investigator injects 7 mg of an experimental drug into an animal. The drug does not bind to plasma proteins and is eliminated unchanged in urine via first-order kinetics. Two hours later, the investigator obtains laboratory values from the animal that reveal the rate of drug elimination is 0.02 mg/min, the plasma drug concentration is 0.04 mg/mL, and the total amount of drug eliminated in urine is 5 mg. Which of the following is the best estimate of the clearance of the drug in the animal at the time of measurement?
221.e: Plasma clearance (CL) is the volume of plasma cleared of a substance in a period of time. It is estimated by dividing a substance's rate of elimination by its plasma concentration: CL = (0.02 mg/min)/(0.04 mg/mL) = 0.5 mL/min. In first-order kinetics, the rate of elimination of the substance and the plasma concentration of the substance decrease with time, but the CL remains constant. Alternatively, the CL of a substance with first-order kinetics can be calculated by multiplying the volume of distribution (Vd) by the elimination constant (Ke) of the substance. For a substance that is minimally protein-bound and excreted unchanged only in the urine, as in this case, the CL is essentially the glomerular filtration rate. In humans, inulin is such a substance Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.52

221.q: Which pharmacokinetic parameters are used to determine the loading dose of an orally administered drug? 1. Volume of distribution (Vd) 2. Half-life 3. Plasma concentration 4. Bioavailability
221.e: Explanation: Loading dose (LD) = (Desired steady-state plasma concentration × Vd) ÷ Bioavailability. Half-life determines maintenance dosing frequency and time to steady state, but it is not a direct component of the loading dose equation (Statement 2 ruled out) For oral drugs , bioavailability (F) must be accounted for because oral dosing is reduced by first-pass extraction and incomplete absorption. Formula (practical): LD (oral) = (C_target × Vd) / F Where: C_target = desired plasma concentration (therapeutic target) Vd = volume of distribution F = fraction absorbed (bioavailability)

221.q: There is no statistically significant difference in the dose-corrected area under the curve (AUC) for the two routes of administration. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this finding?
221.e: This drug is almost entirely absorbed into systemic circulation when orally administered, as indicated by the lack of difference in the dose-corrected AUCs for oral and intravenous administration. indicating that this drug has near 100% bioavailability. Isosorbide mononitrate does not undergo first-pass metabolism by the liver and thus has approx. 100% bioavailability. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.48

221.q: A 56-year-old patient is being treated with oral levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia. The plasma clearance of the drug is calculated as 12.0 L/h. Oral bioavailability of the drug is 50%. Sensitivity analysis of a sputum culture shows a minimal inhibitory concentration of 1 μg/mL for the causative pathogen. The target plasma concentration is 2 mg/L. If the drug is administered twice per day, which of the following dosages should be administered at each dosing interval to maintain a steady state?
221.e: A maintenance dose of 576 mg should be administered at 12 hour intervals to achieve the desired target concentration of 2 mg/L. The corresponding formula needed for calculation requires the following values: Cp = target plasma concentration at steady state (mg/L) = 2 mg/L Cl = clearance (L/h)= 12 L/h τ = dosing interval (hours)= 12 hour F = bioavailability = 50 % Maintenance dose = (Cp * Cl * τ) / F → (2*12*12)/0.50 = 288/0.5 = 576 Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.52

221.q: A 17-year-old woman is given a prescription of fluconazole to be taken daily (q 12 h) for 3 days. The half-life is 12 h. How long will it take for the medication to reach 90% of its final steady state level?
221.e: To calculate the time it takes for a medication to reach 90% of its final steady state, you can use the formula (3.3) * (t1/2). Given that the half-life (t1/2) of fluconazole is 12 hours: Time to Reach 90% of Steady State = (3.3) * (12 hours) = 39.6 hours So, it will take approximately 39.6 hours for the medication to reach 90% of its final steady-state level. Among the given options, the closest one is: C) 40 hours This option is the most accurate representation of the calculated time of approximately 39.6 hours. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Fourteenth Edition, Pg no. 51

221.q: What formula is the dosing rate of a drug based on?
221.e: When a drug is repeated at relatively short intervals, it accumulates in the body until elimination balances input and a steady state plasma concentration ( Cpss ) is attained- Cpss = dose rate/CL From this equation it is implied that doubling the dose rate would double the average Cpss and so on. Further, if the therapeutic plasma Concentration of the drug has been worked out and its CL is known, the dose rate needed to achieve the target Cpss can be determined- Dose rate = target Cpss × CL

221.q: What does the term LD₅⁰ represent in toxicology?
o: The dose that causes death in 50% of a tested animal population
The dose that reduces infection in 50% of a tested population
The dose that produces a toxic effect in 50% of the population
The range where drug efficacy is high and adverse effects are low
221.e: Explanation for answer: The LD₅⁰ (Lethal Dose 50%) is a standard measure of acute toxicity. It represents the single dose of a substance required to kill 50% of a population of test animals under controlled conditions. A higher LD₅⁰ indicates a safer drug. Key Takeaways: LD₅⁰ measures acute lethality in animal studies. Therapeutic Index (TI) = LD₅⁰ / ED₅⁰; a higher TI indicates a safer drug.

221.q: All of the following are advantages of enteric coated tablets except:
o: It protects acid labile drugs from gastric pH
It increases the half-life of the drug.
It increases the absorption of drugs that are preferentially absorbed distal to stomach
It protects stomach from irritant drugs
221.e: Certain drugs are degraded in the gastrointestinal tract, e.g. penicillin G by acid, insulin by peptidases, and are ineffective orally. Enteric coated tablets have acid resistant coating, can be Used to overcome acid lability, gastric irritancy and also used to increase absorption of drugs which are absorbed from the intestine(Options A,C,D) Sustained release preparations have drug particles coated with slowly dissolving material that can increases the half-life of the drug.

222.q: A researcher for a pharmaceutical company is studying a new medication to treat parkinsonism. The medication is dosed at 10 mg and causes improvement in bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity in 99% of patients. However, 100 mg of this medication causes toxicity manifested as seizures in 1% of the population treated with this medication. What is the standard margin of safety of this medication?
222.e: The standard margin of safety (SMS) is a measure of how much safer a drug's effective dose is compared to its toxic dose. It's calculated using the formula: SMS = (LD1 / ED99) - 1 * 100 In this case: Effective dose (ED99): The dose at which the medication causes improvement in bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity in 99% of patients is 10 mg. Toxic dose (LD1): The dose that causes seizures in 1% of the population treated with this medication is 100 mg. Now, calculate the SMS: SMS = (100 mg / 10 mg) - 1 * 100 = 10 - 1 * 100 = 900 So, the standard margin of safety for this medication is 900. The correct answer is D) 900. This indicates that the medication is 900 times safer at the effective dose (10 mg) than it is toxic at the dose that causes seizures (100 mg). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no. 37

222.q: Drug A and Drug B are of equal magnitude. If Drug A and Drug B are combined together, And it produces an effect that is equal in magnitude to the sum of effects when both are given individually, this would be an example of which of the following?
222.e: (A) The additive effects of drugs occur when two drugs with the same effect are added together and produce an effect that is equal in magnitude to the sum of the effects when the two drugs are given individually. (B) Neutralization occurs when two drugs combine with another to form an inactive compound. (C) Potentiation occurs if a drug lacking an effect of its own increases the effect of a second active drug. (D) Synergism occurs if two drugs with the same effect, when given together, produce an effect that is in greater magnitude than the sum of the effects when the drugs are given individually. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.9

222.q: Which of the following is not a feature of type B adverse drug reactions?
o: Symptoms and signs of drug allergy
222.e: Adverse drug reactions can be defined as one of the two types: Type A: Dose dependent common extension of known pharmacological effect Type B: Dose independent uncommon symptoms and signs of drug allergy The most important type to the adverse drug reaction is type B, which encompasses both anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions. Reference: Physics, Pharmacology and Physiology for Anaesthetists, Matthew E. Cross, second edition, pg 151.

223.q: A 42-year-old man with a 6-cm right adrenal tumour is going to undergo a laparoscopic surgical procedure to remove the tumour. It is anticipated that the procedure will take approximately 12 h. The patient has a history of hypertension controlled with a alpha-blocker. Which of the following agents, used intraoperatively, will provide efficacious blood pressure control for the duration of the procedure?
223.e: Nadolol has a half-life of 12 to 24 h and would be the best agent for beta-blockade in a patient who is undergoing a long duration surgical procedure. A single intra-operative dose should suffice the entire case. Acebutolol has a 3- to 4-h half-life. Esmolol has a 10-min half-life. It is the shortest acting Beta-blocker. Metoprolol has a 3- to 4-h half-life. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 166.

223.q: Which of the following patients is most likely to be treated with intravenous glucagon?
o: An 18-year-old woman who took an overdose of cocaine and now has a blood pressure of 190/110 mm Hg
A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes who has not taken her glyburide for the last 3 days
A 62-year-old man with severe bradycardia and hypotension resulting from ingestion of an overdose of Atenolol
A 74-year-old man with lactic acidosis as a complication of severe infection and shock
223.e: Glucagon acts through cardiac glucagon receptors to stimulate the rate and force of contraction of the heart. Because this bypasses cardiac β adrenoceptors, glucagon is useful in the treatment of β-blocker-induced cardiac depression. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 757

223.q: A 45-year-old woman found obtunded in her apartment. She is hypotensive and bradycardic. Intravenous glucagon is administered, and her condition improves. Which of the following intracellular changes is most likely responsible for the improvement in her condition?
o: Decreased cAMP in vascular smooth muscle
Decreased DAG in vascular smooth muscle
223.e: This patient has most likely overdosed on beta blocker medications. Beta blocker overdose causes diffuse non-selective blockade of peripheral beta adrenergic receptors, causing depression of myocardial contractility, bradycardia, and varying degrees of AV block. The result is a low cardiac output state. Glucagon is the drug of choice for beta blocker overdose. Glucagon acts on G protein-coupled receptors, increasing intracellular CAMP and thus increasing the release of intracellular calcium during muscle contraction. This increases heart rate and cardiac contractility. Improvements in heart rate and blood pressure may be observed within minutes. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 192

223.q: A patient presented with suspected cocaine overdose. Which of the following features is not seen in this patient?
223.e: In the periphery, cocaine it blocks uptake of NA and Adr intoadrenergic nerve endings, resulting in higher concentration of the transmitter around the receptors → sympathomimetic effect, potentiation of directly acting sympathomimetics and suppression of indirectly acting sympathomimetics. Local vasoconstriction, tachycardia, rise in BP and mydriasis are the manifestations of its sympathomimetic action.

223.q: While playing in the garden, a 9-year-old boy is stung by 3 bees, now presented to ED for difficulty breathing since 15 minutes. When the symptoms started, his mother noticed a rash and swelling of his tongue and lips. Two years ago, he was diagnosed with asthma. What is the treatment of choice?
223.e: Given clinical scenario of patient's rash, swelling, and difficulty breathing shortly after exposure to bee's stung are suggestive of anaphylaxis. In this case, start initial treatment immediately by administering epinephrine IM 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh. Epinephrine injections for anaphylaxis should always be given intramuscularly in a concentration of 1:1,000 (Option B is correct) Option C: Epinephrine 1:10,000 solution used in cardiac arrest through IV route. Injecting the 1:1,000 solution into a vein can lead to cardiac arrhythmia/arrest. Option A & D: Antihistamines and corticosteroids are sometimes used as supplementary agents, but the prompt parenteral use of epinephrine is mandatory and lifesaving, thus it's treatment of choice for anaphylaxis. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 147.

223.q: A 65-year-old male is given an intravenous infusion of an agent that increases peripheral vascular resistance, increases systolic blood pressure, decreases pulse pressure, and decreases heart rate. Which of the following agents is being described?
223.e: Of the agents given in option, only phenylephrine has the actions described. Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist that causes marked arterial vasoconstriction when administered intravenously. The result is an increase in systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure. The induced blood pressure increase elicits a baroreceptor-mediated increase in vagal tone, which results in decreased stroke volume and a slowed heart rate. The pulse pressure, defined as the systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure, is decreased by phenylephrine because of the reflex decrease in stroke volume and the increased afterload. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 194

223.q: 48-year-old man comes with blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg despite the use of enalapril as well as an appropriate dietary and exercise program. He has had problems with asthma since childhood and having allergy with sulfa drugs. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for this patient?
223.e: This patient is hypertensive despite the use of the ACE inhibitor enalapril, an appropriate diet, and an exercise program. The physician then prescribes a second antihypertensive medication. A beta blocker was likely chosen since the use of a thiazide or loop diuretic is contraindicated in this patient due to a severe sulfa allergy. B1-selective antagonists are often used to control hypertension in patients, such as asthmatics, who might experience bronchoconstriction with nonselective beta antagonists (e.g., propranolol). Remember that beta1 receptors predominate in the heart, while B2 receptors predominate in the lungs. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 187

223.q: Which among the following is a short-acting beta-blocker?
223.e: Explanation: Esmolol is an ultra- short-acting cardioselective beta-1 blocker. Its exceptionally short half-life (~9 minutes) is due to rapid metabolism by erythrocyte esterases . This makes it ideal for use in critical care settings (e.g., supraventricular tachycardia, perioperative hypertension) where precise, short-duration beta-blockade is required. Explanation of other options: Nadolol (Option A): A long-acting, non-selective beta-blocker. Propranolol (Option B): A non-selective beta-blocker with an intermediate half-life. Atenolol (Option D): A cardioselective beta-blocker with a longer half-life, suitable for once-daily dosing. Key Takeaways: Esmolol's short duration of action is due to metabolism by esterases in the blood. It is the beta-blocker of choice when a rapidly titratable and reversible effect is needed.

224.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic myopia comes to the ophthalmologist for regular check-up. Examination shows bilateral narrowing of peripheral visual fields, cupping of the optic discs, and elevated intraocular pressure. Gonioscopy shows no abnormalities. Which of the following first line of treatment for this patient ?
224.e: The loss of peripheral vision, optic disc cupping, and elevated intraocular pressure in this patient with a normal gonioscopy are diagnostic of open-angle glaucoma. Preferred first-line therapy are topical prostaglandin analogs like Latanoprost. Alternative options are Topical beta blockers alone and/or alpha-2 agonists OR Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. For treatment of Refractory glaucoma, oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are used. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 159.

224.q: Topical application of 400 mcg/ml mitomycin C is used for
224.e: Mitomycin is an anti-tumor antibiotic with alkylating agent like property. It is used in superficial cancer of urinary bladder and for squamous cell carcinoma of anus . The drug has radiomimetic effects, and also sensitizes hypoxic tumor cells to the effects of hypoxia. Application of topical mitomycin C after endoscopic dilation of laryngotracheal stenosis reduces the rate of restenosis.

740.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recent onset of weakness of her hands, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing. She has been treated for myasthenia gravis for several years. Which of the following is the best drug for distinguishing between myasthenic crisis and cholinergic crisis ?
740.e: Any of the cholinesterase inhibitors (choices B, C, or D) would effectively correct myasthenic crisis. However, because cholinergic crisis (if that is what is causing the symptoms) would be worsened by a cholinomimetic, we choose the shortest-acting cholinesterase inhibitor, edrophonium. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 113

740.q: A 45-year-old farmer is admitted for Parathion poisoning. Which one of the following is its characteristics?
o: If treated early, its toxicity may be partly reversed by pralidoxime
It is less toxic to humans than malathion
It is more persistent in the environment than DDT
It is poorly absorbed through skin and lungs
740.e: The "-thion" organophosphates (those containing the P=S bond) are activated, not inactivated, by conversion to "-oxon" (P=O) derivatives. They are less stable than halogenated hydrocarbon insecticides of the DDT type; therefore, they are less persistent in the environment. Parathion is more toxic than malathion. It is very lipid-soluble and rapidly absorbed through the lungs and skin. Pralidoxime has very high affinity for the phosphorus atom and is a chemical antagonist of organophosphates. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 115

740.q: A 30-year-old woman complains of severe bloating after undergoing abdominal surgery. She also finds it difficult to urinate. Mild cholinomimetic stimulation without vasodilation is preferred for treatment. Which agent should be preferred ?
740.e: Bethanechol or distigmine is often effective in relieving post-op ileus. Neostigmine and bethanechol in moderate doses have significantly different effects on vascular endothelium. Bethanechol directly acts on muscarinic receptor of vascular endothelium and cause vasodilation, while Distigmine, Indirectly acting AchE inhibitor, does not cause vasodilation. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 132

740.q: Which one of the following can be blocked by atropine?
o: Decreased blood pressure caused by hexamethonium
Increased blood pressure caused by nicotine
740.e: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and inhibits parasympathomimetic effects. Nicotine can induce both parasympathomimetic and sympathomimetic effects by virtue of its ganglion-stimulating action. B & C: Hypertension and exercise-induced tachycardia reflect sympathetic discharge with norepinephrine release and therefore would not be blocked by atropine. D: Exercise-induced sweating is another sympathomimetic response, but it is mediated by acetylcholine released from sympathetic nerve fibers at eccrine sweat glands. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 128

740.q: A 62-year-old man has increased intraocular pressure bilaterally. You start him on drug used to treat his open-angle glaucoma, which also happens to cross the blood-brain barrier better than other drugs in its class. Which of the following drugs is this?
740.e: All of the drugs listed inhibit acetylcholinesterase, but physostigmine best crosses the blood-brain barrier. These drugs increase the effects of endogenous acetylcholine by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, which increase the half-life of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft. Physostigmine decreases intraocular pressure by stimulating contraction of the ciliary muscle, which opens the trabecular meshwork, increasing outflow of the aqueous humor. (A) Echothiophate is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that can also be used for glaucoma but does not cross the blood-brain barrier. (B) Neostigmine is often used after surgeries to hasten recovery from anesthesia. It does not cross the blood-brain barrier. (D) Pyridostigmine is used to treat myasthenia gravis. It does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 110

740.q: A 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increased sweating for the past 6 months. She experiences severe sweating that is triggered by stressful situations and speaking in public. She is failing one of her university classes because of her avoidance of public speaking. She has not had any fevers, chills, weight loss, or night sweats. Her temperature is 36.6°C (98°F). Physical examination shows moist skin in the axillae and on the palms, soles, and face. Which of the following drugs is most likely to be effective for this patient's condition?
740.e: Sweating is an autonomic reflex primarily mediated by acetylcholine receptors of the sympathetic nervous system. Glycopyrrolate is an anticholinergic agent used to treat hyperhidrosis. This drug blocks ACh at muscarinic receptors, which temporarily reduces sweat production. As with any anticholinergic drug, careful dosing is required to avoid adverse effects of excessive ACh inhibition (e.g., flushed skin, cycloplegia, dry mouth, constipation). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 134

740.q: A 38-year-old man has been admitted to the emergency department showing signs of autonomic drug toxicity. Which of the following signs would distinguish between an overdose of a ganglion blocker versus a muscarinic blocker?
o: Dry skin in a warm environment
740.e: Neither ganglion blockers nor muscarinic blockers cause miosis; they cause mydriasis. Both classes of cholinoceptor blockers increase resting heart rate and cause cycloplegia, because these are determined largely by parasympathetic tone. Similarly, both can cause dry skin, since this requires cholinergic transmission. Postural hypotension, on the other hand, is a sign of sympathetic blockade, which would occur with ganglion blockers but not muscarinic blockers. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 133

740.q: A 68-year-old woman referred to you for ECG showing 2:1 second-degree AV block. If you administer atropine intravenously to the patient in, you would expect which of the following to occur?
o: Increase sinus rate and maintain 2:1 AV block
Increase sinus rate and improve heart block to 1:1 conduction
No change in sinus rate and worsen heart block to >2:1
740.e: In heart block occurring at the AV node, the administration of atropine (an anticholinergic agent) will often improve the block as the AV node has a high degree of vagal efferent innervation. The SA node phase 4 action potential slope will increase as well with anticholinergic stimulation, causing faster sinus rate. In heart block occurring below the AV node, anticholinergic stimulation will often cause the appearance of a worse (3:1, 4:1, etc.) heart block as the sinus rate increases and more impulses are transmitted to the infranodal tissue during its prolonged (and unchanged with atropine) refractory period. (Note :One may use this finding to differentiate Wenckebach and type II second-degree heart block during difficult-to-interpret 2:1 conduction.) Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 244

225.q: Which of the following drugs will not produce fixed dilated pupils?
225.e: Pilocarpine causes marked sweating, salivation and increase in other secretions. The cardiovascular effects are complex. Small doses generally cause fall in BP (muscarinic), but higher doses elicit rise in BP and tachycardia which is probably due to ganglionic stimulation (through ganglionic muscarinic receptors). Applied to the eye, it penetrates cornea and promptly causes miosis, ciliary muscle contraction and fall in intraocular tension lasting 4-8 hours.

225.q: A 55-year-old man with recurrent episodes of retrosternal chest pain. He is given a sublingual tablet and reports rapid relief of the pain. This drug most likely improved this patient's symptoms by causing which of the following hemodynamic changes?
o: Decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume
225.e: This patient has a classic presentation of chronic stable angina, which is characterized by chest pain that occurs with activity and is relieved with rest or sublingual nitroglycerin. Nitrates exert their effect by direct vascular smooth muscle relaxation that results in: Vasodilation of the peripheral veins and arteries, predominantly venodilation Decreased left ventricular wall stress due to reduced preload (decreased left ventricular end-diastolic volume and pressure) Modest reduction in afterload due to systemic arterial vasodilation Mild coronary artery dilation and reduction of coronary vasospasm. This results in decreased myocardial oxygen demand, leading to improved exercise tolerance and relief of angina symptoms. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 221

225.q: Which one of the following is not a nitric oxide donor but causes it to be synthesized and released from endogenous precursors, resulting in vasodilation?
225.e: Nitroprusside and organic nitrites (eg, amyl nitrite) and nitrates (eg, nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, and isosorbide mononitrate) contain NO groups that can be released as NO. Arginine is the normal source of endogenous NO. Acetylcho- line, acting on M3 receptors, stimulates the synthesis of NO from arginine. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung

225.q: A 60-year-old male is diagnosed with exertional angina. His treatment regimen includes metoprolol, isosorbide dinitrate and aspirin. He takes isosorbide dinitrate early in the morning and again in the afternoon, but he does not take an evening dose. Such a pattern of drug administration is intended to decrease which of the following?
225.e: Around-the-clock nitrate administration (in any form) rapidly results in development of tolerance to nitrates. This is why a nitrate-free interval must be provided every day in patients that are using daily long acting nitrates. The mechanism by which this occurs has not been fully demonstrated, but it is theorized that it is due to a decreased vascular sensitivity to nitrates and an increased sensitivity to endogenous vasoconstricting agents. Usually the nitrate-free period is timed to occur during the night when the patient is sleeping and cardiac work is the least. Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 214

225.q: A 65-year-old man with known CAD comes with exertional chest tightness. The patient underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery 3 years ago for progressive angina. You discuss about adding isosorbide dinitrate to his current therapy but the patient is concerned about adverse effects. Which of the following is most likely to occur in this patient with the add-on therapy?
225.e: Nitrates are frequently used for symptomatic relief in patients with chronic stable angina. The anti-ischemic effect of nitrates is mediated by systemic vasodilation (predominantly venodilation) with a decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume and wall stress, resulting in decreased myocardial oxygen demand and relief of angina symptoms. The main adverse effects seen with nitrate therapy include headaches, cutaneous flushing, lightheadedness, hypotension, and reflex tachycardia. Nitrates must be avoided in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (due to increased outflow tract obstruction), right ventricular infarction (due to reduction in preload, impairing cardiac output), and those on phosphodiesterase inhibitors (synergism increases the risk of severe hypotension). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 217

225.q: A 67-year-old woman has been put on filgrastim after being treated with anticancer drugs, the therapeutic objective is to prevent which of the following?
225.e: Filgrastim (G-CSF) stimulates the production and function of neutrophils, important cellular mediators of the innate immune system that serve as the first line of defense against infection. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834

226.q: Hypertension and pulmonary edema associated with scorpion sting is managed by:-
226.e: Scorpion sting is a dreadful medical emergency. Scorpion stings cause a wide range of symptoms, from severe local reactions to cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological manifestations. Alpha-receptors play a vital role in the pathogenesis of cardiac failure and pulmonary edema due to scorpion sting. Prazosin is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blocker. It dilates veins and arterioles, thereby reducing preload and left ventricular impedance without rise in heart rate and renin secretion. It also inhibits sympathetic outflow in the central nervous system. It enhances insulin secretion, which is inhibited by venom action. It has also been found useful even in cases with hypotension. Thus, its pharmacological properties can antagonize the hemodynamic, hormonal and metabolic effects of scorpion venom action

226.q: Mechanism by which Ach decreases heart rate is by:
226.e: Ans: A. Delayed diastolic depolarization Acetyl choline decreases heart rate primarily by inhibiting the spontaneous depolarization of cells in SA node; also known as diastolic depolarization. This is achieved by inhibition of the funny current in the SA node. Effect of acetylcholine on cardiovascular system Heart rate Ach inhibits funny current generation in the decreases pacemaker cells of SA node AV conduction Ach blocks L type calcium channels in the AV decreases node Atrial contraction Atrium is supplied by cholinergic fibers more than decreases > the ventricles. Ach opens potassium channels ventricular and decreases cyclic AMP in the myocardial cells. contraction Ach increases calcium in endothelial cells, which Vasodilation stimulates calcium dependent ENOS and releases NO which causes vasodilation.

226.q: Which of the following drugs does not reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?
226.e: Explanation: Digoxin is a positive inotrope used in HFrEF to improve symptoms and reduce hospitalizations due to heart failure. However, large clinical trials have shown it has no significant impact on overall mortality . Explanation of other options: B) Beta-blockers, C) ACE inhibitors, D) H-ISDN: All of these are pillars of HFrEF therapy with robust evidence from clinical trials demonstrating significant mortality benefit . Key Takeaways: Drugs that reduce mortality in HFrEF include ACEIs/ARBs/ARNIs, beta-blockers, MRAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors. Digoxin improves symptoms but not survival.

226.q: Mannitol is used in the management of:-
226.e: Mannitol is very helpful in lowering of intraocular pressure in cases of Acute congestive glaucoma. MOA: Increases the extracellular oncotic pressure hence extracting water from cells and tissues. Uses Its indications are: Increased intracranial or intraocular tension (acute congestive glaucoma, head injury, stroke, etc To maintain GFR and urine flow in impending acute renal failure To counteract low osmolality of plasma and ECF due to rapid haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis (dialysis disequilibrium). Mannitol is contraindicated in renal insufficiency, acute tubular necrosis, anuria, pulmonary edema; acute left ventricular failure, CHF and cerebral haemorrhage.(Options A,C,D ruled out) The most common side effect is headache. Nausea and vomiting may occur; hypersensitivity reactions are rare.

226.q: A patient on digoxin, potassium chloride, clarithromycin, atenolol and triamterene developed ventricular arrhythmia. Serum digoxin levels were raised. Which of the following medications might be responsible for it?
226.e: CYP3A4/5 Carryout biotransformation of largest number(nearly 50%) of drugs. In addition to the liver, these isoforms are expressed in the intestine (responsible for first pass metabolism at this site) and kidney as well. Inhibition of this isoenzyme by erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole is responsible for the important drug interaction with terfenadine, astemizole and cisapride which are its substrates. Verapamil, ritonavir and a constituent of grapefruit juice are other important inhibitors. Enzyme inhibitors [ Virat Kohli Can't Call Every Indians ] V alproate K etoconazole C imetidine C iprofloxacin/ C larithromycin E rythromycin I NH Enzyme Inducers [GPRS Cell Phone] G - Griseofulvin P - Phenytoin R - Rifampicin S - Smoking Cell - Carbamazepine Phone - Phenobarbitone

226.q: A patient receiving digoxin develops side effects such as nausea and vomiting. His serum digoxin concentration is found to be 4 ng/mL, while the therapeutic range is up to 1 ng/mL. Given that digoxin has a half-life of 40 hours, how long will it take before the drug can be safely restarted?
226.e: Explanation: It will take 80 hours before the drug can be safely restarted. The Plasma half-life (t½) of a drug is the time taken for its plasma concentration to be reduced to half of its original value. In the scenario, the digoxin serum concentration of 4 ng/ml is significantly above the therapeutic range. Starting at 4 ng/mL , it would take: 1 half-life (40 hrs) → 2 ng/mL 2 half-lives (80 hrs) → 1 ng/mL (within therapeutic range) Since the therapeutic range is ≤1 ng/mL , the drug can be safely restarted after 80 hours . Therefore, we should wait at least 80 hours before resuming treatment, considering digoxin's half-life of 40 hours.

226.q: Which of the following have convincingly demonstrated mortality reduction for patients with HFpEF?
226.e: While therapeutic targets in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFpEF) are relatively abundant and guided by the targets of disease modification, trials in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) have been largely disappointing. Overall, symptom management and blood pressure control are the goals in HFpEF treatment now. ACE inhibitors (option A) have been studies in many mechanistic studies and have shown no convincing mortality benefit. Similarly, angiotensin receptor blockers (option B) were studied in the CHARM-Preserved and I-PRESERVE studies and were found to have no mortality benefit. Sildenafil (a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor) was shown to improve filling pressures and RV function in patients with HFpEF, but did not show mortality benefit. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 248

226.q: A 70 years old male patient came to OPD with the complaints of cough, difficulty in breathing on exertion and chest pain. On Auscultation, no abnormal heart sound or murmur was heard, bilateral rhonchi were heard over lung fields. His pulse rate is 88/min; BP is 116/78 mm Hg. His chest radiogram was s/o COPD. So, treatment started with oral theophylline. What is the effect on Cardiovascular system of theophylline?
226.e: The methylxanthines have positive chronotropic and inotropic effects. At low concentrations, these effects appear to result from inhibition of presynaptic adenosine receptors in sympathetic nerves increasing catecholamine release at nerve endings. The higher concentrations (> 10 μmol/L, 2 mg/L) associated with inhibition of phosphodiesterase and increases in cAMP may result in increased influx of calcium. At much higher concentrations (> 100 μmol/L), sequestration of calcium by the sarcoplasmic reticulum is impaired. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 345

227.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Methyldopa o Centrally acting sympatholytic antihypertensives are clonidine, methyldopa, guanabenz, guanfacine, moxonidine and rilmenidine.

227.q: A 57-year-old man is found to have a blood pressure of 150/100 mm Hg on three successive occasions. He has begun on an antihypertensive agent. After taking the first dose of the medication, he goes out to play golf and collapses on the golf course. Which one of the following drugs may be responsible for his symptoms?
227.e: Prazosin produces first- dose hypotension, presumably by blocking alpha-1- receptors. This effect is minimized by initially giving the drug in small, divided doses. Other options do not cause first-dose hypotension. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 182

227.q: A 53-year-old man comes with shortness of breath and chest tightness. Blood pressure is 200/110 mm Hg and pulse is 90/min and regular. Lung examination reveals bibasilar crackles. Nitroglycerin infusion is started and results in significant symptomatic improvement. Which of the following intracellular events is most likely responsible for the beneficial effects of this patient's treatment?
227.e: This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with acute pulmonary edema due to severely elevated blood pressure (hypertensive emergency). In such cases, intravenous vasodilators (nitroglycerine, sodium nitroprusside) are often used to improve the acute heart failure by reducing preload and afterload. Nitrates are metabolized within vascular smooth muscle cells to nitric oxide, which activates guanylate cyclase and promotes the conversion of guanosine triphosphate (GTP) to cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). Increased levels of cGMP lead to decreased intracellular calcium (reduces the activity of myosin light-chain kinase) and activation of myosin light chain phosphatase. This promotes myosin light-chain dephosphorylation and vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 221

227.q: 57-year-old homeless man takes an antihypertensive agent but has not been able to obtain the medication. Patient's blood pressure is 190/110 mm Hg. Which one of the following antihypertensive drugs can precipitate a hypertensive crisis following abrupt cessation of therapy?
227.e: Increased sympathetic nervous system activity occurs if clonidine therapy is abruptly stopped after prolonged administration. Uncontrolled elevation in blood pressure can occur. Patients should be slowly weaned from clonidine while other antihypertensive medications are initiated. Other options do not cause increased sympathetic activity after abrupt discontinuation. Reference Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 185

227.q: An investigational study, a newly synthesized drug is found to have antihypertensive effects. Increasing drug concentrations can cause increase in arteriolar radius and decrease beta cell insulin secretion. The mechanism of action of which of the following drugs most closely resembles the mechanism of action of the experimental drug?
227.e: The experimental agent is able to do both vasodilation and to decrease the release of insulin in response to glucose. The question is which known drug has similar effects. The answer is diazoxide, a K+ channel opener with hyperglycemic effects; Diazoxide is a direct acting peripheral vasodilator that decreases both systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Specifically, diazoxide opens K channels on vascular smooth muscle, causing hyperpolarization and vasodilation, resulting in a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance. Opening K channels on pancreatic beta cells causes hyperpolarization and decreased calcium entry through voltage-gated calcium channels. As a result, diazoxide decreases insulin secretion in response to glucose. Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 183-84

227.q: A 56-year-old man with male pattern baldness and hypertension is placed on minoxidil. He has had a lack of response to antihypertensive agents with failure to respond to calcium channel blockers and ACE inhibitors. Prolonged use of this agent can be associated with which of the following effects?
227.e: This drug causes dilation of resistance vessels (arterioles) but not of capacitance vessels (venules). Minoxidil is administered orally for treatment of severe to malignant hypertension that is refractory to other drugs. Reflex tachycardia and fluid retention may be severe and require the concomitant use of a loop diuretic and a beta-blocker. Minoxidil causes serious sodium and water retention, leading to volume overload, edema, and congestive heart failure. Minoxidil treatment also causes hypertrichosis (the growth of body hair). This drug is used topically to treat male pattern baldness. Option(A) This agent is used to treat male pattern baldness. Option(C) This agent is not associated with muscle wasting. Option(D) This agent does not cause uremic pericarditis. Reference Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 178

227.q: A 65-year-old woman with chronic CHF. All of the following drug should be avoided except ?
227.e: Avoidance of drugs that may worsen CHF Most antiarrhythmic agents Calcium channel blockers (except amlodipine) NSAIDs Thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone) Inhalation anesthetics Cautious selection of antidepressants due to numerous interactions and adverse effects when used with HF drugs (SSRIs may be used judiciously) Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 221, 222

227.q: A 59-year-old man with hypertension presents with lower extremity edema. Physical examination reveals pitting edema from the ankles to the knees bilaterally. The patient has begun on furosemide. What could be side effect seen in this patient ?
227.e: Furosemide is a loop diuretic with important interactions that treating we must be aware of. This agent will potentiate the action of other antihypertensives, and the patient can become hypotensive. GO PANDA ”: G out, O totoxicity, low P otassium, A llergy, N ephritis, D ehydration, A lkalosis. Option(A) Hypokalemia will result when combined with corticosteroids. Option(B) Orthostatic hypotension is worsened by furosemide. Option(C) Ototoxicity results when furosemide is combined with aminoglycoside antibiotics. Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 177

228.q: A mild hypertensive patient presented with chronic renal insufficiency and pedal edema. On investigations, serum creatinine was found to be 1.9 mg/dL with GFR <40 ml/min. Which of the following drugs should be used for management of hypertension in this patient?
228.e: Metolazone In common with loop diuretics it is able to evoke a clinically useful response even in severe renal failure (g.f.r. ~15 ml/min), and has marked additive action when combined with furosemide. An additional proximal tubular action has been demonstrated; PO4 reabsorption that occurs in PT, is inhibited. It is excretedunchanged in urine. Metolazone has been usedmainly for edema and occasionally for hypertension

228.q: A 75-year-old man with COPD and chronic heart failure presents to you for follow-up. The patient takes multiple medications for these problems. Which of the following strategies may prove to have additional benefit in the treatment of this patient?
o: Use of calcium channel blockers at high dose
Use of beta-blockers at high doses
228.e: Chronic HF is typically managed by A reduction in physical activity Low dietary intake of sodium ( Treatment of comorbid conditions Judicious use of diuretics, inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin system, and inotropic agents. Drugs that may precipitate or exacerbate HF, such as NSAIDs drugs, alcohol, calcium channel blockers, high-dose beta-blockers, and some antiarrhythmic drugs, should be avoided if possible. Patients with HF complain of dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, and dependent edema. Vigorous exercise in this deconditioned patient may worsen heart function. Use of calcium channel blockers at high doses can worsen heart failure. Use of beta-blockers at high doses can worsen heart failure. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 221

228.q: A 60-year-old patient complains of paresthesias and occasional nausea associated with one of the drugs she is taking. She is found to have hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. She is probably taking
o: Amiloride for edema associated with aldosteronism
Furosemide for severe hypertension and heart failure
228.e: Paresthesias and gastrointestinal distress are common adverse effects of acetazolamide, especially when it is taken chronically, as in glaucoma. The observation that the patient has metabolic acidosis also suggests the use of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor like acetazolamide. Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 262

228.q: A 57-year-old woman with "fainting spell", her blood pressure is 120/60 when lying down and 60/20 when she sits up. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of her fainting spell?
228.e: The case history suggests that the syncope (fainting) is associated with diuretic use. Complications of diuretics that can result in syncope include both postural hypotension (which this patient exhibits) due to excessive reduction of blood volume and arrhythmias due to excessive potassium loss. Potassium wasting is more common with thiazides (because of their long duration of action), but these drugs rarely cause reduction of blood volume sufficient to result in orthostatic hypotension. Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 262

228.q: A patient diagnosed with ascites due to cirrhosis. The diuretic of choice to reduce edema would be?
228.e: Aldosterone antagonists like Spironolactone and Eplerenone are the drugs of choice for Cirrhotic edema, resistant edema and hypertension. Uses of Spironolactone & Eplerenone It is a weak diuretic in its own right and is used mostly in combination with other more efficacious diuretics. To counteract K+ loss due to thiazide and loop diuretics. Edema: Spironolactone is more useful in cirrhotic and nephritic edema in which aldosterone levels are generally high. It potentiates thiazides and loop diuretics and is frequently added to them in the treatment of ascites due to cirrhosis of the liver. It breaks resistance to the thiazide/loop diuretic that develops due to secondary hyperaldosteronism and re-establishes the response. Thus, spironolactone is particularly employed in refractory edema. Hypertension: Spironolactone is used to augment a thiazide in the treatment of resistant hypertension.

228.q: A 34 yr old male with hypertension diagnosed with stage 4 chronic kidney disease with eGFR<30 ml/min. His doctor wants to prescribe a thiazide diuretic. Which of the following can be given?
228.e: Metolazone and Indapamide are two thiazide diuretics that can be administered even in patients with renal insufficiency. Metolazon e: In common with loop diuretics, it is able to evoke a clinically useful response even in severe renal failure (g.f.r. ~15 ml/min), and has marked additive action when combined with furosemide. An additional proximal tubular action has been demonstrated; PO4 reabsorption that occurs in PT, is inhibited. It is excreted unchanged in urine. Metolazone has been used mainly for edema.

228.q: Side effect of thiazide diuretics are all except ?
228.e: Ans. is 'A' i.e., Hypocalcemia Thiazides cause hypercalcemia (see above explanation).

228.q: A 54-year-old man comes with severe pain with tenderness in his first metatarsophalangeal joint. He says that the pain was so bad that it woke him up from sleep. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? Laboratory studies show WBC count is 12 x 103/mL , creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, calcium is 8.6 mg/dL, and uric acid is 9.5 mg/dL.
228.e: Acute gouty arthritis (AGA) is characterized by the rapid onset of pain, swelling, and inflammation. The attack is often monoarticular at first, affecting the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint. Uric acid levels are generally >7.5 mg/dL when an attack occurs. Changes in rate levels, leading to gout flares, can result from acute alcohol intoxication, overindulgence of foods high in purines, rapid weight loss, dehydration, and trauma. Medications (e.g., thiazide or loop diuretics, allopurinol, uricosuric agents, Low-dose aspirin) can also precipitate gout. Mnemonic : TH e NI ce PYR A mid Th iazides(+loop diuretics), ni acin, pyr azinamide, a spirin Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 262

229.q: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a MI with cardiac arrhythmia. A continuous intravenous infusion of lidocaine, 1.92 mg/min, is started at 8 AM. The average pharmacokinetic parameters of lidocaine are: Vd 77 L; clearance 640 mL/min; half-life 1.4 h. What is the expected steady-state plasma concentration?
229.e: The drug is being administered continuously and the steady- state concentration (Cp(ss)) for a continuously administered drug is given by the equation. Thus, Dosage = Plasma level × Clearance 1.92 mg/min = Cp(ss) × CL Rearranging : Cp(ss) = 1.92 mg/min 640 mL/min Cp(ss) = 0.003 mg/mL or 3 mg/L Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Fourteenth Edition, Pg no. 50

229.q: Identify the incorrect choice regarding choice of anti-arrhythmic.
o: A 12-year-old with congenital LQTS = Magnesium sulphate
A 67-year-old on digoxin with supraventricular arrythmia = Propranolol
A 56-year old with ventricular arrhythmia due after MI = lidocaine
229.e: Other choices are correct A 45-year-old with supraventricular arrhythmia = Verapamil A 67-year-old on digoxin with supraventricular arrythmia = Propranolol A 56-year old with ventricular arrhythmia due after MI = lidocaine Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 248

229.q: 56-year-old woman presents with complaints of fatigue, sluggishness, and weight gain. She has been taking T4 since 5 years without significant problems regarding her energy level. Her recent history is significant for diagnosis of arrhythmia, and she is currently taking an anti-arrhythmic drug. What is the most likely cause of her current condition?
229.e: Amiodarone is an iodine-containing anti-arrhythmic drug with complex effects on the thyroid gland and thyroid hormones. One of its actions is to inhibit peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. Note that propranolol also reduces conversion of T4 to T3. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 692

229.q: A 48-year old male had an overdose, and manifested severe acute procainamide toxicity with markedly long QT. Which of the following should be given immediately?
229.e: The most effective therapy for procainamide (and quinidine) toxicity appears to be concentrated sodium lactate due to increase in sodium current by increasing the sodium ion gradient and reduced drug-receptor binding by alkalinizing the tissue . Pressor sympathomimetics are to be used to reverse drug-induced hypotension if indicated. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 14th Edition, Page Number-241.

229.q: Mr. Agrawal underwent tPA administration for STEMI 2 hour previously. He had an excellent response with resolution of his ST- elevation. However, You note a wide complex ventricular rhythm with a rate of 75 bpm. Mr. Agrawal feels well. The next most appropriate step will be ?
229.e: This patient has an accelerated idioventricular rhythm, a common finding in patients with successful reperfusion after thrombolytic therapy. This rhythm is benign and requires no further therapy. It invariably resolves on its own. A & C : Amiodarone or metoprolol would be appropriate therapy if this was ventricular tachycardia or perhaps supraventricular tachycardia. Carotid sinus massage would be appropriate in the setting of supraventricular tachycardia. B : Flecainide (a class I antiarrhythmic) is contraindicated in post-MI patients because it was found to increase mortality. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 244

229.q: You admit a patient and instruct the nurse in-charge to continuously monitor ECG every 4 hours since you gave a drug that can cause a potent change in the ECG. Which of the following medications can cause a prolongation of the QT interval?
229.e: Drugs causing QT prolongation include: Antiarrhythmics : Quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide, propafenone, amiodarone Antimalarials : Quinine, mefloquine, artemisinin, halofantrine Antibacterials : Sparfloxacin, moxifloxacin Antihistamines : Terfenadine, astemizole, ebastine Antidepressants : Amitriptyline and other tricyclics Antipsychotics : Thioridazine, pimozide, aripiprazole, ziprasidone Prokinetic : Cisapride

230.q: A 53-year-old obese man with past history of acute myocardial infarction is on metoprolol and low- dose aspirin. His total serum cholesterol level is 155 mg/dL, with an HDL level of 27 mg/dL and a triglyceride level of 92 mg/dL. Which of the following lipid-lowering agents would be most effective for preventing future cardiovascular events in this patient?
230.e: Patients with low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels (men Nonpharmacologic measures such as exercise, weight loss, and smoking cessation help to raise HDL levels and have significant cardiovascular benefits. In contrast, use of medications to raise HDL levels does not improve cardiovascular outcomes.
