Pharmacologic treatment of patients with low HDL levels should focus on lowering LDL cholesterol with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins), as these are the most effective lipid- lowering drugs for preventing cardiovascular events. Statins are indicated for secondary prevention in all patients with known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, regardless of baseline lipid levels. Cationic exchange resin = cholestyramine Essential fatty acids = Omega-3-fatty acid Pharmacologic vitamin= niacin Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 221

230.q: A 48-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia comes for follow-up with current LDL level of 190 mg/dL. Which of the following should be obtained before starting statin therapy in this patient?
230.e: Serious side effects of statins include myopathy and hepatitis. Although mild elevations of liver enzymes are common, significant liver injury (aspartate transaminase/alanine transaminase levels more than 3 times the upper limit of normal) is seen in less than 1% of patients and is usually reversible if the medication is discontinued. Liver function tests are recommended before starting statin therapy; otherwise, routine monitoring is not necessary unless symptoms of hepatic injury develop (eg, fatigue, malaise, anorexia). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 212

230.q: A 42-year-old woman with persistent hyperlipidaemia despite 6 months of maintaining a healthy diet and exercising regularly. Although her past medical history is significant for biliary colic secondary to gallstones, the patient has refused elective cholecystectomy. Laboratory studies show elevated serum triglycerides and LDL cholesterol levels. Drug therapy is discussed with the patient. Given this patient's pre-existing gallbladder disease, which of the following drugs should be avoided?
230.e: In patients with significant hypertriglyceridemia, fibrates are particularly effective due to their ability to upregulate lipoprotein lipase resulting in increased oxidation of fatty acids (liver, muscles). Gemfibrozil and other fibrates inhibit the rate-limiting enzyme in bile acid synthesis, cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase. The reduced bile acid production results in decreased cholesterol solubility and increased microcrystal precipitation, thereby promoting gallstone formation . As a result, fibrates should be used with caution in patients with preexisting gallbladder disease. Patients on fibrate therapy should also be monitored for myopathy, a risk significantly increased when fibrates are used concurrently with statins. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1098

230.q: A patient who has recently had a myocardial infarction (MI) presents for a follow-up. His cholesterol levels are as follows: total cholesterol 238 mg/dL, triglycerides 125 mg/dL, and HDL 50 mg/dL. He is currently taking atorvastatin, metoprolol, and aspirin. Which of the following medications should be added to his regimen? 1. Ezetimibe 2. Bempedoic acid 3. Evolocumab 4. Gemfibrozil
230.e: Explanation: This patient has elevated LDL cholesterol post-MI despite statin therapy. Therefore, Ezetimibe, Bempedoic acid, and Evolocumab can be added for further LDL reduction. Gemfibrozil is not indicated since triglycerides are normal. Ezetimibe (1): Inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption → ↓ LDL and total cholesterol. Bempedoic acid (2): Inhibits ATP-citrate lyase → ↓ hepatic cholesterol synthesis → ↓ LDL. Evolocumab (3): PCSK9 inhibitor → prevents LDL receptor degradation → ↑ LDL clearance. Explanation of other options: Gemfibrozil (Option D): Incorrect because it is used for severe hypertriglyceridemia and not for LDL lowering. Key Takeaways: Add Ezetimibe , Bempedoic acid , or Evolocumab if LDL remains high despite statins. Gemfibrozil reserved for hypertriglyceridemia. PCSK9 inhibitors are potent LDL reducers post-MI.

230.q: Patients taking which of the following drugs should be advised to avoid drinking grapefruit juice?
230.e: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 in the liver, particularly at high doses. This can cause decreased drug elimination via hepatic metabolism and can increase potential drug toxicities. Atorvastatin is metabolized via this pathway. Drugs that may enhance atorvastatin toxicity via this mechanism include phenytoin, ritonavir, clarithromycin, and azole antifungals. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.60

230.q: A 45-year-old man is also started on high-intensity atorvastatin therapy, along with antiplatelet therapy and appropriate medications to control blood pressure. Four weeks later, the patient's total cholesterol level is 140 mg/dL, down from 200 mg/dL before discharge. Which of the following has most likely increased as the result of the therapy?
230.e: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) inhibit the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis. In response to these changes, hepatocytes increase their surface expression of the LDL receptor to increase uptake of circulating LDL. Treatment generally produces a 20%-50% reduction in serum cholesterol and LDL concentration. High-intensity statin therapy reduces the risk of acute coronary events. This risk reduction is greater than that seen with other classes of lipid- lowering medications and is likely due to additional properties of statins. Besides effects on lipids, statins have anti-inflammatory properties improve endothelial dysfunction, and appear to stabilize atherosclerotic plaques. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 217

230.q: A 57-year-old man with severe hypertriglyceridemia is on fibrate medication in the past but could not tolerate it due to liver toxicity. The physician prescribes the appropriate medications and explains that the patient is likely to experience skin flushing and warmth after taking the pills. Which of the following is the primary agent mediating these side effects?
230.e: Nicotinic acid, or niacin, has been used in the treatment of hyperlipidemia for almost 4 decades. It is effective in raising HDL cholesterol levels, as well as lowering triglycerides and LDL levels. Niacin's main side effects are cutaneous flushing, warmth, and itching; these are primarily mediated by release of prostaglandins (particularly PGD2 and PGE2). Aspirin, which inhibits prostaglandin synthesis, can significantly reduce these side effects if given 30-60 minutes before niacin administration. The side effects are also reduced with slow-release preparations or if niacin is taken with meals. They are worst when niacin is first initiated and tend to fade over time due to tachyphylaxis. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 221

231.q: What is the mechanism of action of Sacubitril?
231.e: Sacubitril: It is an orally active Neutral Endopeptidase(NEP) inhibitor which increases the blood levels of Natriuretic Peptides and other vasodilator peptides resulting in natriuresis, diuresis, vascular relaxation, lowering of AngII as well as aldosterone levels. Combined with Valsartan, it affords symptomatic improvement in CHF patients. Option A: ACE inhibitors: Captopril, Lisinopril etc. Option C: Endothelin antagonist: Ambrisentan, Macitentan etc. Option D: Angiotensin receptor blocker: Valsartan, Telmisartan etc.

231.q: A 58-year-old female with diabetes with microalbuminuria, is started on captopril. What effect does a competitive inhibitor have on enzyme kinetics?
231.e: Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no. 21

231.q: A 78-year-old woman presents with increasing shortness of breath since 3 months. She underwent an emergency PCI for myocardial infarction 12 months ago. At the time of discharge, EDV was 300 mL and ejection fraction was 58%. She admits to rarely taking her medication as she usually feels well and has no symptoms. Current Echocardiography shows left ventricular dilation and an end-diastolic volume of 390 mL; Ejection fraction is 35%. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's worsening of ventricular function?
231.e: This woman did not adhere to medical therapy after the myocardial infarction and presents with dyspnea on exertion and a reduced ejection fraction with left ventricular dilation. These findings are most likely the result of unhindered cardiac remodelling. ACE inhibitors such enalapril have been found to decrease remodelling by slowing down the rate of left ventricular dilation after acute myocardial infarction (MI). This effect is achieved by decreasing preload and after-load due to blockage of angiotensin II. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 222

232.q: A 45-year-old woman with lung cancer has abnormally low serum osmolality and hyponatremia. A drug that increases the formation of dilute urine and is used to treat SIADH is
232.e: Retention of water with hyponatremia and inability to form dilute urine in the fully hydrated condition is characteristic of SIADH. Antagonists of ADH (Tolpvaptan) are needed to treat this condition. Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 268

232.q: Desmopressin is preferred over vasopressin because desmopressin -
232.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., More potent; 'c' i.e., Has little vasconstrictor activity o Desmopressin is longer acting o Desmopressin is V2 selective —) No V, mediated vasoconstriction. o Desmopressin is 12 times more potent than vasopressin.

Answer- A. Positive reinforcement Consistent dry bed training with positive reinforcement has a success rate of 85% and bed and pad alarm systems have a success rate of approximately 75% with relapse rate that are lower than those with pharmacotherapy.

232.q: 5 year old child bed wetting Rx of choice ?
232.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., No treatment o No treatment is given to children below 6 years of age because of high spontaneous cure rate. o After 6 years treatment include. t) Behavioral therapy : This is the treatment of choice. it) Pharmacological treatment : It is used when non-pharmacological (behavioral) therapy fails. Desmopressin is the drug of choice. Other drugs used are impramine and oxybutinin.

233.q: A patient is on long term anticonvulsant therapy. There is progressive contractility of the visual field. The likely anti-epileptic drug responsible for this adverse effect is?
233.e: Vigabatrin is an irreversible inhibitor of GABA transaminase , thus increases GABAergic activity. It is the DOC for infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis (ACTH is DOC for all other cases). It can result in irreversible visual field defects due to retinal atrophy.

233.q: Which statement concerning the proposed mechanisms of action of anticonvulsant drugs is most accurate?
o: Ethosuximide selectively blocks potassium ion (K+) channels in thalamic neurons.
Phenobarbital produces a selective blockade of Calcium ion (Ca2+) channels.
Phenytoin prolongs the inactivated state of the Na+ channel.
233.e: Benzodiazepines facilitate GABA-mediated inhibitory actions. Ethosuximide selectively blocks calcium channels in thalamic neurons. Phenobarbital produces multiple effects, mainly enhancement of GABA-chloride inhibitory activity. Phenytoin selectively blocks the Na+ channel and prolongs the inactivated state. Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 14th Edition, Page Number- 425.

233.q: Which of the following drug may cause irreversible vision loss ?
233.e: Vigabatrine, acts by inhibition of GABA transaminase irreversibly → ↑ GABA, used in Refractory focal seizures (adjunctive therapy) and Monotherapy for infantile spasms (West syndrome). It can cause irreversible vision loss in up to 50% of patients; so used only in patients if other anticonvulsants are ineffective. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number. 431

233.q: A 62-year-old woman is presented with sudden onset of severe left eye pain, blurred vision, nausea, and vomiting. She is on anti-seizure drug. Gonioscopy shows that the iris meets the cornea at an angle of 10° (N = 20-45°). Which of the following drug may precipitate this condition ?
233.e: Topiramate, Blockage of voltage-gated Na+ channels and↑ GABA. Dose-related adverse effects that occur frequently in the first 4 weeks of topiramate therapy are somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, nervousness, and confusion. Acute myopia and angle- closure glaucoma may require prompt drug withdrawal. Urolithiasis occurs in 0.5–1.5% of patients on long-term therapy and is more common in men. In some patients, carbonic anhydrase inhibition is associated with reduced serum bicarbonate that is usually asymptomatic but may result in nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, anorexia, or nausea and vomiting. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number 424

233.q: A 44-year-old woman on long-term Phenytoin therapy for 10 years presents with weakness and fatigue. Her CBC shows: Hb: 8.2 g/dL, MCV: 114 fL (macrocytic anemia). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
233.e: This patient is having megaloblastic anemia, probably due to long term phenytoin therapy. She should be given vitamin B12 + folic acid for the same. Long-term use is associated in some patients with coarsening of facial features and with mild peripheral neuropathy, usually manifested by diminished deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities. Long-term use may also result in abnormalities of vitamin D metabolism, leading to osteomalacia. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number. 428

233.q: ACTH is the treatment of choice for which of the following syndrome?
233.e: Infantile spasms (hypsarrhythmia) Therapy of this condition is unsatisfactory, antiepileptic drugs are generally useless. Corticosteroids(ACTH) afford symptomatic relief but cannot be used for long-term due to adverse effects. Clonazepam, valproate and vigabatrin may afford some relief. Drug of choice for infantile spasms is ACTH whereas infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis are treated with vigabatrin.

233.q: What is the most common and clinically significant side effect of Lamotrigine?
233.e: Explanation: The most common and significant adverse effect of lamotrigine is a skin rash , which can range from a simple maculopapular rash to life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). The risk is heightened by rapid dose escalation or concomitant use with valproate. Explanation of other options: A) Diplopia & B) Tremors: These are more commonly associated with other antiepileptics like carbamazepine or valproate, not lamotrigine. Neutropenia: This is a rare side effect of lamotrigine, not the most common or significant. Key Takeaways: Lamotrigine-induced rash is a major concern requiring careful dose titration. Concomitant valproate use increases lamotrigine levels and the risk of rash.

233.q: Fosphenytoin different from phenytoin in which of the following-
o: Can be used in absence seizures
It is the drug of choice for myoclonic seizures
233.e: Ans. 'b' i.e., Can be mixed with saline While phenytoin cannot be injected in a drip of glucose solution, fosphenytoin can be injected with saline and glucose.

234.q: For plasma level monitoring, when is lithium estimation done?
234.e: Serum-Level Monitoring and Dose Because of the low therapeutic index for Li+, regular determination Serum concentration is crucial. Concentrations considered to be effective and acceptably safe are between 0.6 and 1.5 mEq/L. The range of 1.0-1.5 mEq/L is favored for treatment of acutely manic patients. Somewhat lower values (0.6-1.0 mEq/L) are considered adequate and are safer for long-term prophylaxis. Serum concentrations of Li+ have been found to follow a clear dose-effect relationship between 0.4 and 1.0 mEq/L, but with a corresponding dose-dependent rise in polyuria and tremor as indices of adverse effects. By convention, the serum Li+ concentration is measured from samples obtained 10-12 h after the last oral dose of the day.

235.q: The aminoacid derived neurotransmitter used for treating depression is ?
235.e: Ans. A. Serotonine The three main neurotransmitters involved in depression are dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin (s-HT). When brain Ievels of one or more neurotransmitter are low or unbalanced, depression can result. Generally, antidepressant drugs work by increasing production or decreasing the breakdown of one or more of these neurotransmitters.

235.q: A healthy, 24-year-old man is prescribed sustained-release bupropion (Zyban) for smoking cessation. Twenty-one days after therapy he presents to his family physician with intermittent fever and a generalized rash, at which point the bupropion therapy is discontinued. A month later he develops a dry, intermittent cough and dyspnea. Which of the following pulmonary function test results is consistent with a diagnosis of allergic bronchospasm?
235.e: Bronchospasm increases the resistance to airflow, which makes it more difficult to expel gas rapidly from the lung during expiration, so although both FEV1 and vital capacity decrease, the percent of gas expelled in 1 second as a function of the total amount that can be expelled (the FEV1/FVC ratio) also decreases dramatically. Obstructive disease also produces air trapping, which increases the residual volume, functional residual capacity, and total lung capacity. Reference: Levitzky, pp 34-36, 40-46.

235.q: An 78-year-old man has difficulty sleeping. Triazolam is prescribed for her at one half of the conventional adult dose. Which statement about the use of triazolam in this elderly patient is most accurate?
o: Hypertension is a common adverse effect of benzodiazepines in elderly patients
Over-the-counter cold medications may antagonize the hypnotic effects of the drug
The patient may experience amnesia, especially if he also consumes alcoholic beverages
Triazolam does not cause rebound insomnia on abrupt discontinuance
235.e: In elderly patients taking benzodiazepines, hypotension is far more likely than an increase in blood pressure. Elderly patients are more prone to the CNS depressant effects of hypnotics; a dose reduction of 50% may still cause excessive sedation with possible ambulatory impairment. Additive CNS depression occurs commonly with drugs used in over- the-counter cold medications, especially antihistamines, and rebound insomnia can occur with abrupt discontinuance of benzodiazepines used as sleeping pills. Alcohol enhances psychomotor depression and the amnestic effects of the benzodiazepines. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number 385

235.q: A 45-year-old is started on a drug for recurrent major depression. After a week, she is presented with influenza-like symptoms including fevers and neck stiffness. After thorough investigation diagnosis of HLH (Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis) has been made. Which of the drug may cause secondary HLH ?
235.e: While secondary HLH is usually triggered by infection or malignancy, a through medication history is essential for prompt recognition and cessation of potentially offending agents such as lamotrigine. Outcomes for such patients with with holding of offending drug and prompt initiation of dexamethasone treatment. Although most controlled studies have evaluated lamotrigine as add-on therapy, the drug is effective as mono-therapy for focal seizures, and lamotrigine is now widely prescribed for this indication because of its excellent tolerability. It can also improve depression in patients with epilepsy and reduces the risk of relapse in bipolar disorder. Reference: https://jmedicalcasereports.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13256-019-2295-1

235.q: An 86 years old lady presented with severe constipation. She was a known hypertensive on medications for 10 years. In clinic, her BP was 157/98 mm Hg with a heart rate of 58/min. On taking here BP in the supine position it was found to be 90/60 mm Hg. She had the recent history of depression. She is taking atenolol, thiazide, imipramine, haloperidol and docusate. What will be the next best step in the management?
o: Change atenolol and thiazide to calcium channel blocker and ACE inhibitor and add bisacodyl for constipation
Change imipramine and haloperidol to fluoxetine and risperidone and add bisacodyl for constipation
Only add bisacodyl for constipation and continue rest of the medications
Discontinue all her medications and start her on steroids
235.e: Ans: B. Change imipramine and haloperidol to fluoxetine and risperidone and add bisacodyl for constipation (Ref Harrison 19/e p1623-1624, 18/e p3531: Goodman Gilman 12/e p410. 1333) Effects of Imipramine: Postural hypotension - Due to alpha blockade by Imipramine & thiazides interaction. Anti-cholinergic side-effect. Hence, Imipramine (TCA) must be discontinued. Should be started on SSRI, fluoxetin & laxative (existing constipation). Effect of haloperidol: Anti-cholinergic side effects. Should start on atypical antipsychotic Risperidone.

235.q: Drug "X" is used in the management of insomnia and facilitates the inhibitory actions of GABA, but it lacks anticonvulsant or muscle-relaxing properties and has minimal effect on REM sleep. Its actions are antagonised by flumazenil. Find "X"
235.e: Only two of the drugs listed are used for insomnia, eszopiclone and ramelteon. Eszopiclone, zaleplon, and zolpidem are related hypnotics that, though structurally different from benzodiazepines, appear to have a similar mechanism of action. However, unlike benzodiazepines, these drugs are not used in seizures or in muscle spasticity states. Compared with benzodiazepines, the newer hypnotics are less likely to alter sleep patterns. A : Buspirone is not a hypnotic. BUT IT'S ANXIOLYTIC C : Ramelteon activates melatonin receptors in the suprachiasmatic nuclei; flumazenil does not reverse its effects. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number. 422

235.q: Which of the following statements are true about benzodiazepines and barbiturates? 1) Flumazenil is an antidote for barbiturate 2) They cause additive sedation with alcohol 3) Thiopentone has short duration of action due to metabolism 4) They cause inhibition of GABA chloride channels
235.e: Explanation: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates the two classes of agents, differ markedly in their potencies. Barbiturates act to enhance GABAA receptor function at low micromolar concentrations, while benzodiazepines are considerably more potent, binding with nanomolar affinity. Both benzodiazepines and barbiturates bind to allosteric sites on the GABA-A receptor pentamer and thereby enhance GABA-stimulated Cl-channel function (Statement 4 ruled out) → additive CNS depression with alcohol. Thiopentone has a short duration not due to metabolism, but due to redistribution from brain to peripheral tissues (Statement 3 ruled out) (Thiopentone action) Thiopentone IV → Rapid CNS penetration → Sleep (seconds) → Redistribution to muscle & fat → Recovery Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist , not effective in barbiturate poisoning (statement 1 Ruled out)

235.q: As a medical practitioner in India, how will you prescribe alprazolam to a patient?
o: 1mg OD before bed time for 7 days
0.5 mg daily before bedtime for 7 days
235.e: We as doctors should not write any medical abbreviations in our prescription as it creates confusion for the patients. Hence writing the advice in proper English is what is recommended. Alprazolam The primary indication of this potent and intermediate duration of action BZD is anxiety disorder, but it is also being employed as night-time hypnotic due to rapid oral absorption. Its active metabolite has a short half-life. As such, there are few residual effects the next day. Discontinuation after regular use has produced relatively marked withdrawal phenomena.

236.q: Which of the following drug cannot be used in biliary colic ?
236.e: The opioids contract biliary smooth muscle, which can result in biliary colic. The sphincter of Oddi may constrict, resulting in reflux of biliary and pancreatic secretions and elevated plasma amylase and lipase levels. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 552

The opioid derivatives most commonly used as antitussives are dextromethorphan, codeine, levopropoxyphene, and noscapine (levopropoxyphene and noscapine are not available in the USA). They should be used with caution in patients taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors (see Table 31–5 ). Antitussive preparations usually also contain expectorants to thin and liquefy respiratory secretions. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 559

236.q: Opioid antitussive agents are banned by FDA for children of age under __.
236.e: Importantly, due to increasing reports of death in young children taking dextromethorphan in formulations of over-the-counter “cold/cough” medications, its use in children less than 6 years of age has been banned by the FDA. Moreover, because of variations in the metabolism of codeine, its use for any purpose in young children is being reconsidered. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD, PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 559

236.q: A 40-year-old woman is experiencing a right knee injury. After assessment, she is treated with an opioid analgesic and her knee pain decreases significantly. Soon after administration, however, the patient experiences new-onset upper abdominal pain that makes it difficult for her to lie still. An adverse drug effect involving which of the following structures is most likely responsible for this patient's current condition?
236.e: Administration of mu opioid analgesics, such as morphine, can cause contraction of smooth muscle cells in the sphincter of Oddi, leading to spasm and an increase in common bile duct pressures. Although uncommon, pressures in the gallbladder can also increase, potentially leading to biliary colic. Patients who develop biliary colic will have severe pain and cramping in the right upper abdomen. Management involves discontinuation of mu opioid analgesics and pain control with alternative agents such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (eg, ketorolac, diclofenac). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1103

236.q: Which of the following sentences are FALSE ? 1.Opioids affect sensory and emotional pain 2.NSAIDs affect sensory and emotional pain. 3.Opioids have no effect on emotional pain 4.NSAIDs have no effect on emotional pain
236.e: Opioids have effect on both sensory and emotional pain whereas NSAIDs have no significant effect on emotional pain. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. 236.q: Comparing the given drugs, comment Regarding potency: Morphine and fentanyl
o: Morphine is more potent than fentanyl
236.e: Fentanyl is more potent than Morphine. The doses of fentanyl are given in micrograms to produce the same effect produced by morphine in milligrams (0.1mg per kg) Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology, page no 1285

236.q: Opioid receptors belong to which class?
236.e: Opioids bind to specific receptors located throughout the central nervous system and other tissues Four major opioid receptor types have been identified: mu, kappa, delta, and sigma All opioid receptors couple to G proteins binding of an agonist to an opioid receptor causes membrane hyperpolarization Acute opioid effects are mediated by inhibition of adenylyl cyclase (reductions in intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate concentrations) and activation of phospholipase C Reference : Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

236.q: Opioid with predominant peripheral action is?
236.e: Methyl naltrexone is a peripheral mu opioid receptor antagonist It is a quaternary ammonium compound and hence cannot cross the blood brain barrier Thus, it can reverse the effects of opioid mediated by peripheral opioid receptors , since it cannot cross the blood brain barrier, it does not affect the opioid effects mediated by opioid receptors in the CNS , such as analgesia It was introduced in the treatment of opioid induced constipation refractory to other measures Alvimopan is a similar acting peripheral mu opioid receptor antagonist Reference : Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

237.q: Meperidine is contraindicated in heart failure because of its which action ?
o: Causes negative inotropic effect on heart
237.e: Although fentanyl is now the predominant analgesic in the phenylpiperidine class, meperidine continues to be used. This older opioid has significant antimuscarinic effects, which may be a contraindication if tachycardia would be a problem. Meperidine is also reported to have a negative inotropic action on the heart. In addition, it has the potential for producing seizures secondary to accumulation of its metabolite, normeperidine, in patients receiving high doses or with concurrent renal failure. Given this undesirable profile, use of meperidine as a first-line analgesic is becoming increasingly rare. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 557

237.q: Which properties of Remifentanil makes it useful in anesthesia practice ?
237.e: These opioids differ mainly in their potency and biodisposition. Sufentanil is five to seven times more potent than fentanyl. Alfentanil is considerably less potent than fentanyl, but acts more rapidly and has a markedly shorter duration of action. Remifentanil is metabolized very rapidly by blood and nonspecific tissue esterases, making its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic half-lives extremely short. Such properties are useful when these compounds are used in anesthesia practice. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 557

237.q: Propoxyphene is chemically related to methadone but not suitable for use. Why ?
o: Can be used in combination with aspirin
237.e: Propoxyphene is chemically related to methadone but has extremely low analgesic activity. Its low efficacy makes it unsuitable, even in combination with aspirin, for severe pain. The increasing incidence of deaths associated with its use and misuse caused it to be withdrawn in the United States. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 558

237.q: Which of the following opioid and active metabolite pairs are incorrectly matched?
237.e: Explanation: Active Metabolite Matching: Morphine: Active metabolite is Morphine 6 glucuronide. Diamorphine: Active metabolites are 6 monoacetylmorphine and morphine. Pethidine: Active metabolite is Norpethidine. Codeine: Active metabolites are Norcodeine and Morphine. Tramadol: Active metabolite is O desmethyltramadol known as the M1 metabolite. Paracetamol: Incorrectly matched with Poro paracetamol because its primary active metabolite is N acetyl p benzoquinone imine also known as NAPQI. (Option B) Key Takeaways: Paracetamol is incorrectly paired with Poro paracetamol since its true active metabolite is NAPQI. Correct knowledge of opioid metabolites is essential for safe analgesic use and monitoring toxicity.

237.q: Clinical uses of fentanyl include all except?
o: To blunt the response to laryngoscopy and intubation
As the sole spinal anaesthetic agent
237.e: Fentanyl is administered clinically in a wide range of doses Low doses of fentanyl -> 1 to 2 mg/kg IV , are injected to provide -> analgesia Fentanyl -> 2 to 20 mg/kg IV , may be administered as -> an adjuvant to inhaled anaesthetics to blunt circulatory responses to: (a) direct laryngoscopy for intubation of the trachea (b) sudden changes in the level of surgical stimulation Large doses of fentanyl -> 50 to 150 mg/kg IV , have been used alone -> to produce surgical anaesthesia Analgesia produced by neuraxial opioids, in contrast to regional anaesthesia with local anaesthetics, is not associated with sympathectomy, sensory block, or motor weakness Reference : Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

237.q: All of the following are metabolised in liver except?
237.e: Except for remifentanil , all opioids depend primarily on the liver for biotransformation and are metabolized by the cytochrome P (CYP) system , conjugated in the liver, or both The ester structure of remifentanil makes it susceptible to hydrolysis (in a manner like esmolol) by nonspecific esterase in red blood cells and tissues Reference : Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

238.q: Tocilizumab is a newer monoclonal antibody for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. It acts against:
238.e: Tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody that selectively binds to the interleukin-6 receptor and prevents IL-6 from binding to its receptor (IL-6R) on the liver, lung, and synovial fibroblasts Reference: Tocilizumab - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (nih.gov)

238.q: A 50 years old male patient came to emergency department with complaints of difficulty in breathing, bilateral lower limb oedema, chest pain. Sweating. Patient was on treatment for asthma but he did not take medications for 3,4 months. His SpO2 was 97% on air. On Auscultation, Third heart sound was heard and bilateral coarse crepitus was heard over lung fields. ECG was s/o CCF and Chest X Ray was suggestive of pulmonary oedema. Intravenous morphine is started for pain. Mechanism of action of morphine in pulmonary oedema is ________________.
238.e: The relief produced by intravenous morphine in dyspnea from pulmonary edema associated with left ventricular heart failure is remarkable. Proposed mechanisms include reduced anxiety ( perception of shortness of breath) and reduced cardiac preload (reduced venous tone) and afterload (decreased peripheral resistance). However, if respiratory depression is a problem, furosemide may be preferred for the treatment of pulmonary edema. On the other hand, morphine can be particularly useful when treating painful myocardial ischemia with pulmonary edema. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 553

238.q: A 45 years old patient came to emergency department with the complaints of severe chest pain, sweating, palpitation and pain radiating to back. His pulse rate was 130/minute and BP was 140/90 mm Hg. His ECG was s/o Anterolateral wall MI. All opioid analgesic can be used in this patient except ___________.
238.e: Cardiovascular system- Most opioids have no significant direct effects on the heart and, other than bradycardia, no major effects on cardiac rhythm. Meperidine is an exception to this generalization because its antimuscarinic action can result in tachycardia. Anterolateral wall MI leads to Tachycardia and Hypertension. Most of the opioids causes but Meperidine causes tachycardia so it cannot be used. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 551

238.q: Which are the pure opioid antagonist agents ?
238.e: The pure opioid antagonist drugs naloxone, naltrexone, and nalmefene are morphine derivatives with bulkier substituents at the N 17 position. These agents have a relatively high affinity for μ-opioid binding sites. They have lower affinity for the other receptors but can also reverse agonists at δ and κ sites. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 559

239.q: Advantage of clarithromycin over erythromycin is:
o: Does not inhibit hepatic microsomal enzymes
Eradicate mycoplasma infections in a single dose
239.e: Clarithromycin can be administered less frequently than erythromycin, but it is not effective in single doses against susceptible organisms. Organisms resistant to erythromycin, including pneumococci and methicillin-resistant staphylococci, are also resistant to other macrolides. Drug interactions have occurred with clarithromycin, through its ability to inhibit cytochrome P450. Clarithromycin is more active than erythromycin against Maxium complex, Tgondii, and H pylori.

239.q: A 46-year-old man presents with fever and productive cough. He is an alcoholic. CXR shows lung abscess. What would be the ideal antibiotic therapy for him ?
239.e: This patient with CXR of lung abscess, treated with Clindamycin. It is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by preventing peptide translocation at the 50S (large) ribosomal subunit. It targets anaerobic organisms and is commonly used for the treatment of aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess, which are typically polymicrobial. Clostridioides difficile colitis is a potential complication of clindamycin. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 836

239.q: A 3-year-old child is presented with violent coughing spells followed by a high pitched inspiratory sound during this time. She also has low-grade fevers and a runny nose. Her only vaccinations were received at birth. Which of the following is treatment ?
239.e: As per given clinical scenario, patient with an incomplete immunisation record, signs of an upper respiratory infection (nasal discharge, low-grade fever) and intense paroxysmal coughing with a high-pitched "Whooping" sound indicate pertussis (whooping cough). Azithromycin is the treatment of choice. Early administration of macrolides can lessen symptoms in the catarrhal and paroxysmal stage. Therefore, oral azithromycin is indicated in this patient. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 820

239.q: Your consultant prescribes a drug that blocks peptide transfer by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
239.e: Clindamycin is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by preventing peptide translocation at the 50S (large) ribosomal subunit. It targets anaerobic organisms and is commonly used for the treatment of aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess, which are typically polymicrobial. Clostridioides difficile colitis is a potential complication of clindamycin. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 837

239.q: A patient was prescribed a high dose penicillin along with gentamicin for his symptoms. Which of the following statement is true regarding this:
o: TDM must be done for penicillin
TDM must be done for gentamicin
TDM done for both penicillin and gentamicin
239.e: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is particularly useful in the following situations: Drugs with low safety margin, e.g. digoxin, anticonvulsants, antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycoside antibiotics, lithium, tricyclic antidepressants. If individual variations are large, e.g. antidepressants, lithium. Potentially toxic drugs used in the presence of renal failure, e.g. aminoglycoside antibiotics, vancomycin. In case of poisoning. In case of failure of response without any apparent reason, e.g. antimicrobials. To check patient compliance, e.g. psychopharmacological agents.

239.q: Within 12 h of birth, the baby boy begins to have temperature fluctuations, difficulty breathing, and reduced movements. You suspect neonatal sepsis, so IV gentamicin plus ampicillin is started This increased effectiveness is an example of what principle
239.e: Synergy is a term used to describe a situation when the combined effect of two or more drugs simultaneously is greater than can be explained by arithmetically adding the individual effects. A fine example is the synergistic effect when penicillin such as ampicillin is combined with an amino-glycoside such as gentamicin. An agonist is a molecule that elicits a response from a receptor by binding to it. The term can refer to endogenous or exogenous compounds. Anergy refers to a lack of the body’s immune system to mount a normal response to an antigen. It does not describe cooperation between drugs. Symbiosis refers to a mutually beneficial relationship between organisms. It is not used to describe interactions between medications. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no. 22

239.q: Drug use in initial treatment of mycobacterium Avium?
239.e: Initial regimen for mycobacterium avium: At least two-antimycobacterial drugs; preferred agents include: Macrolide: clarithromycin (first-line) OR azithromycin AND ethambutol Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine - 20 th addition Page no. 1278

240.e: Several classes of antimalarial drugs are available. Drugs that eliminate developing or dormant liver forms are called tissue schizonticides; those that act on erythrocytic parasites are blood schizonticides; and those that kill sexual stages and prevent transmission to mosquitoes are Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal. Page no. 915

240.q: Which of the following sentences are TRUE for use of artemisinin-based combination therapy in pregnancy? 1. Recommended for uncomplicated falciparum malaria in 2nd & 3rd trimester 2. Not recommended for uncomplicated falciparum malaria in 2nd & 3rd trimester 3. Intravenous artesunate can be used for severe malaria in 1st trimester 4. Intravenous artesunate cannot be used for severe malaria in 1st trimester
240.e: WHO recommends: Artemisinin-based combination therapies for the treatment of uncomplicated falciparum malaria during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Intravenous artesunate or quinine for the treatment of severe malaria during the first trimester. And intravenous artesunate for treatment of severe malaria during the second and third trimesters. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. 240.q: Which is the only drug available acting against dormant hypnozoite stages of P vivax and P ovale
240.e: Primaquine is the drug of choice for the eradication of dormant liver forms of P vivax and P ovale and can also be used for chemoprophylaxis against all malarial species. Primaquine is active against hepatic stages of all human malaria parasites. It is the only available agent active against the dormant hypnozoite stages of P vivax and P ovale. Primaquine is also gametocidal against the four human malaria species. Primaquine acts against erythrocytic stage parasites, but this activity is too weak to play an important role. The mechanism of antimalarial action is unknown. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 924

240.q: Which of the following drug provides terminal prophylaxis against vivax and ovale malaria?
240.e: Terminal Prophylaxis of Vivax and Ovale Malaria Standard chemoprophylaxis does not prevent a relapse of vivax or ovale malaria, because the hypnozoite forms of these parasites are not eradicated by chloroquine or other available blood schizonticide agents. To markedly diminish the likelihood of relapse, some authorities advocate the use of primaquine after the completion of travel to an endemic area. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 924

240.q: A 15 years old male patient came to OPD with the complaints of fever with chills for 4-5 days unattended. On laboratory investigation his peripheral smear examination revealed P. vivax malarial parasites. He was admitted into the medicine ward. Due to insufficient stock of oral and intravenous drug of anti-malarial agents, only intravenous chloroquine was available. Nursing attendant infused chloroquine very rapidly. What will happen to the patient?
240.e: The long-term administration of high doses of chloroquine for rheumatologic diseases can result in irreversible ototoxicity, retinopathy, myopathy, and peripheral neuropathy. These abnormalities are rarely if ever seen with standard-dose weekly chemoprophylaxis, even when given for prolonged periods. Large intramuscular injections or rapid intravenous infusions of chloroquine hydrochloride can result in severe hypotension and respiratory and cardiac arrest. Parenteral administration of chloroquine is best avoided, but if other drugs are not available for parenteral use, it should be infused slowly. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal. Page no. 920

240.q: You are a doctor working with doctors without borders. Your latest assignment would be a 6 months service at an African village. You being cautious, take mefloquine prophylaxis. With its consumption, due to its quality of high protein binding, you would expect:
240.e: Oral absorption of MQ is good but peak concentrations are reached 5-15 hours. It is highly plasma protein bound and Concentrated in many organs including liver, lung and intestines. Extensive metabolism occurs in the liver and it is primarily secreted in bile. Considerable enterohepatic circulation of MQ and its tissue binding accounts for the long t½ which is 2-3 weeks. Option A: High plasma protein binding means the drug would remain in the intravascular compartment and hence won’t undergo glomerular filtration Option B: High plasma protein binding means the drug would remain in the intravascular compartment and hence will have a low Volume of distribution Option C: High plasma protein binding increases the duration of action Option D: High plasma protein binding would lead to more drug interactions as many drugs may bind to a similar protein.

241.q: What is the primary target of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin in bacterial DNA replication?
241.e: Explanation: DNA gyrase is an essential bacterial enzyme responsible for introducing negative supercoils into DNA, which relieves the torsional strain generated ahead of the replication fork. Ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone antibiotic, specifically inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. By inhibiting DNA gyrase, ciprofloxacin prevents proper DNA replication and transcription, ultimately leading to bacterial cell death.

241.q: A 25 years old male patient came to OPD with the complaints of high-grade fever, coughing, blood in sputum, dyspnoea. His pulse rate is 120/min, BP is 110/76 mm Hg, SpO2 on room air is 98 %. He is already on ART since 3 years and AKT since 2 months. Blood culture and BAL was sent to rule out secondary bacterial infection. BAL report came positive for Pneumocystis jiroveci. Which regimen offers more tolerance in this patient in comparison to commonly used trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole regimen?
241.e: The combination of clindamycin and primaquine is an alternative regimen in the treatment of pneumocystis, particularly mild to moderate disease. This regimen offers improved tolerance compared with high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or pentamidine, although its efficacy against severe pneumocystis pneumonia is not well studied. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 924

241.q: Mechanism of action of quinolones is?
241.e: DNA gyrase inhibitors REF: Goodman Gillman's 11th ed p. 722 The quinolone antibiotics target bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. For many gram positive bacteria, topoisomerase IV is the primary target. For many gram-negative bacteria, DNA gyrase is the primary quinolone target.

241.q: Supplementary folinic acid may prevent anemia in folate-deficient persons who use this drug; it is a weak base achieving tissue levels similar to those in plasma.

242.q: A 67-year-old man develops dysuria, flank pain, and fever. Examination shows marked tenderness in the right costovertebral area. Treatment with an antibiotic is begun, but his symptoms do not improve. Further evaluation shows that the causal organism produces an enzyme that inactivates the antibiotic via phosphorylation. An agent from which of the following classes of antibiotics was most likely administered?
242.e: This antibiotic is used to treat infections with gram-negative, aerobic bacteria and acts by irreversibly inhibiting the 30S subunit of the initiation complex. Aminoglycosides are bactericidal agents that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit. Microbial resistance develops when enzymes (e.g., transferases) are produced that inactivate the antibiotic via phosphorylation, acetylation, or adenylation. Aminoglycosides, which are effective against gram-negative bacilli (e.g., E.coli, Klebsiella, Serratia, Proteus, Pseudomonas), can be used instead of fluoroquinolones for the inpatient treatment of complicated pyelonephritis. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 839

243.q: What is the first line regimen proposed by NACO for the treatment of HIV-2 infection?
243.e: NACO recommends a combination of 2NRTI+protease inhibitor for treatment of HIV-2 infection. Currently, the first line regimen consists of Tenofovir +Lamivudine +lopinavir -ritonavir Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 335

243.q: Lamivudine is a Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI), which has proven antiviral activity against HIV and HBV. However, some patients infected with HBV are resistant to Lamivudine. Which mutation confers this property of drug resistance?
243.e: Hepatitis B virus infected patients on lamivudine therapy may develop resistance to the drug due to mutation in the YMDD locus present in the HBV reverse transcriptase region of polymerase gene. Pre-core mutants have mutations in pre-core region (which abolishes HBeAg production) or basal core promoter region (down regulates HBeAg production). The escape mutants of HBV have mutations in the S gene ("a" antigen region) which leads to alteration of HBsAg. Reference : Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 20, Pg: 279

243.q: A resident doctor developed needle prick injury while taking blood samples of HIV positive symptomatic patients. Which of the following regimen is best for post exposure prophylaxis of HIV for this doctor?
243.e: Post-exposure prophylaxis: Treatment should be started within 72 hours of exposure, preferably as early as possible At first the wound is washed with soap and water. Secondly before initiating drug therapy blood samples are taken to measure the baseline viral markers Then, triple drug therapy is given which includes Tenofovir, Lamivudine and a boosted protease inhibitor for 28 days. After 6 weeks again viral markers are measured to check for the infection.

243.q: Administration of which of the following drugs would increase the bioavailability of saquinavir?
243.e: Ritonavir being a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor acts as a booster for other antiretrovirals like Saquinavir. Ritonavir (RTV) It is a potent PI; also a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. Drug interactions, nausea, diarrhoea, paresthesias, fatigue and lipid abnormalities are prominent. Though RTV (600 mg twice daily) can be used as an antiretroviral drug, it is more commonly employed in a low dose (100 mg BD) to boost all other PIs except NFV. Low dose RTV produces no additional side effects. 243.q: Which drugs can be used as pre exposure prophylaxis of HIV?
243.e: Tenofovir is often co-administered with emtricitabine, and a once-daily, fixed-dose combination formulation is available, either alone or in combination with efavirenz. A recent placebo controlled. study found that use of emtricitabine and tenofovir was effective as pre-exposure prophylaxis, reducing HIV acquisition in men who have sex with men. In another placebo-controlled study, use of the experimental 1% tenofovir gel as a vaginal microbicide was effective in decreasing the incidence of heterosexual HIV acquisition. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin,MD. Page no. 875

243.q: Which of the following is not approved for HBV treatment?
243.e: HBV infection in the United States: five oral nucleoside/nucleotide analogues (lamivudine, adefovir dipivoxil, tenofovir, entecavir, telbivudine) and two injectable interferon drugs (interferon alfa-2b, pegylated interferon alfa-2a) Reference LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin,MD. Page no. 883

243.q: Which of the following is not the ART agent?
243.e: Six classes of antiretroviral agents are currently available for use: nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), protease inhibitors (PIs), fusion inhibitors, CCR5 receptor antagonist integrase inhibitors. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin,MD. Page no. 869

243.q: Lamividine is ART agent which can be co-administered with__________.
243.e: Lamivudine is often co-administered with abacavir, and a once-daily, fixed-dose combination formulation is available. Lamivudine is also available in a fixed-dose combination with zidovudine, either alone or in combination with abacavir. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin,MD. Page no. 874

244.q: A 84- year-old man with gram stain of CSF shows gram-positive rods resembling diphtheroids, the antibiotic regimen for empiric treatment would include
244.e: Diphtheroid-like Gram-positive rods in the cerebrospinal fluid smear of an elderly patient are indicative of L-monocytogenes. Listeria infections are more common in neonates, elderly patients, and those who have been treated with immunosuppressive agents. Cephalosporins do not cover listeria. ( Mnemonic : “LAME”: listeria, atypicals, MRSA, and enterococcus.) Treatment consists of ampicillin with or without an amino glycoside such as gentamicin. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can also be used. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 802

244.q: A 23-year-old with otitis media treated with amoxicillin. The mechanism of action involves inhibition of
244.e: Penicillins (and cephalosporins) bind to PBPs acting at the transpeptidation stage of cell wall synthesis (the final step) to inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking. Synthesis of N-acetylmuramic acid is inhibited by fosfomycin. Vancomycin inhibits transglycosylase, preventing elongation of peptidoglycan chains. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 800

244.q: Resistance of pneumococci to penicillin G is due to
o: Changes in chemical structure of target penicillin- binding proteins
Changes in the d-Ala-d-Ala building block of peptidoglycan precursor
244.e: Pneumococcal resistance to penicillins is due to changes in the chemical structures of the target penicillin-binding proteins located in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane. A similar mechanism underlies the resistance of staphylococci to methicillin (MRSA strains). A structural alteration in the d-Ala-d-Ala component of the pentapeptide side chains of peptidoglycans is the basis for a mechanism of resistance to vancomycin. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 801

244.q: A 45-year-old woman with CML is admitted to the hospital with malaise, chills, and high fever. A blood culture reveals the presence of Gram-negative bacilli. The initial diagnosis is bacteremia, and parenteral antibiotics are indicated. The records of the patient reveal that she had a severe urticarial rash, hypotension, and respiratory difficulty after oral penicillin V about 6 months ago. The most appropriate drug regimen for empiric treatment is
244.e: Each of the drugs listed has activity against some Gram- negative bacilli. All penicillins should be avoided in patients with a history of allergic reactions to any individual penicillin drug. Cephalosporins should also be avoided in patients who have had anaphylaxis or other severe hypersensitivity reactions after use of a penicillin. There is partial cross reactivity between penicillins and the carbapenems such as imipenem and meropenem, but no cross-reactivity between the penicillins and aztreonam. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 799

244.q: Which of the following statements about beta-lactam antibiotics is most correct?
o: Cephalexin and other first-generation cephalosporins cross the blood-brain barrier
Ceftriaxone and nafcillin are both eliminated mainly via biliary secretion
Instability of penicillins in gastric acid does not limit their oral absorption
Renal tubular reabsorption of amoxicillin is inhibited by probenecid
244.e: First- and second-generation cephalosporins are not effective in meningitis because they do not readily enter the cerebrospinal fluid. Instability of penicillins in gastric acid does limit their oral absorption, renal elimination of amoxicillin is inhibited by probenecid, and ticarcillin has activity against several Gram-negative rods. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 802

244.q: A patient needs antibiotic treatment for native valve, culture- positive infective enterococcal endocarditis. His medical history includes a severe anaphylactic reaction to penicillin G during the last year. The best approach would be treatment with
244.e: In patients who have had a severe reaction to a penicillin, it is inadvisable to administer a cephalosporin or a carbapenem such as meropenem. Aztreonam has no significant activity against Gram-positive cocci, so the logical treatment in this case is vancomycin, often with an aminoglycoside (eg, gentamicin) for synergistic activity against enterococci. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 808

245.q: A 62-year-old man is presented with severe abdominal pain and diarrhea after a recent urinary tract infection. An appropriate workup confirms C difficile colitis. The patient is placed on an oral macrocyclic antibiotic that inhibits the sigma subunit of RNA polymerase. Which of the following agents was most likely administered to this patient?
245.e: Treatment options for Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) typically include oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Fidaxomicin is a macrocyclic antibiotic (related to macrolides) that inhibits the sigma subunit of RNA polymerase , leading to protein synthesis impairment and cell death (bactericidal activity against C difficile). It is administered orally and has minimal systemic absorption, resulting in high fecal concentrations) also has a narrow spectrum of activity with a lesser effect on normal colonic flora than vancomycin. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1105

245.q: Cilastatin is given in combination with imipenem because:-
o: Cilastatin prevents degradation of imipenem in kidney
Inhibits the enzymes that digest imipenem in stomach
245.e: A limiting feature of imipenem is its rapid hydrolysis by the enzyme dehydropeptidase I located on the brush border of renal tubular cells. An innovative solution to this problem is its combination with cilastatin, a reversible inhibitor of dehydropeptidase I, which has matched pharmacokinetics with imipenem (t½ of both is 1 hr) and protects it. Options B,C,D are not the correct reasons why Imipenem is given with Cilastatin.

245.q: A 56-year-old woman presents with productive cough, fever and dyspnea since 2 days. Pulmonary examination shows diffuse crackles. CXR shows a left upper-lobe infiltrate of the lung. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain shows gram-negative rods that are oxidase-positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment ?
245.e: Fever, productive cough, crackles, and an infiltrate on chest x-ray are consistent with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). Gram negative rods and oxidase-positive rods suggest Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most likely causative organism Cefepime and levofloxacin are the first-line treatment for patients with CAP when there is a strong suspicion of P. aeruginosa infection. Other treatment options for CAP with P. aeruginosa include piperacillin/tazobactam, meropenem, or imipenem plus a fluoroquinolone. An aminoglycoside may be added as well. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 838-39

246.q: Pyrantel pamoate is not effective against______________.
246.e: Pyrantel pamoate is a broad-spectrum antihelminthic highly effective for the treatment of pinworm, ascaris, and Trichostrongylus orientalis It is moderately effective against both species of hookworm. It is not effective in trichuriasis or strongyloidiasis. Oxantel pamoate, an analog of pyrantel not available in the USA, has been used successfully in the treatment of trichuriasis; the two drugs have been combined for their broad-spectrum antihelminthic activity Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 53-Clinical Pharmacology of the Antihelminthic Drugs by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 945

246.q: What is the maximum dose of pyrantel that can be given in one day?
246.e: The standard dose is 11 mg (base)/kg (maximum, 1 g), given orally once with or without food. For pinworm, the dose is repeated in 2 weeks, and cure rates are greater than 95%. The drug is available in the USA without prescription for this indication. For ascariasis, a single dose yields cure rates of 85–100%. Treatment should be repeated if eggs are found 2 weeks after treatment. For hookworm infections, a single dose is effective against light infections; but for heavy infections, especially with Necator americanus, a 3-day course is necessary to reach 90% cure rates. A course of treatment can be repeated in 2 weeks. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 53-Clinical Pharmacology of the Antihelminthic Drugs by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 945

246.q: A patient presented with an episode of seizure and CT scan revealed presence of calcified cysts in brain with no evidence of Hydrocephalus. A diagnosis of Neurocysticercosis was made. Which of the following statements regarding treatment of this condition is correct?
o: Only anti parasitic drugs should be given
Anti parasitic drugs should be given and after the completion of course, Steroids should be given
Steroids should be started first followed by anti parasitic drugs
Only anti epileptic drugs should be given
246.e: Steroids to be given first to prevent any hyperinflammatory syndrome due to dying parasites from Albendazole treatment. Neurocysticercosis: When albendazole/praziquantel is used to kill cysticerci lodged in the brain, prednisolone 40 mg/day or equivalent is given for 2-4 weeks to suppress the reaction to the dying larvae. All other options are not the correct ways to treat the patient.

246.q: A 35 years old male patient came to OPD with the complaints of diarrhoea, mild fever and weakness. His pulse rate is 100/min and BP is 100/70 mm Hg. He is already treated with antibacterial drugs which did not work. Physician is suspecting amebiasis. Which is the drug of choice for the treatment of extraluminal amebiasis?
246.e: Metronidazole, a nitroimidazole, is the drug of choice in the treatment of extraluminal amebiasis. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 927

Metronidazole, a nitroimidazole, is the drug of choice in the treatment of extraluminal amebiasis. It kills trophozoites but not cysts of E histolytica and effectively eradicates intestinal and extraintestinal tissue infections. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 927,928

246.q: Which of the following sentences are TRUE for administration of Albendazole? 1. It should be taken on empty stomach for intraluminal parasites 2. It should be taken with fatty meals for intraluminal parasites 3. It should be taken on empty stomach for tissue parasites 4. It should be taken with fatty meals for tissue parasites
246.e: Albendazole is administered on an empty stomach when used against intraluminal parasites but with a fatty meal when used against tissue parasites. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 53-Clinical Pharmacology of the Antihelminthic Drugs by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 938

246.q: Ivermectin is an alternate drug for multiple helminthic infections but it is drug of choice for ___________.
246.e: Ivermectin is the drug of choice in strongyloidiasis and onchocerciasis. It is also an alternative drug for a number of other helminthic infections. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 53-Clinical Pharmacology of the Antihelminthic Drugs by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal,MD. Page no. 940

246.q: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the drug of choice for________.
246.e: Diethylcarbamazine is a drug of choice in the treatment of filariasis, loiasis, and tropical eosinophilia. It has been replaced by ivermectin for the treatment of onchocerciasis. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 53-Clinical Pharmacology of the Antihelminthic Drugs by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal,MD. Page no. 939

247.q: A 32-year-old man with HIV infection comes with recurrent growth of a whitish film on his tongue and buccal mucosa. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of the initial drug of choice for this patient's illness?
o: It blocks ergosterol synthesis by inhibiting squalene epoxidase
It inhibits the CYP450-dependent enzyme lanosterol 14-a-demethylase
It inhibits the synthesis of beta-glucan
It interferes with mitotic spindle function
247.e: This is a case of oral thrush, an overgrowth of the oral cavity with Candida albicans, which is a normal flora organism that may cause several disorders including oral thrush, esophagitis, and pneumonia in immunosuppressed patients. In HIV-infected individuals, oral and/or pharyngeal candidiasis infections are generally treated with clotrimazole lozenges or fluconazole oral tablets. Fluconazole acts as an inhibitor of the fungal cytochrome P-450 dependent enzyme lanosterol 14-a-demethylase. In a fungus, lanosterol 14-0-demethylase functions to convert lanosterol to ergosterol. This is responsible for the fungistatic effect of the "azole" antifungals. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition by Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 880-882

247.q: Which of the following antifungal drugs possess additional anti-inflammatory and antipruritic activity?
247.e: Sertaconazole has additional anti inflammatory and anti pruritic activity. The imidazole derivatives oxiconazole, sulconazole, and sertaconazole are used for the topical treatment of infections caused by the common pathogenic dermatophytes. Oxiconazole nitrate is available as a 1% cream and lotion; sulconazole nitrate is supplied as a 1% solution or cream. Sertaconazole is a 2% cream marketed for tinea pedis.

247.q: A 32-year-old man living in Gujarat was transferred to California for several months. On his return to India, he complains of having influenza-like symptoms with fever and a cough. He also has red, tender nodules on his shins. You suspect that these symptoms are due to coccidioidomycosis contracted during his stay in California. This patient should be treated immediately with
247.e: A travel history can be important in the diagnosis of fungal disease. If this patient has a fungal infection of the lungs, it is probably due to C. immitis, which is endemic in dry regions of the western US. Pulmonary symptoms of coccidioidomycosis are usually self-limiting, and drug therapy is not commonly required in an otherwise healthy patient. Tender red nodules on extensor surfaces constitute a good prognostic sign. Erythema nodosum is a delayed hypersensitivity response to fungal antigens. No organisms are present in the lesions, and it is not a sign of disseminated disease. Reference- Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 862-863

247.q: In which of the following scenario, Treatment with Amphotericin-B should be avoided?
o: A-27-year-old HIV+ man with suspected cryptococcal meningitis
A-65-year-old diabetic with rhino-cerebral mucormycosis, has Sr.creatinine of 2.2
A-9-year-old immunosuppressed man with invasive aspergillosis
247.e: Option A- A-27-year-old HIV+ man with suspected cryptococcal meningitis: Amphotericin B along with fluconazole is the treatment of choice. Option B- A-65-year-old diabetic with rhino-cerebral mucormycosis, has s.creat of 2.2 : Amphotericin B is the drug of choice in mucormycosis, it may cause transient rise in s.creat after large dose, but the benefit of continuing the drug outweigh the risk. It may be prevented by pre-loading patient with 1-2 L of NS. Renal replacement therapy can be done if required. Option C- A-34-year-old HIV+ woman with severe invasive histoplasmosis = Amphotericin B is preferred option in severe histoplasmosis. Option D- A-9-year-old immunosuppressed man with invasive aspergillosis = IV Itraconazole is better option compare to Amphotericin B for invasive aspergillosis. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 877-879

247.q: A 3-year-old-child with ventriculoperitoneal shunt develops fever with chills. On examination, right eye deviated towards left side. Treatment with antibiotics did not improve condition. Culture followed by microscopy identifies C. Glabrata organism. What is the preferred anti-fungal for patient?
247.e: This patient with Candidemia with identified organism C. Glabrata is resistant to fluconazole and amphotericin B. Echinocandins like Caspofungin is Preferred drug for patient Symptoms of Candidemia may vary from fever to sepsis. It's hard to distinguish from bacterial sepsis. Infiltration of organs may occur either directly (e.g., ventriculoperitoneal shunt in meningitis) or hematogenous (e.g., endocarditis with IV drug use). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 882-884

247.q: A patient with pulmonary aspergillosis was treated with voriconazole. Which of the following is false about voriconazole?
o: It should be taken on an empty stomach
It should not be co-administered with pyrazinamide
247.e: Explanation: ]There is no significant interaction between voriconazole and pyrazinamide . Voriconazole primarily interacts with drugs metabolized by CYP2C19, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4 . Explanation of other options: It should be taken on an empty stomach (Option A): Correct - food, especially high-fat meals, reduces voriconazole absorption. It requires therapeutic drug monitoring (Option B): Correct - maintain serum levels between 1-5 mg/L for efficacy and safety. It requires a loading dose (Option D): Correct- a loading dose helps achieve steady-state levels quickly in severe fungal infections. Key Takeaways: Voriconazole → triazole antifungal for invasive aspergillosis. Taken on an empty stomach. Requires therapeutic drug monitoring and loading dose. No known interaction with pyrazinamide.

247.q: Which of the anti-fungal drug cause visual disturbances?
247.e: Voriconazole causes immediate but transient visual disturbances including blurring of vision of unknown cause in more than 30% of patients. Based on animal studies voriconazole is a class D drug in terms of pregnancy risk. Option B- Infusion-related effects of Caspofungin include headache, gastrointestinal distress, fever, rash, and flushing (histamine release). Option C- Visual dysfunction has not been reported with Posaconazole, but the drug is an inhibitor of CYP3A4, increasing the levels of cyclosporine and tacrolimus. Option D- Prolonged high plasma levels of flucytosine cause reversible bone marrow depression, alopecia, and liver dysfunction. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 885-886

247.q: Interactions between this drug and cell membrane components can result in the formation of pores lined by hydrophilic groups present in the drug molecule.
247.e: The polyene antifungal drugs amphotericin B and nystatin are amphipathic molecules that can interact with ergosterol in fungal cell membranes to form artificial pores. In these structures, the lipophilic groups on the drug molecule are arranged on the outside of the pore, and the hydrophilic regions are located on the inside. The fungicidal action of the polyenes derives from this interaction, which results in leakage of intracellular constituents. Reference- Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 858-859

248.q: It is your first day as an intern in the medicine department and in the first case sheet you read, the patient was given teduglutide. On reading about this drug, you would learn all the following about the drug, except?
o: It is used for short-bowel syndrome
248.e: Teduglutide It is a recombinant analog of human glucagon like peptide 2(GLP 2)(Option B) It is used for the treatment of adults with short bowel syndrome(Option A) It works by promoting mucosal growth and possibly restoring gastric emptying and secretion and is a gut hormone.(Option D) It is given by subcutaneous route It is long acting drug because it is resistant to degradation by DPP-4

248.q: Which of the following drug used as 'sterilizing' agent which is active against residual intracellular organisms that may cause relapse?
248.e: Pyrazinamide is an important front-line drug used in conjunction with isoniazid and rifampin in short-course (i.e., 6-month) regimens as a “sterilizing” agent active against residual intracellularorganisms that may cause relapse. Tubercle bacilli develop resistance to pyrazinamide fairly readily, but there is no cross-resistance with isoniazid or other antimycobacterial drugs. REFERENCE: KD TRIPATHI Essential of Medical Pharmacology 7 th Edition Page no. 765-779

248.q: A 64-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to fever, anorexia, and nausea. Several weeks ago, on routine testing, the patient was found to have a positive purified protein derivative test. He had no respiratory symptoms, and a chest x-ray was unremarkable. A month ago, he started isoniazid therapy with pyridoxine supplementation. Currently, temperature is 38.3 O C (100.9 O F). On physical examination, there is mild abdominal discomfort. Laboratory studies are pending. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
248.e: This patient with latent tuberculosis infection (positive tuberculin skin test, no symptoms, unremarkable chest x-ray) was started on isoniazid (INH) therapy and now has fever, anorexia, and nausea. INH is directly hepatotoxic. In 10% - 20% of patients, it causes acute, mild hepatic dysfunction, characterized by transient increases in serum aminotransferases (AST/SGOT, ALT/SGPT). This adverse effect usually occurs during the first 4-6 months of treatment, and, in most cases, liver function tests return to baseline with continued INH therapy. In rare instances ( Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine - 20 th addition Page no. 1273-1274

248.q: M. Kansai (Non-Tubercular Mycobacterium) is resistant to which of the following drugs?
248.e: M kansai is susceptible to rifampin and ethambutol, partially susceptible to isoniazid, and completely resistant to pyrazinamide. A three-drug combination of isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol is the conventional treatment for M kansai infection. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 14th Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page no. 849-850

248.q: Which of the following anti-tuberculosis drug is not bactericidal drug?
248.e: Bactericidal drugs: A substance that directly kills bacteria. Bacteriostatic drugs: A substance that stops bacteria from reproducing (does not directly kill bacteria). Rifampin, Isoniazid and Streptomycin are bactericidal drugs. Where as ethambutol and Pyrazinamide are bacteriostatic drugs. REFERENCE: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 14th Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page no. 842-849
