248.q: Which of the following anti-tubercular drug contraindicated in pregnancy?
248.e: Bactericidal drugs: A substance that directly kills bacteria. Bacteriostatic drugs: A substance that stops bacteria from reproducing (does not directly kill bacteria). Rifampin, Isoniazid and Streptomycin are bactericidal drugs. Where as ethambutol and Pyrazinamide are bacteriostatic drugs. The following antituberculosis drugs are contraindicated in pregnant women: Streptomycin Kanamycin Amikacin Capreomycin Fluoroquinolones Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 14th Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page no. 842-849

248.q: Which of the following Anti-Tubercular Drug have maximum CSF penetration?
248.e: Isoniazid has maximum CSF penetration. And Streptomycin has minimum CSF penetration. REFERENCE: KD TRIPATHI Essential of Medical Pharmacology 7 th Edition Page no. 765-779

248.q: A 31-year-old Woman comes to the emergency department with a 3-week history of fever, night sweats, and productive cough. He has also had a 4-kg weight loss. Chest-x ray reveals a cavitary lesion on the right. Sputum culture is obtained. When exposed to drug A, isolates of the pathogen growing in culture quickly become less resistant to decoloration with an acid-alcohol agent and stop proliferating. Which of the following is drug A most likely to be?
248.e: Isoniazid is an antimicrobial agent that is active only against mycobacteria. Its specificity is derived from its inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis. Mycolic acids form long branched-chain fatty acids in the outer portion of the mycobacterial peptidoglycan cell wall; they are essential for proper cell wall structure and virulence factor synthesis (eg, sulfatides, wax D, cord factor). If mycobacteria are unable to synthesize mycolic acids, they cannot create proper cell walls or divide to form new cells. Mycolic acids in the cell wall cause mycobacteria to be acid-fast as they retain the carbolfuchsin dye and resist decoloration by an acid-alcohol decolorizing agent. REFERENCE: KD TRIPATHI Essential of Medical Pharmacology 7 th Edition Page no. 765-779

249.q: Which of the following is not an indication of using rifabutin/fluroquinolones in patient having mycobacterium avium infection?
o: A high risk of mortality (e.g., CD4 count < 50)
249.e: Initial regimen for mycobacterium avium: At least two-antimycobacterial drugs; preferred agents include: Macrolide: clarithromycin (first-line) ORazithromycin AND ethambutol Optional third and fourth drugs [1] Consider in patients with any of the following: A high risk of mortality (e.g., CD4 count Drug resistance High mycobacterialload Inadequate response to ART Agents (any of the following): Rifabutin Fluoroquinolone: levofloxacin or moxifloxacin Injectable agent: amikacin or streptomycin Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine - 20 th addition Page no. 1278

249.q: Which of the following Anti-Tubercular Drug causing Neuro-Psychiatric Side effect?
249.e: Cycloserine is associated with Neuro-Psychiatric Side effect. Adverse effect of 2 nd line Anti-Tubercular Drug: Thioacetazone (tuberculostatic drug): Hepatitis, bone marrow suppression and Steven Johnson syndrome. Para amino salicylic acid (PAS) can cause kidney, liver and thyroid dysfunction. Ethionamide can cause hepatitis, optic neuritis and hypothyroidism. Cycloserine can cause neuropsychiatric adverse effects. Kanamycin, Amikacin and Capreomycin can cause ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Rifabutin commonly causes gastrointestinal adverse effects. Rarely, it can cause anterior uveitis, clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea, diffuse polymyalgia syndrome, yellow skin discoloration (Pseudo-jaundice) and pancytopenia. REFERENCE: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 14th Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page no. 846-849

250.q: A patient presented with a few hypoesthetic, hairless skin plaques. Diagnosis of leprosy confirmed with tissue biopsy. What is the mechanism of action of drugs used to treat this condition? i) Inhibit dihydropteroate synthase ii) Inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase iii) binding preferentially to mycobacterial DNA and inhibiting replication and growth
250.e: Patient is having presentation of Tuberculoid leprosy. Treatment of tuberculoid leprosy is dapsone and rifampin. Mechanism of action of dapsone and rifampin are inhibit dihydropteroate synthase and Inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase respectively. Lepromatous—presents diffusely over the skin, with leonine (lion-like) facies, and is communicable (high bacterial load); characterized by low cell-mediated immunity with a humoral Th2 response. Tuberculoid—limited to a few hypo esthetic, hairless skin plaques; characterized by high cell mediated immunity with a largely Th1-type immune response and low bacterial load. Treatment: dapsone and rifampin for tuberculoid form; clofazimine is added for lepromatous form. Reference: First Aid Step 1 USMLE 18 th edition Page no. 141

250.q: Which of the following drug given supervised as per national leprosy elimination programme? i) Rifampicin 600 mg once a month ii) Clofazimine 300 mg once a month iii) Dapsone 100 mg daily iv) Clofazimine 50 mg daily
250.e: Under NLEP Rifampicin and Clofazimine are given under supervision for both Multibacillary and Paucibacillary Leprosy. Rifampicin is given 600 mg once a month under supervision. Clofazimine is given 300 mg once a month under supervision and 50 mg daily unsupervised for 28 days. Dapsone is given 100 mg once daily unsupervised for 28 days. Multibacillary Leprosy is treated for 12 months and Paucibacillary Leprosy for 6 months. Under RNTCP, DOTS: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol are administered under supervision. REFERENCE: KD TRIPATHI Essential of Medical Pharmacology 7 th Edition Page no. 780-786

Treatment of choice for type 1 as well as type 2 lepra reaction is corticosteroids. For severe reaction, prednisolone 40-60mg/day is started immediately and continued till the reaction subsides. The dose is then tapered over 2-3 months. For resistant cases of Erythema nodosum leprosum drug of choice is thalidomide. REFERENCE: KD TRIPATHI Essential of Medical Pharmacology 7 th Edition page no. 780-786

251.q: A patient came to OPD with the complaints of generalized body oedema, difficulty in breathing and anuria since 3-4 days. Laboratory investigation and USG was performed. USG was s/o Chronic Renal Failure. What will be the half-life acyclovir in this pt?
251.e: Acyclovir is cleared primarily by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion. The half-life is 2.5–3 hours in patients with normal renal function and 20 hours in patients with anuria. Reference : LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin,MD. Page no. 862

251.q: Which of the following agent is useful against HBV, HIV and Herpesvirus?
251.e: Although initially and abortively developed for treatment of HIV infection, adefovir dipivoxil gained approval, at lower and less toxic doses, for treatment of HBV infection. Adefovir dipivoxil is the diester prodrug of adefovir, an acyclic phosphonated adenine nucleotide analog . It is phosphorylated by cellular kinases to the active diphosphate metabolite and then competitively inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and causes chain termination after incorporation into viral DNA. Adefovir is active in vitro against a wide range of DNA and RNA viruses, including HBV, HIV and herpesviruses. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin,MD. Page no. 884

251.q: Drugs least effective in severe covid-19 infection?
251.e: Favipiravir inhibits SARS-CoV-2 viral replication in vitro with evidence of clinical benefit in open label trials.

251.q: A 34 years old male patient came to OPD with the complaint of bilateral genital vesicles, fever and itching. He is a known case of HIV and on ART since last 4 years. So, he is diagnosed as genital HSV infection in HIV. There are three nucleoside analogues are licensed for treatment of HSV and VZV. Which of the following are three agents?
251.e: Three oral nucleoside analogues are licensed for the treatment of HSV and VZV infections: acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir. They have similar mechanisms of action and comparable indications for clinical use; all are well tolerated. Acyclovir has been the most extensively studied It was licensed first and is the only one of the three that is available for intravenous use in the United States. Comparative trials have demonstrated similar efficacies of these three agents for the treatment of HSV but modest superiority of famciclovir and valacyclovir for the treatment of herpes zoster infections. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin, MD. Page no. 862

251.q: A 35 years old female patient of recurrent herpes labialis came to OPD for 5th episode of herpes labialis. She was prescribed acyclovir topical ointment 5 times daily for 4 days. Acyclovir requires ________ phosphorylation steps for activation.
251.e: Acyclovir ( Figure 49–2 ) is an acyclic guanosine derivative with clinical activity against HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV, but it is approximately 10 times more potent against HSV-1 and HSV-2 than against VZV. In vitro activity against Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) is present but weaker. Acyclovir requires three phosphorylation steps for activation. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin, MD. Page no. 862

251.q: 1. Acyclovir is selectively activated in infected cells 2. It requires viral kinase for initial phosphorylation
o: Sentence 1 and 2 both are True and 2 is correct reason for 1
Sentence 1 and 2 both are True but 2 is not the correct reason for 1
Sentence 1 is True but Sentence 2 is False
251.e: Acyclovir requires three phosphorylation steps for activation. It is converted first to the monophosphate derivative by the virus specified thymidine kinase and then to the di- and triphosphate compounds by host cell enzymes (Figure 49-3). Because it requires the viral kinase for initial phosphorylation, acyclovir is selectively activated and the active metabolite accumulates only in infected cells. Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA synthesis by two mechanisms: competition with deoxyGTP for the viral DNA polymerase, resulting in binding to the DNA template as an irreversible complex. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin,MD. Page no. 862

251.q: Which of the following drug achieves serum levels orally that is approximately those achieved by intravenous acyclovir?
251.e: Valacyclovir is the L-valyl ester of acyclovir.It is rapidly converted to acyclovir after oral administration via first pass enzymatic hydrolysis in the liver and intestine, resulting in serum levels that are three to five times greater than those achieved with oral acyclovir and approximate those achieved with intravenous acyclovir. Oral bioavailability is 54–70%, and cerebrospinal fluid levels are about 50% of those in serum. Elimination half-life is 2.5–3.3 hours. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin, MD. Page no. 864

251.q: AIDS patients who are treated with valacyclovir(8g/d) chronically, had an increased incidence of _____________.
251.e: Valacyclovir is generally well tolerated, although nausea, headache, vomiting, or rash occasionally occur. At high doses, confusion, hallucinations, and seizures have been reported. AIDS patients who received high-dosage valacyclovir chronically (ie, 8 g/d) had an increased incidence of gastrointestinal intolerance as well as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and hemolytic-uremic syndrome; this dose has also been associated with confusion and hallucinations in transplant patients. In a recent study, there was no evidence of increased birth defects in 181 infants who were exposed to valacyclovir during the first trimester. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 49- Antiviral Agents by Dr. Sharon Safrin, MD. Page no. 864

252.q: A 32-year-old woman with amenorrhea, infertility, and galactorrhea is treated with a drug that known to successfully restore ovulation and menstruation. She is advised to take the drug ,Bromocriptine orally. Before being given the drug, What you'll question the woman about previous/present history?
252.e: Bromocriptine, a dopamine receptor agonist, is used to treat the amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome, which is a consequence of hyperprolactinemia. Because of its central dopaminergic effects, the drug should not be used in patients with a history of schizophrenia or other forms of psychotic illness. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 680, 725

252.q: A 47-year-old man exhibited signs and symptoms of acromegaly. Radiologic studies indicated the presence of a large pituitary tumor. Surgical treatment of the tumor was only partially effective in controlling his disease. At this point, which of the following drugs is most likely to be used as pharmacologic therapy?
252.e: The medicines most often used to treat acromegaly are called somatostatin analogs (SSAs) like octreotide. These drugs curb the release of GH and may also reduce the size of the pituitary tumor. Several studies have shown that these drugs are safe and effective for long-term treatment. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 675

252.q: A 26-year-old woman presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Her prolactin level is grossly elevated (200 ng/mL). Which of the following is most useful in the treatment of hyperprolactinemia?
252.e: Bromocriptine is an effective dopamine agonist in the CNS with the advantage of oral activity. The drug inhibits prolactin secretion by activating pituitary dopamine receptors. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 286

252.q: A 4-year-old girl presented with hirsutism, breast enlargement, and a height and bone age that was consistent with an age of 9. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for treatment of this patient ?
252.e: Given clinical scenario suggest the diagnosis of precocious puberty. Treatment involves suppressing gonadotropin secretion with continuous administration of a long-acting GnRH agonist such as leuprolide. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no.622

252.q: A 2-year-old boy with failure to thrive was found to have an inactivating mutation in the gene that encodes the growth hormone receptor. Which of the following drugs is most likely to improve his metabolic function and promote his growth?
252.e: This child’s condition is due to the inability of GH to stimulate the production of insulin-like growth factors, the ultimate mediators of GH effects. Mecasermin, a combination of recombinant IGF-1 and the binding protein that protects IGF-1 from immediate destruction, will help correct the IGF deficiency. Because of the inactive GH receptors, somatropin will not be effective. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 678

253.q: Which of the following is a sign or symptom that would be expected to occur in the event of chronic overdose with exogenous T4?
253.e: In hyperthyroidism, the metabolic rate increases, and even though there is increased appetite, weight loss often occurs. The other choices are symptoms seen in hypothyroidism. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 690

253.q: A 34-year-old woman underwent near total thyroidectomy. She was started on levothyroxine. What hormone is produced in the peripheral tissues when levothyroxine is administered?
253.e: L-thyroxine (levothyroxine, a synthetic form of T4) is peripherally converted to T3 (biologically active) and rT3 (biologically inactive), Indicated in Myxedema & Hypothyroidism. Side effects are Sweating, heat intolerance Tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias, chest pain Tremors Weight loss (this drug is sometimes misused by patients trying to lose weight) Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 694

253.q: Initiating T4 therapy for an elderly patient with long- standing hypothyroidism, is it important to begin with small doses to avoid which of the following?
253.e: Patients with long-standing hypothyroidism, especially those who are elderly, are highly sensitive to the stimulatory effects of T4 on cardiac function. Administration of regular doses can cause overstimulation of the heart and cardiac collapse Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 689

253.q: A 65-year-old woman with MNG is scheduled for total thyroidectomy. Which of the following drugs will be administered for 10-14 days before surgery to reduce the vascularity of his thyroid gland?
253.e: Iodides inhibit the synthesis and release of thyroid hormone and decrease the size and vascularity of the hyperplastic gland. Lugol’s solution contains a mixture of potassium iodide and iodine. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 695

253.q: A 73-year-old woman is brought to you for progressive memory loss She has gained 10kgs in the last year. Her father died from complications of Alzheimer disease. She is oriented but has short-term memory deficits. Examination shows a normal gait and delayed relaxation of the achilles reflex bilaterally. Her skin is dry and she has brittle nails. Treatment with which of the following is most appropriate?
253.e: Hashimoto thyroiditis is characterized by progressive destruction of thyroid tissue by antithyroid peroxidase antibodies and antithyroglobulin antibodies. Initially, it may manifest with transient hyperthyroidism, before progressing to hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism results in a generalized decrease of the basal metabolic rate, which can present with weight gain, fatigue, dry skin and brittle nails, along with concentration and memory impairment. Treatment with Life-long oral administration of L-thyroxine (T4) , commence at a lower and more slow-acting dose with increasing severity of hypothyroidism because of the risk of cardiac side effects. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 699

253.q: A 45-year-old woman is on L-thyroxine therapy for 2 years with adequate therapeutic response. However, with all of the following drugs, dose of L-thyroxine is to be increased except?
253.e: Increased dosage necessary Estrogen & SERM (Increase TBG in the serum) Bile acid-binding resins Omeprazole Calcium carbonate (Reduces absorption of thyroid hormone) Phenytoin Carbamazepine (Increases metabolism of thyroid hormones) Propranolol (Reduces conversion of T4 to T3) Reduced dosage necessary: glucocorticoids (Decrease TBG in the serum) Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 704

254.q: A 56-year-old woman with SLE had been maintained on a moderate daily dose of prednisone for 9 months. Her disease has finally gone into remission. Gradual tapering of a glucocorticoid is required for recovery of which of the following?
o: Depressed release of insulin from pancreatic B cells
254.e: Exogenous glucocorticoids act at the hypothalamus and pituitary to suppress the production of CRH and ACTH. As a result, adrenal production of endogenous corticosteroids is suppressed. On discontinuance, the recovery of normal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal function occurs slowly. Glucocorticoid doses must be tapered slowly, over several months, to prevent adrenal insufficiency. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 712

254.q: A new-born girl exhibited ambiguous genitalia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension. Treatment consisted of fluid and salt replacement and hydrocortisone administration. Which of the following describes the primary therapeutic effect of glucocorticoid administration?
254.e: A 21α-hydroxylase deficiency prevents normal synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone, and causes accumulation of cortisol precursors. The hypothalamic-pituitary system responds to the abnormally low levels of cortisol by increasing ACTH release. High levels of ACTH induce adrenal hyperplasia and excess production of adrenal androgens, which can cause virilization of females and prepubertal males. Glucocorticoid is administered to replace the missing mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid activity and to suppress ACTH release, which removes the stimulus for excess adrenal androgen production. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 715

254.q: A 75 years old male patient is known case of COPD and is on combination therapy of LABA + Corticosteroids. Most important action of corticosteroid is___.
254.e: Corticosteroids have been used to treat asthma since 1950 and are presumed to act by their broad anti-inflammatory efficacy, mediated in part by inhibition of production of inflammatory cytokines. They do not relax airway smooth muscle directly but reduce bronchial reactivity and reduce the frequency of asthma exacerbations if taken regularly. Their effect on airway obstruction may be due in part to their contraction of engorged vessels in the bronchial mucosa and their potentiation of the effects of β-receptor agonists, but their most important action is inhibition of the infiltration of asthmatic airways by lymphocytes, eosinophils, and mast cells. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 347

254.q: Initial Drug of choice for suspected case of acute adrenal insufficiency is:
254.e: Answer is C (Dexamethasone): The treatment of choice for acute adrenal insufficiency is Glucocorticoid Replacement Therapy. In cases where the diagnosis of acute adrenal insufficiency is suspected (not confirmed) Dexamethasone is preferred as the initial steroid of choice because Dexamethasone does not compete with the cortisol assay. Cosyntropin stimulation testing may be performed while the patient is on treatment.

254.q: A 54-year-old man with advanced tuberculosis has developed signs of severe acute adrenal insufficiency. The patient should be treated immediately. Which of the following combinations is most rational?
254.e: In acute adrenal insufficiency, there is loss of salt and water that is primarily due to reduced production of aldosterone. The loss of salt and water can lead to dehydration. A rational combination of drugs should include agents with complementary effects (i.e. a glucocorticoid and a mineralocorticoid). The combination with these characteristics is cortisol and fludrocortisone. (Note that although fludrocortisone may have sufficient glucocorticoid activity for a patient with mild disease, a patient in severe acute adrenal insufficiency needs a full glucocorticoid such as cortisol.) Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 710

254.q: Which of the following is the only drug that reduces mortality in a patient with severe COVID-19 on respiratory support?
254.e: Corticosteroids have mortality benefit in COVID 19 patients Patients with severe or critical COVID-19 develop an overstimulation of the immune system, which can be very harmful to their health. Corticosteroids reduce this overstimulation, which helps balance the immune system responses so that they are effective and do not cause damage to the person themselves.

254.q: A 78-year-male old patient came to the emergency department with the complaint of severe dyspnoea. He is a known case of COPD and is on inhalational LABA + Corticosteroids. His SpO2 on room air is 96%, Pulse rate is 120/min, BP is 140/90 mm Hg. On Auscultation, bilateral fine crepitus is heard. He needs urgent treatment for dyspnoea. What is the dose for intravenous Methylprednisolone every 6-12 hours?
254.e: Urgent treatment is often begun with an oral dose of 30-60 mg prednisone per day or an intravenous dose of 1 mg/kg methylprednisolone every 6-12 hours; the daily dose is decreased after airway obstruction has improved. In most patients, systemic corticosteroid therapy can be discontinued in 7-10 days, but in other patient's symptoms may worsen as the dose is decreased to lower levels. Reference: LANG' Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor, 12th Edition, Page Number-347.

254.q: A 48-year-old male with Cushing's syndrome due to an adrenal tumor. Which of the following drugs would be expected to reduce the signs and symptoms of this man's disease?
254.e: Ketoconazole inhibits many types of cytochrome P450 enzymes. It can be used to reduce the unregulated overproduction of corticosteroids by adrenal tumors. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 714

255.q: Which of the following drugs is most useful for the treatment of hypercalcemia in Paget's disease?
255.e: Paget’s disease is characterized by excessive bone resorption, poorly organized bone formation, and hypercalcemia. Bisphosphonates and calcitonin are first-line treatments. Pamidronate is a powerful bisphosphonate used parenterally to treat hypercalcemia. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 793

255.q: The active metabolites of vitamin D act through a nuclear receptor to produce which of the following effects ?
o: Decrease the absorption of calcium from bone
Increase the absorption of calcium from the gastrointestinal tract
255.e: The active metabolites of vitamin D increase serum calcium and phosphate by promoting calcium and phosphate uptake from the gastrointestinal tract, increasing bone resorption, and decreasing renal excretion of both electrolytes. They inhibit, rather than stimulate, PTH formation. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 781

255.q: Which of the following cause inhibition of the enzyme farnesyl pyrophosphatesynthase?
255.e: Nitrogen-containingbisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronate) cause inhibition of the enzyme farnesyl pyrophosphatesynthase → disturbance of osteoclast metabolism and signaling → reduced osteoclast function and promotion of osteoclast apoptosis. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 698

255.q: Which of the following is NOT true about Teriparatide ?
o: Contraindicated in patient with prior radiation therapy
255.e: Teriparatide: parathyroid hormone analogue Mechanism of action: increases osteoblastic activity →increased bone growth Mainly used for the treatment of osteoporosis and as an alternative for severe osteoporosis (T-score ≤ -3.5) or for patients with contraindications to bisphosphonates Administered in a pulsatile fashion Side effects : Hypercalcemia (usually transitory) Increased risk of osteosarcoma in patients with Paget disease of the bone (or an unexplained elevation of alkaline phosphatases) and Prior cancers or radiation therapy Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 790

255.q: A 60 year old postmenopausal woman having a previous history of Colles fracture presented with backache. Which of the following statements about anti-osteoporosis drugs is false regarding this patient?
o: Calcium requirement is 1200 mg per day
Oral vitamin D3 should be given along with calcium supplements
Bisphosphonates therapy should not be repeated for more than one year
Teriparatide therapy should be followed by bisphosphonate therapy
255.e: Osteoporosis The second and third generation BPNs (e.g. alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate) are effective in preventing and treating postmenopausal osteoporosis in women as well as age related, idiopathic and steroid induced osteoporosis in both men and women. Alendronate is equally or more effective than HRT or raloxifene in conserving bone mineral density BPNs are more effective than calcitonin and continue to afford protection for at least 5 years of continuous use. Thus, theyare the first choice drugs now for osteoporosis. Since the t 1/2 of alendronate in bone is ~ 10 years, treatment beyond 5 years is considered unnecessary.

255.q: Which of the following drug acts by mimicking osteoprotegerin ?
255.e: Denosumab (monoclonal antibody against RANKL) Mechanism of action: targets the RANKL by mimicking osteoprotegerin → interference in osteoclast maturation → ↓ osteoclast activity Indicated in patients with impaired renal function or in whom bisphosphonates therapy failed Reference: Basic & clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 15 th Edition, pg no. 807

256.q: A 67-year-old diabetic male admitted for worsening cardia failure and hyperglycemia. Which OHA can be prescribed for beneficial effect in cardia failure ?
256.e: Some of the characteristics of SGLT-2 inhibitors Glycemic efficacy: lowers HbA1c by 0.6% over 3 months Promotes weight loss ↓ Blood pressure ↓ Risk of cardiovascular mortality in patients with type 2 DM and cardiovascular disease Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzun Pg no. 762

256.q: A 67-year-old diabetic male presents with dizziness due to hypoglycemia. He is on treatment with metformin with acarbose. Hypoglycemia should be treated with ?
256.e: Patients taking an α-glucosidase inhibitor who experience hypoglycemia should be treated with oral glucose (dextrose) and not sucrose, because the absorption of sucrose will be delayed. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 749

256.q: In response to drug X, pancreatic islet cells begin producing increasing amounts of secretory granules. Identify X.
256.e: The secretory granules produced by the pancreatic islet cells in response to X, contain insulin and C-peptide, suggesting that the administered drug works by increasing endogenous insulin production. Glimepiride, a sulfonylurea, stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells. Their principle target is the ATP-sensitive K+ channels in the pancreatic β-cell plasma membrane. Inhibition of K+ channels by sulfonylureas causes depolarization of the β-cell membrane, leading to an influx of Ca2+, which stimulates exocytosis of insulin-containing secretory granules. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 759

256.q: A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus has a HbA1C of 8.5%. Consultant prescribes a drug that reversibly inhibits a membrane-bound enzyme that hydrolyses carbohydrate bonds. Which of the following drugs was most likely added to this patient's medication regimen?
256.e: The drug inhibits alpha-glucosidase, Miglitol, prevents the hydrolysis of polysaccharides to monosaccharides. Since polysaccharides are not absorbed as easily as monosaccharides, alpha-glucosidase therapy results in a slower rise in postprandial blood glucose concentrations. Adverse effects of alpha-glucosidase inhibitors are caused by impaired absorption and include flatulence, diarrhoea, and early satiety. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 14th Edition, Page Number-761.

256.q: In response to a drug X, the pancreatic islet cells began producing increasing amounts of secretory granules. Identify X.
256.e: The secretory granules produced by the pancreatic islet cells in response to X contain insulin and C-peptide, suggesting that the administered drug works by increasing endogenous insulin production. Glimepiride, a sulfonylurea, stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells. Their principal target is the ATP-sensitive K+ channels in the pancreatic β-cell plasma membrane. Inhibition of K+ channels by sulfonylureas causes depolarization of the β-cell membrane, leading to an influx of Ca2+, which stimulates exocytosis of insulin-containing secretory granules. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 14th Edition, Page Number-759.

256.q: A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus has HbA1c = 8.5%. Consultant prescribes a drug that reversibly inhibits a membrane-bound enzyme that hydrolyzes carbohydrate bonds. Which of the following drugs was most likely added to this patient's medication regimen?
256.e: The drug inhibits alpha-glucosidase, Miglitol, prevents the hydrolysis of polysaccharides to monosaccharides. Since polysaccharides are not absorbed as easily as monosaccharides, alpha-glucosidase therapy results in a slower rise in postprandial blood glucose concentrations. Adverse effects of alpha-glucosidase inhibitors are caused by impaired absorption and include flatulence, diarrhea, and early satiety. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 14th Edition, Page Number-761.

256.q: A 12-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes has severe hyperglycaemia, ketoacidosis, and a blood pH of 7.20. Which of the following agents should be administered to achieve rapid control of the severe ketoacidosis ?
256.e: Oral antidiabetic agents are inappropriate in this patient because he has insulin-dependent diabetes. He needs a rapid-acting insulin preparation that can be given intravenously. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 754

256.q: A 25-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes wishes to control of her diabetes to improve her long-term prognosis. Which of the following regimens is most appropriate?
o: Morning injections of mixed insulin lispro and insulin aspart
Evening injections of mixed regular insulin and insulin glargine
Morning and evening injections of regular insulin, supplemented by small amounts of NPH insulin at mealtimes
Morning injections of insulin glargine, supplemented by small amounts of insulin lispro at mealtimes
256.e: Insulin regimens for tight control usually take the form of establishing a basal level of insulin with a small amount of a long-acting preparation (eg, insulin glargine) and supplementing the insulin levels, when called for by food intake, with short-acting insulin lispro. Less tight control may be achieved with 2 injections of intermediate-acting insulin per day. Because intake of glucose is mainly during the day, long- acting insulins are usually given in the morning, not at night. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no.754

257.q: Which of the following is not used in treatment of polycystic ovarian disease?
257.e: Treatment of PCOD Weight loss of more than 5% of previous weight is important. Cigarette smoking should be avoided. Estrogen in combination with progesterone (lacking androgenic properties). Dexamethasone 0.5 mg at bedtime also reduces androgen production. Hirsutism is treated with cyproterone acetate or spironolactone. Infertility is treated with Clomiphene. Ovulation is induced in around 80% of patients and about 40% conceive. However, abortion rate of 25-40% is due to corpus luteal phase defect manifested by Clomiphene. In Clomiphene failed group, ovulation can be induced with FSH or GnRH analogues. Metformin treats the root cause of PCOS, rectifies endocrine and metabolic functions and improves fertility and is the drug of choice.

257.q: A female with unilateral breast cancer is on tamoxifen therapy. Which of the following adverse effects is associated with the use of tamoxifen?
257.e: Tamoxifen is a SERM that acts as an antagonist at estrogen receptors in the breast. It decreases the risk of contralateral breast cancer and is Approved for primary prevention of breast cancer in women at high risk. Adverse effects of Tamoxifen include: Hot flashes Vaginal discharge or bleeding Menstrual irregularities Thromboembolic events (rare) Endometrial hyperplasia/Carcinoma Cataract Hepatotoxicity

258.q: A 50-year-old man is presents with dizziness and confusion. He had an episode of chest pain and took several tablets of nitroglycerin. His current medications include tadalafil for erectile dysfunction. His blood pressure is 50/20 mmHg and his heart rate is 120 beats/min. Which of the following cellular changes is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
258.e: The interaction between nitrates and phosphodiesterase inhibitors used in erectile dysfunction (tadalafil, sildenafil, vardenafil) is well known and very important to understand. Nitrates are converted to nitric oxide by vascular smooth muscle cells, and nitric oxide causes increased intracellular CGMP as a second-messenger. Increased GMP concentration leads to vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Additionally, GMP is metabolized within the cells by phosphodiesterase, and phosphodiesterase inhibitors will lead to increased intracellular GMP. GMP accumulation in vascular smooth muscle cells due to both enhanced synthesis (nitrates) and inhibited degradation (PDE inhibitors) is responsible for profound hypotension due to extreme vasodilatation when these drugs are used together. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 194

258.q: A 78-year-old man presents with the complaint of difficulty urinating. He has difficulty starting his stream and feels his bladder is still full after he urinates. He has to get up about four times a night to urinate. The physician starts him on finasteride, which non-competitively inhibits 5 alpha-reductase. What effect does a noncompetitive inhibitor have on enzyme kinetics?
258.e: Decreases Vmax. Noncompetitive inhibitor decrease the Vmax. Noncompetitive inhibitors block enzyme activity with or without substrates bound, therefore the affinity is unaffected. The Vmax decreases because when the inhibitor is bound, it decreases the amount of active sites available for the substrate. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no. 22

258.q: A patient with pre-existing liver disease consumed a drug and developed worsening of liver dysfunction. The metabolite of the drug responsible is N-acetyl-para-amino-benzo-quinone-imine(NAPQI). The likely implicated drug in this case is
258.e: This is a case of Paracetamol toxicity. Mechanism of toxicity of Paracetamol N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NABQI) is a highly reactive arylating minor metabolite of paracetamol which is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione. When a very large dose of paracetamol is taken, glucuronidation capacity is saturated, more of the minor metabolite is formed-hepatic glutathione is depleted and this metabolite binds covalently to proteins in liver cells (and renal tubules) causing necrosis. Antidote: N-acetylcysteine

258.q: Which of the following drugs act directly without sexual stimulation ?
258.e: Ans. C. Alprostadil Alprastadil (pGEl) is directly injected into corpora cavernusa for erectile dysfunction' It acts by increasing arterial inflow" by vasodilation and reducing outflow by contracting the carporal smooth muscle that occludes draining venules.

260.q: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, such as aspirin act by inhibiting the activity of the enzyme:
260.e: Drugs acting as inhibitors COX NSAID Aspirin: Inhibits COX-1 and COX-2. Indomethacin and ibuprofen-inhibit cyclooxyge- nases by competing with arachidonate. Coxibs: Selectively inhibit COX-2 Some coxibs have been withdrawn or suspended from the market due to undesirable side effects and safety issues. Reference: Harper's 32 nd edition, page 241

260.q: A patient on aspirin presented with occult blood in his stool. Inhibition of which of the following by aspirin would best explain this adverse event?
260.e: Aspirin, even in small doses, irreversibly inhibits TXA2 synthesis by platelets. Thus, it interferes with platelet aggregation and bleeding time is prolonged to nearly twice the normal value. Long-term intake of large doses decreases synthesis of clotting factors in the liver and predisposes to bleeding. This can be prevented by prophylactic vit K therapy. Aspirin particles coming in contact with gastric mucosa promotes local back diffusion of acid. This causes focal necrosis of mucosal cells and capillaries→acute ulcers, erosive gastritis, congestion and microscopic haemorrhages. The occult blood loss in stools is increased by even a single tablet of aspirin.

260.q: A pregnant woman was prescribed indomethacin. What effect could be expected in the fetus?
260.e: Ductus arteriosus closure During foetal circulation ductus arteriosus is kept patent by local elaboration of PGE2 by COX-2. Unknown mechanisms switch off this synthesis at birth and the ductus closes. When this fails to occur, small doses of indomethacin or aspirin bring about closure in the majority of cases within a few hours by inhibiting PG production. Administration of NSAIDs in late pregnancy has been found to promote premature closure of ductus in some cases. Risk of postpartum haemorrhage is increased. Prescribing of NSAIDs near term should be avoided

260.q: Which of the following patient characteristics is the most compelling reason for avoiding celecoxib in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis?
260.e: Celecoxib is a COX-2-selective inhibitor. Although the COX-2 inhibitors have the advantage over nonselective NSAIDs of reduced gastrointestinal toxicity, clinical data suggest that they are more likely to cause arterial thrombotic events. A history of myocardial infarction would be a compelling reason to avoid a COX-2 inhibitor. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 650

260.q: A 6-year-old girl suffering from the effects of an aspirin overdose. Which of the following syndromes is this patient most likely to exhibit as a result of this drug overdose?
o: Bone marrow suppression and possibly aplastic anemia
260.e: Salicylate intoxication is associated with metabolic acidosis, dehydration, and hyperthermia. If these problems are not corrected, coma and death ensue. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 647

260.q: Read the following statements regarding the use of given drugs and choose the correct option. 1. Morphine is used for the treatment of pulmonary oedema 2. Indomethacin can be used in the treatment of headache 3. Aspirin is used in the treatment of dyspepsia 4. Pethidine can be used in treatment of biliary colic
260.e: Morphine helps in pulmonary oedema by reducing the preload by redistributing the blood and therefore reducing the pulmonary capillary pressure. Indomethacin like many other NSAIDS inhibit the synthesis of prostaglandins and relieve symptom of headache. Aspirin is a non competitive inhibitor of COX and causes gastric ulcers, does not relieve dyspepsia. Opioids produce a general increase in resting tone of the gut wall and sphincters. These effects arise from stimulation of both µ- and κ-receptors on neuronal plexuses in the gut wall. An increase in biliary pressure caused by opioid-induced spasm at the sphincter of Oddi can exacerbate biliary colic. Hence, Pethidine can be used in the treatment of biliary colic.

260.q: The main advantage of ketorolac over aspirin is that ketorolac
o: Can be combined more safely with an opioid such as codeine
Does not prolong the bleeding time
Available in a parenteral formulation that can be injected intramuscularly or intravenously
Less likely to cause acute renal failure in patients with some preexisting degree of renal impairment
260.e: Ketorolac exerts typical NSAID effects. It prolongs the bleeding time and can impair renal function, especially in a patient with preexisting renal disease. Its primary use is as a parenteral agent for pain management, especially for treatment of postoperative patients. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 648

260.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease underwent nephrectomy. Which of the following can be used for post-operative pain for this patient?
260.e: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) Actions: The central analgesic action of paracetamol is like aspirin, i.e. it raises pain threshold, but has weak peripheral anti-inflammatory components. Analgesic action of aspirin and paracetamol is additive. Paracetamol is a good and promptly acting antipyretic. Paracetamol has negligible anti-inflammatory action. In contrast to aspirin and other NSAIDs, paracetamol does not stimulate respiration or affect acid-base balance; it does not increase cellular metabolism. It has no effect on CVS. Gastric irritation is insignificant-mucosal erosion and bleeding occur rarely only in overdose. It does not affect platelet function or clotting factors and is not uricosuric.

261.q: Many guidelines prefer to treat acute gout with a corticosteroid or indomethacin because high doses of colchicine are likely to cause
261.e: At doses needed to treat acute gout, colchicine frequently causes significant diarrhea. Such gastrointestinal effects are less likely with the lower doses used in chronic gout. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 656

261.q: Which of the following drugs is most likely to increase serum concentrations of conventional doses of methotrexate, a weak acid that is primarily cleared in the urine?
261.e: Like other weak acids, methotrexate depends on active tubular excretion in the proximal tubule for efficient elimination. Probenecid competes with methotrexate for binding to the proximal tubule transporter and thereby decreases the rate of clearance of methotrexate. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 647

261.q: A 40-year-old woman with renal allograft is currently taking an immunosuppressive drug. Laboratory examination shows a uric acid level of 10.5 mg/dL. Treatment with allopurinol is begun, necessitating a reduction in the dose of the immunosuppressive drug. Which of the following immunosuppressive drugs is this patient most likely taking?
261.e: In this question, you must identify the immunosuppressive drug that interacts with allopurinol, subsequently requiring a dose reduction of the immunosuppressant agent. Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant that ultimately inhibits T-lymphocyte proliferation. This agent is converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which inhibits DNA purine synthesis and subsequent T-cell proliferation. Xanthine oxidase is instrumental in the metabolism of azathioprine metabolites, and coadministration with allopurinol (an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase) can result in azathioprine toxicity. Because azathioprine interacts with allopurinol in the question stem, azathioprine is the correct . Reference- Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1004-1005

261.q: Over the next 7 months, the patient had 2 more attacks of acute gout. Her serum concentration of uric acid was elevated. The decision was made to put her on chronic drug therapy to try to prevent subsequent attacks. Which of the following drugs could be used to decrease this woman's rate of production of uric acid?
261.e: Allopurinol is the only drug listed that decreases production of uric acid. Probenecid increases uric acid excretion. Colchicine and hydroxychloroquine do not affect uric acid metabolism. Aspirin actually slows renal secretion of uric acid and raises uric acid blood levels. It should not be used in gout. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 651

261.q: A 28-year-old woman suffers from intense migraine headaches. She is on fluoxetine for her mental illness. Which of the following drugs should be avoided ? 1.Naproxen 2.Paracetamol 3.Ondansetron 4.Tramadol 5.Linezolid 6.Domperidone
261.e: Patient is on SSRI, therefore 5-HT agonist should be avoided as it combination may lead to serotonin syndrome. Serotonergic drugs : Psychiatric drugs: MAOIs, SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, vortioxetine, vilazodone, trazodone, buspirone Other drugs: tramadol, ondansetron, MDMA, dextromethorphan, meperidine, St. John's wort, triptans, linezolid. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 287

262.q: Not to be given in malignant malaria is -
262.e: Answer- A. Quinolone Artemisinin derivative : Artesunate Quinine or Quinidine Plus one of the following : Doxycycline, Tetracycline and Clindamycin

262.q: A 42-year-old woman with RA comes with 10-month history of joint pain and stiffness in her wrists and fingers. The symptoms are worse in the morning and improve with activity. She is started on first line DMARDs. All of the following are true about treatment except?
o: To minimize adverse effects, administer folic acid.
Pregnancy is contraindication with the treatment.
Avoid administering NSAIDs on the same day as DMARDs.
Need yearly fundoscopy to rule out bull's eye Retinopathy.
262.e: This patient of RA is initiated with methotrexate PO 10-25 mg weekly. Option A- True. Folic acid 7–10 mg PO once weekly 24–48 hours after MTX administration Option B- True. Couple should plan for contraception while she's been on methotrexate treatment. If she plans to conceive, Sulfasalazine should be considered in patients with low disease activity. Option C- True. NSAIDs can inhibit the renal excretion of MTX, which may increase the risk for adverse effects. Option D- False. Given statement is true about CHQ therapy, should be consider in patients with low disease activity after remission. Not a first line of treatment. Reference- Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 995-996

262.q: A 59-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is planned for DEXA scan and result shows a T-score of -1.80, Which of the following drugs is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this finding?
262.e: Patients with refractory rheumatoid arthritis are frequently prescribed glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone), which induce bone resorption and increase the risk of osteopenia and osteoporosis. Glucocorticoid-induced bone resorption is primarily mediated via the RANK ligand signaling pathway, a cascade that upregulates osteoclast activity and induces apoptosis of osteoblasts. Chronic glucocorticoid use can also induce mild hypocalcemia, which leads to PTH-mediated bone resorption. In addition, decreased estrogen levels following menopause increase this patient's risk for osteoporosis and osteopenia. Bisphosphonates and denosumab (anti-RANK ligand antibody) are used to treat glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 713

262.q: Which of the following is a parenterally administered DMARD whose mechanism of anti-inflammatory action is antagonism of tumor necrosis factor?
262.e: Etanercept is a recombinant protein that binds to tumor necrosis factor and prevents its inflammatory effects. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 656

262.q: An 18-year-old was brought to the emergency department by her friends as she had turned blue. She was well otherwise. On examination she has central cyanosis; all other parameters are normal. What is the most likely cause?
262.e: The question deals with cyanosis in an otherwise well patient. Cyanosis is seen in hypoxia. But the patient with hypoxia will be dyspnoeic. Here the patient is otherwise normal. Rare cause of cyanosis is due to abnormal hemoglobins like methemoglobin or Sulfhemoglobin. The causes of methemoglobinemia includes: Nitrates, nitric oxide or nitrobenzene Aniline dyes Propanil(a herbicide) Dapsone Pyridium So the accurate among the options are drinking water contaminated with nitrates. Lead poisoning will not lead to cyanosis but bluish lines in the gums. Carbon monoxide poisoning will cause cherry red discolouration. Anorexia nervosa is a disease of distorted perception of body image, where the patient restricts food intake and will be malnourished. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:459 Pg 3593

262.q: A 17-year-old female presents after taking an overdose of her grandmother's medication. Investigations revealed: Serum potassium 6 mmol/L (3.5-4.9) Which one of the following drugs is the most likely cause of this abnormality?
262.e: Beta blockers , particularly propranolol, in overdose can cause hyperkalaemia by transmembrane shifts. It is useful to think of the opposite - beta-agonists such as salbutamol are far more widely known to cause hypokalaemia. Overdose of digoxin therapy most commonly manifests as rhythm disturbance, and may be exacerbated by hyper- or hypokalaemia. Salicylate overdose causes metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, pg:423

262.q: A 20 year old male has taken a drug overdose of multiple drugs. Which one of the following can be effectively removed by haemodialysis?
262.e: Drugs with a large volume of distribution are poorly dialysed. Haemodialysis is effective in lithium poisoning. LIST OF DIALYZABLE TOXINS Dialysis should be considered in cases of severe poisoning due to: Carbamazepine Ethylene glycol Isopropyl alcohol Lithium Methanol Theophylline Salicylates Valproate. Hemodialysis corrects the acid base balance as well as removal of toxins compared to hemoperfusion. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 459, Pg: 3589.

262.q: A 38 year old man with a history of depression is brought to the accident and emergency department after being found unconscious in a garage. A friend said that he complained of a headache, then had nausea and vomiting. He then became unarousable. Oxygen saturations are 95% on air and breath sounds are clear on auscultation. What is the likely diagnosis?
262.e: The patient has a clear lung field with normal oxygen saturation which rules out primary lung of vascular pathologies like pneumonitis, pulmonary embolism and eosinophilia. Carbon monoxide poisoning is produced by the incomplete combustion of carbon containing fuels such as gas, coal, oil, wood and coke. CO increases the affinity of O 2 to Haemoglobin which results in cellular hypoxia in spite of a normal saturation. The O2 Hb dissociation curve shifts to the left. Headache is the most common symptom (90%) followed by nausea & vomiting, vertigo, alteration in consciousness and weakness. The cherry red skin colour occurs when COHb concentration exceeds 20% but it is rarely seen in life. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:459 Pg 3593

263.q: Romiplostim acts on which of the following receptors:
263.e: Romiplostim: Genetically engineered protein in which the Fc component of a human antibody is fused to two copies of a peptide that stimulates the thrombopoietin receptors; approved for treatment of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura Ref: Katzung 11th edition Chapter 33.

263.q: All of the following are false regarding prasugrel, except:
o: Not much metabolism in the body
Slow onset of action than clopidogrel
263.e: Prasugrel : This is a newer, more potent and faster acting irreversibleP2Y12 purinergic receptor blocker , as when strong antiplatelet action is required.(Option C ruled out) Like its predecessors, it is also a prodrug, but is more rapidly absorbed.(Option B ruled out) It is also more rapidly and more completely activated, resulting in faster and more consistent platelet inhibition.(Option A ruled out) Bleeding complications are also more frequent and more serious. Patients with a history of ischaemic stroke and TIAs are at greater risk of intracranial haemorrhage. Prasugrel is contraindicated in such patients. Key Takeaway: Irreversible P2Y12 blockers(Prodrugs): Clopidogrel, Ticlopidine, Prasugrel Reversible, competitive P2Y12 blocker: Cangrelor Reversible, non competitive P2Y12 blocker: Ticagrelor

263.q: Which of the following most accurately describes the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
o: Clopidogrel directly binds to the platelet ADP receptors
Clopidogrel facilitates the action of antithrombin III
The active metabolite of clopidogrel binds to and inhibits the platelet ADP receptors
The active metabolite of clopidogrel binds to and inhibits the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors
263.e: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that is activated by CYP2C9 and CYP2C19. It irreversibly binds to the ADP receptor on the surface of platelets that serves as a key role in platelet aggregation. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834

263.q: A 56-year-old man undergoes a percutaneous coronary angiography procedure and placement of a stent in a coronary blood vessel. Appropriate pharmacological management will be?
263.e: Patient will need to be on aspirin and clopidogrel for at least a year. Aspirin and clopidogrel help prevent platelet-induced occlusion of coronary stents. Clopidogrel is a prodrug that is activated by CYP2C9 and It irreversibly binds to the ADP receptor on the surface of platelets that serves as a key role in platelet aggregation. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 840-45

263.q: A 59-year-old man with MI is admitted for emergency percutaneous insertion of a coronary stent. Which of the following drugs might cause unexpected results based on the patient's CYP2C19 genotype?
263.e: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that must be metabolised to an active platelet-inhibiting metabolite by CYP2C19. Poor metabolizers achieve inadequate platelet inhibition. Option B & C: Prasugrel and ticagrelor do not require P450 activation and are not subject to this risk. Option D: Cytochrome P450-inducing drugs (e.g., carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, barbiturates) increase warfarin's clearance and reduce the anticoagulant effect of a given dose. Cytochrome P450 inhibitors (e.g., amiodarone, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, cimetidine) reduce warfarin's clearance and increase the anticoagulant effect of a given dose. Genetic variability in cytochrome CYP2C9 and VKOR affect responses to warfarin. Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 14th Edition, Page Number- 79.
Ans. is 'b' i.e., Inhibit ADP mediated cAMP activation

263.q: A 55-year-old man is brought 2 h after the onset of severe chest pain. He has a history of poorly controlled mild hypertension and elevated blood cholesterol but does not smoke. ECG changes of ST elevation and cardiac enzymes confirm the diagnosis of myocardial infarction. The decision is made to attempt to open his occluded artery. Which of the following drugs accelerates the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin?
263.e: Reteplase is the only thrombolytic drug listed. Heparin is anticoagulant. Argatroban is a direct inhibitor of thrombin, and Aminocaproic acid is an inhibitor, not an activator, of the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 836

263.q: A 55-year-old man is brought 2 hrs after the onset of severe chest pain. He has a history of poorly controlled mild hypertension and elevated blood cholesterol but does not smoke. ECG changes of ST elevation and cardiac enzymes confirm the diagnosis of myocardial infarction. The decision is made to attempt to open his occluded artery. Which of the following drugs accelerates the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin?
263.e: Reteplase is the only thrombolytic drug listed. Heparin is anticoagulant. Argatroban is a direct inhibitor of thrombin, and Aminocaproic acid is an inhibitor, not an activator, of the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834-33

264.q: Which enzyme is involved in the management of thrombotic events by converting plasminogen to plasmin?
264.e: Explanation: Urokinase is an enzyme that promotes the breakdown of blood clots by converting plasminogen into plasmin, which then degrades fibrin, the main component of clots. This fibrinolytic action helps dissolve clots in blood vessels. It is used in Pulmonary embolism, Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) etc to dissolve clots.

264.q: Which of the following drugs acts as a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase?
264.e: Explanation: Methotrexate is a structural analogue of folic acid and acts as a competitive inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, preventing the conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, which is essential for DNA synthesis and cell division. This particularly affects rapidly dividing cells, making it useful in cancer and autoimmune diseases.

264.q: Which one of the following compounds is function as antagonist of Vitamin K, and commonly used to reduce blood clotting in patients with high risk of thromboembolism?
264.e: Option A: Antagonists of vitamin K are used to reduce blood coagulation in patients at risk of thromboembolism; the most widely used is warfarin. Option B: Menadione and menadiol diacetate, synthetic compounds that can be metabolized to phylloquinone. It has vitamin K activity. Option C: Menaquinones, synthesized by intestinal bacteria, with differing lengths of side chain. It has also vitamin K like activity. Option D: Tocopherol have vitamin E activity. Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition, CH 44 PN 532

264.q: Which of the following drugs may inhibit the hepatic microsomal P450 responsible for warfarin metabolism?
264.e: Amiodarone is an important anti-arrhythmic drug and has a well-documented ability to inhibit the hepatic metabolism of many drugs. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no.60

264.q: Rifampicin increase elimination of all of the following drugs except?
264.e: Rifampin strongly induces most cytochrome P450 isoforms (CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, and 3A4), which increases the elimination of numerous other drugs including methadone, anticoagulants, cyclosporine, some anticonvulsants, protease inhibitors, some nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors or integrase strand transfer inhibitors, contraceptives, and a host of others. Coadministration of rifampin results in significantly lower serum levels of these drugs. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 14th Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page no. 845-846

264.q: Patients with a history of mitral stenosis and stroke presents with irregularly irregular heart beats. There is no clot in the left atrium on TEE. Patient is already on ACE inhibitors and statins. Which of the following drugs should be added for stroke prevention?
264.e: Anticoagulants are of little value in thrombotic stroke. Neurological sequelae are similar whether they are given or not. Moreover, in the initial stages it is difficult to rule out haemorrhagic stroke. However, they may be given in cerebral embolism because showers of emboli are often recurrent in case of mitral stenosis/atrial fibrillation, and can be prevented by anticoagulants. Antiplatelet drugs are superior to anticoagulants in transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs).

264.q: A 78-year-old woman does not want oral anti-coagulation because she does not want to come to clinic for frequent blood tests. You suggest an oral alternative and start her on apixaban and counsel her on the importance of taking the medication each day, as suddenly stopping can lead to
264.e: Due to the shorter half-life of the oral factor X and thrombin inhibitors, the anticoagulant status of the patient changes rapidly. Sudden cessation of short-acting oral anticoagulants can lead to stroke . Excess bleeding is associated with taking any of the anticoagulants not with stopping them. An increase in INR reflects increased anticoagulation by warfarin. Thrombo- cytopenia is a risk associated with heparin. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834-33

264.q: Unfortunately, because of a calculation error, the heparin drip is running at 100 times the rate it should be running at for a 67 year old patient with DVT. Protamine sulfate is immediately given intravenously. This agent works by which of the following mechanisms of action?
264.e: Chemical antagonist. A chemical antagonist prevents the actions of an agonist by modifying or sequestering the agonist so that it is incapable of binding to and activating its receptor. Protamine sulfate is a chemical antagonist for heparin. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no. 22

265.q: Mechanism of action of leukotriene pathway inhibitors?
265.e: Two approaches to interrupting the leukotriene pathway have been pursued: inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase, thereby preventing leukotriene synthesis; and inhibition of the binding of LTD 4 to its receptor on target tissues, thereby preventing its action. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 349

265.q: A 10-year-old boy with asthma uses an albuterol and low-dose inhaled mometasone. Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate to prevent complications from this treatment?
265.e: Oral rinsing after inhaled steroid use is the most appropriate recommendation. In bronchial asthma, the use of inhaled glucocorticoids such as mometasone results in more targeted steroid delivery to the lungs with much less systemic absorption. However, some of the drug is deposited in the oral cavity, which predisposes patients to local opportunistic fungal infections, especially candidiasis. Gargling or oral rinsing immediately after inhalation is recommended to reduce the local steroid burden and decrease the risk of infection. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 713

265.q: Which of the following is FALSE for deriphyline?
265.e: The methylxanthines have positive chronotropic and inotropic effects. At low concentrations, these effects appear to result from inhibition of presynaptic adenosine receptors in sympathetic nerves increasing catecholamine release at nerve endings. The higher concentrations (> 10 μmol/L, 2 mg/L) associated with inhibition of phosphodiesterase and increases in cAMP may result in increased influx of calcium. At much higher concentrations (> 100 μmol/L), sequestration of calcium by the sarcoplasmic reticulum is impaired. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 345

265.q: 1. Tiotropium does not inhibit M2- receptor- mediated- auto-down-regulation of Acetylcholine release. 2. Tiotropium dissociates most rapidly from M2 Receptors.
o: Sentence 1 and 2 both are True and 2 is correct reason for 1
Sentence 1 and 2 both are True but 2 is not the correct reason for 1
Sentence 1 is True but Sentence 2 is False
265.e: Ipratropium appears to be at least as effective in patients with COPD that includes a partially reversible component. A longer acting, selective antimuscarinic agent, tiotropium, is approved as a treatment for COPD. It binds to M1, M2, and M3 receptors with equal affinity, but dissociates most rapidly from M 2 receptors, expressed on the efferent nerve ending. This means that tiotropium does not inhibit the M2 -receptor–mediated auto–down-regulation of acetylcholine release, and thus confers a degree of receptor selectivity. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 347

265.q: Which of the following anti-muscarinic agent/s is approved for use in COPD?
265.e: Ipratropium appears to be least as effective in patients with COPD that includes a partially reversible component. A longer acting, selective, anti-muscarinic agent, tiotropium, is approved for treatment of COPD. Reference: LANG' Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor, 12th Edition, Page Number-347.

265.q: A 15-year-old girl is diagnosed with asthma and treatment is begun with an albuterol + LD inhaled Beclomethasone inhaler as needed. The patient is at greatest risk for which of the following adverse effects?
265.e: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) is the most common adverse effect of treatment with inhaled corticosteroids. It can be prevented by gargling with water after use of the inhaler and/or by adding a spacer to metered dose inhalers. This patient is experiencing symptoms at night and > 2 times per week on her current regimen of PRN albuterol (SABA). The addition of a daily, low-dose inhaled steroid to her regimen is the preferred management for mild asthma. Because inhaled corticosteroids do not take full effect until they have been used for approx. 1 week, a follow-up visit should be scheduled after this time to assess symptom control. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 709

Some patients appear to have particularly favourable responses, but no clinical features allow identification of “responders” before a trial of therapy. In the USA, zileuton is approved for use in an oral dosage of 1200 mg of the sustained-release form twice daily; zafirlukast, 20 mg twice daily; and montelukast, 10 mg (for adults) or 4 mg (for children) once daily. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 350

265.q: Mechanism of action of theophylline in Bronchial asthma include all of the following Except ?
265.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Beta-2 receptor stimulation Proposed mechanisms of action of theophylline Phosphodiesterase inhibition (Non selective) Adenosine receptor antagonism (A1, A2) Increased histone Deacetylase activity (↑red efficacy of corticosteroids) Inhibition of intracellular calcium release Stimulation of catecholamine release Inhibition of NF - alpha Beta translocation into the nucleus (nuclear translocation) Mediator inhibition (Prostaglandins, TNF alpha)

266.q: A 40-year-old male presents with severe burning chest pain radiating into his neck. His electrocardiogram was normal and test for troponin was negative. A diagnosis of GERD was made and he was sent home with a prescription for a drug that irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase in the parietal cells. Which of the following is not a side-effect of drug?
266.e: Some of the side effects of PPIs Gastrointestinal Nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, flatulence ↑ Risk of C. difficile infection Reactive hypergastrinemia ↓ Absorption of iron and vitamin B12 ↓ Absorption of calcium and magnesium → ↑ risk of osteoporosis in long-term use→ ↑ risk of fractures in elderly individuals Neurological Light headedness, headaches Possibly increased risk of developing cognitive impairment/dementia Others Exanthema Visual disturbances (rare) ↑ Risk of pneumonia In rare cases, acute interstitial nephritis Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1095

266.q: A 12-year-old boy is brought due to chronic diarrhea and failure to gain weight appropriately. He has a history of recurrent respiratory infections, and prior sputum cultures have been positive for pseudomonas aeruginosa. His younger brother died from a severe respiratory infection at age 9. Which of the following agents is most likely to improve this patient's condition in the long term?
266.e: This young Caucasian patient has a history of recurrent respiratory infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. These findings, along with a family history of early sibling death from pulmonary infection, suggest a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. Steatorrhea and failure to thrive occur as a result of malabsorption due to obstructive fibrosis and progressive insufficiency of the exocrine pancreas . Pancreatic lipase supplementation is likely to improve this patient's condition by enhancing macronutrient and vitamin absorption. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1092

266.q: Which of the following is a small molecule that polymerizes in stomach acid and coats the ulcer bed, resulting in accelerated healing and reduction of symptoms ?
266.e: Sucralfate is a small molecule that polymerizes in stomach acid and forms a protective coat over the ulcer bed. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1110

266.q: A 34-year-old woman presents with intermittent burning sensation in her chest with an occasional simultaneous acidic taste at the back of her throat. The symptoms occur soon after she eats a meal. A medication is prescribed for treatment of her symptoms. The patient returns in 2 weeks for a follow-up visit and reports near-complete resolution of her symptoms. The prescribed medication most likely binds to which of the following targets?
266.e: This woman has symptoms of dyspepsia likely due to gastroesophageal reflux (GERD), a common disorder that occurs with reflux of gastric acid into the oesophagus. Management of patients with frequent symptoms includes lifestyle and dietary modifications (eg, weight loss, avoidance of tobacco) and medications to suppress gastric acid secretion, such as H2 receptor antagonists (eg, ranitidine) and proton pump inhibitors ([PPIs] eg, pantoprazole, omeprazole). PPl are the most effective inhibitors of gastric acid secretion; they bind to and irreversibly inhibit the hydrogen-potassium ATPase on parietal cells . Potential side effects are related to the increased gastric pH and include increased risk of Clostridium difficile infections and nutritional deficiencies (eg, calcium, magnesium, iron). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1099

266.q: Which of the following medications is used to treat GERD?
266.e: Explanation: The main treatments for GERD involve proton pump inhibitors and prokinetic agents. Domperidone is a prokinetic drug used to manage GERD. It works by tightening the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), which helps prevent stomach contents from refluxing back into the esophagus. Explanation for other options: Ondansetron (Option A): is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist mainly used to prevent nausea and vomiting, particularly in chemotherapy or post-surgery patients. It is not used to treat GERD. Loperamide (Option C): is an antidiarrheal medication used to manage diarrhea, but it has no role in treating GERD. Diphenoxylate (Option D): is another antidiarrheal drug and does not have any direct application in the treatment of GERD.

267.q: A patient who is taking verapamil for hypertension and angina has become constipated. Which of the following drugs is an osmotic laxative that could be used to treat the patient's constipation?
267.e: A laxative that mildly stimulates the gut would be most suitable in a patient taking a smooth muscle relaxant drug such as verapamil. By holding water in the intestine, magnesium hydroxide provides additional bulk and stimulates increased contractions . A helpful mnemonic is magnesium "magnifies" stool, aluminum halts the stool. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1091

267.q: A 38-year-old woman comes with motion sickness. She is planning a vacation cruise and has previously experienced severe nausea and vomiting while sailing. After the appropriate drug therapy is recommended, this patient should be counselled regarding which of the following side effects?
267.e: Perception of motion and orientation is determined by input from the vestibular, visual, and somatosensory systems. These 3 systems are usually congruent, but conflicting input can lead to motion sickness, characterized by nausea, dizziness, and autonomic symptoms (eg, diaphoresis). Integration of these sensory pathways occurs in the vestibular nuclei via muscarinic M1 and histaminic H1 neurotransmission. As such, antimuscarinic agents (eg, scopolamine) and first-generation antihistamines (eg, meclizine, dimenhydrinate) are most effective for management of motion sickness. Anticholinergic side effects are common with these medications and may include blurry vision, dry mouth, urinary retention, and constipation. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1108

267.q: Which drug stimulates chloride secretion into the gut lumen and is used for irritable bowel syndrome?
267.e: Linaclotide is approved for the treatment of chronic constipation and IBS with predominant constipation. Linaclotide activates guanylyl cyclase-C on the luminal intestinal epithelial surface, which leads to activation of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) leading to increased chloride-rich secretion and acceleration of intestinal transit. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1103

267.q: A patient presented to hospital with three bouts of vomiting and treated with an antiemetic drug. Vomiting subsided but after some time, he developed abnormal movements. Which of the following drugs is used for treatment of these motor symptoms?
267.e: Central anticholinergics These are drugs having a higher central: peripheral anticholinergic action ratio than atropine, but the pharmacological profile is similar. The central anticholinergics act by reducing the unbalanced cholinergic activity in the striatum of parkinsonian patients. These drugs produce 10-25% improvement in parkinsonian symptoms lasting 4-8 hours after a single dose. Generally, tremor is benefited more than rigidity; hypokinesia is improved the least. Sialorrhoea is controlled by their peripheral action. Anticholinergics are the only drugs effective in drug (phenothiazines, other D2 antagonists) induced parkinsonism. The side effect profile is similar to atropine. Impairment of memory and cognition, organic confusional states and blurred vision are more common in the elderly. Urinary retention is possible in elderly males.

267.q: A 32-year-old woman has irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea that is not responsive to conventional therapies. Despite the small risk of severe constipation and ischemic colitis, the patient decides to begin therapy with alosetron. Alosetron has which of the following receptor actions?
267.e: Serotonin plays a major regulatory role in the enteric nervous system, and the potent 5-HT3 receptor antagonist alosetron has shown efficacy in treating women with IBS that is accompanied by diarrhoea.
