287.e: Pralidoxime(2-PAM), a nucleophilic oxime, most effective when treatment is started early and if used within 48 hours and helps in regenerating AChE associated with skeletal muscle neuromuscular junctions(overcome the nicotinic effects of OPCs). Dose: 1-2 g IV(20-40 mg/kg) over 5-20 min dissolved in 0.9% normal saline solution, may be repeated at 1-2 hours if muscle weakness is not relieved and again after 8-10 hours. Alternatively, continuous infusion(200-400 mg/h) of 2-PAM is more effective because of shorter duration of action of a single dose. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition, Page No. 655.

287.q: All are true of OPC poisoning, except:
287.e: Atropinization: Atropine blocks the muscarinic manifestations and has no effect on nicotinic receptors(on muscle weakness or paralysis) and does not affect the rate of regeneration of inhibited AChE. Dose: 2-4 mg IV(0.05-0.2 mg/kg in children) repeated after every 5-15 minutes till atropinization, the dose should be adjusted to maintain this effect for at least 24 hours(maintenance dose: 0.02-0.05 mg/kg). Option A: OP compounds are anti-cholinesterase agents(ChE inhibitors) Option B: The muscarinic manifestations may lead to bradycardia or tachycardia; but predominantly bradycardia. Option D: Nicotinic manifestations on striated muscle leads to initial stimulus results in contraction. Later there is paralysis due to persistent depolarisation. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition, Page No. 655.

287.q: All are true of organophosphorus compounds poisoning, except:
287.e: Explanation: Atropinization: Atropine blocks the muscarinic manifestations and has no effect on nicotinic receptors (on muscle weakness or paralysis) and does not affect the rate of regeneration of inhibited AChE. Dose: 2-4 mg IV (0.05-0.2 mg/kg in children) repeated after every 5-15 minutes till atropinization, the dose should be adjusted to maintain this effect for at least 24 hours (maintenance dose: 0.02-0.05 mg/kg). Anti-cholinesterase agents (Option A): Organophosphorus compounds (OPC) are irreversible acetylcholinesterase (IACh) inhibitors, causing ACh buildup. Bradycardia (Option B): Seen due to excess acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors. Paralysis (Option D): A late nicotinic effect due to persistent depolarization at neuromuscular junctions.

288.q: A woman found comatose in her house is life-flighted to the nearest regional medical center. Blood gases reveal a normal PaO2 but a lower than normal arterial O2 saturation. Which of the following conditions is most consistent with the findings?
288.e: Hemoglobin has 210 x greater affinity for carbon monoxide than for oxygen. Thus, in carbon monoxide poisoning, the amount of dissolved oxygen, as reflected by the PaO2 may be normal, but the saturation of hemoglobin with oxygen will be lower than expected for a given PaO2. V/Q mismatch with low V/Q units, hypoventilation, and right-to-left shunting are all causes of hypoxemia (decreased PaO2). In anemia, hemoglobin concentration is reduced, but the saturation of hemoglobin O2 is normal. Reference: Ganong, pp 683-691. Levitzky, pp 180-183.

288.q: What is the cause of death in smoke inhalation?
288.e: Victims of smoke inhalation are affected by carbon monoxide poisoning . In carbon monoxide poisoning, the cause of death is anaemic hypoxia Carbon monoxide has a higher affinity to haemoglobin compared to oxygen and hence the amount of haemoglobin available for oxygen transport is markedly reduced. It displaces oxygen from its combination with haemoglobin and forms a relatively stable compound known as carboxyhemoglobin . It thus reduces the oxygen content of the blood, and hence, that of the tissues. It acts as a chemical asphyxiant and produces death due to anaemic anoxia. References: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice 5th edition Page no: 113; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 101

288.q: Lee Jones test is used to detect:
288.e: Lee Jones test is used to detect cyanide. Lee Jones test: To 5 ml of stomach contents add few crystals of ferrous sulphate and 5 drops of 2% sodium hydroxide. Boil and cool and add 10 drops of 10% hydrochloric acid. Greenish-blue colour indicates cyanide, and purplish colour salicylates. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 480

288.q: First aid should be given in acid contact ?
288.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Wash with mild alkali agent [Ref Reddy 30Th le p. 485] The most critical aspect of acid burn care is the constant and prolonged washing of the area with water at a room temperature to get the acid out immediately. To try and minimize the damage, the effects of acid should be neutralized by applying a mild alkali solution to the affected area (solution of sodium bicarbonate and water.

288.q: Oochronosis is seen in which poisoning ?
288.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Carbolic acid [Ref Reddy 30th/e p. 489] Chronic carbolic acid poisoning/phenol marasmus The poisoning is characterised by anorexia, weight loss, headache, vertigo, dark urine and pigmentation of skin & sclera. Carbolic acid/ Phenol is converted into hydroquinone & pyrocatechol in the body before being excreted in the urine. Hydroquinone er pyrocatechol may cause pigmentation in the cornea and various cartilages- Oochronosis. Oochronosis is commonly associated with alkaptonuria, in which homegentisic acid gets deposited in cartilages, ligaments & fibrous tissues.

CO combines reversibly with haemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) producing anaemic hypoxia (Blood O 2 -carrying capacity is reduced). It has a high affinity for Hb (about 250 times more than O2). It inhibits electron transport by blocking cytochrome A3 oxidase and cytochrome P450 and hence intracellular respiration. Anaemic hypoxia occurs when the oxygen carrying ability of the blood decreases, and thus, this defect is specifically associated with the blood. This implies that fewer hemoglobin molecules (or oxygen-binding sites) are available for binding oxygen. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th Edition, Page No. 645

289.q: A chronic alcoholic assaulted his neighbour. He had quit drinking 4 days back but now has delirium tremens. He is:
o: Family is responsible for his act
289.e: Medico-legal Aspects of delirium tremens: It is a medical emergency and should be treated on an inpatient basis. When a person is in delirium tremens commits any illegal act, he is not held responsible by the reason that he is considered to be mentally unsound during this state (Sec. 22 BNS). 22 BNS: Act of a person of unsound mind. - Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition. Page No. 606

289.q: An alcoholic patient is brought for medical examination for alleged assault of his neighbour. On examination, abnormal behaviour with irrelevant talk is noted. He has history of abstaining from alcohol for past 4 days and is diagnosed to be a case of delirium tremens. What is true according to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha?
o: He is criminally responsible for his act
He is partially responsible for his act
Have diminished responsible for his act
Not responsible for his act under section 22 BNS
289.e: Sec. 22 BNS: Act of a person of unsound mind.-Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law. Delirium tremens is a psychiatric condition arising as a result of abstinence from alcohol. In case of delirium tremens, he doesn't know that what is he doing. So, he is not criminally responsible for his act under section 22 BNS. Reference: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha, 2023

289.q: An alcoholic patient is brought for medical examination for alleged assault of his neighbour. On examination, abnormal behaviour with irrelevant talk is noted. He has history of abstaining from alcohol for past 4 days and is diagnosed to be a case of delirium tremens. What is true according to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
o: He is criminally responsible for his act
He is partially responsible for his act
Have diminished responsible for his act
Not responsible for his act under section 22 BNS
289.e: Explanation: Delirium tremens is a psychiatric condition arising as a result of abstinence from alcohol. In case of delirium tremens, he doesn't know what he is doing. So, he is not criminally responsible for his act under section 22 BNS. Sec. 22 BNS: Act of a person of unsound mind. Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.

289.q: According to Indian 'Motor Vehicle Act 1988', punishable quantity of alcohol in blood while driving a vehicle:
289.e: According to Motor Vehicle Act 1988, the maximum permissible BAC while driving is 30mg/dl. In India, driving under the influence of alcohol or drunk driving is punishable if the BAC exceeds 30mg/dl. In India, according to Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019, for the first offence, punishment is imprisonment up to 6 months with/without fine up to Rs. 10,000. For the subsequent offence, the punishment is up to 2 years of imprisonment with or without fine up to Rs. 15,000. Under this Act, there can be arrest without warrant, a breath test and a laboratory test can also be carried out. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition. Page No. 604

289.q: Widmark's formula is used for measurement of blood level of
289.e: Widmark’s formula is used to estimate the blood alcohol level in the body. a = cpr where, a - the total amount of alcohol (in grams) absorbed in the body c - the concentration of alcohol in blood (in g/kg) p - the weight of the person (in kg) r- constant (0.68 in men and 0.5 in women) Alcohol level from urine is estimated with the formula: a = 3/4 qpr where, q - concentration of alcohol in urine (in g/l) and 'a' 'p' and 'r' are the same as above. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition. Page No. 604

289.q: A 43-year-old male did not have alcohol for 2 days. He presented with seizures; treatment given:
289.e: Treatment (For both withdrawal symptoms and delirium tremens): Diazepam (40-80 mg/day in divided doses) is used. Oral multi-B vitamins, including thiamine 50-100 mg is given daily for a week or more. Chlordiazepoxide (80-200 mg/day in divided doses) or haloperidol 20 mg or more/day may be used. Intravenous fluids are avoided, unless there is evidence of bleeding, vomiting or diarrhoea. In some withdrawal symptom cases, only restoration of alcoholic drinks helps. In cases of urgent sedation as in delirium tremens- phenobarbitone or chlorpromazine injection can be given, and then detoxification and maintenance of nutrition is carried on with 5% dextrose solution IV and thiamine. Symptomatic treatment. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition. Page No. 606

289.q: Not true about methyl alcohol poisoning:
o: Effects are due to formic acid
289.e: Both ethanol and methanol are metabolized by hepatic alcohol dehydrogenas e 4-methylpyrazole (fomepizole) is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase. It blocks the formation of formaldehyde and formic acid and can be used instead of ethanol. Dose: Loading dose of 15 mg/kg over 30 minutes, followed by 10 mg/kg every 12 hours for 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition. Page No. 609

289.q: Most common drug abuse in India ?
289.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Heroin Amongst the given options, heroin is the most commonly abused substance : Alcohol → 43.9 % Opioids (including heroin) → 26% Cannabis → 11.6 %

290.q: The usual fatal dose of white phosphorous:
290.e: The usual fatal dose of white phosphorous is 60-120 mg. Fulminating poisoning (death within 12 hours) may be seen when the patient takes a large dose. Early death is due to cardiac dysrhythmias, secondary to electrolyte abnormalities, such as hypocalcaemia and hyperkalaemia. Death after the first 24 h is due to hepatic failure. Fatal dose: 60-120 mg (1 mg/kg) of white phosphorus. Fatal period: Within 24 hours but may be delayed by 5-7 days. Diagnosis: Oral and skin burns, luminescent 'smoking' vomitus and stools with a garlic odour, and GIT and biliary damage characterize white phosphorus poisoning. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 565

290.q: M/C Heavy Metal poisoning in The World?
290.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e.,Lead [Ref Park 22"'Ile p. 752] More industrial workers are exposed to lead than any other toxic metal.

290.q: Cardiac arrythmias, myalgia and flaccid quadriplegia are characteristic of poisoning by:
290.e: Cardiac arrythmias, myalgia and flaccid quadriplegia are characteristic of poisoning by Barium carbonate. Signs and symptoms of Barium carbonate poisoning: The most characteristic features are areflexia and paralysis. Barium induces hypokalaemia. (Ba 2+ ion is a muscle poison). GIT: Nausea, vomiting, salivation, abdominal pain and diarrhea. Muscular system: Tingling sensation, tremors, cramps, stiffness of the muscles, paralysis of the tongue and larynx, myoclonus, myalgia, flaccid quadriplegia. CVS: Hypertension, arrhythmia, ectopic beats, ventricular fibrillation, irregular pulse, shock, cardiac arrest. RS: Pulmonary edema, respiratory failure. CNS: Mydriasis, vertigo, headache, confusion, convulsions. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 560

290.q: Which of the following metals can be detected even in conflagrated human remains?
290.e: Arsenic can be detected even in conflagration of human bones. Hence, it is possible to detect poisoning by arsenic even in charred bones and ashes. Arsenic is volatile but much of the arsenic in bones is converted into arsenates, which are non-volatile. In suspected cases of poisoning by arsenic, all the available ashes and burnt bones should be preserved for chemical analysis. Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2 nd Edition, P C Dixit, Page No. 184.

290.q: Which metal can be detected in the charred bones and ashes of conflagrated human remains?
290.e: Explanation: Arsenic can be detected even in conflagration of human bones, so it is possible to detect arsenic poisoning, even in charred bones and ashes. Arsenic is volatile but much of the arsenic in bones is converted into arsenates, which are non-volatile. In India, cremation conditions often do not favour complete combustion. Even if arsenic is present as arsenic trioxide or another volatile form, not all arsenic is lost. Some volatilized arsenic may condense on cooler parts of the funeral pyre, preventing its complete loss. Arsenic is especially detectable in the spongy bones, such as the skull & vertebrae. Arsenic can persist here long after its disappearance from soft organs like the liver, spleen, kidneys, or brain. Thallium, cadmium and mercury are highly volatile and unlikely to be found in conflagrated remains.

290.q: Brutonian lines on gums is seen in poisoning with ?
290.e: :B Ans. is 'a > b' i.e., Lead > Mercury [Ref Reddy 306/e p.497-498] Burtonian line is blue line, which is seen on upper gums in lead poisoning. Similar blue line (but not called burtonian line in these cases) is also seen in poisoning with Mercury (Hg), Copper (Cu), Silver (Ag), bismuth (Bi), and Iron (Fe).

290.q: A person was found dead with bluish green frothy discharge at the angle of mouth and nostrils. Probable cause can be:
290.e: Postmortem findings in copper poisoning Skin may be yellow due to jaundice. Greenish-blue froth from the mouth and nostrils Mucous membrane of the mouth and tongue may have bluish or greenish-blue tinge. Internally, some discoloration is present in the mucous membrane of the esophagus and stomach. Stomach: Gastric mucosa is congested with desquamation and haemorrhages at places. Small intestine: Mucosa (upper part) may show necrosis. Liver: Soft and fatty. It shows centrilobular necrosis and biliary stasis. Kidneys: It may show acute proximal tubular necrosis. Haemoglobin casts may be seen in the tubules. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 553, 554

290.q: Minamata Bay disease refers to chronic toxicity with:
290.e: Explanation: Minamata Bay disease was due to chronic organic mercury intoxication (Methyl mercury). Minamata disease: It is due to chronic organic mercury intoxication caused by eating contaminated fish and shellfish. In Minamata Bay (Japan), a factory discharged inorganic mercury into the water. The mercury was methylated by bacteria and subsequently ingested by fish. Local villagers ate the fish and began to exhibit signs of chronic mercury poisoning. Symptoms include disturbances in hand coordination, gait and speech, chewing and swallowing difficulties, visual blurring, tremors, rigidity, seizures and clouding of consciousness. Key Takeaway: Minamata disease is caused by chronic methylmercury poisoning from consumption of contaminated seafood.

291.q: Several children were hospitalized with symptoms thought to be due to ingestion of food containing botulinum toxin. Which one of the following signs or symptoms is consistent with the diagnosis of botulinum poisoning?
291.e: Botulinum toxin impairs all types of cholinergic transmission, including transmission at ganglionic synapses and somatic motor nerve endings. Botulinum toxin prevents discharge of vesicular transmitter content from cholinergic nerve endings. All of the signs listed except cycloplegia indicate cholinomimetic action. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 114

291.q: A girl, otherwise healthy, sleeping on the floor suddenly develops nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, quadriplegia at night. Diagnosis is:
291.e: Krait: Signs and symptoms are similar to cobra poisoning, but less rapid. The signs and symptoms are Abdominal pain Ptosis Dysarthria Dysphagia Chest pain Quadriparesis Respiratory paralysis Death Common krait hunt nocturnally and are quick to bite people sleeping on the floor, often without waking their victims, since the venom is painless. Victims wake up early morning, paralyzed - mistaken for STROKE Option A: GBS will have a preceding history of diarrhoea 6 to 8 weeks before and will have ascending paralysis. Option B: Poliomyelitis will have gradual onset flaccid paralysis. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition, Page No. 581

291.q: In a snake envenomation, antivenom is started by giving a dose of:
291.e: The recommended initial dose of PASV is 8-10 vials administered slowly via IV route over a period of 1 hour Repeat doses for vasculotoxic species is based on the 6 hours rule (depending on the coagulation profile); the maximum recommended dose is 30 vials. Repeat doses for neurotoxicity is based on the 1-2 hours rule (depending on whether patients have not improved, or worsened); maximum dose is 20 vials. Antivenin treatment should be given, as soon as it is indicated. Ideally PASV should be administered within 4 hours, but effective even if it is given within 24 hours. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5 th edition, Page No. 584

Strychnine competitively blocks ventral horn motor neurone postganglionic receptor sites in the spinal cord and brainstem and prevents the effects of glycine (the presumed inhibitory transmitter). Widespread inhibition in the spinal cord results in 'release' excitation. The action is particularly noted in the anterior horn cells. It stimulates the cerebral cortex. GABA, the neurotransmitter for presynaptic inhibitory neurons is not affected. Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 466

291.q: Socrates was killed by which poisoning:
291.e: Hemlock (Conium Maculatum) was administered to Socrates, the Greek Philosopher in 399 BC as a form of execution. Conium is a peripheral nerve poison which give rise to ascending paralysis. Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 696

292.q: A person of interest in a homicide case is on the run from the police. He wishes to remove the tattoo on his left arm which is very prominent. Which of the following methods may be used for the same? 1. Surgical excision 2. Scarification with sandpaper 3. Caustic soda 4. Rubbing with isopropyl alcohol 5. Electrolysis
292.e: Methods for deliberate tattoo removal include Surgical methods: Complete excision and skin grafting Production of burn by means of red hot iron Scarification with sandpaper Carbon dioxide snow Electrolysis Caustic substances remove pigment by producing inflammatory reaction and a superficial scar, e.g., mixture of papain in glycerine, zinc chloride and tannic acid LASER beam: By exposure to laser beams, the particles of the dye get vapourised and expelled from the tissues in gaseous form Confluent smallpox and sometimes chronic eczema in children can obliterate tattoo marks Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 68

293.q: Which structure of the ear develops from all three germ layers?
293.e: The tympanic membrane develops from all three germinal layers. The outer epithelial layer is formed by the ectoderm The inner mucosal layer of the endoderm The middle fibrous layer is formed by the mesoderm. Explanation of other options: External auditory canal (Option B): The External auditory canal develops from the ectodermal layer. Stapes (Option C): The Stapes develop from the endodermal layer. Vestibular labyrinth (Option D): Forms from the otic placode (ectoderm) and surrounding mesoderm, but does not involve endoderm. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number: 15

Scheibe dysplasia Most common inner ear anomaly. Dysplasia of cochlea and saccule; hence also called cochleosaccular dysplasia.(Pars Inferior) Bony labyrinth is normal. Superior part of membranous labyrinth(utricle and semicircular ducts) is normal.(Pars Superior) Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 135.

o: Always occur as an isolated anomaly
Cochlear implants are used in treatment
May be associated with Pendred syndrome & DiGeorge syndrome
293.e: Mondini dysplasia may be seen in Pendred, Waardenburg, branchio-oto-renal, Treacher-Collins and Wildervanck syndromes along with other anamolies. Mondini dysplasia: Inner ear malformation Only basal coil is present or cochlea is 1.5 turns. There is incomplete partition between the scalae due to absence of osseous spiral lamina. Condition is unilateral or bilateral Can be treated by a cochlear implant. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 135.

293.q: Saccule of inner ear develop from
293.e: During embryonic development, the saccule, one of the two otolith organs in the inner ear, develops from the pars inferior to the otocyst . The saccule is responsible for detecting linear acceleration and head position. Other options: Sacculus anterior This is a small sac that is located in the utricle of the inner ear. It is not involved in the development of the saccule. Pars superior: This is the superior portion of the otic vesicle. It gives rise to the utricle and the semicircular canals.

293.q: Cochlear implant is contraindicated in all except:
o: Persistent otitis media and mastoiditis without eradication of the disease
293.e: Mild intracochlear ossification is not a contraindication for cochlear implant. Option a - Michel aplasia - Complete absence of bony and membranous labyrinth. No hearing aids or cochlear implantation can be used. Option b - Cochlear implant works by stimulating the auditory nerve. So absence of cochlear nerve is a contraindication for its use. Option d - Persistent otitis media and mastoiditis without eradication of the disease - Bone Anchored Hearing Aids should be considered. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 135, 146.

293.q: A congenitally deaf child on radiological evaluation of cochlea and brain with MRI/CT scan has been found to having normal cochlea with absence of eighth nerve on both sides. What is the best method of hearing rehabilitation in this case?
293.e: Indications of ABI include: Neurofibroma type 2 - Bilateral vestibular schwannoma Congenital aplasia of VIII nerve Cochlear aplasia(Michel Aplasia) The prerequisite for cochlear implant surgery is presence of normal VIII nerve. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 147.

o: Used for mild - to - moderate hearing loss
It is implanted through the oval window
Mondini's Cochlear dysplasia is not a contraindication
293.e: Mondini dysplasia of cochlea refers to the condition when there are one and half turns of cochlea rather than two and half. There is absence of the apical modiolus and interscalar septum, resulting in an incomplete partitioning of the cochlea together with an enlarged vestibular aqueduct(EVA) and dilated vestibule. This is not a contraindication of cochlear implantation. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Rehabilitation of the Hearing Impaired, Page number: 145

294.q: A patient with ear wax underwent syringing. During syringing, the patient developed a syncopal episode. Stimulation of which nerve is responsible?
294.e: Auricular branch of the vagus (CN X), also called Arnold's nerve, supplies the concha and corresponding eminence on the medial surface. Vagus nerve has a parasympathetic action on the muscle fibers of the heart, so its stimulation during syringing of the ear canal can cause syncopal episode in some patients. Other Options: By stimulation of the other three nerves given in other three options don't cause syncope on stimulation.

294.q: Which of the following best describes Fissure of Santorini
o: Natural deficiency in cartilaginous part of external auditory canal
Natural deficiency in bony part of external auditory canal
Natural deficiency in fallopian canal of facial nerve
Vertical bony septum in Internal Auditory Canal
294.e: Fissures of Santorini are natural dehiscence in cartilaginous part of EAC. They allow transmission of infection and malignancy from EAC to Parotid gland Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Anatomy of Ear, Page number:3

295.q: Not a true match about the anatomical aspects of ear
o: Korner's septum is remnant of petrosquamous suture
Subiculum is a bony spicule which separates oval and round windows
Processus Cochleariformis indicates the basal turn of cochlea.
Canal for Tensor tympani lies on the anterior wall of middle ear
295.e: Processus cochleariformis is a hook like process on the medial wall of middle ear which marks the first genu of facial nerve. Tendon of tensor tympani takes a turn here to attach to malleus. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page - 5,6, 9

295.q: Infection of CNS spreads to tympanic cavity(=middle ear) through:
295.e: Hyrtl's fissure connects middle ear to middle cranial fossa. Canal of Huguier is the exit point of chorda tympani nerve from middle ear Vestibular aqueduct is the bony cover of Endolymphatic duct Aqueduct of cochlea connects inner ear to CSF in subarachnoid space of brain(not middle ear) Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Some Memorable Nuggets for Rapid Review, Page number: 547

295.q: Which of the following middle ear structure develops from neural crest cells?
295.e: Explanation: Middle ear ossicles begin forming around 6 weeks of development as cartilaginous structures . Malleus and Incus: Derived from mesoderm of the first pharyngeal arch . Stapes: Suprastructure: From mesoderm of the second pharyngeal arch . Footplate: From the otic capsule , which is derived from neural crest cells .

295.q: Which of the following is NOT a branch of 1st part of maxillary artery?
295.e: Branches of maxillary artery: The maxillary artery consists of three parts; mandibular part, pterygoid part, pterygopalatine part. Branches of mandibular part: Inferior alveolar artery Middle meningeal artery Deep auricular artery Anterior tympanic artery Occasionally an accessory meningeal branch. Branches of pterygoid part: Masseteric artery Deep temporal branches Pterygoid branches Buccal artery Branches of pterygopalatine part: Posterior superior alveolar artery Infraorbital artery Descending palatine artery Greater palatine artery Lesser palatine artery Sphenopalatine artery Lateral posterior nasal arteries Posterior septal branches

295.q: Which of the following is not true about tubercular otitis media? a. Blood-stained ear discharge b. Pale granulations in the middle ear & mastoid c. Facial paralysis d. Multiple perforations in tympanic membrane e. Painful due to underlying bone destruction
295.e: Tubercular otitis media Clinical features: Painless otorrhoea - The ear discharge is foul smelling due to underlying bone destruction. Pale granulations in middle ear and mastoid. It does not have blood stained discharge. Multiple perforations in pars tensa of tympanic membrane. Facial palsy → most common complication. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 88, 89.

295.q: Which of these is not found on the medial wall of middle ear?
295.e: Pyramid lies on the posterior wall. Tendon of Stapedius muscle arises from it. The medial wall of middle ear has – Promontary - a bulge on medial wall due to the basal coil of cochlea Lateral semicircular canal bulge Tympanic plexus (IXth N) - lies on promontory Oval window - into which footplate of stapes is fixed Round window - covered by secondary tympanic membrane Processus cochleariformis - hook like process which marks the first genu of facial nerve Ponticulus, Subiculum and Sinus tympani in between these two bony spicules Horizontal segment of Facial nerve canal Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Anatomy of Ear, Page number: 6

295.q: Surgical procedure which involves reconstruction of cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal?
295.e: Meatoplasty is a surgical procedure that involves the reconstruction or enlargement of the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal. It is performed to improve access, drainage, and ventilation of the ear canal.It is the last step of modified radical mastoidectomy. Other options: A. Canaloplasty: Canaloplasty is a surgical procedure used to treat glaucoma by enlarging and restructuring the eye's drainage canal. B. Myringoplasty: Myringoplasty is a surgical procedure to repair a perforated tympanic membrane (eardrum), not involving the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal. C. Tympanoplasty: Tympanoplasty is a surgical procedure to repair or reconstruct the middle ear, including the tympanic membrane and ossicles, but not specifically the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal.

296.q: Which of the following forms lateral wall of mastoid antrum?
296.e: It is a large, air-containing space in the upper part of the mastoid and communicates with the attic through the aditus. Its roof is formed by tegmen antri, a continuation of the tegmen tympani and separates it from the middle cranial fossa. The lateral wall of antrum is formed by a plate of bone which is on an average 1.5 cm thick in the adult. It is marked externally on the surface of mastoid by suprameatal (MacEwen's) triangle Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose & Head and Neck surgery by P L Dhingra, 9 th edition, Pg.no.7,8

296.q: A surgeon while doing mastoid surgery encounters unusual bleeding in the operative site. He can control the bleeding by doing everything except
o: Polish the area with diamond burr
Apply cutting burr to the site of bleeding
Use electrocautery to control the bleeding
Use bone wax to control the bleeding
296.e: Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 566. Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1249.

296.q: Mohan, 22 years old, male gives a history of right sided ear discharge, foul smelling and occasionally blood stained for the last 6 years.For last 3 days patient has developed fever with chills, headache and pitting oedema over mastoid region. The most probable diagnosis is
o: Atticoantral CSOM with sigmoid sinus thrombosis
296.e: Foul smelling and occasionally blood stain discharge, suggest unsafe CSOM also called as Atticoantral CSOM Pitting edema over mastoid is Greisinger sign Mastoiditis do not presents with pitting edema over mastoid or headache Meningitis present with neck, rigidity, vomiting Brain abscess, presence with fever with chills.

297.q: What is capula in the inner ear?
o: Sensory end organ of utricle and saccule
297.e: The sensory end organ of utricle and saccule are called as macula . They are responsible for linear Balance. The sensory end organ of semicircular canals are called cristae . They are responsible for angular Balance. Each semicircular canal have one narrow end and one dilated end. The dilated end is called ampulla. Cristae are present inside ampulla Cristae contains Gelatinous layer which contains cupula.

297.q: Mark the correct statement(s) regarding Inner and Outer hair cells: Inner hair cells are in a single row and transmit auditory impulses.II. Outer hair cells are in 3-4 rows and modulate the function of inner hair cells.III. Outer hair cells are more responsible for movement of the tectorial membrane. IV. Outer and inner hair cells are present in the ratio of 3:1.
o: I, II and IV are correct
I, II and III are correct
297.e: Explanation: Inner hair cells (IHCs): IHCs are single row cells responsible for transmitting auditory impulses to the brain via afferent fibers . Outer hair cells (OHCs): OHCs are arranged in 3-4 rows and modulate the function of inner hair cells via efferent pathways, amplifying cochlear sensitivity. Outer hair cells and tectorial membrane movement: OHCs do not primarily move the tectorial membrane . Their role is mainly cochlear amplification ; tectorial membrane motion is a passive mechanical response. (Statement 3 is incorrect) Ratio of Outer: Inner hair cells: OHCs (~12,000) outnumber IHCs (~3,500), approximately a 3:1 ratio.

297.q: As per the travelling wave theory of hearing given by Von Bekesy, sound energy creates a wave-like movement in which structure of the inner ear?
297.e: Travelling wave theory of hearing has been given by Von Bekesy which states that - A sound wave depending on its frequency, reaches maximum amplitude on a particular place in the basilar membrane and stimulates that segment. Therefore, higher frequencies are sensed in the basal turn and low frequencies are sensed in the apex of cochlea. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number- 20.

297.q: Which of the following is true regarding vestibular system: a. Semi-circular canal responds to linear acceleration b. Utricle responds to Horizontal linear acceleration c. Otolith organs responds to angular acceleration d. Saccule responds to rotational acceleration e. Saccule responds to vertical linear acceleration
297.e: Utricle and saccule are also called VESTIBULE or OTOLITHIC ORGANS. Utricle and Saccule – Linear balance (Receptor: Macula) Utricle – Horizontal balance Saccule – Vertical balance Semicircular canals – Angular balance(Receptor:Crista) Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no - 20

298.q: All are true about malignant otitis externa except
o: Technetium scan is more useful in the prognostic evaluation of this entity
ESR can be used to monitor the progression of disease
Facial nerve is the most commonly involved nerve
298.e: Malignant otitis externa = Skull base osteomyelitis is locally destructive infection of bony EAC which is part of skull base. It is mostly seen in old diabetics and caused by Pseudomonas. Radionucleide gallium(good for prognostic evaluation) and technetium scan(good for diagnosis) are helpful in the management. Also ESR is a good tool to monitor disease activity. \ Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Some Memorable Nuggets for Rapid Review, Page number: 548

298.q: A 62 year old diabetic male with severe pain in ear and granulation with discharge in the external ear. On examination, the patient has facial nerve palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
298.e: Malignant Otitis Externa is an inflammatory condition caused by pseudomonas infection usually in the elderly diabetics, or in those on immunosuppressive drugs. Its early manifestations resemble diffuse otitis externa but there is excruciating pain and appearance of granulations in the ear canal.

298.q: Malignant otitis externa is characterised by all of the follwing except
298.e: Necrotizing otitis externa, also called malignant otitis externa, is caused by pseudomonas infection in an elderly patient with diabetes. Symptoms include severe otalgia, facial nerve palsy can occur. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.548

298.q: A 50 year old female patient has presented with the complaint of long standing left ear discharge, foul smelling, blood stained. She has left sided facial palsy. She also gives history of ear ache which is worse at night. On otoscopy, friable granulations are seen in the middle ear. What is the most probable diagnosis?
298.e: This patient is middle aged with long standing blood tinged ear discharge and ear ache worse at night. She also has granulations in the middle ear. All these point to a diagnosis of Malignancy of the middle ear. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 130, 131.

298.q: While syringing for the ear wax, the cold water should not be used. What is the appropriate reason for this?
o: It may lead to perforation of tympanic membrane
It may lead to infection of external auditory canal.
It may make the wax hard and difficult to remove.
298.e: EAC OCCLUSION BY WAX COLLECTION : Some people produce more wax which leads to EAC occlusion by wax collection. This will lead to conductive hearing loss (30 dB CHL approx.) Treatment is PARADICHLOROBENZENE (wax dissolving drops), use these drops for a few days and the suction clearance or syringing is done. SYRINGING-direction of water is Posterosuperior. Use water at body temperature. In syringing avoid cold water because it can lead to vertigo because of inner ear stimulation. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 49, 63.

298.q: Keratosis obturans is caused due to
o: Abnormal collection of cerumen in the outer part of external auditory canal
Abnormal collection of cerumen in the deeper part of external auditory canal
Abnormal epithelial migration of skin of tympanic membrane
Chronic foul smelling ear discharge present in external auditory canal
298.e: Keratosis Obturans : EAC skin sheds off to produce keratin inside EAC. EAC skin migrates outwards, bringing keratin and wax out of EAC. Rarely this skin migration pattern is absent, that will lead to collection of keratin+ wax as an expansile mass in ear, this disease is called KERATOSIS OBTURANS. Treatment is surgery called CANALPLASTY. \ Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head \and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Diseases of External Ear, Page number: 64

298.q: A 5 year old patient presents with the history of hearing loss. On examination he is found to have a pearly white mass behind the intact tympanic membrane. What is the most possible diagnosis?
298.e: Cholesteatoma : It is the ectopic presence of skin in the middle ear cleft. It is pearly white in colour. It is of 4 types : Primary Acquired Cholesteatoma (mc) Secondary Acquired Cholesteatoma Tertiary Acquired Cholesteatoma Congenital Cholesteatoma Congenital Cholesteatoma: We use LEVENSON’S CRITERIA to diagnose congenital cholesteatoma . It presents as PEARLY WHITE MASS behind INTACT TYMPANIC MEMBRANE It is UNSAFE due to bone erosion . Bone Erosion leads to Complications, so it is called UNSAFE CSOM. Treatment : Surgery → MRM ( Modified Radical Mastoidectomy) also called as Tympanomastoid Exploration. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Cholesteatoma and Chronic Otitis Media, Page number: 80

298.q: Best treatment for traumatic hematoma of the pinna is which of the following measures?
298.e: PINNA HAEMATOMA: It is due to trauma. It is a sub-perichondrial hemorrhage. Treatment is aspiration or drainage + pressure bandage. Otherwise it will lead to Necosis of cartilage which will lead to PINNA DEFORMITY known as BOXER EAR/CAULIFLOWER EAR. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Diseases of External Ear, Page number: 58

299.q: Most common cause of conductive deafness in children less than 12 yrs:
299.e: In above all the condition we see Hearing loss except in acute otitis media .In Acute otitis media patient present with Ear ache . The most common cause of hearing loss in children less than 12 years is Serous otitis media. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Disorders of Middle Ear, Page number: 75

299.q: The most common site of cholesteatoma in the middle ear cleft is
299.e: Prussak's space is the most common site of cholesteatoma formation in middle ear. It lies between the pars flaccida and the neck of malleus. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 80, 549. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1191.

299.q: CT scan of a patient suffering from atticoantral CSOM shows an abscess at petrous apex. Which of the following is not a likely symptom in this case?
299.e: Spread of infection from the middle ear to petrous bone is called Petrositis or Gradinego syndrome. This is a triad of Ear discharge Deep seated ear or Retro-orbital pain(CN V involvement) Diplopia(CN VI involvement - Lateral rectus palsy) It is a complication of CSOM. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 95.

299.q: Which of the following is not the mechanism of bone erosion caused by cholesteatoma in atticoantral CSOM?
o: Collagenase and acid phosphatase release by osteoclasts
Proteolytic enzymes liberated by mononuclear cells
299.e: Mechanism of bone erosion in Cholesteatoma: Inflammatory Osteitis Enzymatic theory-Bone destryoing Enzyme Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Cholesteatoma and Chronic Otitis Media, Page number: 80, 81

299.q: What is the most common site of residual cholesteatoma after mastoid exploration in a case of unsafe CSOM?
299.e: Sinus tympani Sinus tympani is a deep recess on medial wall of middle ear. It is a hidden area and most common site of residual cholesteatoma after mastoid surgery. Boundaries of facial Recess Superior - Ponticulus Inferior - Subiculum Lateral - Limited by vertical segment of facial nerve. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 87.

299.q: Teritary acquired cholesteatoma occurs in which of the following entities
299.e: After a blast injury, a cholesteatoma may arise behind a spontaneously healed tympanic membrane. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra

299.q: The marginal perforation of tympanic membrane if allowed to progress, will lead to:
299.e: A posterosuperior marginal perforation if allowed to progress will lead to secondary acquired cholesteatoma(In these cases, there is already a pre-existing perforation in pars tensa). Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 80.

299.q: Tubercular otitis media is characterized by all except
299.e: Tubercular otitis media is characterized by multiple perforations in the tympanic membrane, pale granulations , and foul-smelling ear discharge . Painful otorrhea is not a typical feature of tubercular otitis media. In laryngeal Tb there will be painful phonation. Other options and why they are wrong: B. Multiple perforations: Multiple perforations in the tympanic membrane are a characteristic feature of tubercular otitis media due to the destructive nature of the disease. C. Pale granulations: Tubercular otitis media is associated with pale or edematous granulations due to the chronic inflammatory process. D. Foul-smelling ear discharge: Foul-smelling or purulent ear discharge is commonly observed in tubercular otitis media due to the chronic infection.

300.q: A patient of right unsafe CSOM has presented with double vision and pain behind the right eye. What is the name of this entity?
300.e: PETROSITIS- GRADINEGO SYNDROME It is an infection of Petrous apex air cells. It's a complication of ASOM or CSOM. Petrous apex has relation with 5th and 6th cranial nerves. It has 3 features- PNEMONIC GERD. G-Gradinego syndrome E-Ear discharge R-Retro Orbital pain due to 5 th nerve D-Diplopia-due to 6 th nerve. CT scan of temporal bone will show abscess at Petrous apex. Treatment :– Surgical exploration. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Complications of Suppurative Otitis Media, Page number: 95

300.q: A patient of right unsafe CSOM has presented with history of diplopia and pain behind the right eye. What is the further ideal investigation in this clinical scenario?
300.e: Retro orbital pain and diplopia are suggestive of petrositis. Along with otorrhoea, it forms the triad of Gradinego syndrome. Diagnosis of petrous apicitis requires HRCT tempral bone which shows abscess at Petrous apex. Treatment - Cortical, modified radical or radical mastoidectomy + IV antibiotics Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 95.

300.q: Mohan, 22 year old, male gives history of right sided ear discharge, foul smelling and occasionally blood stained for last 6 years. He also complains of hearing loss for last 2 years. For last 3 days patient has developed fever with chills, headache and oedema over mastoid region. The most probable diagnosis is
o: Atticoantral CSOM with Lateral sinus thrombosis
300.e: Scanty, foul smelling ear discharge is seen in atticoantral CSOM. The patient recently developed fever with chills, headache and oedema over the mastoid(Griesinger sign). All these point to a diagnosis of Sigmoid sinus thrombosis(Lateral sinus thrombosis). TREATMENT Modified radical mastoidectomy with opening the sinus wall and removal of thrombus + i/v antibiotics. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 101.

300.q: A 6 yrs male child presented to ENT emergency with left ear profuse ear discharge for last 3 days with lateral and forward displacement of pinna. X ray mastoid ( Schuller's view) revealed cloding of air cells and destruction of cotical septations. What is the most probable Diagnosis?
300.e: Acute coalescent mastoiditis is defined by the acute form of destruction of the thin bony septae between mastoid air cells. It may be followed by the formation of abscess cavities and the dissipation of pus into adjacent areas. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra

300.q: All are true about mandible fracture except: a. Condylar neck is most common site b. Malocclusion of teeth may occur c. Anterior superior alveolar nerve is most commonly injured d. Panorex radiographs are useful for diagnosis e. Malnunion & non-union are complications
300.e: Anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the upper jaw and is not injured in mandibular fracture. In fracture of mandible, C ondyle is the most commonly fractured followed by A ngle, B ody and S ymphysis ( CABS ). Malocclusion of teeth and deviation of jaw to the opposite site occur in displaced fractures of condyle. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no - 216 Gray's Anatomy- The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice - 41 st edition - Page - 526

300.q: A young lady presents to OPD with a history of sudden onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness following an episode of acute otitis media two weeks back. On examination, Rinne's test and fistula test were found positive. However, she initially refused treatment and again presented with complaints of worsened hearing loss in the affected ear. Further examination, revealed a negative fistula test. What would be the most likely finding on the Rinne test in this scenario?
300.e: Explanation: The patient with otitis media , has developed labyrinthine fistula as a complication, which caused sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) , tinnitus, and vertigo. This will result in a: Positive Rinne's test Positive fistula test: Due to perilymph leak or fistula Since treatment was refused, the condition progressed, resulting in complete labyrinthine destruction or the dead ear. This caused a negative fistula sign. However, the ear now has profound unilateral SNHL, where Rinne's test remains positive (a true positive result). Rinne's Test: The Rinne test compares bone conduction (BC) to air conduction (AC) of sound. In conductive hearing loss , BC > AC (i.e., the sound is heard better through bone conduction). In sensorineural hearing loss , AC > BC (i.e., the sound is heard better through air conduction).

300.q: A 38-year-old male presents with suspected diagnosis of suppurative labyrinthitis. A positive Rinne test and a positive fistula sign were recorded on initial examination. The patient refused treatment and returned to the emergency department after 2 weeks complaining of deafness on the same ear. On examination, now the fistula sign was found to be negative. What would be the expected finding on repeating the Rinne test?
300.e: The patient was earlier having labyrinthine fistula. Because of no treatment, he developed dead labyrinth. A negative fistula sign in this case indicates a dead labyrinth which implies severe sensorineural hearing loss. In such cases a false negative Rinne's test is most likely. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 26, 48.

300.q: A 20yrs old Male present with unilateral Ear discharge, pallor, fever and positive Crowe Beck Test. The clinical diagnosis is:
300.e: Crowe Beck sign is seen in Sigmoid sinus thrombosis(Lateral sinus thrombosis). It is the engorgement of retinal veins due to pressure on the jugular vein of healthy side seen on fundoscopy. This is absent on the affected side. This is due to blockage of venous drainage of brain. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 100, 101.

301.q: The best description of Gelle's test
o: With increase in pressure in External auditory canal, there is decrease in the intensity of bone conducted sound in normal individuals
With increase in pressure in External auditory canal, there is increase in the intensity of bone conducted sound in normal individuals
With increase in pressure in External auditory canal, there is decrease in the intensity of bone conducted sound in Otosclerosis patients
With increase in pressure in External auditory canal, there is increase in the intensity of bone conducted sound in Otosclerosis patients
301.e: Gelle's test Compares intensity of bone-conducted tuning fork sound, without and with, raising pressure on the tympanic membrane with Siegel's speculum. Normally, Gelle's test is positive because intensity of hearing decreases when air pressure is raised in external auditory canal. In ossicular fixation or ossicular discontinuity, increased air pressure makes no changes in the sound intensity(Gelle's negative). Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 27.

301.q: Which of the following statements is false about sodium fluoride regarding its use in the treatment of otosclerosis?
o: It acts treatment of choice in patients with positive schwartz sign.
It acts by inhibiting osteoblastic activity
Is contraindicated in chronic renal failure
Is indicated in patients with a positive Schwartz sign
301.e: SODIUM FLUORIDE Mechanism of action: Inhibitor of osteoclast activity and so a stabilizer of bone turnover. It also leads to increased calcium deposition in otospongiotic foci and decreased bone remodelling. It inhibits the proteolytic enzymes in the cochlea. Uses: Sodium fluoride is the treatment of choice in Schwartz sign positive patients which represents the active stage of the disease. It is also used in cochlear otosclerosis. Contraindications: Chronic nephritis, Flourosis, in pregnant and lactating women and in children. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1074.

301.q: Which of the following is not a feature of Otosclerosis?
301.e: Rising sun sign is seen in Glomus Jugulare. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page -

301.q: False statement about Schwartz sign in a case of Otosclerosis:
o: Sodium Flouride is the treatment of schoice
301.e: Schwartz sign in otosclerosis is contraindication for surgery . Other treatment for Otosclerosis Hearing aid- is given for patients unwilling for surgery. Sodium fluoride (NaF) oral therapy. It is treatment of choice for Schwartz sign (+) patient. (Early stage of disease) Cochlear otosclerosis. NaF leads to stabilization of disease. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 105. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1079.

301.q: Van der Hoeve syndrome includes all except
301.e: VAN DER HOEVE SYNDROME OSTEOGENESIS IMPERFECTA. OTOSCLEROSIS. BLUE SCLERA. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 103.

301.q: Which of the following is not applicable to Otosclerosis?
o: Dip at 2000 Hz in Bone conduction curve
Worsening of hearing loss during pregnancy
Schwartz sign in early stage of disease
301.e: Diplacusis : Patient can hear the same sound in 2 frequencies. This is seen in MENIERES DISEASE not in OTOSCLEROSIS. Paracusis willisi : Patient can hear better in noisy areas . It is seen in OTOSCLEROSIS. Remaining all other options are true about Otosclerosis. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Otosclerosis, Page number: 104

301.q: A young woman with a history of progressive moderate bilateral hearing loss which has aggravated during her pregnancy. On examination the tympanic membrane was normal. Which surgery should be done to treat this condition?
301.e: The case scenario given in the question is suggestive of Otosclerosis . Surgical management: Stapedectomy/stapedotomy with a placement of prosthesis is the treatment of choice. Here the fixed otosclerotic stapes is removed and a prosthesis inserted between the incus and oval window. Prosthesis employed may be a teflon piston, stainless steel piston, platinum-teflon or titanium-teflon piston. Other options: The case given in the question is of Otosclerosis in which we occasionally manage conservatively (option B) and not by Tympanoplasty (option A) and tympanoplasty with stapedectomy.

301.q: Tone decay test can be used to detect:
301.e: Acoustic neuroma is a retrocochlear lesion. Tone decay Test is a measure of auditory nerve fatigue. Tone decay is faster in retrocochlear lesion. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 31.

302.q: A middle age female patient is complaining of transient sensation of rotational movements of surroundings with nausea while lying down on the bed. She has been experiencing this problem for last 3 days. Which part of the inner ear is the site of origin of pathology that is likely to be responsible for the given complaint?
302.e: This is a case of BPPV(Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo). Otoliths or otoconia are calcium carbonate crystals lying embedded in the gelatinous layer of macula. Macula is the sensory end organ of utricle and saccule whose function is linear acceleration. In certain head positions, the displaced otoconia come to rest against the cupula of SCC causing vertigo. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 52.

302.q: One of the following is not the treatment modality for Meniere's Disease
o: Intermittent Inner ear pulse pressure therapy
302.e: Primary treatment is medical management. Refractory patients are offered further treatments. like transtympanic injection of gentamycin using microwicks or microcatheters. Meniett device is external device used for pulse pressure therapy to labyrinth. Donaldson's line is surgical landmark for localisation of endolymphatic sac to conduct endolymphatic sac decompression therapy. Schwartz operation is other name for cortical mastoidectomy which is done in cases of acute mastoiditis. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Meniere's disease, Page number: 124

302.q: Third window effect is seen in:
302.e: In superior semicircular canal dehiscence, the patient will have conductive hearing loss due to leakage of sound waves from the dehiscence which acts like a third window. This is called third window phenomenon. Reference: Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1192.

302.q: All are characteristic features of superior semicircular canal dehiscence except
o: HRCT temporal bone is helpful in diagnosis
302.e: Patient shows conductive hearing loss on audiometry due to leakage of sound energy from third window which has been created in SCC(apart from oval and round window). This is called third window phenomenon. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Meniere's Disease, Page number: 120

302.q: Which of the following is not a typical feature of Meniere's disease?
302.e: Pulsatile tinnitus is seen in Glomus tumor. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 120.

302.q: All are true about Lermoyez syndrome except
o: Vertigo is the first symptom followed by hearing loss
Hearing loss is the first symptom followed by vertigo
The symptoms are in reverse order as compared to classical Meniere's disease.
302.e: LERMOYEZ SYNDROME- rare variant of Meniere’s disease where hearing loss is followed by vertigo. (Reverse Meniere’s disease). In the classical menieres disease, vertigo is followed by hearing loss. Meniere’s disease Episode finishes within 24hrs. (BPPV-Few second vertigo without hearing loss or tinitus) During an episode some patients can develop diarrhoea. (Very rare) During episodes some people fall down without turning unconscious, this is called as Tumarkin’s crisis (Rare) Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 122.

302.q: All of the following are true about Meniere's disease Except
o: Inner ear ablation required in all cases
Low frequency sensorineural hearing loss in early stages
302.e: Inner ear ablation is only required in all those cases of Meniere's disease who have more frequent disabling episodes of vertigo with no significant residual hearing. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 123, 124.

302.q: A 36 year old male patient is suffering from Meniere's disease for last 3 years. He has developed very frequent disabling episodes of vertigo with normal cochlear function. What will be further appropriate treatment of this patient?
302.e: This patient has normal cochlear function and disabling vertigo. So a treatment method which preserves hearing is preferred. Among the options given, vestibular neurectomy is the correct answer. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 123, 124.

303.q: What is the most common benign tumour of middle ear?
o: Carcinoma of middle ear and mastoid
303.e: GLOMUS JUGULARE It is benign non capsulated locally invasive highly vascular tumour. It is more common in females. Site of origin- it arises from glomus cells lying around the jugular bulb. It is skull based jugular foramen tumour. The red vascular tumor erodes the floor of the middle ear and grows into hypotympanum This is called the Rising Sun sign. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Tumours of Middle Ear and Mastoid, Page number: 128, 129

303.q: 73 year old person with mild unilateral sensorineural hearing loss on right side has been diagnosed with ipsilateral Acoustic neuroma on Gadolinium enhanced MRI scan. The tumour size mentioned in the radiologist report is 1.0 cm. Audiogram reveals mild SNHL on right side, What is the further management of this patient?
o: Neurosurgical removal by middle cranial fossa approach
303.e: Since the tumour size is small and age of the patient is 73, it will be appropriate to go for Gamma Knife therapy, a stereotactic radiotherapy. Indications for Gamma Knife Therapy: Patient unwilling for surgery Patient unfit for surgery Old patient with small tumor with residual hearing. Middle cranial fossa approach is preferred for small tumors with residual hearing. It will lead to hearing preservation. If this patient would have been young, we would have gone for choice D. Translabyrithine approach is good for large size tumours with no residual hearing. Hearing preservation is not possible in this. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 134. Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition, Volume 2, Page - 1263.

303.q: Rising Sun Appearance is typically seen in:
303.e: Glomus jugulare is a benign non capsulated locally invasive highly vascular tumour. It erodes the floor of middle ear and start growing in Hypotympanum as red vascular mass(Rising sun sign). Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Tumours of Middle Ear and Mastoid, Page number: 128, 129

303.q: True about glomus jugulare are all except:
303.e: Glomus jugulare invades the hypotympanum. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 128.

303.q: All are true about Vestibular schwannoma except
o: It is the most common type of cerbellopontine angle tumour
Gamma knife surgery is the treatment of choice for this tumour
Speech discrimination score is very poor in these patients
303.e: Acoustic neuroma Treatment is surgical excision. Indications for Gamma Knife Therapy Patient unwilling for surgery Patient unfit for surgery Old patient with small tumor with residual hearing. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Accoustic Neuroma, Page number: 132

303.q: All statements are true about acoustic neuroma except
o: Gamma knife is the preferred treatment for smaller tumors in old age patient
BERA shows decreased Interaural latency difference of Wave V
Inferior vestibular nerve is main nerve of origin.
303.e: Acoustic neuromas are intracranial, extra-axial tumors that arise from the Schwann cells, investing either the vestibular or cochlear nerve. This can often be demonstrated through audiological testing by a phenomenon called "rollover," in which speech discrimination scores decrease as the volume of the speech stimulus increases. A normal score is 80% or greater. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg no. 426

303.q: What is the most common tumor of cerebellopontine angle?
303.e: Acoustic neuroma (Vestibular Schwannoma) It's a benign slow growing tumor of the 8th nerve. Most common site of origin is Inferior Vestibular division of 8 th nerve. It is common in the 4th-5th decade. It is mostly unilateral except in Neurofibroma-2 (bilateral vestibular schwannoma) It's a brain tumor. It is the most common type of Cerebellopontine angle tumour. Ear examination NORMAL. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Accoustic Neuroma, Page number: 132

303.q: The most common site of origin of Acoustic neuroma is
303.e: Acoustic neuroma (Vestibular Schwannoma) It's a benign slow growing tumor of the 8th nerve. Most common site of origin is Inferior Vestibular division of 8 th nerve. It is common in the 4th-5th decade. It is mostly unilateral except in Neurofibroma-2 (bilateral vestibular schwannoma) Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Accoustic Neuroma, Page number: 132</p

304.q: Which of the following is the surgical landmark for first genu of facial nerve?
304.e: Processuscochleariformis Hook like projection on medial wall of middle ear. Surgical landmark for first genu of facial nerve. It demarcates the geniculate ganglion which lies just anterior to it. Tympanic segment of the facial nerve starts at this level. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. - 7, 108.

304.q: Which of the following is not a boundary of facial recess?
o: Tympanic segment of the facial nerve
Mastoid segment of the facial nerve
304.e: Facial recess is the surgical landmark for posterior tympanotomy. Boundaries: Medial boundary - Vertical segment of the facial nerve (mastoid segment) Lateral boundary - Chorda tympani Superior boundary - Fossa incudis (short process of incus) Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number-6.

304.q: Which of the following is surgical landmark of first genu of facial nerve?
304.e: SURGICAL LANDMARKS OF FACIAL NERVE For middle ear and mastoid surgery Processus It demarcates the geniculate ganglion which lies just anterior to it. Tympanic segment of the nerve starts at this level. Oval window and horizontal The facial nerve runs above the oval window (stapes) and below the horizontal canal. Short process of Facial nerve lies medial to the short process of incus at the level of aditus. Nerve runs behind the pyramid and the posterior tympanic sulcus. Tympanomastoid In vertical or mastoid segment, nerve runs behind this suture. Digastric ridge. The nerve leaves the mastoid at the anterior end of digastric ridge. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.108,109

304.q: A 50-year-old female presented with complaints of progressive facial weakness. MRI showed a facial nerve Schwannoma. What is the most common site of the above lesion?
304.e: Explanation: Schwannomas are rare nerve sheath tumours that can occur throughout the body, and are symptomatic based on location, size, and impingement on adjacent structures. These tumours are often benign lesions that occur sporadically or as part of genetic conditions such as neurofibromatosis. Schwannomas may arise from peripheral nerves, gastrointestinal nerves, spinal nerve roots and cranial nerves. Facial nerve Schwannomas arise from cranial nerve VII and commonly involve the geniculate ganglion, labyrinthine segment, and internal auditory canal . While small lesions are asymptomatic, larger lesions can cause facial nerve paralysis and facial spasms. Lesions in the internal auditory canal can cause hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, and otalgia.

304.q: The physiological bottleneck of facial nerve is present in which part?
304.e: Labyrinthine segment is the narrowest part of the facial nerve. Hence it is the physiological bottleneck of facial nerve. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 107, 108.

304.q: Facial nerve testing can be clinically done in suspected acute facial nerve palsy by all except? A. Orbicularis oculi closure B. Buccinator action C. Chewing D. Elevation of eyebrows E. Checking for angle of mouth
304.e: Chewing is performed by muscles of mastication(Masseter, Temporalis, Pterygoids). These are supplied by the trigeminal nerve. Muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 117.

304.q: Which of the following is not supplied by the anterior division of mandibular nerve (V3)?
304.e: B i.e. Medial pterygoid Temporalis, messeter and lateral pterygoid musclesQ are supplied by anterior division of mandibular nerve whereas medial pterygoid muscleQ is supplied by the main trunk of mandibular nerve.

304.q: In a patient of facial nerve injury, Schirmer's test shows decreased lacrimation, taste sensation is impaired and stapedial reflex is absent. Where is the level of injury?
304.e: Topodiagnostic Tests: Schirmer's Test - Reduced lacrimation - lesion proximal to geniculate ganglion(first genu) Stapedial Reflex - Lost in lesions above Nerve. to Stapedius(second genu) Taste test - Impairment of taste means lesion above chorda tympani origin In this question, Lacrimation - absentl Stapedial reflex - Abscent Taste sensation - Impaired So the level of lesion is above the first genu, in the labyrinthine segment. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 108.

305.q: Not used in the treatment of bell's palsy
305.e: Steroids are the main stay of management. A patient who reports within first three days should be given acyclovir as well. Care of the eye is a very important part of management to prevent exposure keratopathy.Chances of recovery in bell's palsy are 85% and above. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Facial Nerve and its Disorders, Page number: 112

305.q: All of the following are true about temporal bone fractures except
o: Transverse fractures are more commonly associated with facial palsy
Ear bleeding is suggestive of longitudinal fractures
CSF otorrhoea is more common in transverse fractures
Longitudinal fractures more commonly cause conductive deafness
305.e: Temporal bone fracture are two types: Longitudinal fracture This is due to falling on the side. 80% of total fractures. Less dangerous. Cause Ossicular dislocation. Cause CHL Vertigo is uncommon. EAC bleeding and CSF otorrhoea are more Common Facial palsy is less common and delayed, it is due to edema of nerve. So, treatment is or oral steroids. Transverse fracture Due to Fall on front or the back. 20% of total fractures. More dangerous. Damage cochlea. Cause SNHL Vertigo is common. EAC bleeding and CSF otorrhoea less common Facial palsy is more common and immediate it is due to direct injury to nerve by fracture line. So, treatment is immediate Surgery. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Facial Nerve and its Disorders, Page number: 114

305.q: Which of the following is associated with olfactory nerve dysfunction?
305.e: Olfactory deficits have been described in a number of neurological disorders. Olfactory dysfunction may be the first clinical sign of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and idiopathic Parkinson’s disease (PD). In PD, bilateral olfactory deficits occur before the onset of most of the classical neurological signs. Hence smell testing maybe useful. The remaining syndromes are not associated with olfactory nerve dysfunction. Reference – Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, 8 th edition – Volume 1 – Page – 1237

305.q: Which statement is false regarding Bell's palsy?
o: Vesicles seen on pinna and in External Auditory canal
Hyperacusis is seen in these cases
Most common cause of lower motor neuron facial palsy.
305.e: Facial paralysis along with vesicular rash in the external auditory canal and pinna is seen in Ramsay HuntSyndrome(Herpes Zoster Oticus). Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 112-114.

305.q: A patient of head injury has bluish discoloration over mastoid area, bleeding from external auditory meatus with normal facial nerve function. After three days, patient develops facial paralysis. What is the treatment plan for this patient?
305.e: Based on the findings given, this is a case of longitudinal fracture of temporal bone. It presents with delayed onset of facial paralysis. This should be managed by 3 weeks of steroid therapy(as the cause is oedema). Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 116.

305.q: A patient of bell's palsy shows no improvement with 3 weeks of steroid therapy. His electroneuronography reveals no significant facial nerve degeneration. What should be the next step in the management?
o: Acyclovir should be added to treatment
Continue with steroids and repeat assessment
305.e: Treatment of Bell's palsy: Oral steroids for 3 weeks. If no improvement ->Electroneuronography is done If electroneuronography shows no significant facial nerve degeneration, steroid therapy is continued with repeat assessment. Facial nerve decompression would have been done if electroneuronography showed significant facial nerve degeneration Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 113.

305.q: A patient of Bell's palsy shows no improvement with 3 weeks of steroid therapy. His electrophysiological nerve testing reveals degeneration in >90% nerve fibres. What should be the next step in the management?
o: Surgical repair of facial nerve with nerve grafting
Increase the dose of steroid and repeat assessment after one week
305.e: If there is no recovery after 3 weeks of steroid therapy, then next management is to do. Electrophysiological Nerve testing to check for extent for nerve degeneration. If significant degeneration is noted (i.e. 90% fibres show degeneration), Then treatment is switched to surgery called surgical decompression of facial nerve. If it is Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Facial Nerve and its Disorders, Page number: 113

305.q: What is the intervention for facial nerve injury immediately following head trauma and fracture of temporal bone?
305.e: Immediate onset facial paralysis following temporal bone fracture - Surgery in the form of nerve decompression, re-anastomosis of cut ends or cable nerve graft. Delayed onset facial paralysis following temporal bone fracture is treated conservatively like Bell's palsy. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 115.

306.q: A 10-year-old child has fever, pain in ear and Otoscopy shows tympanic membrane to be red & bulging, treatment of choice is:
o: Myringotomy with Grommet surgery and antibiotics
306.e: This is a case of Acute Suppurative Otitis Media(ASOM) with bulging ear drum. It is an impending perforation, hence Myringotomy will be needed in poster inferior quadrant. Grommet is only used in glue ear or Eustachian tube dysfunction. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 75.

306.q: A 10 years old child presented to ENT OPD with history of mouth breathing for last 3 yrs. Otoscopy revealed Bilateral retracted TM with air bubbles visible behind the ear drum. Audiological assesment shows Type B Tympanogram and moderate conductive hearing loss. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?
306.e: INDICATIONS Adenoid hypertrophy causing snoring, mouth breathing, sleep apnoea syndrome or speech abnormalities, i.e. (rhinolalia clausa). Recurrent Chronic otitis media with effusion associated with adenoid Recurrent ear discharge in benign CSOM associated with adenoiditis/adenoid hyperplasia. Dental Adenoidectomy does not correct dental abnormalities but will prevent its recurrence after orthodontic treatment. The grommet insertion. If myringotomy and aspiration combined with medical measures have not helped and fluid recurs, a grommet is inserted to provide continued aeration of middle ear. It is left in place for weeks or months or till it is spontaneously extruded Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg no. 507

306.q: Which muscle is responsible for the opening of Eustachian tube during swallowing?
306.e: EUSTACHIAN TUBE : It connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. Total Length 36 mm → Outer 12mm is bony& Inner 24mm is cartilagenous Angulation at birth it is nearly horizontal tube where as in adults it is 45° with horizontal. Main function of the Eustachian tube is middle ear ventilation. Tensor veli palatini muscle opens the tube during swallowing. Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Eustachian Tube and its Disorders, Page number: 67

306.q: Which of the following tests uses a negative pressure to test eustachian tube function?
306.e: Toynbee's manoeuvre uses negative pressure to test eustachian tube function. It is a more physiological test. It is performed by asking the patient to swallow while nose has been pinched. This draws air from the middle ear into the nasopharynx and causes inward movement of tympanic membrane. The remaining three tests use positive pressure which causes outward movement of tympanic membrane. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 69, 70.

306.q: A patient presents to the hospital with a hypermobile tympanic membrane and hearing his own voice. What is the most possible diagnosis?
