VIII th nerve is not involved in NPC. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 297

o: Level 4 cervical lymph nodes are involved
May be associated with U/L otitis media with Effusion
323.e: All the cranial nerves can be involved in Nasopharyngeal carcinoma except the 1 st , 7 th and 8 th cranial nerves. So facial palsy is not a feature. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 297

323.q: All of the following are true about nasopharyngeal carcinoma except
o: IgA antibody to EBV are present
Bilateral conductive deafness in an adult patient is a common presentation
Cervical lymph node metastasis is seen in 75% patients
Commonest histopathological type is undifferentiated carcinoma
323.e: The nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with unilateral conductive hearing loss in an adult patient due to obstruction of Eustachian tube causing serous otitis media. Presence of unilateral serous otitis media in an adult should raise suspicion of nasopharyngeal growth. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 297

323.q: All of the following are true about nasopharyngeal carcinoma except
o: Trigeminal nerve involvement is a very common occurrence in these patients
Nasophyrangiectomy with bilateral neck dissection is the primary treatment
323.e: Chemoradiation is the treatment of choice for all stages of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Involvement of trigeminal nerve occurs commonly through foramen lacerum presenting as facial pain in the area supplied by V nerve and loss of corneal reflex. Bimodal age distribution is seen with incidence in fifth to seventh decades > younger age groups. Causes jugular foramen syndrome due to involvement of IX th , X th , XI th cranial nerves. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 297

323.q: Which virus has been implicated as an aetiological agent in nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
323.e: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is more common in China and is closely associated with EB virus. Specific viral markers are being developed to screen people in high-incidence areas. EB virus has two important antigens: Viral capsid antigen(VCA) - IgA antibodies of VCA are more sensitive for nasopharyngeal cancer. Early antigen(EA) - IgA antibodies of EA are highly specific for nasopharyngeal cancer. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 296

323.q: Treatment of choice of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is?
323.e: Cure rate is doubled when chemotherapy is combined with radiotherapy. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 298

324.q: Cricoid cartilage lies at which vertebral level ?
324.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., C6 [Ref BDC 5I'Ve Vol. III, p. 237]

324.q: All of the following are true about Juvenile papilloma of larynx except
o: CO2 laser microsurgery is the treatment of choice
324.e: Juvenile papillomas are premalignant. All papillomas should be examined histopathologically to exclude any dysplastic features or malignant transformation. They are caused by HPV-6,11. The infection is transmitted from mother to child at the time of birth. CO2 laser is the treatment of choice. Recurrences are common after surgery. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 356

324.q: Ideal treatment for Keratosis larynx is
324.e: Leukoplakia or keratosis larynx Localized form of epithelial hyperplasia involving upper surface of one or both vocal cords. White plaque or warty growth on the cord without affecting its mobility. Precancerous condition Treatment is stripping of vocal cords followed by histology of tissue for any malignant change. Chronic laryngeal irritants should be eliminated. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 354

324.q: Which cartilage of larynx is paired?
324.e: Larynx has three unpaired and three paired cartilages. Unpaired: Thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis. Paired: Arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra , 8 th Edition, pg. no – 331

324.q: Which is the narrowest part of Infant larynx
324.e: Infant's larynx is small and conical. The diameter of cricoid cartilage is smaller than the size of glottis, making subglottis the narrowest part . Paediatric endotracheal tube selection depends on this. In adults, glottis is narrowest part . Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 335 Scott Brown's Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery - 8 th edition - Volume 3 - Page number - 1081

324.q: The ideal management of Juvenile papilloma of larynx is
324.e: Management of Juvenile papilloma of larynx - Microlaryngoscopy and CO2laser excision avoiding injury to vocal ligament. Recurrence is common and procedure needs to be repeated several times. In the absence of CO2 laser - tumour removed under microscope with cup forceps or a debrider. Medical therapies - can be used as adjuvants. Interferon alpha-2a has shown promising results but has several side effects including fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia, headache, loss of weight and suppression of bone marrow. 13-cis-retinoic acid has also been used. This too has several side effects. REF: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 356

324.q: Which is the narrowest part of the adult larynx airway?
324.e: Explanation: The adult laryngeal airway is divided into three regions: supraglottis, glottis, and subglottis . The glottis , which includes the true vocal cords and the space between them, is the narrowest part of the adult airway. In contrast, the pediatric airway has its narrowest point at the cricoid cartilage (subglottis). Knowledge of the narrowest airway region is crucial for airway management, endotracheal intubation, and recognizing potential sites of obstruction. Explanation of Other Options: Supraglottis (Option A): Includes epiglottis, arytenoids, false cords, and ventricles; wider than the glottis. Subglottis (Option C): Area below the vocal cords to the cricoid; narrowest in children. Trachea (Option D): Continues below the subglottis; larger than glottis in adults. Reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33232069/

324.q: Which of the following statement is true for Lupus larynx
o: Involvement of posterior part of larynx
324.e: Lupus larynx Involves the anterior part of the larynx Epiglottis is the most common site. Painless condition. Associated with lupus of nose and larynx. The remaining points are true for tuberculosis of larynx. (OPTIONS a,c,d) TB larynx is a painful disease associated with pulmonary TB. The earliest lesions form in the posterior part of larynx with turban epiglottis occurring in the later part. Weakness of voice and painful phonation are the classical symptoms of TB larynx. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 343

325.q: A 55-year-old woman has been suffering from COPD with neuromuscular respiratory insufficiency. 1 week back, she underwent tracheostomy for airway support and bronchial toilet. She is now in the ward. During the morning rounds, you find that the tracheostomy tube is blocked and her SpO2 is 72%. What would be the immediate management you will carry out?
o: Do suction of the tube after putting normal saline in the tube
325.e: This is an acute airway emergency. The tube should be removed immediately and replaced with a new tube. Oxygen will not help the patient as the tube is already blocked. Deriphyllin is a bronchodilator. It has no role in management of a blocked tube. Suction of the tube after putting normal saline helps in clearing the crusts. This helps to prevent blockage of the tube but is not helpful after blockage has occurred. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page Number-372.

325.q: Which drug has role as a local application agent in JORP( Juvenile onset respiratory papillomatosis)
325.e: Juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JoRRP) is a condition related to HPV 6 and 11 infection which is characterized by the repeated growth of benign exophytic papilloma in the respiratory tract of children. Cidofovir is used locally in JORP. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra

325.q: Following statements are true about foreign bodies in the air passage in children except:
o: Vegetable foreign bodies are not common.
A normal chest X ray can be seen in early cases within 24 hours.
More common in the right bronchus.
More common in children less than 4 years of age.
325.e: In children, vegetable foreign bodies are common with peanuts being the most common. A normal chest X ray is seen in early cases within 24 hours or when a foreign body causing partial obstruction with full ingress and egress of air does not produce any sign. Most foreign bodies enter the right bronchus because it is wider and more in line with the tracheal lumen. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page Number-377, 375.

325.q: Corkscrew esophagus is seen in which of the following conditions ?
325.e: Ans. is d i.e., Diffuse Esophageal spasm Radiological appearances of diffuse esophageal spasm have been described as: curling esophagus Corkscrew esophagus or - pseudodiverticulosis Diffuse esophageal spasm is a motor disorder of esophagus characterized by repetitive simultaneous non-peristaltic contractions. Symptoms are substernal chest pain and/or dysphagia Diagnosed by manometry Also know Nutcracker esophagus also known as 'supersqueezer' esophagus - it is characterized by extremely high-amplitude peristaltic contraction - Symptoms are pain and dysphagia Diagnosed by manometry study which shows peristaltic esophageal contractions with peak amplitudes greater than two standard deviations above the normal values.

325.q: All of the following conditions affect posterior part of Larynx except:
325.e: Lupus larynx affects anterior larynx. It most commonly involves epiglottis. Intubation granuloma involves the posterior thirds of the vocal cords. Pachydermia laryngis is heaping up of epithelium in interarytenoid region and posterior part of vocal cords. Tuberculosis larynx most commonly forms lesions in posterior part of larynx. REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no – 343, 342, 354

325.q: A child presented with stridor, barking cough and difficulty in breathing since 3 days. He also had low grade fever with increased leukocyte count. All of the following are true except:
o: On X-ray, sub glottic stenosis is seen
Boys are affected more than girls
Antibiotics are the main stay of treatment
325.e: This is a case of acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup). Treatment includes: Hospitalization & IV fluids I/v steroids : to reduce edema especially when child is in distress Humidified air to soften crusts Racemic Adrenaline via a respirator - Bronchodilator Intubation / tracheostomy may be needed Antibiotics are only given to prevent secondary infection. Croup is usually caused by viral infections, and antibiotics are not the mainstay of treatment. Supportive care, such as humidified air, hydration, and sometimes corticosteroids, is more commonly used. Antibiotics are not effective against viral infections. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, pg. no – 339, 340

325.q: One month old Child presents with difficulty in breathing since day seven of birth, which on making the patient prone, improves. The probable diagnosis is Laryngomalacia. What would be the ideal management
325.e: Laryngomalacia manifests at birth or soon after, and usually disappears by 2 years of age . So reassurance is the ideal strategy. Tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction. Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia. Steroids have no role in the management of laryngomalacia. REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no 344

325.q: Commonest cause of acute epiglottitis is:
325.e: Acute epiglottitis Primarily affects children of 2–7 years of age but can also affect adults. The most common organism responsible for this condition in children. Streptococcus Pneumoniae & Haemophilus Infuenzae B is second common aetiological agent. Parainfluenza virus causes croup (Acute laryngotracheobronchitis). Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no – 338

326.q: 1. True about Reinke's oedema: a. Usually unilateral b. Common in smoker c. Corticosteroid is mainstay of treatment d. Involve whole of membranous part of the vocal cords e. Patient has dysphonia
326.e: Reinke’s edema is usually bilateral Usual cause is smoking and vocal abuse Involves whole of membranous part of the vocal cords Patient has a hoarse, low pitched voice Mainstay of treatment – Decortication of vocal cord Re-education in voice production and cessation of smoking Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no – 342, 353 Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery – 8 th edition – Volume 3 – Page number – 952

Reinke's oedema is due to oedema of the subepithelial space of the vocal cord (Reinke's space). TREATMENT- Decortication of the vocal cord (removal of strip of epithelium is done on one side and 3 - 4weeks on the other). Voice rest, speech therapy, cessation of smoking Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no - 342

326.q: All are true about Reinke's odema except
o: Speech therapy and Proton Pump Inhibitor are the mainstay of treatment
Sub-epithelial cordectomy is the treatment of choice
326.e: Under the epithelium of vocal cords is a potential space with scanty subepithelial connective tissues. It is bounded above and below by the arcuate lines, in front by anterior commissure, and behind by vocal process of arytenoid. Oedema of this space causes fusiform swelling of the membranous cords (Reinke’s oedema). Stopping smoking and Subepithelial cordectomy is the treatment of choice. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra, Pg.342

326.q: Type of voice in adenoid hypertrophy is:
326.e: Rhinolalia clausa is hyponasality. It is due to blockage of the nose or nasopharynx. Common causes include common cold, nasal polyp, sinusitis, adenoid hypertrophy, nasopharyngeal mass. Rhinolalia aperta is hypernasality - Seen in cleft palate, palatal perforation, palatal palsy Hot potato voice is seen in peritonsillar abscess(quinsy). Dysphonia Plica ventricularis - Here voice is produced by false vocal cords. May be secondary to impaired function of the true vocal cords like paralysis, surgical excision or cancer. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 366, 368 , 311

326.q: True regarding Acute retropharyngeal abscess? A. Always associated with hoarseness of voice B. Can produce trismus C. Can extend to base of skull D. Produces unilateral bulge on posterior pharyngeal wall E. More common in children
326.e: Trismus is a feature of parapharyngeal abscess. Hoarseness of voice is a common feature of vocal cord problems. Retropharyngeal Space - Between the buccopharyngeal & the prevertebral fascia Extends from base of skull to bifurcation of trachea Divided by a fibrous raphe into 2(spaces of Gilette) Abscess causes U/L bulge on posterior pharyngeal wall Abscess commonly seen in children Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 313, 366

326.q: Treatment of choice of vocal polyp is :
326.e: Vocal polyp is caused by sudden shouting resulting in haemorrhage in the vocal cord and subsequent submucosal oedema. Treatment is surgical excision under operating microscope followed by speech therapy. Reference- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no - 353

326.q: Laryngopharyngeal reflux can lead to all except
326.e: Sulcus vocalis Furrow like depression in vocal cord Due to deficiency of lamina propria, the epithelium dips down forming a furrow. Can be congenital or due to phonotrauma. Laryngopharyngeal reflux causes pseudosulcus vocalis. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no - 355 Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery – 8 th edition – Volume 3 – Page number – 1095

326.q: Most common cause of bilateral vocal cord palsy
326.e: Thyroid surgery (Total thyroidectomy) is the most common cause of bilateral vocal cord palsy. Most common cause of unilateral vocal cord palsy is idiopathic followed by carcinoma bronchus. Reference – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no 348 REFERENCE- Scott Brown’s Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery – 8 th edition – Volume 3 – Page number – 1108

327.q: A child presented with ear infection with foul-smelling discharge. On further exploration, a small perforation is found in the pars flaccida of the tympanic membrane. What would be the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Topical antibiotics and decongestants for 4 weeks
IV antibiotics and follow-up after a month
327.e: Foul smelling discharge with perforation of pars flaccida of the tympanic membrane is suggestive of atticoantral CSOM. It is always managed surgically. So tympanomastoid exploration(MRM) is the correct answer. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 85, 87.

327.q: The ideal treatment for T1N0M0 glottic cancer larynx is
327.e: T1N0M0 glottic malignancy - Tumour limited to vocal cord(s) with normal mobility. Carcinoma of the mobile membranous vocal cord is traditionally treated with radiotherapy. Now such lesions are precisely excised with CO2 laser under microscope with the same good results . Laser excision has the advantages of lower cost, lower duration of treatment and morbidity. REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no - 363

327.q: Which is the preferred treatment for verrucous glottic malignancy of larynx stage T1N0M0?
327.e: Carcinoma of the mobile membranous vocal cord is traditionally treated with radiotherapy. Now such lesions can be precisely excised with CO2 laser under microscope with the same good results. Laser excision has the advantages of lower cost, lower duration of treatment and morbidity. Similar T1 lesions of the supra- or infrahyoid epiglottis with or without neck nodes have been treated with CO2 laser. Cervical nodes in such cases are managed surgically with appropriate neck dissection. Endoscopic CO2 laser is getting popular at some centers where facilities of CO2 laser and expertise are available. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page Number-363.

327.q: A 50 yrs old male chronic smoker complains of hoarseness for the past 4 months. Microlaryngoscopy biopsy shows it to be keratosis of the larynx. All the suggested treatment modalities for this condition, except
327.e: Leukoplakia or keratosis of larynx is a premalignant epithelial hyperplasia involving the upeer surface of vocal cords. Treatment includes Stripping of vocal cords followed by histology of tissue for any malignant change. Laser vaporizer can also be used. Chronic laryngeal irritants should be eliminated. Partial laryngectomy is done for T2 stage of carcinoma larynx. Reference - Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 354

327.q: Vertical partial laryngectomy is done for
327.e: Vertical partial laryngectomy is done for T2N0Mo glottic cancer. The growth should be limited to one side and other side should be free. Horizontal partial laryngectomy is done for T2N0M0 supraglottic cancer. The pre-requisite is the growth should be limited to supraglottis and both vocal cords are free and mobile. The lung functions should be also good REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no - 363

327.q: Horizontal partial laryngectomy is done for
327.e: Horizontal partial laryngectomy is done for T2N0M0 supraglottic cancer. The pre-requisite is the growth should be limited to supraglottis and both vocal cords are free and mobile. The lung functions should be also good. Vertical partial laryngectomy is done for T2N0Mo glottic cancer. The growth should be limited to one side and other side should be free. REF:- Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra ,8 th Edition, pg. no - 363

327.q: Which of the following is the best description of Type 3 cordectomy
327.e: Transmuscular cordectomy (type III) is performed by cutting through the vocalis muscle. The resection encompasses the epithelium, lamina propria, and part of the vocalis muscle. The resection may extend from the vocal process to the anterior commissure. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose, AND Throat by PL Dhingra

327.q: A 48-year-old man with a history of trauma to the right ear presents with pain and hearing loss. Examination showed blood clots filling the ear canal. What is the next step in management?
o: Keep the ear dry and give analgesics
327.e: Explanation: The patient is most likely to have sustained traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, resulting in blood clots in the ear canal. In cases of traumatic tympanic membrane perforation with blood clots, the safest initial step is to keep the ear dry and provide analgesics. Traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane usually heals automatically. Its important to keep the ear dry to prevent infections, thus use of ear drops and syringing is best avoided. (Option B, D ruled out). Aspirating the clot, which seals the bleeding, may potentially cause further complications and is usually unnecessary, as the clot typically resolves spontaneously. (Option A ruled out) Overall, conservative management allows for natural healing of the tympanic membrane and pain relief.

328.q: All of the following are helpful in the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea except -
328.e: Muller's manoeuvre - An endoscope is used to look for collapse of soft tissues in the oropharynx when the patient inspires vigorously. Level of pharyngeal obstruction can be found. It plays a role in the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea but has no role in its treatment. Treatment options for OSA include - A. Lifestyle changes Weight loss Quit alcohol and smoking Dietary modification B. Positional therapy – Sleeping on the side as supine position may cause OSA. C. CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure) or BiPAP (bilevel positive airway pressure) when CPAP is not tolerated. These devices maintain a positive pressure and keep the airway open. D. Surgical -Laser Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty(UPPP) - The aim is to increase the size of airway. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 327, 328

328.q: All of the following are true about cochlear implant except
o: Receiver stimulator is surgically implanted inside the body
Eighth nerve integrity should be established before cochlear implantation
Mondini's dysplasia of cochlea is not a contraindication of cochlear implantation
Veria approach is the classical facial recess approach
328.e: Surgical technique : The classical approach is posterior tympanotomy(facial recess approach) Other surgical technique is Veria approach. This is transcanal approach Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Rehabilitation of the Hearing Impaired, Page number: 145

328.q: All of the following are true about bone anchored hearing aid except
o: It has surgically implantable titanium fixture
It transmits sound directly to cochlea through the bone conduction.
The BAHA device is implanted on the side of deaf ear.
328.e: Osseointegration takes 2-6 months. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 142, 143.

328.q: True statement regarding use of head mirror & Bull lamp in ENT examination: a. Distance between the doctor and the patient must be more than 10 inches b. Applied on right eye c. Right eye should be closed during examination d. Both eye should be open while examining e. Light from bull lamp is diffuse but strong
328.e: Head mirror and Bull lamp in ENT: Distance between the doctor and patient must be less than 10 inches Applied on right eye Both eyes should be open while examining The light is diffuse but strong Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 444, 445.

328.q: Cochlear implant electrode is placed in
328.e: Cochlear Implant (Electrode) Insertion of Electrode into scala tympani of Cochlea through Round window. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Page - 146.

328.q: Which focal length in the objective piece of microscope is commonly used for ear surgery?
328.e: The focal length in objective piece of microscope commonly used in ENT is: Ear surgery-200/250mm Nose-300mm Larynx-400mm Reference : Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Chapter name: Page number:

329.q: Iris cloboma is most common in ?
329.e: Ans. C. Inferonasal All clobomas (including iris) are mostly inferonasal.

329.q: What is the anteroposterior diameter of an adult eyeball?
329.e: Dimensions of an adult eyeball Anteroposterior diameter : 24 mm Horizontal diameter : 23.5 mm Vertical diameter : 23 mm Circumference : 75 mm Volume : 6.5 ml Weight : 7 g Reference: Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th ed. – A.K.Khurana, Ch-1 Anatomy and development of eye

329.q: What is the volume of an adult eyeball?
329.e: Dimensions of an adult eyeball Anteroposterior diameter : 24 mm Horizontal diameter : 23.5 mm Vertical diameter : 23 mm Circumference : 75 mm Volume : 6.5 ml Weight : 7 g Reference : Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th ed. – A.K.Khurana, Ch-1 Anatomy and development of eye

329.q: Which of the following is true about Cloquet's canal?
o: The hyaloid artery in a foetus runs through it
Contains the primary vitreous at birth
Runs from lens to optic disc
329.e: Cloquet’s canal, which contains the primary vitreous at birth, runs straight from the lens to the optic disc. The secondary vitreous eventually becomes liquefied and shrinks. Between 40 and 70 years of age in most individuals and earlier in myopes, vitreous liquefaction or syneresis occurs; the vitreous mass gradually shrinks and collapses, causing its separation from the retina, a condition known as PVD. Condensations of the vitreous fibrils are present within this liquefied vitreous and are visible as floaters. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the eye, 23 rd ed. Ch 17-Diseases of retina and vitreous

329.q: Which muscle originates in the orbital apex above the annulus of Zinn?
329.e: Explanation: The superior oblique and levator palpebrae muscles originate in the orbital apex superior to the annulus. All the recti muscles arise in a fibrous ring around the optic foramen to the nasal side of the axis of the eye, the annulus of Zinn, and are inserted in the sclera by flat tendinous insertions about 10 mm broad. The medial rectus is inserted into the sclera about 5.5 mm to the nasal side of the corneoscleral margin, the inferior rectus 6.6 mm below, the lateral rectus 7 mm to the temporal side and the superior rectus 7.75 mm above The inferior oblique originates behind the lacrimal fossa.

329.q: The ophthalmic artery provides blood supply to which of the following structures of the eye?
o: The nucleus of the crystalline lens
329.e: The cornea and the crystalline lens are the avascular structures of the eye. The remaining structures are supplied by the branches of ophthalmic artery which is a branch of internal carotid artery. Reference: Parson, 22nd Edition, Pg no. 238-244.

329.q: Each rectus muscle is supplied by two to three anterior ciliary arteries, except:
329.e: The lateral rectus is supplied by one anterior ciliary artery. Reference : kurana 2/e, p. 47

329.q: The only extraocular muscle taking origin from anterior part of orbit is
329.e: The inferior oblique muscle has its origin on the maxillary bone just posterior to the inferior medial orbital rim and lateral to the nasolacrimal canal. The inferior oblique is the only extraocular muscle to have its anatomic origin in the anterior orbit. Reference: Kanski, 5 th ed, Page no. 529.

330.q: True about rigid gas-permeable lenses are
o: Copolymer of PMMA and silicone and cellulose acetate butyrate.
They resist deposits and are less likely than soft contact lenses to harbour bacteria.
330.e: Oxygen-permeable or rigid gas-permeable lenses are made of a firm, durable plastic that transmits oxygen, e.g., a copolymer of PMMA and silicone and cellulose acetate butyrate. As they do not contain water, they resist deposits and are less likely than soft contact lenses to harbour bacteria. Oxygen-permeable lenses are easy to clean and disinfect, do not dehydrate and last longer than soft lenses. The rigidity of oxygen permeable lenses also means that they are easier to handle than soft lenses. As they retain their shape better, they provide sharper vision. Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 87

330.q: A 15-year-old girl experiences blurry vision OS and a frontal headache. Her acuities are 20/20 OD and 20/60 without correction OS. With -2.00 D refraction she sees 20/20 OS. In the light, pupils measure 6 mm OD and 1 mm OS and in the dark they measure 7 mm OD and 1 mm OS. The right pupil is briskly reactive; the left does not react to light or near stimuli. Her examination is otherwise unremarkable. What type of drop did she use?
330.e: A sympathomimetic drop would dilate the pupil, not constrict the pupil. It would not produce a myopic shift, and the pupil would remain reactive to light and near stimuli. A prostaglandin inhibitor would have no effect on the pupil, and an alpha adrenergic agent would have the same effect as a sympathomimetic. Only a parasympathomimetic drop would constrict the pupil and induce the myopic shift. Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 222/424.

330.q: An emmetropic 12 year old child has a near point of 10 cm. So amplitude of accommodation is
330.e: 1/ 0.1 - 1 / infinity = 10 D Range of accommodation Distance between far (infinity) and near point (30 cm) Power of accommodation Refractive power of eye in fully accommodative state - power at rest = power to focus at near - power to focus at far. The amplitude of accommodation is a measure of the closest point at which the eyes can focus: it is the range from the far point to the near point in dioptres. Because it is measured from the far point, the measurement needs to be taken with the distance correction in place. The amplitude of accommodation (Am) is mathematically expressed as the dioptric difference between the far point (fp) and the near point (np) of the eye and it is related to the maximum power variation that can perform an eye. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

330.q: Spherical equivalent of this prescription +3DS / + 2 DC at 90 degree is
330.e: Take half the value of the cylinder and Add it to the sphere power. In other words, as a formula the spherical equivalent Spherical Equivalent = Sphere + (Cylinder)/2 Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

330.q: The critical angle refers to the angle of incidence in the denser medium, corresponding to which angle of refraction in the rarer medium is:
330.e: The angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is 90 degrees is called as the critical angle. The critical angle is the angle of incidence above which the total internal reflection occurs. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

330.q: The end point of streak retinoscopy is:
o: Streak disappears and the pupil appears completely light or dark
Just reversal of the red reflex
330.e: When streak retinoscopy is performed, the width of the reflex widens progressively as the neutralization is approached, and at the end point, streak disappears and the pupil appears completely illuminated or completely dark Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

330.q: While performing duochrome test, if the patient reports that he sees red letters more clear than green, it indicates that he is slightly:
330.e: If the letters of the green side are clearer +0.25 D sphere is added If the letters on the red side are clearer -0.25 D sphere is added Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

330.q: Soft contact lenses are made of:
330.e: Types of contact lenses Hard contact lenses Semi soft Soft Modern soft contact lenses are made of hydrogel and silicon hydrogel polymers. Hard contacts are made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) or Plexiglas. Soft contacts are mass-produced, but hard contact lenses are made to fit the wearer. The main hydrogel material used for soft contacts is poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate), usually called poly-HEMA Soft contact lenses Problems of deposits Daily disposables, Weekly, Monthly Continuous wear lenses – over 30 nights Increased water content and permeability for oxygen Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

331.q: Calculate amplitude of accommodation where patient is myopia - 2D, near point 10 cm
331.e: 2 D is already given as power to focus at far so Amplitude will be 1/ 0.1 - 2 = 10 -2 = 8 D Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

331.q: One millimeter decrease in axial length of the eyeball leads to hypermetropia of:
331.e: Shortening of eyeball induces a hypermetropia of + 3 D Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

Pseudo Myopia: This type of myopia is called as false appearance of myopia that occurs due to excessive accommodation and spasms of accommodation.This type of myopia usually manifest the execessive amount of myopia and decreased amount of hypermetropia. It could cause severe headache with asthenopic complaints. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

331.q: One millimeter increase in the radius of curvature of cornea leads to hypermetropia of:
331.e: (Normal axial length is 24mm). A decrease of 1mm in axial length produces a hypermetropia of 3.0D. Curvature Hypermetropia: When the curvature of the cornea or lens is flatter than normal. An increase of 1mm in its radius of curvature produces a hypermetropia of 6. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

331.q: A female patient wants LASIK surgery for her eye. She asks for your opinion. All the following things are suitable for performing LASIK surgery except:
331.e: C/I of LASIK Age CCT Unstable refractive error for last 6 months Keratoconus Pregnancy Any active inflammatory/ infective intraocular disorder Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

Pathological/degenerative myopia More frequency of degenerations like lattice, snow flake More chances of Retinal detachments Choroidal hemorrhage in macula: foster fuch’s spot Lacquer cracks: breaks in bruch’s membrane Myopic crescent: disparity b/t sclera ( globe enlarges) and RPE Posterior staphyloma: ectasia of sclera Large disc, large disc cup ratio Visibility of choroidal vessels, RPE thinning Tilted disc: dragging of retina nasally over disc Other features in myopia Large eyeball Far point comes near Does not accommodate for near → convergence insufficiency → exophoria Deep AC POAG, Pigmentary glaucoma, nuclear cataract Low ocular rigidity Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

331.q: During retinoscopy with a plane mirror from a distance of 1 M, no movement of pupillary red reflex with the movement of the mirror indicates:
331.e: With movement of the red reflex along the movement of the retinoscope indicates either emmetropia or hypermetropia or myopia of less than 1D. Against movement of the red reflex to the movement of the retinoscope implies myopia of more than 1D No movement implies myopia of – 1D Bright and fast shadow is seen in the pupillary area which moves rapidly with the movement of the mirror, in patients with low degrees of refractive errors. Dull reflex which moves slowly with the movement of the mirror is seen in patients with high degrees of ametropia. When using a streak retinoscope of red reflex is narrow with a high degree of ametropia and the wide reflex means a low degree of ametropia. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

331.q: Foster fuch spots can be seen in
331.e: Two typical ophthalmoscopic appearances are seen in high myopia—changes at the disc typified in the development of a myopic crescent, and changes in the central area of the fundus described as chorioretinal myopic degeneration. Degenerative changes also occur at the periphery of the retina which may lead to a retinal detachment, and degenerative changes in the vitreous are common, giving rise to dust-like vitreous opacities or large floaters composed of elements of the vitreous framework. These 'floaters' are seen more plainly by myopic than by other eyes because the entoptic image is larger. These degenerative changes may have serious visual consequences; in fact, they are among the more common causes of severe visual disability. Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 79

332.q: While performing subjective verification of refraction, the cross cylinder is used to check:
o: Axis of the cylinder to be prescribed
Power of the cylinder to be prescribed
332.e: Cross cylinder examination (otherwise known as Jackson's cross cylinder, JCC) is an examination used to refine the astigmatic refraction by fine-tuning the axis and strength of astigmatism. While a rough estimate can be obtained via retinoscopy or automated refractometry, cross-cylinder examination remains invaluable in fine-tuning the refraction for best vision. It confirm the axis and power of cylinder both Eg of types of JCC 0.25 JCC = +0.25DS/-0.50DC X 90 0.50 JCC = +0.50DS/-1.00DC X 90 1.00 JCC = +1.00DS/-2.00DC X 90 Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

332.q: Causes of premature presbyopia include all of the following except:
332.e: Rather in uncorrected myopia presbyopia occurs late, as they already have a good near vision without glasses Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

332.q: If the youth is in poor health or does much near work the perpetual overaction of the ciliary muscle is likely to produce symptoms; the condition is often called
332.e: In the young, the condition may cause no symptoms. When symptoms are present or arise, they are chiefly referable to the abnormal amount of accommodation to which these eyes are subjected, and to the lack of balance between accommodation and convergence. A healthy youth has an ample reserve of accommodation, and if hypermetropic, can accommodate for distant and near objects without being conscious of the act. If the youth is in poor health or does much near work the perpetual overaction of the ciliary muscle is likely to produce symptoms; the condition is often called accommodative asthenopia or 'eye strain' Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 79

332.q: Which of the following is an example of compound myopic, against the rule astigmatism:
332.e: When eyewear prescriptions are written, they can be classified into different areas depending on the power or refractive error. There are seven categories to which prescriptions can fall: Simple Hyperopia, the Rx will be (+) sphere Simple Myopia, the Rx will be (-) sphere Simple Myopic Astigmatism, the Rx will be plano (-) Simple Hyperopic Astigmatism, the Rx will be (+) Compound Hyperopic Astigmatism, major meridian power will be (+)(+) on both 90 and 180 degree axis Compound Myopic Astigmatism, major meridian power will be (-)(-) on both 90 and 180 degree axis Mixed Astigmatism, major meridian powers will be opposites (-)(+) (+)(-) on both 90 and 180 degree axis

o: Vertical meridian is more curved than the horizontal
Horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical
332.e: Astigmatism WTR is produced when the corneal curvature is steepest in the vertical meridian; conversely astigmatism ATR is produced when the steepest corneal meridian is horizontal. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

332.q: Which type of astigmatism is most likely associated with keratoconus?
332.e: The cornea is at first transparent and the vision is impaired due to myopic astigmatism. The patient becomes myopic, but the error of refraction cannot be satisfactorily corrected with ordinary glasses owing to the parabolic nature of the curvature which leads to irregular astigmatism in the later stages. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

332.q: Cases in which astigmatism causes asthenopic symptoms
332.e: If the astigmatic error is small (less than 0.5 D) and not associated with symptoms, spectacles are unnecessary unless the highest visual acuity is desired. However, in all cases in which astigmatism causes asthenopic symptoms, full optical correction should be ordered for constant use, that is, both for distant and near vision. Other measures are rigid contact lenses, Toric contact lenses, astigmatic LASIK (1.5-5 D), arcuate keratotomy and Toric phakic IOLs. Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 82

332.q: Because of circle of least diffusion, the distant vision is comparatively good in:
332.e: Circle of least confusion/diffusion: The smallest cross-section of a blur circle between the two focal lines formed by the astigmatic lens. Also defined as “At the dioptric midpoint of focal lines the cross-section of sturm's Conoid appears as a circular patch of light rays with best overall focus. If the retina is placed at the ” Circle of least diffusion” of Strum's conoid, the distant vision is often found to be surprisingly good with a relatively high degree of mixed astigmatism. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

333.q: Which of the following are indications for Pterygium surgery?
333.e: A pterygium is best left alone unless it is progressing towards the pupillary area, causes excessive astigmatism, a restriction of ocular motility or is disfiguring. Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

333.q: Which of the following is/are indications for Pterygium surgery?
333.e: Explanation: Indications for removal of Pterygium: Progression towards the pupillary area Excessive astigmatism Restriction of ocular motility Cosmetic disfigurement

333.q: Which is false regarding viral conjunctivitis
o: Topical antibiotics are treatment of choice
333.e: Topical antibiotics have a role in bacterial conjunctivitis In viral they can be given for prophylaxis from secondary bacterial infection Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva
Ans. A. Squamous cell Ca Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant lesion of the conjunctiva"

333.q: Where does the limbal part of conjunctiva derive its blood supply from?
333.e: Explanation: The limbal part of the conjunctiva derives its blood supply from Both the anterior and posterior conjunctival arteries. Blood Supply of the Conjunctiva: Marginal Conjunctiva: Supplied by the marginal arcade of the eyelid. Forniceal Conjunctiva: Supplied by the peripheral arcade of the eyelid. Limbal (Bulbar) Conjunctiva: Supplied by both: Posterior conjunctival arteries: Branches of the peripheral arterial arcade of the eyelids. Anterior conjunctival arteries: Branches of the anterior ciliary arteries. These two systems anastomose near the limbus (corneal margin) to form the pericorneal plexus.

333.q: Sub-mandibular nodes receive lymphatics from which part of conjunctiva?
333.e: The lymphatic drainage is to the submandibular nodes, which drain the medial one-third of the superior conjunctiva and the medial two-thirds of the inferior conjunctiva, and the preauricular nodes, which drain the lateral two-thirds of the superior conjunctiva and lateral one-third of the inferior conjunctiva. Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

333.q: Which type of conjunctival secretions are most likely seen in Vernal Kerato-Conjunctivitis?
333.e: The nature of the secretion is of diagnostic importance. Bacterial: Muco-purulent/ purulent Viral: Serous Allergic (VKC): White stringy/ ropy Acute allergic ( Bee sting): Chemosis+lid edema Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

333.q: Which of the following statements regarding management of bacterial conjunctivitis is incorrect?
o: Topical antibiotics are mainstay in treatment.
Topical steroid use is not indicated.
Systemic antibiotics will be required in pre-septal cellulitis.
Use of bandage is recommended for associated photophobia.
333.e: Management of Bacterial conjunctivitis: Topical anti-biotics: Broad spectrum drugs ( Ofloxacin/ chloramphenicol) 4-6 times a day Topical steroids: Not indicated Systemic anti-biotics: in case of pyrexia/ pre-septal cellulitis Use of bandage: contra-indicated- prevents drainage of secretions/ increases local temperature and promotes bacterial growth For photophobia, sun glasses can be used. Pad and bandage can promote growth of more bacteria Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

334.q: Sclera is outer coat of eye ball. It is
334.e: The sclera is the white outer coating of the eye. It is tough, fibrous tissue that extends from the cornea(the clear front section of the eye) to the optic nerve at the back of the eye. The sclera gives the eyeball its white color. Reference: Parson 22/e, Pg: 67.

334.q: Sclera is not transparent due to
o: Collagen bundles in sclera are of varying sizes and are irregularly arranged
334.e: The sclera proper, also known as the scleral stroma, is also called the substantia propria. Ultrasructurally, sclera is composed of: Collagen bundles Elastic fibers Fibroblasts Ground substances These components are responsible for its non-transparent nature. The ground substances consist of proteoglycans and glycoproteins. The collagen bundles in the sclera vary in size and are irregularly arranged, which is why the sclera is not transparent like the cornea. These variations in scleral collagen fibers are more pronounced in the mid-sclera, where the diameter of the fibers ranges from 50 to 400 nm. Reference: Parson 22/e, Pg: 45.

334.q: Most common systemic association of scleritis is
334.e: RA is the most commonly associated with scleritis, which is an inflammation of the sclera characterized by vasodilation of the superficial and deep episcleral vessels. Occasionally, scleritis may present before the onset of joint symptoms in the RA patient. It may also occur as a manifestation of systemic vasculitis. However, The most common eye-related symptom of rheumatoid arthritis is dryness. Reference: parson's 22/e section II chapter 16 diseases of the sclera. Pg 228.

335.q: Most common protozoan causing keratitis is
335.e: Ans. is `b' i.e., Acanthamoeba [Ref Kanski 8th/e p. 197] "Acanthamoeba keratitis is the most common keratitis caused by a protozoan especially in contact lens users".

335.q: All of the following microbial organisms are implicated in development of ICK except?
335.e: It is hypothesized that commensal organisms from periocular skin or the ocular surface gain access to the stroma via suture tracks or through compromised unhealthy corneal epithelium. Microorganisms that can produce this type of infection include α haemolytic Streptococcus, Peptostreptococcus, Pseudomonas and Candida, and prolonged treatment with topical vancomycin, moxifloxacin or gatifloxacin eyedrops with discontinuation or minimization of topical steroid use is generally required. Recurrence of infection and stromal scarring are common which may then require keratoplasty. Neisseriae Gonnorhoea is a highly virulent micro-organism that can invade healthy corneal epithelium whereas ICK is caused by low grade (low virulent) commensal micro-organisms that affect damaged corneal epithelium. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

335.q: Which of the following organisms is not implicated in development of marginal corneal ulcers?
335.e: Marginal/ Catarrhal ulcers occur near the limbus, especially in old people. Aetiology: As an immune reaction to toxins produced by staphylococcal organisms residing in the conjunctival sac or lids in patients with chronic meibomianitis or blepharitis; they also occur in association with a chronic conjunctivitis and may be caused by Moraxella or Haemophilus. Pseudomonas is implicated in development of contact lens induced keratitis. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

335.q: Where are the corneal stem cells situated?
335.e: The corneal physiology is designed in such a way to maintain transparency and take care of healing and/or regeneration capacity of the cornea. In case the cornea sustains injury due to any cause such as trauma, infection or surgery, and if the injury is superficial involving only the epithelium, the stratified squamous epithelium covering the anterior surface of the cornea rapidly regenerates. This regeneration of corneal epithelial cells is mainly from stem cells, which are epithelial cells present as palisades of Vogt at the limbus. These mitotically active cells with an increased surface area of basal cells present in folds, and palisades are ideally suited for this purpose. There is very little mitotic activity in the basal cells at the centre of the cornea. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Edition 23rd- Chap 12- Diseases of the cornea

335.q: Ocular involvement with Herpes Simplex can include which of the following conditions?
335.e: Ocular involvement with the herpes simplex virus (HSV) has varied manifestations which include blepharitis, conjunctivitis, keratitis and iridocyclitis. The corneal involvement can be epithelial (dendritic or geographic keratitis), stromal (necrotizing and non-necrotizing stromal keratitis) and endothelial. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

335.q: Which type of corneal vascularisation is seen in Cogan's Syndrome?
335.e: Deep vascularization occurs, consisting of radial bundles of brush-like vessels, and since they are covered with a layer of hazy cornea, their bright scarlet is toned down to a dull reddish pink (‘salmon patches’), wherein separate vessels can be seen only with difficulty. The opacity extends a little beyond the vessels, which seem to push the opacity in front of them and at the height of the condition the vessels run in radial bundles almost, but seldom quite, to the centre of the cornea. There is often a moderate degree of superficial vascularization, but it never extends far over the cornea and at the limbus the conjunctiva may be heaped up. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

335.q: Which virus is implicated in development of Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO)?
335.e: Herpes zoster is caused by the same virus that causes chickenpox (varicella zoster virus). Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

335.q: How long does it take for a superficial epi-defect to heal?
335.e: Loss of epithelium is termed as epithelial defect and can be demonstrated clearly by staining with 1% sodium fluorescein dye and viewed with cobalt blue filtered light. If superficial without any inflammation, an epithelial defect is also called an abrasion or erosion and usually heals within 12–24 hours by regeneration of the epithelial cells from the periphery, which slide over to cover the defect. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Edition 23rd- Chap 12- Diseases of the cornea

336.q: Which drug is implicated in development of Argyrosis?
336.e: Pigmentation may occur from the prolonged topical use of silver nitrate (argyrosis). It is due to the permanent impregnation of the elastic fibres, particularly the Descemet's membrane, with metallic silver. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 - Diseases of Cornea

336.q: Which of the following investigations / results support diagnosis of keratoconus?
o: Topography: cone shaped lesion with astigmatism
336.e: Keratometer: The keratometer mires are malformed, malaligned and malfocussed. Corneal topography: In the early stages, the condition is diagnosed with corneal topography, which demonstrates the cone and typical astigmatic pattern. Corneal thinness can also be measured with ultrasonic pachymetry or the Orbscan II corneal topography system. With the ophthalmoscope or a plane mirror at a distance of 1 m, a ring of shadow, concentric with the margin, is seen in the red reflex (resembling a droplet of oil), which alters its position on moving the mirror. It is due to a zone through which a few rays pass into the observer’s eye, as the emergent rays in the centre are convergent while those on the periphery are divergent. Refraction: irregular myopic astigmatism Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

336.q: Which of the following tests are performed as part of donor screening for eye donation?
336.e: Cadaveric allograft corneal tissue and sclera are made available for transplantation by eye banks by the process of eye donation organized by eye banks. With consent of the legal next of kin (parents/spouse/sibling/progeny/grandparents/grandchildren), the eyes are harvested and tissues processed before releasing for transplantation. Donors are screened for known contraindications by medical and social history, clinical examination and serological screening of a donor blood sample for transmissible infectious diseases such as HIV/AIDS, HbsAG, hepatitis C and syphilis. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

336.q: What is the pattern of corneal opacities seen in Theil-Behnke dystrophy?
336.e: Corneal opacities in Theil-Behnke dystrophy: typically reticular (honeycomb) in pattern . Corneal opacities in Reis-Bucklers dystrophy: irregular, coarse, geographic shaped opacities at the level of the Bowman layer and superficial stroma. Finger print/ dot pattern is seen in Epithelial Basement Membrane dystrophy-EBMD Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Edition 23rd- Chap 12- Diseases of the cornea

336.q: Following corneal transplantation, most common infection occur ?
336.e: Ans. A. Staph epidermidis Pneumococcus and staphylococcus aureus have been found to be the commonest microorganisms in the developed world, whereas staph epidermidis is the commonest in developing countries, for causing infectious keratitis after corneal transplantations.

336.q: What is the allowed time frame for harvesting corneas from cadaveric donors?
336.e: Donor corneas are harvested from cadaveric donors within 6–8 hours after death, sometimes up to 12 hours after death in countries with cold climates or if the donor is refrigerated. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

336.q: Which of the following is /are likely causes of graft failure?
336.e: Major causes of graft failure include primary failure due to poor donor endothelium, graft infection, graft rejection and recurrence of the primary disease in the graft. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

336.q: Which of the following elements is not useful for keratoprosthesis fixation?
336.e: The basic design of a keratoprosthesis includes a central optical cylinder made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) with a surrounding fixation device which is of different designs in terms of shape, size and material. Some of the materials used for the latter include methacrylate, Teflon, Dacron mesh, polycarbon, tooth and bone (osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis), cartilage (chondro-keratoprosthesis) or nail (onycho-keratoprosthesis). PMMA is used for central optical cylinder making. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

337.q: A 78-year-old man experienced unilateral sudden loss of vision 1 year previously. Currently, he complains of severe pain in that eye. Examination reveals no light-perception vision, intraocular pressure of 72 mm Hg, iris neovascularization and evidence of a central retinal vein occlusion. What would the least helpful topical therapeutic agent be at this time?
337.e: The management of a painful blind eye with end-stage glaucoma can include topical cycloplegia (anticholinergic agent) and a corticosteroid agent for comfort. A topical beta blocker may provide relatively little intraocular pressure lowering but may provide some increased comfort. Eyes with end-stage iris neovascularization and neovascular glaucoma have completely or near completely closed angles. A cholinergic agent, such as pilocarpine, will not successfully reduce intraocular pressure in these eyes and will often increase pain and inflammation. Reference: Parsons 22nd Edition/303

337.q: Which statement regarding Muller cells is false?
o: They are modified glial cells that provide structural framework supporting neural elements in the retina.
Their nuclei lie in the outer nuclear layer
Their basal processes extend out to form the inner surface of the retina (inner limiting membrane).
The apical or outer cell processes extend beyond the outer nuclear layer, where they are connected to the photoreceptors by a system of terminal bars that comprise the external limiting membrane.
337.e: The nuclei of the Muller cells lie in the inner nuclear layer, whereas the nuclei of the photoreceptors lie in the outer nuclear layer. Reference : kurana 3/e,p. 46

337.q: Which statement about the RPE is false?
o: The RPE interdigitates with the apical processes of the rod and cone segments.
RPEs are densely adherent to Bruch's membrane
RPEs comprise the inner blood-retinal barrier
RPE cells are taller and contain a greater concentration of pigment in the macula
337.e: RPE cells comprise the outer blood–retinal barrier; the inner blood– retinal barrier consists of the endothelium lining the retinal blood vessels. Reference : kurana 4/e, p. 40

337.q: There is increased risk of Rhegmatogenous RD in all of the following except
337.e: Rhegmatogenous RD Pathophysiology The essential lesion is a rhegma (retinal break) through which the liquefied vitreous gains access to the retina. This liquefied vitreous accumulates beneath the neurosensory retina leading to RD. This is commonly seen in: High myopes: Peripheral retinal degenerations like lattice degeneration, holes and breaks with used liquefaction of overlying vitreous predispose to RD Trauma Aphakia Pseudophakia Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition/648

337.q: Which gas is used in Pneumatic Retinopexy
337.e: Pneumatic retinopexy: In this procedure, the neurosensory retina is pushed towards the RPE by injecting an expansile gas in the vitreous cavity. The break is then sealed with laser. The gases commonly used are Sulphur Hexafluoride (SF6) and Perfluoropropane (C3F8) Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition/648

Purtscher's retinopathy It is blockage of the retinal capillaries by emboli leading to multiple hemorrhages and cotton wool spots throughout the retina Causes are Acute pancreatitis Head and chest trauma. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Fat embolism Chronic renal failure Amniotic fluid embolism SLE Scleroderma Reference: Yanoff and Duker 6th edition/479

337.q: Normal ratio of artery: vein in retina is
337.e: Retinal arteries are end arteries, branch dichomatously Artery : venous caliber ratio (AV ratio) = 2 : 3 Anastomosis at : lamina cribrosa Reference: parson's 22/e section IV chapter 20. pg 310-retinal vessels

337.q: What is the presumed cause of venous obstruction in branched retinal vein occlusion?
o: The retinal artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath
Retinal hemorrhages result in reduced venous flow
337.e: Systemic hypertension causes hardening of the retinal arterioles. At the point where the retinal arterioles and venules cross, they are connected by a common adventitial sheath, which binds them together. The sclerotic arteriole causes a deformation of the venule's lumen, resulting in turbulent blood flow and a blood clot. Reference: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 8th Edition, Page Number-539.

338.q: All of the following are seen in RP except
338.e: Rather the vessles become thin and attenuated in retinitis pigmentosa. This is most consistent sign in RP also. Reference: parson's 22/e section IV, chapter 20. pg. 328.RP

338.q: A patient is suffering from gyrate atrophy of choroid which is due to the deficiency of enzyme Ornithine aminotransferase. Which of the following is beneficial for the patient?
338.e: Ornithine aminotransferase deficiency (also known as gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina) is an inborn error of ornithine metabolism, caused by decreased activity of the enzyme ornithine aminotransferase. Biochemically, it can be detected by elevated levels of ornithine in the blood. Clinically, it presents initially with poor night vision, which slowly progresses to total blindness . It is believed to be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Research suggests there can be some adverse effect on muscles and also the brain. The cause of this is somewhat unclear but may relate to very low levels of creatine often found in this population. Treatment may include vitamin B6, lysine or dramatic dietary change to minimize arginine from patient's diet . Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 473.

338.q: Which of the following is not a common ocular association in retinitis pigmentosa?
338.e: Ocular associations of retinitis pigmentosa include myopia, primary open-angle glaucoma, microphthalmos, conical cornea (keratoconus) and posterior subcapsular cataract. Reference: Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th edition – A.K.Khurana, Chapter-12 Diseases of retina.

338.q: What is the most common cause of choroidal neurovascularization?
338.e: Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) consists of a blood vessel complex that extends through Bruch membrane from the choriocapillaris into the sub-retinal pigment epithelium (type 1) or subretinalspace (type 2). Age related macular degeneration is the most common causative association, followed by myopic degeneration. Causes of choroid neovascularization(CNV): Degenerative conditions - Age related macular degeneration, myopia, angioid streaks. Inflammatory or infectious conditions - Histoplasmosis, sarcoidosis, multifocal choroiditis Choroidal tumors Choroidal rupture Laser photocoagulation Idiopathic Hypermetropia does not cause CNV. Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 462.

338.q: Epiretinal membrane is most commonly associated with which one of the following conditions?
338.e: Although epiretinal membrane may be associated with trauma, retinal venous occlusion, and uveitis, it is most commonly associated with posterior vitreous detachment. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/618

338.q: Which of the following is true for feature of fundus flavimaculatus?
o: Scrambled egg appearance at the fovea
White or yellowish-white deep retinal flecks
338.e: Fundus flavimaculatus is a flecked retinal dystrophy affecting both eyes and appears usually in the third or fourth decade of life. White or yellowish white deep retinal flecks resembling fish tails with fuzzy outlines as seen with the ophthalmoscope are characteristic. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the eye, 23 rd edition, Chapter 17 - Diseases of retina and vitreous.

338.q: Which of the following is not a feature of Refsum's syndrome?
338.e: Refsum's syndrome is characterised by retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy and cerebellar ataxia. Reference: Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th edition – A.K.Khurana, Chapter-12 Diseases of retina.

338.q: A 20 year old male presents with complaints of diminished night vision since two years. On fundus examination, he was found to have features of retinitis pigmentosa. Systemic examination showed obesity, mental defect, polydactyly and hypogonadism. What is the most probable syndrome he's suffering from?
338.e: Laurence-Moon-Biedl-Bardet syndrome is characterised by retinitis pigmentosa, obesity, hypogenitalism, polydactyly and mental deficiency. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the eye, 23 rd edition, Chapter 17 - Diseases of retina and vitreous.

339.q: What is not a cause of monocular diplopia
339.e: Monocular Diplopia Monocular diplopia is usually attributable to refractive or media abnormalities. Common causes include uncorrected astigmatism, corneal irregularities, tear film abnormalities, cataract, etc. The hallmark of monocular diplopia from refractive abnormalities is improvement with pinhole. KIDS(pneumonic) Keratoconus/astigmatism Incipient cataract Double pupil/trauma Subluxated lens Reference: kanski, 5 th Edition, Page no. 544.

339.q: What is the inheritance pattern of Wagner's syndrome ?
339.e: Wagner's syndrome has an autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance with following features: Vitreous is liquified with condensed membranes. Retina shows narrow and sheathed vessels, and pigmented spots in the periphery. Choroid may be atrophied. Cataract may develop as late complication. Reference : Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7 th ed. – A.K.Khurana, Ch-12 Diseases of retina

339.q: The most frequent cataract type seen in adult retinitis pigmentosa patient is
339.e: Cataracts are recognized as the most common anterior segment complication of RP. The opacity of lens generally happens at the mid stage of the disease course with obvious clinical symptoms and signs, and the major symptom is glare, especially in bright light. As these are complicated cataracts and are posterior subcapsular cataracts the most common prob is that of glare. Reference: parson's 22/e section IV, chapter 20. pg-327-328. RP

339.q: Crystalline lens absorbs light rays shorter than:
339.e: The crystalline lens absorbs almost all incident energy to wavelengths of nearly 400 nm. In youth, a very small amount of UV-A reaches the retina, but the lens becomes more absorbing with age. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

339.q: Accommodation is maximum at the age of:
339.e: Accommodation is a dynamic process in which the curvature of the eye's natural lens is temporarily adjusted to improve focus at near or in eyes that are hyperopic (far-sighted). Accommodative convergence described the normal convergence of the eyes in response to accommodation of the lens It is strongest in children, gets weakened with age Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

339.q: Which of the following is most common type of congenital cataract causing diminished vision?
339.e: Zonular or lamellar cataract is the most common type of congenital cataract associated with diminished vision. A zone in the foetal nucleus is usually affected. Hypocalcemia in pregnancy is an important cause. Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 415/416

339.q: Rubella in pregnancy is important cause in causing which of the following cataracts?
339.e: Nuclear cataract usually affects the embryonic nucleus . Rubella in pregnancy is an important cause. In maternal rubella infection, after 6 weeks of gestation , the virus can penetrate the lens capsule causing unilateral or bilateral, dense, nuclear opacities at birth, or they may develop several weeks or months later. Extra information - lamellar/ zonular cataract can also be seen in rubella. The congenital rubella retinitis may present as a salt and-pepper fundus appearance. Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 415/416

339.q: True about lens of the eye is all except
339.e: Origin is from surface ecotoderm, not neural ectoderm. Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition/329

340.q: Intraocular lens (IOL) which can correct astigmatism is
340.e: Toric IOLs have an integral cylindrical refractive component to compensate for pre-existing corneal astigmatism . The main potential problem is rotation within the capsular bag (rare), and may be corrected by early surgical repositioning. Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 368

340.q: Endophthalmitis involve all the layers of the eyeball except
340.e: Endophthalmitis is the most dreaded and worst possible complication of cataract surgery. It is a suppurative inflammation starting from the vitreous which extends to all the parts of the eye except the sclera . If the sclera also becomes involved , the condition is then called as panophthalmitis . Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 724/725

340.q: Which of the following is/are not complications noted in early post-operative period of keratoplasty?
340.e: Complications in the early postoperative period include wound leak, shallow anterior chamber, persistent or nonhealing epithelial defect, secondary glaucoma, graft oedema, uveitis, graft infection, inflammatory ‘sterile’ suture infiltrates and primary graft failure. In the late postoperative period (after 3 weeks), complications include graft rejection, graft infection, secondary glaucoma, loose sutures and high astigmatism. Very late complications (after 1 year) include graft rejection and wound dehiscence from minor trauma and recurrence of the primary disease. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

340.q: Treatment of traumatic cataract in children ?
340.e: Ans. A. ECCE + IOL Traumatic cataract in children is a common cause of unilateral loss of vision. Penetrating injuries are usually more common than blunt injuries. At the time of presentation after trauma to eye, primary repair of the corneal or scleral wound is usually preferred, Cataract surgery GCCE) with IOL implantations is performed later following complete evaluation of damage to the intraocular structures by ancillary methods such as B-scan ultrasonography.

340.q: Expulsive hemorrhage in cataract surgery is from?
340.e: Ans, B. Ciliary artery Expulsive hemorrhage after cataract extraction or glaucoma surgery = Rupture of ciliary artery. Expulsive hemorrhage in Retinal/Vitrous operation = Direct trauma to choroidal or vortex vein.

340.q: Best option to correct aphakia is
340.e: IOL implantation has the following advantages: Minimal after-care of patient Minimum aniseikonia (difference in image size seen by the eyes) Rapid return of binocularity and Normal peripheral vision Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 85

340.q: Which one of the following single changes results in the selection of a lens more powerful than intended?
o: Using an A-constant of 116.8 instead of 117.3
Axial length measured as 20.5 mm rather than 20.2 mm
Average keratometry of 44.50 D in place of 44.00 D
Placing the lens in the ciliary sulcus instead of in the capsular bag
340.e: The lens power formula is dependent on axial length (in millimetres) and keratometry (in dioptres) as follows: Lens power = A − 2.5 (axial length) − 0.9 (average keratometry) A higher 'A-constant', 'decreased axial length', or 'decreased keratometry' readings would result in the calculation of a stronger lens. Moving a convex (plus) lens more anteriorly in the eye and away from the nodal point also effectively increases its power. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e, P. 45

340.q: A patient had a -10 D myopic LASIK treatment years ago. Now, she presents for cataract surgery. All of the following measurements would be helpful in the calculation of the lens power for cataract surgery in this patient except:
340.e: A number of formulas have been developed to calculate the IOL power after LASIK and refractive surgery, including the Aramberri Double K method, clinical history method, Masket method, and others. These rely upon pre- and postoperative refractions and keratometry, the LASIK treatment, and adjustments to these measurements. Although corneal thickness may influence the curvature of the cornea, the actual corneal curvature measurements and refractions are the most useful in the calculations for lens power post-LASIK. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e, P. 51

341.q: All are considered emergencies in eye except
341.e: CRVO is not an emergency in eye The ocular emergencies are Ischemic optic neuropathy: rule out giant-cell arteritis (GCA) Central retina artery occlusion: rule out GCA and causes of emboli/thrombus Mac-on rhegmatogenous retinal detachmen Acute third nerve palsy: rule out intracranial aneurysm Open globe: rule out intraocular foreign body Acute angle closure glaucoma Endophthalmitis Alkali injury: requires urgent and copious irrigation Orbital cellulitis Reference: kanski 9/e chapter 22 pg. 892-916

341.q: In what condition are cycloplegic agents contraindicated during refraction?
o: Adverse side effects to anticholinergic drugs
341.e: The use of cycloplegic agents for cycloplegic refraction is an important part in the evaluation of patients with complaints pertaining to binocular vision and ocular motility. Adverse reactions to cycloplegic agents(anticholinergics) include allergic or hypersensitive reaction with conjunctivitis, eyelid edema and dermatitis. Psychological effects have been observed in children receiving the drug. Adverse reactions occur more frequently with atropine compared to other agents. Systemic intoxication from atropine manifests as dry mouth, fever, flushing of the face, rapid pulse, nausea, dizziness, delirium and erythema. Patients with previous adverse side effects are at risk for adverse reactions to further use of the offending cycloplegic agents. In none of the other conditions are cycloplegic drops contraindicated. Reference: Kanski, 6th edition, Pg no. 756.

341.q: Not a risk factor for angle closure glaucoma ?
341.e: Ans. D. Small lens Predisposing factors for PACG :- i) Shallow anterior chamber,ii) Short eye (short axiallensth),i1i) Smaller corneal diameter, iv) Anterior location of iris-lens diaphragm, v) Hlpermetropic eye, vi) Large lens (older cataractous).

341.q: Which type of cataract causes phacolytic glaucoma?
341.e: Morgagnian cataract can lead to phacolytic glaucoma and phacoanaphylactic uveitis. Hypermature cataract has two varieties. Sclerotic cataract : The lens becomes shrunken and small with calcification on the anterior capsule. There is wrinkling of the lens capsule. It predisposes to subluxation of lens. Morgagnian cataract : There is total liquefaction of the cortex as a result of which the nucleus sinks inferiorly. The liquefied cortex leaks through the intact capsule and blocks the trabecular meshwork. This leads to phacolytic glaucoma or lens protein glaucoma. It also causes phacoanaphylactic uveitis . Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 415-416

341.q: A male patient with a history of hypermature cataract presents with a 2 day history of ciliary congestion, photophobia, blurring of vision and on examination has a deep anterior chamber in the right eye. The left eye is normal the diagnosis is
341.e: This describes a case of HMSC morgagnian cataract with lens proteins blocking the TM and hence increase the IOP. It is a type of secondary open angle glaucoma. Reference: parson 21st edition pg 288

341.q: Epicanthal fold, Hypertelorism and Microphthalmos is seen in
341.e: Trisomy 13 Patau Syndrome Microphthalmos Colobomas Retinal dysplasia Cataract Corneal opacities Optic nerve hypoplasia Cyclopia Intra-ocular cartilage Trisomy 18 Edwards syndrome Blepharophimosis Ptosis Epicanthal fold Hypertelorism Microphthalmos Uveal coloboma Congenital glaucoma Corneal opacities Cataract and hypoplasia of optic nerves in both eyes, retinal dysplasia and Bergmeister's papilla Trisomy 21 G Trisomy or Down's syndrome Upward slanting palpebral fissure(Mongoloid slant) Almond-shaped palpebral fissure Epicanthus Telecanthus Narrowed interpupillary distance Esotropia High refractive errors Cataract Iris hypoplasia Keratoconus Reference: A. K. Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 439/440.

342.q: Recurrent anterior uveitis with increased intraocular tension is seen in ?
342.e: Ans. A. Posner schlossman syndrome Glamatocyclitic crisis (posner - Schlossman syndrome) is a unilateral recurrent non- granulomatous iritis that is associated with an elevated ocular pressure during the attacks'

342.q: All are complications of anterior uveitis except
342.e: Complications of uveitis Early: Secondary glaucoma - angle closure, trabeculitis Seclusio pupillae Occlusio pupillae Late: Secondary glaucoma - synechiae formation, steroid induced Cataract - complicated cataract Band shaped Keratopathy, Hypotony, Cystoid macular edema: cause of low vision in uveitis Optic neuritis, Phthisis bulbi: In chronic disorders of eye sometimes there is shrinkage of eyeball, architecture is lost, IOP becomes very low, sclera gets thickened and there is calcification. Reference: parson's 22/e, chapter 17 pg. 241 sequelae

342.q: Which ocular disease is generally characterized by normal intraocular pressure interrupted by recurrent episodes of markedly elevated intraocular pressure associated with low-grade anterior chamber inflammation?
342.e: Glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome) is a rare form of open-angle glaucoma characterized by recurrent attacks of mild anterior uveitis and marked elevation of intraocular pressure, often to 40-60 mm Hg. The condition is usually unilateral and affects middle-aged patients. The iritis is generally mild with small, discrete, round keratitic precipitates. The acute attack usually resolves within a few weeks. The intraocular pressure typically returns to normal between attacks, but a chronic glaucoma may develop over time with recurrent episodes. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis, pseudoexfoliation glaucoma, and pigmentary glaucoma are generally associated with chronic pressure elevation. Reference: Parsons 22nd edition/300pg

342.q: A 50-year-old man has recurrent episodes of markedly elevated IOP and low-grade anterior chamber inflammation. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Glaucoma associated with elevated episcleral venous pressure
342.e: Glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome) is a rare type of open-angle glaucoma typically affecting middle-aged adults. It usually presents with unilateral eye pain and blurred vision associated with markedly increased IOP (40-60 mm Hg). A mild iritis is present and resolves spontaneously within a few weeks. The IOP usually remains normal between episodes, but a chronic secondary glaucoma may develop with an increasing number of attacks. Angle-recession glaucoma, glaucoma associated with elevated episcleral venous pressure, and exfoliation glaucoma are all chronic forms of glaucoma that are not typically associated with ocular inflammation. Reference: PARSONS 22ND EDITION/300

342.q: Which of the following is not a possible cause of the salt and pepper appearance of the fundus in a patient?
342.e: Explanation: Tuberculosis is not associated with 'salt and pepper' appearance of fundus. Differential diagnoses of Salt & pepper fundus: Prenatal Rubella (Option A ruled out) Congenital Syphilis (Option B ruled out ) Varicella Mumps Retinitis pigmentosa Leber congenital amaurosis Drugs: Thioridazine (anti-psychotic) Ocular features of Tuberculosis: Anterior uveitis (granulomatous) Choroiditis: serpiginous pattern, multifocal Choroidal granulomas: known as Tubercles , focal elevated dome-shaped lesions Retinal vasculitis: retinal hemorrhages Interstitial keratitis Lupus vulgaris: Reddish-brown eyelid nodules Neuroretinitis (Optic neuropathy
