Ans. B. Cataract The most common complication of intermediate uveitis (pers ptanitis) is cystoid macular edema, which may decrease the visual acuity. 2nd most common complication is complicated cataract' Other complication includes retinal detachment.

342.q: Which ocular disease is characterized by the triad of iris heterochromia, iridocyclitis, and cataract?
342.e: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is an uncommon form of chronic iridocyclitis characterized by iris heterochromia with loss of iris pigment in the affected eye, low-grade iritis with stellate keratic precipitates, and posterior subcapsular cataract. The condition is usually unilateral and typically affects middle-aged adults. A secondary open angle glaucoma develops in approximately 15% of patients. Gonioscopy may reveal fine vessels in the anterior chamber angle, but these vessels do not lead to peripheral anterior synechiae formation or secondary angle closure. Cataract and heterochromia are not typical of Posner-Schlossman syndrome. ICE syndrome and Peters anomaly do not share any features of the triad. Reference: PARSONS 22ND EDITION/300

342.q: Which of the following statements is true about ciliary body?
o: Consists of pars plana and pars plicata
Contraction of ciliary body helps in accommodation
342.e: The ciliary body has three basic functions: Aqueous production and removal Helps in accommodation Formation of vitreous mucopolysaccharide The inner surface of the ciliary body is divided into two regions. The anterior part ( pars plicata ) is corrugated with a number of folds running in an anteroposterior direction. The posterior part (pars plana) is smooth . The arterial supply to the ciliary body is via the long posterior ciliary and anterior ciliary arteries. Reference: Parson, 22nd Edition, Pg no. 239-244.

343.q: Uveal effusion syndrome may be associated with all of the following, except
343.e: Uveal Effusion Syndrome(Ciliochoroidal Effusion) is an idiopathic disease of the retina and choroid characterized by abnormal accumulation of serous fluid in the outer layer of ciliary body or choroid. Clinical Features: Structurally abnormal sclera(Thick Sclera) Abnormal accumulation of serous fluid in the outer layer of ciliary body and choroid leading to Detachment of Ciliary body(Exudative) Detachment of Choroid(Exudative) Deep Ciliochoridal detachments Detachment of Retina(Exudative) Absence of inflammation or neoplastic disease Eyes maybe nanopthalmic (small) or hypermetropic Phthisis and hypotonia is usually due to ciliary body shutdown from chronic detachment which compromises the blood supply to the ciliary processes Mottling of pigment epithelium( Leopard spots ) may be seen after spontaneous resolution. Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 484.

343.q: Head light in fog appearance is seen in ?
343.e: Ans. B. Toxoplasmoss On fundoscopic examination, there is diffuse "headtightinthe fogappearance, in congenital toxoplasmosis. This is due to combination of active retinal lesion in the center with depigmentation (the headlight) and severe vitreous inflammation (the fog).

343.q: Which of the following is true about Birdshot Chorioretinopathy?
343.e: Birdshot chorioretinopathy is an uncommon idiopathic chronic/recurrent bilateral disease which predominantly affects females . Over 95% patients are positive for HLA A29 . The disease involves both the retina and choroid independently. Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 429, 467.

343.q: An individual infected with HIV has a necrotizing retinitis on fundus examination. Which of the following will be most helpful to make a diagnosis?
o: Serologic testing for herpes virus, including CMV
Blood culture for herpes virus, including CMV
343.e: Infection is the most likely cause of necrotizing retinitis in a HIV patient . The most common causes could be viral or parasitic(Toxoplasmosis). Vitreous biopsy is the most specific way to determine the cause. Option a/d - blood culture and serologic testing do not prove an intraocular infection, they are helpful only in ruling out the possibility of a viral infection. Option b - due to anergy, unreliable Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 450.

343.q: A 20 year old man complains of difficulty in reading the newspaper with his right eye, three weeks after sustaining a gun shot injury to his left eye. The most likely diagnosis is
343.e: Bilateral granulomatous non suppurative panuveitis after penetrating injury to ciliary body(Danger area of eye) It is thought that the penetrating trauma or surgery activates the afferent phase of an autoimmune reaction. This may be due to the exposure of sequestered ocular antigens to the immune system after trauma or an alteration of the immune tolerance to ocular antigens Occurs between 2 weeks to 3 months after injury, but cases are seen as early as 1 week and late as 10 years also. Symptom - loss of accommodation, photophobia Signs - Retrolental flare(inflammation behind lens) 1 st sign Hence loss of accommodation is the first symptom in this condition Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 12 trauma pg. 448

343.q: Which of the following structures is not a part of the posterior segment of the eye?
343.e: Explanation: Inside the eye, the globe is broadly divided into the anterior segment and posterior segment by the lens. The posterior segment, i.e. the part of the eye that lies behind the lens, is bounded internally by the ciliary body anteriorly and retina posteriorly. Structures present in the posterior segment include the retina, choroid, and the optic disc, and the cavity is filled with a transparent gel-like substance called the vitreous humour.

343.q: What organisms are responsible for acute retinal necrosis (ARN) and progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN)?
343.e: The organisms most commonly responsible for acute retinal necrosis (ARN) and progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) are varicella-zoster and herpes simplex. Rubella and rubeola do not cause acute retinitis in post-natal humans. Borrelia bergdorferi is the causitive organism of Lyme disease. Bartonella henselae is the causitive organism of cat-scratch disease. Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Treponema pallidum may cause retinitis and/or choroiditis, but are not the causitive organisms of acute retinal necrosis (ARN) and progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN). Reference: Kanski 8th edition/439-440
Ciliary body is called as the danger area of eye Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 12 uveitis pg. 448 sympathetic ophthalmitis

344.q: Most common malignant tumour of eyelid is ?
344.e: Ans, b. Basal cell carcinoma Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumour of the eyelids and constitutes 85-90% of all malignant epithelialeyelid tumours.
The most common malignancy of the eyelid is basal cell carcinoma. Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10 th edition, 1308

344.q: Extra row of cilia in the lid margin is
344.e: Distichiasis is a rare condition in which there is an extra posterior row of cilia , occasionally in all four lids. The posterior row of cilia arise from the orifices of the Meibomian glands . Reference: Kanski 8/e, Pg. 32.

344.q: When planning to surgically repair a congenital ptosis in a patient, what is the most important pre-operative assessment?
344.e: The surgical technique used for congenital ptosis depends primarily on levator function; patients with poor levator function often require some form of frontalis sling. The severity (in mm) of ptosis is secondary. Patients with marked ptosis and good levator function can still benefit from levator surgery. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/41-44

344.q: Chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis is commonly a presenting sign of which one of the following?
344.e: Sebaceous cell carcinoma commonly presents as a unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis. The other entities would be much less likely to involve the conjunctival surface of the eyelid to a significant degree and usually present differently. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/19

344.q: Ectropion and loss of eyelashes should alert one to the possibility of which one of the following?
344.e: Ectropion combined with alteration of eyelid anatomy, or loss of eyelashes, should suggest the possibility of malignancy and need for a biopsy. Loss of eyelashes is not typical of involutional changes, facial palsy, or eyelid rubbing. Reference: Kanski 8th edition 13/45

344.q: What is the most important predictor for recurrence and survival in patients with eyelid skin lesion?
344.e: Breslow thickness is the most important predictor of recurrence and survival in patients with eyelid skin melanoma. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/19

344.q: All the following are surgeries for ptosis correction except
344.e: Muller recession -Weakening procedure Muller resection -Strengthening procedure In ptosis, Muller's resection needs to be done. Muller's muscle is an eyelid elevator which is weakened in ptosis. Reference: Kanski 8/e, Pg. 42 -44.

345.q: Which structure divides the lacrimal gland into two lobes?
345.e: The lacrimal gland is split into two lobes by the lateral extent of the levator aponeurosis. Reference : kurana 4/e, p. 35

345.q: What is the most common site of congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction?
345.e: Congenital dacryocystitis is the inflammation of the lacrimal sac in a newborn, most commonly due to delayed/incomplete canalization of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD), most often at the lower end of NLD and near valve of Hasner - occlusion is membranous. Presents with epiphora, swelling and purulent discharge at inner canthus. Treatment Massage over lacrimal sac with topical antibiotics -initial treatment of choice for 1 year. Syringing is attempted usually by 9-12 months of age. Most of us do it after 1 year only Probing of NLD should be undertaken after 12 months of age, as spontaneous resolution is likely to occur by 12 months. Dacryocystorhinostomy after 4 years of age. Reference: Parson's 21/e p. 464, 466

345.q: What is the initial management of congenital dacryocystitis?
345.e: Congenital dacryocystitis is the inflammation of the lacrimal sac in a newborn, most commonly due to delayed/incomplete canalization of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD), most often at the lower and near valve of Hasner -occlusion is membranous. Presents with epiphora, swelling and purulent discharge at inner canthus. Treatment Criggler Massage over lacrimal sac with topical antibiotics -initial treatment of choice. Syringing is attempted usually by 9-12 months of age Probing of NLD should be undertaken after 12 months of age, as spontaneous resolution is likely to occur by 12 months. Dacryocystorhinostomy after 4 years of age. Reference: Parson's 21/e p. 464, 466

345.q: What is the anatomical relationship of the upper lacrimal punctum with respect to lower punctum?
345.e: The upper lacrimal punctum lies 0.5mm medial to the lower punctum. Upper punctum is directed downwards and backwards while the lower punctum is directed upwards and backwards. Reference: Khurana Anatomy, 2/e, P. 368

345.q: Which of the following is a cause of epiphora?
345.e: Causes of epiphora (overflow of tears at the eyelid margin) include - Hypersecretion secondary to anterior segment disease such as dry eye ('paradoxical watering') or inflammation. Defective drainage due to a compromised lacrimal drainage system; this may be caused by: Malposition of the lacrimal puncta. Obstruction at any point along the drainage system, from the punctal region to the valve of Hasner. Ex: Nasolacrimal duct block Lacrimal pump failure , which may occur secondarily to lower lid laxity or weakness of the orbicularis muscle. Ex: Facial nerve palsy Reference: Parson's 20/e, p.449

345.q: Probing and irrigation is contraindicated in:
345.e: Contraindications to probing and irrigation include - Acute dacryocystitis Acute canaliculitis In the setting of active infection , probing and irrigation are most likely to cause trauma because the lacrimal sac wall is inflated and friable, it also can cause unnecessary pain and anxiety for the patient. Reference: Parson 20/e, P. 478-479

345.q: What is the most common organism implicated in dacryocystitis?
345.e: Gram-positive organisms are most common in dacryocystitis. Consider gram-negative organisms in patients with diabetes mellitus, immunocompromised patients, or nursing home residents if there is no response to initial treatment. Fungal infection would be a rare cause of dacryocystitis. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/73

345.q: A patient with acute dacryocystitis, reflux of pus from the canaliculi, and preseptal cellulitis should be treated with which of the following?
o: Probing and irrigation for diagnosis confirmation
345.e: A patient with obvious dacryocystitis should not be probed. Probing would be painful and not provide additional information. Antibiotics will help inflammation subside prior to dacryocystorhinostomy. Massage may have some role in chronic dacryocystitis. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/75

346.q: True about chemical injury to eye all except
o: Acid injury are more severe in eye
Wash is to be done by ringer lactate
Steroids are given to decrease inflammation
IOP can be high in initial period
346.e: Alkali (penetrate inside) burns are more severe as compared to acid(coagulate on surface) Corneal epithelial and stromal damage by coagulase enzyme released by damaged epithelium and cause a lot of inflammation. Limbal ischaemia results from loss of stem cells. Vascularisation and conjuctivalisation of cornea occurs. Severe cases can have corneal ulceration and perforation. Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 912 chemical injury

346.q: Most dangerous intraocular foreign body is
346.e: Chalcosis, also called chalcosis bulbi, is a chronic reaction to a copper-containing intraocular foreign body (IOFB) When copper enters the eye, it is oxidized from its uncharged elemental form, Cu, to Cu 2+ ions. Though the ions are free to diffuse throughout the vitreous, they have a propensity to deposit in intraocular basement membranes including Descemet's membrane of the cornea (KF ring) and the internal limiting membrane (ILM) Foreign bodies containing less copper ( 85%) show a generalized pattern of intraocular copper deposition and are associated with more devastating outcomes such as suppurative endophthalmitis and phthisis bulbi. Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 911 IOFB

346.q: Cherry Red spot in children after trauma is seen in
346.e: Commotio retinae Commotio retinae is caused by concussion of the sensory retina resulting in cloudy swelling that gives the involved area a grey appearance. It most frequently affects the temporal fundus. If the macula is involved, a 'cherry-red spot' may be seen at the fovea. Severe involvement may be associated with intraretinal haemorrhage that can involve the macula. The prognosis in mild cases is good, with spontaneous resolution in around 6 weeks. Sequelae to more severe commotio may include progressive pigmentary degeneration and macular hole formation Reference: Kanski 8th edition/873

346.q: All are features of concussion injury to eye except
346.e: Intra ocular foreign body is due to penetrating injury. Other options mentioned here are due to blunt trauma. Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 899 blunt trauma

346.q: Which one of the following statements describing the adult orbit is false?
o: The volume of the orbit is 30 ml.
The maximum width is 1 cm behind the anterior orbital margin.
The depth of the orbit averages 50 mm from the orbital entrance to the apex.
The medial walls are parallel and border the nasal cavity, ethmoid air cells, and sphenoid sinus posteriorly.
346.e: The depth of the orbit varies from 40 to 45 mm from the orbital entrance to the orbital apex. The distance to the apex becomes important in the dissection or excision of a tumor in the posterior orbit or in the repair of an extensive blowout fracture Reference : kurana 4/e, p. 48

346.q: In which of the following quadrants are retinal dialyses most often found following blunt trauma?
346.e: Blunt trauma may result in a variety of retinal breaks including retinal dialyses, macular holes, giant retinal tears, horseshoe retinal tears, operculated retinal tears, and large, necrotic, sometimes posterior retinal breaks often associated with chorioretinitis sclopetaria. Retinal dialyses, however, are the most common retinal breaks found following blunt ocular trauma. Retinal dialyses resulting from blunt trauma are most often found in the inferotemporal and superonasal quadrants. All patients with a history of blunt trauma need to be given a careful retinal examination with scleral depression to look for retinal breaks after their pain, iritis, or hyphema, if any, has resolved. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/873

346.q: Which of the following is the most common indication for repair of medial orbital wall fractures?
346.e: Medial orbital wall fractures often cause enophthalmos and/or medial rectus entrapment with restrictive strabismus, both of which are indications for surgical repair. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/866

346.q: What is the MC site of intra ocular FB
346.e: The most common site of entry of an IOFB is the cornea (82.9%) followed by the sclera (11.4%), and the limbus (5.7%). The most common location of an intraocular foreign body lodged in the posterior segment is intravitreal (61%), followed by intra-retinal (14%) and sub-retinal(5%). Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 911 IOFB

347.q: Cavernous sinus syndrome can be differentiated by orbital apex syndrome by
347.e: Early vision loss; visual loss is early in orbital apex syndrome as apex has optic canal optic nerve also Orbital apex syndrome (inflammation of the posterior orbit, including the superior orbital fissure through which cranial nerves III, IV, V, and VI and the superior ophthalmic vein traverse, as well as the optic canal involving the ophthalmic artery and optic nerve and characterized by less edema and proptosis but more vision loss than cavernous sinus thrombosis) Reference: Parson 21st edition pg 476

347.q: Which of the following is common feature of Orbital Apex Syndrome and Cavernous sinus thrombosis?
347.e: Total ophthalmoplegia: In this condition all extraocular muscles including LPS and intraocular muscles, viz., sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle are paralysed. It results from combined paralysis of third, fourth and sixth cranial nerves. It is a common feature of orbital apex syndrome and cavernous sinus thrombosis. Reference: A k Khurana, 5th edition, Pg: 333.

347.q: A child of 10 year age presented with UL painful proptosis following nasal congestion. After two days he developed diplopia while looking at left side and severe headache and decreased vision. What could be the diagnosis
347.e: Cavernous sinus thrombosis; diplopia occurs because of 6th nerve involvement in cavernous sinus Nasal congestion suggests it might be sinusitis leading to orbital cellulitis and finally to cavernous sinus thrombosis Cavernous sinus thrombosis is usually caused by a bacterial infection that spreads from another area of the face or skull. Many cases are the result of an infection of staphylococcal (staph) bacteria, which can cause: sinusitis Reference: Parson 21st edition pg 482

347.q: What is a common sign of a malignant lymphoproliferative lesion?
347.e: Common malignant lymphoproliferative lesions in the orbit include non-Hodgkins lymphoma and myeloma and these commonly present with insidious subacute mass effect rather than pain and vision loss, as can be seen with idiopathic orbital inflammation and some epithelial malignancies. Reference: Kanski, 8th Edition, Page no. 13.

347.q: Which condition is closely associated with thyroid eye disease?
347.e: Thyroid eye disease may be associated with other autoimmune manifestations such as myasthenia gravis. Both Parinaud's dorsal midbrain syndrome and eczema may cause eyelid retraction, but are not closely related to thyroid eye disease. Myotonic dystrophy causes ptosis and is not closely related to thyroid eye disease. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/82-84

347.q: Which of the following CT findings is not commonly seen with thyroid-related orbitopathy?
347.e: Thyroid-related orbitopathy is an immunologically related inflammatory condition that affects orbital tissues, particularly the extraocular muscles. The most common cause for unilateral orbital proptosis in an adult is thyroid-related orbitopathy. Even though the clinical finding may indicate a unilateral problem, a CT scan or MRI often show bilateral disease. The CT findings consist of fusiform enlargement of the extraocular muscle, commonly the inferior and medial rectus muscles, with sparing of the tendons. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/82-84

347.q: What are the 2 most commonly affected rectus muscles in thyroid eye disease?
347.e: The inferior rectus is most commonly involved in thyroid eye disease, followed by the medial rectus and superior rectus. The sequence of muscle involvement - I M SLOw. ( pneumonic ) I - IR M - MR S -SR L - LR O - obliques Reference: Kanski 8th edition/82-84

347.q: MC cause of proptosis in adults is
347.e: In children it is orbital cellulitis Reference: Parson 21st edition pg 484

348.e: AMBLYOPIA Amblyopia is a unilateral or bilateral reduction of best corrected visual acuity in the absence of any organic cause. Clinical Features: Unilateral or bilateral reduced vision Crowding phenomenon may be seen: The patient is able to identify a Snellen's chart character with the amblyopic eye when the character is presented in isolation. If the character is shown along with other letters, the patient may not be able to recognize it. Neutral Density Filter Test(NDF): When the patient is asked to read through a NDF, the amblyopic eye shows no change, while in the normal eye, there is a drop in visual acuity Amblyopia treatment should be tried till the child is 12 years old. Best results are seen between 5-8 years of age. Reference: Kanski, 8th Edition, Page no. 746.

348.q: Angle evaluation can be done by
348.e: Angle evaluation is clinically done with Gonioscope but there are machines available for the same They are Anterior Segment OCT Ultrasound Biomicroscopy(UBM) Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th Edition, Pg No. 1024

348.q: Which of the following test programmes on the Humphrey's automated perimeter is best suited for evaluation of visual fields in neurologic disease?
348.e: Visual field defects are best detected by Goldmann kinetic perimetry (full field) and Humphrey automated threshold perimetry (30-2 programme for central field or neurological programmes). 10-2, 24-2 are used in evaluation of fields in glaucoma. 120-2/ full fields can be used for neurological evaluation but very time consuming/ poor compliance by patients due to attention fatigue. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye 23rd edition-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

348.q: The Antagonist muscle of left medial rectus is
348.e: Agonist-antagonist: Muscles of same eye which have opposite functions, e.g. MR and LR of the same eye. Synergist: Muscles of the same eye which move the eye in the same direction, e.g. SR and IO of the same eye are synergists in elevation. Yoke muscles: A pair of muscles of opposite eyes which produce a conjugate ocular movement, e.g. LR of right eye and MR of left eye are yoke muscles for dextroversion. Reference: Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, Pg no. 1186.

348.q: What is the study of choice for the evaluation of fractures in acute orbital trauma?
348.e: Computerized tomography is superior for evaluation of bone disorders. Magnetic resonance imaging and orbital ultrasound would be of less utility and nerve conduction is not commonly done in the setting of acute orbital trauma. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/865

348.q: What is the use of alternate cover test
348.e: Cover test: The occluder is held in front of the eye for a few seconds and then removed. When the fixing eye is occluded, the examiner will observe the non-occluded eye move to pick up fixation if a tropia is present. If no tropia is present, the non-occluded eye will remain stationary. Uncover test: To assess for a phoria or latent deviation, the examiner observes the eye behind the occluder. If a phoria is present, the uncovered eye does not move, however the eye that is behind the occluder will deviate and return to a straight position when the occluder is removed. Alternate Cover Testing(ACT) determines the total amount of manfiest and latent deviation of the eye. A cover-uncover test is done before moving on to alternate cover testing. Reference: AAO basics by Kara M. Cavuoto, M.D. 2023.

348.q: A 4-year-old child presents for evaluation of a recent onset esotropia. What step should be considered next?
o: Autorefraction with the use of accommodative control
348.e: Cycloplegic refraction is used to determine the objective determination of refractive error by relaxing accommodation. It is especially important in young children and patients with strabismus. Dry retinoscopy, manifest refraction and autorefraction are not satisfactory techniques to fully assess refractive errors in young children or patients with strabismus. Reference: Kanski, 6th edition, Pg no. 756.

348.q: What type of tropia is seen in a V-pattern strabismus?
348.e: V-pattern strabismus is a pattern in which the eyes are more abducted in downgaze than in upgaze. The etiology is unknown except in cases of extraocular muscle palsies. Multiple theories suggest primary or secondary muscle dysfunction, which can involve inferior oblique muscle overaction, superior oblique muscle underaction, horizontal rectus muscle dysfunction or extorsion of the globe and bony orbit which may lead to a V- or A- pattern. Infantile esotropia usually presents with a V-pattern. Refractive esotropia, intermittent exotropia and sensory exotropia are not commonly V-patterned. Reference: Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, Pg no. 1221.

349.q: A regular contact lens user presents with complaints of severe pain, redness, photophobia and blurring of vision for more than two weeks not responding to standard treatment. On examination, a paracentral ring shaped lesion with stromal infiltrates and overlying epithelial defects is observed in the affected eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis
349.e: A history of contact lens usage and a corneal ulcer not responding to standard treatment ( antibiotics and cylcoplegics ) suggest acanthamoeba ulcer. Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

349.q: Which of the following patient scenarios is/are not suitable for keratoprosthesis implantation?
349.e: A keratoprosthesis is a device designed to replace the cornea. Unfortunately, an ideal keratoprosthesis has not yet been devised. Implantation of a keratoprosthesis is considered only as a last resort where penetrating keratoplasty is not possible or has repeatedly failed. Implantation of a keratoprosthesis is reserved for bilaterally blind patients suffering from severe ocular surface disorders such as following chemical burns, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, severe dry eyes and recurrent graft rejections. Preoperative prerequisites include a minimum vision of light perception and absence of gross posterior segment disorders as evaluated by ultrasonography. Advanced keratoconus: first line of treatment : keratoplasty Fungal endophthalmitis: requires vitrectomy, not keratoprosthesis Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

349.q: Which of the following is the treatment of Candida endophthalmitis?
349.e: Treatment of Candida endophthalmitis includes: Antifungal treatment : Agent is decided based on culture sensitivity. Intravenous amphotericin-B in combination with oral flucytosine is given, but resistance is a concern. Voriconazole orally or intravenously has a broad spectrum of antifungal action with low reported resistance and high ocular penetration; adjunctive intravitreal treatment may be given(100 µg in 0.1 ml), with serial injections probably needed. Pars plana vitrectomy should be considered at an early stage, especially for severe or unresponsive disease. Along with providing a substantial culture specimen, it reduces fungal and antigen load, facilitates therapeutic agent penetration and clears the ocular media. Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 454.

349.q: Which of the following doesn't require treatment
349.e: Severe non proliferative diabetic Retinopathy Indications of treatment in DR PDR NPDR with CME Reference: parson's 22/e section IV chapter 20. pg 312-315

349.q: Guanethidine is used in the treatment of which of the following condition?
349.e: Guanethidine (10%) eye drops is useful in decreasing lid retraction in Thyrotoxic ophthalmopathy. It is an adrenergic neuron blocker which acts by inhibiting the release of noradrenaline in response to nerve stimulation.

349.q: Blood-tinged tears should prompt what treatment?
349.e: Malignancy should be considered in patients with blood-tinged tears. Biopsy is necessary to establish the diagnosis. Probing or balloon dacryoplasty would fail to establish the diagnosis, and dacryocystorhinostomy could spread the tumor. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/65

349.q: What is the appropriate treatment for acute dacryocystitis with localized abscess?
o: Irrigation and probing of the lacrimal system followed by application of warm compresses
Oral antibiotics and drainage of abscess or immediate dacryocystorhinostomy.
Surgical creation of a permanent dacryocutaneous fistula
349.e: Dacryocystitis with localized abscess is best treated with systemic antibiotics and prompt drainage of the abscess. Dacryocystorhinostomy surgery will accomplish drainage, but often cannot be performed in a timely fashion, and can be technically challenging due to local cellulitis and the possibility of rupture and fistulization. Probing is likely to damage the inflamed canaliculi or the valve of Rosenmuller, and topical antibiotics are inadequate. Dacryocutaneous fistula is an undesired outcome. Reference: Kanski 8th edition/75

349.q: Adaptation mechanism in patients with LR palsy includes
349.e: Strabismus or any ocular deviation may result in diplopia, but the individual undertakes certain adaptations to overcome this diplopia. The compensatory mechanisms may vary according to the type of Diplopia and the age of individual. Reference: Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, Pg no. 1225.

350.q: A 40-year old woman develops blurred vision at near in the left eye. She has a mid-dilated pupil that reacts only to near stimulus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
350.e: An isolated dilated pupil that reacts to near better than light is typically from a tonic(Adie) pupil. Loss of accommodation frequently occurs with pupillary dilation. Accommodative insufficiency and accommodative spasm are not associated with pupillary dilation. Third nerve palsy would be expected to have other features, including ptosis and an ocular misalignment. In Adie's Tonic Pupil, the affected pupil is larger(anisocoria). Its exact cause is not known. It is usually unilateral, associated with absent knee jerk and occurs more often in young women. Adie's pupil constricts with weak pilocarpine(0.125%) drops, while normal pupil does not. Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 293.

350.q: Swinging light test is positive in ?
350.e: Ans. C. Retrobulbar neuritis Swinging flash light is used for relative efferent pathway defect (RAPD) which is most characteristic of Iesions in the optic nerve. Thus it is positive in retrobulbar neuritis.

350.q: A 42-year-old woman has anisocoria that is greater in light. The right pupil is sluggishly reactive to light and she has normal ocular motility, alignment and normal eyelid position. What would be the best next step?
350.e: The findings suggest a problem with the pupillary sphincter(greater anisocoria in light). Normal lid position, alignment and eyelid position make third nerve palsy unlikely. Cocaine is useful in the diagnosis of Horner syndrome. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy would be the most helpful to distinguish abnormalities in the iris that might suggest a tonic pupil or trauma as the cause of anisocoria. Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 293, Parsons, 22nd, Edition, Pg: 33.

350.q: A person is able to read 6/6. At what distance he should be able to read 6/ 36
350.e: It is about a normal individual’s visual acuity. If he reads 6/6, at 36 mtr he should be able to read 6/36 line. Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

350.q: Which of the following pupillary sign is seen during concussion injury to brain?
350.e: Concussion injuries to the brain These are usually associated with subdural hemorrhage and unconsciousness which may produce the following ocular signs. Hutchinson's pupil: It is characterised by initial ipsilateral miosis followed by dilatation with no light reflex due to raised intracranial pressure. If the pressure rises still further, similar changes occur in the contralateral pupil. Therefore, presence of bilateral fixed and dilated pupils is an indication of immediate cerebral decompression. Papilledema: When it appears within 48 hours of the trauma, it indicates extra or intracerebral hemorrhage and is an indication for immediate surgical measures. While the papilledema appearing after a week of head injury is usually due to cerebral oedema. Reference: AK Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 311.

350.q: Major arterial circle is present at

350.e: Explanation: It is an anastomosis of long PCA and ACA at the root of the iris From it several branches arise to reach ciliary process. One goes to pupillary margin and forms minor arterial circle

351.q: Which clinical condition shows most resemblance to IIH?
351.e: Retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, hard exudates and disc edema may be seen in many retinal vascular pathologies. Features characterisitic of each are as follows: Diabetic Retinopathy: Hard exudates and micro-aneurysms involving posterior pole. Malignant Hypertension: Changes centred around disc +/- exudative retinal detachment CRVO: Disc edema plus tortuous veins plus hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants CRAO: Retinal pallor plus cherry red spot at macula Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

351.q: A 30-year-old woman is referred to you by her neurosurgeon after removal of a cerebellar hemangioma. Which of the following are you most likely to find?
351.e: Capillary hemangioma of the retina is associated with cerebellar and other central nervous system hemangiomas as part of the Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Choroidal hemangiomas are seen in Sturge-Weber syndrome. Racemous angiomas of the retina and cavernous hemangiomas of the retina most commonly occur as isolated entities. Reference: Kanski, 8th Edition, Page no. 506.

351.q: Which of the following blood vessels are compromised in Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy?
351.e: Posterior ischemic Optic neuropathy This entity shares the features of AION except for the site of involvement. Posterior optic nerve ischaemia is believed to occur due to disorders affecting the small pial vessels which supply the intraorbital portion of the optic nerve away from the eyeball. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

351.q: Lesion of the medial longitudinal bundle causes
351.e: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: In this condition there is lesion of the medial longitudinal bundle. It is the pathway by which various ocular motor nuclei are linked. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is characterized by: defective action of medial rectus on the side of lesion, horizontal nystagmus of the opposite eye. Reference: A k Khurana, 5th edition, Pg: 333.

351.q: Which part of visual fields is most likely affected in patients of optic neuritiis?
351.e: Clinical signs include a variable degree of decreased visual acuity, decreased colour vision, abnormal contrast sensitivity, decreased stereoacuity and visual field defects which could be central, centrocaecal, arcuate, sectorial, altitudinal focal pattern defects or a generalized nonspecific depression in retinal sensitivity. Perimetry shows visual function depression over the entire field but is more marked in the central 20° with varied patterns of field defects. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

351.q: Which of the following conditions is/are associated with development of papilledema?
351.e: By definition, papilloedema is disc oedema due to increased intracranial pressure. An intracranial tumour in any position may induce it. In general, those tumours which tend to produce internal hydrocephalus are most likely to cause papilloedema. The site of the tumour is more important than its nature, size or rate of growth. Other intracranial causes include a brain abscess, thrombosis of the cavernous sinus or other intracranial veins, aneurysm, subarachnoid haemorrhage, pseudotumour cerebri andhydrocephalus. Malignant hypertension can also cause papilloedema, usually by raising the intracranial tension, but may produce signs of disc oedema in the absence of raised intracranial pressure as seen in grade IV hypertensive retinopathy. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye 23rd edition-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

351.q: which of the following features helps differentiate papillitis from papilledema?
351.e: In optic neuritis due to inflammation (papillitis), the appearance of the disc is often ophthalmoscopically indistinguishable from that in papilloedema. The swelling is usually moderate (2-3 D), shelving off gradually into the surrounding retina. Vision in papilledema is normal, but in papillitis it is lost Vitreous opacities are usual, although they may be very fine. The visual symptoms are usually marked in papillitis. The acute depression of central vision, presence of a definite afferent pupillary defect or a relative afferent pupillary defect and the absence of signs of an intracranial space-occupying lesion form the most important differentiating features. Involvement in papillitis is usually unilateral whereas in papilledema it is bilateral. Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

351.q: Ataxia, nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia is seen in -
351.e: Ans. B. Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia The most commonidentifiableetiologies are ischemia, aneurysm, tumor and trauma, some 20% remain unexplained.

352.q: Most common distant site of metastasis in malignant melanoma
352.e: Uveal melanoma is a malignant tumor arising from melanocytes in the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, or choroid). It is the most common primary intraocular tumor in adults with an age-adjusted incidence of 6 per million. The choroid is the most common site involved and gives rise to 90% of uveal melanomas. Melanomas arising within the ciliary body comprise 7% and melanomas of the iris account for 2% There is a strong tendency for metastasis, particularly to the liver, and prognosis is poor when the tumor has disseminated. Reference: Kanski's Synopsis of Clinical Ophthalmology (Fourth edition) 2023, Page 322

352.q: What is treatment of choice for conjunctival melanomas?
352.e: β-Irradiation, either primary or after tumour excision, is the treatment of choice for conjunctival melanomas. Malignant lesions may become radioresistant, in which case the only effective treatment is wide excision with exenteration of the orbit and extensive reconstitution by skin grafting. Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

352.q: Most common site of metastasis in eye is (FMG)
352.e: The uvea is the most common site for ocular metastasis. Within the uvea, 88% of metastases are to the choroid, followed by metastases to the iris (9%) and ciliary body (2%) Ocular or eye metastasis are usually from a breast cancer (in women) and lung cancer (in men). Other less common sites of origin include the prostate, the kidney, the thyroid, and gastrointestinal tract. Reference: Parson 21st edition pg 481

352.q: What is the preferred management of pediatric optic nerve gliomas confined to orbit?
o: External radiation if confined to the optic nerve
352.e: Optic nerve gliomas that are confined to the orbit can be observed, particularly if vision is good. Radiation is used if the tumor is unresectable because of chiasm or tract involvement and symptoms are progressing. Chemotherapy is effective in progressive chiasmal or hypothalamic gliomas and may avoid complications of radiation. Surgery may be used for progressive lesions expanding toward the chiasm. 356.q: Burden of disease in a society is best indicated by
356.e: Disability-adjusted life years (DALY) : DALY is a measure of overall disease burden, expressed as a number of years lost due to ill-health, disability or early death. The DALY is becoming increasingly common in the field of public health and health impact assessment. The Global Burden of Disease project combines the impact of premature mortality with that of disability. It captures the population impact of important fatal and nonfatal disabling conditions through a single measure. It is calculated by formula : DALY = YLL + YLD The DALY relies on an acceptance that the most appropriate measure of the effects of the chronic illness is time. One DALY, therefore, is equal to one year of healthy life lost.

356.q: Sexual dysfunction is associated with a deficiency of which of the following minerals?
356.e: Explanation: Zinc deficiency is closely associated with sexual dysfunction. Zinc is crucial for hormone synthesis, especially testosterone, and supports normal reproductive function in males. A deficiency can result in decreased testosterone levels, erectile dysfunction, reduced libido, and impaired spermatogenesis. Explanation of other options: Copper (Option B): While important for enzymatic activity and iron metabolism, copper is not directly implicated in sexual dysfunction. Magnesium (Option C): Magnesium plays a role in over 300 biochemical reactions but is not directly linked to sexual health or dysfunction. Molybdenum (Option D): A trace element involved in enzymatic processes, but no clear evidence supports a role in sexual function. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9778609/

363.q: Which vaccine follows open vial policy
363.e: Explanation: Pentavalent vaccine (which protects against Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B, and Hib) is a liquid vaccine that comes in multi-dose vials and does follow the open vial policy . If stored correctly (2-8°C), not expired, unopened vials are clean, and aseptic technique is followed, it can be used up to 28 days after opening. Explanation for other options: BCG (option A): Does not follow open vial policy. It is a lyophilized (freeze-dried) vaccine that must be reconstituted and used within 4-6 hours. After that, it must be discarded. JE (option C): incorrect it is also a lyophilized vaccine, and once reconstituted, it must be used within a short time (usually 4 hours). Does not follow open vial policy. MMR (option D): incorrect it is also lyophilized, and must be used within 4 hours of reconstitution. Does not follow open vial policy.

364.q: Which of these vaccines are not covered under the open vial policy?
364.e: Explanation: The measles vaccine does not follow the open vial policy. The open vial policy states that vaccine vials, once opened, can be used for multiple sessions over a period of up to 28 days, as long as they are kept under proper cold chain conditions to minimize vaccine wastage. This policy applies to all liquid vaccines, such as Hepatitis B , DPT, Pentavalent, OPV, IPV, PCV, and Td. However, reconstituted vaccines like MMR, BCG, JE , Yellow Fever, and Rotavirus vaccines do not follow the open vial policy.

366.q: A researcher finds a sensitive test to be positive for a person. For diagnosis, which of the following will hold true?
o: It confirms that the person does not have the disease
it suggests that if the disease is rare, the person surely has the disease
it confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common
it is an expected finding in case the disease is prevalent
366.e: Sensitivity of a screening test is the ability of the test to identify correctly those who have the disease. It confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common. Reference: Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 25 th Edition, pg- 152

366.q: A test for Hepatitis C is performed on 200 patients with biopsy-proven disease and 200 patients free of the disease. The test shows positive results on 180 of the patients with the disease and negative results on 150 of the patients without the disease. Which of the following is appropriate?
o: Has a positive predictive value of 90%
Has a negative predictive value of 75%
366.e: To determine the appropriate statement, let's define the terms: Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The probability that a person with a positive test result truly has the disease. Negative Predictive Value (NPV): The probability that a person with a negative test result truly does not have the disease. Sensitivity: The proportion of true positive cases that the test correctly identifies. Specificity: The proportion of true negative cases that the test correctly identifies. Given the information: True positives (TP): 180 True negatives (TN): 150 False positives (FP): 50 (200 - 150) False negatives (FN): 20 (200 - 180) Sensitivity=TP/(FN+TP)=180/(20+180)=180/200=0.9 = 90% Reference: Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 25th Edition, pg- 152

366.q: A test for Hepatitis C is performed on 200 patients with biopsy-proven disease and 200 patients free of the disease. The test shows positive results on 180 of the patients with the disease and negative results on 150 of the patients without the disease. Which of the following is appropriate?
o: Has a positive predictive value of 83%
Has a negative predictive value of 88%
366.e: NPV= TN/(TN+FN) x 100= 150/170 x 100= 88% Reference: Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 25 th Edition, pg- 152

368.q: A pregnant woman with a 2-year-old child reports that she completed all recommended antenatal vaccinations during her previous pregnancy. Which of the following is recommended for her current pregnancy?
o: Give a booster dose of TT
Give a booster dose of Td
368.e: Explanation: The Td vaccine (Tetanus and Diphtheria) is recommended as a booster during pregnancy for women who have completed the required tetanus immunizations in previous pregnancies. Current Indian guidelines emphasize the following points: Td vaccine provides immunity against both Tetanus and Diphtheria , whereas the older TT (Tetanus Toxoid) vaccine only targets tetanus. For women with a history of prior antenatal TT vaccination, a single booster dose of Td is sufficient in the current pregnancy to maintain protective immunity. (Options A, C & D ruled out) Timing: The first dose is administered at the start of pregnancy (preferably before 20 weeks). The second dose is scheduled between 20-26 weeks if the first dose was given early or if additional coverage is required.

369.q: Organism included in Category A Bioterrorism is/are a. Vibrio cholerae b. Clostridium botulinum c. Yersinia pestis d. Bacillus anthracis
369.e: Category A bioterrorism agents are those that pose the highest risk to national security because they can be easily disseminated or transmitted from person to person, result in high mortality rates, and have the potential for major public health impact. Explanation for why not the other options: a. Vibrio cholerae: Vibrio cholerae is the bacterium responsible for causing cholera, a severe diarrheal disease. While cholera can cause significant morbidity and mortality, it is not typically considered a Category A bioterrorism agent due to its lower potential for deliberate dissemination and widespread impact compared to other agents in Category A. 369.q: The causative agent of endemic typhus is:
369.e: Explanation: Endemic typhus (also called murine typhus ) is caused by Rickettsia typhi . Transmission: Flea bite (commonly from rats). Clinical features: Mild febrile illness, headache, myalgia, sometimes rash. Usually self-limiting. Differentiation from epidemic typhus: Epidemic typhus → caused by Rickettsia prowazekii , transmitted by body lice , more severe. Explanation of Incorrect Options: Rickettsia prowazekii (Option A): Causes epidemic typhus , not endemic typhus. Salmonella typhi (Option C): Causes typhoid fever , a bacterial enteric fever, not a rickettsial infection. Orientia tsutsugamushi (Option D): Causes scrub typhus , transmitted by chiggers , not fleas.

369.q: What is the correct composition and dosing schedule of the Shanchol vaccine?
369.e: Explanation: Shanchol is a bivalent oral cholera vaccine given in 2 doses This refers to a vaccine that targets two different strains of Vibrio cholerae and requires two doses for complete immunisation. The Shanchol vaccine is bivalent, meaning it covers two different strains of Vibrio cholerae (01 and 0139) and typically requires two doses for full protection.

369.q: A patient presents with high-grade fever with chills and macular rashes over the neck, along with a positive tourniquet test. What is the probable diagnosis?
369.e: Explanation: Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever (DHF): Caused by dengue virus (Flavivirus). Clinical features: High-grade fever with chills Macular rash, often starting on the neck and chest Positive tourniquet test (capillary fragility) Hemorrhagic manifestations in severe cases Lab findings may include thrombocytopenia and hemoconcentration . The positive tourniquet test is a classic sign of capillary fragility in DHF . Explanation of Incorrect Options: Malaria (Option A): Fever with chills is common, but rash and positive tourniquet test are absent. Filariasis (Option B): Chronic infection with lymphedema and elephantiasis ; acute fever is rare. Typhoid (Option D): Presents with prolonged fever, rose spots , and gastrointestinal symptoms, but tourniquet test is not positive .

370.q: There is an outbreak of encephalitis in school children due to lack of proper childhood vaccination. According to universal immunization schedule, Which of the following type and route of vaccine that could have prevented this
370.e: JENVAC is a single dose inactivated Japanese Encephalitis (JE) Vaccine. This Vero cell derived vaccine is prepared from an Indian strain (Kolar- 821564XY) of the JE virus. JENVAC has been developed in collaboration with the National Institute of Virology, India. It is a safe and highly-effective vaccine that protects against all known strains of Japanese Encephalitis. Data of 2-dose study shows that a single dose of JENVAC is sufficient to elicit the immune response as the subjects who received a single dose were 98.67% sero-protected and the 4-fold sero-conversion was at 93.14% for the ≥1 year to ≤50 years age group. Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 111

371.q: Sachin visited the Emergency Department after he had received a Category 3 wound by a cat at his Veterinary centre. He had received pre-exposure prophylaxis. What should be the next line of management?
371.e: In case a person has received Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis, HRIg is not needed to be given. Hence, in this case, Wound management + ARV is only given. Post-Exposure prophylaxis in a person who has already received Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis: Cat 1: Wound Management Cat 2: Wound Management Cat 3: Wound Management + ARV (only 2 doses are administered on Day 0&3) Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis: 3 doses on Day 0, 7 & 21/28 Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

371.q: In a CHC area in a particular day, in which of the following diseases the prevalence may be zero though the incidence may be quite high in the area
371.e: All new cases of rabies (Incidence) are dying fast, so Prevalence will be zero at one point Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th edition, Chapter Principles of Epidemiology & Epidemiology methods.

371.q: A patient presents with a history of category 3 dog bites. He received rabies prophylaxis for a monkey bite 6 months ago. What is the next step in management?
o: Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3
371.e: Explanation: For patients who have previously completed rabies vaccination (within the last 3-6 months), management after a new category 3 exposure includes: Immediate wound cleaning Booster rabies vaccination on days 0 and 3 This approach triggers a rapid anamnestic immune response , providing sufficient protection without additional interventions like rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) . Explanation of Other Options: Wound cleaning only (Option A) : Category 3 bites require vaccination even in previously vaccinated individuals. Wound cleaning + rabies vaccine on day 0, 3 & 7 (Option C) : Only 2 booster doses are needed for previously vaccinated patients. Wound cleaning + IM vaccine + RIG (Option D) : RIG is reserved for rabies-naive patients or those without prior vaccination.

372.q: True about source of leptospirosis (contaminated) EXCEPT:
372.e: Surface water reservoirs : True. Contaminated water, especially during floods, is a primary source of Leptospirosis . The bacteria can survive in water, and humans can get infected through direct contact. Mud and soil : True. Soil and mud contaminated with the urine of infected animals, particularly rats , can be a source of Leptospirosis . Food : True. Although rare, Leptospirosis can be transmitted through contaminated food, especially when food is exposed to infected animal urine. Bite of carrier animal : Incorrect. Leptospirosis is primarily transmitted through direct contact with contaminated water, soil, or food, not by the bite of infected animals. Key Takeaways: Tags: INICET JUNE 2020 Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive & Social Medicine, K.park, 27 th Edition, Chapter-5, Page no: 338-339.

373.q: Second most common STD after gonococcus ?

Most common STD in India is herpes genitalis (20%) followed by chancroid (11%), viral warts/HPV (11%), syphilis (11%) and gonorrhoea (9%). Overall (in world) most common STD is chlamydia followed by gonorrhoea.

373.q: Five clean practices under strategies for the elimination of neonatal tetanus include all except?
373.e: The "Five Clean Practices" are part of the WHO-recommended strategies to prevent neonatal tetanus , especially during home or non-institutional deliveries. These practices are focused on ensuring cleanliness during delivery and cord care, which are the primary sources of Clostridium tetani infection in newborns. The Five Clean Practices include: Clean surface for delivery Clean hands of the birth attendant Clean cord-cutting instrument (e.g., new or sterilized blade) Clean cord tie Clean cord care (e.g., avoiding the application of unclean substances) Additional practices include: Clean water : For washing hands, the perineal area, and cleaning the newborn. Clean towel : To dry and wrap the baby immediately after birth (reduces risk of hypothermia and infection). Reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive Medicine, 27th Edition, Page 261

374.q: Which of the following is not included in the STEP approach?
374.e: Explanation: The WHO STEPwise approach (STEPS) is a standardized framework for countries to collect, analyze, and disseminate data on key risk factors for non-communicable diseases (NCDs) . It is designed to be simple and flexible, gathering information in three sequential "steps." Step 1: Questionnaire-based assessment of demographic, behavioral, and historical risk factors (e.g., tobacco use, alcohol consumption, diet, physical activity). Step 2: Simple physical measurements (e.g., height, weight, waist circumference, blood pressure ). (Option B ruled out) Step 3: Biochemical measurements (e.g., fasting blood sugar , blood lipids like cholesterol). (Options C & D ruled out) Blood group is a fixed genetic characteristic and is not considered a modifiable risk factor for NCDs in the context of this surveillance tool. Therefore, it is not included in the STEPS approach.

375.q: Cervical cancer screening using the co-test includes:
o: Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) and Pap smear together
Pap smear and HPV DNA test together
Blood test for antibodies and Pap smear together
375.e: Explanation: Co-testing for cervical cancer involves performing both a Pap smear (cytology) and HPV DNA testing Purpose: Pap smear: Detects cellular abnormalities (pre-cancerous changes). HPV DNA test: Detects high-risk HPV strains associated with cervical cancer. Recommended for women ≥30 years for improved sensitivity compared to either test alone. Explanation of Incorrect Options: VIA and Pap smear together (Option A): VIA is a visual screening method ; co-testing specifically refers to cytology + HPV DNA. Blood test for antibodies and Pap smear (Option C): No role of blood antibodies in cervical cancer screening; not part of co-testing. VIA alone (Option D): VIA is a stand-alone screening method , not a co-test.

Corpulence index [Ref Park 22nd le p. 369, 370] Different indices use to determine obesity are i) Body mass index (Qetelet's index) It is used internationally as reference standard for assessing the prevalence of obesity. It is dependent both on height and weight (has been explained earlier). ii) Ponderal index It is dependent both on height and weight. It is defined as height (cm) divided by cube root of weight (kg). iii) Broca indexà deal weight = Height (cms) - 100 iv) Corpulence indexà It is dependent only on weight (height independent. 375.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., 90% [Ref Park 22"/e p. 358] Approximately 90% of oral cancers in South East Asia are linked to tobacco chewing and tobacco smoking" -- Park

375.q: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) definition, what is the threshold for visual acuity in the better eye (with best possible correction) that classifies a person as "blind"?
375.e: Explanation: The correct WHO definition of blindness is a visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye with the best possible correction. This means a person classified as blind cannot see at 3 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 60 meters. The WHO classification for distance vision impairment is: Mild: Visual acuity worse than 6/12 Moderate: Visual acuity worse than 6/18 (Option C ruled out) Severe: Visual acuity worse than 6/60 (Option A ruled out) Blindness: Visual acuity worse than 3/60 Explanation of other options: 1/60 (Option D): This is not a standard WHO cut-off for defining any category of visual impairment. Key Takeaways: Memorize the WHO cut-off for blindness: . Understand the progression: 6/18 (Moderate) -> 6/60 (Severe) -> 3/60 (Blindness). Reference: World Health Organization (WHO) - Visual impairment and blindness.

376.q: Which of the following drugs are used for clinical cure of malaria? Artemether Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine Chloroquine Primaquine
376.e: Explanation: Clinical cure refers to the treatment that clears the parasite burden from the blood, relieving the acute symptoms of malaria. This is achieved by schizonticidal drugs . Artemether (an artemisinin derivative), Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (a sulfa drug combination), and Chloroquine are all blood schizonticides and are used for clinical cure. Primaquine is a tissue schizonticide (acts on hypnozoites in the liver for P. vivax and P. ovale) and a gametocidal It is not used for clinical cure of the acute attack but for radical cure (preventing relapse) and preventing transmission. Key Takeaways: Blood schizonticides (e.g., Chloroquine, Artemisinin, SP) are for clinical cure. Primaquine is for radical cure and gametocidal action.

376.q: In a town with population of 1,00,000, the number of slides examined is 50,000. Out of these, 100 slides were positive for malaria. The API is-
376.e: The Annual Parasite Index (API) is a measure used to assess the intensity of malaria transmission in a specific area. It is calculated by the formula: API = (Number of positive blood slides for malaria / Total population) × 1,000 Given: Total population = 100,000 Number of slides examined = 50,000 Number of slides positive for malaria = 100 API= (confirmed cases during one year/population under surveillance) x 1000= (100/100000) x 1000= 1 Reference - Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 306

376.q: According to WHO, what proportion of a country's Gross National Product (GNP) should ideally be allocated to health services?
376.e: Explanation: The WHO recommends that 5% of a country's GNP be spent on health services. This allocation is intended to: Ensure adequate healthcare delivery to the population Strengthen public health infrastructure Meet the healthcare needs of the community effectively

377.q: HIV post exposure prophylaxis should be started within?
377.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., 1-2 hrs Anti-retroviral drug for post-exposure prophylaxis should be initiated as soon as possible after the exposure within the first few hours and no later than 72 hours. So, the best answer here is 1-2 hours (first few hours).

377.q: A patient diagnosed to have both HIV and TB, which of the drug regimen should be followed
o: Start ART first followed by ATT
Start ATT first followed by ART
377.e: If a person is positive for both HIV and TB, Treatment for TB should be started first . In a person positive with both HIV and TB, signs and symptoms of TB are less prominent due to decreased cellular immunity (due to decreased CD4 count ) If ART is given 1st to this person, the cellular immunity will be increased, there will be flare up of signs and symptoms of TB. This is known as Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome ( IRIS) . Hence, ATT is given first to prevent this. ATT is given for minimum of 2 weeks followed by ART . With rifampicin containing regimen : Additional dose of DTG 50mg should be taken after 12 hours on the same day, as rifampicin decreases the bio-availability of dolutegravir ( DTG) Reference -Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 235

378.q: Recently, the Government of India added a vaccine to the national immunisation schedule against a certain agent which is the leading cause of viral gastroenteritis in children. What is the dosing schedule of this vaccine?
378.e: The rotavac vaccine has been added to the national immunisation schedule in 2020 in selected states. It is given at 5drops/dose, orally at 6,10,14 weeks, along with Pentavalent vaccine and OPV. Reference : Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 425

378.q: For a population of 70,00,000 with 30% of it belonging to the slum population, how many Urban PHCs are required for the slum population according to NUHM?
378.e: Explanation: According to NUHM, 42 U-PHCs are required for this scenario. According to NUHM guidelines, an Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC) is typically established for every 50,000-60,000 population. When targeting slum areas specifically, one U-PHC is recommended for approximately 25,000-30,000 slum population. In exceptional cases, such as highly dense or isolated slum clusters, one U-PHC may be set up for populations as low as 5,000-10,000. In the given question, the total population is 70,00,000. Out of this, 30% is the slum population, which means the slum population is 21,00,000 (30% of 70,00,000). Using the standard norm of one U-PHC per 50,000 people, we divide the slum population by 50,000. 21,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = 42 Therefore, to serve the slum population of this city, 42 Urban PHCs would be required.

378.q: Which of the following is correct about fiPV dosing schedule in NIS?
378.e: Explanation: Fractional Inactivated Polio Vaccine (fIPV) is included in the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) of India. As per the latest guidelines, fIPV is given at: 6 weeks 14 weeks 9 months (along with measles-containing vaccine) This schedule is designed to boost immunity against poliovirus while complementing the doses of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV). Explanation of other options : 6wk 10wk 9m (Option A): The second dose is given at 14 weeks , not 10 weeks . 6wk, 10wk, 14wk (Option C): The third dose is given at 9 months , not 14 weeks . 6wk, 10wk, 12wk (Option D): This is not in line with the recommended schedule, as the second and third doses are at 14 weeks and 9 months , respectively. Key Takeaways: The correct fIPV dosing schedule in India is 6 weeks, 14 weeks, and 9 months , aligning with the National Immunization Schedule to ensure robust protection against polio.

378.q: Rukmini is attending the village health nutrition and sanitation program day. How frequently is this conducted?
378.e: Explanation: The Village Health, Nutrition and Sanitation Day (VHND) is conducted once every month. (Option B,C and D ruled out) It is typically held at the Anganwadi Center (AWC) and serves as a crucial platform for providing integrated health, nutrition, and sanitation services to the community, particularly targeting women and children. Location: Primarily held at the Anganwadi Center (AWC). Day: Preferably on Wednesdays, but can be scheduled on any other day in the same month if a village is missed. Key Activities: Immunization, antenatal care, health education, nutrition services, and sanitation promotion. Key Takeaways: VHND is a monthly outreach activity. It is a cornerstone of primary healthcare delivery at the village level under the National Health Mission (NHM).

378.q: Check-ups conducted for children aged 9-18 years under Rashtriya Bal Swasthya karyakram is done for every?
378.e: Explanation: Under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) , school-going children in the age group of 6-18 years are screened by mobile health teams twice a year , which is semi-annually.(Option A,B and C ruled out) This frequent screening schedule is designed for the early detection and management of the 4 Ds: Defects at birth Diseases Deficiencies Developmental delays. Target Group: Children aged 6-18 years in government and government-aided schools. Screening Team: Comprises Mobile Health Teams with a Medical Officer, Pharmacist, and Lab Technician. Purpose: Early identification and intervention for health conditions to reduce child mortality and morbidity. Key Takeaways: RBSK mandates semi-annual (twice-a-year) health screening for school children aged 6-18 years. This ensures regular monitoring and timely intervention for common childhood health conditions.

378.q: Which of the following is a service provided under Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat - Health and Wellness Centres ?
378.e: Explanation: Under the Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (PM-ABHWC, also called Arogya Mandir) , essential services include: Dietary services (nutritional support, therapeutic diet where needed) Outpatient and preventive care Maternal and child health care Non-communicable disease screening and management Essential drugs and diagnostics Referral services Dietary services are specifically included to ensure nutritional support during illness and recovery . Explanation of Incorrect Options: Laundry (Option A): Supportive/hospital maintenance service, not part of Arogya Mandir package . Security (Option C): A general facility requirement, not a defined service under PM-ABHWC. Potable water (Option D): Availability of safe water is a basic infrastructure requirement , but not classified as a health service under Arogya Mandir.

378.q: Which of the following is correct regarding the Ayushman Bharat scheme?
o: Rs 5 lakh/per family per year is given
Rs 10 lakh/per family per year is given

Rs 2 lakh/per family per year is given

It provides: Health insurance coverage up to Rs 5 lakh per family per year (Options B, C & D ruled out) Coverage applies for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization Targeted towards poor and vulnerable families (over 10.74 crore families) Benefits are cashless and paperless , available across empaneled public and private hospitals in India This makes it a critical scheme in reducing out-of-pocket expenditure and improving access to healthcare.

Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th Edition, Chapter Concept Of Health & Disease.

o: Expectancy of life at age one
380.e: Life expectancy at age 1, infant mortality and literacy are used as indicators of development, describing progress in health, sanitation, education and women's status Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th Edition, Chapter Concept Of Health & Disease.

380.q: Which is not a mortality indicator
380.e: Years of potential life lost, IMR are mortality indicators Life expectancy is a positive mortality indicator Incidence and prevalence are morbidity indicators Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th edition, Chapter Principles of Epidemiology & Epidemiology methods.

380.q: According to the National Health Policy (NHP) 2017, what were the target numerical goals set to be achieved for the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) and the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) by the year 2023?
380.e: Explanation: The National Health Policy (NHP) 2017 outlined specific, time-bound targets for key health indicators. The goal for 2023 was to reduce the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) to below 70 per 100,000 live births and the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) to below 30 per 1,000 live births . This target of "70/30" represented a crucial mid-term milestone in India's efforts to significantly improve maternal and child health outcomes. Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR): The number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. Infant Mortality Rate (IMR): The number of infant deaths per 1,000 live births. Key Takeaways: The NHP 2017 target for 2023 was MMR and IMR . These targets are distinct from the final goals set for 2030, which align with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

380.q: According to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) proposed targets for 2030, what are the global reduction goals for the maternal mortality ratio (MMR) and under-5 mortality rate?
380.e: Explanation: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a set of 17 global goals established by the United Nations, with a target year of 2030. Goal 3 of the SDGs is to "Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages." Within Goal 3, the specific targets for maternal and child mortality are: Target 3.1: Reduce the global maternal mortality ratio (MMR) to less than 70 per 100,000 live births . Target 3.2: End preventable deaths of newborns and children under 5 years of age, with all countries aiming to reduce under-5 mortality to at least as low as 25 per 1,000 live births . References: Sustainable Development Goal 3: United Nations. https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal3

380.q: The number of live births per 1000 women in the reproductive age group in a year refers to
380.e: d. General Fertility Rate (GFR): The General Fertility Rate (GFR) is a demographic measure that calculates the number of live births per 1,000 women of reproductive age (usually defined as women aged 15-49) in a given population over a specific period, typically a year. GFR provides similar information to GRR but specifically focuses on the fertility level of women within the reproductive age group, rather than the entire population of women in that age group. Reference: Park's Preventive and social medicine, 27th EDITION Pg 564

380.q: In a population with a total of 4050 births, there are 50 stillbirths, 50 neonatal deaths within the first 7 days, and 150 deaths between 8 and 28 days of life. What is the Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) for this population?
380.e: Explanation: The Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) is calculated as the number of deaths of infants within the first 28 days of life per 1000 live births. Step-by-step calculation: Calculate Live Births: Live births = Total births - Stillbirths Live births = 4050 - 50 = 4000 Determine Total Neonatal Deaths: Neonatal deaths include all deaths from 0 to 28 days. Total Neonatal Deaths = Deaths (0-7 days) + Deaths (8-28 days) Total Neonatal Deaths = 50 + 150 = 200 Calculate NMR: NMR = (Total Neonatal Deaths / Live Births) × 1000 NMR = (200 / 4000) × 1000 = 50 (Option A,C and D ruled out) Key Takeaways: NMR includes all deaths from birth up to (and including) the 28th day of life. The denominator for NMR is the number of Live Births (Total births minus stillbirths). NMR is a critical indicator of perinatal and newborn care quality.

380.q: In a village with a given population, the total number of live births in a year is 4000. 40 newborns died within the first 7 days of life whereas 40 died due to various causes between 8 to 28 days of life. There were 50 deaths between the age of 1 month to 6 months of life and 0 of them died in utero. What is the neonatal mortality rate in this population?
380.e: Explanation: The Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) is calculated as the number of deaths during the first 28 days of life (the neonatal period) per 1000 live births. Calculation: Total Neonatal Deaths = Deaths (0-7 days) + Deaths (8-28 days) = 40 + 40 = 80 Total Live Births = 4000 NMR = (Total Neonatal Deaths / Total Live Births) * 1000 NMR = (80 / 4000) * 1000 = 20 per 1000 live births (Option A,C and D ruled out) The neonatal period is the most vulnerable time for a child's survival. NMR is a key indicator of the quality of perinatal and neonatal care. Key Takeaways: Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) includes all deaths from 0 to 28 days of life. Formula: NMR = (Number of neonatal deaths / Number of live births) x 1000

381.e: CONTRAINDICATIONS ABSOLUTE : Suspected pregnancy Pelvic inflammatory disease Vaginal bleeding of undiagnosed etiology Cancer of the cervix, uterus or adnexa and other pelvic tumours Previous ectopic pregnancy. Malignant trophoblastic disease or known pelvic tuberculosis RELATIVE : Anemia Menorrhagia History of PID since last pregnancy Purulent cervical discharge Distortions of the uterine cavity due to congenital malformations, fibroids etc Unmotivated person. KEY TAKE AWAY The ideal IUD candidate : The Planned Parenthood Federation of America (PPFA) has described the ideal IUD candidate as a woman : Who has borne at least one child Has no history of pelvic disease Has normal menstrual periods Is willing to check the IUD tail Has access to follow-up and treatment of potential problems, and Is in a monogamous relationship.

381.q: Which of the following is not a component of the RCH program?
381.e: Explanation: The Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) program focuses on improving maternal and child health. Its core components include: Family Planning: Services for contraception and fertility regulation. Maternal Health (Safe Motherhood): Essential and emergency obstetric care to reduce maternal mortality. ( Option A ruled out ) Child Health: Immunization, management of childhood illnesses, and newborn care (Child Survival component). ( Option C ruled out ) Prevention and Management of RTI/STD: Screening and treatment of Reproductive Tract Infections (RTIs) and Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs) . ( Option D ruled out ) While women's education and empowerment is an important aspect of broader public health and gender programs, it is not a direct component of the RCH program , which focuses specifically on health services related to reproduction and child health .

381.q: Mr. X married Mrs. Y, and the couple had two children, born in 2002 and 2005. In 2020, Mr. X's father, who was employed with the State Bank of India (SBI), retired and moved in with Mr. X and his family, accompanied by his wife. Which of the following best describes the family transition?
381.e: Explanation: Family extension occurs when a new member (such as a child) is added to the family. In this case, Mr. X and Mrs. Y had their first child in 2002 , which extended their family. Explanation of other options: Formation in 2002 (Option A): Incorrect, because the family was formed when Mr. X and Mrs. Y got married (before 2002) . Regression in 2020 (Option B): Regression occurs when family members leave or die, which is not the case here. Dissolution in 2020(Option D): Dissolution happens when a family breaks apart (e.g., through divorce or death), but here, the family remained intact. Key Takeaways: Extension of a family occurs when new members, such as children or dependent relatives, are added. The birth of the first child in 2002 marks the extension of the nuclear family. Family formation relates to marriage; regression and dissolution involve loss or breakdown.

382.q: When should a primigravida initiate breastfeeding after a normal delivery of a healthy newborn?
382.e: Explanation: Early initiation of breastfeeding, ideally within the first hour after birth , is recommended for all healthy newborns, especially for primigravida mothers. Early initiation is important because: It stimulates milk production in the mother. The newborn receives colostrum , which is rich in nutrients and antibodies, providing protection against infections . Promotes mother-baby bonding and helps establish successful breastfeeding.

382.q: The following statements about breast milk are true except:
o: The maximum milk output is seen at 12 months
The coefficient of uptake of iron in breast milk is 70%
Calcium absorption of human milk is better than that of cow's milk
It provides about 70 K cals per 100 ml
382.e: Maximum milk output occurs around 3 to 6 months postpartum , not 12 months, as infant demand peaks and the mother’s milk supply is well-regulated. Iron uptake from breast milk is 70% , due to high bioavailability, allowing infants to absorb it efficiently. Key Takeaways: Peak milk production is around 3-6 months postpartum . Breast milk provides highly bioavailable iron and calcium and approximately 70 Kcals per 100 ml . 392.q: What is the term used to describe the process that occurs in an oxidation pond?
o: Aerobic during day, anaerobic during night
Anaerobic during day, aerobic during night
392.e: Explanation: Oxidation ponds (also called stabilization ponds or lagoons) are large, shallow basins used for sewage treatment. Their functioning depends on the interaction between algae and bacteria . Daytime: Algae perform photosynthesis → release large amounts of oxygen into the pond. This oxygen supports aerobic bacteria , which break down organic matter into simpler, non-toxic compounds. Hence, the pond environment is predominantly aerobic . Nighttime: Photosynthesis stops in the absence of sunlight. Microorganisms continue to consume oxygen through respiration . Oxygen levels fall rapidly, and anaerobic conditions may develop, particularly at the bottom layers. This daily oscillation between aerobic (day) and anaerobic (night) conditions is a characteristic feature of oxidation ponds and helps in effective sewage stabilization. (Options A, B & D ruled out)
