424.q: A 58-year-old woman is referred by the Ortho department after attending with a vertebral fracture, the second in the last 3 years. She underwent a total hysterectomy with oophorectomy at the age of 38 for carcinoma. Bone densitometry confirms osteoporosis. The calcium and parathyroid hormone assays are normal. Which of the following is the most likely concerning her underlying pathophysiology?
o: She has suffered predominantly cortical bone loss
She has probably suffered an equal mix of cortical and trabecular bone loss
She has probably suffered predominantly trabecular bone loss
424.e: Hypo-estrogenization, as in this case, is usually characterized by predominantly trabecular bone loss. Involutional bone loss of old age is characterized by a mixed picture of trabecular and cortical bone loss. In the presence of normal calcium and parathyroid hormone levels, parathyroid disease is ruled out. Hormone replacement therapy was formerly the mainstay of treatment, but this has fallen out of favor due to increased thromboembolic disease and the risk of breast carcinoma. The current line of therapy for osteoporosis include either anti-resorption agents like bisphosphonates and denosumab or anabolic agents like Teriparatide. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3192-93

424.q: Which one of the following statements is true for the actions of parathyroid hormone (PTH)?
o: Acts directly on renal, bone, and intestinal cells
Acts directly on renal cells and indirectly on bone and intestinal cells
Acts directly on renal and bone cells and indirectly on intestinal cells
Has no direct actions on renal, bone, and intestinal cells
424.e: PTH shares a receptor with PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), and this receptor is a member of the G protein–coupled receptor (GPCR) family. PTH/PTHrP receptors are expressed by kidney and bone cells, and PTH acts directly on renal and bone cells. PTH acts indirectly on intestinal cells to enhance calcium absorption as follows: PTH stimulates renal 1α-hydroxylase activity to promote synthesis of the active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), which then acts on the intestine to enhance calcium absorption. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, page number 3171

425.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Rotor syndrome Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is seen when ? i) Impaired secretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile -> Dubin Johnson syndrome, Rotor syndrome. ii) Impaired bile flow —> Obstructive jaundice, primary biliary cirrhosis, Neonatal cholestasis, e.g. Extrahepatic biliary atresia/neonate idiopathic hepatitis, Choledocal cyst, Sclerosing cholangitis, Caroli disease, Metabolic (Tyrosinemia, Wolman disease, Nieman pick disease, Galactosemia, Fructosemia).

Answer- D. All of above Impaired bile flow → Obstructive jaundice, primary biliary cirrhosis, Neonatal cholestasis, e.g. Extrahepatic biliary atresia/neonate idiopathic hepatitis, Choledocal cyst, Sclerosing cholangitis, Caroli disease, Metabolic (Tyrosinemia, Wolman disease, Nieman pick disease, Galactosemia, Fructosemia).

425.q: A 42 year old man has worsening jaundice and has deranged liver function tests which have worsened over the last 3 months. He has positive IgG to hepatitis C. Which of the following investigations is most useful for management of the condition?
425.e: Liver biopsy is useful to determine the severity of the disease and for monitory progression when treatment with ribavirin and interferon is instigated. Cirrhosis develops in 20-25 percent of patients with chronic hepatitis C after 10 years. It is also important to rule out liver carcinoma which may be a complication of long standing hepatitis C infection Hepatitis C is an RNA virus and hence option C is incorrect. ERCP is done in cases of obstructive jaundice. CT abdomen is not going to help in this patient Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2592

425.q: A 28 year old intravenous drug user complains about severe epigastric pains, nausea and vomiting. He has upper GI endoscopy which shows small areas of ulceration and white plaques. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
425.e: This is a patient with possible HIV who has oesophageal candidiasis (white plaques on endoscopy). Candida is normally found in the throat but can become pathogenic and produce esophagitis in a compromised host. Candida albicans is most common cause. Oral fluconazole for 14-21 days is the preferred treatment. Patients refractory to fluconazole may respond to voriconazole or posaconazole. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2432

425.q: A 30 year old lady is referred for investigation of abnormal liver function tests. She has been taking several drugs to treat tuberculosis for a long period of time.Her albumin is 3.0 g/dl, bilirubin 5 mg/dl, ALP is 250 U/l and ALT is 300 U/l.She has a liver biopsy which shows histological evidence of liver necrosis eroding the portal zone and extending into the liver lobule. What is the likely diagnosis?
425.e: Periportal necrosis, portal inflammation, bridging necrosis and interface hepatitis are features of active liver inflammation. Inflammatory conditions (e.g Wilson's disease) and drugs such as methyldopa and isoniazid can precipitate chronic active hepatitis. Autoimmune hepatitis is associated with antinuclear antibodies (70%), anti-smooth muscle (30%) and liver specific antibodies (ASGP-R asialoglycoprotein receptor; LKM liver kidney microsomal antibodies). Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2592

425.q: A 20-year-old patient complains of ankle swelling and breathlessness. Her CXR shows pleural effusions. Blood tests show: urea 17 mg/dl creatinine 0.90 mg/dl sodium 138 mmol/l potassium 4.2 mmol/l alanine transferase 20 U/L bilirubin 0.9 mg/dl albumin 2 gm/dl total cholesterol 340 mg/dl. What is the next best investigation?
425.e: The given patient has hypoalbuminemia, hyper cholesterolemia, edema and pleural effusion. So the edema is attribute to hypoalbuminemia. Hypoalbuminemia can be due to either decreased albumin production as in CLD or excessive albumin loss through urine or gut. However here the cholesterol levels are high which is an indirect indicator of nephrotic syndrome. So the next investigation will be to confirm the urinary loss, which is 24 hour urine estimation. Followed by a renal biopsy, once proteinuria is confirmed. The classic features of nephrotic syndrome are: Proteinuria >3g/24 hours Hypoalbuminemia( Generalized Oedema Hypercholesterolemia Lipiduria Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

426.q: Which blood group is more prone to helicobacter and cholera infection?
426.e: In most people (80%), A, B, and H antigens are secreted by the cells and are present in the circulation as well as in various secretions such as saliva ( Se phenotype ). Others, called "nonsecretors" do not secrete A, B, and H antigens ( se phenotype ). ABO and Se/se systems influence the susceptibility to a variety of diseases. Malaria is less severe in O than non O patients. Group O is associated with enhanced susceptibility to Helicobacter pylori (and gastric ulcer) as well as to cholera bacillus or to norovirus . Group O individuals exhibit a lesser procoagulation phenotype when compared to non O individuals. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 113, Pg: 884

426.q: A patient has been diagnosed as having epidemic typhus. By which vector is he most likely to have become infected?
426.e: The chief vector of epidemic typhus is the human body louse. The hard tick is a vector for a number of rickettsial diseases. Larval trombiculid mites spread scrub typhus. Rat fleas are responsible for the spread of endemic (murine) typhus. The Aedes aegypti mosquito is the vector for dengue fever Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition, Ch:187 Pg:1435

426.q: Which of the following secondary causes of hyperlipidemia result in predominantly hypercholesterolemia, as opposed to hypertriglyceridemia?
426.e: Hypercholesterolaemia rather than hypertriglyceridaemia : nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, hypothyroidism Hyperlipidaemia: secondary causes Causes of predominantly hypertriglyceridemia diabetes mellitus (types 1 and 2) obesity alcohol chronic renal failure drugs: thiazides, non-selective beta-blockers, unopposed estrogen liver disease Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:400 Page number:2897

426.q: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index and various factors can affect its plasma concentration. Which of the following conditions is most likely to increase the risk of digoxin toxicity?
426.e: The factors that can increase digoxin toxicity include: Electrolyte imbalances like hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia Drugs that increase digoxin levels like amiodarone, verapamil or spironolactone Myocardial ischemia and hypoxemia Renal failure Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 350

426.q: A 24-year-old woman has ingested an unknown quantity of paracetamol tablets four hours ago.She now presents with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and right subchondral pain.Which of the following features suggest that she should be transferred to the liver unit?
426.e: A pH of less than 7.3 is a poor prognostic factor for this patient. The criteria for transfer to a ICU are: Encephalopathy INR >2.0 at 3.5 at Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dl Blood pH Systolic BP Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 340 Pg: 2588

426.q: A 39 year old alcoholic is admitted to ER with unsteadiness and confusion. BM is 58 mg/dl. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
426.e: This patient is likely to have Wernicke's encephalopathy causing confusion. IV thiamine should be given to reduce the progression. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:333, Pg: 2526

426.q: A young patient with hypoglycaemia is administered glucagon. Which of the following actions of glucagon would be most likely to be effective in treating this condition?
426.e: Glucagon acts mainly on the liver and has no action on muscle. It increases glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and also stimulates lipolysis in adipose tissue. Adenylate cyclase is a key enzyme involved in the breakdown of glycogen polymers to increase availability of glucose. Activation of this and other enzymes is responsible for restoring blood glucose levels in this case. Insulin induces the synthesis of phosphofructokinase, which increases glycolysis, and stimulates acetyl-CoA carboxylase to increase the synthesis of fatty acids. Glucagon acts via cyclic AMP to stimulate lipolysis, producing free fatty acids that can act as a major source of energy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:3107

426.q: Which of the following parameters are used to calculate Maddrey's Discriminant Function?
426.e: In patients diagnosed with alcoholic hepatitis, short-term mortality can be predicted using the Maddrey discriminant function (MDF; calculated as 4.6 × [the prolongation of the prothrombin time above control {seconds}] + serum bilirubin [mg/dL]). Other scores are MELD score Age-Bilirubin-INR-Creatinine (ABIC) score. Patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis (AH), defined as Maddrey discriminant function (MDF) ≥32 or Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score >20, without contraindications for glucocorticoids are candidates for such treatment. Non responders or patients with contraindications for treatment should be considered for early liver transplantation (LT) or supportive or palliative care, as clinically appropriate. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 342 pg. 2619

427.q: An obese 55 year old woman with Type II diabetes is referred as she has been found to have raised ALT and AST levels. She does not have a history of pruritus or jaundice. She is not on any medication and does not take alcohol. On examination, she has a smooth hepatomegaly of 3 cm edge. There are no xanthelasma and she does not have signs of chronic liver disease. What is the likely diagnosis?
427.e: This diagnosis is non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. The mildest type is simple fatty liver (steatosis), an accumulation of fat within the liver that usually causes no liver damage. This disease is usually nonprogressive and rarely causes liver cirrhosis. A potentially more serious type, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), is associated with liver fibrosis. NAFLD is the most common chronic liver disease in many parts of the world, including the United States. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease affects more women than men, and is associated with insulin resistance /diabetes and obesity . Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 343Pg: 2621

427.q: Which of the following is not a cause of necrotizing myopathy?
427.e: IMNM, or autoimmune necrotizing myopathy, is characterized by the acute or insidious onset of symmetric, proximal more than distal weakness. Specific autoantibodies associated are: (anti-3-hydroxy-3methyl-glutaryl-coenzyme reductase [HMGCR] and anti-signal recognition particle [SRP]). Anti-HMGCR myopathy can be seen in patients receiving statins, inhibitors of HMGCR, particularly in patients aged >50 years. However, anti-HMGCR myopathy can develop in children and young adults without a history of statin use and can mimic a limb girdle muscular dystrophy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 365,: 2822

427.q: Most common microbial trigger for Type 1 DM are all except
427.e: Numerous environmental events have been proposed to trigger the autoimmune process in genetically susceptible individuals; however, none have been conclusively linked to diabetes. Identification of an environmental trigger has been difficult because the event may precede the onset of DM by several years(Putative environmental triggers include viruses (coxsackie, rubella, enteroviruses most prominently), bovine milk proteins, nitrosourea compounds, vitamin D deficiency, and environmental toxins. Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 403, Pg: 3100

427.q: A 38 year old lady has noticed mild jaundice, worsening joint pains and is complaining of itching on her skin for the past 8 months. On examination, she has palpable hepatomegaly and a bronze pigmentation on her skin.Her liver function tests show a bilirubin of 1.5 mg/dl, ALT 100 U/l, ALP 480 U/l. ANA is negative, anti-mitochondrial antibody is positive at 1:320.Which of the following medications is helpful?
427.e: Primary biliary cirrhosis is described. Liver transplantation does not cure the condition. Histology shows white cell damage to the biliary epithelium with non necrotising granuloma formation in the portal triad.Ursodeoxycholic acid lowers serum bilirubin and symptoms of itching, and prolongs the progression towards requirement for liver transplantation. IgM levels are particularly high in PBC. Desferrioxamine is used to treat hemochromatosis Prednisolone is used to treat autoimmune hepatitis Propranolol is for prophylaxis of upper GI bleed in patients of portal hypertension. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 244, Pg: 2627

427.q: Which one of the following statements is true of autoimmune hepatitis?
o: It may be associated with keratoconjunctivitis sicca
It rarely interferes with menstruation except in later stages
It rarely presents before 20 years of age
427.e: It occurs frequently in young (10-20 years) and middle-aged women. Twenty five per cent present as acute hepatitis, but usually the onset is insidious.Some may be asymptomatic for years and then are found to have signs of chronic liver disease. Amenorrhoea is common. It is associated with hyperglobulinemia and other autoimmune diseases. Sixty per cent are associated with HLA-B8, DR3 and Dw3. Extrahepatic features include: arthritis Sjögren syndrome thyroiditis nephritis ulcerative colitis Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia. Reference :Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:341 , Pg: 2613-2615
Ans. is 'a' i.e., Autoimmune hemolytic anemia Most common cause of spherocytes is immunehemolytic anemia.

427.q: Which of the following is associated with autoimmune hepatitis?
427.e: Cross-reactivity between viral antigens (HCV NS3 and NS5A) and host autoantigens (cytochrome P450 2D6) explains the association between hepatitis C and autoimmune hepatitis. Rarely, autoimmune hepatitis occurs after acute hepatitis A and B. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition page Ch: 341 Pg 2615

427.q: A 46 year old man presents with lethargy and pruritus. He has lost one stone in weight over the past two years.He does not smoke. There is no family history of bowel malignancy.On examination he looks pale but is not jaundiced. There is no hepatomegaly and there are no signs of chronic liver disease. Liver ultrasound shows small gallstones. The gallbladder is not inflamed. There is no biliary duct dilatation. Bilirubin is 1.2 mg/dl, ALT is 180 U/l, ALP is 800 U/l. ANA and AMA are negative but pANCA is positive.What is the diagnosis?
427.e: Primary sclerosing cholangitis presents at this age, there is cholestatic picture on the liver function tests, but not necessarily high bilirubin. pANCA is positive in about 90% of patients with PSC. A small proportion of patients (3%) will progress to cholangiocarcinoma at a later age. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch: 344, Pg: 2627-2628

428.q: Which site is Most commonly involved in gastrointestinal TB among the following?
428.e: Although any portion of the gastrointestinal tract may be affected, the terminal ileum and the cecum are the sites most commonly involved in gastrointestinal TB Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1366

428.q: A 35-year-old man is admitted following a serious attempt at paracetamol overdose. Despite efforts to treat him he develops liver failure. Which of the following is most likely with the ensuing liver failure?
o: Better prognosis in those with high alcohol consumption
Hypoglycaemia rarely happens within 12 hours of onset of encephalopathy
428.e: Lactic acidosis is due to decreased hepatic lactate clearance,compounded by poor peripheral perfusion and increased lactate Use of intravenous N-acetylcysteine reduces morbidity and mortality in fulminant hepatic failure. Severe hypoglycemia affects 40% of patients with fulminant liverfailure, which exacerbates encephalopathy. Reference: Harrison 20 th pg. 2370

428.q: A 25-year-old woman is referred from the Emergency department with a paracetamol overdose.Which of the following is an indication for liver transplantation in acute liver failure as a result of paracetamol overdose?
428.e: Prothrombin time > 100 seconds in acute liver failure with paracetamol poisoning is one of the selection criteria for liver transplantation. The remainder of the selection criteria for liver transplantation in acute liver failure with paracetamol overdose are as follows: Arterial pH Creatinine > 2.5 mg/dL Grade III or grade IV encephalopathy. Serum bilirubin > 15 mg/dl is part of the selection criteria for liver transplantation in non-paracetamol induced acute liver failure. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 340, Pg: 2589

428.q: A 37 year old man has chronic liver disease secondary to hepatitis. He comes on having had a depressive episode but also feels tired and unwell. He reveals that he has had a bottle of wine a day for a week.On examination he has gross abdominal distension. A peritoneal tap is done. Results from the tap show that it has albumin of 2.5g/dl, LDH of 320 U/l, RBS of 70 mg/dl and a white cell count of 700 per mm3 (90% neutrophils).What is the diagnosis?
428.e: A white cell count of > 250/mm 3 is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. There is underlying cirrhotic liver disease and this should always be considered related to decompensation. Tuberculous peritonitis will cause lymphocyte predominant ascites with high protein and low glucose. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2632

428.q: A 54 year old man has a long history of alcohol use. On the average he drinks two bottles of wine a day. He presents with tremors, hallucinations and has signs of chronic liver disease as well as ascites. A senior resident doctor assesses the status of chronic liver disease with the Child Pugh Classification. Which of the following is one of the criteria used to assess severity?
428.e: Child Pugh classification includes: (Mnemonic: A BEAP) A lbumin B ilirubin level E ncephalopathy A scites P rothrombin time AST is not used to assess severity of liver disease. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:345 Pg: 2635

428.q: Which of the following hepatic porphyrias present during adult life?
428.e: Four of the five hepatic porphyrias present during adult life: acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) hereditary coproporphyria(HCP) variegate porphyria (VP) ALA-dehydratase porphyria (ADP) acute attacks of neurologic manifestations and elevated levels of one or both of the porphyrin precursors, ALA and PBG, and are thus classified as acute porphyrias. Patients with ADP have also presented in infancy and adolescence. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 20 th Edition, chapter. 409, page number.2989

428.q: A 46 year old man is known to have alcoholic liver cirrhosis. He drinks 60 units of alcohol per week. He presents unwell and confused. Temperature is 38°C and blood pressure is 96/50 mmHg. Abdominal palpation reveals hepatomegaly and ascites. What should be done next?
428.e: There is a high chance of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in this patient with cirrhotic liver disease. When analysis of ascitic fluid reveals a white blood cell count of more than 250 cells/cc, SBP is likely. Cefotaxime should be commenced after a tap is done and blood cultures are sent. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2632

428.q: A 45 year old man has had long standing jaundice, malaise and poor appetite. Over the past 6 months he has lost 2 stones in weight. On examination he has palmar erythema, jaundiced sclera, spider naevi, hepatomegaly and ascites. His bloods reveal: Bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl ALT: 150 U/l ALP: 240 U/l Hep C core antibody Positive HBsAg: Negative Hep A antibody Negative What is the likely diagnosis?
428.e: This patient has features of chronic liver disease, as evidenced by the presence of ascites and spider angiomas. The patient also gives history of jaundice with deranged SGPT , which indicates an active hepatitis. Acute infection with Hepatitis E or C will cause SGPT elevation of the order of 1000. So from among the options the most probable option is HCC. The risk of HCC is increased as well in patients with chronic hepatitis C almost exclusively in patients with cirrhosis, and almost after at least several decades, usually after three decades of disease. Among such cirrhotic patients with chronic hepatitis C, the annual risk of HCC is ~1-4%. 30% of patients with hepatitis C develop hepatocellular carcinoma over 30 years. 20% develop cirrhosis over 20 years. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 82, Pg: 643

429.q: A 59-year-old man presents with a painful swollen left knee as well as pain and stiffness of both his hands. On examination his skin is pigmented. There is tenderness and swelling of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands, he has hepatomegaly of 8 cm below the costal margin. His knee is swollen and aspiration of the joint yields turbid, straw coloured fluid. Which one of the following diagnoses is likely?
429.e: The patient has haemochromatosis as evidenced by the pigmentation and the hepatomegaly. Hemochromatosis involves joints mainly the second and the third MCP joints. It mainly causes chondrocalcinosis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21 st ed, Ch: 374, Pg: 2871

Ans. is 'c' i.e., Increased copper in liver Diagnosis of Wilson disease The gold standard for diagnosis is liver biopsy with quantitative copper assay --> concentration of copper in a liver biopsy sample > 200 mg/g dry weight. Other tests are ? Serum ceruloplasmin level --> low o Urine copper excretion --> increased KF rings o DNA Haplotype analysis.

429.q: A 15-year male child presented with hepatomegaly, involuntary movements, poor scholastic performance. His sister died at 5 years of age. Eye examination is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
429.e: The presence of hepatomegaly, involuntary movements points to Wilson's disease. Wilson Disease is an inherited condition that causes the body to retain excess copper. The copper buildup leads to damage in the kidneys, brain, and eyes. If not treated, Wilson Disease can cause severe brain damage, liver failure, and death.

429.q: A 25-year-old man has loin pains on the left. His urine dipstick shows blood and no protein. MSU culture shows no growth. An abdominal XR shows 2 calculi in the left kidney with a ground glass appearance. How should this patient be managed?
o: He should be advised to drink less water
He should have the calculi removed surgically
429.e: The ground glass appearance of the stones suggests cystine stones . Hexagonal crystals are seen in Cystinuria. Autosomal recessive disorder. Abnormal reabsorption of basic aminoacids.(COAL - cystine, ornithine, arginine, lysine). Visible on plain radiograph. Form staghorn calculi. Raising urinary pH using potassium salts, as sodium can cause increased cystine excretion. Drugs that covalently bind Cystine and facilitate its solubility are also used. Eg: D Penicillamine and Tiopronin. The latter has a better side effect profile. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 318, Pg: 2370-2373.

Ans. is 'a' i.e., Copper Copper containing protein ceruloplasmin is necessary for transport of iron in the Ferric form across membranes Copper is an integral component of ALA synthase, which is necessary for heme synthesis Copper helps in the uptake of iron across normoblasts

429.q: A 40 year old man presents with slurring of his speech and unsteadiness.He has a coarse tremor in his hands and ataxic, shuffling gait on examination. His blood tests show normal renal function. AST is 250 (1-30) U/l, ALP is 350 (1-250) U/l and Bilirubin is 2.2 mg/dl. Which is the best investigation to confirm a diagnosis?
429.e: Wilson's disease can present with early Parkinson's, psychiatric symptoms and dysarthria. It also causes abnormal liver function. It is an autosomal recessive condition. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low. Urinary copper excretion is raised. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 415, Pg: 3235-3236

429.q: The KF ring is associated with which of the following conditions?
429.e: Explanation: The Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring is due to copper deposition in Descemet's membrane of the cornea . It is a hallmark feature of Wilson's disease , an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism characterised by hepatic, neurological, and psychiatric manifestations . Slit-lamp examination is the best method to visualise KF rings. Explanation of other options: Hemochromatosis (Option A): Characterised by iron overload affecting the liver, pancreas, heart, and skin ("bronze diabetes"), but no KF ring is seen. Alzheimer's disease (Option C): A neurodegenerative disorder with memory loss and amyloid plaques, not associated with copper deposition. Huntington's disease (Option D): A genetic movement disorder due to CAG repeats, with chorea and psychiatric features, but no ocular signs like KF rings.

429.q: All of the following statements about. Wilson's disease are true, EXCEPT-
o: It is an autosomal recessive disorder
Zinc acetate is effective as maintenance therapy
429.e: Answer is C (Urinary copper excretion is 100 p (>1.6 umol) per 24 hours. Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder It is caused by a mutation of a gene on chromosome BQ which promotes Cu excretion (ATP 7B gene) Symptomatic patients with Wilson's disease invariably have urinary copper excretion of >100 lig, per 24 hours (>1.6 innol /24 hr) Zinc is the treatment of choice for maintainance therapy in Wilson's disease Zinc is the treatment of choice in Wilson's disease for A. Initial therapy in patients with hepatitis without decompensation(2 A. Maintainance therapy B. Presymptomatic patient C. Pediatric patients D. Pregnant patients

430.q: A 22-year-old male is evaluated by his primary care physician for dysuria. A urethral swab is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. He receives appropriate antibiotic treatment. He returns to the clinic four weeks later complaining of pain in the knees, ankles, and lower back. Repeat testing is negative for both Chlamydia and Neisseria gonorrhea. Which additional finding might be expected on examination?
o: Right upper quadrant pain and hepatomegaly
Nontender subcutaneous nodules over several large joints
430.e: Conjunctival injection mainly affects the posterior conjunctival blood vessels. Because these vessels are more superficial than the ciliary arteries, they produce more redness, move with the conjunctiva, and constrict with the application of topical vasoconstrictors. Reference: Robbins, 10 th edition Page number - 822

430.q: A 35 year old woman has abdominal pain, jaundice and worsening ascites. She drinks 20 units of alcohol each week, and takes the oral contraceptive pill. Which of the following findings would make a diagnosis of Budd Chiari syndrome likely?
430.e: Budd-Chiari syndrome is an uncommon condition induced by thrombotic or nonthrombotic obstruction to hepatic venous outflow.The classic triad of abdominal pain,ascites, and hepatomegaly is observed in the vast majority of patients but is nonspecific. Ascetic fluid protein may be high or low in Budd Chiari syndrome. Tender hepatomegaly on examination is one of the hallmark signs. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch:50, Pg: 323

430.q: A 37 year old man presents with 2 bowls full of hematemesis. He drinks 10 pints of beer a day and has done so for 10 years. Upper GI endoscopy reveals oesophageal varices. Which of the following is effective in reducing the rates of rebleeding in the future?
430.e: Non selective beta blockers (propranolol, nadolol) can be used for reducing rebleeding in oesophageal varices. They work by decreasing hepatic venous pressure gradient and thereby decreasing portal hypertension. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 344, Pg: 2630

430.q: A 39 year old man who has a history of heavy alcohol intake presents with hematemesis and melena. On admission, he was in a pre-shock state with severe anemia and was resuscitated with blood and fresh frozen plasma. Endoscopic examination identified bleeding from the varices in the lower esophagus. Which one of the following drugs should be used for treatment?
430.e: Octreotide and terlipressin are widely used in acute variceal hemorrhage to reduce the bleeding rate octreotide is often used for emergency treatment of bleeding oesophageal varices in patients with cirrhosis of the liver. It is given intravenously.It acts by causing splanchnic vasoconstriction and should be given for a minimum 48 hours . Propranolol and Nadolol are used for prophylaxis of bleeding in a patient known to have esophageal varices. They should not be used in an acute condition as they can cause hypotension. Vitamin K is used to treat hepatic coagulopathy in acute liver failure, warfarin overdose and vit K deficiency of the newborn. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21 st Ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2630

430.q: A 60-year-old man takes atenolol for hypertension. Which of the following side effects is he most likely to be aware of two hours after taking atenolol?
430.e: Atenolol is a water soluble beta blocker, taken once daily and is not associated with drowsiness/sleep disturbance like the lipid-soluble β-blockers. It is not associated with nausea or hesitancy of micturition and would be unlikely to produce significant postural hypotension in a hypertensive subject. However, fatigue is a frequent side effect which typically is felt two hours and beyond after taking the drug. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:271 pg:1903

430.q: Pontine hemorrhage most common cause is
430.e: Answer- A. Hypertension Most common cause of pontine hemorrhage is hypertension.

430.q: Portal hypertension is defined as hepatic venous pressure gradient above __mm Hg?
430.e: Portal hypertension is defined as the elevation of the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) to >5 mm Hg. clinically significant portal hypertension is defined as a HVPG ≥10 mmHg , when there is substantial risk of decompensation with variceal bleeding. Cirrhosis is the most common cause of portal hypertension Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 344 pg. 2629

430.q: Resistant hypertension is defined as when BP control is not occurring with use of 3 drugs. Among these, which of the following drug patients has to be on to meet the definition?
430.e: The term resistant hypertension refers to patients with blood pressures persistently >140/90 mmHg despite taking three or more antihypertensive agents, including a diuretic.

431.q: A 34 year old patient has had a hepatitis test for investigation of jaundice. He has a positive Hep BsAg (HBsAg) and has IgM antibodies to Hep B Core (anti-HBc). What is he likely to have?
431.e: The positive anti-HBc (IgM) and HBsAg suggests acute infection. When the infection resolves, HBsAg becomes negative and anti-HBc (IgG) is positive. In patients who have been vaccinated, HBsAg is negative and anti-HBs is positive. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 339, Pg: 3577

431.q: Which of the following enzyme elevation is/are less specific for the cholestasis jaundice?
431.e: ENZYMES THAT REFLECT CHOLESTASIS The activities of three enzymes-alkaline phosphatase, 5′-nucleotidase, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)-are usually elevated in cholestasis. Alkaline phosphatase and 5′-nucleotidase are found in or near the bile canalicular membrane of hepatocytes, whereas GGT is located in the endoplasmic reticulum and in bile duct epithelial cells. Reflecting its more diffuse localization in the liver, GGT elevation in serum is less specific for cholestasis than are elevations of alkaline phosphatase or 5′- nucleotidase. Some have advocated the use of GGT to identify patients with occult alcohol use.

431.q: A 47 year old man has painless jaundice. He has pale stools and dark urine. On examination he is deeply jaundiced and has scratch marks all over his body. On palpation of the abdomen Courvoisier's sign is positive. Where is the level of biliary obstruction?
431.e: Courvoisier's sign is a palpable distended gallbladder on examination of the abdomen. Obstruction below the level of the cystic duct causes this, probably due to carcinoma of the pancreas. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine Ch:83, Pg: 659,

431.q: A 33 year old man presents with jaundice. He has been on a drug which was prescribed by his GP for several weeks. His blood tests show a bilirubin of 2.6 mg/dl, ALP of 450 U/l and AST 50 U/l. Which one of the following drugs is likely to cause cholestatic jaundice?
431.e: Drugs causing Cholestasis: anabolic steroids containing an alkyl or ethinyl group at carbon 17 azathioprine cetirizine cyclosporine Chlorpromazine Co amoxiclav Erythromycin estolate diclofenac estrogen febuxostat indinavir mercaptopurine methyltestosterone tamoxifen ticlopidine. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21 st Ed, Ch: 340 Pg: 2587

431.q: A 38 year old presents with a 10-day history of loose stools and mild abdominal discomfort, and recent onset of blood in stool. Ulcerative colitis was suspected by the gastroenterologist. Which one of the following is the investigation of choice?
431.e: Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice to evaluate ulcerative colitis (UC). Colonoscopy in UC shows continous involvement of mucosa with no skip lesions. Features such as loss of haustral pattern, erythema, oedema, granular mucosa, blood, pseudopolyps, erosion, ulceration are seen. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:326 Pg: 2475

431.q: A 72 year old woman with longstanding hip osteoarthritis presents complaints of constipation and loose stool. She undergoes a sigmoidoscopy. A rectal biopsy shows pigment-laden macrophages in the lamina propria. What is the most likely cause?
431.e: The pigment laden macrophages suggest that there is melanosis coli. The most common association is with laxatives. To a lesser extent, melanosis coli is also associated with ulcerative colitis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 46 Pg: 307

431.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a five day history of lower abdominal pain and diarrhea.He has a history of chronic obstructive airways disease (COAD) and has had numerous acute infective exacerbations over the last three months.On examination he was dehydrated, with a temperature of 38.6°C, a blood pressure of 102/72 mmHg and has a distended, tender abdomen.Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation for this patient?
431.e: This is pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridium difficile secondary to antibiotic usage for his COPD. Plain AXR is useful for diagnosing toxic dilatation and would be the investigation of choice here due to his abdominal distension, so toxic dilatation should be excluded prior to sigmoidoscopy. However it does not establish the diagnosis.Stool microscopy has no value but stool toxin assay is useful. A patient with diarrhea normally has involvement of the distal colon and rectum, and sigmoidoscopy with biopsy is helpful for rapid diagnosis but should not be performed if toxic dilatation is suspected.Patients with involvement of right colon usually have little or no diarrhoea. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1069

432.q: A 29 year old lady presents with abdominal pain to the GP who suspects irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following is a recognized feature of irritable bowel syndrome?
432.e: Irritable bowel syndrome is a clinical diagnosis characterized by- Abdominal pain relieved by defecation Bloating Alternating bowel habits - constipation, diarrhoea - alone or alternating with each other. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 327 pg: 2490

432.q: A 66-year-old lady presents with symptoms suggestive of irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following would represent a 'red flag' indicator and prompt further investigation?
o: Change in bowel habit for last two years
More frequent stools last two months
432.e: The 'red flag' indicators listed in the NICE guidelines as: Unintentional and unintended weight loss Rectal bleeding A family history of bowel or ovarian cancer A change in bowel habit to loose and / or more frequent stools persisting for more than six weeks in a person aged over 60 years. Also, on clinical examination the other 'red flag' indicators are: Anaemia Abdominal mass Rectal mass Inflammatory markers for inflammatory bowel disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 327 Pg: 2493

432.q: What is the differentiating feature between IBS and organic GI disease?
432.e: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional bowel disorder which is non inflammatory. The unifying feature of inflammatory diarrhea due to any cause is the presence of leukocytes or leukocyte derived protein Calprotectin in stools. Another inflammatory marker in stool is Fecal Lactoferrin, which is also present in activated neutrophils. Both of them can be used in diagnosis of relapses of inflammatory bowel disease from IBS or bacterial overgrowth. Fecal calprotectin is also having the advantage of being a sensitive marker of Colonic or ileocolonic inflammation rather than isolated ileal inflammation. Abdominal pain, diarrhea and presence of mucous in stools can be seen in IBS as well as inflammatory diarrhea. Blood in stools, nocturnal symptoms and weight loss is uncommon in IBS.

433.q: A 44 year old man has a diagnosis of Ulcerative Colitis. He was incidentally found to have positive anti smooth muscle antibodies by the GP who sent an autoimmune screen. Which is the next recommended test for this patient?
433.e: A positive anti smooth muscle antibody test is suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis . Liver function tests may demonstrate elevated levels of bilirubin, AST and ALT. A liver biopsy may then be warranted. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg: 2482

433.q: A 44 year old man has a diagnosis of Ulcerative Colitis. He was incidentally found to have positive anti smooth muscle antibodies by the family doctor who sent an autoimmune screen. Which is the next recommended test for this patient?
433.e: The features are suggestive of autoimmune hepatitis. Liver function tests may demonstrated elevated levels of bilirubin, AST and ALT. A liver biopsy may then be warranted. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch:341 , Pg: 2613-2615

433.q: A 43 year old man has recurrent episodes of bloody diarrhea and lower abdominal cramping. Histologic evaluation of a biopsy from flexible sigmoidoscopy reveals acute inflammation without architectural distortion consistent with ulcerative colitis.Which of the following conditions is associated with the condition?
433.e: 75% of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis have inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease of unknown etiology. In the absence of underlying bile duct abnormalities, a generalized beading and stenosis of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree characterize PSC. PSC is usually progressive, leading to cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and liver failure.Typically, a cholestatic jaundice picture is seen with the liver function tests. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch: 344, Pg: 2627-2628

433.q: A 24 year old man presents with a 10 month history of weight loss, oral ulceration and diarrhoea. A flexible sigmoidoscopy is performed and a colonic biopsy was taken. Which of the following histological features would favour a diagnosis of Crohn's disease over ulcerative colitis?
433.e: Crohn's disease is characterized by transmural inflammation (inflammation of all layers of the gut), fissures, preservation of crypt architecture and non caseating granulomata. Ulcerative colitis is typified by mucosal inflammation, general inflammatory cell infiltration, goblet cell mucus depletion and crypt abscesses. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

433.q: Which of the following features seen on barium studies is typical of both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease?
433.e: Pseudopolyps are seen in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. The remainder of options listed are features of Crohn's disease rather than ulcerative colitis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg: 2475-2477

433.q: A 26-year-old woman had ulcerative colitis (UC) for seven years and was prescribed mesalazine 1.5 g per day. She smokes upto 20 cigarettes per day and is 10 weeks pregnant. She complaines of worsening symptoms with six bloody stools per day. Which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Initiation of an elemental diet risks fetal malnutrition.
Oral mesalazine therapy should be withdrawn.
433.e: The effect of pregnancy on ulcerative colitis is variable. In general, the health of a mother with UC is the best predictor of the outcome of the pregnancy. Hence drug treatment is preferred to leaving active disease untreated. Azathioprine should not generally be started during pregnancy, but it is only relatively contraindicated . However, azathioprine is concentrated in breastfeeding. In the context of pregnancy, an elemental diet does not risk maternal and/or fetal malnutrition. Oral corticosteroids and mesalazine are not contraindicated in pregnancy. Additional folate supplementation should be given. Topical 5- ASA is also not contraindicated. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 326, Pg: 2488

433.q: A 25-year-old man has been admitted with severe ulcerative colitis. He has been on high-dose steroids intravenously for three days but there have been no signs of improvement. The gastroenterology team have decided to commence cyclosporine. Which of the following is a recognized adverse effect of cyclosporine?
433.e: The side effects of cyclosporine include - Hypertension Nephrotoxicity Gum hypertrophy Hirsutism Convulsions The indications for cyclosporine use include - Eczema, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 313 Pg: 2328

433.q: A 44 year old man has 5 year history of bloody diarrhoea mixed with mucus. He had lost 2 stones in weight over this time. Flexible sigmoidoscopy showed loss of vascular appearance, erythema, and superficial ulceration consistent with ulcerative colitis. Which one of the following features is associated with the condition?
433.e: The extraintestinal manifestations of Inflammatory Bowel Disease include- Ocular - Episcleritis , uveitis Rheumatological - Ankylosing spondylitis, peripheral migratory arthritis Dermatological - Erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum Primary sclerosing cholangitis – most common in ulcerative colitis Nephrolithiasis ( calcium oxalate stones - most common)- most common in crohn's disease (CD) T erminal ileum is the most commonly involved site in CD. Megaloblastic anaemia occurs in CD as vitamin B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 326, Pg: 2480-2482

434.q: A 55-year-old man on no current treatment for his quiescent ulcerative colitis (UC) is found to have an ESR of 95 mm/hr (0-20mm/1st hour). Investigations show: Haemoglobin 13.2g/dL (13.0-18.0) WCC 4.5 x 10^9/L (4-11) Platelets 160 x 10^9/L (150-400) Corrected Calcium 8.8 mg/dl IgG 25g/L(6-13) IgA 1.8g/L(0.8-3.0) IgM 1.6g/L(0.4-2.2) What is the most appropriate next investigation?
434.e: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate ( ESR) is not raised in quiescent UC . Hence there must be another reason in this case. The only abnormal result given is a raised IgG . This suggests that myeloma is a possible diagnosis. Plasma immunoelectrophoresis to look for an M band is the most appropriate next investigation. A bone marrow trephine is the definitive investigation but is traumatic and painful to the patient and so is not the next investigation of choice. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st d, Ch:111 Pg: 867

435.q: A patient who has had a subtotal thyroidectomy for hyperthyroidism is on thyroxine replacement. She has a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), normal tri-iodothyronine (T3) and low free thyroxine (T4) levels. What is the most likely reason for those results?
o: The patient's results are as expected - no change in treatment is required
435.e: Once on a full replacement dose, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels should be checked at intervals of 1-3 years, depending on their stability. Fluctuating or elevated TSH levels in a previously stable patient, or thyroxine requirements in excess of 200 mg/day, usually indicate compliance problems. It is important to rule out malabsorption or abnormal thyroxine kinetics caused by drugs: cholestyramine, ferrous sulphate, lovastatin, aluminium hydroxide, rifampicin, amiodarone, carbamazepine, and phenytoin all alter the absorption or clearance of thyroxine. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:377 Pg:2705-07

435.q: A 24 year old woman has type 1 diabetes. She has weight loss over the past 3 months, and irregular menstrual cycles. Her bowel habit has been unchanged. On examination her BMI was 24 kg/m2. Investigations show: haemoglobin of 8.1 g/dl with a MCV of 69 fl. Which is the likely diagnosis?
435.e: This patient has type 1 diabetes – an autoimmune condition. She now presents with iron deficiency anemia along with weight loss. So the possibility of celiac disease should be ruled out as people with type 1 diabetes are at up to six times greater risk of having celiac disease. Dietary deficiency of iron and heavy menstrual loss will not cause weight loss there is no abdominal pain or blood in stools to suggest a Chron's Disease. Antibodies to gliadin should be sent and the diagnosis of celiac disease can be confirmed by a biopsy of small intestine which will show villous atrophy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2463

435.q: A 44 year old man has drunk 50 units a week of alcohol for 20 years. During investigations, she has :Haemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 110 fL (80-96), white cell count 2.1 x 10^9/L (4-11), platelet count 75 x 10^9/L (150-400). What might explain these results?
435.e: The haematological picture is that of macrocytic anemia (most commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency). Folate deficiency occurs in the majority of binge-drinking alcoholics and is a common cause of anemia. Inadequate dietary intake, intestinal malabsorption, and impaired folate storage in the liver all contribute to folate deficiency. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine21 st ed, ch: 99, Pg: 773

435.q: A 64-year-old lady has a six month history of abdominal discomfort, bloating and altered frequency in stools. Her symptoms seem to be worse following a large meal where she also feels nausea. Clinical examination is normal. She is suspected of fulfilling the criteria for irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following investigations should be undertaken to exclude other diagnoses?
435.e: Patients who fulfil the diagnostic criteria for irritable bowel syndrome should be screened for other conditions with- Complete blood count to rule out anemia Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C reactive protein to rule out inflammatory etiology Anti-endomysial antibodies, Tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies to rule out celiac disease. Some patients with IBS-D may have undiagnosed celiac sprue. Because the symptoms of celiac sprue respond to a gluten-free diet, testing for celiac sprue in IBS may prevent years of morbidity and attendant expense Other tests can be done to rule out any other suspected pathology depending on the presenting symptoms. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 327 Pg: 2493

435.q: A 46 year old man has a diagnosis of celiac disease. He presents with a one month history of intermittent, colicky, central abdominal pain and weight loss of 5 kg. There is positive fecal occult blood. What is the most appropriate investigation?
435.e: Colonoscopy is necessary to exclude a colonic carcinoma. There is a relatively high prevalence of colorectal neoplasia among older patients with coeliac disease who can present with iron deficiency or altered bowel habit. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 325 Pg: 2464

435.q: A 36 year man has abdominal pains, weight loss and diarrhoea. He was subsequently found to be lactose intolerant and a small bowel biopsy showed changes consistent with celiac disease. He has also noticed that he is developing itchiness and a generalised rash. Which one of the following skin conditions is it likely to be?
435.e: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease. It presents as an intense pruritic rash consisting of papules and vesicles. Commonly presents on the extensor surface of extremities, buttocks and neck. Occurs due to granular IgA deposits in epidermal basement membrane. Treatment – Dapsone and gluten free diet. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed Ch: 325, Pg: 2463

435.q: Secretory diarrhea is not seen in:
435.e: Answer is B (Celiac Disease) Celiac Disease is associated with Steatorrheal diarrhoea from mucosa! malabsorption. Secretory Diarrhea Certain Bacterial Infection Vibrio Cholera Enterotoxigenic E.Coli Non Osmotic Stimulant Laxatives Hormone Producing Endocrine Tumors Carcinoid, VlPomas, Gastrinomas, Medullary Carcinoma Thyroid (Calcitonin) Bile acids (endogenous laxatives) Bowel resection / disease or fistula Addison's Disease Congenital Electrolyte Absorption defects Chronic Alcohol Ingestion Diabetic Diarrhea Steatorrheal Diarrhea Intraluminal maldigestion Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, Bacterial overgrowth, Bariatric surgery, Liver disease Mucosal malabsorption Celiac sprue, Whipple's disease, Infections, Abetalipoproteinemia, Ischemia Postmucosal obstruction (1° or 2° lymphatic obstruction)

435.q: A 43 year old man has had intermittent diarrhoea and joint pains for 6 months. On examination he has limited vertical eye movements. Which pathogen is the likely cause of his symptoms?
435.e: Whipple's disease characteristically occurs in middle-aged men, who present with weight loss, fever, abdominal pain, arthralgias and intestinal symptoms of diarrhea and malabsorption. CNS and cardiac system are commonly involved. Confusion, memory loss, or uncontrolled eye movements indicate that the infection has travelled to the CNS. Trimethoprim - sulfamethoxazole is recommended; treatment is continued for one year. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg:

436.q: During an epidemic of hepatitis E, fatality is maximum in
436.e: In outbreaks of waterborne hepatitis E in India and Asia, the case-fatality rate is 1-2% and up to 10-20% in pregnant women. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 339 pg. 2577

436.q: A 76-year-old woman presents with acute monocular visual loss. Fundoscopy reveals a swollen pale optic disc in the affected eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
436.e: The presence of a swollen optic disc suggests ischaemic optic neuropathy. In elderly people giant cell arteritis is a common presentation of acute monocular visual loss. Optic neuritis is very rare in people over the age of 50. You would expect bilateral swollen optic discs in raised intracranial pressure. In central retinal vein occlusion you would expect diffuse retinal haemorrhages. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3343

436.q: What is the Most common source of E. coli bacteremia?
436.e: The urinary tract is the most common source of E. coli bacteremia, accounting for one-half to two-thirds of episodes Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1071

436.q: Which of the following factors decrease large intestinal motility?
436.e: Anticholinergic agents decrease large intestinal motility. The other options and cholinergic agents increase large intestinal motility. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:327, Pg: 2494

436.q: What will you give to stop chyluria in diet?
436.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e.,Medium Chain FA [Ref Harrison's 18thie p. 294] Medium chain fatty acids directly enter the portal vein on absorption,bypassing the lymphatics.Hence,they are used in chyluria

436.q: A 75 year man presents with right foot drop, hand numbness, fevers, malaise, weight loss, polymyalgia and diffuse joint pains for 2 months. On examination, he appears unwell and has a temperature of 38°C. Investigations reveal:Hb 8.5 g/dL erythrocyte sedimentation rate 95 mm/hr serum creatinine 2.0 mg/dL urine analysis: blood ++ urine microscopy: white cells & red cell casts seen Which one of the following is the LEAST likely diagnosis?
436.e: This patient presents with multi system involvement as characterized by the presence of multiple peripheral nerve involvement, arthralgia and fever. His laboratory reports show features of inflammation characterized by anemia, high ESR. He also has renal impairment with hematuria and RBC cast which indicates glomerulonephritis. The entire constellation of symptoms points towards the diagnosis of a vasculitis. PAN is a disease of medium sized vessels and it does not cause glomerulonephritis. Renal impairment and hypertension can be seen in PAN due to involvement of the renal artery or its branches. All the other options are small vessel vasculitis and can cause glomerulonephritis. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2810

436.q: A 35-year-old female presented with claudication in forearm, transient loss of vision and abdominal pain. She also had weak femoral pulses. Fundus also showed retinal haemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
436.e: In this question, we have a young female with symptoms of upper limb claudication, visual loss, abdominal pain and weak femoral pulses. The history points to the involvement of the branches of Aorta. The retinal hemorrhage could be secondary to hypertension. The involvement of large and medium vessels in a young female points towards the diagnosis of Takayasu Arteritis. PAN typically involves renal and visceral vessels, ie, small and medium sized arteries. It does not produce absent peripheral pulses. Microscopic polyangiitis is a small vessel vasculitis, mainly presenting as glomerulonephritis and pulmonary vasculitis. Thromboangiitis obliterans(Buerger's disease) is an inflammatory occlusive vascular disorder of small and medium sized arteries of the distal upper and lower limb and is seen in men

436.q: Atheromatous changes of blood vessels affects early in -
436.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Heart Sites of Atherosclerosis Atherosclerotic plaques develop primarily in elastic arteries (e.g., aorta, carotid and iliac arteries), and large & medium sized muscular arteries (e.g., coronary artery and poplitial arteries). In descending order, the vessels most commonly involved are - Abdominal aorta (most common) → Causing aneurysm Coronary arteries (heart) → Causing MI Popliteal arteries → Causing ischemic gangrene of lower limbs. Internal carotid arteries → Causing stroke a Circle of willis Vessels usually spared are Vessels of upper extremities Mesentric and renal vessels, except at their ostia.

437.q: A patient with Wegener's glomerulonephritis presents with sinusitis and hemoptysis. His chest radiograph shows several large cavitary pulmonary nodules, consistent with ventilation- perfusion imbalance with low V'/Q' units. Which of the following will be greater than normal in a patient with a low V'/Q' ratio?
437.e: Areas with low V/Q ratios produce hypoxemia or a decreased PaO2, which leads to A decrease in the dissolved oxygen content of the blood and A decrease in PaCO2, due to stimulation of the peripheral chemoreceptors. At lower PaO2 levels, arterial oxygen saturation is decreased, which decreases the oxyhemoglobin content. Because the mixed alveolar PO2 is normal and the arterial PO2 is less than normal, the A-a gradient is greater than normal. Reference: Levitzky, pp 113-116, 122-123.

437.q: Risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma after HCV infection are:
o: Infection in infancy or early childhood.
437.e: HCC usually occurs after three decades of disease. And occurs exclusively in patients with cirrhosis. 50-70% - Develops chronic HCV 20-25% - Develops Cirrhosis. 1-4% - Develops HCC Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition page Ch: 341 Pg 2615

437.q: Which of the following is true regarding laboratory findings of Zieve's Syndrome?
437.e: A unique form of hemolytic anemia (with spur cells and acanthocytes) called Zieve's syndrome can occur in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. Platelet counts are often reduced early in the disease, reflective of portal hypertension with hypersplenism. Serum total bilirubin can be normal or elevated with advanced disease. Prothrombin times are often prolonged and usually do not respond to administration of parenteral vitamin K. Serum sodium levels are usually normal unless patients have ascites and then can be depressed, largely due to ingestion of excess free water. Transient hyperlipidemia may also be seen. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 344 pg. 2625

437.q: A 26 year old man has had behavioural disturbance recently. His parents mentioned that his brother has been investigated for liver problems recently. On examination, he has a MMSE score of 28/30. He has a mask like face and was noticed to have hypersalivation. When investigations are complete, which drug is most likely to be used for treatment?
437.e: The likely diagnosis is Wilson's disease. Most patients who present with neuropsychiatric manifestations have cirrhosis. The most common presenting neurologic feature is asymmetric tremor, occurring in approximately half of individuals with Wilson disease. Frequent early symptoms include difficulty speaking, excessive salivation, ataxia, masklike facies, clumsiness with the hands, and personality changes. The disease is autosomal recessive. Zinc is used for treatment of Wilson disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 415Pg: 3236

437.q: A 50 year old female presents with history of palpable purpurae for the last 6 months. Now she has cough and hemoptysis and she presents with desaturation. Her investigations shows Hb of 9g/dL, ESR of 100mm/ 1st hour. A biopsy of her skin lesions shows fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas. Which of the following is the most likely disease?
437.e: Patient here presents with cutaneous symptoms and pulmonary involvement and histologically shows fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas. Among the small vessel vasculitis, Microscopic polyangiitis presents lacks granulomas and presents with fibrinoid necrosis. Among the given potions PAN also presents with fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas. So PAN is also a possibility. But what makes PAN unlikely is the pulmonary involvement. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2809

437.q: A young boy presents with PAN like vasculitis. Which of the following diseases is he likely to harbor?
437.e: PAN like vasculitis is seen with Hepatitis B, C, Adenosine deaminase deficiency Type 2 and Hairy cell leukemia. PAN is a disease of middle aged, and is common in males. If a very young boy presents with PAN like symptoms Adenosine deaminase deficiency should be suspected. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 363, Pg 2810-2811

437.q: A 67 year old man presents with dysphagia of solids for the past three months. There is a history of 10 kg weight loss in 4 months following loss of appetite. He has had symptoms of indigestion and heartburn for 10 years. He regularly takes Gaviscon and milk of magnesia. He is a heavy smoker. He undergoes endoscopy, which reveals a small tumour at the lower part of the oesophagus. What is the likely aetiological cause?
437.e: The history is suggestive of gastro oesophageal reflux for the past 10 years. Continuous acid reflux causes metaplasia of the stratified squamous epithelium (which normally lines the distal oesophagus) to an abnormal columnar epithelium. This is known as Barrett's oesophagus . Barrett's oesophagus increases the risk of development of adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus . Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 323 Pg: 2430

437.q: A 48 year old man presents with chronic recurrent sinusitis and occasional haemoptysis. He has a middle lobe patchy shadowing on his chest X-ray. His creatinine is 1.40 mg/dl and urine dipstick shows ++ protein and blood. Which test result is most likely?
437.e: The presence of hematuria and proteinuria indicates renal involvement in the form of a glomerulonephritis. Glomerulonephritis along with upper respiratory tract involvement in the form of recurrent sinusitis and pulmonary involvement indicates a small vessel vasculitis- Wegener’s Granulomatosis. 90% of patients Wegener’s granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with polyangiitis) is associated with c ANCA positivity directed against anti proteinase 3. Positive ANA may be seen in a variety of collagen vascular diseases especially SLE. Positive Kveim test is seen in Sarcoidosis Positive ASO titre is seen in Acute Rheumatic fever. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2806

438.q: All of the following statements regarding Atopic kerato-conjunctivitis are true except?
o: Associated history of Asthma/ allergic rhinitis frequently noted
438.e: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis: Demographics: Generally seen in young adults. Associated Atopic Diseases: Often associated with a history of other atopic diseases such as: Asthma Allergic rhinitis Atopic eczematoid dermatitis in the patient or their family. Disease Characteristics: Responsible for an extremely severe and chronic form of ocular surface disorder. The disease spectrum varies in range of severity: Ranging from mild cases to chronic and persistent inflammation. Comparison to VKC (Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis): Similar in nature to VKC but tends to be more: Severe Chronic Extends into adulthood. Reference: Parson's Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

438.q: A 50 year old male with history of SSc, complaints of fatigue and exertional dyspnoea of 3 months duration. He has also noted malena. On examination, he was pale with spooning of nails. What will be the likely finding on upper GI endoscopy?
438.e: The cause of chronic GI blood loss in a patient with SSC is Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia. The endoscopic appearance is Water melon stomach. Reference : Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2781

438.q: A 40 year old lady has tightening of the skin around her hands and mouth. She has several telangiectasia on her hands, and complains of severe cold hands in winter. She was noticed to be pale. Investigations show : Hb 4.5 g/dl MCV 105 fl WCC 6 x 10^9/L platelets 230 x 10^9/L Iron 22 (14-29) μmol/l Ferritin 155 (15-200)μmol/l total iron binding capacity 50 (45-72) umol/l Folate 11 (3-20) ng/l Vitamin B12 - 85 (120-700 pmol/l) What is the likely cause of anaemia?
438.e: Scleroderma can cause folate deficiency due to malabsorption. However, in this case, the folate levels are normal and there is B12 deficiency. B12 deficiency can occur in conditions where there is bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine (blind loop syndromes) such as jejunal diverticulosis, Crohns disease, fistulas and scleroderma. The anaerobic organisms metabolise vitamin B12 and impair absorption. When systemic sclerosis (SSc) involves the small intestine, normal peristaltic movements are lost and motility is impaired leading to stasis and dilatation. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:360 Page number:2781

438.q: Which of the following is false regarding Systemic Sclerosis?
o: Calcinosis cutis is more seen with long standing SSc, with anti SCl-70 positivity
The calcium and phosphate levels are normal
Crystals are composed of calcium hydroxypetite
Paraspinal sheet calcifications may occur with neurological complications
438.e: Calcinosis cutis is more seen with long standing systemic sclerosis, especially the anti centromere positive limited SSc. The serum calcium and phosphate levels are normal and the deposits are composed of calcium hydroxyapatite. The calcifications usually occur in finger pads, palms, extensor aspects of forearm. Large deposits can cause local nerve compression. Paraspinal sheet calcification can be seen with neurological complications. The lesions can ulcerate the overlying skin too. Reference : Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2779

438.q: Which is not included in the pathologic triad for Systemic sclerosis?
438.e: Three cardinal pathomechanistic processes underlie the protean clinical manifestations and pathologic changes of SSc: diffuse microangiopathy, inflammation and autoimmunity, and visceral and vascular fibrosis affecting multiple organs. In general, autoimmunity and reversible vascular reactivity are early features of SSc, whereas fibrosis and atrophy occur later in the disease. Diffuse Microangiopathy is the first and primary pathogenic event and is responsible for most of the clinical symptoms, including, telangiectasis, Raynaud's Phenomenon, digital ulcers, renal crisis, myocardial involvement and PAH. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:360 Page number:2773

438.q: Which antibody does not have Scleroderma as its phenotype?
438.e: Anti-Ribosomal antibodies are not typically associated with Scleroderma as their phenotype. Anti-Pm-Scl antibodies : These are often found in patients with overlap syndromes involving features of both Scleroderma and Polymyositis. Anti-Ku antibodies : These are associated with some cases of Scleroderma, particularly the limited cutaneous form. Anti-U1 RNP antibodies : These are more commonly associated with Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD), which can have overlapping features of Scleroderma among other autoimmune conditions. Anti-Ribosomal antibodies : These antibodies are primarily associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and are not a typical feature of Scleroderma. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:360 Page number:2776

438.q: Therapeutic usage of Chloroquine is not indicated in which of the following conditions?
438.e: CQ is being used in RA not in ARF CQ is being used in the following conditions. My RED LIP M-malaria R- RA E- Extraintestinal Amebiasis D- Discoid Lupus L- Lepra Reaction I- Infective Mononucleosis P-Photogenic reaction Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1732

438.q: A 50 year old lady has a diagnosis of scleroderma. She is admitted with dizziness. On examination, her pressure is 182/100 and there is bilateral papilloedema. Blood tests reveal a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dl. What is the best medication for treatment?
438.e: Accelerated hypertension and bilateral papilledema in a patient with Scleroderma indicates Scleroderma Renal Crisis. Accelerated hypertension There will be a rapid decline in renal function, with nephrotic range proteinuria. First line treatment is with ACE inhibitors. ARBs are given only if patient is intolerant to ACEI. Goal is to reduce BP by 20/10mmHg every 24 hours till normal. UIII RNP is a predictor of risk of renal crisis in Scleroderma Anti centromere antibody is a negative predictor. Renal biopsy shows changes of accelerated hypertension. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:317, Pg:2366.

439.q: Which of the following genotypes is associated with the lowest levels of alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT)?
439.e: α-1antitrypsin deficiency is due to the insufficient plasma activity of the enzyme that degrades several proteins like neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G and proteinase 3. It is an AR disease and is characterized by emphysema and cirrhosis. The wild genotytpe is PiMM seen in > 90% of individuals. The clinically significant mutation is PiZZ, which is associated with The null phenotype (not in the list of options) is the least common but the most severe form of the disease where there is no detectable AAT in the serum. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2615

439.q: Which one of the following statements is true of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
o: Patients show at least a 15 % improvement in the FEV1 after nebulised bronchodilator
Inhaled corticosteroid usage does not improve long-term prognosis
Breathlessness is uncommon until the FEV1 falls to approximately 50 % of predicted
Emphysema is associated with increased transfer factor
439.e: 15% improvement in FEV1 level of improvement would mean the presence of asthma. High dose inhaled steroids have been shown (ISOLDE) to improve quality of life and reduce hospitalisation rates by reducing the number of exacerbations, but it does not slow the rate of decline of FEV1 (hence does not affect prognosis). Breathless is common but subjective. Mild COPD (60 - 79% predicted FEV1) are often unknown to their GP. Those with moderate COPD (40 - 59% predicted) are seen intermittently seen by GP, whilst those with severe disease ( It is asthma which is associated with normal or increased transfer factor. COPD is associated with decreased transfer factor. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: Ch:202, Pg: 2187

439.q: A 70 year old man attends the hospital with a history of proximal muscle weakness. He also gives a history of cough of 12 weeks duration and complains of pain of the small joints of the hands. He has small haemorrhages in the nail folds, but is not clubbed. On examination of the chest he has bibasal crackles, and a chest radiograph reveals diffuse reticular infiltrates. Lung function tests confirm a restrictive pattern. What is the likely cause of his interstitial lung disease?
439.e: The patient has a restrictive lung disease with proximal muscle weakness and arthritis. Arthritis and ILD can be seen in diseases like RA and SLE, Sarcoidosis, Systemic Sclerosis etc. But here there is proximal muscle weakness and the patient is an elderly male with nail bed hemorrhages, which could indicate telangiectasia. So the diagnosis is Dermatomyositis. In polymyositis and dermatomyositis patients often develop proximal muscle weakness and of pain in the small joints of the fingers. They may have ragged cuticles and haemorrhages at the finger nail folds. Interstitial lung disease can occur. Underlying malignancy (lungs, ovaries, breasts and stomach) is present in 5% Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 365, Pg: 2820

439.q: A 54-year-old man presents with a two-month history of progressive painless weakness affecting the proximal arms and legs. He has noticed difficulty getting out of a low chair and some difficulty swallowing but denies any rashes or visual symptoms. Investigations shows a CK of 5000 IU/l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
439.e: Proximal muscle weakness with high CPK suggests an inflammatory myopathy. Among the options Polymyositis is an Inflammatory myopathy. GBS does not cause elevated CPK. Hypothyroidism may cause weakness but here there are no clues to suggest a hypothyroidism. PMR causes girdle pain. Weakness is rare. Polymyositis classically presents with relatively painless progressive proximal muscle weakness. Dysphagia is common but the ocular muscles are very rarely involved unlike myasthenia gravis where this is a predominant feature. Diagnosis of polymyositis confirmed by elevated muscle enzymes (creatine kinase) and typical EMG and muscle biopsy findings. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:365 Pg:2819

440.q: Organisms commonly causing Non gonococcal urethritis in males are all except:
440.e: C.trachomatis caused ~30-40% of cases of non- gonococcal urethritis (NGU). M. genitalium - probable cause of many Chlamydia-negative cases. U. urealyticum but not U. parvum is associated with NGU. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 136, Pg: 1080

440.q: IVC filter is used in following except -
o: To prevent progress of native blood vessel disease
440.e: Answer is 'b' i.e. Negligible size of emboli

440.q: A 34 year old lady has developed worsening pruritus and jaundice over the past year. Investigations revealed a positive antimitochondrial antibody and a liver biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of primary biliary cirrhosis. Which of the following is associated with the condition?
440.e: Primary biliary cirrhosis is more common in females and is usually associated with raised IgM levels. Xanthelasma are present due to cholestasis. Connective tissue disorders such as Sjogren's syndrome are associated. A positive antimitochondrial antibody and liver biopsy are the best ways to confirm the diagnosis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21 st Ed, Ch: 344 Pg: 2627

440.q: Which of the following is NOT fitting criteria for APLA?
o: Death of normal fetus at 12th week of gestation
Premature birth at 35th week of gestation
440.e: Clinical criteria include vascular thrombosis, defined as one or more clinical episodes of arterial, venous, or small vessel thrombosis in any tissue or organ; and pregnancy morbidity, defined as one or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond the 10th week of gestation; one or more premature births of a morphologically normal neonate before the 34th week of gestation because of eclampsia, severe preeclampsia, or placental insufficiency; or three or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before the 10th week of gestation. Laboratory criteria include LA, anticardiolipin (aCL), and/or anti-β2 GPI antibodies, at intermediate or high titres on two occasions 12 weeks apart. Reference: HARRISON'S PRINCIPLES OF INTERNAL MEDICIENE, ED 21 st , CHAPTER 357 pg 2749

440.q: Features of SLE include all of the following except:
440.e: Answer is B (Sterility): Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. Recurrent Abortions in SLE may be seen as a manifestation of Antiphospholipid Antibody syndrome. Small proportion of patients with SLE may have a Coomb's Positive Haemolytic anemia. Psychosis is a known neurological manifestation of SLE.

440.q: The autoantibody in Type 1 DM which has highest rate of persistence is:
440.e: Anti-GAD has highest persistence rate in Type 1 DM after initial diagnosis Anti GAD is also the most common antibody identified in subjects with Type 1 DM Anti insulin antibody is the earliest appearing antibody in Type 1 DM and has the highest risk of progression to overt DM Reference: ISPAD Guidelines on Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes - 2022

440.q: The first-line therapy for a 50 year old man with severe aplastic anemia is best described as follows?
o: A myeloablative allogeneic stem cell transplant from an unrelated donor
Immunosuppressive therapy with horse anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) followed by ciclosporin
Supportive care only with red cells, platelets and G-CSF
440.e: The treatment of choice is immunosuppression with horse ATG, which is safer than currently available rabbit ATG. Horse ATG should be followed by ciclosporin as longer-term immunosuppression. It induces hematologic recovery (independence from transfusion and a leukocyte count adequate to prevent infection) in 60-70% of patients. Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is reserved as first -line treatment for young patients ( Supportive care is important but not as sole therapy and there is no proven useful role for G-CSF. Long-term glucocorticoids dramatically increase the risk of fatal fungal infection in neutropenic patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal med 21st ed chap 102, pg. 797

440.q: The pathogenesis of most cases of acquired aplastic anemia can be attributed to:
o: Environmental exposure to benzene and benzene derivatives
