440.e: Environmental exposure to myelosuppressive chemicals and radiation are now uncommon causes of aplastic anemia. Fanconi anemia and dyskeratosis congenita (disorders of DNA repair and telomere maintenance, respectively, account for no more than 20% of cases). The majority of patients with acquired aplastic anemia have an autoimmune disease characterized by oligoclonal T-cell populations that function to repress stem cell function. This accounts for the favorable responses to immunosuppressive therapy in such patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 116 pg. 911

441.q: Which is the antibody associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
441.e: Explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune thyroid disease characterized by marked lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid, follicular atrophy, and fibrosis . The disease is primarily mediated by T-cell-induced thyroid cell destruction , but autoantibodies serve as important clinical markers . The most relevant antibodies in Hashimoto's thyroiditis are: Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) antibodies → most commonly present, clinically useful for diagnosis. Anti-thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies → also present in many cases. (vs Option C) TSH-receptor blocking antibodies → seen in some patients, especially in thyroid atrophy, but less common. (vs Option B) Among these, anti-TPO antibodies are the most strongly associated and are the standard diagnostic marker. Anti-CCP (Option A): Seen in rheumatoid arthritis , not thyroid disease.

441.q: A 66 year old man is investigated for lower back pain. He also complains of weight loss and fevers. On reviewing his history, he has been told before that he has ankylosing spondylitis. On admission, his blood tests show a urea of 66 mg/dl and a creatinine of 3.50 mg/dl. An ultrasound of the kidneys shows hydronephrosis bilaterally. CT scan shows fibrotic para-aortic masses. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
441.e: The symptoms of fevers, weight loss and lower back pain are classical for retroperitoneal fibrosis. There is an association with inflammatory conditions such as SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis and glomerulonephrosis. CT or MRI shows fibrotic para-aortic masses causing ureteral obstruction. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 319 Pg: 2375

441.q: Which of the following drugs used in RA is given orally?
441.e: Among the newer agents, JAK inhibitors are the drugs that are given orally among the options. Conventional DMARDS are also oral agents. Biologicals are all parenteral agents. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2761-2764

441.q: A 15 year old female who is diagnosed with SLE has come to your OP for review. Which of the following statements is true? 1. Permanent remission is seen only in 2. Aim of treatment is disease remission on treatment or Low Lupus Disease Activity. 3. Anti ds DNA or C3 levels are used as markers of disease flare 4. SLEDAI 2k score of >3 indicates active disease.
441.e: The question deals with treatment endpoints in SLE. Complete permanent remission(no disease activity without any treatment) is seen in Aim of treatment in SLE is disease remission on treatment or low level disease activity. Disease activity is measured using SLEDAI 2k score and a score of > 4 indicates an active disease. Anti ds DNA titres and C3 complement levels are used as markers of disease flare. From among the given options, SLEDAI2K score of > 3 does not indicate active disease. Hence it is wrong. So statements 1,2 and 3 are correct. Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch : 356 Pg: 2740, 2746

441.q: Which of the following is a ts DMARD used in treatment of RA?
441.e: TS DMARDS or targeted synthetic DMARDS are inhibitors of JAK and are therapeutically used in RA. The JAK family links the extracellular domains of the cytokines involved in RA to the intra cellular signals. They include Tofacitinib : JAK 1 and JAK 3 inhibitor Baricitinib: JAK 1 and JAK 2 inhibitors Upadacitinib: JAK 1 inhibitor They can be used as monotherapy or in combination with methotrexate. They cause neutropenia, increase in cholesterol levels and rise in serum creatinine and transaminases. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2761-2764

441.q: A 55 year old woman with psoriasis has significant joint pains.Which one of the following is effective in the treatment of psoriatic arthropathy?
441.e: The conventional DMARDs that are useful in Psoriatic Arthritis are: Methotrexate, Sulfasalazine, Leflunomide. Biologicals that are used include: anti TNFα agents, anti IL17/23 agents and anti JAK agents like Tofacitinib. Phosphodiesterase inhibitor Apremilast is also used. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2800

441.q: Which joints are Most frequently involved in reactive arthritis?
441.e: The knees are most frequently involved in reactive arthritis, next most commonly affected are the ankles and small joints of the feet Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2797

441.q: What are the parameters that you use in a patient with SLE for assessing the disease activity?
o: Anti ds DNA and serum Complement levels
441.e: The disease activity in SLE can be assessed by measuring the Serum ds DNA activity and a decrease in Serum complement levels(C3 or C4). ESR and CRP can be raised in disease flare or during infections and hence cant be used to differentiate them. Reference : Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed Ch: 356, Pg:2745

442.q: A patient complains of paroxysmal episodes of not being able to catch her breath. When no abnormalities are detected with conventional pulmonary function screening, the pulmonologist orders a methacholine challenge test. Which of the following will increase as a result of stimulating cholinergic receptors on the bronchial smooth muscle?
442.e: Methacholine is a cholinergic agonist, which causes constriction of bronchial smooth muscle. Bronchoconstriction reduces airway radius, which increases airway resistance, and thus the resistive work of breathing. Methacholine-induced bronchoconstriction decreases the anatomic deadspace but has no significant effect on the lung compliance, and thus does not affect the elastic work of breathing. Reference: Ganong, pp 649-650, 654, 657-659. Levitzky, pp 34-36, 49-50.

442.q: A 68-year-old man who has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to his pulmonologist with fatigue, dyspnea at rest, and peripheral edema. His blood gases on room air are PaO2 = 60 mmHg, PaCO2 = 60 mmHg, and pH = 7.36. His alveolar-arterial (A-a) O2 gradient, at a barometric pressure of 760 mmHg and a respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, is approximately what?
442.e: The A-a O2 gradient is the partial pressure difference between the alveolar gas and arterial blood. The PaO2 has been measured. The alveolar oxygen tension must be calculated using the modified alveolar gas equation PAO2 = PIO2 - PaCO2/ R PAO2 = [0.21 x (760 - 47 mmHg)] - 60 mmHg/0.8 PAO2 = 150 mmHg - 75 mmHg = 75 mmHg (A-a) O2 gradient = 75 mmHg - 60 mmHg = 15 mmHg The patient's low arterial oxygen tension (hypoxemia; hypoxic hypoxia) results from a low PAO2 due to hypoventilation (as evidenced by the elevated PaCO2), and thus the (A-a) O2 gradient is within the normal range. Reference: Levitzky, pp 75, 180-181, 262.

442.q: A 28-year-old man presents with symmetrical tremor, worsens with voluntary movements, and resolves completely at rest. He has history of asthma. Which of the following drugs is most suitable for management?
442.e: This patient having essential tremor which is symmetrical, worsens with voluntary movements, and resolves completely at rest. Increased activation of β adrenoceptors has been implicated in essential tremor, and management commonly involves administration of propranolol. However, the more selective β1 blocker metoprolol may be equally effective and is more suitable in a patient with pulmonary disease like asthma. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 511

442.q: A 70 year old patient with COPD presents with cough and breathlessness which has worsened over 2 months. On admission, he has the following arterial blood gas results. pH 7.32, pO2 52 mmhg, pCO2 60 mmhg, HCO3 34mmol/l, Base Excess -1. Which one of the following biochemical states fits best?
442.e: There is a mild respiratory acidosis (pH > 7.3 and pCO2 > 60 mmhg) and base excess is also not elevated (in this case only -1). There is metabolic compensation, as indicated by a high bicarbonate ( >30). The patient's history of COPD suggests that he has chronic hypoxia and chronic CO2 retention, hence causing the picture of chronic respiratory acidosis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 55, Pg: 359

442.q: Most common site for tuberculous lymphadenitis is
442.e: The most common presentation of extrapulmonary TB in both HIV-seronegative individuals and HIV- infected patients (35% of cases worldwide and >40% of cases in the United States in recent series), lymph node disease is particularly frequent among HIV-infected patients and among children. In the United States, besides children, women (particularly non-Caucasians) seem to be especially susceptible Once caused mainly by M. bovis, tuberculous lymphadenitis today is due largely to M. tuberculosis. Lymph node TB presents as painless swelling of the lymph nodes, most commonly at posterior cervical and supraclavicular sites (a condition historically referred to as scrofula) Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178 Pg: 1364

442.q: The 2nd line anti-TB drug in the following is?
442.e: The first line anti tubercular drugs are: INH,rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin. The second line agents are the drugs that are having a low effectiveness and tolerability and hence are used only for the treatment of resistant tuberculosis. The WHO has categorized them into 3 groups. Group A: Fluoroquinolones(Moxifloxacin and levofloxacin). Linezolid, Bedaquiline Group B: Clofazimine and cycloserine Group C: Delamanid, Imipenem-cilastatin/meropenem, amikacin/streptomycin, prothionamide and PAS. The first line agents Ethambutol and pyrazinamide are also included in group c. High dose INH is also used for the treatment of MDR TB

442.q: Why a TB patient is recommend a regimen of 4 drugs on 1st visit -
442.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., To avoid emergence of persistors Two phase chemotheraphv o There are two phase of treatment of tuberculosis i) Intensive phase This is short phase in the early course of treatment and lasts for 1- 3 months. Three or more drugs are given to kill as many bacilli as possible, which prevents emergence of persisters. The risk of relapse is also lessened. Continuation phase It is aimed at sterilizing the smaller number of dormant or persisting bacilli.

442.q: TB multidrug regimen is given to-
442.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Prevent resistance o Multidrug treatment in TB is given to ? i) Prevent emergence of persisters ii) Prevent relapse iii) Prevent emergence of resistance iv) shorten the duration of treatment

443.q: Which of the following is the most sensitive test for diagnosing tubercular pleural effusion?
443.e: The fluid is straw-colored and at times hemorrhagic; it is an exudate with a protein concentration >50% of that in serum (usually ~4&6 g/dL), a normal to low glucose concentration, a pH of ~7.3 (occasionally 45 IU/L) is the most sensitive test for pleural effusion. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21th edition, ch: 178 Page no 1364

443.q: A 72-year-old man presents with an acute onset of severe pain and swelling of the left elbow. He mentions that he had a chest infection 3 weeks ago. On examination, he had a temperature of 38°C and the left elbow was erythematous, swollen and tender. What is the most appropriate investigation?
443.e: The differential diagnosis of acute monoarthritis includes- septic arthritis, crystal induced arthritis and hemarthrosis. The management of acute monoarthritis is always joint aspiration followed by appropriate therapy. In the context of an elderly male presenting with monoarthritis after a recent history of pneumonia should make us raise suspicion of a septic arthritis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 370, Pg: 2852 20th edition Ch:355 Pg:2570

443.q: A 63-year-old diabetic presents with pyrexia, productive cough, and shortness of breath for 5 days. She has RLL consolidation and a small unilateral pleural effusion on CXR. Which is a marker of poor prognosis?
443.e: Indicators of poor prognosis in pneumonia include: Age >65 Co-existing morbidity including diabetes mellitus, chronic renal failure, stroke, coronary artery disease. Respiratory rate>30 Mental impairment Biochemical/haematological markers which include white blood count 30,000/µL; hypoxia needing CPAP or FiO2>60%, positive blood culture and blood urea>7 mmol/L. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:126Pg 1015

443.q: A 34 year old man presents with a hot swollen elbow joint. He has a temperature of 37°C and CRP of 350 mg/l. A diagnosis of septic arthritis is suspected.Which of the following organisms is most commonly isolated from joints?
443.e: Staph aureus is the commonest organism (over 50%). Neisseria gonorrhoeae can occur in patients with sexually transmitted diseases. β-haemolytic streptococci can cause impetigo, sore throat and rheumatic fever. Moraxella is a gram negative coccus which can cause pneumonia in COPD patients. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed Ch: 130, Pg: 1040

443.q: What is The Most common infectious complication of varicella?
o: Secondary bacterial superinfection of the skin
443.e: The most common infectious complication of varicella is secondary bacterial superinfection of the skin, which is usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus, including strains that are methicillin-resistant Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 193, Pg: 1480

443.q: In Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), What are the dominant cells?
443.e: In Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), Lymphocytes are the dominant cells; next most common are histiocytes and plasma cells. In about half of cases, epithelioid cells--scattered individually or forming compact granulomas are seen Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 226Pg 1746 Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 1746

443.q: Patient is scheduled for an elective splenectomy. At least how long before the operation should pneumovax be given?
443.e: All patients undergoing an elective splenectomy should be immunised with polyvalent pneumococcal vaccine (Pneumovax), which currently gives variable protection against 23 strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae. Where possible, it should be given at least 2 weeks and preferably at least 4 weeks prior to splenectomy to allow immunoglobulin G (gG) antibody production. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 146, Pg: 1177

443.q: Complications of Viral hepatitis does not include:
443.e: Rare complications of viral hepatitis include pancreatitis,myocarditis, atypical pneumonia, aplastic anemia, transversemyelitis, and peripheral neuropathy. In children, hepatitis B may present rarely with anicteric hepatitis, a nonpruritic papular rash of the face, buttocks, and limbs, and lymphadenopathy (papular acrodermatitis of childhood or Gianotti-Crosti syndrome) Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 339 pg. 2565

444.q: A 48-year-old coal miner complains of shortness of breath and a productive cough. The history reveals that he has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day since he was 16 years old. Pulmonary function studies are ordered including an esophageal balloon study to measure intrapleural pressures. Normally, intrapleural pressure is negative throughout a tidal inspiration and expiration because of which of the following?
o: The lungs have the tendency to recoil outward throughout a tidal breath
The chest wall has the tendency to recoil inward throughout a tidal breath
The intact pleura causes the lungs and chest wall to recoil away from each other throughout a tidal breath
The intact pleura causes the lungs and chest wall to recoil in the same direction throughout a tidal breath
444.e: When the pleura, and hence the lung-chest wall system, are intact, the inward elastic recoil of the lung opposing the outward elastic recoil of the chest wall results in a subatmospheric (negative) pressure with the pleural space. When one reaches lung volumes in excess of ~70% of the total lung capacity, the chest wall recoil is also inward. Reference: Ganong, pp 665-655. Levitzky, pp 17-23, 29-31.

444.q: Tinea capitis occurs Most commonly in Which age group?
444.e: Tinea capitis occurs most commonly in children 3-7 years old. Children with tinea capitis usually present with well-demarcated scaly patches in which hair shafts are broken off right above the skin; alopecia can result. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 219 Pg 1691

444.q: A 35 year old male presents with history of weakness of both the lower limbs of insidious onset, for the past 2 years. He has mild difficulty in swallowing liquids too. There are no sensory symptoms. On examination, he has fasciculations and areflexia. You also notice gynecomastia. He is also undergoing investigation for infertility. What is the likely molecular abnormality be seen in this patient?
444.e: The given patient has an LMN type of weakness without any sensory symptoms and with associated androgen insensitivity as evidenced by the gynecomastia and the sub fertility. This is classical of the Spinobulbar muscular atrophy or the Kennedy syndrome. It is an X linked disorder and is associated with CAG trinucleotide repeats on the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. CGG trinucleotide repeats is seen in Fragile X syndrome. It is associated with mental retardation. There may be ataxia and ovarian failure associated with it. GAA trinucleotide repeats are seen in Friedrich's Ataxia. CTG trinucleotides are seen in Myotonic dystrophy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 347, Pg: 3415

444.q: A 75-year-old man with established sarcoidosis presents for review. He suffers from a degree of pulmonary fibrosis due to previous pulmonary infiltration and has been taking corticosteroids intermittently. His serum calcium concentration is 12.5 mg/dl. His renal function is normal and parathyroid hormone is just below the lower end of the normal range. What is the most likely cause of his hypercalcaemia?
444.e: In this case, parathyroid hormone is virtually in the normal range (less than 20 pg/ml suggestive of PTH independent hypercalcemia) and his renal function is normal, so there is nothing to suggest a diagnosis of the milk-alkali syndrome/CRF. Hypercalcaemia is found in 10% of established cases of sarcoid, and may eventually lead to nephrocalcinosis. The cause is increased 1 alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D by sarcoid macrophages in the granuloma, in addition to that taking place in the kidney. Other granulomatous conditions like tuberculosis, histoplasmosis and berylliosis also cause hypercalcemia by this mechanism Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3180

444.q: A child with fever with ABCs & pus in stools, causative organism is ?
444.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., EHEC [Ref Harrison 18thle p. 1084] Fever with RBC and pus in stools suggest inflammatory diarrhea. Amongst the given options EHEC causes invasion.

444.q: Which among the following is not a component of initial treatment of orthostatic hypotension?
o: Elevate head end of BED 10cm to minimize supine hypertension.
444.e: Initial treatment of orthostatic hypotension (OH) includes: Patient education: Mechanisms and stresses of OH High salt diet (10-20 gm/day) Compression garments Correct anemia Raise the head end of bed 10 cm to reduce supine hypertension Maintain postural stimuli Learn physical counter - Maneuvers Reference: Harrison 20 th pg.127

444.q: A couple attend the GP with their 2 year old daughter. She has a history of repeated chest infections, failure to thrive, and steatorrhoea (fatty stools). They also have an 8 year old child who is fit and well. What is the likely diagnosis?
444.e: The gene defect in cystic fibrosis is in a mutation on chromosome 7. The inheritance is autosomal recessive so the other child without symptoms has not inherited two CF genes. Pulmonary disease develops over a few months after birth. Common infective organisms are pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 291 Pg 2176

444.q: Which of the following is a typical feature of Farmer's lung?
444.e: Commonest occupational extrinsic allergic alveolitis, due to thermophilic actinomycetes. Crackles are typically heard at the bases. Eosinophilia can be seen but is not typical. Immunoglobulin levels are frequently elevated but not a Para protein. P02 may be decreased particularly with exercise. A restrictive pattern on LF studies is seen. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 288, Pg: 2160

445.q: A 30 year old man gives a six-month history of worsening breathlessness and coughs up half a cupful of sputum daily. He was occasionally wheezy with viral illnesses as a young child, works in a factory and has smoked 25 cigarettes per day for the last four years. The most likely diagnosis is:
445.e: Bronchiectasis is most likely due to the extensive amounts of sputum production. In a young person, cystic fibrosis and hypogammaglobulinemia should be considered. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 290 Pg 2173

445.q: The most common extra intestinal manifestation of Amebiasis is?
445.e: Extraintestinal infection by E. histolytica Most often involves the liver. Of travelers who develop an amebic liver abscess after leaving an endemic area, 95% do so within 5 months. Young patients with an amebic liver abscess are more likely than older patients to present in the acute phase with prominent symptoms of Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1716

445.q: The most common complication of Amebiasis is?
445.e: Pleuropulmonary involvement, which is reported in 20-30% of patients, is the most frequent complication of amebic liver abscess. Rupture into the pericardium, usually from abscesses of the left lobe of the liver, carries the gravest prognosis; it can occur during medical therapy and requires surgical drainage. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1717

445.q: A 26 year old woman with cystic fibrosis presents with abdominal pain. The abdominal pain is colicky and localized in the lower abdomen. On examination, she has pyrexia and tachycardia. Her abdomen was distended. There was guarding and bowel sounds were present. Which of the following is likely to be the cause?
445.e: Meconium Ileus is the earliest clinical manifestation of cystic fibrosis (CF) and occurs in approximately 16% of patients with CF. Contents of the intestinal lumen are often difficult to excrete, leading to meconium ileus (a presentation in 10–20% of newborns with CF) or distal intestinal obstructive syndrome in older individual. Signs of peritonitis include tenderness, abdominal wall edema, distension, and clinical evidence of sepsis. A palpable mass may indicate pseudocyst formation. Surgical exploration is indicated for patients with progressive distension, signs of peritonitis, or clinical deterioration. Complicated Meconium Ileus requires resection more often than simple cases and always requires temporary stomas. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:291 Pg: 2176

445.q: Secondary lung abscess is due to all except
445.e: Lung abscesses are usually characterized as either primary (~80% of cases) or secondary. Primary lung abscesses usually arise from aspiration, are often caused principally by anaerobic bacteria, and occur in the absence of an underlying pulmonary or systemic condition. Secondary lung abscesses arise in the setting of an underlying condition, such as a post obstructive process (e.g., a bronchial foreign body or tumor) or a systemic process (e.g., HIV infection or another immunocompromising condition). Lung abscesses can also be characterized as acute ( Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 127, Pg: 1020

445.q: A 63 year old woman has recently been treated with amoxycillin for a tooth abscess. Since then, she has developed diarrhea up to 15 times a day. There is blood in the stools.Her Hb is 13 g/dl, WCC 13 x 10^9/l, platelets 500 x 10^9/L. Her CRP is 80 mg/l. What is the likely infective organism?
445.e: In a patient who has recently had antibiotics, Clostridium difficile is the most likely infective organism. Clindamycin, ampicillin, and cephalosporins are the implicated drugs. Discontinuation of the offending antibiotic is important (not always easy if an infection such as a dental abscess persists). Oral administration of fidaxomicin or vancomycin is the treatment. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 134, Pg: 1068

445.q: A 38-year-old diabetic patient presents with a 2-day history of worsening pain and swelling of his left upper arm and subjective fevers. He tells you that he is penicillin allergic. His temperature is 99.8° F, and other vital signs are normal. On physical examination, there is a 5-cm-diameter tender, red, indurated lesion with central fluctuance over the triceps area. You perform incision and drainage, which yields about 3 mL of pus. Which one of the following antibiotics should not be used as empirical therapy for this community-acquired skin abscess?
445.e: Clindamycin, doxycycline, minocycline, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are active in vitro against both MRSA and MSSA strains and have been recommended and used to treat skin and soft tissue infections in areas with high prevalence of MRSA. Many MRSA strains and some MSSA strains are fluoroquinolone resistant, and therefore fluoroquinolones should not be used in the absence of documented in vitro susceptibility Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 129 Pg: 1039

Ans. B i.e. Terminal pulp space infection a painful abscess of the deep tissues of the palmar surface of the fingertip that is typically caused by bacterial infection (as with a staphylococcus) and is marked by swelling and pain

446.q: The wife of a recently married 24-year-old medical student reports that even though her husband doesn't snore, he stops breathing for periods of 1 to 2 minutes while he is sleeping. His physician refers him for a polysomnography study and pulmonary function testing, including ventilatory response curves. The tests confirm the apneic episodes during sleep and show depressed ventilatory responsiveness of both the peripheral and central chemoreceptors. Peripheral and central chemoreceptors both contribute to the increased ventilation that occurs as a result of which of the following?
o: A decrease in arterial oxygen content
A decrease in arterial blood pressure
An increase in arterial carbon dioxide tension
A decrease in arterial oxygen tension
446.e: Both the central chemoreceptors, located on or near the ventral surface of the medulla, and the peripheral chemoreceptors, in the carotid and aortic bodies, cause an increase in ventilation in response to an increase in PaCO2. The peripheral chemoreceptors also cause an increase in ventilation in response to a decrease in arterial pH and a decrease in PaO2, but the central chemoreceptors are unresponsive to hypoxemia and do not cause an increase in ventilation in response to a decrease in arterial pH because the blood-brain barrier is relatively impermeable to hydrogen ions. Neither the central chemoreceptors nor the carotid bodies are stimulated by a decrease in arterial blood pressure or O2 content. Reference: Ganong, pp 662, 672-677, 686-688. Levitzky, pp 114-116, 180-182, 201-210.

446.q: A patient with congestive heart failure, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is referred for pulmonary function testing in the supine and upright positions. Which of the following is higher at the apex of the lung than at the base when a person is upright?
446.e: The alveoli at the apex of the lung are larger than those at the base so their compliance is less. Because the compliance is reduced, less inspired gas goes to the apex than to the base. Also, because the apex is above the heart, less blood flows through the apex than through the base. However, the reduction in airflow is less than the reduction in blood flow, so that the V/Q ratio at the top of the lung is greater than it is at the bottom. The increased V/Q ratio at the apex makes PACO2 lower and PAO2 higher at the apex than they are at the base. Reference: Ganong, pp 643-644, 662-663, 686-688. Levitzky, pp 123-128. Stead et al., pp 25-27.

446.q: Which extrapulmonary site is Most commonly involved in TB ?
446.e: In order of frequency, the extrapulmonary sites most commonly involved in TB are the lymph nodes , pleura , genitourinary tract , bones and joints, meninges, peritoneum, and pericardium. Reference :Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178 Pg: 1364

446.q: Which of the following will be incorrect in Rh incompatibility?
446.e: In rh incompatibility, there will be hemolysis and the picture will be similar to any other hemolytic anemia. In hemolytic jaundice, in the blood we will get indirect bilirubinemia. Liver function tests will be normal. Since unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin, it will not be excreted in urine and hence urine will be colorless. Whatever bilirubin is formed will be conjugated by the liver and excreted through the bile, where in the gut it will be converted into stercobilin and subsequently to urobilin. A part of the urobilin will enter the systemic circulation where it will be excreted in the urine.

446.q: A 65-year-old man was advised to start oral digoxin at a dose of 250 μg daily. His doctor explained that the full effect of this treatment would not be apparent for at least a week. Which one of the following pharmacokinetic variables did the doctor use to give this explanation?
446.e: Digoxin follows first order kinetics and has a half-life of 36 to 48 hours in a patient with normal renal function. Sixty-five per cent of the drug absorbed remains in the system after one day. Subsequent doses gradually accumulate until a steady state is achieved after four to five days. The bioavailability of digoxin is around 70%. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1949

446.q: Which of the following goes against a diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
446.e: Clubbing is not a feature of COPD, its presence should raise the suspicion of an underlying lung malignancy. Physical findings of COPD: Nicotine staining of fingernails Signs of respiratory distress: pursed lip breathing, accessory muscle use, tripod position, inspiratory in drawing of ribs (esp lower ribs, ka Hoover's sign) Cachexia (poor prognostic finding) Signs of hyper inflated lungs: barrel chest, hyper resonance on percussion Auscultation: coarse crepitations (fibrosis), polyphonic rhonchi Signs of right heart failure (cor pulmonale): Elevated JVP, Pedal edema, ascites. Labs may show a 2° polycythaemia and chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st edition, chapter. 292 page number. 2185

446.q: Which of the following is not common in primary pulmonary tuberculosis?
446.e: Because most inspired air is distributed to the middle and lower lung zones, these areas are most commonly involved in primary TB. In the majority of cases, the lesion heals spontaneously and becomes evident only as a small calcified nodule. Pleural reaction overlying a subpleural focus is also common. The Ghon focus, with or without overlying pleural reaction, thickening, and regional lymphadenopathy, is referred to as the Ghon complex. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 172 Pg: 1362

446.q: A 45 year man has a long history of productive cough. He had complained of frequent chest infections. Examination reveals bilateral inspiratory crackles in the bases of the lungs and clubbing of the fingers. Which of the following treatments is likely to reduce the frequency of exacerbations?
446.e: The patient has bronchiectasis , in which the common complication is difficulty expectorating, postural drainage of secretions is helpful. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:290 Pg: 2175

447.q: A 27-year-old man develops adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) after near-drowning. Conventional mechanical ventilation on 100% O2 together with inhaled nitric oxide do not provide sufficient oxygenation. Porcine surfactant is instilled via fiberoptic bronchoscope, and the PaCO2, fraction of inspired oxygen (FIO2), and shunting improve impressively. The improvements in respiratory function occurred because surfactant increased which of the following?
o: The pressure gradient needed to inflate the alveoli
447.e: Pulmonary surfactant increases lung compliance by lowering alveolar surface tension. As a result, the pressure gradient needed to inflate the alveoli decreases, as does the work of breathing. Reference: Ganong, pp 654-6558. Kasper et al., pp 1583, 1592-1595. Levitzky, pp 26-28. Stead et al., p 270.

447.q: A 6 feet 3 inches tall, 140-lb, 20-year-old male was watching television when he felt pain in his shoulder blades, shortness of breath, and fatigue. His father noticed how pale he was and took him to the Emergency Department, where a chest X-ray revealed a 55% pneumothorax of the right lung due to rupture of a bleb on the surface of the lung. Which of the following is true?
o: The intrapleural pressure in the affected area is equal to atmospheric pressure
The chest wall on the affected side recoils inward
There is hyperinflation of the affected lung
The V/Q ratio on the affected side is higher than normal
447.e: When air enters the pleural space due to interruption of the pleural surface through either the rupture of the lung or a hole in the chest wall, the pressure in the pleural space becomes atmospheric, the lung on the affected side collapses because of the lung's tendency to recoil inward, and the chest wall on the affected side recoils outward. Because the intrapleural pressure is atmospheric, the mediastinum shifts farther to the normal side with each inspiration. With collapse of the lung, the V / Q ratio on the affected side decreases. Reference: Ganong, p 688. Kasper et al., p 1568. Levitzky, pp 12, 116-Stead et al., pp 273-274.

447.q: A hospitalized patient is found semicomatose. Arterial blood gases reveal hypercapnia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the high arterial PCO2?
447.e: Profound hypoxia depresses the central nervous system, including the medullary respiratory centers. As a result, alveolar ventilation may decrease, resulting in an increased PaCO2. A decrease in metabolic activity would decrease the rate of production of carbon dioxide (VCO2), which would decrease PaCO2, assuming that alveolar ventilation does not change. If an alveolar capillary block is severe, retention of CO2 could briefly occur, but the coexistent hypoxemia would cause reflex hyperventilation with a decrease in PaCO2. At a constant tidal volume and respiratory rate, a decrease in the deadspace volume would increase alveolar ventilation, and thus lower the PaCO2. Reference: Kasper et al. pp 209-210, 1624-1637. Levitzky, pp 66, 73-74, 136-138.

447.q: Which of the following concerning the use of intravenous bicarbonate in cardiorespiratory arrest is correct?
o: Has a positive inotropic effect on ischaemic myocardium
Improves oxygen release to the tissues
447.e: If metabolic acidosis persists after successful defibrillation and with adequate ventilation, 1 mEq/kg sodium bcarbonate may be given. Bicarbonate therapy can increase extracellular pH only if the CO2 produced can be removed by adequate ventilation . Indeed if hypercapnia occurs then as CO2 crosses cell membranes easily, intracellular pH may decrease even further with further deterioration of cellular function. Sodium bicarbonate has - Negative inotropic effect Reduces cerebral blood flow Shifts oxygen dissociation curve to the left inhibiting oxygen release to tissues Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:299 pg:2063

447.q: All form boundaries of triangle of auscultation except
447.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Rhomboid major Triangle of auscultation has the following boundaries Superiorly and medially, by the inferior portion of the Trapezius. Inferiorly, by the Latissimus Dorsi. Laterally, by the medial border of the scapula. The superficial floor of the triangle is formed by the Serratus anterior and the lateral portion of the erector spinae muscles. Deep to these muscles are the osseous portions of the 6" and 7th ribs and the internal and external intercostal muscles. Typically, the Triangle of Auscultation is covered by the Scapula. To better expose the triangle and listen to respiratory sounds with a stethoscope, patients are asked to fold their arms across their chest, medially rotating the scapulae, while bending forward at the trunk, somewhat resembling a fetal position.

447.q: Indications for emergency thoracotomy are all of the following except
447.e: Answer- D. Tension Pneumothorax Emergency thoracotomy is indicated after chest trauma in following conditions : Cardiac arrest (resuscitative thoractomy) Massive hemoththorax (>1500 mL of blood through the chest tube acutely or > 200-300 ml/hr after initial drainage. Penetrating injuries of the anterior aspect of the chest with cardiac tamponade. Large open wounds of the thoracic cage. Major thoracic vascular injuries in the presence of hemodynamic instability

447.q: A 48 year old male is referred to with impotence. He has a history of angina, hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Which one of the following drugs that he takes would present a contraindication towards him receiving Sildenafil?
447.e: Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor used in management of erectile dysfunction. Like nitrates it also increases the release of NO resulting in hypotension. There is a significant risk of hypotension when sildenafil is used with nitrates . There should be at least 24 hours gap between administration of nitrates and short acting PDE5 inhibitors like sildenafil and 48 hours between the use of long acting Tadalafil. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2050

447.q: A 12-year-old boy with bilateral gynaecomastia is being investigated. Which one of the features points towards hypogonadotropic hypogonadism being a likely cause?
447.e: Hypospadias, micropenis and cryptorchidism point towards reduced androgen exposure in utero Kallmann syndrome is characterised by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia. Although hypogonadotropic hypogonadism can be caused by pituitary disorders, a common presentation in childhood is with anosmia (Kallman's syndrome). Causes of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism:. Genetic : Mutations in following genes: KAL1 FGFR1 GNRHR PC1 Acquired: (more common) Stress Athletes Chronic illness Obesity Hyperprolactinemia Sellar lesions Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3014

448.q: A 27-year-old man is noted to have cyanosis of the lower limbs and clubbing of the toes but not the fingers. The blood pressure in the arm and lower limb is the same. Which of the following statements is true?
o: He has coarctation of the aorta.
He is likely to have a loud continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle.
He is likely to need urgent surgery.
448.e: Differential cyanosis (cyanosis only in lower extremities) is seen in a patient with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) when there is reversal of shunt. There is a right-left shunt from the pulmonary artery to the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery. This is Eisenmenger's syndrome. Coarctation causes radiofemoral delay and a lower blood pressure in the leg as compared to the arm. It may be associated with PDA but there is no suggestion in this patient. Continuous machinery murmur is the classic murmur of PDA but when the shunt reverses (as in patients with a large PDA and/or pulmonary disease) the murmur becomes softer and shorter. When Eisenmenger's syndrome has developed surgery is associated with a very high mortality. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:264 pg:1838,1839

448.q: Which of the following concerning congenital heart disease is correct?
o: ASD is the commonest cardiac malformation at birth
Congenital complete heart block is always associated with Anti-Ro antibodies in the mother
Ebstein's anomaly is associated with maternal exposure to lithium carbonate
Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is characterised by a large, dilated left ventricle
448.e: Ebstein's anomaly is associated with maternal exposure to lithium carbonate in the first trimester . It causes malformed tricuspid valve leading to tricuspid regurgitation. Option 1 - VSD is the most congenital heart disease. Option 2 - In the vast majority of cases of neonates with complete heart block the cause is unknown but in the minority it may be caused by autoimmune disease, particularly Anti-Ro antibodies, in the mother. Option 4 -In hypoplastic left heart syndrome, LV hypolasia occurs as the left sided chambers fail to develop and blood enters the systemic circulation from the right ventricle via the pulmonary artery and a patent ductus arteriosus. Reference: Braunwald's heart disease 12 th edition, page no.1559

448.q: Small cell lung cancer are associated with
448.e: Nearly 90% of SCLCs harbor mutations in TP53 and RB1. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 78, Pg: 597

448.q: Which lung cancer stains positive for CD56, NCAM, synaptophysin and chromogranin?
448.e: CD 56, NCAM, synaptophysin and Chromogranin are neuroendocrine markers and will be positive in small cell carcinoma lung. Nap-A and TTF 1 are other immunohistochemical markers that can be used in the diagnosis of lung cancer. Primary lung adenocarcinoma (Nap-A positive, TTF-1 positive) Primary lung squamous cell carcinoma (Nap-A negative, TTF-1 negative) Primary SCLC (Nap-A negative, TTF-1 positive). Cytokeratins 7 and 20 used in combination can help narrow the differential diagnosis; nonsquamous NSCLC, SCLC, and mesothelioma may stain positive for CK7 and negative for CK20, whereas squamous cell lung cancer often will be both CK7 and CK20 negative Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 78, Pg: 596

448.q: What is the gene mutation associated with Marfan syndrome?
448.e: Explanation: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15, which encodes fibrillin-1 , an important component of elastic fibres. Defective fibrillin leads to abnormal connective tissue, causing skeletal (tall stature, long limbs), ocular (lens subluxation), and cardiovascular manifestations (aortic root dilation, dissection) . Explanation of other options: FGFR3 (Option B): Mutation causes achondroplasia , leading to short-limb dwarfism, not Marfan's tall stature. COL1A1 (Option C): Mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta , characterised by brittle bones, blue sclera, and hearing loss. TSC1 (Option D): Mutation causes tuberous sclerosis , a neurocutaneous syndrome with cortical tubers, seizures, and skin lesions.

448.q: Cyanotic heart disease with increased pulmonary blood flow is seen in?
448.e: Cyanotic heart disease with decreased pulmonary blood flow: TOF Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum Tricuspid atresia Double outlet right ventricle TGA with Pulmonary stenosis and VSD Ebstein anomaly Cyanotic heart disease with increased pulmonary flow: D TGA D TGA with intact ventricular septum TGS with VSD L TGA DORV with PS DORV with malposition of arteries (Taussig Bing anomaly) Total anomalous pulmonary venous return Tricuspid atresia Single ventricle Hypoplastic left heart syndrome

448.q: Which of the following is not a cyanotic heart disease?
448.e: Cyanotic congenital heart diseases Tetralogy of Fallot (most common) Persistent truncus arteriosus Transposition of great arteries Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection Tricuspid atresia Ebstein anomaly Eisenmenger syndrome Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation Examples of non-cyanotic heart diseases include ASD, VSD, PDA, coarctation of aorta, pulmonary stenosis etc. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:256 pg:1804,1805

448.q: Which of the following syndromes is not associated with patent ductus arteriousus (PDA) ?
448.e: Syndromes associated with PDA: Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18- ASD, VSD) Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13 - ASD, VSD) Cri du chat syndrome (deletion of 5p) Noonan syndrome (Pulmonary stenosis, HCM, ASD) Congenital rubella syndrome Cardiac manifestations of Marfan syndrome include Mitral valve prolapse, Aortic root dilatation, Aortic regurgitation, Aortic dissection (rarely) Reference: Harrison,s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:264 pg:1833

449.q: A 36-year-old man visits his doctor because his wife has long complained of his snoring, but recently observed that his breathing stops for a couple of minutes at a time while he is sleeping. He undergoes polysomnography and ventilatory response testing to ascertain the extent and cause of his sleep apnea. The activity of the central chemoreceptors is stimulated by which of the following?
o: An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain
A decrease in the PO2 of blood flowing through the brain
An increase in the pH of the CSF
A decrease in the metabolic rate of the surrounding brain tissue
449.e: The central chemoreceptors, located at or near the ventral surface of the medulla, are stimulated to increase ventilation by a decrease in the pH of their extracellular fluid (ECF). The pH of this ECF is affected by the PCO2 of the blood supply to the medullary chemoreceptor area, as well as by the CO2 and lactic acid production of the surrounding brain tissue. The central chemoreceptors are not stimulated by decreases in PaO2 or blood oxygen content but rather can be depressed by long-term or severe decreases in oxygen supply. Reference: Ganong, pp 675-678. Levitzky, pp 206-208.

449.q: A 30-year-old male presents with hematuria and hemoptysis of two weeks duration. His urinalysis showed 2+ protein and dysmorphic RBC. His physician suspected a pulmonary renal syndrome and performs a renal biopsy. The pathologist uses a special stain to visualize the basement membrane. What is it?
449.e: Referring to the previous question, this patient is also suffering from a pulmonary renal syndrome. If the pathologist wants to stain the basement membrane, he might be suspecting Goodpasteur's syndrome. Jone's Methanamine silver is the stain used for basement membrane. Congo red is used for Amyloid. Masons Trichrome for collagen PAS for staining carbohydrate moiety in the cell membranes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2336.

449.q: Most common symptom of the Pertussis is
449.e: Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 160, Pg: 1257

449.q: A 50-year-old woman who is morbidly obese presents with a plasma creatinine of 2.8 mg/dl.Which form of disease is likely?
449.e: As with MPGN, FSGS is not a specific disease entity, it is a morphology of renal injury in several conditions that presents as nephrotic syndrome. The important ones are: Adaptive response to loss of renal mass as post nephrectomy, in obesity and in hyperfiltration. Hep B, Parvo virus, HIV Reflux nephropathy Sickle nephropathy Analgesics and heroine Hereditary podocytopathies: NPHS mutation, WT1 mutation, Fabrys disease, N acetyl neuraminidase deficiency, PLCE mutation, INF2 mutation, TRPC mutation, ACTN mutation. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch: 314, Pg: 2342.

449.q: The correct description of Bruns garland syndrome is:
449.e: Bruns garland syndrome is also known as diabetic amyotrophy/lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy Asymmetrical, painful weakness involving quadriceps, iliopsoas and adductors of thigh; spares the hamstring muscles Most common form of Diabetic neuropathy is the distal symmetric sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy Most common cranial nerve involvement in Diabetes mellitus is Oculomotor nerve followed by abducens and facial nerves. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 3124

449.q: A 39-year-old woman gives an eight month history of bloody diarrhoea. On average she has six bowel motions per day with associated urgency. She also reports weight loss of approximately 3 kg. On examination she is dehydrated and tachycardic. There is evidence of pallor and abdominal examination reveals left-sided tenderness. Which of the following pathological features would you expect to find given the likely underlying diagnosis?
449.e: Chronic bloody diarrhoea in a young patient is very suggestive of a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC) . The time course is too long for an infective cause and whilst Crohn's disease (CD) may cause a colitis, this is less frequent. CD often presents watery diarrhoea. The predominant left sided symptoms (urgency and anatomical distribution of the tendency) should also point towards UC. The answer here therefore is diffuse mucosal inflammation . All the remaining options are histological features of Crohn's disease . Transmural inflammation is seen in CD. Sub serosal lymphoid aggregates are seen in CD Normal crypt architecture is found in CD while crypt abscesses and goblet cell depletion are seen in UC. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

450.q: You review a 67-year-old man for dyslipidemia. He is taking atorvastatin 40 mg/day. Which of the following drugs should be used with caution?
450.e: The risk of statin induced myopathy is high when drugs like Erythromycin, anti fungals, immunosuppressive drugs and gemfibrozil is used along with statins, as these drugs interfere with the metabolism of statins. Statins will increase the drug levels of warfarin and digoxin too. Hence A,.B And C are right options. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, ch: 407, Pg: 3149

450.q: A 37-year-old woman presents to her GP with a vaginal discharge. She has been taking the combined oral contraceptive pill (OCP). What is the most common infection associated with the use of the OCP?
450.e: Women on oral contraceptives have a higher incidence of chlamydial endocervicitis. Vaginal warts are also common in these women. However, it is believed that human papillomavirus infection may occur even before the woman starts taking the pill, and that there is no actual increase in the risk of acquiring infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:389 P page number :2814-15

450.q: Which of the following is the functional effect of Hypokalemia on kidney function?
450.e: The functional effects of hypokalemia on the kidney can include Na+-Cl- and HCO3 - retention, polyuria, phosphaturia, hypocitraturia, and an activation of renal ammoniagenesis. Bicarbonate retention and other acid-base effects of hypokalemia can contribute to the generation of metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalemic polyuria is due to a combination of central polydipsia and an AVP-resistant renal concentrating defect. Structural changes in the kidney due to hypokalemia include a relatively specific vacuolizing injury to proximal tubular cells, interstitial nephritis, and renal cysts. Hypokalemia also predisposes to acute kidney injury and can lead to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in patients with long-standing hypokalemia due to eating disorders and/or laxative abuse. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 350

450.q: A 54-year-old male patient from Chattisgarh having progressive motor symptoms and leg cramps for 1 month. What history will you enquire for making a diagnosis?
450.e: The question deals with neurolathyrism , due to ingestion of chick pea, containing the excito toxin beta oxalylamino L alanine causing spastic paraplegia. This disease is having high prevalence in chhattisgarh as the legume was consumed as staple food during the time of drought.

450.q: A 72 year old man is admitted with pruritus, lethargy and jaundice. He has not drank any alcohol for five years.One month ago, he completed a course of Co-Amoxiclav which was prescribed by his GP. He also takes diclofenac for osteoarthritis. Investigations reveal: Albumin 3.7 g/dL Bilirubin 9 mg/dL AST 220 iu/L Alkaline Phosphatase 210 iu/l Abdominal ultrasound reveals gallstones without biliary duct dilatation. What is the likely cause of his jaundice?
450.e: Drugs causing Cholestasis: anabolic steroids containing an alkyl or ethinyl group at carbon 17 azathioprine cetirizine cyclosporine Chlorpromazine Co amoxiclav Erythromycin estolate diclofenac estrogen febuxostat indinavir mercaptopurine methyltestosterone tamoxifen ticlopidine. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21 st Ed, Ch: 340 Pg: 2587

450.q: Match the following drugs used in the treatment of RA according to the mechanism of action? 1. Anakinra - i. Anti IL-6 2. Tocilizumab - ii. Co-stimulation inhibitor 3. Rituximab - iii. Anti IL-1 4. Abatacept - iv. Anti CD 20
450.e: The question deals with the various biologics used in RA and their mechanism of action. The chief biologicals are the anti TNFα agents, which are described in the previous question. Anakinra is anti IL-1. It has limited use in RA and is used in other autoinflammatory syndromes and Juvenile idiopathic arthritis or Still's Disease. Tocilizumab is anti IL6 antibody. Another agent is Sarilumab. IL-6 is the chief cytokine in Ra which leads to activation of osteoclasts. Rituximab is anti CD 20 antibody. It is used in seropositive RA, refractory to other biologics. Abatacept is a fusion protein consisting of CTLA-4 linked to IgG. It inhibits the co-stimulatory signal for CD4 cells. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2761

450.q: False regard to thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura (TTP) is:
o: Platelet transfusion is recommended to maintain a platelet count of 10 x 10^9/L.
The principal abnormality occurs due to the production of an abnormal WF cleaving protein.
The diagnosis includes proven or suspected arterial or venous thrombosis.
Administration of solvent/detergent-treated fresh frozen plasma isa useful treatment option
450.e: Thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura (TTP) is a rare thrombotic microangiopathy, occurring due to a deficiency of a specific von Willebrand factor cleaving protein known as ADAMTS13 The diagnostic pentad includes acute kidney injury, altered mental state, low platelets, fever and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.Not all features are necessary to make the diagnosis Platelet transfusions are essentially contraindicated in the absence of serious bleeding. Treatment options include plasmapheresis as first line, fresh frozen plasmaadministration, steroids, rituximab and aspirin. Reference: Harrison 20 th 886

450.q: Which of the following is correct about the drugs used in gout? a. Aspirin is not used as it decreases the uric acid secretion b. Diclofenac is used as it concentrates in the joint c. Indomethacin is used as it acts by multiple pathways d. Aspirin is used as it is most powerful NSAID
450.e: Aspirin is not used in gout as it decreases urate secretion . Aspirin has to be given in large doses for anti-inflammatory action. There are more potent anti-inflammatory drugs than aspirin. A, B and C are correct.

451.q: Helmet cells are characteristic of anemia of?
451.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Hemolytic uremic syndrome Schistocytes, helment cells, triangle cells, burr cells are seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). Changes in erythrocyte morphology

451.q: Which of the following is a cause for secondary hypertriglyceridemia?
451.e: Causes of secondary hyperlipidemia include: Type 2 diabetes mellitus chronic renal failure alcoholism (hypertriglyceridemia) drugs including: thiazides, glucocorticoids, oestrogens, cyclosporine, protease inhibitors hypothyroidism (Hypercholesterolemia) nephrotic syndrome. (Hypercholesterolemia) Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:400 Page number:2897

451.q: Renal papillary necrosis is almost always associated with one of the following conditions: March 2004
451.e: Ans. A i.e. Diabetes mellitus `Renal papillary necrosis, an accompaniment of acute pyelonephritis is most often seen in diabetics and is characterised by necrosis of renal papillae of one or both kidneys with sharped demarcation between necrotic and living tissue' — Dorlands Thus while papillary necrosis is a feature of more than one conditions mentioned in the question, it is most commonly seen with diabetes mellitus.

451.q: A 67-year-old man has been receiving dialysis for 6 years. His PTH is elevated at 345 pg/ml(Normal Range 25-65), phosphate 6.6 mg/dl and corrected calcium 8 mg/dl. Of the following, which is the most likely to be responsible for renal osteodystrophy?
451.e: This patient has low calcium, high phosphate and very high PTH levels, which is suggestive of secondary hyperparathyroidism. Among the options 1α hydroxylase deficiency leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:311, Pg:2313.

451.q: Which one of the following conditions is associated with large kidneys despite advanced renal failure?
451.e: Other causes include: Stage 1 diabetic nephropathy Hydronephrosis Acromegaly Renal vein thrombosis Adult polycystic kidney disease Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:311, Pg:2318

451.q: Which of the following drugs are used in CKD to reduce the intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria? 1. ACEI 2. ARB 3. Non dihydropyridine CCBs 4. Beta blockers
451.e: ACE inhibitors and ARB's reduce the intra glomerular pressure by the efferent arteriolar dilation. Non dihydropyridine CCB, Diltiazem and Verapamil are also antiproteinuric and renoprotective. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 311, Pg: 2319.

451.q: A patient with chronic renal failure presents with anaemia. What is the most likely cause?
451.e: Causes of Anemia is CKD patients: Relative deficiency of erythropoietin due to decreased production by the diseased kidneys is the primary cause of anemia. Diminished red blood cell survival Bleeding diathesis Iron deficiency due to poor dietary absorption and gastrointestinal blood loss Hyperparathyroidism/bone marrow fibrosis Chronic inflammation Folate or vitamin B12 deficiency Hemoglobinopathy Comorbid conditions: hypo-/hyperthyroidism, pregnancy, HIV-associated disease, autoimmune disease, immunosuppressive drugs The target hemoglobin recommended in CKD is 10-11.5g/dL Apart from erythropoietin, prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors of endogeneous Hypoxia Inducible Factor are used in CKD. Eg: Roxadustat. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 311, Pg: 2316.

452.q: A 27-year-old woman is in end-stage renal disease. She has been started on regular haemodialysis. She complains of pain in her fingers. An X-ray shows digital subperiosteal erosions. What is the primary metabolic cause for her bony condition?
452.e: Digital sub periosteal resorption is classical of Osteitis fibrosa cystica of hyperparathyroidism. In CKD secondary hyperparathyroidism may progress to tertiary hyperparathyroidism. The series of events that happen in CKD is: Declining GFR leads to reduced excretion of phosphate and thus, phosphate retention The retained phosphate stimulates increased synthesis of both FGF-23 by osteocytes and of PTH and also stimulates growth of parathyroid gland mass PTH production is stimulated by decreased levels of ionized calcium, which in turn, result from decreased levels of renal calcitriol production with reduced kidney mass and suppression of calcitriol production due to phosphate retention and elevated levels of FGF-23, which also increases degradation of calcitriol. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:311, Pg:2313

452.q: A 60-year-old man with long-standing type-2 diabetes, who has recently started on peritoneal dialysis, is admitted with a fractured femoral neck. His serum calcium concentration is 2.9 mmol/l, phosphate is 2 mmol/l and PTH is 5.6 pg/ml(normal range 25-65). Medications include alfacalcidol 0.5 mg daily and calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily. What would a bone biopsy show?
o: Aluminium deposition at the osteoid bone interface
452.e: Referring to the above question, we can clearly say that this patient is suffering from adynamic bone disease. Note that the calcium and phosphorous given here are in mmol/l. Ca value has to be multiplied by 4. So the Ca is 11.6mg/dl. Phosphorous has to be multiplied by 3. So the value is 6mg/dl. Aluminium deposited can cause osteomalacia like picture and is seen with use of aluminium as phosphate binder and Al in dialysate. Osteitis fibrosa cystica is severe secondary hyperparathyroidism. An increase in plasma cells cause hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:410, Pg:3181, 3182.

452.q: Which of the following statements are true regarding the management of Lupus nephritis? 1. HCQS should be included as treatment for all classes since it reduces the accrual of tissue damage. 2. Management of class I and Class II should be guided by the extra renal manifestations. 3. Class III and IV requires aggressive immunosuppression. 4. Isolated Class V has got better prognosis than class IV. 5. Isolated class V without nephrotic range proteinuria requires only supportive management.
452.e: The question deals with the management and prognosis of Lupus Nephritis. HCQ should be in the management of allclasses of lupus nephritis. Class I and II should be treated mainly based on the extra renal manifestations. Class III and IV are the proliferative and serious forms and require aggressive immunosuppression with high dose glucocorticoid with either MMF or Cyclophosphamide. Isolated Class V presents with proteinuria alone and has got better outcome than class IV. But class V often co exists with class III and IV. Class V with nephrotic range proteinuria should be treated with immunosuppression, usually steroid with calcinurin inhibitors. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2739-2747 KDIGO guidelines

452.q: A 47 year old man has a renal transplant. He presents with a hot swollen ankle on the left and fevers. The symptoms have been present for 2 days. What should be done?
o: Send joint fluid for microscopy and culture
452.e: Acute monoarthritis with fever should raise the suspicion of septic arthritis especially in immunosuppressed patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, Ch: 370, Pg: 2845

452.q: A 70-year-old man with no previous past medical history presents with a BP of 180/100 mm Hg, frothy urine and peripheral oedema. There is 1+ blood and 3+ protein on urinalysis. 24-hour protein loss is 5 grams. Plasma albumin is 2.5 g/dL. Plasma C3 is 0.1 (low). Plasma creatinine is 1.80 mg/dl. A renal biopsy is performed. ANA is negative. ESR is 110. Which of the following is most likely to be found on the biopsy?
452.e: This is patient has low C3 levels. So we may tend to think of PSGN. But here, there is no history of sore throat or preceeding streptococcal illness. Another point against PSGN is the presence of nephrotic range proteinuria which is very rare in PSGN. So the answer is MPGN. We should know that mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis are the same and is just a histologic diagnosis and noy etiologic. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

452.q: A 58-year-old man with CKD has been on EPO injections 3 times a week for several years. Which one of the following is a side effect of erythropoietin therapy?
452.e: EPO therapy may lead to hypertension and seizures. Other side effects of treatment with erythropoietin include hyperkalaemia in uraemic patients, increased PCV, thrombocythemia, shunt thrombosis, iron deficiency and urticaria. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, Ch:305, Pg: 2117, 2118, 393, 499, 729

452.q: Which among the following statements is false?
o: In renal transplantation, Kidneys with high KDPI are allocated to those expected to have high post-transplant survival.
Living donor transplants fare better than deceased donor kidneys
Immunosuppression is required lifelong for patients after transplant, except if donated by an identical twin or simultaneous kidney-bone marrow transplantation.
ATG and Alemtuzumab are used as depleting agents
452.e: Kidney Donor Profile Index(KDPI) is a score designed to estimate the risk of graft survival, ranging from 0-100%. Lower KDPI is associated with lesser chance of rejection. KDPI of Living donor transplants do well than deceased donor transplant. Immunosuppression is not required for identical twin and combined kidney-bone marrow transplant. Induction therapy will be done with depleting agents like ATG or Alemtuzumab or non-depleting agents directed against IL2 receptors to reduce the risk of acute rejection. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 313, Pg: 2325-2328.

452.q: A 19-year-old male is unwell. He has previously had a history of renal transplantation 5 years ago. Within three days of admission he developed acute renal failure with evidence of haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia. A clinical diagnosis of haemolytic uraemic syndrome was made and he was treated with plasma exchange. Which one of the following drugs could have caused this?
452.e: Cyclosporine can cause HUS in renal transplant recipients, especially in those also receiving rapamycin, which increases tissue concentrations of ciclosporin. Drugs causing thrombotic microangiopathy: Calcineurin inhibitors Mitomycin C Clopidogrel Gemcitabine Proteasome inhibitors(Bortezomib) Oral contraceptives Interferon Tacrolimus and Sirolimus These drugs cause direct endothelial damage and is dose dependent. Antibody mediated TMA can occur with Clopidogrel, Quinine. It is dose independent. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 317, Pg: 2365.

453.q: What is the most common etiology of complicated UTI?
453.e: In complicated UTI (e.g., CAUTI), E. coli remains the predominant organism Organisms causing UTI: SEEK PP Staph saprophyticus coli Enterococcus Klebsiella Proteus Pseudomonas Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1071

453.q: A 35-year man has been referred for management of hypertension. On examination, he had palpable kidneys. This was confirmed by abdominal ultrasound which showed multiple cysts. Which of the following is likely to be associated?
453.e: A young hypertensive with palpable kidneys and cysts on ultrasound points to the diagnosis of ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease). Polycystic kidney disease is associated with increased levels of EPO which lead to polycythemia. Associations of ADPKD: Cardiovascular: Intracranial aneurysm (5 times more common than general population), can rupture to cause subarachnoid hemorrhage. Diffuse arterial dolichoectasia of the anterior and posterior cerebral circulation → predisposed to arterial dissection and stroke. Mitral valve prolapse. Insufficiency of the mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valves. Gastrointestinal: Colonic diverticula Abdominal wall hernia Polycystic liver disease Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Edition, Page Number 2350-2354.

453.q: A 52 year old man presents with lower back pains and lethargy. Investigations subsequently confirmed obstructive nephropathy and retroperitoneal fibrosis. His medication is reviewed on the ward round. Which medication is well known to cause retroperitoneal fibrosis?
453.e: Retroperitoneal fibrosis is a disease featuring the proliferation of fibrous tissue in the retroperitoneum, the compartment of the body containing the kidneys, aorta, renal tract and various other structures. It may present with lower back pain, renal failure, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis and other obstructive symptoms. It may have an autoimmune etiology. 1/3 rd cases are secondary to malignancy, medications, aortic aneurysm or certain infections. Methyldopa, methysergide, amphetamines, beta blockers, cocaine and LSD are drugs which cause retroperitoneal fibrosis. Azathioprine is used to treat the condition. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 319 Pg: 2375

454.q: A 75-year-old man visits his GP for a new-patient screen. His only previous complaints have been type-2 diabetes and mild long-standing back pain. Screening tests reveal an elevated serum creatinine of 2.15 mg/dl and anaemia with Hb of 10.1 g/dl. A back X-ray shows collapse of the lumbar spine and there is a monoclonal band on serum protein electrophoresis. What is the most likely cause of his deteriorated renal function?
454.e: This patient is suffering from Myeloma as evidenced by the presence of anemia, renal impairment and bone involvement. Myeloma can affect the kidney in several ways - the filtered light chains are toxic to the tubules and can cause acute obstruction: Cast nephropathy The light chain impairs the proximal tubular function and cause RTA Hypercalcemia can cause tubulointerstitial disease Amyloidosis LCDD All forms of renal involvement is reversible to a certain extend with treatment of myeloma. Among the given options Amyloidosis is the best pick Amyloidosis presents predominantly between the ages of 60 and 70 years. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:111, Pg:870.

454.q: A 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension has renal impairment. His creatinine is 2.8 mg/dl. Urine dipstick shows blood ++ and protein +. What is the most useful investigation?
454.e: A urinalysis of 2+ blood and 1+ protein are strong pointers towards glomerular disease. Hence among the options, biopsy is the most useful investigation. Renal ultrasound may be useful in assessing the kidney size and echoes, but it may not help us arrive at a diagnosis. IV urogram is used in the investigation of Obstruction to urinary tract and DTPA nucleide scan is used to asses the functional status of kidneys. Indications of Renal biopsy(when suspected): Glomerulonephritis Nephrotic Syndrome Vasculitis Interstitial nephritis Myeloma kidney HUS and TTP Allograft rejection Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21 st edition, Ch: 310, Pg: 2305.

454.q: Which of the following drugs cause renal impairment by causing interstitial nephritis?
454.e: Quinolones, penicillins, cephalosporins, sulphonamides and rifampicin are antibiotics that cause interstitial nephritis. Vancomycin, Aminoglycosides, Amphotericin B, Acyclovir, Foscarnet, Tenofovir and Cidofovir are toxic to the tubules of kidney. Vancomycin and acyclovir cause intra tubular obstruction. Amphotericin B causes RTA like picture with hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia. Hypomagnesemia is also seen with Aminoglycosides. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Chap 310, Pg. 2300

454.q: Which type of malaria is associated with renal failure -
454.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Falciparum Nephrotic syndrome —> quarta malaria (P. malariae) Acute tubular necrosis (renal failure) malignant tertian malaria or pernicious malaria (caused by P falciparum).

454.q: Which of the following is not a cause of hypokalemic distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis?
454.e: Hypergammaglobulinemia causes hyperkalemic distal renal tubular acidosis hypogammaglobulinemia is not reported to cause the distal renal tubular acidosis Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:55 Pg: 364

454.q: Which of the following drugs cause proximal RTA?
454.e: Proximal RTA is caused by Ifosfamide, Streptozocin, outdated tetracyclines, gentamicin and Tenofovir. Amphotericin B causes distal RTA. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Chap 310, Pg. 2301

455.q: Which of the following denotes normal cardiac axis?
455.e: The cardiac axis represents the overall direction of electrical activity as it spreads through the cardiac conduction system The normal cardiac axis is directed downward and slightly to the left. It falls within the range of -30° to +90°. Left Axis Deviation (LAD): When the QRS axis is less than -30°. Right Axis Deviation (RAD): When the QRS axis is greater than +90°. Extreme Axis Deviation: Occurs when the QRS axis lies between -90° and 180° ("Northwest Axis") Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1870

455.q: A 24-year-old patient is admitted after falling asleep drunk in a toilet cubicle. On examination his BP 130/70, pulse 98 bpm and there is no pericardial rub. There is 'boggy' tenderness of his right calf and both thigh muscles. Biochemistry reveals urea 125 mg/dl, creatinine 4.0 mg/dl, bicarbonate 15 mmol/l, pH 7.1, potassium 7.8 mmol/l and creatine kinase 17 000 IU/l. (Ref values: s. creat: 0.6-1.4 mg/dl; S. urea: 17- 43 mg/dL; S. potassium: 3.5-5 mmol/l; S. bicarbonate: 22 to 32 mmol/L; S. creatine kinase: 5 to 25 IU/L IU/l) What is the most appropriate form of treatment?
455.e: This patient was immobilized for prolonged period, which can lead to rhabdomyolysis and renal failure, as evidenced by the high Creatine kinase levels. In addition, he has hyperkalemia and severe metabolic acidosis. Also, he has boggy swelling and tenderness of his muscles, suggestive of compartment syndrome or bilateral DVT. So he is having multiple issues that requires rapid correction. Hence hemodialysis is the best treatment Forced alkaline diuresis may renal failure is established with life-threatening hyperkalemia and acidosis, it is inappropriate. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, chp:310, pg: 2307.

455.q: All of the following are the side effects of cocaine toxicity. Except?
455.e: Cocaine is a psychostimulant . The other agents belonging to this group are, Methamphetamine, MDMA and Cathinone. There are certain therapeutically used psychostimulants too. These include Methylphenidate and Dextroamphetamine, used in the treatment of ADHD. Phenylpropanolamine was a psychostimulant used previously for weight reduction and is now withdrawn due to the risk of intracerebral bleed. The table depicts the symptoms of overuse of all the psychostimulants. Their cardiovascular effects produce tachycardia and not bradycardia. Withdrawal produces hypersomnia, depressed mood and increased appetite.

455.q: In Diapragmatic Hernia. Most common anomaly is seen in
455.e: Answer- A. Cardiovascular anomalies Diaphragmatic Hernia is defined as a communication between abdominal & thoracic cavities with or without abdominal contents in thorax. Females are affected more than males. More common on left side and is posterolateral. Associated anomalies may be seen 30% of cases CNS lesions, esophageal atresia, omphalocele and CVS lesions. Most cases are sporadic. Cardiac anomalis is MC anomalis.

455.q: An elderly man develops syncope. He is known to have ischaemic heart disease. Peripheral pulses are absent, and ECG reveals wide-complex tachycardia. Immediate management consists of which of the following?
o: A bolus dose of intravenous lidocaine
455.e: The patient has ventricular tachycardia and is hemodynamically unstable indicated by loss of consciousness. Immediate treatment consists of cardioversion followed by a suitable anti-arrhythmic such as lidocaine IV or amiodarone and correction of any electrolyte imbalance. Myocardial infarction (MI) is the likely cause of ventricular tachycardia, hence treatment for MI would be indicated if required. Programmed stimulation may only be carried out when the patient is stable. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2252

455.q: Which of the following is a characteristic finding of Tricuspid regurgitation?
o: Diastolic murmur in left sternal border
455.e: Tricsupid regurgitation - Around 90% is secondary to left sided valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension - Syndromes associated with primary TR include Marfan syndrome, Carcinoid syndrome and with Ebstein anomaly - Clinical examination shows elevated JVP with prominent c-v waves (Lancisi sign) and pulsatile hepatomegaly - Pansystolic murmur is typically heard in the left lower sternal border that increases during inspiration (Carvallo sign) Pansystolic murmur at apex is typically caused by mitral regurgitation. PSM at left lower sternal border can be caused by TR and VSD. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2003

455.q: A 22-year-old man presents with tremor, sweating, flushing and weight loss. On examination his pulse is 135 bpm and his blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg. Which of the following is the least likely diagnostic possibility?
455.e: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine secreting tumours arising from the adrenal gland. Pheochromocytoma may occur in patients with von Recklinghausen's disease (NF-1) and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Skin neurofibromas and multiple cafe au-lait spots occur in peripheral (NF1) neurofibromatosis, while haemangioblastomas are commonly seen in those with the von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Carney's triad includes Pheochromocytoma /paraganglioma, pulmonary chondroma and Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) Ataxia telangiectasia is not associated with pheochromocytomas. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2976

455.q: A 27-year-old woman presented with a history of sudden onset right-sided weakness and dysphasia lasting 8 hours. She had returned to India from US 2 days previously. There was no significant past medical history and physical examination was normal. Chest X-ray, ECG and a CT head scan were all normal. Which one of the following investigations is most likely to reveal the underlying cause of this episode?
455.e: The history here suggests a lower limb deep vein thrombosis with peripheral embolus through a patent foramen ovale, leading to a left sided cerebrovascular event. This is termed the paradoxical embolus - so-called because a thromboembolus arising from the venous circulation can end up in the systemic circulation.
