Transoesophageal echocardiography is the investigation of choice to investigate for a patent foramen ovale, although transthoracic echocardiography with contrast may be an alternative. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:273 pg:1913

456.q: Mr. Kohli is a 26-year-old cricketer comes to you for regular check-up. On your assessment, you note a resting heart rate or 45 bpm with an occasional pause of up to 2 seconds. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. He feels well and reports no syncopal or presyncopal episodes at rest or during exercise. ECG is normal. Which of the following would be next step ?
o: Follow-up after 1 week. Avoid cricket for a week
He should undergo a treadmill stress ECG to determine the presence of chronotropic competence.
456.e: Sinus bradycardia and pauses up to 3 seconds are common in young individuals, particularly in highly trained athletes. (You know Mr. Kohli) Given the normal ECG, lack of symptoms, and normal physical examination, no further testing is warranted. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 245

456.q: A 74-year-old woman presents with a feeling of shortness of breath and choking on lying down. Around 4 months earlier she had been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and was started on aspirin and digoxin by her physician. On examination her physician could feel a goitre. Plain radiography confirmed retrosternal extension, which was presumed to be contributing to her shortness of breath. Her TSH level was less than 0.05 mU/l. Thyroid autoantibodies were negative. What diagnosis best fits with this clinical picture?
456.e: Toxic multinodular goitre usually occurs in women over 55 years of age and is more common than Grave's disease in the elderly. Her atrial fibrillation may well be related to this. Her goitre is obstructing, with significant retrosternal extension, and surgery is the treatment of choice. Initially, however, she should be rendered euthyroid with antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2948

456.q: A 56 year old chronic alcoholic is found on the street with a low conscious level. His GCS is 3/15 on arrival in casualty. On examination, his BP is 110/65 and he is jaundiced. There is marked ascites and he has 7 spider naevi. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 120. Which is the most practical test to elucidate why he is unconscious?
456.e: In a patient with liver disease, it is important to exclude hypoglycemia as a cause of unconsciousness. Following confirming that baseline observations and BM is normal, the next best step is to perform a CT of his head to exclude a central neurological cause of decreased conscious level. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 28, Pg: 187

456.q: A 64-year-old man presents with evidence of gynaecomastia. He has been taking long-term digitalis and warfarin therapy for persistent atrial fibrillation. In addition, he takes another tablet for heartburn. Results of tests for androgens, HCG, liver function and thyroid function are all normal. What is the most likely cause of his gynaecomastia?
456.e: Digitalis is one of a number of drugs that may be associated with gynaecomastia. Causes of gynaecomastia; Drugs: (DISCCO) D igoxin I soniazid S pironolactone C imetidine C yproterone O estrogen Other causes: Thyrotoxicosis Liver disease Estrogen-producing tumors HCG-producing tumors Starvation/refeeding Carcinoma of the breast Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3018

456.q: A 66 year man who is on warfarin for atrial fibrillation is complaining of worsening breathlessness over the last 2 months. On examination, he has an irregular heart beat, blood pressure of 110 / 60 mmHg and he looked pale. There was no evidence of organomegaly. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 8.5 g/dL MCV 70 fL PLT 160 x 10^9/L His upper gastrointestinal tract endoscopy and colonoscopy were normal. What is the next best investigation?
456.e: This patient has microcytic anaemia and is also on warfarin. So the priority is to rule out bleeding. Since upper GI endoscopy and colonoscopy were normal, the next step would be capsule endoscopy which helps to see bleeds in small bowel . In this case angiodysplasia of small bowel could be a cause of bleeding. In capsule endoscopy, a patient swallows a small pill which emits a radio frequency which is picked up by a sensor that the patient wears over several hours. Images are then downloaded as a continuous movie. Another possible cause of GI bleed in a patient with AF is mesenteric insufficiency, which will be characterized by abdominal pain post prandial. In that case mesenteric angiography will be the investigation. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 322, Pg:2417

456.q: A 35 year old patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis has history of palpitations and irregular heartbeat. She presents unwell with fast Atrial Fibrillation and was DC cardioverted successfully. Which of the following medications is most effective for maintenance of sinus rhythm?
456.e: Amiodarone is most effective for maintenance of sinus rhythm. Beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are used to control ventricular rate in patients with Atrial fibrillation. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1907

456.q: A 50-year-old politician presented with a strange fluttering sensation in his chest, but no chest pain. The symptoms lasted 24 hours. An ECG revealed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 130 beats per minute. His blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Which one of the following drugs is most likely to restore sinus rhythm?
456.e: A patient with atrial fibrillation and hemodynamic instability (hypotension/shock/impaired consciousness/heart failure/angina) is treated with DC cardioversion. In a patient with AF without hemodynamic instability, the two approaches to management include controlling the heart rate or restoring sinus rhythm. Flecainide is the drug most likely to restore sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation. Other drugs include Amiodarone, sotalol, dronaderone, propafenone etc. Adenosine is used in patients with supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Digoxin and Bisoprolol are indicated for rate control and are not normally associated with the restoration of sinus rhythm. Verapamil can be used for rate control in atrial fibrillation, and may be used in the treatment of SVT. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1907

456.q: A 71 year old man who had multiple episodes of unilateral amaurosis fugax. He has risk factors of being a smoker and hypertension. He is on atenolol and aspirin. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Carotid dopplers show 80% right carotid stenosis. What is the most appropriate management?
o: High dose aspirin 300mg with a proton pump inhibitor
456.e: As there is > 70% carotid artery stenosis and symptoms suggestive of emboli, endarterectomy is recommended. The patient should also be anticoagulated afterwards in view of atrial fibrillation. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3347

457.q: -30° to -60° left axis deviation is seen in
457.e: Answer- A. Left ventricular hypertrophy Normally, QRS axis ranges from -30° to 90°C An axis more negative than -30° is referred to as left axis deviation and an axis more positive than +100° is called right axis deviation Left axis deviation Axis more negative than -30° Associated with Left ventricular hypertrophy Left anterior fascicular block Inferior M.I.

457.q: A 60-year-old man has had a myocardial infarction. His pulse rate is 45/min and he is feeling lightheaded. Blood pressure is 90/65 mm Hg. In which one of the following conditions is temporary pacing indicated even when symptoms are absent?
457.e: Asymptomatic patients with first- or second-degree Mobitz type I AV block do not require any specific therapy. Patients should undergo treatment of any potentially reversible cause (ie, myocardial ischemia or medication effect) Symptomatic patients with any degree of heart block should be treated urgently with atropine (initial dose 0.5 mg given intravenously) or temporary pacing (transcutaneous or transvenous). Indications for permanent pacing: Symptomatic Brady arrhythmias with any degree of AV block Asymptomatic high-degree AV block (second degree Mobitz type II or third- degree heart block) with slow ventricular rates (less than 40 beats/min). Patients with presumed cardiac syncope with normal heart rates and rhythm but bifascicular or trifascicular block on ECG Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1883

457.q: A 52-year-old man had a ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest whilst at a railway station. He was successfully resuscitated by a co-passenger. Further evaluation at the hospital including coronary angiography showed no stenotic lesions in the coronary arteries. Which is the most appropriate step for long term management?
457.e: A cardiac electrophysiological study would be necessary to help confirm whether this patient has inducible ventricular tachycardia, and ablation of the pathways if so. However in a young patient with no coronary artery disease demonstrable to revascularize, ICD is necessary to treat a possible further cardiac arrest. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1873

457.q: A 47-year-old man presents with broad complex tachycardia. He has a BP of 102/70 and a pulse rate of 176/min. The doctor on duty is considering administration of antiarrhythmic. Which one of the following medications is contraindicated in this patient?
457.e: The patient is likely to have ventricular tachycardia in view of the very fast ventricular rate and broad complexes on ECG. Amiodarone is the preferred pharmacological agent for acute agent in VT without hemodynamic compromise. Verapamil is contraindicated in VT because it can cause the blood pressure to drop drastically due to negative inotropic action. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1922

457.q: All of the following electrocardiograph waveforms are matched correctly to the cardiac cycle that it represents except:
457.e: The electrocardiogram waveforms are labelled alphabetically, beginning with the P wave, which represents atrial depolarization. PR interval shows the AV nodal delay to allow for the filling of ventricles The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization, and the ST-T-U complex (STsegment, T wave, and U wave) represents ventricular repolarization. The J point is the junction between the end of the QRS complex and the beginning of the ST segment. Atrial Repolarization (STa and Ta) is usually too low in amplitude to be detected, but it may become apparent in conditions such as acute pericarditis and atrial infarction. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1866

457.q: The drug of choice in a patient with torsades de pointes is:
457.e: Torsades de pointes is characterised by twisting pattern of ventricular tachycardia in ECG that occurs in the background of prolonged QT interval The drugs, metabolic abnormalities etc. that can prolong QTc can potentially lead to torsades de pointes. IV Magnesium sulphate given at a bolus dose of 1-2 gm is considered to be effective in this condition and is considered the treatment of choice Metoprolol and lignocaine may also be effective in some cases but are not the first line agents. Amiodarone is avoided in such patients as it can further prolong the QTc interval Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1924

457.q: Patient is on metoprolol and if he is given Verapamil, what is the effect that occurs ?
457.e: Metoprolol is a beta blocker. It causes bradycardia by acting on the β 1 receptor in the heart. Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker and is an AV nodal blocking agent . It causes bradycardia by blocking the AV node. In the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, where depolarization is due primarily to a Ca2+-dependent slow inward current, the Verapamil slow the sinus pacemaker and inhibit atrioventricular conduction. So the combined effect will be bradycardia with AV blocks.

457.q: Paradoxical splitting of second heart sound is seen in?
457.e: Answer is C (LBBB) Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) is typically associated with Reversed or Paradoxical Splitting of S2 Paradoxical splitting of second heart sound is caused by delayed A2 or early P2. Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) is associated with delayed Aortic closure (delayed A2) due to delayed electrical activation of the left ventricle. ASD and RBBB are associated with a wide physiological (non- paradoxical) split of second heart sound due to delayed pulmonic closure (Delayed P2) while VSD is associated with a wide physiological (non-paradoxical) split second heart sound from early aortic closure (Early A2).

458.q: Which of the following is not a described association for Mitral valve prolapse?
458.e: Syndromes with MVP as a feature Marfan syndrome Ehler Danlos syndrome Klinefelter syndrome Osteogenesis imperfecta Autosomal dominant Polycystic kidney disease Pseudoxanthoma elasticum Barlow syndrome is synonymous with Mitral valve prolapse Noonan syndrome is associated with peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and atrial septal defect. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2000

458.q: A 65-year-old man has renal bruits, renal impairment and hypertension. Which one of the following tests is most appropriate?
o: Magnetic resonance angiography(MRA) of renal arteries
458.e: From the options above, For renal artery stenosis, MRA remains the best investigation with high sensitivities and specificities. MRI is not effective for detecting stent thrombosis. CT angiography provides excellent imaging of the vessels and is less affected by stents. Risk of contrast nephropathy in renal impairment. Though Intra Arterial angiography remains Gold standard for diagnosis of Large vessel diseases. Doppler is very less expensive but is operator dependent and not useful for distal renal arteries and Fibromuscular dysplasia. Captopril renography has strong negative predictive value. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 278, Pg: 2088-2089.

458.q: A 34-year-old man presented for a routine check-up from company. He was symptom free, but clinical examination suggested a small ventricular septal defect. Which one of the following findings was most likely to have been present?
o: A short systolic murmur at the right sternal edge
A systolic murmur maximal at the apex
A systolic murmur with thrill at the left sternal edge
458.e: Typically, a small VSD generates a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border(LSB) accompanied by a thrill. The murmur may be heard at the apex but is usually loudest at the LSB . Very small defects may generate an early/late systolic murmur. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:234,264 pg:1673,1833

458.q: A 30-year-old heroine addict was found dead in his room. He was last seen alive by his neighbours around 4 weeks ago and he was presumed to be unwell over the past 4 weeks. At autopsy, his kidneys had a flea bitten appearance and renal biopsy showed sub epithelial and sub endothelial deposits of Immunoglobulin and C3. What could be the possible cause of these findings?
458.e: The patient is a IV drug abuser, who was presumed to be not well for the past few weeks. IV drug abuse increases the risk of Infective endocarditis. So the patient probably died of an untreated Infective endocarditis. The appearance of kidneys in IE is 'Flea Bitten' and microscopy shows immune complex deposition. It is more common in Sub Acute Bacterial endocarditis than Acute, since acute will be more symptomatic and the patient would have got treated. SLE presents with varying degrees of proliferation. Moreover, the history of drug abuse cant be ignored. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Pg: 2337.

458.q: Which of the following cardiac conditions is not associated with continuous murmur?
458.e: Causes of continuous murmur These murmurs persist throughout systole and diastole . Causes include : Patent ductus arteriosus Coronary arteriovenous fistula Rupture sinus of Valsalva aneurysm Aortopulmonary window ASD with MS Anomalous left coronary artery Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2012

458.q: A 39-year-old healthy woman has a faint systolic murmur on physical examination. An echocardiogram is performed, and she is found to have a bicuspid aortic valve. In explaining the meaning of this finding to her, the most appropriate statement is that?
o: An aortic valve replacement is eventually likely to be required.
Other family members are not likely to have the same condition
She should be treated with a cholesterol-lowering agent
Down syndrome is a common association of this condition
458.e: Bicuspid aortic valve is perhaps the most common form of congenital heart disease in adults (0.5-1.4% of population). Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) tends to occur sporadically although it can also be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The prevalence of BAV disease among first-degree relatives of an affected individual is ~10%. Complications that can occur in BAV include aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation and increased risk of aortic dissection. Aortic aneurysm may also be coexistent with BAV. Bicuspid valves have a propensity to wear out and calcify with aging . So an aortic valve replacement is eventually likely to be required in the 5th and 6th decades of life. BAV is seen in association with turner's syndrome . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:256 pg:1803,1804,1807

458.q: A patient presented with an episode of TIA. On examination he was found to have an irregularly irregular pulse. A 2d echo showed he had severe mitral stenosis. ECG showed atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is true regarding prevention of stroke. A. Aspirin is the only drug needed B. Warfarin is indicated C. NOACs are not indicated D. Patient with MS can be recommended for a mitral valve surgery
o: B, C and D are correct
458.e: Warfarin is the anticoagulant of choice in valvular AF, For patients with AF or atrial flutter and an elevated CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or greater in men or 3 or greater in women, anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2.0-3.0), is recommended.

458.q: A 72-year-old lady presented with dyspnoea and fever. She has a history of weight loss which has been investigated with colonoscopy which found a tumor of the sigmoid colon and she is awaiting surgery.On examination she has a systolic murmur and and ECHO shows vegetations on the mitral valve. A diagnosis of infective endocarditis is made. Which of the following organisms is associated with a high incidence of colorectal tumors?
458.e: Up to half of patients presenting with Streptococcus bovis endocarditis have colorectal tumors. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 81 Pg: 638

459.q: Which one of the following sets of components of cigarette smoke is a causal agent of coronary artery disease -
o: Nicotine and carbon monoxide and tar
459.e: Ans. is `b' i.e., Nicotine and carbon monoxide and tar Mechanisms for smoking-induced Coronary heart disease Carbon monoxide induces atherogenesis. Nicotine stimulation of adrenergic drive raising both BP and myocardial oxygen demand. Lipid metabolism with fall in protective high-density lipoproteins. Note : Tar is associated with carcinogenesis (not atherosclerosis). But amongst the given options option b is the best answer as it consists of both nicotine and CO.

459.q: The earliest ECG abnormality in a patient with hyperkalemia is:
459.e: ECG changes start to manifest usually when serum K > 6 mEq/L The earliest ECG finding in a patient with hyperkalemia is tall, tented T waves It is followed by other changes like P wave flattening, PR prolongation, QRS widening, appearance of sine wave pattern Hypokalemia is characterised by ECG changes like T wave flattening/inversion, ST segment depression, appearance of 'u' wave and prolonged QU interval. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1911

459.q: A 62-year-old smoker is admitted with nausea, sweating and central crushing chest pain. A 12 lead ECG reveals ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which coronary artery is most likely to have been affected in this case?
459.e: Right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle, the posterior third of the interventricular septum, the inferior wall of the left ventricle and a portion of the posterior wall of the left ventricle. (leads II, III, aVF corresponds to inferior wall) Occasionally the posterior interventricular septum may be supplied by a branch of the of the left circumflex artery, called left dominant circulation. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries arise at the left main coronary artery bifurcation and supply the anterior left ventricle, the bulk of the interventricular septum (anterior two thirds), the apex, and the lateral and posterior left ventricular walls. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2035

459.q: Which of the following is the most commonly affected coronary artery in a patient with myocardial infarction?
459.e: The frequency of involvement of coronaries in MI is left anterior descending artery > right coronary artery > left circumflex artery Left anterior descending artery is also referred to as 'widow's artery'. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2044

459.q: Which of the following pharmacological agents is most likely to benefit a patient with angina due to cardiac syndrome X?
459.e: Nitrates are often effective in patients with syndrome X, which is currently termed 'microvascular angina'. Cardiac syndrome X consists of angina-like chest pain during exertion, characteristic ECG changes during exercise testing, normal coronary arteries on cardiac catheterisation and no inducible coronary artery spasm during catheterisation. It should not be confused with the metabolic syndrome X, which comprises central obesity, glucose intolerance, dyslipidemia, and high blood pressure. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2031, 2034

459.q: Which of the following is seen in a patient with Right ventricular myocardial infarction?
o: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF
Occlusion of the left circumflex artery
459.e: Right ventricular myocardial infarction (RVMI) usually occurs in association with an inferior-wall left ventricular infarction, as revealed by the ECG. In ECG, along with ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF which suggests an inferior wall MI, a patient with RVMI may also have ST elevation in V1 and in right sided chest leads V3R-V6R. The typical clinical findings in RVMI include bradycardia (due to AV node involvement), hypotension, raised JVP with positive Kussmaul sign (inspiratory rise of JVP). Hypotension is typically treated with IV fluids (0.9% saline) There is usually a right coronary occlusion. Characteristic clinical features include a low cardiac output syndrome with jugular venous distension but no pulmonary vascular congestion. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2062

459.q: Correct about presentation of neurogenic shock is?
459.e: Neurogenic shock is associated with bradycardia and hypotension. It is a type of distributive shock.

459.q: A 74-year-old male presents with sudden loss of vision in his right eye, associated with a relative afferent pupillary defect. He has poorly controlled systemic hypertension and raised cholesterol.What is the most likely aetiology of his presentation?
459.e: The history of acute loss of vision affecting one eye suggests an acute vascular occlusion, especially given the associated vascular risks. The others cause a more chronic visual loss. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 222

460.q: A 68-year-old man has a 2 cm adenoma removed from his sigmoid colon. The biopsy results confirm an adenocarcinoma in situ with moderately differentiated dysplastic cells. The pathology report confirms total excision with clear resection margins. What is the most appropriate follow up management for this patient?
460.e: The first thing to note is the question is about planned management. This patient has been picked up early and has had a tumor resected. His CEA would be normal and would not be expected to be elevated until the disease was quite established on the TNM scale. However, this patient'' prognosis would be excellent but he is by definition someone with increased risk. Therefore, he should continue to be reviewed with colonoscopy annually for at least two years. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:81 Pg: 640

460.q: Which of the following drug-eluting stent belongs to first generation with higher rates of stent thrombosis?
460.e: First generation drug eluting stents include Sirolimus and Paclitaxel which have higher risk of restenosis and late stent thrombosis. Second generation stents including Biolimus, Zotarolimus and Everolimus have lower chances of these complications. Reference: Harrison Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2067

460.q: A patient presents with sudden onset aphasia and hemiparesis. The Deficit resolved within 2 hours and the CT Scan of the patient is normal. On examination BP is 160 /110 mm Hg. What is the next best step in management?
o: MRI head to check for ischemia
CT Angiography to look for occlusion in vessel
460.e: The patient in the question has a TIA(Transient Ischemic Attack). The next best step is to find out the source of the thrombus and treat it to prevent the recurrence and stroke. CT angiography of vessels in the head and neck to find the source of the clot.

460.q: A 28 year old man presents with a 6 month history of low back pain. The pain radiates to his buttocks. There is associated stiffness which is worse in the morning and after periods of inactivity. Which of the following signs is most likely to be present?
460.e: The presence of low back ache with morning stiffness in indicative of an inflammatory low back ache. The features of inflammatory back ache includes: Age of onset Morning stiffness of > 30 minutes Improvement with exercise No improvement with rest Pain during the second half of night which improves up on awakening Alternating buttock pain Axial spondyloarthritis are a common cause of inflammatory back ache in young patients and among the given options the test used in diagnosing an axial spondyloarthritis is Sacroiliac tenderness. Others include stretching of the Sacroiliac joint- FABER (Flexion abduction and external rotation) test or the Patrick test. Tenderness in the posterior spinous process of the vertebrae. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2793

460.q: Which of the following interleukins chiefly drive PsA?
460.e: The chief interleukins that drive PsA are IL17 and IL 23. The biologics that are used in treatment of PsA act by antagonizing these cytokines. They include: Anti IL 17: secukinumab and ixekizumab Anti IL-23/IL-12p40 : ustekinumab, a monoclonal antibody to the shared subunit. Anti IL-23 (p19 subunit)-guselkumab, risankizumab, and tildrakizumab Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2800

460.q: A 31 year old man has had a year's history of bilateral hip pains and back pains with early morning stiffness. There is no past medical history of trauma to the back. Non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs helped to relieve his symptoms. What is the likely diagnosis?
460.e: Pain and stiffness in the lower back or buttocks, especially in the morning is typical of sacroiliitis. It is typically helped by NSAIDS or steroids . X rays will help to confirm the diagnosis. It is associated with various inflammatory diseases e.g. ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, arthritis associated with IBD, Reactive arthritis etc Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2790

460.q: For the patient described in the question above, what will you give for long term management initially?
460.e: The cornerstone in the management of RA are DMARDS. Conventional DMARDS are the first choice, Methotrexate is the DMARD of choice for RA. It can be started either as a monotherapy or with other conventional DMARDS like HCQ, Sulfasalazine. Leflunomide is another DMARD that can be used which is equally efficacious as Methotrexate. The recent approach is early intensive therapy with combination of DMARDs to minimize disability. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2761-2764

460.q: A 60 year old male patient who is a known case of lung cancer presents to the physician with complaints of generalized weakness and serum calcium of 16.4mg/dl. What would be the next step in the management of the patient?
460.e: The patient presents with an acute hypercalcemic crisis which can result in the development of systolic arrest of the heart. Therefore, it is imperative to decrease serum calcium of the patient with administration of normal saline and eventually furosemide drip.Normal saline will cause hydration and once the rehydration is complete then initiate furosemide drip. This will result in urinary loss of calcium.Eventually, bisphosphonates and intranasal calcitonin are administered.In the case of AKI, hemodialysis is needed. Reference: Harrison 20 th chap. pg.314

461.q: Which is not correct regarding RA?
o: The incidence of RA increases between 25 and 55 years of age, after which it plateaus until the age of 75 and then decreases
The most common pattern of joint involvement is symmetrical and polyarticular.
Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark of RA
Macrocytic anemia is the most common hematologic abnormality in RA
461.e: A normochromic, normocytic anemia often develops in patients with RA and is the most common hematologic abnormality. Macrocytic anemia may occur in RA due to Methotrexate toxicity. Flexor tenosynovitis can occur in RA. It causes trigger fingers. The most common tendon involved is Flexor Pollicis Longus. The age of onset of RA is between 25 to 55 years of age, after which it plateaus until the age of 75 , after which it decreases. The most common pattern of involvement is symmetrical, polyarthritis. DIP is usually not involved, but if so, it is often due to OA. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2753

461.q: Which of the following drugs target TNF ?
461.e: Etanercept is an Anti TNFα agent used in the management of RA. TNFα agents used in the management of RA includes: Monoclonal antibodies: Infliximab, Adalimumab, Golumumab and Certrolizumab pegol Etanercept is a soluble fusion protein comprising of TNFα receptor 2 in covalent linkage with Fc portion of IgG. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2761

461.q: Which drugs are unsafe and unequivocally contraindicated during pregnancy in a RA patient? 1. HCQ 2. Methotrexate 3. Sulfasalazine 4. Leflunomide 5. TNF alpha inhibitors 6. Glucocorticoids Choose the correct combinations of unsafe drugs?
461.e: Flares during pregnancy are generally treated with low doses of prednisone; hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are probably the safest DMARDs to use during pregnancy. Methotrexate and leflunomide therapy are contraindicated during pregnancy due to their teratogenicity in animals and humans. Biologicals are thought to be safe in the second trimester. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, Ch:358, Pg:2765

461.q: A 5 year old boy presents with history of fever of 1 week duration, along with bilateral cervical adenopathy, bilateral conjunctival congestion, erythema of the oral cavity and desquamation, especially of the finger tips. He has evidence of myocarditis too. He has an ESR of 100mm/1st hour, elevated CRP, and elevated liver enzymes. Which infection will you suspect?
461.e: This patient presents with a multi system involvement. The salient features are involvement of mucosa and desquamation of the skin especially the finger tips. He also has myocarditis. This fits into the picture of Kawazaki Disease. An infection which presents with clinical features resembling Kawazaki Disease is MIS-C, caused by COVID 19. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2816

461.q: A 65-year-old male attends a clinic complaining of breathlessness and persistent fatigue. He has end stage cardiac failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy. Currently he takes Furosemide, Lisinopril, Spironolactone and Carvedilol. Which one of the following drugs should be added to his current therapy?
461.e: Digoxin has a positive inotropic effect; it can be used in patients with heart failure who are in sinus rhythm but presenting with severe symptoms with no response to guideline mediated medical therapy including an ACE inhibitor, diuretic and beta blocker. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic window, hence should be used cautiously to avoid the risk of serious adverse effects including arrhythmias. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1946

461.q: Which of the following is not true regarding dilated cardiomyopathy?
o: Functional mitral regurgitation may be seen
Ejection fraction is usually preserved till later stages
Left sided failure occurs earlier than right sided heart failure
461.e: Dilated cardiomyopathy Ejection fraction is usually significantly reduced ( Left ventricular wall thickness is reduced with increase in LV diastolic dimension Mitral regurgitation is commonly seen due to annular and atrial dilatation Left sided symptoms are predominantly present unlike restrictive cardiomyopathy which presents with right predominant disease Most common cause is ischemic followed by infectious, toxin related, inflammatory and endocrine diseases related. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21 st edition, pg:1955

461.q: Which of the following is the most common infective cause of cardiomyopathy?
461.e: Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by reduviid bug is the most common infectious cause of cardiomyopathy. Typical features include conduction system abnormalities commonly AV blocks Parvovirus B19, Coxsackie and Echoviruses are the most common infectious causes of myocarditis Bacterial causes of myocarditis include legionella, salmonella, Corynebacterium diphtheria etc Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1972

461.q: A 55-year-old man with a longstanding history of alcohol excess has had a progressive abdominal distension for several months.On physical examination he has a non-tender abdomen with no masses palpable, but there is a fluid thrill. An abdominal ultrasound scan shows a large abdominal fluid collection with a small cirrhotic liver. A chest x ray shows increased cardiothoracic ratio with bilateral pleural effusion. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be present?
461.e: Alcohol when consumed in significant amounts for 5-10 years is a risk factor for development of alcohol induced cardiomyopathy which presents with features of dilated cardiomyopathy. Toxicity is attributable to acetaldehyde, the primary metabolite of ethanol. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 259, Pg: 1959

462.q: A 52-year-old patient who has had chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer 6 months earlier comes to the clinic complaining of shortness of breath on exertion. Her BP is 125/78 mmHg, her pulse is 94/min and her apex beat is displaced to the anterior axillary line. CXR - Cardiomegaly, increased shadowing consistent with mild pulmonary oedema at both bases Which chemotherapeutic agent is most likely to be responsible for this patient's symptoms?
462.e: Doxorubicin can be associated with cardiac failure, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and tachyarrhythmias. Platinum based chemotherapies are associated with peripheral neuropathy, and bleomycin with interstitial pneumonitis and a specific skin lesion called 'flagellate dermatitis'. Drugs causing dilated cardiomyopathy Doxorubicin (Adriamycin) Trastuzumab (Herceptin) Tacrolimus Zidovudine Drugs like NSAIDs, Thiazolidinediones can cause fluid retention and thus worsen heart failure in patients with underlying disease. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 737,1964

462.q: A 52-year-old man suffers an extensive anterior myocardial infarction but recovers well in hospital. His pre-discharge ECHO shows him to have an ejection fraction 35%. He is otherwise asymptomatic. His medications on discharge should include which of the following?
o: Aspirin, metoprolol, ramipril and a statin
Aspirin, atenolol, ramipril, furosemide and a statin
Aspirin, isosorbide mononitrate, ramipril and a statin
Aspirin, nitrate, losartan and a statin
462.e: Following a myocardial infarction, patients with LV dysfunction benefit from taking β-Blockers and RAAS blockers. There is strong evidence supporting the use of aspirin and a statin post-MI. In the absence of anginal pain, prophylactic use of nitrates is not mandatory. Diuretics is indicated for patients with symptomatic heart failure and those with fluid overload. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2048-50

462.q: Kussmaul's sign is classically described in:
462.e: Answer is C (Constrictive pericarditis) Kussmaul's sign is classically described in association with Constrictive Pericarditis. Kussmaul's sign refers to paradoxical elevation of JVP/CVP during inspiration (In healthy persons venous pressure falls during inspiration because pressures in the right heart decrease as intrathoracic pressures fall) The Kussmaul's sign is classically described in association with Constrictive pericarditis. Kussmaul's sign is however also seen in association with Right Ventricular Infarction, Restrictive Cardiomyopathy, Pulmonary Embolism and Advanced Systolic Severe Heart Failure

462.q: A 54-year-old obese woman presents to the casualty department with worsening dyspnoea and ankle swelling due to NYHA 3 heart failure. Her renal functions are within normal limits and her potassium is 4.4 mmol/l. Which of the following combinations of drugs is best suited for her in terms of mortality benefit?
462.e: Diuretics are useful in patients with heart failure and features of fluid overload though they don't confer mortality benefit. Beta blockers shown to have mortality benefit include carvedilol, metoprolol, bisoprolol. While administering ACE inhibitor and spironolactone, we need to be cautious about the risk of hyperkalemia. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1945-47

462.q: A 50 year old man with a history of hypertension was investigated for renal impairment. Renal angiography confirms renal artery stenosis. Which one of the following features is an indication for stenting in renal artery stenosis?
462.e: Revascularization is considered when: Progressive decline in GFR during treatment of systemic hypertension Failure to achieve adequate blood pressure control with optimal medical therapy(medical failure) Rapid or recurrent decline in the GFR in association with a reduction in systemic pressure Decline in the GFR during therapy with ACE inhibitors or ARBs Recurrent congestive heart failure in a patient in whom the adequacy of left ventricular function does not explain a cause Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:278, Pg: 2090.

462.q: A 65-year-old man with a known history of hypertension presents with ankle oedema after taking an antihypertensive prescribed by his General Practitioner. He is now found to have a Blood Pressure of 160/100 mmHg. Which of the following would be the preferred drug for this patient?
462.e: The patient has ankle oedema which is usually due to vasodilatation by calcium channel blockers . The preferred initial antihypertensive therapy for the elderly patient will be hydrochlorthiazide . ACE inhibitors are preferred for those patients with heart failure or diabetic nephropathy. β-blockers are preferred for post-myocardial infarction and ischemic heart disease. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:271 pg:1901,1903

462.q: A 42 year old man is referred to the renal physician due to symptoms of haemoptysis and haematuria. These symptoms have been going on for 6 months. Investigations show: Sodium 135 mmol/l Potassium 4.6 mmol/l Urea 108 mg/dl Creatinine 3.6 mg/dl. The likely disease is caused by an antibody against which of the following?
462.e: The patient has pulmonary renal syndrome, and among the given options, the diagnosis would fit Wegener's granulomatosis, which is commonly cANCA positive. In patients with vasculitis, approximately 90 percent of cytoplasmic ANCA are PR3-ANCA and approximately 90 percent of perinuclear ANCA are MPO-ANCA. Option A: Anti smooth muscle antibody is seen in autoimmune hepatitis Option B: Anti dsDNA antibody is a specific antibody of systemic lupus erythematosus Option D: Anti Mi-2 antibodies are found in patients of dermatomyositis Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2340.

462.q: A 63 year old man is on treatment for chronic heart failure with diuretics. He has previous history of athma. He presents with sudden onset of pain and swelling of the metatarso-phalangeal joint of his right big toe. Aspiration of the joint demonstrates crystals of monosodium urate. What is the recommended treatment?
462.e: In this particular patient, colchicine is the best option. In acute gout, either colchicine or NSAIDs can be used. However, asthma contraindicates NSAIDs. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 372, Pg: 2865

463.q: A 24-year-old woman collapsed in a New York City subway station. An autopsy showed that a blood clot had travelled to her lung and caused her death. The medical examiner ultimately ruled that the blood clot was caused by the use of a birth control patch. Which of the following occurs if the blood flow to an alveolus is totally obstructed by a pulmonary thromboembolism?
o: The V/Q ratio of the alveolus equals zero
The PO2 of the alveolus will be equal to that in the inspired air
The PO2 of the alveolus will be equal to the mixed venous PO2
There will be an increase in shunting (venous admixture) in the lung
463.e: A pulmonary thromboembolism results in areas of the lung that are ventilated, but not perfused, yielding V/Q ratios of infinity and an increase in alveolar deadspace. When the V/Q ratio equals infinite, the PAO2 of the affected alveoli will be the same as that in the humidified inspired air because atmospheric air enters the alveoli via the process of ventilation but no gas exchange takes place because the alveoli are not perfused. Areas of the lung that are perfused but not ventilated constitute areas of shunting (venous admixture), characterized as a V/Q ratio equal to 0, and having PAO2 values that equilibrate with the mixed venous blood. Reference: Kasper et al., pp 282, 1561. Levitzky, pp 114-117. Stead, pp 272-273.

463.q: Causes of a small pupil include which of the following?
463.e: Causes of small pupils include: Horner's syndrome Old age Pontine haemorrhage Argyll Robertson pupil Drugs and poisons (opiates, organophosphates). Causes of dilated pupils include: Holmes-Adie (myotonic) pupil Third nerve palsy Drugs and poisons (atropine, cobalt [CO], ethylene glycol). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 216

463.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a small amount of haemoptysis and breathlessness. He does not have pleuritic chest pain and has normal oxygen saturation. In considering the potential diagnosis, haemoptysis can occur with which of the following diagnoses?
463.e: Haemoptysis can be caused by pulmonary embolism, tuberculous infection, aspergilloma, bronchial carcinoma, good pasture's syndrome and Wegener's granulomatosis. Interstitial lung disease presents with dry cough along with progressive dyspnoea. Asthma presents with episodic breathlessness and cough in exposure to cold or allergens. Goitre presents as neck swelling; if large, it may compress the trachea causing stridor and breathlessness; retrosternal extension causes venous congestion due to compression of superior vena cava. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 39, Pg:270-272

463.q: A 34-year-old woman presented with a dry cough, thorax constriction, and generalised weakness. During the preceding 5 months, she had experienced these dry cough episodes twice a week. A lung function test showed a restriction of the vital capacity (71% of the adjusted reference value), and the diffusion capacity was also reduced (66 to 68%). Broncho alveolar lavage specimens were obtained, the lymphocytes were increased up to 41% (norm, <10%), and neutrophils were increased up to 6% (norm, <2%) with a normal total cell count. What is the likely diagnosis?
463.e: Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis is type IV hypersensitivity. There is no eosinophilia, IgG and lymphocytes are involved in immune response. Antigens of micropolyspora faeni and thermoactinomyces are 0.5-5 microns. Assaying for IgG antibodies against specific antigens, either through precipitin testing or direct serum measurement, can be a useful adjunct in the diagnosis of HP High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) is a common component in the diagnostic workup; In subacute forms of the disease, ground-glass airspace opacities are characteristic, as is the presence of centrilobular nodules. Expiratory images may show areas of air trapping that are likely caused by involvement of the small airways BAL shows a lymphocytic predominance with a greater proportion of CD8 positive T cells . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 288, Pg: 2161

463.q: You are called to a cardiac arrest in the Emergency Department where a patient who is known to the dialysis unit has been brought by ambulance. On reviewing her drugs, you note that she is taking a statin, three antihypertensive agents, aspirin and has been receiving erythropoietin injections. Unfortunately, resuscitation is unsuccessful. Which of the following is the commonest cause of death in renal dialysis patients?
463.e: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with CKD at all the stages. Hypertension and dyslipidemia are the risk factors that accelerate atherosclerosis in CKD. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:311, Pg:2315

463.q: A 26 year old woman has symptoms of lethargy, bloody diarrhoea and a previous history of DVT in the leg. On examination, the left eye was inflamed and multiple mouth ulcers were noted. Colonoscopy was organized and this confirmed colitis. She also has vulval ulcers. What is the likely diagnosis?
463.e: Recurrent oral ulceration is the commonest manifestation and the presenting feature in Behcet's disease. Diagnosis of Behcet’s disease requires - Recurrent oral ulcers plus two of the following four clinical manifestations: Recurrent genital ulcers – cause scarring Skin lesions - Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopastular or acneiform nodules Eye lesions - Anterior or posterior uveitis, corneal ulceration, conjunctivitis, papillitis, Positive pathergy test Vasculitis, pustules and subcutaneous nodules can also occur. Vascular thrombosis occurs in about 10% of patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 364, Pg: 2818

463.q: A 44-year-old man presents with a week history of a painful right leg. He has had previous episodes of erythema nodosum, recurrent oral and scrotal ulceration. Examination reveals a diffusely swollen left leg.What is the likely cause of his swollen leg?
463.e: The overall diagnosis is Behcet's syndrome. There is a thrombotic tendency (venous>>arterial), hence the likely cause of a DVT. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:364 Pg:2817

463.q: Which of the following associations is matched correctly?
o: Pulmonary embolism and left bundle branch block
463.e: Pneumoconiosis is not associated with clubbing. Pulmonary embolism causes right heart strain and may present with RBBB Rv strain and Ischemia in ECG. Lung Carcinoids are rarely associated with pleural effusion. Bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is associated with wheezing. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: Ch: 288, Pg: 2165

464.q: Kluver bucy syndrome is due to the lesion in which of the following structure
464.e: Kluver-Bucy Syndrome Occurs due to Bilateral Ablation of the Amygdala Characterized by, Not able to recognize objects by sight - Visual agnosia Tendency to examine objects excessively by mouth Hyperorality Compulsion to intensively explore the immediate environment - Hypermetamorphosis No longer show fear or anger, even when such a reaction is appropriate - Placidity Eat excessively even when not hungry, or may eat objects that are not food - Hyperphagia Augmentation in sexual behavior - Hypersexuality Reference: Guyton, 13th edition page no.760

464.q: A 74-year-old man developed ataxia, then exhibited incontinence, frequent confusion, and difficulty with memory. Neurologic examination shows a bradykinetic, broad-based, magnetic gait, prominent memory loss, and decreased executive functioning. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
464.e: This patient has normal pressure hydrocephalus (PH), which is a clinical syndrome produced by the build-up of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Patients have enlarged ventricles often with normal opening pressures on lumbar puncture. It is characterized by the classic triad (with the accompanying mnemonic): "Wet": urinary incontinence "Wacky": dementia (memory loss, slowed thought) "Wobbly" gait abnormality (apraxic "magnetic" gait) PH is thought to be caused by impaired CSF absorption by arachnoid granulations. It is idiopathic in half of the cases. Secondary causes include meningitis, brain trauma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or prior brain surgery. The treatment for NPH is ventricular shunting. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt drains excess CSF to the abdomen, where it is absorbed. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 503-504

464.q: Unable to consolidate long term memory. Which lobe of the brain is involved
464.e: Answer- C. Parietal Medial temporal lobe is the area of brain responsible for consolidation, i.e. processing of short term memory into long term memory. 1043. Gerstmanns syndrome all except a) Acalculia b) Agraphia c) Aphasia d) Agnosia Correct Answer - C Answer- C. Aphasia Gerstmann syndrome consists of :

464.q: A 69-year-old male presents with cognitive impairment and a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease is suspected. What is the most appropriate test of short term memory?
o: Knowledge of the capital of the India
Recall of the doctor's name at the end of the consultation
464.e: Short term memory impairment is the commonest clinical presentation of Alzheimer's disease. Usually patients are fully orientated in time, person and place. Long term memory is usually intact. The best way to test short term memory is to ask the patient to recall new information in the next few minutes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 29, Pg: 192

464.q: Imaging changes in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) start initially in which parts of the brain?
464.e: Damage to the hippocampus and parahippocampus results in memory problems and has early involvement in Alzheimer's disease. Entorhinal cortex is also involved The corpus callosum can be involved in multiple sclerosis where so-called Dawson's fingers can be seen. Posterior parietal lobe is involved in DLB Cortical ribboning and basal ganglia and thalamus hyperintensity is seen in CJD Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 29, Pg: 192

464.q: A 64 year old man has had a 6 month history of progressive worsening of confusion. He had left the cooker on several times and accused the neighbours of spying on him. On examination, his face is expressionless and he has a monotonous speech. Cranial nerve are normal. Increased tone is present in all 4 limbs. Reflexes, power and sensation are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
464.e: This patient has parkinsonism, with bradykinesia and rigidity. In view of the deterioration in mental function and delusion, Lewy body dementia is more likely than Parkinson's disease. In Parkinson's disease dementia occurs in long standing disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 434 Pg: 3385

464.q: A 60-year-old woman experiences a gradual loss of language abilities. She struggles to find the right words, has difficulty understanding spoken language, and exhibits reduced vocabulary. The relatives also notice changes in personality, socially inappropriate behavior. She also exhibits changes in personality, loss of empathy, and increased preference for sweet foods. Neurological examination shows no significant motor deficits. What is she most likely suffering from?
464.e: This patient is definitely suffering from a dementing disease. The chief domains affected are language, social skills and hyperorality. These are the characteristic features of Frontotemporal dementia. Other features that may be seen include, symptoms of MND and dystonia. PD presents with memory loss only later after the progression of motor symptoms. In DLB, the chief domain affected are visuospatial skills and psychiatric manifestations like visual hallucination. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 432, Pg: 3378

o: Flexion of arm & extension of lower limb
464.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., More dangerous than decerebrate lesion Decortical Posture o Also known as flexor posturing or Mummy baby o Arms flexed/bent over chest, hand fisted, leg extended & rotated inward o Damage to area in cerebral hemisphere, internal capsule, thalamus & upper part of brain. o Decorticate posture is ominous sign of severe brain damage. Decerebrate posture o Also known as extensor posturing o Extension of upper limb & lower limb (ELBOW EXTENDED) o Indicates brain stem damage (Below level of red nucleus) o Decerebrate posture is more ominous than decortical posture

465.q: A 58-year-old woman with epilepsy refractory to medical therapy is hospitalised for deep brain stimulation. This new modality uses a pacemaker-like device to stimulate which of the following structures?
465.e: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) therapy uses a pacemaker-like device to deliver targeted electrical stimulation to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. The therapy is FDA-approved with conditions for adjunctive treatment for partial-onset seizures in adults with medically refractory epilepsy. DBS is also FDA-approved for treatment of advanced Parkinson disease and essential tremor. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number. 417

465.q: A 26-year-old woman with lifelong epilepsy controlled with medication has just found out that she is pregnant. She has seizures once a month but seem to be controlled at present. Which of the following statements about epilepsy in pregnancy is true?
o: Valproate is considered a drug of choice
She should be taking high doses of folic acid
She will likely have no change in seizure activity during pregnancy
465.e: Women with epilepsy are often very concerned about pregnancy and what effect the medications might have on fetal development. Planning is the most important component. All women considering pregnancy should be on high doses of folic acid prior to conception. Valproate and barbiturates should be avoided. Those women already on valproate and barbiturates should be switched to other drugs before pregnancy when possible. When seizures are controlled, maintenance medication may be reduced, if possible, to the lowest dose that provides control. If seizures are not controlled, medications and dosages will need to be adjusted prior to pregnancy, if possible. The frequency and severity of seizures may change during pregnancy. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Page number 430

465.q: A 66-year-old man presents with seizures. Past medical history includes a smoking history of 30 cigarettes a day for many years. His family report a weight loss over the past 8 months.Serum electrolytes show: Sodium 109 mmol/L (135-145) Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0) Glucose 126 mg/dL Urea 3.0 mmol/L (3.2-8.1) Urine sodium : 68 mmol/ L These findings are most likely to be due to:
465.e: The biochemistry points to a syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, with a low serum osmolality [2(Na + K) + urea + glucose]. The clinical picture is consistent with small cell carcinoma of the lung, which is often associated with SIADH. SIADH should be diagnosed only after ruling out hypothyroidism and cortisol deficiency. Diuretic use associated hyponatremia could be associated with low normal serum potassium. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2924

465.q: True with respect to the tumour lysis syndrome (TLS):
o: High-dose intravenous steroid therapy is a reasonable initial treatment option.
TLS is most commonly associated with squamous cell and neuroendocrine tumours.
Clinical TLS can be diagnosed in a patient with seizures and the presence of appropriate laboratory findings.
An increase in serum calcium and potassium levels by >25% is the hallmark feature of laboratory TLS.
465.e: Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is a potentially life-threatening complication of massive cellular lysis in cancer, often encountered in bulky, rapidly progressive or chemo-sensitive tumours. It is most commonly seen in haematological malignancy. Hypocalcaemia is a hallmark feature due to precipitation of ionised calcium with phosphate, which is released in large quantities in tumour lysis. Other laboratory features of TLS include: increase in serum uric acid by >25% from baseline; increase in serum potassium by >25% from baseline; increase in serum phosphate by >25% from baseline. Intravenous hydration and rasburicase are first-line treatments and prophylaxis agents in high-risk groups. Reference: Harrison 20 th 2103,3001

465.q: Woman with morning stiffness which gradually resolves over one hour. Which is correct about the treatment and findings? a. NSAIDS improve symptoms and have disease modifying activity b. Absence of erosion on x-ray rules out diagnosis c. Raised ESR and CRP d. HLA DR4 is related to prognosis
465.e: The question deals with RA. NSAIDS are not disease modifying agents. They are analgesic and anti-inflammatory. ESR and CRP may be raised in RA. RA has a strong HLA association to DR locus. RA classically causes erosive arthritis. But plain X ray may not be always showing erosions. It can be viewed using MRI or ultrasound.

465.q: Seizures are seen in what percentage of RTA patients with brain contusion/loss of consciousness?
o: No relation between trauma and seizures
465.e: Explanation: Post-traumatic seizures occur in approximately 17% of patients with brain contusion, subdural hematoma, or prolonged loss of consciousness. Convulsions are uncommon immediately after traumatic brain injury, though brief tonic extensor posturing or clonic movements may occur at impact. Penetrating injuries carry a particularly high risk of subsequent epilepsy development.

465.q: Which of the following features are not compatible with the diagnosis of motor neurone disease (MND)?
465.e: Optic atrophy is not a feature of MND. Other features not compatible with the diagnosis are sensory impairment and bladder and bowel dysfunction. Muscle cramps occurring with volitional activities especially in early morning hours can be seen in very early disease. Even though there is severe brain stem dysfunction, Ocular motility will also be spared in MND till late stages ALS especially familial ALS is associated with behavioural dysfunction suggesting a frontal lobe dysfunction. Cognitive changes don't occur in MND. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3411-3412

465.q: A 63 year woman with a long history of alcohol abuse has been on Phenytoin for epilepsy. On examination, she has a palpable a liver edge. Her full blood count reveals: Hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL MCV 116 fL white blood count 2.3 x 10^9/L platelet count 95 x 10^9/L What is the likely explanation for these results?
465.e: This patient presents with a clinical picture consistent with megaloblastic anemia . Megaloblastic anemia is either due to Folic acid or Vitamin B12 deficiency. Given her history of heavy alcohol intake and phenytoin usage, folate deficiency is the most likely cause. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch: 99, Pg: 773

466.q: A patient with parkinsonism is being treated with levodopa. He suffers from irregular, involuntary muscle jerks that affect the proximal muscles of the limbs. Which of the following statements about these symptoms is most accurate?
o: Coadministration of muscarinic blockers prevents the occurrence of dyskinesias during treatment with levodopa
Drugs that activate dopamine receptors can exacerbate dyskinesias in a patient taking levodopa
Dyskinesias are less likely to occur if levodopa is administered with carbidopa
The symptoms are usually reduced if the dose of levodopa is increased
466.e: The form and severity of dyskinesias resulting from levodopa may vary widely in individual patients. Dyskinesias occur in up to 80% of patients receiving levodopa for long periods. With continued treatment, dyskinesias may develop at a dose of levodopa that was previously well tolerated. Muscarinic receptor blockers do not prevent their occurrence. They occur more commonly in patients treated with levodopa in combination with carbidopa or with other dopamine receptor agonists. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 506-508

466.q: Extrapyramidal syndrome like side effects are seen in -
466.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Haloperidol Drugs causing extrapvramidal effects o Butyrophenones (Haloperidol) o Methyldopa o OCP'S o Reserpine o Levodopa o Metoclopromide o Phenothiazines o Tricyclic Antidepressants

466.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with slowed mentation, lack of coordination, and brief writhing movements of her hands that are not rhythmic with delusions. Her mother has had similar symptoms. Genetic testing shows mutation on chromosome 4. It is very likely that the most appropriate drug for treatment will be
466.e: Although further diagnosis is desirable, choreo-athetosis with decreased mental abilities and psychosis (paranoia) suggests that this patient has the symptoms of Huntington’s disease. Drugs that are partly ameliorative include agents that deplete dopamine (eg, tetrabenazine) or that block dopamine receptors (eg, haloperidol). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 509-511

466.q: A 53-year-old woman is started on a medication for early symptoms of Parkinson disease one week ago. Vital signs show blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg when supine and 90/60 mm Hg upon standing. Examination of the lower extremities shows a lacy, purple rash and 2+ pitting edema. The patient is most likely experiencing adverse effects caused by which of the following drug?
466.e: This patient shows signs of amantadine toxicity, including orthostatic hypotension, livedo reticularis and peripheral edema. Amantadine can be used as initial short-term monotherapy in patients with mild symptoms of Parkinson disease, mainly for those with prominent tremor. In addition to the side effects seen in this patient, amantadine is associated with anticholinergic-like side effects (e.g., dry mouth, constipation), prolonged QT interval, and psychological disorders (e.g., hallucinations, anxiety). Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition by Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 500-508,512

466.q: A 72 years old woman complaints that sometimes she sees a dog in her kitchen and at other times she sees a snake in her garden, both of which no one else can see. She has Parkinson disease and is on treatment. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
466.e: Levodopa (L-DOPA), a dopamine precursor, is the most effective medication for controlling the motor symptoms of Parkinson disease. Primary effects of L-DOPA are achieved by stimulating D2-receptors in the substantia nigra and striatum. However, overstimulation of D2-receptors by levodopa may also induce psychosis and hallucinations (usually visual). The risk for developing psychiatric symptoms increases with age, other psychiatric conditions, long duration of levodopa treatment, and high doses. Since this patient has been taking levodopa for 3 years and is elderly, her symptoms are most likely the result of levodopa therapy. Other adverse effects of L-DOPA therapy include dizziness, somnolence or insomnia, anxiety, and aggressive behavior. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 513

466.q: A 72-year-old man complains that he has had increased tremor and bradykinesia. He has started on levodopa, regarding side effects of the drug, the patient need not be informed that
o: He may feel dizziness, especially when in supine
He should take the drug in divided doses to avoid nausea
His symptoms will probably improve for a period of time but not indefinitely
He may feel uncontrollable muscle jerks.
466.e: In prescribing levodopa, the patient should be informed about adverse effects, including gastrointestinal distress, postural hypotension (dizziness while standing), and dyskinesias. It is reasonable to advise the patient that therapeutic benefits cannot be expected to continue indefinitely. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 502-503

466.q: A 51-year-old patient with parkinsonism is being maintained on levodopa-carbidopa with adjunctive use of low doses of tolcapone but continues to have off-periods of akinesia. A drug used to "rescue" the patient that provides temporary relief is
466.e: Apomorphine, via subcutaneous injection, is used for temporary relief of off-periods of akinesia (rescue) in parkinsonian patients on dopaminergic drug therapy. Pretreatment with the antiemetic trimethobenzamide for 3 days is essential to prevent severe nausea. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 503-504

466.q: A 77-year-old patient with Parkinsonism is being maintained on levodopa-carbidopa but continues to have off-periods of akinesia. A subcutaneous injection is used to "rescue"the patient that provides temporary relief. With which of the following drug you will pretreat to prevent nausea?
466.e: Apomorphine, via subcutaneous injection, is used for temporary relief of off-periods of akinesia (rescue) in parkinsonian patients on dopaminergic drug therapy. Pretreatment with the antiemetic trimethobenzamide for 3 days is essential to prevent severe nausea. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 503-504

467.q: All of the following drugs worsen myasthenia gravis except:
467.e: Drugs that may exacerbate myasthenia gravis and potentiate the action of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants are: Antibiotics Aminoglycosides e.g Streptomycin Tetracyclines Quinolones e.g ciprofloxacin Macrolides e.g erythromycin Non-depolarizing muscle relaxants e.g d-Tubocurarine Beta-blockers like propranolol, atenolol, metoprolol Local anaesthetics Botulinum toxin Quinine derivatives like quinine, quinidine, chloroquine, mefloquine Magnesium Penicillamine

467.q: A 50 year old patient has a 2 year history of weight loss and diarrhea. He also gives a history of episodes of flushing. VIP syndrome is considered by the admitting physician. Which one of the following is a feature of VIPoma syndrome?
o: Induction of VIP release by somatostatin
467.e: VIPomas [vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) originate in amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation (APUD) cells of the gastroenteropancreatic endocrine system and in adrenal or extra-adrenal neurogenic sites. Features of VIP syndrome include watery diarrhea (100%), hypochlorhydria (70% in adults), hyperglycemia (20-50% in adults), hypercalcemia (20-50% in adults), flushing (20% in adults) and hypokalemia due to diarrhea. Initial treatment is directed toward correcting volume and electrolyte abnormalities by using potassium chloride and sodium bicarbonate. Octreotide controls diarrhea in 80% of cases. Glucocorticoids reduce symptoms in 50% of patients with VIPoma. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 84 Pg: 665

467.q: A 56-year-old man presents with a history of abdominal discomfort that is relieved by passing stool. In the past month his stools have been looser in nature and he has had a feeling of urgency and incomplete evacuation. His symptoms seem to be worse with eating. He has also noticed that he has passed mucus per rectum. He is overweight with a BMI of 28 kg/m2. His weight has fallen. He says that he has adjusted his diet in the last six months. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
467.e: Weight loss, tenesmus and a recent change in bowel habit all point towards an underlying diagnosis of colorectal cancer. Onset of symptoms in later life and a relatively short duration (that is, weeks rather than years) also point towards a 'biological' cause rather than irritable bowel syndrome. The passage of mucus per rectum is a normal physiological function and not indicative of underlying pathology. The symptoms are not suggestive of malabsorption. Diverticulitis and inflammatory bowel disease are both potential diagnoses but given the duration of symptoms less likely than a colonic neoplasm. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, CH: 81, Pg: 639

467.q: A 36 year old woman presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhoea and mouth ulcers. Full blood count reveals normocytic normochromic anaemia, inflammatory markers are raised, and biochemical investigation reveals a raised alkaline phosphatase. Barium follow through shows terminal ileal inflammatory disease. Long term remission may be maintained by the use of which of the following drugs?
467.e: This is a case of Crohn’s disease . Remission of Crohn's disease may be achieved by the use of steroids, elemental diet, surgery or infliximab. Mesalazine may maintain remission if induction has been achieved by surgery and if an 8-week course of metronidazole is administered. It has many side effects. In other scenarios, the most useful drug to maintain long term remission is azathioprine . Steroids (prednisolone) are only used for induction of remission. They are not appropriate for long term maintenance therapy. Cyclosporine is used in severe cases of ulcerative colitis refractory to steroid therapy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg: 2488

467.q: An 18-year-old student presents with a 15 week history of diarrhea. He has lost 2 kg in weight, and has no recent travel abroad.A smear of a duodenal biopsy reveals many trophozoites.What is the best treatment option?
467.e: The diagnosis here is giardiasis, caused by Giardia lamblia. Giardia has been reported as a cause of chronic diarrhea.Most patients respond to oral metronidazole 250-400 mg three times daily for five days. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 229, Pg: 1765

467.q: Which of the following describes the best prescription for active RA in a 45 year old healthy female without any contraindications?
467.e: The current recommendations are early aggressive therapy to reduce joint deformity using combination therapy. Methotrexate is the cornerstone in treatment of RA and combination therapy should be built with Methotrexate as the base. The accepted combinations include Methotrexate plus HCQ plus Sulfasalazine Methotrexate with biologicals Methotrexate with Leflunomide Combination therapy involves starting the treatment with Methotrexate and to rapidly step up to the desired combination in 3-6 months. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2761-2764

467.q: Which of the following statements is false?
o: Hematological abnormalities may not be seen in approximately 40% of patients with Sub acute combined degeneration due to cobalamine deficinecy.
In patients with food cobalamine malabsorption, oral cobalamine is sufficient to correct the deficiency.
Treatment of cobalamine deficiency will completely reverse the neurological manifestations.
Methylmalanoic acid and Homocysteine levels may be elevated in Cobalamine deficiency.
467.e: This question deals with the clinical features of Cobalamine deficncy. Haematological abnormalities like macrocytic anemia will not be seen in 40% of patients with Subacute combined degeneration. In cobalamine deficiency, there will be blocade of steps that require cobalamine as cofactor and hence homocysteine and methyl manioc acid will be accumulated. In patients with pernicious anemia, the management is parenteral cyanocobalamine. But in food cobalamine malabsorption, the patients can absorb free cobalamine and hence oral supplementation is enough, at the dose of 1000mcg/day. The haematological abnormalities completely respond to cobalamine replacement. But the neurologoical manifestations tend to be permanent in about 50% patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch:446, Pg: 3496

467.q: A 26 year old bartender has had abdominal pains and loose stools for 3 years. He also has symptoms of myalgia and profound fatigue. He mentions that the abdominal pains are often worse after he has bread. An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay test was conducted and it showed positive reactions to gluten, albumin, lactose, barley, and rye. Which of the following is not found in the disease?
467.e: This is a case of celiac disease . The following antibodies are found- Antibodies against tissue transglutaminase IgA Antiendomysial antibodies Deamidated anti-gliadin antibodies. Serum IgA levels are measured to detect false-negative results from IgA deficiency. Deamidated anti-gliadin IgG antibodies or tissue transglutaminase IgG antibodies are detectable and diagnostic in IgA-deficient patients. Small intestinal biopsy is the confirmatory test . Biopsies typically show characteristic villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and inflammation, including increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 318, Pg: 2251 - 2253

468.q: A 22 year old female patient presents with a 5-day history of ascending muscle weakness in both hands and feet. EMGs confirm acute demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy. What treatment should be started?
468.e: The diagnosis is Guillain Barre syndrome . It is preceded by diarrhea (e.g. campylobacter) or chest infections (e.g. mycoplasma) in two thirds of cases. Autonomic dysfunction and hyporeflexia are associated. P rogressive symmetric ascending weakness is characteristic . Management: Plasma exchange (OR) IVIG (IV immunoglobulins) - 2 g/kg/day for 5 days. As effective as plasma exchange. Easier to administer and fewer side effects. No benefit in combining both treatments. Steroids and immunosuppressants have not been shown to be beneficial. Regular FVC (Forced vital capacity ) to monitor respiratory function and assess need for ventilation. ICU admission is recommended when FVC is less than 20 mL/kg and intubation is recommended in most cases when FVC is less than 15 mL/kg . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 ST Ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3503

468.q: Which type ofAmyloidosis is caused by mutation of the transthyretin protein ?
468.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy Transthyretin (TTR) is normal serum protein that binds and transport thyroxine and retinol. TTR can cause following types of amyloidosis :? Mutant TTR : - Mutation in TTR can cause syndrome of familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy or familial amylodotic cardiomyopathy. Wild (non-mutant) TTR : - There is no mutation of TTR and wild type TTR forms fibrils which results in senile systemic amyloidosis (senile cardiac amyloidosis).

468.q: The basic abnormality in increased fasting blood glucose is:
468.e: The basic abnormality in increased fasting glucose is high hepatic glucose output mainly due to reduced basal secretion of insulin or hepatic insulin resistance Raised post-prandial glucose values is due to decreased peripheral utilization (muscle and adipose tissue) First and second phase insulin secretion occurs in response to meals Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 3096-3099

468.q: Which of the following is not an FDA approved drug for Diabetic peripheral neuropathy?
468.e: Though tricyclic antidepressants like amitriptyline are commonly employed for managing positive symptoms of diabetic neuropathy, they are not FDA approved Tapentadol is a central acting opioid analog with lesser evidence which is FDA approved Capsaicin patch has also been approved by FDA which works by interfering with the function of TRPV1 Venlafaxine, Oxcarbexapine, tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentin etc are others useful in the symptomatic treatment of neuropathy Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 3124

468.q: Which of the following clinical manifestations suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS)?
o: Bulbar involvement in about 50% of cases
468.e: GBS is associated with bulbar involvement occurs in 50%, with a risk of aspiration and respiratory insufficiency. In GBS, Symmetric involvement is typical. Asymmetrical involvement is present in only 9% of patients. CSF protein is elevated to more than twice the upper limit of normal, with normal glucose and no pleocytosis. Areflexia is commonly present. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3501

468.q: A 57-year-old female is admitted with progressive weakness following a trivial flu-like illness. Which of the following would exclude Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) as the diagnosis?
468.e: A sensory level is not a feature of GBS and would suggest cervical myelopathy. Guillian Barre Syndrome (GBS) is a post-infectious acute polyneuritis typified by elevated CSF protein with few cells and often normal glucose. There is a profound weakness associated with areflexia and peripheral sensory neuropathy. Ophthalmoplegia is associated in particular with the Miller-Fisher variant.
