Muscle wasting is typical with prolonged illness. Autonomic dysfunction can also occur. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3501

468.q: Guillain Barre Syndrome treatment consists of all except?
468.e: Steroids have no role in the treatment of GBS. Plasma exchange and I.V immunoglobulins are the mainstay treatment whereas ventilatory support may be needed during the course of GBS.

468.q: Predominantly sensory neuropathy is/are caused by:
468.e: Answer is A and B (Cisplatin and Pyridoxine excess): Cisplatin and Pyridoxine are associated with predominantly sensory neuropathies.

469.q: In multiple sclerosis slow conduction of sensory and motor pathway is due to
469.e: Autoimmune inflammation and demyelination of CNS (brain and spinal cord) with subsequent axonal damage. Most often affects females aged 20-40 Symptoms may exacerbate with increased body temperature (eg, hot bath, exercise). Relapsing and remitting is most common clinical course. ↑IgG level and myelin basic protein in CSF. Oligoclonal bands aid in diagnosis. MRI is gold standard. Periventricular plaques A (areas of oligodendrocyte loss and reactive gliosis). Multiple white matter lesions disseminated in space and time.

469.q: patient underwent adrenalectomy and developed pigmentation and fatigue diagnosis?
469.e: Removal of adrenal gland leads to Addison's disease. Deficiency of mainly 3 hormones Due to mineralocorticoid deficiency: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, small heart, nausea, vomiting Due to glucocorticoids deficiency: Hypoglycemia, fatigue, anorexia, skin pigmentation, weight loss, myalgia Due to adrenal androgen deficiency: Lack of energy, dry & itchy skin, loss of libido in women & loss of axillary & pubic hairs in women.

469.q: With regard to a patient with a neuromuscular disorder on the critical care unit which is true:
o: Potassium-sparing diuretics should be avoided in patients with hypokalemic periodic paralysis.
Rocuronium use should be avoided in patients with myasthenia gravis
Patients with motor neurone disease typically require double the standard dose of suxamethonium to provide optimum intubating conditions.
Local anesthesia can exacerbate symptoms of multiple sclerosis
469.e: The use of suxamethonium is challenging in patients with neuromuscular disorders. Key points to remember include relative resistance to depolarisation in myasthenia gravis, often requiring an increased dosage, and the development of extrajunctional receptors in many of the myotonias, leading to extensive depolarisation and potentially fatal hyperkalemia with the use of depolarising neuromuscular blockade. In addition, there are disease-specific aspects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade that should be noted,including the relative sensitivity in conditions such as Guillain-Barré syndrome. Hence dose reduction to 10-20% should be considered in addition to ongoing monitoring of blockade. Reference: Harrison 20 th 3188-3200

469.q: Chronic subdural haematoma in a 77-year-old man is not associated with the presence of which of the following?
469.e: Chronic subdural haematoma is classically associated with fluctuating conscious level and cognitive function. Bilateral papilloedema may occur with raised intracranial pressure. Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia is associated with multiple sclerosis and unilateral lesions of medial longitudinal fasciculus may occur with small brain stem infarcts. Unequal pupils are associated with rapid transtentorial coning in extradural haemorrhage leading to ipsilateral dilated pupil followed by bilateral fixed dilated pupils. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 443, Pg: 3457

469.q: A 47 year old man was referred for assessment of unsteady gait, which has been present for 6 months. He has lost a stone in weight over the several months. An MRI of the brain shows multiple high signal areas. A biopsy was taken of one of the lesions. The report shows perivascular infiltrates of lymphocytes affecting white and gray matter. There was minimal myelin loss. CSF examination shows raised white cell count, and oligoclonal bands were not raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
469.e: The white matter lesions suggest either multiple sclerosis or lymphoma. Infiltration with lymphocytes can be seen in Multiple Sclerosis too. In around 10% of patients with MS, OCB can be absent. However, the presence of constitutional symptoms makes the possibility of CNS lymphoma more likely. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine. 21 st Ed, Ch:90 Pg: 705

469.q: Raynaud's phenomenon what change is seen in vessels initial stage -
469.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., No change Structural changes in the arterial walls are absent except late in the course, when intimal thickening can appear.

469.q: A 59-year-old woman presents with poly-symptomatology. On examination she has prominent fasciculations. From which of the following conditions is she unlikely to suffer?
469.e: Fasciculation suggest lower motor neurone disease . It is seen usually in diseases affecting the anterior horn cells of spinal cord. It can also be seen in diseases of the nerve roots and peripheral nerves. However, it is absent in diseases of the muscles or neuromuscular junction. Cervical spondylosis is a disease which affects the spinal cord as well as the nerve roots. So it can cause fasciculations. Motor neurone disease is the prototype illness that presents with fasciculations. Spinal muscular atrophy is an LMN type of MND and hence can cause fascicuations. Multiple Sclerosis is a disease causing demyelination of the white matter of the central nervous system and hence presents with predominant UMN symptoms and can have sensory symptoms as well. Hence MS is the less likely cause. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3411-3415

469.q: A 35 year old female comes to you with paraplegia of one day duration, with a sensory level at T10, she has bladder involvement and is catheterized. She gives a history of loss of vision in her left eye, one year back, with residual defective vision. She was not on any follow up. Her MRI brain and spinal cord shows multiple T2 hyperintense lesions. What will be the treatment of this patient?
469.e: This patient who has a background history of an defective vision, now presents with symptoms suggestive of a spinal cord transection and MRI showing T2 hyperintense lesions. This is typical of Multiple Sclerosis. The acute episodes of Multiple Sclerosis is treated with steroids. Methylprednisolone 500-1000mg for 3-5 days, followed by a taper with oral steroids 60-80mg/day for two weeks. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 444, Pg: 3468

470.q: A 37-year-old female presents with headaches. Examination reveals papilloedema. Which of the following would make the diagnosis of benign intracranial hypertension (BIH) unlikely?
o: Normal ventricles on CT or MRI scan
470.e: BIH is typically associated with papilloedema, reduced venous pulsation and normal appearances of the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A VIth nerve palsy is a recognised association. Reflexes are preserved and plantars are flexor. Extensor plantars suggest an alternative diagnosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 16Pg: 116

470.q: A 30 year old male comes to you with history of recurrent retro orbital pains that occurs once or twice in a day, each lasting for around an hour, associated with ipsilateral lacrimation. He has had similar episodes before which occurred for a period of 1week, after which he remains asymptomatic for around 6-8 months. Which of the following statements is false regarding the preventive therapy of the above condition?
o: Since the episodes lasts only for around 3 weeks, steroids are a good option for preventive therapy
Verapamil is the first line treatment for episodes that lasts longer
Lithium is a drug that is of proven benefit in preventing the episodes of this head ache
CGRP monoclonal antibody is useful in chronic cluster head ache
470.e: The patient in the question suffers from cluster head ache. The bouts or episodes occur for a very short period of 1 weeks. The preventive therapy of cluster head ache depends up on the duration of bouts. For shorter bouts the drugs that are approved are: Prednisolone CGRP monoclonal antibody Galcanezumab Great Occipital nerve injection with lignocaine or steroids Verapamil For bouts that are longer, the drugs that are approved are Verapamil 160-960mg/day Lithium 400-800mg/day Non invasive vagal stimulation Deep brain stimulation Melatonin, Topiramate and Gabapentin are of unproven benefits So among the options, the CGRP monoclonal antibody is useful not for chronic cluster head ache or longer bouts, but for shorter bouts of head ache. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 430, Pg: 3367

470.q: Which of the following statements regarding CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy) is correct?
o: Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain is diagnostic
It is associated with an abnormality of the X chromosome
470.e: CADASIL is a diffuse disease of small arteries, predominantly in the brain. It starts during mid adulthood and is characterised by: Recurrent ischaemic events (transient or permanent) Attacks of migraine with aura Severe mood disorders Sub-cortical dementia and A wide spread leukoencephalopathy on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). CT brain is not diagnostic. Characteristic MRI changes include T2 weighted hyperintensity of the periventricular white matter. A family history is almost always present, as it is an autosomal dominant condition, located to chromosome 19. Infarcts are subcortical, and the thalami and basal ganglia are usually involved. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3343

470.q: Which of the following statements regarding CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy) is correct?
o: Computerised tomography (CT) of the brain is diagnostic
It is associated with an abnormality of the X chromosome
470.e: CADASIL is a diffuse disease of small arteries, predominantly in the brain. It starts during mid adulthood and is characterised by: Recurrent ischaemic events (transient or permanent) Attacks of migraine with aura Severe mood disorders Sub-cortical dementia and A wide spread leukoencephalopathy on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). CT brain is not diagnostic. Characteristic MRI changes include T2 weighted hyperintensity of the periventricular white matter. A family history is almost always present, as it is an autosomal dominant condition, located to chromosome 19. Infarcts are subcortical, and the thalami and basal ganglia are usually involved. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch:427, Pg: 3343-3344

470.q: A 78-year-old lady presents with a 5 day history of severe left temporal headache radiating from her eye to the scalp. She had also experienced jaw discomfort during eating. Which of the following drugs should be given while awaiting results of diagnostic tests?
470.e: The history suggests temporal arteritis. In view of the vision threatening nature of disease, the patient should be commenced on steroids, pending the confirmatory tests. Typically 60 mg of prednisolone per day is recommended. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2811-2812

470.q: An elderly woman on treatment for migraine presents with new onset chest pain, without any previous history of angina/MI. The drug with which of the following mechanisms of action might have caused this presentation?
470.e: Triptans are a group of anti migraine drugs that cause vasoconstriction. So they have the propensity to precipitate angina.

470.q: A 31-year-old woman has known migraine. She gets periodic episodes of headaches with associated visual symptoms. Which one of the Following drugs should be used first in a migraine attack?
470.e: In acute migraine attack, the first line treatments are simple analgesics such as aspirin, ibuprofen or paracetamol. Second line treatment in acute migraine are the triptans (e.g. sumatriptan) which work by selectively stimulating 5-hydroxytriptamine 1 (5HT1) receptors. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch: 430, Pg: 3361

470.q: A 42-year-old patient has been diagnosed with migraine recently. The migraines seem to have increased in frequency since being on a triptan What is the next medication to use?
470.e: This patient requires prophylaxis as the symptoms are not getting controlled on triptans. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 430, Pg: 3361-3364

471.e: Transferrin saturation , which is normally 25-50%, is obtained by the following formula: Transferrin saturation = (Serum iron × 100) ÷ TIBC, where TIBC is total iron binding capacity. Iron-deficiency states are associated with saturation levels Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 63, Pg: 436

471.q: Microcytic erythrocytosis is seen in all except
471.e: Only three situations cause microcytic erythrocytosis: β-thalassemia trait, hypoxic erythrocytosis, and PV. With β-thalassemia trait, the RDW is usually normal, whereas with hypoxic erythrocytosis and PV, the RDW may be elevated due to associated iron deficiency. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 103, Pg: 804

Vitamin B6 dependency syndromes that require pharmacologic doses of vitamin B6 are cystathionine β-synthase deficiency, pyridoxine-responsive (primarily sideroblastic) anemias, and gyrate atrophy with chorioretinal degeneration due to decreased activity of the mitochondrial enzyme ornithine aminotransferase. In these situations, 100-200 mg/d of oral vitamin B6 is required for treatment.

471.q: Sympathetic segments? supply to the heart arises from which of the following spinal
471.e: Sympathetic nerve cells supplying the heart are located in the intermediolateral horn of spinal segments T1 to T5. Sympathetic supply is cardio-acceleratory, and on stimulation, they increase the heart rate, and also dilate coronary arteries. Both parasympathetic and sympathetic nerves form the superficial and deep cardiac plexuses, the branches of which run along the coronary arteries to reach the myocardium.

471.q: What is the Most common site of spinal TB in adults?
471.e: Weight-bearing joints (the spine in 40% of cases, the hips in 13%, and the knees in 10%) are most commonly affected in skeletal TB The upper thoracic spine is the most common site of spinal TB in children The lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae are usually affected in adults Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1365

471.q: What is the Most common site of spinal TB in children?
471.e: While the upper thoracic spine is the most common site of spinal TB in children, the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae are usually affected in adults Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1365

471.q: A 38 year old alcoholic presents with unsteadiness whilst walking. On examination he has increased tone and brisk reflexes in the right leg. Proprioception is abnormal in the right leg. There is loss of vibration sense in the right leg. There is decrease in pain and temperature sensation in the left leg. Which one of the following conditions is most likely to be responsible for his weakness?
471.e: Brown Sequard syndrome which describes hemisection of the spinal cord, causes ipsilateral UMN signs and proprioception loss (corticospinal tract and dorsal column decussate at the medulla), and contralateral sensory loss in pain and temprature (the spinothalamic tracts decussate at the same level). The rest of the conditions (syringomyelia, subacute degeneration of cord, Friedrich's ataxia) can cause cerebellar signs or patchy sensory loss but should be bilateral. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3446

471.q: Enterococci are commonly associated with all of these clinical manifestations except:
471.e: Enterococci act as opportunistic pathogens in severely ill and compromised patients Enterococci are known to cause urinary tract infections; intra abdominal abscesses; wound infections; bacteremia, including catheter-associated blood stream infections; and endocarditis; less commonly, they cause osteoarticular infections and meningitis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 149 Pg: 1200

472.q: Most common infectious agents that cause facial palsy is?
472.e: The most common infectious agents that cause facial palsy are herpes simplex virus type 1 (Bell's palsy) and varicella-zoster virus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 193, Pg: 1480

472.q: A 44 year old bank clerk presents with a headache, nausea and ptosis of the left eye with blurred vision. She does not have fatiguability of her eye movements. Examination revealed swelling on the left side of face, proptosis and chemosis of the left eye, left mastoid swelling and left ophthalmoplegia involving cranial nerves. The pupil sizes were equal. A CT of her head is normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
472.e: A history of headache and no other obvious cause of ptosis is suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Third nerve palsy is associated with dilated pupil and Horner's syndrome is associated with miosis. A CT can be normal, and diagnosis is confirmed with MRI. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3444

472.q: An 80 year old lady is admitted complaining of acute onset weakness in both legs and low back pain for the previous 4 weeks. She has lost 5 kg of weight recently, and has a Hb of 8.5 g/dl. Her cranial nerves and upper limbs were normal but she has reduced power in both lower limbs of 3/5. She has a sensory level at T12 and plantar reflexes are upgoing. Rectal tone was normal. Which is the best next investigation?
472.e: This patient is likely to have cord compression from a metastases to the spine. Urgent MRI scan is required to confirm the diagnosis and a referral for either surgery or radiotherapy can then be made. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3447

472.q: Which of the following cranial structures is not pain producing?
472.e: The pain producing structures in brain includes: scalp, meningeal arteries, dural sinuses, falx cerebri and proximal portion of large pial vessels. The ventricular ependyma, choroid plexus, pial veins, and much of the brain parenchyma are not pain producing Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 16 Pg:112

472.q: A 41 year old man presents with finger weakness which was diagnosed as an ulnar nerve lesion. Which of the Following muscles is supplied by the ulnar nerve?
472.e: The interossei muscles and medial two lumbricals are supplied by the ulnar nerve. The lateral two lumbricals (anatomical position), opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis are supplied by the median nerve. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

472.q: A 32 year old lady is found to have a left sided posterior communicating artery aneurysm on cerebral angiography. Which of the Following would you expect to find?
472.e: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm will cause compression of the third nerve, and therefore pupillary involvement from compression of the parasympathetic fibres that run on the outside of the third nerve. This leads to a dilated pupil. Other features of a third nerve palsy include ptosis, and a 'down and out' eye. Upgaze and adduction is affected. On the contrary, ischemia of the 3rd nerve due to long standing diabetes and atherosclerosis would lead to a palsy which spares the pupillary reflex. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3441

472.q: A 61 year old patient has diplopia looking to the left. When the left eye is covered, the outer image disappears. Which nerve is involved?
472.e: Covering the affected eye causes the false image (outer image) to disappear. In this case, the left eye is involved hence left lateral rectus (abducens nerve). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3441

472.q: A 47-year-old man presents with an insidious onset of binocular horizontal diplopia and left sided facial pain. On examination he has a left abducens nerve palsy and numbness over the maxillary division of the left trigeminal nerve. Of the following which is the most likely anatomical site of his neurological lesion?
472.e: In the pre-antibiotic era, an abducens nerve palsy with ipsilateral pain and numbness was due to petrous osteitis (Gradenigo syndrome) but is now more likely the result of a meningioma or nasopharyngeal carcinoma of the petrous apex. The cavernous sinus syndrome consists of variable involvement of Oculomotor (III) Trochlear (IV) Abducens (VI) Trigeminal (ophthalmic and maxillary division) (V) and Oculo-sympathetic nerves. The superior orbital fissure syndrome is similar to the cavernous sinus syndrome except for the presence of proptosis. Lesions of the cerebellopontine angle causes compression of cranial nerves V (trigeminal), VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear). Lesions of the midbrain cause a variety of symptoms, depending on the exact area affected. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 441 Pg: 3444

473.q: A 25-year-old female presented with a sudden onset of left sided head and neck pain. 24 hours later she presents with sudden onset of right hemiparesis, facial weakness and homonymous hemianopia and left Horner's syndrome. A CT brain showed a left middle cerebral artery territory infarction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
473.e: The presence of neck pain on the left side, followed by a right sided weakness points to the diagnosis of carotid dissection. The two commonest causes of young onset stroke (less than 40 years) are cardio-embolism and carotid artery dissection. Carotid artery dissection is either spontaneous or traumatic. Facial/head/neck pain and Horner's syndrome are characteristic features. Migrainous stroke usually affects the posterior circulation (posterior cerebral artery territory is the commonest). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3341

473.q: A 72-year-old woman presented with an acute, severe occipital headache, unsteadiness of her gait and vomiting. She had a history of poorly controlled hypertension. On examination there was nystagmus to the left, ataxia of the left limbs and gait ataxia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
473.e: Cerebellar haemorrhage The most common symptoms are of severe nausea and vomiting and ataxia. Headache may be severe. Patients with cerebellar haemorrhage can rapidly become comatose within hours after the onset from herniation, because of its limited space in the posterior fossa. Pontine haemorrhage There are numerous nuclei located within the pons. Rapidly deteriorating level of consciousness, impaired extraocular movement and extensive sensorimotor deficits are clinical clues to pontine haemorrhage. Basal ganglia haemorrhage Contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, or hemi-inattention. Aphasia, especially non-fluency and impaired comprehension, is frequently seen if haemorrhage occurs in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 428, Pg: 3350

473.q: A 41 year old man complained of a severe headache. Following this, he then developed nausea and vomiting and came to the ER to be assessed. A CT scan demonstrated blood in the left sylvian fissure. Which of the Following is the most likely cause?
473.e: The history is consistent with a subarachnoid haemorrhage, caused by rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm. Migraine will not cause blood in the Sylvian fissure. Carotid dissection will result in ischemia in the brain rather than bleed. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3355

473.q: A 48-year-old man with chest pain of 1-hour duration is diagnosed as having acute myocardial infarction. Which of the following features, if present, would most contraindicate thrombolytic therapy?
o: History of likely ischaemic stroke within the past month
473.e: There is an approximate 1% risk of stroke and a 0.7% risk of major hemorrhage associated with the use of thrombolysis. Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (TPA) is connected with a lower rate of intracranial hemorrhage and hence is the drug of choice for thrombolysis in acute myocardial infarction of less than 12 hour's duration. Absolute contraindications for thrombolytic therapy Aortic dissection Previous cerebral hemorrhage Known history of cerebral aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation Known intracranial neoplasm Recent (within the past 6 months) thromboembolic stroke Active internal bleeding (excluding menstruation) Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2059

473.q: A 44 year old lady died of Subarachnoid hemorrhage due to cerebral aneurysm. As per her sister who is conscious at present, there is a family history of other deaths from subarachnoid haemorrhage. She is, however, asymptomatic. What should be done?
473.e: This may be a case of familial subarachnoid haemorrhage. In those who have a first degree relative who genuinely suffered a SAH, their risk of also suffering one is 3-7 times that of the general population. MRI is better than CT scan for screening. Angiography is diagnostic but too invasive for screening. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3355

473.q: A 77-year-old woman has had worsening shortness of breath for several years.She now has to sleep sitting up on two pillows. She has difficulty swallowing. There is no history of chest pain. She is afebrile. Recently, she suffered a stroke with left hemiparesis. A chest x ray reveals a near-normal left ventricular size with a prominent left atrial border.Which of the following conditions is most likely to account for these findings?
473.e: Mitral valve stenosis leads to left atrial enlargement, but the left ventricle is usually small. An enlarged left atrium may lead to pressure posteriorly on the oesophagus. Most mitral valvular disease in adults results from rheumatic heart disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3337

473.q: A 35 year old male is evaluated for young stroke. He gives history of burning pains in both his feet since his late teenage. What can be seen on examining this patient?
473.e: We have a patient with stroke presenting at a very young age along with symptoms of peripheral neuropathy. This should make us thing of Fabry's Disease. It is an X linked dominant disorder. The characteristic skin lesions that are seen in Fabry's disease are Angiokeratomas. They are dark red to blue black maculopapular lesions that are seen in the area between the umbilicus and knee most abundantly. Other features are hypohidrosis, vascular diseases of the heart, kidneys and brain. Lenticular and corneal opacities may also e seen. Xanthomas, Central obesity can also occur in familial dyslipidemias that can also cause stroke in young. But here there is history of burning parasthesias due to peripheral neuropathy which is seen in Fabry's disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 418, Pg: 3259

473.q: Which of the following antiplatelet agents has been proven effective in the acute treatment of ischemic stroke?
473.e: Aspirin is the only antiplatelet agent that has been proven to be effective for the acute treatment of ischemic stroke; there are several antiplatelet agents proven for the secondary prevention of stroke. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, chapter 427 page number. 3338

474.q: An 18-year-old college student living in a dormitory contracts meningitis, which causes a centrally mediated increase in his respiratory rate. The basic respiratory rhythm is generated in which of the following regions of the brain?
474.e: The main components of the respiratory control pattern generator for the automatic control of breathing are located in the medulla. The basic respiratory rhythm is initiated by a small group of synaptically coupled pacemaker cells in the pre-Botzinger complex on either side of the medulla between the nucleus ambiguus and the lateral reticular nucleus. This basic rhythm can be modified by many factors, including higher centers in the cerebral cortex and hypothalamus and input from the reticular activating system and pontine respiratory centers, including the pneumotaxic center in the nucleus parabrachialis. Reference: Ganong, pp 192-193, 671-673. Levitzky, pp 188-194, 200.
Enterococci are well-known causes of nosocomial UTI-the most common infection caused by these organisms. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 149 Pg: 1199

474.q: Which is true of herpes simplex encephalitis?
474.e: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is associated with high signal in one or both temporal lobes (limbic encephalitis). Seizures are commonly present in HSE. Herpes simplex virus type 1 is the causative virus (not type 2 which is associated with genital herpes). PCR for herpes simplex virus on cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) is a highly specific test. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch:137 Pg: 1095-1097

474.q: Which of the following is correct regarding herpes simplex encephalitis?
o: Is associated with a polymorphonuclear pleocytosis in the CSF
Produces a diffuse, evenly distributed inflammation of cerebral tissues
Produces a typical EEG pattern with lateralized periodic discharges at 2 Hz
Should be treated with acyclovir as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed by urgent CSF viral antibody titres
474.e: This EEG pattern is seen but is not diagnostic. Peak incidence occurs in winter A lymphocytosis is characteristic in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Temporal lobe location is typical Immediate treatment is required on clinical suspicion. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:137 Pg: 1095-1097

474.q: A 44 year old patient has been having fevers, neck stiffness and confusion. There was a past medical history of HIV infection and diabetes. A CT scan was normal and lumbar puncture was performed. The opening pressure during LP was normal, and there were elevated CSF lymphocytes (88), and elevated CSF protein (5.5 g/l), and a low glucose. Gram staining and India ink preparation revealed 4-7 micron, round budding yeasts with capsule and 8-10 lymphocytes per high power field. What is the diagnosis?
474.e: Cryptococcal meningitis is often seen in immunosuppressed patients. The organism is Cryptococcus Neoformans . Meningitis manifests with diffuse, nonfocal findings (eg, altered mental status, vomiting). A CT scan or MRI in patients with cryptococcal infection may reveal diffuse atrophy or cerebral edema with focal, homogenous, or contrast-enhanced areas. An India ink preparation is commonly used with CSF to identify the organism and to support a presumptive diagnosis. If performed correctly, 25-50% of patients with cryptococcal meningitis show Cryptococci. In patients with AIDS, amphotericin B is given for 2 weeks, with or without 2 weeks of flucytosine, followed by fluconazole at 400 mg/d for a minimum of 10 weeks. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 202, Pg: 1576

475.q: PNH patients will be having deficient surface proteins that normally protect the red cells from activated compliments. What are the two deficient surface proteins?
475.e: The definitive diagnosis of PNH is based on the demonstration that a substantial proportion of the patient's red cells have an increased susceptibility to complement (C), due to the deficiency on their surface of proteins (particularly CD59 and CD55). Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th Edition, Page

475.q: A 65 year old man presents with an immune-mediated thrombocytopenia. He has been treated with antibiotics during a recent hospital admission. Which of the following is most likely implicated in the new development?
475.e: Drugs causing Thrombocytopenia Trimethoprim/ sulfamethoxazole Penicillin Vancomycin Rifampin Ethambutol Amphotericin B Quinine Heparin Digoxin Amiodarone Ethanol Quinidine H2 -antagonists NSAIDs Acetaminophen Chemotherapy Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 115, pg. 908

475.q: A 71 year old patient has a set of investigations due to lethargy. She complains of polyuria and generalised back pains. Upon investigation, she has the following results: Hb 8 g/dl MCV 100 fl Platelets 190 x 10^9/L total protein 9 g/dl Albumin 3.4 (3.7-4.9) g/dl calcium 12 mg/dl phosphate 1.8 mg/dl What is the appropriate next investigation?
475.e: The patient in this question has bone pains, hypercalcemia with impaired renal function and AG reversal, all pointing to the diagnosis of Myeloma. Hence the next best step would be a serum protein electrophoresis. 24 hour urine albumin or protein and LFT is of little use in this clinical scenario. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 111 Pg : 865-867

475.q: Which of the following diseases presents with Thrombotic microangiopathy without Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?
475.e: Thrombotic microangiopathy(TMA) is a pathological lesion characterized by the presence of endothelial injury in the terminal arteriole and capillaries of organs, causing hyaline platelet thrombi, resulting in partial or complete occlusion of vessels. In kidneys it leads to a membranoproliferative pattern in glomerulus. Usually TMA is associated with Micro angiopathic hemolytic anemia(MAHA) characterized by schistocytes and thrombocytopenia. Typical examples of TMA include: Hemolytic uremic syndrome Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura Malignant hypertension Scleroderma renal crisis APLa syndrome HELLP syndrome HIV infection Radiation nephropathy TMA without MAHA is seen in POEMS Syndrome TMA associated with Myeloproliferative neoplasias Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 217, Pg: 2364.

475.q: A 23-year-old woman was referred for investigation of iron deficiency anemia.Her mother died aged 28 years from colonic carcinoma complicating Peutz-Jegher syndrome.Which is the most likely mode of inheritance of Peutz-Jegher syndrome?
475.e: Peutz-Jegher syndrome is a condition characterized by perioral pigmentation and numerous hamartomas of the bowel.Originally it was assumed that these did not predispose to malignancy but studies now suggest the contrary.The condition is autosomal dominant. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 81, Pg: 638

475.q: Which of the following is a cause of macroglossia?
475.e: Macroglossia, Raccoon eyes, hepatomegaly, anemia are features of amyloidosis Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus. Aphthous ulceration is common in active disease. Aphthous ulcers and glossitis are both features of celiac disease. Patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome have characteristic mucocutaneous pigmentation, that leads to perioral freckling. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 112, Pg: 880

475.q: Marker of small cell cancer of lung is -
475.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Chromogranin Small cell carcinoma contains. Polypeptide hormore e.g. PTH like peptide. Neuroendocrine markers -4 chromogranin, Synaptophysin, Leu7 458. Collapse of lung is called - a) Emphysema b) Bronchiactasis c) Atelectasis d) Bronchitis Correct Answer - C Ans. is 'c' i.e., Atelectasis Atelectasis (collapse) Atelectasis refers to:-

475.q: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a syndrome characterized by:
o: Thrombocytosis, anemia, neurologic abnormalities, progressive renal failure and fever.
Thrombocytopenia, anemia, neurologic abnormalities, progressive hepatic failure and fever
Thrombocytosis, anemia neurologic abnormalities, progressive renal failure and fever
Thrombocytopenia, anemia, neurological abnormalities, progressive renal failure and fever
475.e: Answer is D (Thrombocytopenia, anemia, neurological abnormalities, progressive renal failure and fever) Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) is characterized clinically by the Pentad of Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia, Thrombocytopenia. Decreased Renal Function. Disturbed Neurological function and Fever.

476.q: A 36 year old man presents with acute stiffness swelling of his knees and ankles, a painful rash on his legs. The ESR was 107 mm/hour. Chest Xray showed hilar lymphadenopathy bilaterally. What is the likely progression of the arthralgia?
476.e: The description typical of acute sarcoidosis - erythema nodosum, oligoarthropathy and hilar lymphadenopathy. This usually has a good prognosis, with resolution over 6-8 weeks. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 367, Pg: 2833

476.q: Which of the following is false :
o: Cystitis is a risk factor for recurrent cystitis and pyelonephritis.
Recurrent infection leads to renal failure.
ASB is common among elderly but does not in itself increase the risk of death.
Infection plays prime role for development of Chronic Interstitial Nephritis
476.e: Cystitis is a risk factor for recurrent cystitis and pyelonephritis. ASB is common among elderly and catheterized patients but does not in itself increase the risk of death. infection does not play a primary role in chronic interstitial nephritis; the primary etiologic factors in this conditions are analgesic abuse, obstruction, reflux, and toxin exposure. In the presence of underlying renal abnormalities Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1078

476.q: A 25-year-old man has symptoms of lethargy. Blood results reveal a urea of 55 mg/dl and creatinine of 3.9 mg/dl. Which of the following indicates chronic(rather than acute) renal failure?
476.e: The clinical clues to chronicity of renal impairment is symptoms of azotemia > 3 months, renal osteodystrophy, bilaterally scarred kidneys and broad cast in urinary sediments. Anemia can occur in both AKI and CKD. Disorders of Calcium and Phosphorus homeostasis can also be seen in AKI and CKD. Renal osteodystrophy(bone changes) and small sized kidney with a destroyed renal parenchyma, with increased echogenicity and thinned out cortex with isosthenuria and broad cast are the only conclusive findings of chronicity. However, anemia and Ca Phosphate levels in AKI are not the rule but exception. Hence anemia is the best option here. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 52, Pg: 332, 333.

476.q: Which of the following viral infections contributes the most to the prevalence of chronic hepatitis?
476.e: Chronic hepatitis B afflicts 248 million people worldwide (2 billion overall have been infected; endemic areas include Asia and sub-Saharan Africa) Whereas, 71 million people are infected with HCV, with the highest rates in central and east Asia, north Africa, and the Middle East. Hence prevalence of hepatitis B is greater Risk of chronicity is maximum with hepatitis C infection (85% risk) Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 341, Pg: 2592

476.q: Cytogenetic abnormalities seen in myelodysplastic syndromes include all except
476.e: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder characterized by disordered cell proliferation, impaired differentiation, and aberrant hematopoiesis, resulting in cytopenias and risk of progression to leukemia . Both chromosomal and genetic instability have been implicated; both are aging-related . Cytogenetic abnormalities are found in approximately one-half of patients. Aneuploidy (chromosome loss or gain) is more frequent than translocations . Loss of all or part of chromosomes 5, 7, and 20, and trisomy of 8 may be related to etiology ( 11q23 following topoisomerase II inhibitors ). The type and number of cytogenetic abnormalities strongly correlate with the probability of leukemic transformation and survival. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 102, Pg: 801

476.q: All are criteria for accelerated blast phase except
476.e: Criteria of accelerated-phase CML (Chronic Myeloid Leukemia) includes the presence of - 15% or more peripheral blasts 30% or more peripheral blasts plus promyelocytes 20% or more peripheral basophils Cytogenetic clonal evolution (presence of chromosomal abnormalities inaddition to Ph) Thrombocytopenia 9 /L ( unrelated to therapy ) Accelerated phase of CML is historically associated with median survival of Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 105, Pg: 821

476.q: Is L-Asparaginase useful for the treatment of?
476.e: Induction regimens are centered around vincristine, glucocorticoids, and anthracyclines with or without cyclophosphamide or cytarabine. L-Asparaginase is the only ALL-specific drug and is now more intensively used in adults. Pegylated asparaginase has the advantage of a significantly longer period of asparagine depletion. Dexamethasone is often preferred to prednisone because it penetrates the blood-brain barrier and also acts on resting leukemic blast cells Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 106 pg. 831

476.q: What is Median age of diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
476.e: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is primarily a disease of older adults , with a median age at diagnosis of 71 years. Reference: Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 107, Pg: 834

477.q: A 36-year-old man with a history of AIDS and Pneumocystis infection presents to the Emergency Department with severe respiratory distress. The patient is placed on a ventilator at a rate of 16, tidal volume of 600 mL, and FIO2 of 1.0. An arterial blood sample taken 20 minutes later reveals a Po2 of 350 mmHg, a Pco2 of 36 mmHg, and a pH of 7.32. At a barometric pressure of 757 mmHg, and assuming a normal respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, the patient's alveolar oxygen tension is approximately which of the following?
477.e: The alveolar air equation is used to calculate the PAO2. PAO2 = PIO2 - (PaCO2/ R ) Given the barometric pressure of 757 mmHg, FIO2 = 1.0 (100% O2), PaCO2 = 36 mmHg, and R = 0.8, then PAO2 = (1.0)(757 - 47) - (36/0.8) = 710 - 45 = 665 mmHg Pneumocystis is an opportunistic fungal pulmonary pathogen that is an important cause of pneumonia (pneumocystosis) in immunocompromised hosts. HIV patients with a CD4 + cell count below 200/μL have an increased risk of developing Pneumocystis pneumonia. According to new, and still evolving nomenclature, Pneumocystis carinii is the name of the organism derived from rats, and Pneumocystis jiroveci is the name of the organism derived from humans. Reference: Ganong, p 660. Kasper et al., pp 1194-1196, 1583, 1592-1595. Levitzky, p 75. Stead et al., pp 202-204.

477.q: Which is the most common form of localized lymphadenopathy in adults?
477.e: In adults, the most common localized form is inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy In children, it is cervical lymphadenopathy Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 66 Pg: 458

477.q: Which of the following statements is true? 1. In the context of a decreased GFR, autoregulatory mechanisms lead to prostacyclin mediated dialation of afferent arteriole and ACE mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. 2. NSAIDS cause inhibition of afferent arteriolar vasodilation and a decrease in GFR 3. NSAIDS cause inhibition of efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and a decrease in GFR. 4. NSAIDS cause inhibition of efferent arteriolar vasodilation and a decrease in GFR.
477.e: This question deals with renal autoregulatory mechanism. Under circumstances of reduced perfusion pressure, within the autoregulatory range, the GFR is maintained by the dialation of the afferent arteriole and constriction of the efferent arteriole . The former is mediated by prostaglandins and the latter by Angiotensin II. So drugs that inhibit the production of vasodilatory prostaglandins, eg NSAIDS, will reduce the GFR by inhibiting prostaglandin mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation. ACEI or ARBs reduce the GFR by inhibiting Angiotensin II mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. Hence statements 1 and 2 are correct. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Chap 310 Pg. 2298

477.q: What is the Most common hematologic abnormality in HIV infected patients?
477.e: Anemia is the most common hematologic abnormality in HIV infected patients and, in the absence of a specific treatable cause, is independently associated with a poor prognosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 202, Pg:74

477.q: A 35-year-old man has been diagnosed with diarrhea. His blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, and temperature 38°C.Blood results show Na 118 mmol/l, K 2.8 mmol/l urea 8 mg/dl, creatinine 0.4 mg/dl, chloride 70 mmol/l, bicarbonate 20 mmol/l. Serum osmolality is 287 mosm/l and urine osmolality is 700 mosm/l. Which is the most likely diagnosis for hyponatremia?
o: Blood taken from a drip arm
477.e: There is hyponatremia, hypokalemia and low urea with normal osmolality. This is most likely due to inaccurate sampling from a drip arm. In the other causes of hyponatraemia (true hyponatremia), the plasma osmolality should be low as well. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2964

477.q: A 48-year-old woman who works in a pharmacy presents with episodes of tiredness and lethargy. Her blood pressure is 115/75mmHg. Her bloods reveal hypokalaemia and a raised serum bicarbonate level. Urine collection reveals hypercalciuria. Otherwise the findings are unremarkable. What is the likely diagnosis?
477.e: This picture could fit Bartter's syndrome , although Bartter's syndrome is rare (1 per million), has an autosomal-recessive pattern of inheritance and commonly presents below the age of 5 years. Features of Bartter's syndrome include volume depletion, tetany and muscle weakness. This woman's occupation is the clue, which unfortunately makes furosemide abuse very much more likely. Conn's syndrome is associated with hypertension and is due to aldosterone excess. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 350

477.q: A 51-year-old woman presents with increasing lower back pain for the last six months. The pain is increased by working as a floor-layer, and is worse in the evening. There is no weight loss, night pain, or fever. Her back is stiff for 15 minutes in morning. Over the last few months she has developed firm to hard swelling on several distal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and has anterior knee pain worsened by climbing stairs. A full blood count, ESR, and CRP done by the GP have been normal. What is the diagnosis?
477.e: This patient has generalised osteoarthritis (GOA), as there are OA related symptoms in at least three joint areas, namely Bony swellings at distal and proximal IPJs termed Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes respectively Anterior knee pain, worse on climbing stairs, suggesting patella-femoral joint OA, and Low back pain, suggesting spinal degenerative changes. Ankylosing spondylitis typically occurs in young men, and associates with pronounced early morning stiffness and buttock pain. Osteoporosis is not symptomatic, unless accompanied by a spinal fracture. Osteoporotic spinal fractures present with acute pain which improves over a period of few weeks to a couple of months. There are no red-flag symptoms to raise the possibility of discitis or malignancy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 371 Pg: 2858-2859

477.q: Best provocative test for diagnosis of Gastrinoma is:
477.e: Answer is B (Secretin injection test) Gastrinomas (Zollinger Ellison Syndrome) are characterized by peptic ulceration due to hypersecretion of gastrin by a non-beta cell tumor. Secretin injection test is the most valuable provocative test in identifying patients with ZES.

478.q: At what intervals should monitoring of patients on HAART should be done?
478.e: CD4 cell count and viral load have to be monitored every 3-6 months to monitor the response to treatment. Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 334

478.q: A 38-year-old man presents with a 16 week history of indigestion. Five years previously he had been treated for a duodenal ulcer. Investigations reveal: Fasting gastrin 120 pmol/l (<55) Which one of the following statements regarding gastrin is correct?
o: It acts upon the G cells of the stomach
It inhibits the secretion of pancreatic bicarbonate
It is produced by the parietal cells of the stomach
Its release is stimulated by gastric luminal peptides
478.e: Gastrin is produced in response to Stimulation by neural reflex pathways By the direct effect of digested peptides on the G cells themselves. Gastrin is mainly produced by the G cells of the gastric antrum. Gastrin stimulates the production of bicarbonate by pancreas. It stimulates the parietal cells to produce hydrochloric acid. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 324, Pg: 2435

478.q: A 44-year-old woman presents with a mass in her neck and symptoms of choking/ shortness of breath when she lies down. Investigations; Hb 14.1 g/dl WCC 5.4 x 10^9/L PLT 235 x 10^9/L Na+ 140 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 0.6 mg/dl TSH 0.9 U/l You suspect that she may have retrosternal extension of the goitre. Which of the following would be the investigation of choice for this patient to determine the degree of retrosternal involvement?
478.e: Whilst a plain radiograph may be used to demonstrate retrosternal thyroid extension and tracheal deviation, a CT of the chest is more sensitive and specific in determining the extent of disease. Thyroid ultrasound is most useful for determining the nature of thyroid nodules. Radioisotope scanning has a role to play in determining the uptake of thyroid hormone and as such the underlying diagnosis behind thyrotoxicosis, or in identifying cold nodules within the gland which may raise the suspicion of an underlying neoplasm. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2946

478.q: A 33 year old lady presents with stiffness, pain and swelling of her hands and wrists. Investigations reveal a normocytic, normochromic anemia, elevated ESR and CRP. What antibody would you use if you wanted to do A test for detecting RA factor?
478.e: IgM, IgG, and IgA isotypes of RF occur in sera from patients with RA, although the IgM isotype is the one most frequently measured by commercial laboratories. The sensitivity of RA is only 75%, therefore a negative test does not exclude the presence of the disease. False positive in other connective tissue diseases, such as primary Sjogren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, and type II mixed essential cryoglobulinemia, as well as chronic infections such as subacute bacterial endocarditis and hepatitis B and C. Serum RF may also be detected in 1-5% of the healthy population. Anti CCP has sensitivity almost similar to RA factor, but is almost 95% specific for RA. Anti CCP has a role in predicting the outcomes too, as it is associated with worse outcomes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2759

478.q: A 44-year-old male attends for a routine medical and is in good health. Examination was normal but investigations reveal that he has a serum urate concentration of 9.2 mg/dl (4.2-7.5). Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
478.e: The most appropriate treatment for this asymptomatic man with an isolated slightly elevated urate is lifestyle advice with an appropriately reduced purine diet, increased exercise and reduced alcohol consumption. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 372, Pg: 2863-2865

478.q: A 36-year-old HIV-positive man, evaluated for weight loss and weakness has been found to have disseminated tuberculosis. On examination, he is hypotensive and has hyperpigmentation of the mucosa, elbows and skin creases. Further investigations confirm a diagnosis of Addison's disease. Which of the following is likely in this condition?
478.e: In adrenal destruction, serum Na, Cl and HCO3 levels are reduced, and serum potassium is elevated. The hyponatraemia is due to both loss of sodium in the urine (due to aldosterone and cortisol deficiency) and to movement into the intracellular compartment. Hyperkalemia is due to a combination of aldosterone deficiency, impaired glomerular filtration (due to hypotension) and acidosis. Mild to moderate hypercalcemia occurs in 10-20% patients, the cause of which is uncertain. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2971

478.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with generalised oedema. There was no relevant past medical history. Investigations revealed: Creatinine 0.65 mg/dl, Albumin 2 g/dl, 24-hour urine protein excretion 3.2 g. Ultrasound scan shows normal renal size. Renal biopsy was performed which was normal by light microscopy and showed minimal IgM deposit on IF. Which of the following should the patient be treated with initially?
478.e: This question deals with Nephrotic syndrome in pedaitric patient. The most common cause is Minimal change disease. Light microscopy will be normal. If will either show no deposits or minimal IgM and electron microscope shows effacement of foot processes. The treatment is steroids. 80% of patients achieve remission with prednisolone therapy. Cyclophosphamide treatment can be started for those who are steroid resistant Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

478.q: A 51 year old presents with tiredness and heavy periods. She is known to drink large amounts of alcohol. Her investigations reveal: Hemoglobin 7.3 g/dl MCV 72 fL white cell count 7500/μL platelet count 250000/μL serum ferritin 7 μg/L, (15-300) She was commenced on oral iron therapy one month later but her hemoglobin concentration was 7.8 g/dl. What is the likely cause of the failure of her hemoglobin to respond?
478.e: The likely explanation for failure of an iron deficiency anemia to respond iron therapy in a patient with heavy periods is poor compliance. Folate deficiency will cause a Megaloblastic picture with MCV>100 fL Sideroblastic anemia would cause an increase in serum iron and ferritin. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:97 Pg:752

479.q: The most significant risk factor for cancer is
479.e: The most significant risk factor for cancer overall is age. 2/3 rd of all cases were seen in those aged >65 years. Reference: Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 72, Pg: 508

479.q: Overall % of developing cancer in males during lifetime is
479.e: Overall, men have a 40.5% risk of developing cancer at some time during their lives; women have a 38.9% lifetime risk Reference: Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 69, Pg: 482

479.q: A 74-year-old man was admitted with pallor, light-headedness and loss of energy. On the day prior to admission he had reported loose dark stools. Examination revealed a pulse of 110 per minute and a blood pressure of 106/70 mmHg. Investigations revealed: Haemoglobin 6.2 g/dl (14-18) MCV 72 fl (80-96) White cell count 11.3 x 10^9/L (4-11) Platelet count 480 x 10^9/L (150-400) What is the most appropriate next step in his management?
479.e: This patient has significant microcytic anaemia with a hemoglobin of He should be resuscitated with blood transfusion and then sent for upper GI endoscopy. Red cell administration may be a part of volume replacement even without hemorrhage in order to optimize oxygen delivery if hemoglobin content is A barium meal will not help a bleeding vessel. Parenteral iron administration is for chronic anaemia, not acute bleeds. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch : 303, Pg: 2240

480.q: All of the following can be seen in refeeding syndrome except:
480.e: This is characterized by shift in fluid and electrolyte shift in malnourished patients undergoing refeeding. It is more common with parenteral fluids . It results in hypophosphatemia, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 25, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 338

480.q: Early management of shock focuses on restoring circulating volume, maintaining perfusion and using appropriate fluids. Several principles guide initial resuscitation. One of the following statements is false. Identify the incorrect statement.
o: First line therapy is putting a short wide bore intravenous cannula and start infusion
Albumin should not be the start in immediate period
Ringer lactate is most physiological fluid and ideal crystalloid
It is ideal to give inotropic agents regardless of preload to heart
480.e: Explanation: Inotropic agents should never be started without ensuring adequate preload. In shock, the first step is to restore circulating volume with crystalloids. Starting inotropes before correcting hypovolemia can worsen ischemia, increase oxygen demand and cause arrhythmias. Principles of fluid therapy in shock: The first step is to gain rapid venous access with a short, wide-bore cannula and begin crystalloid infusion. (Option A) Ringer lactate is considered the most physiological crystalloid solution due to its electrolyte composition. ( Option C) Colloids (like albumin) are not recommended in the immediate resuscitation period because crystalloids are faster, safer and more accessible. (Option B) Inotropes are only considered after adequate fluid resuscitation if hypotension persists. (Option D)

480.q: Calculate the calories from TPN containing 100 grams of dextrose, 30 grams of amino acids and 40 grams of lipids:
480.e: 100*3.4=340 kcal from dextrose 40*10=400 kcal from lipid 30*4=120 kcal from aminoacid Total 860 kcal Reference: https://jamieberray.weebly.com/uploads/5/3/0/9/53090885/parenteral nutrition calculations.pdf

480.q: Which of the following statement is false regarding parenteral nutrition?
o: Peripheral feeding is appropriate for short term feeding up to 3 weeks.
Thrombophlebitis is more commonly seen with peripheral feeding.
For central feeding, Hickman lines are ideal.
Fluid retention is indicated by change in weight of >1 kg/day.
480.e: Option A : Peripheral feeding is appropriate for short term feeding up to 2 weeks. Option B : Common disadvantage which is seen after peripheral feeding is Thrombophlebitis, which irreversibly damage vein. Option C : For central parenteral feeding Hickman lines are preferable as they Minimize possibility of line dislodgement and reduce the possibility of Sepsis. Option D : Common metabolic complications following central feeding includes fluid overload, hyperglycaemia, abnormalities of liver function and vitamin deficiencies. Fluid overload can be avoided by daily weighing of the patient. A weight change of >1 kg/day normally indicates fluid retention. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 25, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 338-340

480.q: All of the following fluids are isotonic in body except:
480.e: Please remember that 5%dextrose in water is isotonic when it is in pint form but when administered in body, Dextrose will rapidly utilize and then it will act as hypotonic fluid. So, if asked without mentioning in body go with 5% Dextrose as isotonic Fluid. Ringer solution is similar to Ringer lactate, but it has no lactate as content. Reference: Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of surgery 28 th edition Chapter 2 page no 18

480.q: In a 65-kg adult male recovering from shock, the maintenance fluid rate is calculated using the standard formula recommended for adults weighing more than 40 kg. Based on this rule, what should be his maintenance fluid rate?
480.e: Explanation: According to the provided guideline, adult maintenance fluid rate is calculated as: weight in kilograms + 40. For a 65-kg patient, maintenance fluid would be 65 + 40=105 ml/hour. This is the safest and most accurate maintenance rate for an adult of this weight after stabilization from shock.

480.q: Patients who are unable to maintain adequate oral intake are at risk of malnutrition and complications. Clinical guidelines recommend initiating nutritional support once intake has been insufficient for a defined period. After how many days of inadequate intake should nutritional support be considered?
480.e: Explanation: Nutritional support (enteral or parenteral) should be considered when a patient has inadequate intake for 5 days or more , as metabolic stress and protein-energy deficit begin to significantly affect clinical outcomes around this timeframe. Guidelines for initiating nutritional support: 5 days of inadequate intake - initiate support to prevent malnutrition Earlier initiation (within 1-3 days) is recommended in critically ill or high-risk patients Enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral whenever feasible Goals: maintain lean body mass, support immune function, reduce complications

480.q: Nutritional support should be considered in patients with inadequate intake for how many days?
480.e: Any patient who has sustained 5 days of inadequate intake or who is Anticipated to have no or inadequate intake for this period. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery; chapter: 25; Edition: 28 th ; Pg: 335

481.q: A child was brought to the ER with a lesion on the forearm as seen. As a surgery resident, you decide to excise the lesion in emergency ot. Which of the following investigations will test for the entire coagulation?
481.e: Thromboelastography can be used for guiding intra operative transfusion. But it cant be employed in other disorders of bleeding and thrombosis. It has some role in venom induced coagulopathy

481.q: What would be maintenance fluid rate in case of shock in a man with 65 kgs of weight?
481.e: For patient weighting more than 40 kgs simple rule to calculate maintenance water is = weight in kgs +40 So, in our patient maintenance fluid would be 65 + 40=105 ml/hour. Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 4, Edition: 21 st

481.q: Which of the following is not the complication of massive transfusion?
481.e: Complications from massive transfusion Complications from massive transfusion include: coagulopathy; hypocalcaemia; hyperkalaemia; hypokalaemia; hypothermia.

481.q: All of the following statements are true except:
o: In patient with active bleeding due to major trauma first step should be controlling Bleeding rather than starting high fluid therapy.
In patient with Bowel obstruction first step should be to resuscitate a patient
In patient with active bleeding due to major trauma first step always be fluid therapy.
Airway and breathing must be ensured in every patient presenting with shock.
481.e: In patients who are actively bleeding (major trauma, aortic aneurysm rupture, gastrointestinal hemorrhage), it is counterproductive to institute high-volume fluid therapy without controlling the site of hemorrhage. Increasing blood pressure merely increases bleeding from the site while fluid therapy cools the patient and dilutes available coagulation factors. Thus operative hemorrhage control should not be delayed and resuscitation should proceed in parallel with surgery. Conversely, a patient with bowel obstruction and hypovolemic shock must be adequately resuscitated before undergoing surgery otherwise the additional surgical injury and hypovolemia induced during the procedure will exacerbate the inflammatory activation and increase the incidence and severity of end-organ insult. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28th

481.q: In case of blood loss, ideal replacement fluid is?
481.e: In case of blood loss, blood products are the ideal replacement fluids as crystalloids and colloids have no oxygen carrying capacity and also don't contain coagulation factors, RBCs etc. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28th, Pg: 21

481.q: In case of shock amount of bolus of fluid required to see response would be?
481.e: 250 to 500 ml of fluid should be given as bolus to see dynamic response. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28th, Pg: 18

481.q: When evaluating a patient in shock, a fluid challenge is often given to assess responsiveness to volume expansion. This involves administering a small but adequate bolus of fluid and observing the hemodynamic response. What is the commonly recommended bolus volume to assess fluid responsiveness?
481.e: Explanation: A 250 ml fluid bolus is the standard amount used to assess fluid responsiveness in shock. This volume is large enough to produce measurable hemodynamic changes, yet small enough to avoid fluid overload, especially in critically ill or borderline patients. It is used in both emergency and critical care settings. Fluid challenge principles: Quickly determine whether the patient is "fluid responsive" Typically uses 250 ml crystalloid bolus Response assessed by: Blood pressure improvement Heart rate reduction Improvement in perfusion (urine output, mental status) Ultrasound assessment of IVC or stroke volume variation A positive response suggests hypovolemia, while lack of response indicates need for vasopressors or search for other causes of shock.

481.q: All of the followings are correct regarding storage of blood products except:
o: Packed red cell stored at -2° C with shelf life of 5 weeks
Fresh frozen plasma stored at -40 to -50°C with shelf life of 2 years
Cryoprecipitate is stored at -30° C with shelf life of 2 years
Platelets are stored at 20° C with shelf life of 5 days
481.e: Packed red cells are stored in a SAG-M solution to increase shelf life up to 5 weeks at 2-6°C. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 21

482.q: Best gas used for creating pneumoperitonium at laparoscopy is :
482.e: CO2 CO, is the gas used to create pneumoperitoneum during laparoscopy. Other option is - N20 : But it is expensive, less soluble in blood and supports combustion. Also know : Instrument used for creating pneumoperitoneum is veress needle. Flow Rate of CO, for creating pneumoperitoneum 200 - 2000 ml/min & pressure between 15 - 25 mm of Hg.

482.q: Which among the following is a false statement for physical structure of suture material?
o: Monofilament sutures have poor knotting ability
Multifilament sutures have good knotting ability
Multifilament sutures have less bacterial contamination
482.e: Physical structure . Suture material may be monofilament or multifilament. Monofilament suture material is smooth and tends to slide through tissues easily without any sawing action, but is more difficult to knot effectively. Such material can be easily damaged by gripping it with needle holder or forceps and this can lead to fracture of the suture material. Multifilament or braided sutures are much easier to knot, but have a surface area of several thousand times that of monofilament sutures and thus have a capillary action and interstices where bacteria may lodge and be responsible for persistent infection or sinuses. In order to overcome some of these problems, certain materials are produced as a braided suture, which is coated with silicone in order to make it smooth. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 90

482.q: Which among the following is an absorbable suture material?
482.e: Polygalactin also known as vicryl is a monofilament synthetic absorbable suture used in CBD, ureter and bowel surgeries Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 92

482.q: All of the following statements are incorrect regarding Torsion of testis except?
o: Torsion of testis must be relieved within 6-8 hours of onset of symptoms
At operation, viability of testis is assessed before de rotation
If salvageable, three point fixation of both testes with absorbable suture is performed
482.e: Option A Testicular torsion is most common in adolescents, but may occur at any age and is usually inside the tunica vaginalis. Perinatal torsion differs and is usually extravaginal. Option C At operation, viability of the testis is assessed after de rotation. Option D If salvageable, three-point fixation of both testes with non-absorbable sutures is performed. Reference: Bailey and love’s short practice of surgery, 27 th edition, Page - 125

482.q: What should be the minimum length of the suture material left after cutting to avoid unravelling?
482.e: When the suture is cut after knotting, the ends should be left about 1-2 mm long to prevent unraveling. This is particularly important when using monofilament material. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 96

482.q: The conversion factor to find out the outer diameter of a cannula in millimeters, expressed in French size is
482.e: The French scale begins at zero, and each increment of one French unit represents an increase of 1/3 (0.33) millimeter in outer diameter (3): i.e., French size × 0.33 = outside diameter (mm). Thus, a catheter that is 5 French units in size will have an outer diameter of 5 × 0.33 = 1.65 mm Reference: E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 33 Page No 339 -334.

483.q: A 16-year-old boy was brought to the emergency ward with wheeze and an extensive rash after eating at a Chinese restaurant. On examination, he had extensive wheezes in his chest, stridor, as well as urticaria covering his upper and lower limbs. His BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
483.e: The scenario is consistent with a food allergy, e.g. nuts, leading to an anaphylactic reaction. The patient should be treated with hydrocortisone (IV or IM) as well as antihistaminic drugs. Hereditary angioedema is an autosomal dominant condition caused by C1 esterase deficiency which leads to recurrent attacks of angioedema Bronchitis presents with a productive cough, fever and dyspnoea. It is usually caused by a viral infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-2728.

483.q: Which of the following defines sepsis according to SEPSIS-3 criteria?
o: Suspected or documented infection & increase in any two of the SOFA points
Suspected or documented infection plus vasopressor therapy needed to maintain MAP>65 mmHg and serum lactate >2.0mmol/L despite adequate fluid restriction
Suspected or documented infection plus two SIRS criteria
483.e: Sepsis is defined by SEPSIS-3 criteria as suspected or documented infection and an acute increase in >2 sepsis-related organ failure assessment (SOFA) points. Documented or suspected infection + Need for vasopressors to maintain MAP more than or equal to 65mmHg and elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L ) defines the septic shock according to SEPSIS -3 criteria.SIRS criteria were included in earlier criteria (SEPSIS I & II). Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 20th Ed chap 297, pg.2045

483.q: All electrolyte abnormalities are seen in immediate postoperative period except:
483.e: Option A : Due to increased catabolism in response to surgical stress there will be Negative nitrogen balance occuring. Option B : There is frequently shifting of potassium into cells as well as losses occur in postoperative period that leads to hypokalemia. Option C : Following surgical stress there will be increased glucose production but decreased glucose utilization at tissue level due to insulin resistance, that leads to glucose intolerance. Option D : Following surgery there will be shifting of fluid into extracellular space seen that leads to Hypernatremia. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 1, Edition: 28 th

483.q: Which marker is best measure of organ perfusion?
483.e: Urine output is ideal indicator to measure organ perfusion and to monitor adequacy of fluid therapy. CVP is ideal to measure response to fluid therapy but it is not ideal to Measure organ perfusion Base deficit and lactate level are also good indicators but they are more Invasive and not rapidly available in all places. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28th, Pg: 19

483.q: All of the following are shunt complications except?
483.e: Complications of shunt include - Overdrainage can result in low-pressure headaches, which are typically worse on standing. Collapse of the ventricles can cause accumulation of fluid or blood in the subdural space, resulting in subdural hygroma or subdural haematoma. The slit ventricle syndrome occurs in children treated with shunts, whose ventricles and subarachnoid spaces are underdeveloped, resulting in poor brain compliance. In these patients normal fluctuations in ICP are exaggerated so that coughing and straining may cause symptoms of raised ICP. Shunts are vulnerable to disconnection, infection and blockage . Any shunt blockage may not be evident on scan, as the ventricles fail to enlarge. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 705-706

483.q: Cryoprecipitate is rich in which factor?
483.e: Cryoprecipitate is a supernatant precipitate of FFP and is rich in factor VIII and fibrinogen. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 21

483.q: Ideal time to give preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis is?
483.e: Antibiotic should be given in such a way that maximum blood and tissue level of antibiotic is present before putting an incision. So, the ideal time to give antibiotics is 1 hour before surgery . Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, Edition: 21 st

483.q: All of the following statements are correct regarding REBOA except
o: REBOA is Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta
REBOA is done through common femoral artery
It is advanced distal to level of injury
It acts by shunting blood to the heart and brain
483.e: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) has emerged over the past decade as a promising method of obtaining temporary hemorrhage control in the decompensating trauma patient. Depending on the zone of trauma, REBOA is introduced through the common femoral artery, advanced proximal to level of injury , and inflated, effectively shunting blood to the heart and brain while also decreasing hemorrhage Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21st, Pg: 395

484.q: All of the following are component of revised trauma score except
484.e: The Revised Trauma Score is another well-studied physiologic scoring system that characterizes the condition of the injured patient by incorporating - Glasgow Coma Scale Systolic blood pressure Respiratory rate. These scores have been of value for research purposes and have been successfully used to make triage decisions. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 389

484.q: Which one of the following is the first priority if you are performing a primary survey on a patient?
o: Ensuring patient is oriented to time place and person
484.e: Ensuring a patent airway is the first priority in the primary survey. This is essential, because efforts to restore cardiovascular integrity will be futile unless the oxygen content of the blood is adequate. Simultaneously, all patients with blunt trauma require cervical spine immobilization until injury is excluded. This is typically accomplished by applying a hard collar or placing sandbags on both sides of the head with the patient's forehead taped across the bags to the backboard. Soft collars do not effectively immobilize the cervical spine. For penetrating neck wounds , however, cervical collars are not believed useful because they provide no benefit, but may interfere with assessment and treatment Reference : Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 11th, Pg: 184

484.q: Injury severity score to categorise an injury as a severe injury is?
484.e: Baker and colleagues presented the ISS, calculated by summing the squares of the AIS severity codes for the three most severely injured body regions. The ISS ranges from 1 to 75 , with severity groupings being defined as - Minor injury (ISS less than 9) Moderate injury (ISS between 9 and 16) Serious injury (ISS between 16 and 25) Severe injury (ISS more than 25). Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21st, Pg: 389

484.q: Identify the fourth stage from the philosophy of 'damage control orthopedic' or the 'damage control surgery'
484.e: Knowledge acquired at the molecular level related to the immune-inflammatory response to injury and the concepts of the phenomena of the first hit (the impact exerted on the homeostatic mechanisms as a result of the original trauma sustained) and the second hit (the additional physiological stress induced by surgical procedures) led to the acceptance and implementation of the so call 'damage control orthopaedics' (DCO) philosophy, which is called damage control surgery (DCS ) in more generalized settings. The stages of DCO are: Resuscitation Hemorrhage control Decompression Decontamination Fracture splintage Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 26, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 350-351

484.q: A patient of RTA was brought to the hospital with a left flank bruise associated with hematuria. Patient was hemodynamically stable. Which of the following investigations should be done for hematuria?
484.e: Renal trauma Ominous sign is : hematuria and flank bruise Investigation: Stable patients: IOC- CECT Unstable patient: IOC: IVP( on table IVP is done) IVP( intravenous pyelogram is done to all patients undergoing surgery for renal trauma to look for renal perfusion RTA having left flank bruise associated with hematuria suggest renal trauma. Conservative management with close surveillance is sufficient in the majority of cases of isolated renal trauma. Lower grade injuries, sometimes including grade IV, can be managed conservatively with bed rest, antibiotics in case of penetrating injuries and serial hemoglobin estimation. Re-imaging is usually done after 2-4 days in cases of falling hemoglobin levels, fever or expanding fank mass. Persistent urinary leak can be managed with an internal DJ stent or PCN.

484.q: All of the following are indications for radiological assessment in renal injury except
484.e: The indications for radiological assessment are: Penetrating injuries. Gross haematuria. Shock in combination with microscopic haematuria. Children: in whom the kidneys are much lower and less well protected. Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 76, Edition: 27th, Pg: 1413-1414

484.q: RTA with multiple fractures initial treatment would be -
