484.e: Answer- C. Airway management Management of trauma begins with primary survey. The ATLS (Advanced Trauma Life Support) defines primary survey as assessment of the `A,B,C' i.e., Airway with cervical spine protection, Breathing and circulation.

485.q: Inferior thyroid artery supplies which structures 1. Esophagus 2. Thyroid 3. Parathyroid 4. Thymus
485.e: The inferior thyroid artery (ITA) is considered the principal blood supplier of the thyroid gland . The ITA gives rise to the ascending cervical artery, the inferior laryngeal artery, and also gives pharyngeal, tracheal , and esophageal ITA also supplies the four parathyroid glands . Blood supply of esophagus: Cricopharyngeal muscle (inlet of esophagus) is supplied by superior thyroid artery Cervical esophagus: predominantly by inferior thyroid artery Thoracic esophagus: aorta, both right and left bronchial artery, along with descending branch from inferior thyroid artery, intercostal artery and ascending branch from inferior phrenic artery Abdominal esophagus: left gastric artery and inferior phrenic artery Blood supply to the thymus comes from the internal thoracic artery .

485.q: Gold standard investigation for a patient having signs of multiple injuries
485.e: Explanation: Whole-Body CT (WBCT) in Severe Blunt Trauma WBCT (head-to-pelvis with IV contrast) is the gold standard for evaluating the severely injured adult with blunt trauma. Selective (region-specific) imaging has no role in these patients due to the high likelihood of multisystem injury and the need for comprehensive assessment. WBCT is time-critical and should be performed as early as possible during resuscitation to guide timely interventions. If a patient requires immediate trauma laparotomy without prior WBCT , Apply a pelvic binder and do not remove it until a pelvic fracture is excluded. Obtain an immediate pelvic X-ray , either in the emergency department or on arrival to the operating theatre. Key Takeaways: Whole-body CT is the preferred investigation when there are signs of multiple injuries or deranged physiology.

485.q: All of the following statements are incorrect regarding evaluation of patient with chest injury except
o: CT chest is almost universally performed during the initial evaluation of patient with risk of thoracic injury
Deviation of trachea at sternal notch suggest intrathoracic pressure on same side of deviation
Thoracic MDCTA is useful for evaluation of pericardium
Thoracic MDCTA has become the standard approach to evaluation of chest injury
485.e: Thoracic MDCTA has become the standard approach to evaluation of the chest and provides superior visualization of the chest wall, vasculature, pleural spaces, and lung parenchyma. Option A : Chest radiography is almost universally performed during the initial assessment on patients at risk for thoracic injuries. Option B : Deviation of the trachea at the sternal notch may reveal intrathoracic tension on the side opposite the trachea. Option C: Thoracic MDCTA is unreliable for evaluation of pericardium, given cardiac motion degradation. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21st, Pg: 405

485.q: Cardiac injuries causing cardiovascular collapse requires urgent thoracotomy. Which kind of thoracotomy requires in this case?
485.e: For cardiac injuries that cause cardiovascular collapse, a left anterolateral thoracotomy is performed in the emergency department and may be extended to a contralateral (“clamshell”) incision if needed. When time permits, most cardiac injuries are best approached through a median sternotomy. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21st, Pg: 409

486.q: Which of the following statement about breast tissue is false?
o: Fibrous stroma is absent beneath the areola
Alveolar epithelium is columnar in the resting phase
15-20 lactiferous ducts open in the nipple
Myoepitheliocytes facilitates the passage of the milk along the ducts
486.e: Alveolar epithelium is cuboidal in the resting phase, and columnar during lactation. The fibrous stroma forms septa (suspensory ligaments of Cooper) which anchor the skin and gland to the pectoral fascia. It forms the major part of the gland but is absent beneath the areola and nipple. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 749

486.q: In lymphatic drainage of the breast, the major portion (about 75%) enters eventually into which group of nodes?
486.e: About 75% of the lymph draining the breast goes to the axillary lymph nodes, via the pectoral lymph nodes. All of this lymph from the pectoral lymph nodes must drain to the central lymph nodes as well. This is why it is so important to examine all these groups of axillary lymph nodes when performing a breast exam. Most of the rest of the lymph drainage from the breast goes to the parasternal nodes, although a small amount goes to the opposite breast and a small amount drains to the abdominal wall. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 737

486.q: Which among the following flaps is not used in breast reconstruction surgery?
486.e: Autologous tissue reconstruction in breast surgery is done using the following muscle flaps- Latissimus dorsi flap - based on the thoracodorsal pedicle Muscle-preserving perforator abdominal flaps - Ex: Deep inferior epigastric perforator flap Transverse rectus abdominis flap - based on superior or inferior epigastric artery or both. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 53, Edition: 27th, Pg: 879

486.q: Where does the lymphatic spread occur for a tumour in the posterior one-third of the breast?
486.e: Lymphatic metastasis- Occurs primarily to the axillary and the internal mammary lymph nodes. Tumours in the posterior one-third of the breast are more likely to drain to the internal mammary nodes . Involvement of supraclavicular nodes and of any contralateral lymph nodes represents advanced disease. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 932

486.q: Which among the following is not the clinical finding of the staphylococcal breast abscess?
486.e: Staphylococcal abscess - Present with point tenderness, erythema, and hyperthermia . Treatment - Initial approach is with analgesics, antibiotics and repeated aspiration of the abscess. Incision and drainage is done if Abscess is not resolving with repeated aspiration and antibiotic therapy Thinning or necrosis of the overlying skin Staphylococcus aureus (localised, involves deeper breast tissue) and Streptococcus species (diffuse superficial involvement) are the organisms most frequently recovered from nipple discharge from an infected breast. Reference : Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 11 th , Pg: 550

486.q: Which among the following is the most common cause of spontaneous nipple discharge from the single duct of the breast?
486.e: The most common cause of spontaneous nipple discharge from a single duct is a solitary intraductal papilloma (60%-80%) in one of the large subareolar ducts under the nipple. Subareolar duct ectasia producing inflammation and dilatation of large collecting ducts under the nipple is common (20%) and usually involves discharge from multiple ducts. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 35, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 814

486.q: Which among the following findings is seen in duct ectasia of breast?
486.e: Duct ectasia/periductal mastitis- This is a dilatation of the breast ducts, which is often associated with periductal inflammation. The disease is more common in smokers . Nipple discharge (of any colour), a subareolar mass, abscess, mammary duct fistula and/or nipple retraction are the most common symptoms. Pathogenesis - Initially, there is a dilatation in one or more of the larger lactiferous ducts, which fill with a stagnant black or green secretion . This may discharge. These fluids then set up an irritant reaction in surrounding tissue, leading to periductal mastitis or even abscess and fistula formation. In some cases, a chronic indurated mass forms beneath the areola, which mimics a carcinoma. Fibrosis eventually develops, which may cause slit-like nipple retraction. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 929

486.q: What is the size in diameter of giant fibroadenomas?
486.e: Giant Fibroadenoma Occasionally occur during puberty . They are over 5 cm in diameter and are often rapidly growing. Other features are similar to fibroadenoma. Enucleated through a submammary incision . They are more common in the Afro-Caribbean Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 922

487.q: For which type(s) of cancer is prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) typically given? 1. Lung cancer 2. Liver cancer 3. Prostate cancer 4. Breast cancer
487.e: Explanation: Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) is primarily used to reduce the risk of brain metastases in cancers that have a high likelihood of spreading to the central nervous system. Lung Cancer: PCI is most commonly administered in small cell lung cancer (SCLC) due to its aggressive nature and high tendency to metastasize to the brain. It has been shown to improve overall survival and decrease the incidence of brain metastases in patients who respond to initial treatment. Breast Cancer: PCI may be considered in select cases of breast cancer, particularly in patients at high risk for brain metastases. This includes aggressive subtypes such as HER2-positive and triple-negative breast cancer . Options A, B, and D are incorrect. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9020164/ https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4477380/

487.q: Where is the most common skeletal metastasis seen in the patient of breast tumour?
487.e: Skeletal metastases occurs via the bloodstream in breast carcinoma. The commonly involved sites in order of frequency include - Lumbar vertebrae - most common Femur Thoracic vertebrae Ribs Skull The deposits are generally more osteolytic than osteoblastic . Metastases may also commonly occur in the liver, lungs and brain and, occasionally, the adrenal glands and ovaries via the bloodstream. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 53, Edition: 27th, Pg: 873

487.q: Which among the following is not a clinical finding of the fibrocystic disease of the breast?
487.e: Nipple discharge is not a feature of fibrocystic disease of the breast. Fibrocystic disease of the breast - Common during the fourth and fifth decades of life , generally lasting until menopause. There is an exaggerated response of breast stroma and epithelium to various circulating and locally produced hormones and growth factors. Characterized by the constellation of premenstrual cyclic breast pain, tenderness, and nodularity. As per Bailey it is not seen, so go with choice 3 Reference: Bailey & Love's SHORT PRACTICE of SURGERY, 28th edition, PART 8: ENDOCRINE AND BREAST, Chapter no.58

487.q: Which among the following is not commonly associated with male breast carcinoma?
487.e: Risk factors for carcinoma of the male breast include- Gynaecomastia Excess endogenous or exogenous oestrogen. BRCA2 mutation Klinefeltor syndrome Infiltrating ductal carcinoma is the most common type of breast cancer in men. Diagnosis, grading, treatment and prognosis are the same as female breast cancer. BRCA2 mutation mostly causes a hormone receptor positive tumor. Hence tamoxifen can be used for treatment. Reference : Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 11 th , Pg: 551, 600

487.q: Which of the following benign breast conditions has the LEAST associated risk of developing invasive ductal carcinoma?
487.e: Explanation: Based on consensus pathological classification (e.g., from the American College of Pathologists), benign breast conditions carry varying risks for subsequent breast cancer: No Increased Risk: Conditions like squamous metaplasia , adenosis, cysts, and fibroadenoma. Slightly Increased Risk (1.5-2x): Florid epithelial hyperplasia and papilloma with a fibrovascular core . (Option A and B ruled out) Moderately Increased Risk (~5x): Atypical hyperplasia (a high-risk lesion). (Option C ruled out) Therefore, squamous metaplasia is a benign change with no documented increased risk of breast cancer development. Key Takeaways: Not all benign breast disease carries the same cancer risk. Atypical hyperplasia confers the highest risk among the options given.

487.q: All of the following are risk factors for infection of shunt except?
o: Staff movement in and out of the theatre
487.e: 75% of shunt infections present within 1 month, reflecting introduction at the time of insertion. Risk factors include - Very young patients Open myelomeningocoele Long operation time Staff movement in and out of theatre Treatment - Removal of shunt Antibiotic therapy Shunt reinserted at a new site after infection resolves. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 705-706

487.q: All of the following are risk factors for aneurysmal bleeding except?
487.e: Aneurysmal bleeding has an incidence of 10 - 15 per 100 000 population per year. Risk factors include age, female sex, hypertension, smoking, cocaine abuse and A family history with two first-degree relatives affected. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 709

487.q: Pressure to cause the pressure sore is:
487.e: Pressure sores occur as a result of friction or persisting pressure on soft tissues. The pressure to cause the pressure sore is 30mm Hg. They particularly affect the pressure points of a recumbent patient, including the sacrum, greater trochanter and heels. Order of involvement of bed sores: ischium> greater trochanter> sacrum Risk factors are poor nutritional status, dehydration, lack of mobility and nerve block anaesthesia technique. Early mobilisation of the patient and regular inspection of pressure points by the nursing team can act to prevent pressure sores. High-risk patients may be nursed on an air mattress, which automatically relieves the pressure areas. Keep patients mobile or regularly turned if bed-bound

488.q: Best diagnostic method for parathyroid adenoma is
488.e: Preference investigations for parathyroid diseases in terms of reliablity ( from best to least ) PET - CT - MOST RELIABLE Sestamibi SPECT - better than Tc99m sestamibi scan Tech 99m - Sestamibi scan- most commonly used USG - LEAST RELIABLE The sensitivity of sestamibi SPECT is 79% for Parathyroid adenoma. The sensitivity of PET\CT is 93 % for Parathyroid adenoma.

488.q: A 45 year old female patient on examination of her breast a 4.5cm * 3cm size irregular mass is felt in the left upper quadrant of the right breast which is not fixed to the pectoralis major muscle and no skin changes, a 2cm*1.5cm lymph node is also palpated in the right axilla. No mass felt in the opposite breast. What all investigations will you do to this patient? 1. Mammography 2. PET scan 3. Biopsy of the breast mass 4. USG guided biopsy of the enlarged axillary lymph node
488.e: According to the case scenario-staging of breast carcinoma - T2N1 - early breast cancer Mammography in two planes and ultrasonography are the first line investigations for imaging the breast, it is done for both the breast and also to look for multicnetricity PET scan is done for locally advanced breast cancer TRU CUT biopsy of lump is the gold standard investigation as it is a tissue diagnosis USG guided biopsy of the enlarged axillary lymph node is of no use as, if axillary lymph node are enlarged itself indicates local metastasis, which should be managed by axillary dissection.

489.q: Which among the following statements is false for inflammatory carcinoma of the breast?
o: Presents with painful, swollen breast with cutaneous oedema
It results from blockage of intramuscular lymphatics with carcinoma cells
489.e: Inflammatory carcinoma - Rare Highly aggressive Presents as a painful, swollen breast, which is warm with cutaneous oedema. Due to blockage of the subdermal lymphatics with carcinoma cells. Inflammatory cancer usually involves at least one-third of the breast and may mimic a breast abscess. A biopsy will confirm the diagnosis and show undifferentiated carcinoma cells. It used to be rapidly fatal but with aggressive chemotherapy and radiotherapy and with salvage surgery the prognosis has improved considerably. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 53, Edition: 27 th , Pg: 872

489.q: Which among the following is not the modality for staging carcinoma?
489.e: The goals of preoperative staging are to gain information on prognosis, to counsel the patient effectively, and to determine the extent of disease to decide the most appropriate course of therapy. The three main treatment pathways are upfront resection (with or without subsequent adjuvant therapy), neoadjuvant therapy followed by resection, or treatment of systemic disease without resection The main modalities for staging gastric adenocarcinoma are upper endoscopy; EUS; cross-sectional imaging such as CT, MRI, and/or positron emission tomography (PET); and diagnostic laparoscopy. Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 49, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1222

490.q: After mastectomy, breast reconstruction is done by
490.e: Answer- B. latissimus dorsi If the skin at the mastectomy site is poor (e.g. following radiotherapy) or if a larger volume of tissue is required, a musculocutaneous flap can be constructed either from the latissimusdorsi muscle (an LD flap) or using the transversusabdominis muscle (a TRAM flap as). The latter gives an excellent cosmetic result in experienced hands but is a lengthy procedure and requires careful patient selection.

490.q: What is the most prevalent condition that leads to the occurrence of heartburn and chest pain in a patient?
490.e: Explanation: Esophagitis refers to inflammation of the esophageal mucosa. It presents with chest pain, heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia. Proton pump inhibitors are the mainstay of treatment. Explanation of other options: Barrett's esophagus (Option A): Involves squamous-to-columnar mucosal change in the lower esophagus, usually after long-standing reflux. Pneumonia (Option B): A lung infection causing cough, fever, and infiltrates, not isolated heartburn or chest pain. Myocardial infarction (Option C): Due to ischemia; presents with crushing chest pain radiating to the arm/neck, not relieved by PPIs.

491.q: A 27-year-old female presents with a thyroid swelling. Which of the following symptoms is unlikely to occur due to compression of adjacent structures?
o: Hoarseness of voice due to recurrent laryngeal nerve compression
491.e: Explanation: Thyroid enlargement can compress adjacent structures, producing multiple clinical manifestations. Hoarseness of voice due to recurrent laryngeal nerve compression (Option A): The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs posteromedial to the thyroid. Compression may cause hoarseness , vocal cord paresis, or paralysis. Dysphagia due to esophagus compression (Option B): The esophagus lies medial and posterior to the thyroid. Compression can lead to difficulty swallowing or dysphagia. Superior vena cava syndrome (Option C): Although the SVC is located in the superior mediastinum and is rarely affected, large substernal goiters or massive thyroid enlargements can rarely cause SVC compression, leading to facial and upper limb edema, dyspnea, and facial plethora.

491.q: In a 35-years old pregnant female with hyperthyroidism, which antithyroid drug should be given in the first trimester?
491.e: Antithyroid drugs Those in common use are carbimazole and propylthiouracil : these are ANTI-TPO drugs. Antithyroid drugs are used to restore the patient to a euthyroid state and to maintain this for a prolonged period in the hope that a permanent remission will occur, i.e. that production of TSH-RAb will diminish or cease. Propylthiouracil has no teratogenicity effect. Antithyroid drugs cannot cure a toxic nodule. The overactive thyroid tissue is autonomous and recurrence of the hyperthyroidism is certain when the drug is discontinued. Anti-thyroids in pregnancy: 1 st trimester: propylthiouracil is used (carbimazole not used because it's teratogenic and may cause aplasia cutis) 2 nd trimester onwards: carbimazole (propylthiouracil not used throughout pregnancy due to risk of hepatitis)

491.q: Which among the following radioactive substance is not used in the thyroid scintigraphy technique?
491.e: Thyroid scintigraphy is performed using either technetium-99m pertechnetate or a radiolabelled iodine nuclide (typically 123I or 131I). Depending on the specific study, the tracer can be administered intravenously, orally, or via inhalation, and images are obtained anywhere from 30 minutes (for intravenous [IV] injection) to 24 hours (for oral administration) afterward. The thyroid normally displays symmetric uptake bilaterally. Nodular disease can be classified into whether there is increased focal uptake (the so-called "hot" nodule) or not (the "cold" nodule). Classically, "hot" nodules in the setting of hyperthyroidism are thought to be benign toxic nodules with extremely low risk of malignancy, whereas "cold" nodules carry a 15% risk of malignancy. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 882

491.q: Which of the following is not an indication for parathyroidectomy in a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism?
o: Serum calcium > 1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal
491.e: Explanation: Creatinine clearance Indications for Parathyroidectomy: Serum calcium > 0.25 mmol/L (1.0 mg/dL) above the upper limit of normal. (Option A ruled out) Bone Mineral Density (BMD) by DEXA : T-score ≤ -2.5 at the lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, or distal one-third of radius . Vertebral fracture . Creatinine clearance 60 mL/min . 24-hour urinary calcium > 10 mmol/dL (>400 mg/day) (Option B ruled out) or increased risk of stone formation Age

491.q: Which of the following is a false statement regarding cystic masses of the neck?
o: Type 3 branchial fistula has its internal orifice on cricopharyngeus
Cystic hygroma is filled with clear lymph
Thyroglossal cyst moves upwards on swallowing and tongue protrusion
Fluctuation is positive in branchial cyst
491.e: Explanation: Type 3 branchial fistula passes between the internal and external carotid arteries and may open into the lateral pharyngeal wall or reach the skull base. It does not open on the cricopharyngeus muscle. Explanation of other options: Cystic hygroma is filled with clear lymph (Option B): Correct. It is a congenital lymphatic malformation. Thyroglossal cyst moves upwards on swallowing and tongue protrusion (Option C): Correct. Classical clinical sign due to attachment to the tongue. Fluctuation is positive in branchial cyst (Option D): Correct. Branchial cysts are fluctuant swellings, often soft and sometimes transilluminant.

491.q: Investigation of choice for studying Renal Cortical mass
491.e: C i.e. 99 - Tc - DMSA DTPA (Renogram) DMSA (Isotope Scanning) - DTPA is freely filtered at - Tc.99 DMSA is used for renal glomerulus with no morphological tubular reabsorption or (anatomic) imagine excretion (i.e. GFR = - This compound gets fixed in renal Excretory function) tubules & images - DTPA is useful for evaluating may be obtained after 1-2 hours of perfusion and injection. Lesions excretory function of each such as tumors & benign lesions as kidneyQ cysts show filling - Indications:defectQ

491.q: Appropriate FNAC specimen in case of thyroid contains:
o: 3 follicular cell groups containing 10-12 cells each
6 follicular cell groups containing 10-15 cells each
10 follicular cell groups containing 6-8 cells each
6-8 follicular cell groups containing 10-15 cells each
491.e: All Bethesda categories were included in the present study. The parameter used to determine the satisfactoriness of the specimens was the presence of at least six clusters of thyroid follicular cells , with each cluster including at least 10 follicular cells with good preservation . All specimens were obtained by an endocrinologist and without using ultrasound. The prepared slides were stained with the Papanicolaou stain . The histological diagnoses were classified into three types: Benign and nonneoplastic, Benign and neoplastic, and Malignant. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4707785/

491.q: Which among the following thyroid carcinoma is associated with adrenal pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism?
491.e: Some tumours are familial and account for 10–20% of all cases. Medullary carcinoma may occur in combination with adrenal phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism (HPT) (usually due to hyperplasia) in the syndrome known as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN-2A). The familial form of the disease frequently affects children and young adults, whereas the sporadic cases occur at any age with no sex predominance. When the familial form is associated with prominent mucosal neuromas involving the lips, tongue and inner aspect of the eyelids, with a Marfanoid habitus, the syndrome is referred to as MEN type 2B. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 870-871

492.q: Which among the following thyroid malignancy shows the symptom of diarrhoea?
492.e: Are tumours of the parafollicular (C cells) derived from the neural crest. rather than the cells of the thyroid follicle as are other primary thyroid carcinomas. The cells are not unlike those of a carcinoid tumour and on histological analysis a characteristic amyloid stroma is seen. High levels of serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen are produced by many medullary tumours, which should be tested for in suspected cases. Calcitonin levels fall after resection and rise again with recurrence, making it a valuable tumour marker in the follow-up of patients with this disease. Diarrhoea is a feature in 30% of cases and this may be due to 5-hydroxytryptamine or prostaglandins produced by the tumour cells. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 870-871

492.q: Which among the following cancer shows the presence of psammoma bodies?
492.e: Explanation: Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common type of thyroid cancer overall, comprising 84% of all incident cases. Histologically, PTC is characterised by complex branching papillae with pseudo-inclusions, nuclear grooving, and psammoma bodies. The so-called follicular variant of PTC (fvPTC) has a similar prognosis to classical PTC and histologically has well-defined follicles with minimal papillary projections. Other less common but more aggressive histologic subtypes of PTC include tall cell, hobnail, diffuse sclerosing, and columnar variants, which together comprise less than 1% of all PTCs.

492.q: Which among the following is the most aggressive thyroid malignancy?
492.e: This is one of the most aggressive malignancies in humans. Thankfully it is rare. It may develop de novo , or present as dedifferentiation of a papillary or poorly differentiated carcinoma. The disease is characterised by rapid growth, visceral invasion and distant metastases. The surgeon’s role in this disease is crucial. Thyroid lymphoma can be incorrectly diagnosed as anaplastic cancer and so biopsy is critical. This can be done using a core or open technique. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 868

492.q: Which among the following is not the criteria for total thyroidectomy in a patient of differential thyroid carcinoma?
492.e: Total thyroidectomy remains the preferred evidence-based approach for DTCs associated with higher risk factors, such as: Tumor size of at least 4 cm. Presence of gross extrathyroidal extension. Evidence of metastatic disease. Radiation-induced DTC. Familial non medullary thyroid cancer. Multifocal bilateral DTC. In summary, the management of differentiated thyroid carcinomas has evolved to consider a more tailored approach, with total thyroidectomy reserved for higher-risk cases. Smaller tumors, between 1 and 4 cm, without specific high-risk features may be managed with thyroid lobectomy or near-total thyroidectomy based on the patient's clinical profile. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 903

492.q: After a total thyroidectomy under GA, the anesthetist tried to extubate the patient but he was unable to extubate. What is the most probable reason?
492.e: In b\l recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, both the abductor's of vocal cords(posterior cricoarytenoid-safety muscle of larynx) is paralysed So the vocal cords come into cadaveric position which is very dangerous leading to stridor If u\l recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, there will be only hoarseness of voice If external laryngeal nerve injury, there will be husky voice If internal laryngeal nerve injury -leads to aspiration, as sensory innervation of larynx is lost

493.q: A 44 year old Asian man presents with epigastric pains of burning nature. The pain was worst at night. He was prescribed combinations of antacids for a year and but this did not relieve his symptoms entirely. He had an endoscopy which did not show any significant abnormalities 3 months ago. Which is the best test for further investigation for this patient?
493.e: This patient presents with features of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). In some cases of GERD, endoscopic signs may be absent due to- A partially treated disease In nonerosive reflux disease - most common cause. In such instances, 24 hour oesophageal pH study can demonstrate excessive esophageal exposure to refluxed gastric fluid, the physiologic abnormality of GERD. Urease breath test is done to identify Helicobacter pylori. Gastric biopsy is done in cases of suspected gastric carcinoma. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2424

493.q: A 38 year old man presents with epigastric pains which are burning in nature and worse at night. He undergoes endoscopy and the investigation confirms a diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). Which of the following is most likely to relieve his symptoms?
493.e: The most effective drugs in Gastro-oesophageal reflux are proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole. Treatment for GORD includes - Lifestyle changes - Avoiding foods that reduce LES pressure like coffee, alcohol, fatty foods Avoiding acidic foods like citrus fruits, tomato based foods Weight loss Pharmacological treatment -PPI like omeprazole >> H2 receptor antagonists like ranitidine Surgical management -Nissen fundoplication -In refractory cases Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st , Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

493.q: A 58-year-old male presents with dysphagia, retrosternal discomfort and weight loss. Studies reveal achalasia. Which of the following is most definitive way to provide symptomatic relief?
493.e: The only durable therapies for achalasia are pneumatic dilation and LES myotomy (Heller myotomy). The patient shows excellent symptom improvement. Reflux is the most common side effect and a concomitant anti-relfux procedure (Nissen's fundoplication) may be performed. Both calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) and nitrates relax the lower oesophageal sphincter. However the effect on symptoms is variable, short-lived and usually suboptimal. Use is frequently limited by adverse effects. Consequently medical therapy is typically limited to those patients too frail or unwilling to undergo definitive treatment or other therapies. Latest treatment is POEM. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 23,Pg: 2427-2428

493.q: A 42 year old man who usually drinks only 2 units of alcohol a day went on an alcohol binge with his friends. On that day, he vomited 10 times and was brought to hospital feeling very unwell. He has not previously had any symptoms of dyspepsia or abdominal pains. During physical assessment, he vomits a large bowlful of blood. What is the likely cause of his haemetemesis?
493.e: This is a case of Mallory Weiss tear . Longitudinal tear in the mucosa at the gastroesophageal junction . Caused by forceful or prolonged vomiting or coughing. They may also be caused by epileptic convulsions. Usually seen in alcoholics, bulimia nervosa patients. The tear may be followed by vomiting bright red blood or by passing blood in the stool. Active bleed can be treated by endoscopy (band ligation or coaptive coagulation). A transmural rupture at gastroesophageal junction is called Boerhaave's syndrome. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2433

493.q: A 40-year-old man is referred with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD).Which of the following concerning GERD is correct?
o: Acid suppressant therapy should not be given continuously
Esophageal pH monitoring is a good guide to therapy
Symptoms do not correlate with mucosal status at endoscopy
493.e: Symptoms of GERD do not correlate with the mucosal appearances at endoscopy. PPIs can be given continuously where the diagnosis has been satisfactorily proven and relapse of symptoms persist after withdrawal. Although endoscopy can be performed in cases that are not clear cut or do not respond to proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), it is not mandatory. The doubt of Barrett's oesophagus can only be clarified with biopsy. Monitoring of pH is not a good guide to therapy. Symptomatic improvement is a good guide to the efficacy of therapy. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st , Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

493.q: Which among the following cytokines is not a contributing factor in intestinal inflammatory disease?
493.e: Immunologic factors. Humoral and cell-mediated immune reactions directed againstintestinal cells in Crohn disease suggest an autoimmune phenomenon. Attention has focused on the role of cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1, IL-2, IL- 8, and TNF-α, as contributing factors in the intestinal inflammatory response. The role of the immune response remains controversial in Crohn disease and may represent an effect of the disease process rather than an actual cause. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 1259

493.q: A young girl presented with reflux and retrosternal discomfort. Best investigation for this?
493.e: Ambulatory reflux monitoring is considered one of the most important confrmatory tests for GORD. There are two types of monitoring devices: catheter based and wireless capsule. Both measure the pH value at 5-6 cm above the upper border of the LOS, Ambulatory refux monitoring is considered one of the most important confrmatory tests for GORD. There are two types of monitoring devices: catheter based and wireless capsule. Both measure the pH value at 5-6 cm above the upper border of the LOS, A composite score (Johnson-DeMeester) consists of six parameters that can be calculated. The patient needs to record their symptoms throughout the study period, so that symptom correlation with pH data can be calculated.

494.q: Which is the first line investigation for oesophageal cancer?
494.e: Investigation Endoscopy is the first-line investigation for most patients. It provides an unrivalled direct view of the oesophageal mucosa and any lesion allowing its site and size to be documented. Cytology and/or histology specimens taken via the endoscope are crucial for accurate diagnosis. The combination of histology and cytology increases the diagnostic accuracy to more than 95%. The chief limitation of conventional endoscopy is that only the mucosal surface can be studied and biopsied. Other investigations are therefore usually required to define the extent of local or distant spread. The improved image resolution of modern endoscopes and novel techniques involving magnification and the use of dyes to enhance surface detail may lead to more early lesions being recognised. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1136-1137

494.q: What is the margin of resection in oesophageal cancer?
494.e: PRINCIPLES The principle of oesophagectomy is to deal adequately with the local tumour in order to minimise the risk of local recurrence and achieve an adequate lymphadenectomy to reduce the risk of staging error. Although studies in Japan would indicate that more extensive lymphadenectomy is associated with better survival, this may simply reflect more accurate staging. A number of studies support the view that the proximal extent of resection should ideally be 10 cm above the macroscopic tumour and 5 cm distal. When such a margin cannot be achieved proximally, particularly with squamous cell carcinoma, there is evidence that postoperative radiotherapy can minimise local recurrence, although this does not improve survival. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1141

494.q: Rat tail appearance in contrast radiography is seen in?
494.e: Carcinoma esophagus REF: sabiston's 18' edition chapter 41 See table in the previous question "Rat-tail" appearance on barium study is seen in carcinoma esophagus.

494.q: Which of the following is the best investigation to establish a diagnosis of GERD?
494.e: Explanation: 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring is considered the gold standard for objectively diagnosing GERD. It directly measures the frequency and duration of acid reflux episodes (pH Explanation of other options: Upper GI endoscopy (Option B): Endoscopy is excellent for visualizing complications of GERD (esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, strictures) but is often normal in patients with non-erosive reflux disease (NERD), making it less sensitive for establishing the initial diagnosis. CECT & MRI (Options C and D): Cross-sectional imaging like CT and MRI have no role in the routine diagnosis of GERD, as they cannot detect acid reflux. Key Takeaways: 24-hour pH monitoring is the gold standard for diagnosing GERD. Endoscopy is used to assess for complications, not primarily for diagnosis.

494.q: Which among the following is not the symptom for gastric carcinoma?
494.e: The symptoms of gastric cancer are generally vague and nonspecific, contributing to its frequently advanced stage at the time of diagnosis. Symptoms include epigastric pain, early satiety, and weight loss . These symptoms are frequently mistaken for more common benign causes of dyspepsia including PUD and gastritis. The epigastric pain associated with gastric cancer tends to be constant and non radiating and is generally not relieved by eating. More advanced lesions may manifest with either gastric outlet obstruction or/strong> dysphagia depending on the location of the tumor. Some degree of GI bleeding is common, with 40% of patients having some form of anemia. Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 49, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1222

494.q: What are the laboratory findings seen in medullary carcinoma of thyroid?
o: Low calcitonin and high carcinoembryonic antigen
Low calcitonin and low carcinoembryonic antigen
High calcitonin and high carcinoembryonic antigen
494.e: These are tumours of the parafollicular (C cells) derived from the neural crest. rather than the cells of the thyroid follicle as are other primary thyroid carcinomas. The cells are not unlike those of a carcinoid tumour and on histological analysis a characteristic amyloid stroma is seen. High levels of serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen are produced by many medullary tumours, which should be tested for in suspected cases. Calcitonin levels fall after resection and rise again with recurrence, making it a valuable tumour marker in the follow-up of patients with this disease. Diarrhoea is a feature in 30% of cases and this may be due to 5-hydroxytryptamine or prostaglandins produced by the tumour cells. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 870-871

495.q: A 46 year woman is admitted due to a single episode of haematemesis after taking a tablet of ibuprofen 6 hours previously. On examination, she had a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg (lying) and 95/60 mmHg (standing). Her haemoglobin concentration is 7.5 g/dL. What is the likely cause of the haemetemesis?
495.e: The likely answer is gastric erosions because the bleeding occurred after only one dose of Ibuprofen. There is no previous history of dyspepsia or upper GI bleeding. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs ( NSAIDs ) such as aspirin, ibuprofen, and naproxen cause gastric erosions via - Can be direct irritants of gastric mucosa Prostaglandins have a protective role in maintaining mucosal integrity. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin production . Because of gravity, the irritants lie on the greater curvature of the stomach, and therefore, gastritis and ulcers are seen distally on or near the greater curvature of the stomach . Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 48, Pg: 312

495.q: A 52 year old lady complains of epigastric burning pains due to stress. She finally undergoes an UGI endoscopy which shows gastro-oesophageal reflux. Which medication is the most effective for her condition?
495.e: The main pharmacological therapy for GERD is inhibition of gastric acid suppression . Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, lansoprazole and pantoprazole are more effective than H2 receptor blockers such as ranitidine, cimetidine or nizatidine. Healing in oesophagitis is better with a PPI. Bismuth is a mucosal protective agent used in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease. Magnesium hydroxide is an antacid. It is not as effective as PPI for GERD. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

495.q: A 35 years old male with gastric outlet obstruction presented to emergency with multiple episodes of vomiting. Which of the following fluids is preferred for this patient?
495.e: Treatment of gastric outlet obstruction: Treating the patient involves correcting the metabolic abnormalities and dealing with the mechanical obstruction. The patient should be rehydrated with intravenous isotonic saline with potassium supplementation. Replacing the sodium chloride and water allows the kidney to correct the acid-base abnormality. The metabolic abnormalities may be less if the obstruction is due to malignancy, as the acid-base disturbance is less pronounced.

495.q: A new born child presented with bilious vomiting. What will be the most appropriate test to diagnose the condition in this baby?
495.e: With the above history , bilious vomiting suggest the obstruction may be form duodenum and beyond Barium meal follow through helps in delineating the small bowel hence is used for diagnosis Gastrograffin dye is used most of the time instead of barium

495.q: Which is the common site for peptic ulcer?
495.e: Common sites for peptic ulcers are the first part of the duodenum and the lesser curve of the stomach , but they also occur on the stoma following gastric surgery, the oesophagus and even in a Meckel's diverticulum , which contains ectopic gastric epithelium. In general, the ulcer occurs at a junction between different types of epithelia, the ulcer occurring in the epithelium least resistant to acid damage. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1157

495.q: Which among the following condition shows hourglass contraction of stomach?
495.e: Pathology This is essentially similar to that of a duodenal ulcer, except that gastric ulcers tend to be larger. Fibrosis, when it occurs, may result in the now rarely seen hourglass contraction of the stomach. Large chronic ulcers may erode posteriorly into the pancreas and, on other occasions, into major vessels such as the splenic artery. Less commonly, they may erode into other organs such as the transverse colon. Chronic gastric ulcers are much more common on the lesser curve (especially at the incisura angularis; than on the greater curve and, even when high on the lesser curve, they tend to be at the boundary between the acid-secreting and the non-acid secreting epithelia. With atrophy of parietal cell mass, non-acid-secreting epithelium migrates up the lesser curvature. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1158

495.q: Which among the following factors is not associated with poor outcome in case of perforated peptic ulcer?
495.e: There are patients who have small leaks from a perforated peptic ulcer and relatively mild peritoneal contamination, who may be managed with intravenous fluids, nasogastric suction and antibiotics. These patients are in the minority. A number of factors have been associated with poor outcome after perforated peptic ulcer, including: Delay in diagnosis (>24 hours); Medical comorbidities; Shock; Increasing age (>75). Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1164-1165

495.q: What is the most common site of abdominal tuberculosis?
495.e: The most common site of the gastrointestinal TB is ileocecal location (ileocecal TB), followed by jejunum and colon. The esophagus, stomach and duodenum are rarely involved. Reference: www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4209546

496.q: A 56--year-old male stomach cancer patient underwent surgery. After surgery, lab reports show Hb = 7.8, MCH= 28, MCV= 120. His anemia is caused by a deficiency of X and can be treated with Y.
o: X = intrinsic factor; Y = folic acid
X = intrinsic factor; Y = vitamin B12
X = extrinsic factor; Y = parenteral iron
496.e: Resection of the stomach does lead to loss of intrinsic factor and the patient will be deficient in vitamin B12. Prevention or treatment of iron deficiency anemia (microcytic cell size) is the only indication for iron administration. Sargramostim is a GM-CSF and is used to stimulate the production of neutrophils and other myeloid and megakaryocyte progenitors. Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834-39

496.q: With respect to gastric carcinoma, which of the following statements is true?
o: Aspirin use is a risk factor for gastric carcinoma
Early diagnosis of gastric carcinoma results in a five year survival rate of 20%
Endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning for local tumour staging
Helicobacter pylori infection is not associated with gastric carcinoma
496.e: Incidence of distal stomach tumors is actually decreasing while the incidence of tumors in the proximal stomach is increasing. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use is associated with decreased risk of certain gastric tumors. pylori infection has been associated in a number of studies with increased risk of gastric carcinoma. Screening for gastric carcinoma in Japan detects up to 40% of gastric carcinomas at an early stage and in skilled hands five year survival can be upwards of 90%. Computed tomography (CT) with gastric dilatation is a useful complementary investigation in the staging of gastric carcinoma, but endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning as it is able to assess depth of infiltration and lymphatic dissemination of tumor. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 80, Pg: 629-632

496.q: A visible mass in epigastrium with CD117 positive, but cytokeratin and S-100 negative. What is the diagnosis?
496.e: Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) may arise in any part of the gastrointestinal tract but 50% will be found in the stomach. Previously named leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma, the term GIST is now used, recognising the distinct phenotype. They are tumours of mesenchymal origin and are observed equally commonly in males and females. The tumours are universally associated with a mutation in the tyrosine kinase c-kit oncogene. Most GISTs occur due to gain of function mutation in receptor tyrosine kinase KIT or PDGFR-alpha. Most useful marker is CD-117. Carney triad - GIST + paraganglioma + pulmonary chondroma.

497.q: The immediate postoperative period is associated with predictable hormonal and metabolic shifts. Several electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities commonly occur, while some do not. Which one of the following is not typically seen in the immediate postoperative period?
497.e: Explanation: In the immediate postoperative period, patients often develop hyperkalaemia or normal potassium levels due to tissue breakdown, acidosis and decreased renal excretion. Hypokalaemia is not typically seen . Normal metabolic changes in the immediate postoperative period include: Negative nitrogen balance due to catabolic stress hormones (Option A) Glucose intolerance due to increased cortisol, catecholamines and insulin resistance (Option C) Hyponatremia due to ADH surge and water retention (Option D) Potassium tends to be normal or high , not low, because of increased catabolism, acidemia and reduced renal clearance

497.q: Which among the following is helpful in determining organ function after transplant?
497.e: The factors determining organ function after transplantation include - A] Donor characteristics - Extremes of age Presence of pre-existing damage in transplanted organ Haemodynamic and metabolic instability B] Procurement-related factors - Warm ischaemic time Type of preservation solution Cold ischaemic time C] Recipient-related factors - Technical factors relating to implantation Haemodynamic and metabolic stability Immunological factors Presence of drugs that impair transplant function Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th Edition, Chapter 82, Transplantation, Pg: 1549.

497.q: Which among the following statements is false for action of thyroid hormones?
o: Metabolic effects are due to bound T3 and T4
T3 is more important physiological hormone
497.e: The metabolic effects of the thyroid hormones are due to unbound free T4 and T3 (0.03% and 0.3% of the total circulating hormones, respectively). T3 is the more important physiological hormone and is also produced in the periphery by conversion from T4. T3 is quick acting (within a few hours), whereas T4 acts more slowly (4-14 days). Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 852

497.q: Which of the following is the most common deficiency observed after gastric bypass/bariatric surgery?
497.e: Explanation: Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB). This occurs due to two main reasons: Bypass of the Duodenum: The primary site of iron absorption is bypassed. Reduced Gastric Acid: The new gastric pouch produces little acid, and iron requires an acidic environment for conversion into its absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) form. This often leads to iron-deficiency anemia, presenting as fatigue and pallor. Copper and zinc deficiencies may occur but are less common than iron deficiency, while calcium deficiency is frequent due to reduced intake and vitamin D malabsorption, yet iron deficiency remains the most common. (Options B,C and D ruled out) Key Takeaways: Iron deficiency is the most prevalent micronutrient deficiency after gastric bypass. Lifelong supplementation and monitoring are required after bariatric surgery.

497.q: All of the following metabolic responses are seen in response to starvation except:
o: After 12 hours of fast liver glycogen converted into glucose.
After 24 hours of fasting, gluconeogenesis started from non-carbohydrate precursors.
After 1week of fasting, Central nervous system adapts to using ketone bodies as their primary Fuel.
Even though muscle contain glycogen it cannot be utilized directly.
497.e: Option A : After 12 hours of fast plasma insulin level falls and glucagon level rise which Facilitates conversion of liver glycogen into glucose. Option B : After more than 24 hours of fasting, Gluconeogenesis started from Amino acids particularly glutamine and alanine. Option C : After 48-72 hours not a week, central nervous system may adapt to using ketone bodies as their primary fuel source. Option D : Glycogen also exist in muscle but cannot be utilized directly. Muscle Glycogen is converted to lactate which is then exported to liver where It is converted to glucose. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 25, Edition: 28th, Pg: 329

497.q: All of the following are true regarding intussusception except?
o: In majority, the cause is hyperplasia of Peyer's patches
In 10% children, there is pathological lead point, such as a Meckel's diverticulum, enteric duplication of cyst or small bowel lymphoma
Sausage shaped mass is palpated in infra umbilical region
497.e: In the majority, the cause is hyperplasia of Peyer’s patches (lymphoid tissue), which may be secondary to a viral infection. In 10% of children, there is a pathological lead point, such as a Meckel’s diverticulum, enteric duplication cyst or even a small bowel lymphoma. Such cases are more likely in children over the age of 2 years and in those with recurrent intussusception. Classically, a previously healthy infant presents with colicky pain and vomiting (milk then bile). Between episodes, the child initially appears well. Later, they may pass a ‘redcurrant jelly’ stool. Clinical signs include dehydration, abdominal distension and a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Rectal examination may reveal blood or rarely the apex of the intussusceptum. Reference: Bailey and love’s short practice of surgery, 27 th edition, Page –129

497.q: The first structure to encounter at renal hilum during laparoscopic nephrectomy is?
497.e: At the renal hilum, The first structure encountered (i.e. the uppermost) is the renal vein Then the renal artery Lastly the renal pelvis . Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27 th Edition, Chapter 76, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1399.

497.q: Which among the following structures is not removed in the patey's mastectomy?
497.e: In Patey's mastectomy, the breast and associated structures are dissected en bloc and the excised mass is composed of - Whole breast tissue Skin over the breast tissue Nipple areola complex Fat, fascia and lymph nodes of the axilla. The pectoralis minor muscle is either divided or retracted to gain access to the upper two-thirds of the axilla. The axillary vein and nerves to the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi should be preserved . Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 935

498.q: Nutritional complications are more with which fistula?
498.e: Proximal small intestine fistulas will have high output → so metabolic and electrolyte complications are more common with proximal fistula The maximum malnutrition is caused by duodenal fistulas. Although gastric and duodenal fistulas receive almost the same food and enzymes, duodenum receives extra bile from gallbladder and pancreatic enzymes from pancreas hence duodenal fistula are more notorious for nutritional complications. Fistulas which are difficult to heal: F - foreign body in tract R - radiotherapy I - inflammatory bowel disease E - epithelialised tract N - neoplasia D - distal obstruction S - short fistulous tract ( Principles of management of enterocutaneous fistula (SNAP) S - elimination of Sepsis and skin protection N - Nutrition - a period of parenteral nutrition may well be required. A - Anatomical assessment P - definitive Planned surgery

498.q: A young man met with a motor bike accident and had injury to ileum and jejunum. Therefore the entire ileum and part of jejunum was resected. Which of the following would the patient suffer from?
498.e: If the jejunum is resected, the ileum can assume all the required absorptive functions, but resection of the terminal ileum will result in a diminished bile salt pool, vitamin B12 deficiency and may lead to deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. The ileum also plays an important role in water absorption, possibly because the tightness of the intercellular junctions supports a concentration gradient across its lumen. Significant ileal resection therefore commonly results in very troublesome diarrhea. The small intestine plays an important role in the metabolism of plasma lipoproteins, as it is the main site of synthesis of high-density, low-density and very low-density lipoproteins (HDL, LDL, VLDL).

498.q: A 45 years old male presents with complaints of pain in the abdomen, vomiting on and off and Diarrhea. Measurement of Serum creatinine is high. What is the probable diagnosis?
498.e: In the gastrointestinal tract, especially the small intestine, they secrete excess 5-HT , which is rapidly metabolized by the liver. In the presence of liver metastases, NET metastases secrete 5-HT into the IVC, avoiding hepatic first-pass metabolism and leading to symptoms of 5-HT excess, known as carcinoid syndrome . The cardinal features are sweating, flushing, bronchospasm and restrictive cardiomyopathy secondary to fibrotic right heart valvular disease (Hedinger syndrome ).

498.q: Which among the following obstruction leads to profuse early vomiting, rapid dehydration and minimal distention?
498.e: Features of obstruction In high small bowel obstruction, vomiting occurs early, is profuse and causes rapid dehydration. Distension is minimal with little evidence of dilated small bowel loops on abdominal radiography In low small bowel obstruction, pain is predominant with central distension. Vomiting is delayed. Multiple dilated small bowel loops are seen on radiography In large bowel obstruction, distension is early and pronounced. Pain is less severe and vomiting and dehydration are later features. The colon proximal to the obstruction is distended on abdominal radiography. The small bowel will be dilated if the ileocaecal valve is incompetent. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1381

498.q: What is the length of small intestine?
498.e: The length of the small bowel varies from 300 to 850 cm between the duodenojejunal (DJ) flexure to the ileocaecal valve . It is notoriously difficult to establish the length of the small intestine, and estimates gathered at surgery, at postmortem and during radiological investigations may vary widely, even in the same individual. In addition, there is considerable inter-individual variability and the small intestine has been said to be longer in men. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 74, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1306

498.q: Which vasoactive peptide is not produced by carcinoid tumour?
498.e: Carcinoid tumours These neuroendocrine tumours occur throughout the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly in the appendix, ileum and rectum in decreasing order of frequency. Appendicular carcinoid tumours are commonly noted as an incidental finding at appendicectomy, and are said to occur in approximately 2% of appendices removed surgically. The tumour arises from Kulchitsky cells at the base of intestinal crypts (of Lieberkuhn). Carcinoid tumours can produce a number of vasoactive peptides, most commonly 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin), but also histamine, prostaglandins and kallikrein. Plasma markers of tumour bulk, such as chromogranin A concentrations, may be useful markers of disease recurrence, as well as of prognostic value. CARCINOID TUMOR OF THE SMALL INTESTINE Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 74, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1310

498.q: Which type of pathological change is seen in Crohn's disease?
498.e: Crohn Disease Crohn disease is a chronic, transmural inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract for which the definitive cause is unknown, although a combination of genetic and environmental factors has been implicated. Crohn disease can involve any part of the alimentary tract from the mouth to the anus but most commonly affects the small intestine and colon. The most common clinical manifestations are abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and weight loss. Crohn disease can be complicated by intestinal obstruction or localized perforation with fistula formation. Medical and surgical treatments are palliative; however, operative therapy can provide effective symptomatic relief for patients with complications from Crohn disease and produces a reasonable long-term benefit. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 1258

498.q: Which among the following is not the common manifestation seen in Crohn's disease?
498.e: Crohn Disease Crohn disease is a chronic, transmural inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract for which the definitive cause is unknown, although a combination of genetic and environmental factors has been implicated. Crohn disease can involve any part of the alimentary tract from the mouth to the anus but most commonly affects the small intestine and colon. The most common clinical manifestations are abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and weight loss. Crohn disease can be complicated by intestinal obstruction or localized perforation with fistula formation. Medical and surgical treatments are palliative; however, operative therapy can provide effective symptomatic relief for patients with complications from Crohn disease and produces a reasonable long-term benefit. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 1258

499.q: When present with dynamic ileus, the C.difficile infection is identified by
499.e: Diarrhea is the most common manifestation caused by C. difficile. Stools are almost never grossly bloody and range from soft and unformed to watery or mucoid in consistency, with a characteristic odor. Clinical and laboratory findings include fever in 28% of cases, abdominal pain in 22%, and leukocytosis in 50%. When dynamic ileus (which is seen on x-ray in ~20% of cases) results in cessation of stool passage, the diagnosis of CDI is frequently overlooked. A clue to the presence of unsuspected CDI in these patients is unexplained leukocytosis , with ≥15,000 white blood cells (WBCs)/uL. Such patients are at high risk for complications of C. difficile infection, particularly toxic megacolon and sepsis . Reference : Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:134 Pg: 1068

499.q: Which of the following is most commonly associated with the development of pseudomembranous colitis?
499.e: Clostridium difficile a Gram positive anaerobic bacterium is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis. Studies show that when C. difficile colonise the gut they release two potent toxins, toxin A and toxin B, which bind to certain receptors in the lining of the colon and ultimately cause diarrhoea and inflammation of the large intestine or colon (colitis). Commonly the disease is caused by broad spectrum antibiotics most commonly cephalosporins , broad spectrum penicillins and clindamycin . Less commonly, macrolides and quinolones have been reported to cause the disorder. Oral Vancomycin and Fidaxomycin are the agents used for mild infections. Metronidazole is reserved for fulminant cases. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1069

500.q: What is the time range for air exchange in laminar airflow theatres?
500.e: Ultra-clean ventilation systems use high-efficiency particulateair (HEPA) filters that remove 99.9% of particulate matter >0.3 mm in diameter (bacteria are 0.5 mm). They also use vertical laminar airflow over the operating table to minimise turbulence, reduce contamination at the surgical site (horizontal laminar air flow is less effective (Salvati et al . 1982)). Laminar airflow theatres have an air exchange every 2-3 minutes. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, Appendix: 1, Edition: 27 th , Pg: 1563

500.q: What should be the optimum temperature in the operating rooms?
500.e: The operating lights disturb the laminar airflow and are optimally placed to either side of the operative wound with 0.6 m between the lights to minimise obstruction to the vertical airflow (Refaie et al . 2015). Temperature in the operating theatre should be between 18 and 25°C. Reference : Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, Appendix: 1, Edition: 27th, Pg: 1564

500.q: In which disease appendicectomy proves to be protective?
500.e: Aside from its tendency to cause surgical pathology the appendix, long thought to be a vestigial organ, may also have important roles in both immune function and maintaining the gut microbiota. The putative role of the appendix in the pathogenesis of ulcerative colitis (appendicectomy seems to be protective) for example, may be explained by its interaction with the intestinal flora and gut immune function. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1335

500.q: What is the name of the sign when deep palpation of the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa?
500.e: Deep palpation of the left iliac fossa may cause pain in the right iliac fossa, Rovsing's sign, which is helpful in supporting a clinical diagnosis of appendicitis. Occasionally, an inflamed appendix lies on the psoas muscle, and the patient, often a young adult, will lie with the right hip flexed for pain relief (the psoas sign). Spasm of the obturator internus is sometimes demonstrable when the hip is flexed and internally rotated. If an inflamed appendix is in contact with the obturator internus, this manoeuvre will cause pain in the hypogastrium (the obturator test; Zachary Cope). Cutaneous hyperaesthesia may be demonstrable in the right iliac fossa, but is rarely of diagnostic value. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1339

500.q: What will be the position of the appendix in silent appendicitis?
500.e: Retrocaecal Rigidity is often absent, and even application of deep pressure may fail to elicit tenderness (silent appendix), the reason being that the caecum, distended with gas, prevents the pressure exerted by the hand from reaching the inflamed structure in case of retrocaecal appendix. However, deep tenderness is often present in the loin, and rigidity of the quadratus lumborum may be in evidence. Psoas spasm, due to the inflamed appendix being in contact with that muscle, may be sufficient to cause flexion of the hip joint. Hyperextension of the hip joint may induce abdominal pain when the degree of psoas spasm is insufficient to cause flexion of the hip. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1339

500.q: After appendectomy, exploration was done for the bleeding. Ligation of which artery is beneficial?
500.e: The appendicular artery, a branch of the lower division of the ileocolic artery , passes behind the terminal ileum to enter the mesoappendix a short distance from the base of the appendix.

501.q: Which of the following autoinflammatory syndrome shows clock like regularity of episodes?
501.e: Periodic Fever with Aphthous Stomatitis , pharyngitis and cervical adenitis presents with clock like periodicity. It is the Most common autoinflammatory syndrome in children. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch; 369 Pg: 2843

501.q: A 50-year-old woman has investigations for recurrent renal calculi. A 24 hour urine collection revealed: calcium 18 mmol/24 hours(2-7) oxalate 180 mmol/24 hours (90-450) uric acid 2.8 mmol/24 hours (1.5-4.4) citrate 2 mmol/24 hours (0.3-0.4). Which form of treatment is likely to be successful?
501.e: Hypercalciuria is the most common identifiable cause of calcium kidney stone disease. The commonest type of renal stone is Calcium Oxalate. Currently there is no normal or cut off to define hypercalciuria. High calcium along with high urine oxalate and low urinary citrate cause Calcium oxalate stones. Pharmacological management of Calcium Oxalate stones Thiazide diuretics, usually Chlorthalidone, along with sodium restriction. Sodium restriction, if not followed will not lead to the desired effect on calcium. The other significant causes are hyperoxaluria, hyperuricosuria, low urinary volume, and hypocitraturia. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 318, Pg: 2372.

501.q: A 62 year old man with history of colorectal polyps presents with low grade fever, weight loss and night sweats. ECHO showed vegetations on the aortic valve. Which is the most likely organism to be grown in blood culture?
501.e: Streptococcus bovis bacteremia and endocarditis have been strongly associated with colorectal neoplasia. Patient identified to have S. bovis endocarditis should be evaluated for the presence of colorectal polyps or cancer. Penicillin G is the treatment of choice for S. bovis endocarditis typically given for 4 weeks. Staphylococcus aureus is the most commonly isolated organism from endocarditis occurring in IV drug abusers, which preferentially affects the tricuspid valve. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1023-25

501.q: An alcoholic patient who is diagnosed with chronic hepatitis has been admitted to emergency room for vomiting of blood since last 2 days due to variceal bleeding. Patient is in shock. You are the doctor and you have started the first line treatment, but the patient died. What is the underlying cause of death in this patient?
501.e: Varices are ubiquitous in patients with portal hypertension irrespective of the etiology and usually present with an acute, large-volume haematemesis associated with a high morbidity and significant mortality. The lower esophagus is the most common site and the diagnosis should be suspected in a patient known to have cirrhosis, but confirmation of the source is required following initial resuscitation. Variceal hemorrhage is a medical emergency and failure to control variceal bleeding with current medical management occurs in 10-20% of cases. The most common cause of death in these patients are HEMORRHAGIC SHOCK -> HYPOVOLEMIC SHOCK Patients with massive hemorrhage should be admitted to an intensive therapy unit, venous access obtained through two large-bore peripheral cannulae and resuscitation commenced, ideally with blood.

501.q: All of the following are aim of emergency department thoracotomy except
o: Clamping of the ascending aorta to cut off the blood supply to the heart and brain
Control of intrathoracic haemorrhage from other sources
501.e: The aim of EDT is to perform: Internal cardiac massage; Control of haemorrhage from injury to the heart or lung; Control of intrathoracic haemorrhage from other sources; Control of massive air leak; Clamping of the thoracic aorta to preserve the blood supply to the heart and brain, and cutting off the arterial supply distally, in a moribund patient with a major distal penetrating injury. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 29, Edition: 28th, Pg: 378

501.q: All of the following are considered as futile for emergency department thoracotomy except
o: CPR in the absence of endotracheal intubation for more than 5 minutes
CPR for more than 10 minutes (despite endotracheal intubation)
Blunt trauma when there have been no signs of life at the scene
501.e: In certain situations, EDT is considered futile: CPR in the absence of endotracheal intubation for more than 5 minutes; CPR for more than 10 minutes (despite endotracheal intubation); Blunt trauma when there have been no signs of life at the scene Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 29, Edition: 28th, Pg: 378

501.q: Treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism true is/are
o: All symptomatic patients should be offered surgery.
501.e: All symptomatic patients should be offered surgery. An expert panel recently published recommendations on which asymptomatic patients should be considered for surgical intervention (Bilezikian et al., 2014). When criteria have been met and where a single adenoma has been identified by radiological means, a minimally invasive parathyroidectomy may be offered. Conversely, where there is discordant imaging or where imaging fails to identify any parathyroid abnormalities, then a bilateral neck exploration and three and a half-gland parathyroidectomy or a four- gland parathyroidectomy and autotransplantation should be performed. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, CHAPTER 56, The parathyroid glands, Pg:879.

501.q: Only definite treatment for secondary hyperparathyroidism
501.e: Renal transplantation remains the only definite treatment for secondary hyperparathyroidism . Other therapies are a bridge to this or aim to provide symptom relief. Standard management includes replacement of calcium and vitamin D and the reduction of phosphate levels by the use of phosphate binders. Treatment of this disease changed radically with the introduction of calcimimetic drugs, such as cinacalcet. Calcimimetics alter the set point of the CaR, thereby reducing the constant stimulation of the parathyroid glands and lowering the PTH level. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, CHAPTER 56, The parathyroid glands, Pg:885.

502.q: What is the length of rigid sigmoidoscope?
502.e: Sigmoidoscope length should be 60cm. Rigid sigmoidoscope is 25 cm is correct In the past, the sigmoidoscope was a rigid stainless steel instrument of variable diameter and normally 25 cm in length , but this has been replaced by disposable plastic instruments. The rectum must be empty for proper inspection. Direct inspection of the rectal mucosa may alert the clinician to inflammation or This procedure can be performed in the outpatient setting. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 79, Edition 28th, Pg: 1395

502.q: During a routine check-up, a male patient is found to have a rectal mass on digital rectal examination (DRE). His bowel habits are normal. What is the next best investigation to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate further?
502.e: Explanation: A colonoscopy with biopsy is essential to confirm rectal carcinoma and to assess for synchronous lesions elsewhere in the colon. Biopsy provides histological confirmation and influences staging and management decisions. Explanation of other options: CT scan of the abdomen (Option A): Helps in staging but not the initial confirmatory step. Rigid sigmoidoscopy and biopsy (Option B): Limited to distal rectum and sigmoid; cannot assess entire colon. Barium enema (Option D): Largely replaced by colonoscopy, which is superior for diagnosis and biopsy. Key Takeaways: Colonoscopy + biopsy = diagnostic and rules out synchronous cancers. CT/MRI = staging investigations, not primary diagnostic.

502.q: What is the length of the large bowel?
502.e: The large bowel including the colon and rectum is a tube of variable diameter, approximately 150 cm in length. The terminal ileum empties into the cecum through a thickened, nipple-shaped invagination, the ileocecal valve. The cecum is a capacious sac-like segment of the proximal colon, with an average diameter of 7.5 cm and length of 10 cm. Although it is distensible, acute dilation of the cecum to a diameter of more than 12 cm, which can be measured by a plain abdominal radiograph, can result in ischemic necrosis and perforation of the bowel wall. Surgical intervention may be required when this degree of cecal distention is caused by obstruction or pseudo-obstruction Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 1321

502.q: Which among the following is not the clinical presentation of familial adenomatous polyposis?
502.e: Clinically, FAP is characterized by early development of a wide range of colorectal adenomatous polyps after the second decade of life and many extracolonic manifestations. Patients with FAP may be asymptomatic or may present with bleeding, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, or mucous discharge per rectum. Other symptoms such as anaemia, obstruction, or weight loss usually occur as polyps grow larger in size or number and may foreshadow the presence of cancer. A variety of benign and malignant extracolonic manifestations have been described in FAP. These include gastroduodenal adenomas and carcinoma, desmoids, osteomas, epidermoid cysts, papillary thyroid carcinoma, small bowel polyps and carcinoma, congenital hyperplasia of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), and dental anomalies. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 1368

502.q: What is the length of adult rectum?
502.e: Anatomy of the rectum The rectum measures approximately 15 cm in length It is divided into lower, middle and upper thirds The blood supply consists of superior, middle and inferior rectal vessels The lymphatic drainage follows the blood supply. The principal route of drainage is upwards along the superior rectal vessels to the para-aortic nodes, although the lower rectum can drain to lymphatics along the lateral pelvic side walls Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 79, Edition 28th, Pg: 1393

502.q: Which structure separates coccyx and lower two sacral vertebrae from the rectum posteriorly?
502.e: The lower third of the rectum is separated by distinct fascial layers from the prostate/vagina anteriorly (Denonvilliers fascia), and from the coccyx and lower two sacral vertebrae posteriorly (Waldeyer's fascia). These fascial layers are surgically important as they act as barriers to malignant invasion and form the anatomical envelope for total mesorectal excision (TME) to achieve complete oncological clearance of rectal cancer. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 79, Edition 28th, Pg: 1393

503.q: Parrot beak appearance is seen in
503.e: Answer- A. Volvulus Barium/gastrograffin enema - demonstrates the point of obstruction, pathognomonic "Bird beck deformity" or parrot beak deformity. Contrast enema is contraindicated if gangrene is suspected. "Parrot beaked" clawing of neils is also seen in chronic cocaine abuse.

503.q: Which among the following is not a presenting sign in a patient of Budd-Chiari syndrome?
503.e: Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) is a posthepatic cause of portal hypertension characterized by the obstruction of hepatic venous outflow . Patients may present with - Acute signs and symptoms of abdominal pain Ascites Hepatomegaly BCS is defined as primary when the obstructive process involves an endoluminal venous thrombosis . BCS is considered as a secondary process when the veins are compressed or invaded by a neighbouring lesion originating outside the vein. Reference : Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 31, Liver, Pg: 1368.

503.q: Which among the following diseases is referred to as jeep disease?
503.e: Pilonidal sinus The term pilonidal sinus describes a condition found in the natal cleft overlying the coccyx, consisting of one or more, usually non-infected, midline openings, which communicate with a fibrous track lined by granulation tissue and containing hair lying loosely within the lumen. A common affliction amongst the military, it has been referred to as ‘jeep disease’. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 80, Edition 28th, Pg: 1423

503.q: The fibres of internal oblique contribute to which component of inguinal canal?
503.e: The inguinal canal is about 4 cm in length and is located just cephalad to the inguinal ligament.
