The canal extends between the internal (deep) inguinal and external (superficial) inguinal rings. The inguinal canal contains the spermatic cord in men and the round ligament of the uterus in women. Structures contributing to the walls of inguinal canal Roof: oblique fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis Anterior wall: external oblique aponeurosis and internal oblique aponeurosis Floor: inguinal ligament and lacunar ligament Posterior wall: transversalis fascia and transversus abdominis

504.q: Which investigation is useful for intra-abdominal and hepatic metastasis?
504.e: LAPAROSCOPY This is a useful technique for the diagnosis of intra-abdominal and hepatic metastases. It has the advantage of enabling tissue samples or peritoneal cytology to be obtained and is the only modality reliably able to detect peritoneal tumour seedlings. This is particularly important for tumours arising from the intra-abdominal portion of the oesophagus, cardia and where there is a potential communication between a full-thickness tumour and the peritoneal cavity, for instance where there is a hiatus hernia. Laparoscopy Laparoscopic staging is useful in adenocarcinomas, especially those of the OGJ, but not for squamous cell cancer. Laparoscopy should be reserved for patients in whom confirmation of metastatic disease that is not otherwise obtainable is essential in deciding on treatment. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1139

504.q: Which are the two fix points around which the stomach rotates in the volvulus of stomach?
504.e: Volvulus of the stomach Rotation of the stomach usually occurs around the axis and between its two fixed points, i.e. the cardia and the pylorus . In theory, rotation can occur in the horizontal (organoaxial) or vertical (mesenteroaxial) direction but, commonly, it is the former which occurs. This condition is usually associated with a large diaphragmatic defect around the oesophagus ( paraesophageal herniation ). Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1180

504.q: Hypertranslucent chest X-ray is seen in all except
504.e: Answer- C. Pneumonectomy Causes of opaque hemithorax Technical : - Rotation, Scoliosis. Pleural : - Pleural effusion, Pleural thickening, Mesothelioma. Surgical : - Pneumonectomy, Thoracoplasty. Congenital : - Pulmonary agenesis. Mediastinal : - Gross cardiomegaly, tumors. Pulmonary : - Collapse, Consolidation, fibrosis, Foreign body. Diaphragmatic hernia

504.q: Which among the following is not the component of the seroma?
504.e: Seroma A seroma is the collection of fluid containing fat, serum, and lymph that develops at surgical wound or dead space from surgery. Seromas are common in surgical procedures, which create dead space or interruption of lymphatic drainage. Examples of this include breast or axillary surgery and hernia surgery. The use of prosthetic mesh in hernia surgery may contribute to poor flap adherence and trigger inflammation which can increase the risk of seroma formation. Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 12, Edition: 21st, Pg: 239

504.q: Which among the following conditions shows absent or inadequate peristalsis?
504.e: Dynamic, in which peristalsis is working against a mechanical obstruction. It may occur in an acute or a chronic form. Adynamic, in which there is no mechanical obstruction; peristalsis is absent or inadequate (e.g. paralytic ileus or pseudo-obstruction). Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1375

504.q: Which among the following is not an indication for early surgical intervention?
504.e: Indications for early surgical intervention Obstructed external hernia Clinical features suspicious of intestinal strangulation Obstruction in a 'virgin' abdomen Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1386

504.q: All of the following statements are correct regarding midline hernias in children except?
o: An umbilical hernia caused by incomplete closure of the umbilical ring
Most umbilical hernia resolved by age of 1 year
Supraumbilical hernia caused by defect in linea alba above the umbilical ring
Epigastric hernia are repaired if symptomatic
504.e: In the embryo, the umbilical ring is a relatively large defect in the ventral abdominal wall transmitting several structures that connect the fetus to the placenta.An umbilical hernia is common and caused by incomplete closure of the umbilical ring; incarceration is very rare. Most umbilical hernias resolve by 4 years of age. Supraumbilical hernias occur through defects in the linea alba just above the umbilical ring and do not close but are still repaired at around 4 years of age. Epigastric hernias are defects higher still that allow a small amount of preperitoneal fat to prolapse. They are repaired if symptomatic. Reference: Bailey and love's short practice of surgery, 27 th edition, Page - 127

504.q: Which among the following do follow the rule of absolute constipation in intestinal obstruction patient?
504.e: The rule that absolute constipation is present in intestinal obstruction does not apply in: Richter’s hernia; Gallstone ileus; Mesenteric vascular occlusion; Functional obstruction associated with pelvic abscess; All cases of partial obstruction (in which diarrhoea may occur). Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1380

505.q: After resection of bladder tumour, check cystoscopies are recommended for all of the following conditions, except?
505.e: The factors that result in an increased recurrence and progression rate are: high grade; pT1 disease; concomitant CIS; multiple primary tumours; recurrent disease at the first check cystoscopy 3 months after diagnosis. Patients with known bladder tumours should always be screened for upper tract tumours. Very few present with advanced constitutional symptoms and a palpable mass. Microscopic haematuria should be evaluated to exclude urothelial malignancy in the high-risk adult (chronic smokers, occupational exposure, older age) population. Reference : Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28 th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1481.

505.q: Which among the following conditions requires emergency surgery in a patient with variceal bleeding?
505.e: The most common situations requiring urgent or emergency surgery for the management of variceal bleeding are - Failure of acute endoscopic treatment Failure of long-term endoscopic therapy Hemorrhage from gastric varices or portal hypertensive gastropathy Failure of TIPS placement. Reference : Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1446.

505.q: Which among the following is not the potential route of bacterial exposure in pyogenic liver abscess?
505.e: The liver is probably exposed to portal venous bacterial loads on a regular basis and usually clears this bacterial load without problems. The development of a hepatic abscess occurs when an inoculum of bacteria, regardless of the route of exposure, exceeds the liver's ability to clear it. This results in tissue invasion, neutrophil infiltration, and formation of an organized abscess. The potential routes of hepatic exposure to bacteria are the biliary tree, portal vein, hepatic artery, direct extension of a nearby nidus of infection, and trauma. Reference : Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21 st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1428

505.q: Which among the following is the most commonly affected region of the liver in pyogenic liver abscess?
505.e: Most hepatic abscesses involve the right hemiliver, accounting for about 75% of cases. The explanation for this is not known, but preferential laminar blood flow to the right side has been postulated. The left liver is involved in approximately 20% of the cases; the caudate lobe is rarely involved (5%). Bilobar involvement with multiple abscesses is uncommon. Approximately 50% of hepatic abscesses are solitary. Hepatic abscesses can vary in size from less than 1 mm to 3 or 4 cm in diameter and can be multiloculated or a single cavity. At abdominal exploration, hepatic abscesses appear tan and are fluctuant to palpation, although deeper abscesses may not be visible and can be difficult to palpate. Surrounding inflammation can cause adhesions to local structures. Reference : Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1453

507.q: Which among the following is not a common site for hematogenous spread in phyllodes tumour?
507.e: Metastases from malignant phyllodes tumors occur via hematogenous spread. Common sites of metastasis include lung, bone, abdominal viscera, and mediastinum . Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 35, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 832

507.q: Which among the following is the causative agent for malignant thyroid lymphoma?
507.e: Aetiology of malignant thyroid tumours The great majority of thyroid cancers have no known aetiological factor. The most important identifiable aetiological factor in differentiated thyroid carcinoma (particularly papillary) is irradiation of the thyroid under 5 years of age. Short latency aggressive papillary cancer is associated with the ret/PTC3 oncogene and later developing, possibly less aggressive, cancers with RET/PTC1. The incidence of follicular carcinoma is high in endemic goitrous areas, possibly due to TSH stimulation. Malignant lymphomas sometimes develop in autoimmune thyroiditis, and the lymphocytic infiltration in the autoimmune process may be an aetiological factor. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 867

507.q: What is the most common primary malignant tumor in adults?
507.e: The most common primary malignant tumor in adults is Glioblastoma . The most common primary malignant tumor in children is Medulloblastoma. The most common primary CNS tumor in adults is Astrocytoma. The most common primary CNS tumor in children is Pilocytic astrocytoma. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 715

507.q: Which among the following is the most common type of malignant anal cancer?
507.e: Anal malignancy is rare and accounts for less than 2% of all large bowel cancers. The crude incidence rate is 0.65 per 100 000. Those arising below the dentate line are usually squamous, whereas those above are variously termed basaloid, cloacogenic or transitional. Collectively they are known as epidermoid carcinomas , and account for >70% of anal malignancies; management and prognosis is similar for this group. Adenocarcinomas are the next commonest. Other tumours include melanoma, lymphoma, and sarcoma. Reference : Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page Number-1443.

508.q: Which among the following is not a component of Reynold's pentad?
508.e: Clinical Manifestations Cholangitis may present as anything from a mild, self-limited episode to a fulminant, potentially life-threatening septicaemia. Patients with gallstone-induced cholangitis are most commonly older and female. The most common presentation is fever, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain,and jaundice. These classic symptoms, known as Charcot's triad , are present in about two-thirds of patients. The illness can progress rapidly with the development of shock and altered mental status, known as Reynolds' pentad (e.g., fever, jaundice, right upper quadrantpain, septic shock, and mental status changes ). However, the presentation may be atypical, with little if any fever, jaundice, or pain. Reference : Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11 th edition, Chapter 32, Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, pg no: 1408

508.q: What do you expect in a lady after gallbladder removal most commonly?
508.e: Complications of cholecystectomy Cholecystectomy affects the storage and excretion of bile acids (BAs), which can alter the metabolism of BAs and the gut microbiota.These changes can lead to metabolic disorders Hyperglycemia :Cholecystectomy can lead to hyperglycemia, or high blood glucose level Dyslipidemia :Cholecystectomy can lead to dyslipidemia, or abnormal levels of lipids and lipoprotein Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) :Cholecystectomy can increase the risk of NAFLD Metabolic syndrome :Cholecystectomy can increase the risk of metabolic syndrome (MetS), even in patients without other risk factors like hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia

508.q: Which is the most common histological subtype of gallbladder carcinoma?
508.e: Pathology and Staging Gallbladder cancer is generally adenocarcinoma . It is staged by the standard tumour node metastasis (TNM) staging system. Gallbladder cancer spreads via lymphatics, hematogenously, and notoriously into the peritoneal cavity or along biopsy or surgical wound tracts. Reference : Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21 st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, 55. Biliary System, Pg no: 1516.
Patients are mostly asymptomatic; symptoms if present are Early presentations: Right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting Late features includes: Jaundice and anorexia, a palpable mass.

508.q: Which among the following is not a consistent predictor of malignancy in gall bladder polyp?
508.e: Gallbladder polyp. The only polypoid lesions that have malignant potential and are associated with a significant rate of harbouring malignancy are adenomatous polyps . The most consistent predictors of malignancy in gallbladder polyps are single polyp,size greater than 1 cm, and age older than 50 year s. Cholecystectomy is generally recommended for polyps larger than 1 cm and can safely be performed laparoscopically. Polyps smaller than 1 cm can undergo surveillance to demonstrate stability, with the exception in the setting of PSC, where the threshold for cholecystectomy should be lower in the population. Reference : Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21 st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, 55. Biliary System, Pg no: 1518

508.q: A patient presents with pain in the right hypochondrium. Blood investigations showed AST-22IU/L and ALT- 27 IU/L. Serum Bilirubin levels - 5 mg/dl and also ALP-200 mg%. What should be the initial investigation in this patient?
508.e: Ultrasonography Transabdominal ultrasonography (USG) is the initial imaging modality of choice as it is accurate, readily available, inexpensive and quick to perform . However, it is operator dependent and may be compromised by excessive body fat and intraluminal bowel gas. The size of the gallbladder and presence of stones or polyps can be determined. Acute calculous cholecystitis is diagnosed radiologically (sensitivity 90-95%) by thickening of the gallbladder wall (>3 mm), presence of pericholecystic fluid or direct tenderness when the probe is pushed against the gallbladder (ultrasonographic Murphy's sign). Additionally, the presence of inflammation around the gallbladder, the size of the CBD and, occasionally, the presence of stones within the extrahepatic biliary tree can be determined.

508.q: Which among the following statements is false for the incidence of gallbladder carcinoma?
o: Usually occurs in 6th decade of life
Ethnicity plays an important role in the development of gall bladder carcinoma
Most common biliary tract carcinoma in united states
508.e: Incidence Gallbladder cancer generally occurs in the sixth and seventh decades of life and is two to three times more common in women than in men. Ethnicity plays an important role in the development of gallbladder cancer, with the highest incidence in women from India and Pakistan. Among North American populations, Native Americans and immigrants from Latin America have the highest rates. In the United States overall, gallbladder cancer is the most common cancer of the biliary tract and the fifth most common gastrointestinal cancer. Reference : Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21 st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, 55. Biliary System, Pg no: 1516

509.q: Which sphincter surrounds the wall of the cystic duct?
509.e: The cystic duct is about 3 cm in length but the length is variable. The lumen is usually 1-3 mm in diameter. The mucosa of the cystic duct is arranged in spiral folds known as the valves of Heister and the wall is surrounded by a sphincteric structure called the sphincter of Lutkens . The cystic duct joins the supraduodenal segment of the common hepatic duct in 80% of cases, however the anatomy may vary and the junction may be much lower in the retroduodenal or even retropancreatic part of the bile duct. Occasionally, the cystic duct may join the right hepatic duct or even a right hepatic sectorial duct. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27 th edition, Chapter 67, The gallbladder and bile ducts, Pg no: 1188

509.q: Which among the following is not a benign neoplasm causing biliary obstruction?
509.e: Benign tumours of the bile duct These are uncommon and may be an incidental finding. For symptomatic patients, the duration of symptoms may vary from a few days to months and their clinical presentation may in fact mimic conditions such as cholecystitis,choledocholithiasis, cholangiocarcinoma or pancreatic cancer. Benign neoplasms causing biliary obstruction may be classified as follows: papilloma and adenoma; multiple biliary papillomatosis; granular cell myoblastoma; neural tumours; leiomyoma; endocrine tumours. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27 edition, Chapter 67, The gallbladder and bile ducts, Pg no: 1207

509.q: Which among the following tumour marker is elevated in cholangiocarcinoma?
509.e: Investigations Biochemical investigations will confirm the presence of obstructive jaundice (elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transferase) in case of cholangiocarcinoma. The tumour-marker CA 19-9 may also be elevated . Imaging studies such as ultrasound, MDR-CT and MRI/MRCP are essential for diagnosis and staging. These studies allow the level of biliary obstruction to be defined and determine the locoregional extent of disease and the presence of metastases. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, Chapter 71 Gallbladder and bile ducts Pg no: 1256-1257.

510.q: Which of the following should not be given before a splenectomy patient?
510.e: Postsplenectomy septicaemia may result from S. pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae or Escherichia coli. Published guidelines emphasize that most infections after splenectomy could be avoided through measures that include offering patients appropriate and timely immunization, antibiotic prophylaxis, education and prompt treatment of infection Immunization in post - splenectomised pt. includes Hib + meningococcal + pneumococcal vaccines.

510.q: Which among the following is not the OPSI associated risk factor?
510.e: Reference : Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21 st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 57, The Spleen, Pg: 1579.

510.q: Which among the following organisms doesn't cause infection after splenectomy?
510.e: Splenic filtration may be particularly important for removal of microorganisms for which the host does not have a specific antibody. The immune functions of the spleen become evident after splenectomy, when patients are noted to be at risk for specific infections related to encapsulated bacteria Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenza, and Neisseria meningitidis. Asplenia and hyposplenism could be a result of surgical absence of spleen or lack of functioning of an anatomically present spleen. The most serious sequela is overwhelming postsplenectomy infection (OPSI). Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, Chapter 70, The Spleen, Pg: 1231.

510.q: What is the mechanism of anaemia in hereditary spherocytosis?
510.e: This is usually classified into: defects of the RBC membrane (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis ); defect in erythrocyte enzyme (e.g., glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency [G6PD]); and defect in hemoglobin synthesis (e.g., thalassemia, sickle cell anemias [hemoglobin S]). Reference : Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21 st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN,Chapter 57, The Spleen, Pg: 1571.

511.q: Which among the following is not a complication of bladder drainage of exocrine pancreas?
511.e: Bladder drainage of the exocrine pancreas may result in the following complications - Bladder/duodenal anastomotic leaks Cystitis (owing to effect of pancreatic enzymes) Urethritis/urethral stricture Reflux pancreatitis Urinary tract infection Haematuria Metabolic acidosis (due to loss of bicarbonate in the urine). Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th Edition, Chapter 82, Transplantation, Pg: 1553.

511.q: Most common pituitary tumour in clinical practice is:
511.e: Explanation: Among pituitary adenomas that present clinically, prolactin-secreting (prolactinomas) are the most common functioning tumours. Functioning adenomas (especially prolactinomas) produce hormonal syndromes that bring patients to clinical attention earlier. Non-functioning adenomas are also common (often present as macroadenomas with mass effect), but prolactinomas are the most common single subtype encountered in clinical practice. Explanation of other options: GH producing adenomas (Option A) : causes acromegaly; are less common than prolactinomas. ACTH adenomas (Option B ): causes Cushing's disease and are less common. Non-functional adenomas (Option D) : are common (often diagnosed by mass effect), but among clinical presenting tumours with endocrine features , functioning adenomas (especially prolactinomas) are the most common single type.

511.q: 40-year-old female came with Intractable or recurrent peptic ulcer disease (hemorrhage, perforation), complications of peptic ulcer, diarrhea. CT showed SOL of pancreas likely diagnosis is
511.e: Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, CHAPTER 57, The adrenal glands and other abdominal endocrine disorders, Pg:905.

511.q: Most common functioning Neuroendocrine Tumor of pancreas
511.e: Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, CHAPTER 57, The adrenal glands and other abdominal endocrine disorders, Pg:905.

511.q: Not seen in a case of gastrinoma
o: Fulminating ulcer diathesis in the stomach, duodenum
Non-beta islet cell tumours of the pancreas
511.e: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES)/gastrinoma is a condition that includes: (1) fulminating ulcer or atypical sites; (2) recurrent ulceration despite 'adequate' therapy; and (3) non-beta islet cell tumours of the pancreas (gastrinoma). Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, CHAPTER 57, The adrenal glands and other abdominal endocrine disorders, Pg:907.

511.q: When you compare pancreas adenocarcinoma (PDAC) with non-functioning Neuroendocrine Tumor (NF-Neuroendocrine Tumor), NF-Neuroendocrine Tumor usually show all except
511.e: Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, Chapter, The adrenal glands and other abdominal endocrine disorders, Pg:908.

511.q: VIPoma is associated with which syndrome:
511.e: Ans is 'b' i.e. Verner Morrison VlPomas are endocrine tumors that secrete excessive amounts of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), Excessive VIP causes a distinct syndrome characterized by large- volume diarrhea, hypokalemia, and dehydration. This syndrome also is called Verner-Morrison syndrome, pancreatic cholera, and WDHA syndrome for watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria. The principal symptoms are large-volume diarrhea (100%) severe enough to cause hypokalemia (80-100%), dehydration (83%), hypochlorhydria (54-76%), and flushing (20%). In adults 80-90% of VlPomas are pancreatic in location, with the rest due to VIP-secreting pheochromocytomas,

512.q: A 65 year old man has a cystoscopy to investigate haematuria. He develops pyrexia a day after the procedure. Which one of the following organisms is most likely to be implicated?
512.e: The commonest organisms infecting UTI are E coli and following that, klebsiella, proteus are next commonest and then enterococci. However, following cystoscopy/instrumentation, staph epidermidis(coagulase negative staph) infection is the commonest. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1071.

512.q: A 32 year old man presents with longstanding epigastric pains. An abdominal CT was organized and this showed dilated pancreatic ducts. The secretin test is positive. The patient has a HB of 13 g/dl, MCV of 105 fl and platelet count of 350 x 10^9/l. The high MCV is most likely due to:
512.e: In chronic pancreatitis, trypsin secretion is reduced. Trypsin is required in the release of protein bound dietary B12 which enables absorption and hence B12 deficiency is the most likely in this case. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 348, Pg: 2668

512.q: Which is the most specific and sensitive laboratory investigation for pancreatic damage?
512.e: When the pancreas is damaged, enzymes such as amylase, lipase, trypsin, elastase and chymotrypsin are released into the serum. Measurement of serum amylase is the most widely used test of pancreatic damage (serum lipase is more sensitive and specific, but is not widely available). The serum amylase rises within a few hours of pancreatic damage and declines over the next 4-8 days. A markedly elevated serum level is highly suspicious but not diagnostic of acute pancreatitis. Urinary amylase and amylase-creatinine clearance ratios add little to diagnostic accuracy. If confirmation of the diagnosis is required, computed tomography (CT) of the pancreas is of greater value. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th Edition, Chapter 68, The Pancreas, Pg: 1214.

512.q: What is the normal duration for decline of serum amylase levels in pancreatic damage?
512.e: When the pancreas is damaged, enzymes such as amylase, lipase, trypsin, elastase and chymotrypsin are released into the serum. Measurement of serum amylase is the most widely used test of pancreatic damage (serum lipase is more sensitive and specific, but is not widely available). The serum amylase rises within a few hours of pancreatic damage and declines over the next 4-8 days. A markedly elevated serum level is highly suspicious but not diagnostic of acute pancreatitis. Urinary amylase and amylase-creatinine clearance ratios add little to diagnostic accuracy. If confirmation of the diagnosis is required, computed tomography (CT) of the pancreas is of greater value. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th Edition, Chapter 68, The Pancreas, Pg: 1214.

512.q: A 36-year-old man with alcoholic pancreatitis 5 weeks ago now presents with epigastric pain, jaundice, and a palpable mass. CT scan image is shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
512.e: Correct Answer: A) Pancreatic pseudocyst Explanation: A pancreatic pseudocyst typically develops >2 weeks after acute pancreatitis, especially in alcoholics. Clinically, a tense, cystic epigastric mass is palpable. Common sites: between stomach & colon, or near liver/stomach. Explanation of other options: Choledochal cyst (Option B): Congenital biliary cyst, not alcohol related. Gastric duplication cyst (Option C): Congenital, near greater curvature, not epigastric. Mesenteric cyst (Option D): Congenital, usually in umbilical region. Key Takeaways: Alcoholic pancreatitis → pseudocyst after 2 weeks. Presents as tense epigastric cystic swelling. References: NCBI Bookshelf - Pancreatic Pseudocyst

512.q: A 40 years old patient, with previous history of MI, presented to the emergency with history of multiple episodes of vomiting, pain abdomen and blood in stool. On examination, BP-90/60 mmHg, PR-112/minute and pulse were irregularly irregular. Abdomen was soft, non-distended and bowel sounds were absent. What is the most probable diagnosis?
512.e: The above clinical scenario suggest a case of ACUTE MESENTERIC ISCHEMIA Acute mesenteric occlusion may be either thrombotic (following atheromatous narrowing) or embolic. Embolic occlusion results in sudden, severe abdominal pain, with bowel emptying (vomiting and diarrhoea) and a source of emboli present (usually cardiac). Unfortunately, the diagnosis is often only made at laparotomy with widespread infarction of the small and large bowel present; in this situation it is often fatal. Occasionally, the degree of bowel infarction is more limited; resection of the dead bowel and embolectomy of the superior mesenteric artery, or bypass surgery, can reduce the otherwise high mortality rate in these patients. A 'second look' laparotomy 24 hours later to check the viability of the bowel may be indicated

513.q: A 60 year old man presents with severe pain in his left loin radiating to the left groin. Bedside testing of urine demonstrates haematuria. Abdominal ultrasound does not demonstrate any abnormality and X-ray KUB does not show any visible stones. Which form of calculus might the patient have?
513.e: Radiopaque stones are: Calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, triple phosphate, cystine stones. Radiolucent stones are: Uric acid, xanthine stones. Uric acid stones can be visualized by helical CT. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 318, Pg: 2370.

513.q: A 60 year old man has presented with chronic projectile vomiting and significant weight loss. Which of the following electrolyte abnormality is seen in this patient?
o: Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypernatremia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypercalcemia
Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesemia
513.e: Metabolic effects Vomiting hydrochloric acid results in hypochloremic alkalosis . Initially the sodium and potassium may be relatively normal; however, as dehydration progresses, more profound metabolic abnormalities arise, partly related to renal dysfunction. Initially, the urine has a low chloride and high bicarbonate content , reflecting the primary metabolic abnormality. With time the patient becomes progressively hyponatremic and more profoundly dehydrated. Because of the dehydration , sodium is retained and potassium and hydrogen ions are excreted . This results in the urine becoming paradoxically acidic and hypokalaemia ensues . Alkalosis leads to a lowering in the circulating ionized calcium, and tetany can occur.

513.q: 35 year old male, chronic smoker came to OPD with right calf muscle pain and ulcer over the great toe with surrounding black pigmentation. What is the next investigation you do to this patient?
o: Duplex scan of lower limb vessels
513.e: The history given here is suggestive of buerger's disease The next investigation is to do DUPLEX scan to know the distal blood flow in lower limbs. This major non-invasive technique uses B-mode ultrasound to provide an image of vessels IOC for atherosclerotic diseases is DIGITAL SUBSTARCTION ANGIOGRAPHY (DSA)

513.q: Which among the following is not an aspect of assessing the patient with suspected chronic liver disease?
513.e: The key aspects of assessing a patient with suspected chronic liver disease or complications of portal hypertension are the following - Diagnosis of the underlying liver disease Estimation of functional hepatic reserve - helps to determine whether definitive (e.g., hepatic transplantation) or palliative (e.g., endoscopic variceal ligation or a shunt procedure) treatment is indicated Definition of portal venous anatomy and hepatic hemodynamic evaluation Identification of the site of upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage , if present. Reference : Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1445.

513.q: Which of these is incorrectly paired?
513.e: Explanation: The Los Angeles (LA) classification grades reflux esophagitis (endoscopic mucosal breaks). Achalasia is classified by high-resolution manometry using the Chicago classification (types I-III). So LA classification does not apply to achalasia Explanation of other options: Chronic pancreatitis (Option A)- M-ANNHEIM : the M-ANNHEIM classification (pronounced "Mannheim") is an accepted classification and scoring system for chronic pancreatitis (etiology, stage, severity). So this pairing is essentially correct (note the common spelling M-ANNHEIM). Colonoscopy - Boston score (Option C) : the Boston Bowel Preparation Scale is used to grade bowel prep quality for colonoscopy. Parathyroid resection - Miami criteria (Option D) : t he Miami intraoperative PTH criteria (drop of >50% from baseline at 10 min) guides adequacy of parathyroidectomy.

513.q: Which among the following is not a risk factor for chronic rejection of kidney transplant?
513.e: Long cold ischemic time is a risk factor. Chronic rejection usually occurs after the first 6 months. All types of transplants are susceptible to chronic rejection, and it is the major cause of allograft failure. Interestingly, the liver is more resistant than other organs to the destructive effects of chronic rejection. The risk factors for chronic rejection of a kidney transplant are: Previous episodes of acute rejection Poor HLA match Long cold ischaemia time Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection Raised blood lipids Inadequate immunosuppression (including poor compliance) The single most important risk factor for chronic rejection after kidney transplantation is acute rejection (with vascular inflammation) and recurrent episodes of acute rejection . Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th Edition, Chapter 82, Transplantation, Pg: 1536.

513.q: Which among the following chemotherapeutic agent is effective agent VEGF receptors?
513.e: Bevacizumab is effective against VEGF receptors . Erlotinib, cetuximab are effective against EGFR receptors. Ibrutinib is effective against bruton’s tyrosine kinase receptors. Used in the management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Reference: Schwartz 11 th edition page 343

513.q: A chronic smoker starts having pain in the calf on walking distance of 400 meters initially. Gradually he starts developing pain on walking distance of 200 meters only. Gradually he is having pain even during sleeping so decides to sleep in sitting position which makes him feel better. What is the likely dioagnosis?
513.e: Rest pain As disease progression occurs the claudication distance decreases and perfusion to the leg may be so severely compromised that anaerobic respiration occurs even at rest , typically affecting the foot and/or calf. The pain is exacerbated by lying down or elevation of the foot because of the loss of gravitational effects on the perfusion pressure in the foot. The patient characteristically describes pain that is worse at night and may be lessened by hanging the foot out of bed or by sleeping in a chair (effects of gravity restored). Even the pressure of bedclothes on the foot may exacerbate the pain.

514.q: Which among the following metastasis is common in pancreatic tubular adenocarcinoma?
514.e: Ductal adenocarcinomas infiltrate locally, typically along nerve sheaths, along lymphatics and into blood vessels. Liver and peritoneal metastases are common. Peritoneum Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter 72, The Pancreas, Pg: 1281.

514.q: Not a risk factor of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) after Whipple procedure for gastrinoma
514.e: Whipple procedure for gastrinoma Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27 th Edition, CHAPTER 20, Postoperative care, Pg:299

514.q: Which is the most common site of occurrence of ductal adenocarcinoma?
514.e: Ductal adenocarcinomas - Arise most commonly in the head of the pancreas . They are solid, scirrhous tumours, characterised by neoplastic tubular glands within a markedly desmoplastic fibrous stroma . Infiltrate locally , typically along nerve sheaths, along lymphatics and into blood vessels. Liver and peritoneal metastases are common. Proliferative lesions in the pancreatic ducts can precede invasive ductal adenocarcinoma. These are termed pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN), and can demonstrate a range of structural complexity and cellular atypia. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter 72, The Pancreas, Pg: 1281

515.q: A 27-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of headaches and sweating. Her mother had renal calculi and died of a tumour in her neck. On examination a nodule is felt in the patient's neck in the region of the thyroid gland. A surgeon advises complete thyroidectomy. What is the most important investigation the surgeon must undertake prior to surgery?
515.e: This patient probably has medullary carcinoma of the thyroid , which is usually associated with phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism as part of the MEN-2A syndrome. Here, the serum TSH level is unchanged, while a 24-h urine test for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid is performed for the diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome. Phaeochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery. If present, the effect of catecholamines must be blocked prior to surgery. MEN-1 is associated with Pituitary adenoma, Parathyroid hyperplasia and Pancreatic tumours. MEN-2A (multiple endocrine neoplasia) is associated with Parathyroid hyperplasia, Medullary carcinoma thyroid and Pheochromocytoma MEN-2B is also associated with a marfanoid appearance, Mucosal neuromas whereas MEN-2a is not. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2953

515.q: A 40-year-old patient with renal calculi has further investigation. High urinary levels of the following substances predispose to urinary tract stone formation, EXCEPT FOR:
515.e: Animal protein, oxalate, cystine and urate are all stone-forming substances, so high urinary levels promote stone formation. Low urinary citrate levels promote stone formation. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 318, Pg: 2369.

515.q: A 42-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for left flank pain and hematuria. Urinalysis reveals a pH of 6.9 and hematuria only. There is no evidence of UTI. Renal ultrasound shows the presence of kidney stones. He has no deafness. Serum chemistry and ABG show mild hypokalemic hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Serum creatinine is normal. He has a family history of kidney stones, and several members have mild hypokalemic hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Which one of the following renal tubular acidoses (RTAs) is the MOST likely diagnosis in this patient?
o: Type IV RTA with aldosterone deficiency
515.e: This patient has hereditary form of distal RTA with autosomal dominant inheritance. It occurs in adults. Autosomal recessive forms are diagnosed in infancy and childhood with or without deafness. Hyperkalemic RTA with a defect in voltage gradient is seen in patients with mild to moderate renal dysfunction. Type 4 RTA patients with aldosterone deficiency have mild renal impairment and can acidify their urine. Patients with incomplete RTA may have a combination of both proximal and distal RTA. They may present with acid urine, but the diagnosis is established only after an acid load. Proximal RTA patients present with severe hypokalemia, but nephrolithiasis is uncommon. Thus, options A, C, and D are incorrect. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:55 Pg: 364

515.q: A young girl presents with continuous urinary dribbling since birth, despite normal voiding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
515.e: Explanation: In females, an ectopic ureter that opens below the sphincter (into the urethra or vagina) presents as continuous dribbling of urine despite normal voiding . This history is pathognomonic. Explanation of other options: Ureterocele (Option B): Causes recurrent UTIs and bladder outlet obstruction, not continuous dribbling. Congenital megaureter (Option C): Presents with hydronephrosis and infections, not continuous leakage. Vesicoureteric reflux (Option D): Causes recurrent UTIs and hydronephrosis, not continuous wetting.

516.q: 65 years old male presented with a mass in the left lumbar region which was ballotable. He was having abdominal discomfort and on investigations he was found to have a 7*5*3 cm which was confined within the kidney and diagnosed as Renal cell carcinoma. What would be the treatment in this patient?
516.e: Nephron-sparing surgery with the recent increase in incidental detection of small renal masses (tumours Partial nephrectomy should be the treatment of choice in tumours less than 4cm, in well-selected tumours between 4 and 7cm, in bilateral tumours, in tumours in solitary kidneys and in patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction. Radical nephrectomy is limited to tumors >7cm Minimally invasive techniques by laparoscopy or robots have reduced postoperative morbidity. Because of the limitation of ischaemia time, minimally invasive techniques should be reserved for tumours with non-complex anatomy, as predicted by nephrometry scores. Alternative techniques such as surveillance, cryoablation or radiofrequency ablation of small renal tumours may be offered in patients with high surgical risk (e.g. elderly patients, patients with multiple comorbidities).

517.q: According to Weigert-Meyer's rule of ureteral duplication, the lower pole ureter inserts into the urinary bladder:
o: Lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter
Lateral and caudal to the upper pole ureter
Medial and cephalad to the upper pole ureter
Medial and caudal to the upper pole ureter
517.e: Explanation: The Weigert-Meyer law describes the anatomical relationship of the upper and lower renal moieties in duplicated collecting systems and their corresponding inferior drainage into the bladder. Weigert Meyer's rule states that The upper and lower renal moieties each have separate ureters, each with its own orifice in the bladder. The upper renal moiety ureter typically inserts ectopically, medially and inferior to the lower renal moiety ureter, often leading to a The lower renal moiety ureter inserts orthotopically , laterally, and superiorly to the upper moiety's ureter, which has a risk of vesicoureteral reflux.

517.q: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and was discharged after drain removal on day 1. On day 2, he returned with abdominal pain, tachycardia, fever, and ultrasound showing a 5 × 5 cm subhepatic collection. What is the most likely cause?
517.e: Explanation: Early post-cholecystectomy subhepatic collections are most often due to a bile leak, commonly from the cystic duct stump or an accessory bile duct. Explanation of other options: Infection (Option A): Takes 5-7 days to develop; not an early cause of subhepatic collection. Surgical site pain (Option B): Does not explain fever, tachycardia, or localized fluid collection. Retained gallstones (Option D): Can cause colic or cholangitis, but not an early subhepatic collection.

517.q: After a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, what should the expected urine output be in a patient with normal renal function?
517.e: Explanation: The normal urine output is around 1500 ml/day for a healthy adult, which roughly translates to 0.5-1.5 ml/kg/hour . (1x70(kg)x24(hours) ~ 1700 ml). Minimum urine output to excrete end products of protein metabolism: 500ml/day Ideal urine output in a normal 70kg adult: 1500 ml

517.q: Diversion of urine is best done at
517.e: Answer- A. Ileum Ileal segment is the best for urinary diversion after cystectomy. Still better method is "Continent cutaneous diversion" method. But the best method is "Orthotopic neobladders".

518.q: Most common cause of cancer death?
518.e: Lung cancer is one of the most common cancers throughout the world. In the UK, there are approximately 45 000 new cases a year. From the time of diagnosis, 60% of patients are dead within 1 year and only 15% survive 5 years, making lung cancer the most common cause of cancer death. Survival is dependent on the stage that the patient presents with lung cancer. Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 984.

518.q: Which of the following does not cause bladder outlet obstruction?
518.e: Vesico-ureteral reflux (VUR) does not cause bladder outlet obstruction (BOO). VUR is the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder to the ureter. Urodynamically proven BOO may result from- BPH - Benign prostatic hyperplasia Bladder neck stenosis Bladder neck hypertrophy Prostate cancer Urethral strictures Functional obstruction due to neuropathic conditions Urodynamically proven BOO may result from: BPH; bladder neck stenosis; bladder neck dyssynergia or functional bladder neck obstruction; bladder neck hypertrophy; prostate cancer; urethral stricture; functional obstruction due to neuropathic conditions. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, Chapter 84, The prostate and seminal vesicles, Pg: 1524.

518.q: Which of the following iodine isotopes is used in the management of prostate cancer?
518.e: brachytherapy for prostate cancer is passed via trans- perineal needles Radio-isotopes commonly used are- iodine-125 and palladium-103 Theses isotopes deliver an intense, confined radiation dose. Iodine-125 ( 125 I) is a radioisotope of iodine which has uses in biological assays, nuclear medicine imaging and in radiation therapy as brachytherapy to treat a number of conditions, including prostate cancer, uveal melanomas, and brain tumors. It is the second longest-lived radioisotope of iodine, after iodine-129. Permanent seed implants are used as monotherapy in cases of prostate tumors with a high probability of being limited to the prostate, without any need to combine it with external radiotherapy or hormone therapy https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11103823/

518.q: In a patient with a carcinoma prostate with high Gleason score, bone scan was done. Bone scan shows increased uptake with bones and reduced in kidney and soft tissues. This is reported as super scan because of:
o: Increased uptake because of osteoblastic lesions
518.e: Once the diagnosis has been established, if metastatic spread is suspected (on the basis of a high PSA [>10 ng/mL], locally advanced disease or presence of Gleason 7 or higher) a bone scan should be carried out. This is because prostate cancer is predominantly osteoblastic lesions which shows increased uptake in bone scans.

518.q: Which of the following is not true regarding radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer?
o: Should be carried out only in men with a life expectancy of < 10 yrs
Exclusion of metastases would be required before surgery
Results in a high incidence of impotence
518.e: Radical prostatectomy is suitable for- Localised disease Carried out only in men with a life expectancy of >10 years . Exclusion of metastases would require a negative bone scan and MRI of the pelvis. Procedure - Removal of the prostate down to the distal urethral sphincter , in addition to the seminal vesicles . The bladder neck is reconstituted and anastomosed to the urethra. It results in a high incidence of impotence , but a low incidence of severe stress incontinence ( Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, Chapter 84, The prostate and seminal vesicles, Pg: 1536.

519.q: Not true regarding non ischaemic priapism?
o: Consequence of traumatic damage to the central penile artery, usually as a consequence of blunt perineal trauma
Blood gas analysis shows the characteristics of venous blood
519.e: This rarer form of priapism arises as a consequence of traumatic damage to the central penile artery, usually as a consequence of blunt perineal trauma. A fistula develops between the artery and the sinusoidal space, which results in a persistent erection that is painless, in contrast to the ischaemic priapism. Blood gas analysis shows the characteristics of arterial blood and Doppler scanning and selective arteriography will demonstrate the fistula. Treatment is not an emergency, since there is no ischaemia, and is most appropriately achieved by selective arterial embolisation. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 85, Urethra and Penis, Pg: 1551.

519.q: All of the following are indications for circumcision, except?
o: An inability to retract the foreskin for intercourse
519.e: Explanation: In infants and young boys, circumcision is most usually performed at the request of the parents for social or religious reasons . Medical indications for circumcision in boys include true phimosis , Balanitis xerotica obliterans (rare under the age of 5 years), recurrent attacks of balanoposthitis and recurrent urinary tract infections with an abnormal upper urinary tract . In adults, circumcision is indicated because of an inability to retract the foreskin for intercourse, for splitting of an abnormally tight frenulum or for recurrent balanitis.

519.q: Which statement is not correct regarding male urethra?
o: The membranous urethra lies just distal to the verumontanum
Bulbar urethra is located where the urethra penetrates the pelvic floor and it is the usual site of urethral rupture at the time of a pelvic fracture
The bulbar urethra extends from the membranous urethra to the penoscrotal junction
The urethral lining changes from transitional cell epithelium proximally to stratified squamous cell epithelium distally
519.e: Membranous urethra is located where the urethra penetrates the pelvic floor and it is the usual site of rupture at time of pelvic fracture. All other statements are correct. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 85, Urethra and Penis, Pg: 1538.

519.q: Most common site for urethral stricture?
519.e: Post Inflammatory strictures are less common since the introduction of effective antibiotic treatment of gonorrhoea. The stricture is most commonly seen in the bulbar urethra but submeatal strictures also occur. There is infection in the periurethral glands, which persists after inadequately treated gonorrhoea. The infection spreads to cause a periurethritis, which heals by fibrosis. Most strictures appear within 1 year of infection but may not cause difficulty in micturition for some time later. The common causes of urethral stricture are: lichen sclerosus (LS); iatrogenic (post catheter and/or instrumentation); sexually transmitted diseases (gonorrhoea); post radiation; traumatic; idiopathic; congenital. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 85, Urethra and Penis, Pg: 1542.

519.q: Which is not true regarding Fowler's syndrome?
o: Often associated with polycystic ovaries and causes urinary retention
There is some evidence that sacral neuromodulation can be effective
519.e: This idiopathic condition, which was described by Fowler and Kirby, is associated with an abnormal myotonic discharge in the striated urethral sphincter that can be detected by sphincter electromyography. It is often associated with polycystic ovaries and causes urinary retention in women and should not be confused with a urethral stricture. Urethral dilatation is ineffective and the retention is best treated by intermittent self-catheterisation. There is some evidence that sacral neuromodulation can be effective Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th Edition, Chapter 79, Urethra and Penis, Pg: 1485.

519.q: Which is not true regarding ischaemic priapism?
o: The commoner and is due to venous congestion
The penis remains erect and remains painless
Blood taken from the penis shows hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis
519.e: lschaemic priapism lschaemic or veno-occlusive priapism is the more common. It is due to venous congestion, with consequent thrombosis and ischaemia. The penis remains erect and becomes painful. This is a pathological erection and the glans penis and corpus spongiosum are not involved. The condition is most commonly seen as a side effect of medication, most notably antipsychotic medication and intracavernosal injections. It can also arise as a complication of hypercoagulable blood disorders such as sickle cell disease or leukaemia. A small proportion of cases are caused by malignant disease in the corpora cavernosa or the pelvis. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 85, Urethra and Penis, Pg: 1551.

519.q: Aetiology of penile cancer are all except?
519.e: Circumcision soon after birth confers immunity against carcinoma of the penis. Later circumcision does not seem to have the same benefit, with the assumption that smegma is in some way carcinogenic. Human papillomavirus infection (HPV types 16 and 18) is a risk factor, as are BXO and smoking. Phimosis and chronic balanoposthitis are known to be contributory factors, and there are definite pre carcinomatous states including leukoplakia of the glans, which is similar to the condition seen on the tongue, and penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN) Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 85, Urethra and Penis, Pg: 1551.

519.q: An elderly patient with Ca Penis underwent partial penile amputation. Biopsy report came as a T2 lesion. What will be the appropriate timing for lymph node management (clinically N0 nodes)?
o: Patient is kept on follow up, when nodes become palpable
No lymph node dissection for him
519.e: Here the primary lesion is T2 hence lymph node dissection becomes mandatory even if it is clinically N0. The best results are from immediate adjuvant lymph node dissection (5 year survival 83%) and the worst results are from surveillance and delayed lymphadenectomy (5 year survival 36%). Several studies have analyzed the survival of men undergoing early versus delayed lymphadenectomy according to pathologic evaluation of nodal status The best results were from immediate adjunctive lymph node dissection (83%), with the next best from immediate therapeutic lymphadenectomy (66%). The worst results were from the surveillance and delayed lymphadenectomy group (36%), in whom dissection was delayed until palpable nodes developed. Reference : Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology 12th Edition, Pg: 1757.

520.q: A patient presented with painless hard enlargement of the testis. LDH values are increased. Next best step is?
520.e: The c/f and the raised AFP levels are suggestive of a testicular tumor, probably a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT) and the next best step in management is high inguinal orchidectomy. Painless testicular enlargement: Testicular Tumor Syphilis Testicular tumors are of: Seminoma: most common type, with normal alpha fetoprotein and HCG, and mild elevation of LDH Non seminomatous: very high levels of alpha fetoprotein and HCG Transcrotal biopsy is contraindicated as it causes dissemination of tumor cells Next step in case of testicular tumor - chevassu's manuvere where testis is delivered by high inguinal orchidectomy

520.q: A young male was found to have a testicular swelling. After evaluation- HIGH INGUINAL ORCHIDECTOMY was done. What will be the probable diagnosis?
520.e: HIGH INGUINAL ORCHIDECTOMY is done for seminoma of testis or any other testicular tumor, because if operated via scrotum there is increased risk of dissemination of cancer cells. Option a) torsion testis- orchidopexy is done if the testis is viable Option c) fourniers gangrene: testis not affected in this condition, so ORCHIDECTOMY is not done Option d) hematocele initially aspiration is done, if recurrent excision of the cyst is done

520.q: A 14 years old boy is presented with absent left testis in scrotum. On examination, left testis was found in the superior inguinal pouch. What is the diagnosis?
520.e: Ectopic testis: an ectopic testis is one that has ended up away from the normal path of descent. The commonest site is the superfcial inguinal pouch, just inferior and medial to the superfcial inguinal ring. Other rarer ectopic sites include the femoral triangle, root of the penis and perineum

521.q: All of the following are correct regarding meningitis except
o: Raised ICP should be excluded before LP
CSF should be sent for microscopy and culture
Treatment is broad spectrum antibiotics including anaerobic coverage
521.e: Meningitis is a feared complication of neurosurgery and head injury. CT scan allows exclusion of raised intracranial pressure and should be done prior to lumbar puncture. CSF should be sent for microscopy and culture, along with protein and glucose level assay. Treatment is with broad spectrum antibiotics including anaerobic coverage. Empirical therapy is started with 3rd generation cephalosporin + Vancomycin ± Ampicillin . Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 706

521.q: Reperfusion injury occurs when blood flow is restored after a period of ischemia. During this phase, accumulated metabolites and ions re-enter circulation, creating systemic disturbances. According to surgical principles described in Bailey and Love, which substance is chiefly responsible for the clinically significant component of reperfusion injury?
521.e: Explanation: During prolonged ischemia, cells lose membrane integrity and release potassium and acid into surrounding tissues. Once reperfusion occurs, this accumulated potassium rapidly enters the systemic circulation. This sudden potassium surge can cause myocardial depression, dangerous cardiac arrhythmias, vasodilation, worsening hypotension and can contribute significantly to multi organ injury. During ischemia: Cells lose ATP and membrane pumps begin to fail Potassium leaks out of cells into the interstitial space Acidity increases due to anaerobic metabolism Inflammatory pathways are activated locally During reperfusion: The accumulated potassium and acids enter systemic circulation Inflammatory mediators and cell fragments activate leukocytes These changes may contribute to acute lung injury, acute kidney injury and multi organ failure

521.q: All of the following statements are correct regarding GCS score except:
o: GCS is composed of a measure of eye opening, verbal response, and motor function
Verbal response is reflective of outcomes after TBI
521.e: Explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) reflects the level of consciousness. Scores range from 3 to 15 and assess: Eye opening Verbal response Motor function The motor score alone, not the verbal response, is most reflective of outcomes after traumatic brain injury (TBI). Head Injury Severity & GCS Severity classification of head injury is based on the post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) GCS, especially the motor score, is the best predictor of neurological outcome. Alcohol and drugs may complicate assessment. GCS-Based Classification: Minor head injury: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness (LOC) . Mild head injury: GCS 14 or 15 with LOC . Moderate head injury: GCS 9-13 . Severe head injury: GCS 3-8 . Key Takeaways: Motor component of GCS is the best predictor of TBI outcomes.

521.q: Patient had trauma, GCS score of the patient was 10. What is the severity of injury?
521.e: GCS classification severity Minor- GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness Mild: GCS 14 or 15 with loss of consciousness Moderate: GCS 9-13 Severe: GCS 3-8

521.q: A young male with head injury was brought to the emergency in unconscious state. The patient was not able to breath properly, put on ventilatory support. On examination, GCS was 8 with findings of raised ICT. NCCT brain and spinal imaging were normal. What is the most probable diagnosis?
521.e: This is a form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy accidents that usually renders the patient comatose; it is associated with poor outcomes. It is strictly a pathological diagnosis made at postmortem, but haemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum and dorsolateral rostral brainstem on CT may be suggestive, although CT often appears normal Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically. IOC for diffuse atonal injury is SWI-MRI

522.e: The premalignant lesions of oral cavity are leukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral submucous fibrosis, lichen planus, chronic hyperplastic candidiasis. Erythroplakia is a red patch or plaque on the oral mucosal surface. Aphthous ulcers are recurrent and superficial ulcers usually involving movable mucosa of oral cavity. Fordyce Spots - Aberrant sebaceous glands present under the buccal or labial mucosa and shine through it as yellowish or yellow-brown spots. They are considered normal. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 265, 257, 255.

522.q: A 45-year-old male patient, known case of carcinoma tongue, underwent hemiglossectomy with modified radical neck dissection. His primary tumour and excised lymph nodes were sent for histopathology examination. In which of the following conditions will adjuvant radiotherapy not be required by the patient?
522.e: Explanation: Multiple lymph node involvement is an indication for adjuvant radiotherapy, not single lymph node involvement. Indications of Adjuvant radiotherapy: Advanced stage T3 or T4. (Option D) Presence of lymphovascular invasion Presence of Perineural invasion Positive surgical margins (Option B) Multiple lymph node involvement Extra capsular nodal extension. (Option C)

522.q: A 55-year-old male smoker presented with a mass on the left side of the neck at the level 2 region. An FNAC was done, which was suggestive of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma. A careful endoscopic and radiological examination was done, which revealed the absence of any primary tumour. Which of the following is not a theory for this condition?
o: Squamous element of brachial remnants in lymph nodes turning malignant.
Subclinical primary with nodal metastasis, either due to faster growth rate of the nodal metastasis or sloughing of necrotic carcinoma.
Primary regressing due to immune hyperactivity.
522.e: Explanation: The incidence of a neck node with unknown primary origin in head and neck region is about 3%. Carcinoma of unknown primary is defined as histological confirmation for at least one of the cervical lymph nodes to be metastatic , in the absence of a primary tumour, which is confirmed by thorough physical, endoscopic and radiological examination. Theories of occurrence include the following: The squamous element of brachial remnants in lymph nodes turning malignant. (Option A) The subclinical primary with nodal metastasis, either due to the faster growth rate of the nodal metastasis or the sloughing of necrotic carcinoma. (Option B) The primary regressing due to immune hyperactivity. (Option C) The small hidden primary in tonsil/base of tongue crypts with aggressive nodal metastasis.

522.q: Which of the following is false regarding tongue tie:
o: Usually lead to severe respiratory difficulty
Significant tongue tie needs surgical release
522.e: Ankyloglossia(Tongue Tie) Causes speech defects if tongue cannot be protruded beyond the lower incisors. A mobile tongue is important to maintain orodental hygiene-to clean the debris and prevent formation of dental plaques. Treatment of any significant tongue tie is transverse release and vertical closure. Thin mucosal folds can be simply incised. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, Pg. no. 257

522.q: What is the most common salivary gland tumor?
522.e: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign salivary gland tumor, also known as a mixed tumor . It can occur in both major and minor salivary glands. Pleomorphic adenoma is composed of a mixture of different cell types, including epithelial and myoepithelial cells, and it is encapsulated. A. Adenocarcinoma: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumor derived from glandular epithelial tissue. It is less common than pleomorphic adenoma and represents a cancerous (malignant) tumor. C. Mucoepidermoid tumor: Mucoepidermoid tumor is a common malignant salivary gland tumor that includes both mucus-secreting and squamous cells. It is less common than pleomorphic adenoma. D. Basal cell carcinoma: Basal cell carcinoma is a type of skin cancer that arises from basal cells in the epidermis.

522.q: Fibular flap is commonly used for reconstruction of defects of Hemi mandibulectomy. This flap is based on which of the following artery. What is type of this flap?
o: Anterior tibial vessels and regional flap
Dorsalis pedis vessels and free flap
522.e: Explanation: The fibular flap is an example of a free flap, which means that in this type of flaps the donor site and recipient sites are distant from each other and the flap carries it's blood vessels along with it. Fibular flap is based on peroneal vessels. The fibular flap provides good bone stock and it's robust peroneal supply ensures that multiple osteotomies can be performed. The flexor hallucis longus muscle and skin can be harvested along with the flap to provide soft tissue reconstruction along with the bone. Up to 25 cm of bone can be harvested. Key takeaway: The fibular flap is an example of free flap which means that in this type of flaps the donor site and recipient sites are distant from each other and the flap carries it's blood vessels along with it. Fibular flap is based on peroneal vessels.

522.q: Most common cause of acute parotitis -
522.e: Answer- A. Staphylococcus Aureus MC organism is Staphylococcus Aureus >> streptococcus viridans >> pneumococcus. Acute bacterial parotitis: is most often caused by a bacterial infection of Staphylococcus aureus but may be caused by any commensal bacteria. Usually ascending infection Staphylococcus aureus Ref- Manipal Manual of Surgery 5th edition

522.q: Which among the following is not a risk factor for potential malignant transformation in oral cavity cancer?
o: Premalignant lesion on posterior aspect of tongue
522.e: Potential for malignant change The potential risk for malignant transformation includes: Severity/grade of dysplasia Increases with increasing age of the patient Increases with increasing size of the lesion May be higher in smokers (although contradictory evidence exists to suggest non-smokers are at higher risk) Increases with alcohol consumption Depends on the anatomical site of the premalignant lesion Is particularly high for premalignant lesions on the lateral/ventral surface of the tongue, particularly in younger women, even in the absence of associated risk factors. Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 48, Edition: 27 th , Pg: 762

523.q: In patient with ___%TBSA, inflammatory reaction causes fluid loss in vessels remote from the burn injury
523.e: The overall effect of these changes is to produce a net flow of water, solutes and proteins from the intravascular to the extravascular space. This flow occurs over the first 36 hours after the injury, but does not include red blood cells. In a small burn, this reaction is small and localised but, as the burn size approaches 10-15% of total body surface area (TBSA), the loss of intravascular fluid can cause a level of circulatory shock. Furthermore, once the area increases to 25% of TBSA, the inflammatory reaction causes fluid loss in vessels remote from the burn injury. This is why such importance is attached to measuring the TBSA involved in any burn. It dictates the size of inflammatory reaction and therefore the amount of fluid needed to control shock. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 46, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 666

523.q: All of the following statements are correct regarding escharotomy except
o: Upper limb - Mid-axial, anterior to the elbow medially to avoid the ulnar nerve
Hand - Midline in the digits. Release muscle compartments if tight
Lower limb - Mid-axial. Posterior to the ankle laterally to avoid the saphenous vein
Chest - Down the chest lateral to the nipples, across the chest below the clavicle and across the chest at the level of the xiphisternum
523.e: Key features of escharotomy placement. Upper limb - Mid-axial, anterior to the elbow medially to avoid the ulnar nerve Hand - Midline in the digits. Release muscle compartments if tight. Best done in theatre and with an experienced surgeon Lower limb - Mid-axial. Posterior to the ankle medially to avoid the saphenous vein Chest - Down the chest lateral to the nipples, across the chest below the clavicle and across the chest at the level of the xiphisternum General rules extend the wound beyond the deep burn. Diathermy any significant bleeding vessels. Apply haemostatic dressing and elevate the limb postoperatively Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 46, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 673

523.q: A patient who had burns some years back now presents with ulceration over the burns area indicative of malignancy. What is it?
523.e: Marjolin's ulcer: is a squamous cell carcinoma arising from Chronic burns scar Keloid scar Long standing venous ulcer scar Chronically inflamed wounds are susceptible to neoplastic transformation. Squamous cell carcinoma was originally reported in chronic burn scars by Marjolin . Chronic osteomyelitis, pressure sores, venous stasis ulcers, and hidradenitis may also develop neoplastic change. Biopsies should be performed in cases of chronic wounds that appear clinically atypical. Cutaneous wounds may first exhibit pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasiaa premalignant condition. Such a diagnosis on biopsy should prompt additional biopsies to exclude squamous cell carcinoma, which may already be present in other areas of the wound.

523.q: Flash burn, tender, red & painful, which of the following type is the burn-
523.e: Answer- B. First degree burn First degree burn (also k/a Superficial or Epidermal burn) These burns involve only the epidermis They do not blister, Are erythematous because of dermal vasodilation Blanch to touch (i.e. show capillary refilling) Are quite painful Heal without scarring in 5 to 10 days. They result in pain and reddening of the epidermis (outer layer of the skin). The clinical fearures are blistering and/or loss of the epidermis. The underlying dermis is pink and moist. The capillary return is cleariy visible when blanched

524.q: In a female abdominal intestinal perforation operated has serous discharge on 5th day with wound gap. What is your diagnosis
524.e: Answer- A. Wound dehiscence Dehisence most often develops 7 to 10 days postoperatively but may occur anytime after surgery, from 1 to more than 20 days."- Sabiston

524.q: Pressure greater than how many mmHg causes pressure sores?
524.e: Explanation: Pressure sores (also known as decubitus ulcers or pressure ulcers) develop when sustained external pressure on the skin exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, resulting in ischemia and eventual tissue necrosis. The critical threshold is when pressure rises above 33 mmHg , which surpasses normal capillary pressure (≈25-32 mmHg). At this point, tissue perfusion becomes inadequate, leading to ischemic damage. Explanation of other options: Options B, C, and D (45 mmHg, 54 mmHg, 67 mmHg): Although higher pressures can cause more rapid and severe necrosis, ischemia begins once pressure exceeds 33 mmHg. Prolonged lower-level pressure, particularly over bony prominences like the sacrum and heels , can also result in ulcer formation if unrelieved.

524.q: Graft taken from identical twin is called as:
524.e: Autograft: a graft of tissue from one point to another of the same individual's body Isograft: graft of tissue between two individuals who are genetically identical( monozygotic twins). Allograft: an organ or tissue transplanted from one individual to another. Heterotopic graft: a graft placed in a site different from that where the organ is normally located Xenograft: graft from animal to human

525.q: Which among the following tumour shows predominance of Askanazey cells histologically?
525.e: Follicular carcinoma can normally only be differentiated from follicular adenoma by the architecture on histology. For this reason, follicular lesions on FNA are unable to be diagnosed as malignant in the absence of clinical features such as metastases. Multiple foci of follicular carcinoma are seldom seen and lymph node involvement is much less common than in papillary carcinoma. Blood-borne metastases are more common and the eventual mortality rate, although still low, is twice that of papillary cancer. Hurthle cell tumours are a rare variant of follicular neoplasm in which oxyphil (Hurthle, Askanazy) cells predominate histologically. Hurthle cell cancers are associated with a poorer prognosis. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 868

525.q: Which is not true regarding renal agenesis?
o: The ipsilateral testis and vas deferens are usually absent
525.e: Renal agenesis is the complete absence of one kidney. It results from failure of connection between the metanephric blastema and the ipsilateral ureteric bud . This condition is an autosomal dominant trait with incomplete penetrance. Typically, there is an absent ipsilateral ureter and the ipsilateral hemi-trigone is missing in the bladder. The remaining kidney is usually hypertrophic but may also be dysplastic. In addition, the ipsilateral testis and vas deferens are usually absent and in some patients the adrenal gland on the affected side is missing as well. Females with the condition may have an absent ovary or Fallopian tube . Renal agenesis is different from renal aplasia where there is a small dysplastic kidney. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28 th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1466.

525.q: All of the following are causes for vesico-vaginal fistula, except?
525.e: Anterior colporrhaphy can lead to formation of vesicovaginal fistula. Causes of vesicovaginal fistula include - Obstetric - Protracted or neglected labour. Gynaecological - Total hysterectomy and anterior colporrhaphy. Radiotherapy . Direct neoplastic infiltration . Exceptionally, carcinoma of the cervix ulcerates through the anterior fornix to implicate the bladder. Reference : Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28 th Edition, Chapter 83, The Urinary Bladder, Pg: 1505.

525.q: All of the following are components of trauma triad of death except:
525.e: The concept of damage control surgery (DCS) was developed because severely traumatised patients with impaired physiology have poor outcomes after lengthy and complex surgical reconstructive procedures performed shortly after their trauma. Prolonged procedures result in additional trauma and further immune and physiological derangement The 'triad of death' is a cycle of: Acidosis Coagulopathy Hypothermia, may develop and result in multi-organ failure and death Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 27, Edition: 28th, Pg: 358

525.q: How much length is increased in Z plasty when it is done at 60 degrees?
525.e: Ans is 'c' i.e. 75% Z-plasty is a very common interposition surgical technique utilized in plastic and reconstructive surgery to revise scars. In general, the greater the angle, the greater the gain in wound length. Tissue Lengthening with Z-Plasty Type of Z-Plasty Increase in Length of Central Limb (%) Simple 45-degree 50 Simple 60-degree 75 Simple 90-degree 100 Four-flap with 60-degree 150 angles Double-opposing 75 Five-flap 125 Or Angles compared to gain in length are as follows: 30-degree angle results in a 25% gain in length 45-degree angle results in a 50% gain in length 60-degree angle results in a 75% gain in length 75-degree angle results in a 100% gain in length 90-degree angle results in a 125% gain in length

525.q: Presence of which microorganism is contraindication for split thickness skin grafting?
525.e: The group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus can destroy split grafts completely (and also convert a donor site to a full-thickness defect) and so the presence of this microorganism is a contraindication to grafting. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 47, Plastic and reconstructive surgery, Pg: 686

526.q: Which among the following diseases is also known as serocystic disease of the Brodie?
526.e: Phyllodes tumour (Serocystic disease of Brodie or Cystosarcoma phyllodes) - Benign Usually occur in women over the age of 40 years but can appear in younger women. They present as a large, sometimes massive tumour with an unevenly bosselated surface . Occasionally, ulceration of overlying skin occurs because of pressure necrosis. Mobile on the chest wall Only very rarely develop features of a sarcomatous tumour. These may metastasise via the bloodstream. Treatment Treatment for the benign type is enucleation in young women or wide local excision . Massive tumours, recurrent tumours and those of the malignant type will require mastectomy. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28 th , Pg: 922-923

526.q: Which among the following diseases shows Kantor string sign on barium enema study?
526.e: Radiology. CTE or magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) are often used as the initial assessment of Crohn disease to complement direct ileocolonoscopy. Imaging studies can provide information regarding severity of inflammation, length, and focality and identify complications (e.g., obstruction or fistula). In addition, these studies support surgical planning and the evaluation of response to medical therapy. Previously, barium enema was commonly used to identify features of Crohn For example, long lengths of narrowed terminal ileum (Kantor string sign ) may be present with long-standing disease. Segmental and irregular patterns of bowel involvement may be Fistulas between adjacent bowel loops and organs may be apparent Reference : Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21 st , Pg: 1263

526.q: Imminent gangrene in peripheral vascular disease (PVD) is associated with an ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) of less than:
526.e: Explanation: ABPI - ankle-brachial pressure index is the ratio of the systolic pressure at the ankle to that in the ipsilateral arm. It is interpreted as the highest pressure in the dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial or peroneal artery serving as the numerator, with the highest brachial systolic pressure being the denominator. Patients with an ABPI of 0.50, and a deteriorating ABI is predictive of future limb loss. Interpretation of various measurements of ABPI is as follows: ≥0.9 - normal (Option A ruled out) 7-0.9 - mild arterial disease (claudication may be absent or mild) (Option B ruled out) ~0.5 - suggests critical ischemia / rest pain may occur (Option C ruled out) It should be noted that low ABPI reflects very poor distal perfusion. When ABPI drops below about 0.3 the perfusion is insufficient to sustain tissue and necrosis/gangrene is imminent. Key takeaways: ABPI .

527.q: Most common cause of spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage?
527.e: Spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is usually the result of - Bleeding from a ruptured aneurysm (~80% of SAH) Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) Most ruptured aneurysms are located in the circle of Willis , at branch points in the arterial tree associated with turbulent blood flow. Reference : Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 708-709.

527.q: Which of the following statements is not true regarding autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)?
o: Polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 play a critical role
Visible haematuria occurs in up to 40% of patients with ADPKD
