567.e: Menstrual problems occurring in TB patients: M/C menstrual complain oligomenorrhea/Amenorrhea 1st menstrual complain – Menorrhagia (due to Endometritis in acute phase) Pelvic examination – M/C finding = Normal pelvic examination 2nd M/C finding – tenderness present Reference: J B Sharma, Textbook of Gynecology 1 st edition p380

567.q: A 19-year-old girl with painless ulcer in labia majora with everted margins:
567.e: The M/c causes of genital ulcers in young, sexually active women are: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) Treponema pallidum (syphilis) Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid). In this case, a painless ulcer with an everted margin leaves no doubt that the cause of the ulcer is syphilis (treponema pallidum). reference: J B Sharma, Textbook of Gynecology 1 st edition p359

567.q: The following are the primary sites of acute gonococcal infection except:
567.e: Ectocervix is covered by squamous epithelium and squamous epithelium is resistant to Gonococcal infection Primary genital sites of involvement of gonorrhea : Endocervix Urethra Skene’s gland Bartholin’s gland Reference: Dutta Gynae 6th/ed p 147.

567.q: True statement about female genital tuberculosis:
o: Genital tract involvement results from lymphatic spread
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques have got higher sensitivity in detection
Reproductive outcome following antituberculous chemotherapy is satisfactory
567.e: Genital tuberculosis is usually secondary to primary infection (lungs, bones, lymph nodes). It spreads by haematogenous route (not lymphatic route) leading to endosalpingitis. Caseous granulomatous lesions with giant cells on pathological examination are suggestive of TB but are not diagnostic as it can be seen in fungal infection and sarcoidosis. PCR is more sensitive (85–95%) than microscopy and bacteriological culture. This method can detect fewer than 10 organisms in clinical specimens compared to 10,000 necessary for smear positivity. Reproductive outcome even after treatment is poor. Pregnancy rate is about 20%, live birth rate is only 7%. The risk of miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy are high. Reference: Dutta Gynae 6th/ed p 140

568.q: A 44-year-old female complains of lower abdominal pain and vaginal discharge. On examination, there is cervicitis along with a mucopurulent cervical discharge. The Gram smear of the discharge shows presence of abundant pus cells, but no bacteria. The best approach to isolate the possible causative agent would be:
o: Culture on chocolate agar supplemented with hemin
Culture on a bilayer human blood agar
568.e: Patient is complaining of abdominal pain and vaginal discharge. On examination, cervicitis and mucopurulent discharge is seen - which indicates she is having PID. The presence of pus cells in the absence of an organism indicates chlamydial infection (most common STD today). It is an intracellular organism that grows only on McCoy or HeLa cell cultures. It cannot be grown on other media and hence, often goes unnoticed, later leading to infertility. Culture in McCoy cells is 100% specific for chlamydia but is inexpensive, technically difficult and takes 3-7 days to obtain the result. Reference: Harrion 18th/ed p 1426.

568.q: In the perspective of the busy life schedule in the modern society, the accepted minimum period of sexual cohabitation resulting in no offspring for a couple to be declared infertile is:
568.e: If a couple fails to achieve pregnancy after one year of “unprotected” and regular intercourse, it is an indication to investigate the couple for infertility. Infertility: Primary When no previous pregnancies have occurred. Secondary When a prior pregnancy although not necessary although not necessarily a live birth, has occurred Reference : Shaw 15 th /ed, p 200 Reference : Novak 13 th /ed, p 973

568.q: Most commonly used ovulation induction drug is
568.e: M/C used drug for ovulation Induction: clomiphene citrate Clomiphene Citrate: It is a racemic mixture of enclomiphene and zuclomiphene. Enclomiphene is a more potent isomer responsible for its ovulation-inducing action. Dose = 50–250 mg. However, the US FDA-approved maximum dose for clomiphene citrate is 100 mg Clomiphene blocks “Estrogen” receptors → increase FSH from pituitary →growth of follicles Thus it can be used only in patients with intact hypothalamic –pituitary ovarian axis With clomiphene success rate for ovulation is 80% and success rate for pregnancy is 40% Reference: JB Sharma textbook of Gynecology e1 p218

568.q: The following are the contraindications of tubal reconstructive surgery except:
o: Reversal done after 5 years of sterilization
568.e: Tubal reconstruction surgery can be done for a number of reasons including for reversal of sterilisation procedure. The most favourable outcome is seen when it is done for reversal of sterilisation procedures. Factors for Poor Outcome Following Tuboplasty Dense pelvic adhesions. Loss of fimbriae. Bilateral hydrosalpinx > 3 cm. Length of the reconstructed tube Reversal done after 5 years of sterilization operation. Presence of other factors for infertility Reference: Dutta Gynae 6 th /ed p 248.

568.q: A patient treated for infertility with clomiphene citrate presents with sudden onset of abdominal pain and dis tension with ascites, the probable cause is:
568.e: Side effects of clomiphene: Multiple pregnancy (6-8%) Ovarian cysts Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome ( Anti Estrogenic side effects Hot Flashes, osteoporosis Long Term use-ovarian malignancy Note: No congenital malformation seen Most common effects are hot flashes and ovarian cyst formation. Reference: Jeffcoate 7 th /ed p 652

568.q: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in a 28-year-old obese woman presenting with Oligomenorrhea, infertility and hirsutism?
568.e: A young woman presenting in the third decade with obesity, oligomenorrhea, infertility and hirsutism leaves no doubt for the diagnosis of PCOS. Ovulatory dysfunction such as oligomenorrhea or hyperandrogenism. Clinical or biochemical evidence of hyperandrogenism. USG criteria Since this female has oligomenorrhea and hirsutism, 2 of the criteria are being fulfilled. Reference: Shaw 15th/ed pg no: 371

568.q: In hysterosalpingography, fallopian tubes are seen beaded in appearance with clubbing of the fimbrial end and ampulla. What is likely cause :
568.e: HSG showing 'Bead-like fallopian tube and clubbing of ampulla are suggestive of genital tuberculosis' HSG findings in case of tuberculosis: Rigid non-peristaltic pipe like tube called as lead pipe appearance. Beading of tube and variation in filling density. Elongated and distended tube with everted fimbriae and patent abdominal ostium called 'tobacco pouch' appearance. Calcification of tube, Bilateral cornual block. Vascular or lymphatic intravasation of dye. Tubal diverticula Uterine cavity - irregular outline, honeycomb appearance or presence of uterine synechiae (Asherman’s syndrome). In a proven case of genital tuberculosis, HSG is contraindicated as it may spread the infection. So, HSG should not be performed until pelvic tuberculosis is excluded by endometrial study. Reference : Dutta Gynae 5th/ed p 137-38

568.q: In hysterosalpingography, fallopian tubes are seen beaded in appearance with clubbing of the fimbrial end and ampulla. Most likely cause is:
568.e: HSG findings in case of tuberculosis: Rigid non-peristaltic pipe-like tube called lead pipe appearance. Beading of tube and variation in filling density. Elongated and distended tube with everted fimbriae and patent abdominal ostium called ‘tobacco pouch’ appearance. Calcification of tube. Bilateral cornual block. Vascular or lymphatic intravasation of dye. Tubal diverticula and/or fluffiness of tubal outline. Uterine cavity—irregular outline, honeycomb appearance or presence of uterine synechiae (Asherman’s syndrome). Reference: Shaw 15th/ed p 157; Dutta Gynae 5th/ed p 137-38

569.q: Chronic constipation in children is seen in all A/E?
569.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Jejunal polyp Organic causes of constipation are : i) Intestinal: Hirschprung disease, Anal/rectal stenosis, Anal fissure, anteriorly displaced anal opening, strictures. ii) Drugs: Narcotics, vincristine, Psychotropics. iii) Metabolic/endocrine: Cystic fibrosis, hypothyroidism, Panhypopituitrism iv) Neuromuscular: Cerebral palsy, Psychomotor retardation, spinal cord lesions, Myotonic dystophy, Neuropathy or myopathy of GIT v) Other causes: Low fibre diet, Milk protein allergy.

569.q: Which of the following statements is not true about cervical glands discharge
o: Cervical gland discharge is alkaline in nature and rich in mucoprotein
Vagina has no glands and acidic discharge of cervical glands makes vaginal ph low
Cervical gland secretions contain sodium chloride
None of the above (all are true)
569.e: Secretion of the cervical glands is alkaline and thick, rich in mucoprotein, fructose and sodium chloride. The vaginal pH , from puberty to menopause, is acidic because of the presence of Döderlein’s bacilli which produce lactic acid from the glycogen present in the exfoliated cells. The pH varies with the estrogenic activity and ranges between 4 and 5. Reference : DC Dutta textbook of obstetrics, 8th edition; chapter 1

569.q: Metropathica hemorrhagica is best treated by:
569.e: Metropathia hemorrhagica is a type of anovulatory DUB, hence logically speaking it should be best treated by progesterone therapy. It is mostly seen in premenopausal women. Patients complain of a variable period of amenorrhea followed by excessive painless bleeding. On HPE-cystic glandular hyperplasia, Swiss cheese pattern is seen, and secretory changes are absent Treatment: In DUB due to anovular causes: Progesterones are the mainstay of therapy. They diminish the effects of estrogen on target cells by inhibiting oestrogen receptors. Reference: Dutta Gynae 5 th /ed pp 184,187.

569.q: Sarita, a 30 year old woman develops a deep vein thrombosis in her left calf on fourth postoperative day following cesarean section done for fetal distress. The patient is started on heparin and is scheduled to begin a 6 weeks course of warfarin therapy. The patient is a devoted mother who wants to breastfeed her baby. What is the advice which is given to the patient?
o: Patient may continue breastfeeding at her own risk
Patient should breast feed her baby only if her INR is at <2.5
Patient can breast feed her baby after 6 weeks course of warfarin is over
Warfarin is not a contraindication for lactation
569.e: Remember: Warfarin is contraindicated in the first trimester of pregnancy as it can lead to contradi syndrome comprising of microcephaly, optic atrophy, nasal hypolplasia and chondrodysplasia punctate.It can also lead to IUGR, abortions and IUD. But warfarin is absolutely safe during lactation as an extremely minute quantity of it is excreted in breast milk. Reference : Dutta Obs 7/e, pg 146

569.q: Postpartum decidual secretions present are referred to as:
569.e: LOCHIA: It is the vaginal discharge for the first fortnight during puerperium The discharge originates from the uterine body, cervix and vagina. Its reaction is alkaline tending to become acid towards the end. Depending upon the variation of the color of the discharge, it is named as: Lochia rubra (red) 1-4 days. Lochia serosa (5-9 days) - the color is yellowish or pink or pale brownish. Lochia alba — (pale white) - 10-15 days Reference : Dutta Obs. 7/e, pg 146

569.q: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is indicated in all except:
569.e: Prevention of CHD. But recent trials have shown an increase in the Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) is generally indicated for conditions such as osteoporosis, hot At flushes, and atrophic vaginitis. However, it is not recommended for the prevention of cardiovascular disease. 49 In fact, studies have shown potential risks associated with HRT, particularly in relation to cardiovascular events, which has led to a more cautious approach in prescribing HRT for this purpose. Reference: Novak 15th/ed p 1242

569.q: A 45-year-old multipara lady has a single fibroid detected on a routine USG. The fibroid is in fact palpable clinically and is found to be 14- 16 cms in size. The patient is currently asymptomatic. What is the next line of management?
569.e: Since she is perimenopausal and her childbearing is complete we can go for hysterectomy. Indications for Operating an Asymptomatic Fibroid: Fibroids larger than 12-14 weeks pregnancy. Rapidly growing fibroids. Subserous and pedunculated fibroid prone to torsion. If it is likely to complicate a future pregnancy. If there is doubt about its nature Unexplained infertility and unexplained recurrent abortion. Uncertain diagnosis: If patient is symptomatic decide whether you give medical. Treatment or surgical treatment. Indications of Medical Management To treat anemia and recover hemoglobin levels before To reduce the size of large fibroid and facilitate Treatment of women approaching menopause to avoid In women with medical contraindication to surgery or those who are postponing surgery. For preservation of fertility in women with large myomas before conservative surgery like myomectomy.

569.q: GnRH analogues are useful in all except
569.e: GnRH is the controlling factor for gonadotropin release (LH and FSH). Indications for using Synthetic GnRH In females: (In all those conditions where there is increased estrogen, GnRH analogues are useful). In males: Cryptorchidism: short-term intranasal nafarelin is used. Carcinoma prostate: GnRH agonists are as effective as orchidectomy in Ca prostate but if there are neurological symptoms or life-threatening metastatic disease - androgens should first be started followed by GnRH agonist. BPH: Daily administration of leuprorelin or nafarelin decreases obstructive urinary symptoms in 1-6 months time. Adverse Effects of GnRH Local allergic reactions may occur at injection sites. They cause menopause like symptoms-hot flushes, vaginal dryness, headache, joint and muscle stiffness, depression, osteoporosis, and irregular vaginal bleeding. Reference: Jeffcoate 7 th /ed p 652

570.q: All of these secrete hormone, except:
570.e: Dysgerminoma: "The tumor is neutral and does not secrete either male or female sex hormones but secretes placental alkaline phosphatase, lactate dehydrogenase and beta hCG". Granulosa cell tumor : Secretes estrogen Theca cell tumor : Secretes estrogen Hilus cell tumor : Secretes androgens Reference: Shaw 15 th /ed p 378

570.q: The most common pure germ cell tumour of the ovary:
570.e: Germ cell Tumors of ovary: In contrast to slow growing epithelial ovarian tumors, germ cell malignancies grow rapidly and are characterized by subacute pelvic pain. Most common germ cell Tumor – Mature teratoma or Dermoid cyst (Benign in nature). Most common malignant GCT – Dysgerminoma. Second most common malignant GCT –Immature cystic teratoma Reference: CGDT 10 th/ed p 875; Devita 7th/ed p 1391; Novak 14th/ed p 1506; 15th/ed p 1394; Williams Gynae 1st/ed p 741

570.q: False about dermoid cyst of ovary:
570.e: Dermoid cyst: Dermoid cyst is a benign teratoma. It is most common benign tumour of ovary in reproductive age group. Most common benign neoplasm diagnosed during pregnancy. Most common Germ cell tumor. It is the commonest tumor to undergo torsion. Characteristically they are unilocular cyst containing hair and cheesy sebaceous material, teeth, bones, thyroid tissue and cartilage. If teeth or bone are seen in X-ray in adnexal mass, this finding is pathognomic for teratoma and thus X-ray is diagnostic. Malignant change in a dermoid cyst occurs in 0.5 – 2% cases in patients > 40 years. Most common malignancy which develops is, squamous cell carcinoma. Reference: Textbook of Gynaecology Sheila Balakrishnan 1 st /ed p 183 Reference: Shaw 15 th /ed p 376-7; Williams Gynae 1 st /ed p 214-5

570.q: Nerve supply of ovaries are derived from spinal segment
570.e: The ovaries derive their nerve supply from Sympathetics via renal and aortic plexus and celiac and mesenteric ganglia (derived from T9 T10 spinal segment) which follow the course of the ovarian vessels. Ovaries are developed from genital ridge (abdominal organ) then descend to the pelvis at 33 week of gestation. Ovarian artery is a direct branch of the aorta, other pelvic organs are mainly supplied by the internal iliac artery. Reference: D C Dutta's textbook of gynecology, 7th edition, chapter 1

570.q: Which of the following ovarian tumour is most prone to undergo torsion during pregnancy?
570.e: "Incidence of dermoid cyst increases two times in pregnancy and it becomes the most commonly diagnosed ovarian tumour during pregnancy." -Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 310 "A benign cystic teratoma is the most common neoplasm to undergo torsion." -Novak 14/e, p 510 Note: Benign cystic teratoma is another name for dermoid cyst. From the above two lines it is clear that dermoid cyst is the most common ovarian tumour to undergo torsion during pregnancy. For more details on dermoid cyst and other ovarian tumours kindly see" Self-Assessment and Review Gynaecology" by the same author. Reference : Novak 14/e, pg 510; Dutta Obs. 6/e, pg 310

570.q: Sample should be taken from which wall of vagina, for hormonal analysis;
570.e: Vaginal study gives a fair idea about the hormonal status and, in turn, about ovulation/ovarian cycle. For hormonal study, sample should be taken from: Lateral wall For cytological study (Papsmear), sample should be taken from: Posterior wall Squamous epithelium is resistant to gonococcal infection hence theoretically gonococcal vaginitis can occur in new born females Vagina does not have any mucus-secreting glands. Since vagina does not have any glands, vaginal discharge is not derived from vagina. The components of vaginal secretion are derived from: Endocervical glands Endometrial glands Bartholin’s glands Vagina does not have any serosal covering except for the area covered by cul de sac posteriorly. Apart from Doderlein’s bacilli, it contains many other pathogenic organisms including Cl. welchii. Reference: Self-assessment and review of gynecology, ch-1, page 10.

570.q: Smt. Pushpa is a suspected case of ovarian tumors. On laparotomy bilaterally enlarged ovaries with smooth surface was seen:
570.e: Krukenberg tumor: Krukenberg tumor by definition represents carcinoma of stomach metastasis to ovary . But the eponym is commonly used to denote any gastric cancer metastatic to ovary Tumor arises by retrograde lymphatic spread e. carcinoma cells pass from the stomach to the superior gastric lymph node which also receives lymphatics from the ovary. Characteristics of Krukenberg Tumour: Always bilateral Have smooth surface No tendency to form adhesions Freely mobile No infiltration through the capsule. Histologically the tumour has signet ring cells in the background of myxomatous stroma. They retain the shape of a normal ovary. Have waxy consistency. Reference : Shaw 15 th /ed pg 425-6; CGDT 10 th /ed pg 877

In breastfeeding females, prolactin levels are increased in response to the suckling stimulus of breastfeeding. These observations suggest that high concentrations of prolactin can work at both central level (by inhibiting pulsatile secretion of GnRH) and peripheral level i.e. ovarian sites (by inhibiting synthesis of progesterone and by changing testosterone/dihydrotestosterone ratio i.e. increasing local antiestrogen concentrations) to produce lactational amenorrhea and anovulation. The principle of GnRH suppression by prolactin is reinforced by the demonstration that treatment of amenorrheic, lactating women with pulsatile GnRH, fully restores pituitary secretion and normal ovarian cyclic activity. Reference : Leon Speroff 7 th /ed, pg no: 582

571.q: What is the age group distribution for vulval cancer
571.e: Vulval Cancer Vulval cancer accounts for 2%-4% of all malignancies of the female genital tract. The women are generally elderly, in the sixth or seventh decade of life. Thirty per cent of cases are older than 70 years, and 40% of cases are between the age of 60 and 70 years. M/C variety- Squamous cell carcinoma Most common symptom of vulval cancer - pruritis Most common site: Labia majora and minora Most common type of spread: Lymphatics( First lympnode involved-Superficial Inguinal lymphnode, and then Deep inguinal LN and femoral group of lymphnodes). For lateral tumors only ipsilateral lympnodes involved whereas for midline leisons, B/L lymphnodes are involved Sentinel lymphnode biopsy is helpful in vulval cancer Most important prognostic factor- Lymph node status.

571.q: A 38-year-old woman approaches a physician for contraceptive advice. On examination, there were two symmetrical ulcers on her vulva, which were well-defined with a firm base. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
571.e: Painless well-defined ulcers with a firm base should raise the suspicion of a chancre. Chancre is the primary lesion of primary syphilis. It is most commonly found on the labium majus, labium minus, fourchette, clitoris, urethral orifice, or cervix, but can be found anywhere on the lower genital tract. In 10% cases, more than one primary lesion is present. The first manifestation is a small papule which breaks to form an ulcer. Ulcer is firm, painless with raised edges and a granulomatous base. In fact, any sort of discrete, relatively painless ulceration on the vulva may be a primary syphilitic lesion. Inguinal glands enlarge when the primary is on the vulva or lower vagina. Lymph nodes are hard, painless, and do not suppurate. Reference: Williams Gynaecology, 1st Edition, Page Number-58.

571.q: A lady approaches a physician for contraceptive advice. On examination, there were two symmetrical ulcers on the vulva, which were well-defined with a firm base. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
571.e: Chancre is the primary lesion of primary syphilis. It is most commonly found on the labium majus, labium minus, fourchette, clitoris, urethral orifice or cervix but can be found anywhere on the lower genital tract. In 10% cases more than one primary lesion is present. The first manifestation is a small papule which breaks to form an ulcer. Ulcer is firm, painless with raised edges and granulomatous base. In fact any sort of discrete relatively painless ulceration on the vulva may be primary syphilitic lesion. Inguinal glands enlarge when the primary is on the vulva or lower vagina. Lymph nodes are hard, short, painless, and do not suppurate. Reference: Harrison 17th/ed p 1040; William’s Gynae 1st/ed p 58-9 Current diagnosis and treatment of STDs p 21

571.q: A 38 year old woman approaches a physician for contraceptive advice. On examination, there were two symmetrical ulcers on vulva, which were well-defined with a firm base. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
571.e: Painless well-defined ulcers with firm base should raise the suspicion of chancre. Chancre is the primary lesion of primary syphilis. It is most commonly found on the labium majus, labium minus, fourchette, clitoris, urethral orifice or cervix but can be found anywhere on the lower genital tract. In 10% cases more than one primary lesion is present. The first manifestation is a small papule which breaks to form an ulcer. Ulcer is firm, painless with raised edges and granulomatous base. In fact any sort of discrete relatively painless ulceration on the vulva may be primary syphilitic lesion. Inguinal glands enlarge when the primary is on the vulva or lower vagina. Lymph nodes are hard, shotty, painless, and do not suppurate Reference: William's Gynae 1st/ed p 58.

572.q: Pap smear of janki, 46 years female shows CIN grade III. Which of the following is the next step in management?
572.e: Pap smear is only a screening test. To confirm we need to do a biopsy. In all visible lesions punch biopsy should be done In the case of invisible lesions, colposcopic directed biopsy is the gold standard. Thus, in this case since it is not mentioned growth is visible so we do colposcopy guided biopsy. Reference: Williams Gynecology 1 st /ed pg 628, Table 29-6

572.q: A 56-year-old female patient has carcinoma ovary with bilateral involvement with ascitic fluid in the abdomen. The stage is:
572.e: Bilateral involvement and malignant ascites is seen in category IC. In IC also- according to the new classification it is IC 3. Superficial liver metastasis is included in Stage III. Metastasis to liver parenchyma is included in Stage IV. Reference : Novak 14 th /ed pg 1477; Shaw 15 th /ed pg 427

572.q: A 42-year-old female P3 + 0 + 0 + 3 is found to have carcinoma in situ. Best treatment would be:
572.e: "Carcinoma in situ (stage 0) can be managed successfully by cone biopsy or by abdominal hysterectomy." Reference : Harrison 17 th /ed pg 608 Friends, carcinoma in situ is managed in young women with cone biopsy, whereas in older women or females who had completed their families (> 40 years), simple hysterectomy is the TOC. Reference : Harrison 17 th /ed pg 608; Reference : Novak 14 th /ed pg 581; Reference : Jeffcoate 6 th /ed pg 398

572.q: Which of the following is not a risk factor for CA cervix?
572.e: Factors Predisposing to CIN/Ca cervix: Human Papillomavirus infection Sexually transmitted infection Coitus before 18 years of age Multiple sex partners Multiparity Poor personal hygiene Poor socioeconomic status Smoking, Immunosuppressed individuals Women on OCP, Progesterone therapy for a long time are predisposed to adenocarcinoma of endocervix. In utero exposure to DES "HPV is central to the development of cervical neoplasia. HPV - DNA is found in 95% of all squamous cell carcinoma & 90% of all adenocarcinomas." Reference : Novak 15 th /ed pg 1306.

572.q: HPV triage strategy includes all except:
572.e: HPV triage strategies are used to determine the next step in cervical cancer screening when HPV is detected. These strategies typically involve Conventional Pap smear (A) - Used for cytological evaluation of cervical cells. Liquid-based cytology (B) - A more advanced method of cytology that improves sample quality. Hybrid Capture 2 (HC2) for HPV DNA (C) - A molecular test used to detect high-risk HPV DNA. Colposcopy (D) is not a triage strategy but rather a diagnostic procedure performed if abnormal cytology or persistent high-risk HPV is found Reference : Dutta Gynae 6 th /ed pg 323-4

572.q: The following is always an indication of cesarean section, except:
o: Untreated stage of I b Ca cervix
572.e: Cesarean Section is not indicated in all cases of abruptio placentae. 'An attempt at vaginal delivery is indicated if the degree of separation appears to be limited and if continuous FHR tracing is reassuring. When the placental separation is extensive but the fetus is dead or of dubious viability, vaginal delivery is indicated'. - COGDT 10/e, p 334 In carcinoma cervix, classical cesarean section should be done, vaginal delivery should not be allowed because of cervical dystocia and injuries. - Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 308 Cesarean section is indicated in an active primary genital HSV infection where the membranes are intact or recently ruptured. - Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 300 In a severe degree of placenta previa (Type II posterior, Type III or Type IV), cesarean section is indicated for maternal interest even if the baby is dead. Reference : Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 308, 301, 250; COGDT 10/e, p 334

572.q: Patient diagnosed as squamous cell intraepithelial lesion which of the following has the highest risk for progression to carcinoma:
o: Squamous intraepithelial neoplasia associated with HIV
572.e: There are various nomenclatures/classification systems for reporting of Pap smear. The one which is classically used is by WHO, which uses the terms CIN-I, CIN-II and CIN-III. Another system as discussed earlier is Bethesda which classified the disease as LSIL=low grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and HSIL high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and as discussed in chapter on cancer cervix chances of progressing to cancer are maximum with HSIL which includes CIN11, CIN111 and Ca in situ Reference: Shaw 15 th /ed p 402; Williams Gynae 1 st /ed p 629

572.q: A 45 year old woman Complains of contact bleeding. She has positive pap smear. The next line of management is:
572.e: 44 years old patient presenting with post coital bleeding and positive pap smear raises suspicion of carcinoma cervix / CIN which needs to be confirmed (as pap smear is only a screening procedure). In the question it is not mentioned whether lesion is visible nor the size of lesion is given so we take it to be invisible. As already discussed for invisible lesions, colposcopy should be done to confirm the diagnosis. Reference : Williams Gynae 1 st /ed pg 628, Table 29.6

573.q: Which of the following investigations should be conducted in a 7-month-old child who has a hemoglobin level of 6.3, a history of recurrent blood transfusions, an MCV of 70 fl, normal MCH, normal MCHC, and a peripheral smear indicating a hypochromic microcytic image?
573.e: Explanation: In an infant with severe microcytic hypochromic anemia requiring transfusions, the most likely diagnosis is beta-thalassemia major . Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the definitive test, which would show a significant increase in Hemoglobin F (HbF) and possibly Hemoglobin A2 (HbA2) , with absent or reduced Hemoglobin A (HbA). Explanation of other options: Serum iron (Option A): Would be normal or elevated in thalassemia (due to transfusions), but low in iron deficiency. It is not the definitive test. Direct coomb's test (Option B): Used to diagnose autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Osmotic fragility test (Option C): Used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis, which causes a normocytic or macrocytic anemia, not microcytic. Key Takeaways: Thalassemia major presents in infancy with severe transfusion-dependent microcytic anemia. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the key diagnostic test.

Metropathia hemorrhagica is the same as cystic glandular hyperplasia and is a causative factor for endometrial cancer. Gynandroblastoma is a virilising tumor which secretes androgens (not estrogens) and so does not lead to endometrial cancer Dysgerminoma is a neutral tumor which doesnot secrete either male or female sex hormones but secretes placental alkaline phosphatase, LDH and BHCG and therefore doesnot lead to endometrial cancer. Reference : Shaw 14 th /ed pg 3386 Reference : Dutta Gynae 5 th /ed pg 184

573.q: Pain of ovarian carcinoma is referred to:
573.e: Ovarian pain is referred along the medial side of thigh The obturator nerve during its course, when runs in front of the internal iliac vessels is separated from the normally situated ovary by only the parietal peritoneum lining the pelvic wall, thus pain from the ovary may be referred along the nerve to the skin on the medial side of thigh. Also know Simpson Pain - colicky pain in patients of Ca Endometrium. It is referred to the hypogastrium or to both iliac fossae. It is not severe and tends to appear at the same time each day lasting only 1–2 hours. Reference : Lasts Anatomy 10th/ed pg 302

Long-term tamoxifen therapy is a predisposing factor for endometrial hyperplasia and cancers. Malignancies caused by long-term tamoxifen therapy: Carcinoma endometrium-it is the most common carcinoma associated with it. Uterine sarcoma. Rarely liver cancer with long-term high dose. Non malignant effects of tamoxifen on uterus: Endometrial hyperplasia Endometriosis Fibroid uterus Ovarian cysts Menstrual irregularities or amenorrhea. Reference : Shaw 15 th /ed pg 417, Reference : Novak 14 th /ed pg 1345

Before answering these questions I want all of you to quickly revise staging of Ca Endometrium. Vaginal metastasis means stage IIIB Lymph node involvement is seen from stage IIIC onwards. Bowel involvement /rectal involvement means stage IVA. Lung metastasis means stage IVB. Serosa involvement/positive peritoneal cytology means stage IIIA. The question is about stage IIIB, so everything involved before it is also included. Reference : Novak 15 th /ed pg 1265; Reference : Shaw 15 th /ed pg 420.

573.q: Indication of adjuvant radiotherapy in Ca endometrium are all except:
573.e: Indications of adjuvant radiotherapy: Extrauterine extension. Lower uterine or cervical involvement. Papillary serous or clear cell histology. Poor histologic differentiation (Grade III). Myometrial penetration greater than 1/2 of thickening. Pelvic node involvement. Reference : Shaw 15 th /ed pg 420; Reference : Novak 15 th /ed pg 1275.

573.q: The following are precursors of endometrial carcinoma except:
573.e: Premalignant Lesions of Endometrium are: Simple hyperplasia: Endometrium is thick. The glands are dilated and have outpouching and invaginations. They are crowded and have irregular outlines. The stroma is more dense and cellular. Complex hyperplasia: Endometrium is thicker. The glands are crowded and arranged back to back with reduced stroma. Most glands have irregular outlines. There are papillary processes and intraluminal bridges within the glands. Epithelial pseudostratification is present. Atypical hyperplasia: The endometrial glands have cytologic atypia. The gland outlines are of complex hyperplasia in type. The nuclei of the glands show enlargement, irregular size and shape, hyperchromasia and coarse chromatin. Carcinoma-in-situ: Commonly describes a lesion with severe cytologic as well as architectural abnormalities of the glands. Reference : Dutta Gynae 6 th /ed pg 330

573.q: Living ligature of the uterus is:
573.e: Arrangement of muscle fibres in the uterus are arranged in 3 layers. Outer longitudinal Inner circular Intermediate: – Is the strongest and thickest layer arranged in criss-cross fashion. Through this layer blood vessels run. Apposition of two double curve muscle fibre gives the figure of 8 form. When the muscle contracts they occlude the blood vessels running through the fibres and hence called Living Ligature. Reference : Dutta Obs. 7/e, pg 46

574.q: Narrowest part of fallopian tube is:
574.e: Parts are: Interstitium (Intramural): 1.25 cm long and 1 mm diameter (narrowest part). It has no longitudinal muscles; only circular muscles are present and acts as anatomical sphincter. Isthmus: 2.5 cm long and 2 mm in diameter (second narrowest part); acts as physiologic sphincter. Ampulla: Widest and longest part (5 cm) and fertilization occurs here. Fimbriae/infundibulum: 1.25 cm long with a maximum diameter of 6 mm Total length = 4 inches or 10–12 cm. Reference: Chapter 1, page 8, JB Sharma textbook of Gynecology

574.q: Glands of littre are homologous to:
574.e: The glands of labia minora are homologous to the glands of littre (glandulas prepuciales) of the penile portion of the male urethra Skene's Tubules Skene's tubules are the paraurethral glands equivalent to prostrate in males. Both Bartholin's glands and Skene's tubules arise as downgrowths of urogenital sinus. Bartholin's Glands Bartholin's Glands are homologous to Cowper's gland/bulbourethral glands in males. They are 2 in number and of racemose type. Lie in the superficial perineal pouch embedded in the posterior part of vestibular bulb. Glands are oval in shape and are the size of a pea. They are impalpable unless enlarged. The acini is lined by a single layer of low columnar or cuboidal cells. Reference: Shaw, 15/e, page 8

574.q: Which kind of epithelium is present in vagina?
574.e: In adult females, vagina is lined by stratified squamous epithelium. In newborn females, it is lined by transitional epithelium. Squamous epithelium is resistant to gonococcal infection. Thus, gonococcal vaginitis cannot occur in young/adult females. Reference : J B Sharma, Textbook of Gynecology 1 st edition pg 327

574.q: Which of the following is present in labia minora
574.e: Structurally, the labia minora are composed of connective tissue with many small vessels, elastin fibers, but very little smooth muscle. Nerve fibers are numerous. The epithelia of the labia minora differ by location. Thinly keratinized stratified squamous epithelium covers the outer surface of each labium. Medial to this line, each labium is covered by squamous epithelium that is nonkeratinized. Labia minora lack hair follicles, eccrine glands, and apocrine glands but have many sebaceous glands. Reference: williams obstetrics 26th edition chapter 2

574.q: The uterine blood flow at term
574.e: Uterine blood flow in nonpregnant females = 50 ml/min Uterine blood flow in pregnant females = 750 ml/min Reference: Dutta 8/e

574.q: How much iron a patient can tolerate at a time given intravenously?
574.e: If the dose is more than 50 ml (each ml has 50 mg of iron i.e. 2500 mg iron), then half the dose is given on day one and second half on next day. Thus maximum iron which can be given in a day is 2500 mg. ACOG recommends the use of iron sorbitol as it is safer than iron dextran. Reference: Dutta Obs. 7/e, p 269

574.q: Maximum dose of oral labetalol per day is (mg/day)
574.e: The maximum recommended dose of oral labetalol is generally 2,400 mg per day. This is typically divided into two to three doses throughout the day. However, dosing may vary based on individual patient needs and specific clinical situations. Reference : Arias 5 th edition pg no 195

574.q: Therapeutic range of MgSO4 in mEq/L is
574.e: Therapeutic range = 4-7m Eq/L Disappearance of patellar reflex is the first sign of impending toxicity of MgSO4. Patellar reflex is lost when Mg++ concentration reaches 10 mEq/L.-12 mEq/L (12 mg/dl). Respiratory depression occurs with Mg concentration >12 mEq/L and arrest when >15 mEq/L. Cardiac arrest occurs when >30 mEq/L Reference : Arias 5th edition pg no 199 Reference : Arias 5 th edition pg no 198

575.q: What is the normal color of stool in the newborn after first week of life?
575.e: Meconium (first stool) is passed within 24 hours. After that meconium stools (black tarry)can be passed upto 3 days. On 4th-5th days transitional stools (greenish) are passed. After 5 days regular milk stools (golden yellow) are passed. Tags: Topic: MISCELLANEOUS Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW Reference: Ghai essential pediatrics, 9 th ed, pg no: 133

575.q: What is the venous hematocrit level at which you will diagnose polycythemia in a newborn?
575.e: Definition of polycythemia: a. Venous haematocrit of over 65%. b. Venous haematocrit of over 64% at 2 hours age. c. An umbilical venous or arterial haematocrit over 63% or more. The mean venous haematocrit of term infants is 53 in cord blood, 60 at 2 hours of age, 57 at 6 hours of age and 52 at 12-18 hours of age. As the haematocrit increases, there is increased viscosity and decreased blood flow. When haematocrit increases to more than 60% there is a fall in O2 transport. Definition of hyperviscosity: Viscosity greater than 14.6 centipose at a shear rate of 11.55 as measured by a viscometer. (normal is 1.4- 1.8 centipoise).

575.q: You have to IV cannulate a newborn. The following things are available: 1. 22 G Cannula 2. 26 G Cannula 3. Gloves 4. Normal Saline 5. 5 ml Syringe Which among the following you shall be using for cannulation in this newborn?
575.e: This question is a practical application-based question and very similar to an actual question asked recently. The correct answer is D. For IV cannulating a neonate, we need Gloves, Cannula, Normal saline (to flush) and a 2 ml syringe (not a 5 ml syringe) In neonates, 26G Cannula is used. Reference: The Harriet Lane Handbook 23 rd Edition

575.q: In a neonate with leaky meningomyelocele with CSF dripping out, it should be covered with which among the following before surgery is undertaken?
575.e: The exposed meningomyelocele sac containing neural tissue should be covered with a sterile Saline-soaked gauze. REMEMBER: Exposed neural tissue should not be covered or wiped with any irritant, not even Povidone-Iodine! Perinatal Care for Meningomyelocele Prone or lateral position nursing Cover the sac with a sterile, saline-moistened gauze Prophylactic antibiotics Consider a doughnut ring to prevent sac rupture in MC & MMC Monitor OFC, AF & Vitals closely Reference: AIIMS NICU Protocols 3 rd Edition

575.q: A baby receiving KMC is now stable enough for the procedure to be stopped. What shall be the baby's weight at which you shall decide stopping KMC?
575.e: When to Discontinue KMC? If the mother and baby are comfortable, KMC is continued at the hospital and at home for as long as possible. Often this is desirable until the baby's gestation reaches term or the weight is around 2500 g. Once the weight cut off is reached or crossed and the neonate starts wriggling to show that she is uncomfortable, pulls her limbs out, cries, and fusses whenever put in skin-to-skin contact, the mother can wean the baby from KMC. Reference: AIIMS Protocols In Neonatology, 3 rd Edition, Volume 2, Page 527

575.q: A 7-month-old male infant is at his pediatrician's office for his routine check-up and immunizations. He can roll over from his tummy to back but unable to roll over supine to prone. He is passing objects with his hands, and he cannot sit. His nurse mentions this to the pediatrician. There is a family history of maternal uncle (mother's brother) dying at 16 years of age after being bed-ridden for many years. Of the following, the BEST next step in evaluation and management would be to:
575.e: This infant has development delay predominantly involving motor domain with history of maternal uncle dying between 15-20 years age, who was bed-ridden prior. All this indicates a likely muscle dystrophy with X-linked recessive inheritance, causing death in the 2 nd decade of life. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked, recessive condition affecting male infants should be ruled out in such cases Since targeted therapies are available with more emerging for DMD, sending a creatine kinase (CK) in a male infant with development delay is the next best step at the pediatrician's office. Early detection and diagnosis will enable early treatment. Serum Creatine kinase (CK) is the primary biomarker for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and often used as a screening test. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA edition, pg. 2967

575.q: A preterm neonate could not be started on mother's feed due to some maternal issues. Which among the following is the best alternative to administer in such a case?
575.e: DONOR HUMAN MILK Donar human milk [DHM] is the milk expressed and voluntarily donated by lactating women other than the biological mother of the recipient baby. This donor human milk is pasteurized using the Holder pasteurization method [pasteurized donor human milk; PDHM] and dispensed for use of the recipient. Donation should be free and without any monetary benefit. The recipient should also be provided the DHM free of cost. World health Organization [WHO] and National Neonatology Forum [NNF], India recommends DHM as the preferred choice if mother's own milk is not available for feeding of preterm or low- birthweight [LBW] infants, including very preterm [ Reference: AIIMS Protocols In Neonatology, 3 rd Edition, Volume 2, Page 543

575.q: You are called by the newborn nursery nurse secondary to see a 1-day-old infant vomiting with every feed. The patient takes the formula well but vomits large amounts soon after his feed. The emesis is nonbilious. The only significant history is polyhydramnios during his mother's pregnancy. You obtain an abdominal radiograph and find a large, dilated stomach. What is the most likely diagnosis?
575.e: It is a tough question, but such questions can be answered by ruling out other options easily. Option A- Pyloric stenosis is an acquired condition and would NEVER present in the first few days of life, nor would it be associated with a large stomach at birth and polyhydramnios. Option B- Duodenal webs and atresia would likely present with bilious vomiting. Option C- Jejunoileal atresia would also likely present with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. Option D- Neonates with pyloric atresia will present with early onset of vomiting that is nonbilious, as well as a dilated stomach at birth. The mother may also have polyhydramnios during her pregnancy. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1801

576.q: A 3-year-old child presented with trouble walking to paediatrician. He is diagnosed with DMD (Duchenne muscular dystrophy) by polymerase chain reaction. Genetic analysis shows that the patient's gene for the muscle protein dystrophin on X chromosome contains a mutation. Mutation is found in its promoter region. Which would be the most likely defective process in this child?
o: Post translational modification in dystrophin protein
Post transcriptional modification in dystrophin mRNA
576.e: Option A & Option B: Translation is synthesis of protein from mRNA. Mutation in promoter regions does not lead to any problem during translation or post translational modifications. A deficiency of dystrophin mRNA will result in a deficiency in the production of the dystrophin protein. Option C: Mutations in the promoter typically prevent formation of the RNA polymerase II transcription complex, resulting in a decrease in the initiation of mRNA synthesis during transcription. Option D: Post transcriptional modifications like capping, splicing and tailing defects are not a consequence of promoter mutations. Reference: Harper’s illustrated biochemistry 32 nd edition CH 36 PN 379

576.q: A 14 year old boy has fevers. He has had elbow , shoulder and hip and knee pains over the last few months. On examination, he has a temperature of 37.5°C and palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations show a CRP of 30 and negative ANA. What is the likely diagnosis?
576.e: Any arthritis that occurs in individuals Oligoarticular Polyarticular Rheumatoid factor positive Polyarticular Rheumatoid factor negative Systemic onset Psoriatic arthritis and Enthesitis related arthritis. Systemic onset JIA. It is characterised by Fever Evanescent rash Hepatosplenomegaly Generalized Lymphadenopathy Serositis They are prone for developing a life-threatening complication called Macrophage Activation Syndrome. They will be negative for ANA and RA factor. There will be anemia, raised ESR and CRP with transaminase elevation. Ferritin may be elevated and coagulation screen may be abnormal. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:58, Pg: 394

576.q: The use of prostaglandin to keep the ductus arteriosus open is necessary in which of the following?
576.e: Ductus dependent congenital heart disease (require a patent ductus for maintaining pulmonary / systemic circulation) - Transposition of Great arteries - Tetralogy of Fallot - Tricuspid atresia (Ebstein anomaly) - Coarctation of aorta - Hypoplastic left heart syndrome - Pulmonary stenosis PGE1 is used to maintain an open ductus arteriosus in neonates with heart lesions that depend on it for survival. In Gerbode defect, there is a direct communication between right atrium and left ventricle. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2011-12

576.q: A 7-day-old female newborn had an abnormal result on newborn screening revealing an absence of T-cell receptor excision circles (TREC), which raises concern regarding severe combined immunodeficiency. Of the following, the MOST appropriate next test to confirm the diagnosis is
o: A complete blood cell counts with differential
576.e: Severe combined immunodeficiency represents a group of genetic primary immunodeficiencies defined by dysfunction of humoral and cell mediated immunity. The definitive test for quantifying lymphocyte subsets is flow cytometry. Left untreated, children with severe combined immunodeficiency die early in life owing to infection, but the condition is curable with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Tags : Topic : IMMUNE DISORDERS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1004

576.q: All the following vaccines must be given before splenectomy except?
576.e: Spleen takes care of infections caused by encapsulated bacteria. Hence, before splenectomy we must vaccinate the child against these capsulated organisms i.e., Pneumococcus, Meningococcus and H. Influenzae. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 2352

576.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with swelling and tenderness of his left maxilla, and left subconjunctival haemorrhage after falling on his head in the playground at school. There was no loss of consciousness during or after the incident. He is alert & conscious and his vital signs are stable including GCS 15/15 at the time of presentation and one hour later. He is exquisitely tender in palpation of his left maxillary bone. Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
576.e: There is absolutely no indication in the stem indicating of neurological deficit to order CT scan or MRI. Moreover, there are no signs of intracranial haemorrhage. Swelling and tenderness over left maxilla could represent a maxillary fracture. Tags: Topic: TRAUMA Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Manual of paediatric emergencies & critical care, 2 nd ed., pg. 254

576.q: Which of the following children are considered at-risk babies? 1. Baby with a birth weight of 2.5 kg 2. Baby on artificial feeding 3. Baby of working mother/single parent 4. Baby with weight 5. Birth order of 3 or more
576.e: Explanation: Among the given options, babies on artificial feeding and those with a working mother or single parent fall under the "at-risk" category. These infants are more vulnerable to malnutrition, infection, and inadequate care, requiring closer monitoring. Criteria for At-Risk Infants: Low birth weight ( Twins Higher birth order (≥5). Artificial feeding. Weight Failure to gain weight for 3 consecutive months. Children with PEM or recurrent diarrhea. Babies of working mothers or single parents. These risk factors are used to identify infants who need special attention to reduce morbidity and mortality. Key Takeaways: At-risk infants include those with low birth weight, artificial feeding, PEM, frequent diarrhea, high birth order, and social risk factors . Early identification allows for targeted interventions to reduce neonatal and infant mortality.

576.q: Neonatal reflex which is not present at birth?
576.e: All primitive reflexes are present at birth in a term neonate except Symmetric tonic neck reflex Parachute reflex Landau reflex Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 608

577.q: Treatment of simple febrile convulsion is based on
577.e: Answer- A. Control of fever Prompt reduction of temperature by hydrotherapy (sponging) and antipyretics (paracetamole, ibuprofen) is the most important measure. If seizures lasts for more than 5 minutes, diazepam (rectal or IV) is the anticonvulsant of choice. Phenobarbitone is an alternative

577.q: A baby is born at 43 w 4 d of gestational age. Which of the following morbidity is not to be anticipated in this baby?
577.e: Morbidities associated with post-term pregnancy include the presence of Meconium-stained amniotic fluid ( option a) Meconium aspiration Oligohydramnios Non-reassuring fetal heart rate tracing in labor Low apgar scores, Birth injury ( option c) Fetal macrosomia (option d) Fetal weight loss Tags : Topic : HIGH RISK NEWBORN Difficulty level : MUST KNOW Reference : Cloherty and Stark's Manual of Neonatal care, SA ed., pg. 88

577.q: A 2-day old neonate in the neonatal ICU develops seizures. Which of the following would be the next best investigation for the child?
577.e: In such a situation, BEDSIDE CRANIAL USG is a very useful and informative investigation. Cranial Ultrasound (CUS) in neonates is safe and radiation free. Safety of sonography is well established in fetus and infants CUS can be easily performed at the bedside. Reliable for commonly occurring neonatal events like hemorrhage, cystic lesions, major malformations and fluid collections. CUS can be initiated even immediately after birth and hence suitable for screening. It can be repeated as often as possible without any adverse effects and hence helps in proper follow up of babies with neurological problems. CUS is a significantly cheaper modality of neuroimaging compared with other techniques Reference: AIIMS NICU Protocols, 3 rd Edition

577.q: While giving phototherapy to a neonate for neonatal jaundice, the effectiveness of phototherapy depends on all except
577.e: The therapeutic effect of phototherapy depends on Light energy emitted in the effective range of wavelengths, Distance between the lights and the infant, Surface area of exposed skin Rate of hemolysis and in vivo metabolism and excretion of bilirubin. Dark skin does not reduce the efficacy of phototherapy . Tags : Topic : NEONATAL JAUNDICE Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : AIIMS JULY 2020 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 877

577.q: True regarding management and resuscitation in a baby born through meconium-stained liquor (MSL)?
o: Intrapartum suctioning of mouth and oropharynx
Tracheal suction in all vigorous MSL babies
Positive-Pressure Ventilation in all non-vigorous MSL babies
Gentle suction of mouth and nose in vigorous MSL babies
577.e: Let us evaluate the options sequentially Option A is False- Intrapartum suctioning is not indicated anymore in neonates Option B is False- Tracheal suction is not indicated anymore in neonates. Furthermore, vigorous MSL babies do not need resuscitation, including suction Option C is True- PPV is life-saving in non-vigorous MSL babies Option D is False- Vigorous babies do not need suction or any other initial steps of resuscitation. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 122-123; NRP 8 th Edition Guidelines

577.q: A female delivered a 1.2 kg baby prematurely at 31 wk. The child has hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, petechial rash. The child failed neonatal hearing screen. CT scan showed periventricular calcification. Likely congenital infection?
577.e: Clues in the question Preterm delivery Periventricular calcification Hepatosplenomegaly with jaundice Petechial Rash Failure of neonatal hearing screening, indicating likely SNHL This entire picture corresponds to a likely diagnosis of Congenital CMV Infection. Remember that petechial rash occurs commonly due to thrombocytopenia in such children. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 285

577.q: In a neonate undergoing resuscitation, PPV and chest compressions are being administered. Epinephrine should be administered in which of the following situations?
o: HR<60/min with Chest Compressions & PPV for 30 sec
HR<60/min with Chest Compressions & PPV for 60 sec
577.e: Medications are rarely required in neonatal resuscitation since the mainstay of management is adequate ventilation with or without chest compressions, but epinephrine should be administered when the heart rate is The umbilical vein can generally be readily cannulated and is the preferred method for administration of medications like epinephrine and volume expanders during neonatal resuscitation. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition Chapter 121, NRP Guidelines 8 th Edition

577.q: Which of the following is an effective indicator or perinatal asphyxia?
577.e: Essential Criteria For Perinatal Asphyxia Prolonged Metabolic or Mixed Acidemia (pH Persistence of APGAR Score of 0-3 for >5 min Neurological manifestations e.g., Seizures, coma, hypotonia or HIE Evidence of multiorgan dysfunction in the immediate neonatal period Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Table 9.23

578.q: Mouthing of objects tends to significantly reduce by what developmental age in a child?
578.e: According to OP Ghai 10 th Ed, at 6 months, as the ability to chew develops, the child can take a biscuit to his mouth and chew. At this age, he tends to mouth all objects offered to him. This is called mouthing of objects and can be a reason for inadvertent foreign body ingestion or aspiration. This tendency abates by around 1 year of age in most children. According to other texts and sources, mouthing reduces between 12-18 months. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 31

578.q: A child with developmental delay, can ride a tricycle, can copy a circle, can say name, knows own sex, but cannot narrate a story. What is the developmental age?
578.e: Age of attaining milestones normally Riding a tricycle comes normally at 3 years of age Saying full name and gender also comes at 3 years of age Copying a circle comes at 3 years of age Narrating a story comes at 4 years of age. Now, in this question, the child is able to perform the milestones corresponding to 3 years, but unable to do milestones related to 4 years. Hence, the developmental age of the child should be 3 years. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Tables 3.1, 3.2 and 3.4

578.q: A normal infant is able to sits leaning forward with hands, reaches for and grasps cube with one hand, transfers objects between hands, cannot wave bye-bye, cannot hold objects between finger and thumb. Most probable age is?
578.e: Let us evaluate the information given in the question. A normal infant can sit with own support from 6 months onwards, also called as Tripod position. Reaching for and grasping a cube with one hand, also called as Unidextrous grasp comes at 6 months of age Transferring objects hands to hands develops between 6 to 7 months of age. Waving bye-bye develops at 9 months Immature Pincer grasp comes by 9 months and mature one by 12 months. So, the child is able to do milestones of at or before 7 months of age, but not attained milestones related to 9 months and beyond. Hence the probable age of the child is 7 months. References: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Tables 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20 th edition, pg-69

578.q: A boy has now learnt to feed himself with spoon without spillage, can dress and undress himself with supervision, knows that he is a boy. These milestones are most likely developed between which age?
578.e: Let us evaluate the information given step-wise. Feeding self with spoon with spillage is achieved by 15 months & without spillage by 18 months of age. Can undress self with assistance or supervision by 2 years of age. Can dress self with assistance or supervision by 3 years of age. Knowing gender comes by 3 years. Hence best possible answer here is 2 to 3 years. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Table 3.3; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20 th edition, pg-76

578.q: An infant can sit leaning forwards, on his own hands. When made to stand, he bounces actively. He laughs loudly but becomes concerned when mother moves away and a new person enters the household. What is his most likely age?
578.e: Let us understand the information given here. The child is able to sit with own support, laughs loudly & has stranger anxiety. All of this is pointing towards a likely developmental age of 6 to 7 months. Thus the best answer is option D, i.e., 28 weeks. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 28-35.

578.q: A 10-month-old female infant presents with jerky movement of limbs towards the body; EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. The baby also has delay in attaining developmental milestones. Drug of choice for management in this condition?
578.e: The child in the question has West Syndrome. West syndrome starts between the ages of 2 and 12 months and consists of a triad of infantile epileptic spasms that usually occur in clusters (particularly in drowsiness or upon arousal), developmental regression, and a typical EEG picture called hypsarrhythmia. West syndrome is best treated with ACTH. However, if West Syndrome occurs as a part of Tuberous Sclerosis, then Vigabatrin is the preferred agent. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 2836

578.q: A 10-month-old female infant was admitted to ICU with complaints of recurrent, intermittent jerky movements of limbs on the body. There are delayed milestones in the child. Her EEG revealed a pattern of hypsarrhythmia. What shall be the anti-epileptic therapy of choice?
578.e: Recurrent jerky movements + Delayed milestones + Hypsarrhythmia on EEG indicates a likely diagnosis of West Syndrome. West syndrome is best treated with ACTH. High-dose ACTH is preferred over low-dose ACTH Vigabatrin is considered by some as a drug of second choice for infantile spasms and by some even as an alternative to ACTH as a drug of first choice in Tuberous Sclerosis patients. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 582, AOCN 2021 Guidelines On West Syndrome

578.q: A 2-year-old boy was found to have hepatosplenomegaly and delayed milestones. The liver biopsy and bone marrow biopsy revealed PAS positive histiocytes. Electron microscope finding of these histiocytes will most likely be?
o: Parallel rays of tubular structure in lysosomes
578.e: Hepatosplenomegaly with PAS positive histiocytes suggests diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). The hallmark of LCH is clonal proliferation of monocyte lineage. The presence of birbeck granules in the cytoplasm of tumor cells is characteristic of LCH. Birbeck granules are tennis racket shaped bilaminar granules. They are not seen in all tumor cells by electron microscopy, hence detection of S-100 and CD1a by immunohistochemistry are needed for confirmation of diagnosis. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA edition, pg. 2487

579.q: A baby boy born at 30 weeks of gestation is brought to you at 8 months of chronological age with complaint of not able to roll from prone to supine. What is the best next step of management?
o: Send genetic studies to find congenital disease
Send chromosomal array to find trisomy
Send to development pediatrician and occupational therapist for early intervention
579.e: Corrected gestational age = Chronological age- Preterm age = 32 weeks - 10 weeks = 22 weeks = 5.5 months Hence, the corrected age of the child is 5.5 months and usual age for the prone to supine is 6 months. Hence, the parents are to be reassured that child is normal for age. Till 2 years of age, correction of gestational age has to be applied. Tags : Topic : NORMAL DEVELOPMENT & ASSESSMENT Difficulty : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2023 Reference : Ghai's Essential pediatrics, 8 th ed., pg. 50

579.q: Tanya had her first birthday party recently. During her party she was able to commando crawl with ease, but could not walk. She picked up all the gems from her cake. She could speak 2 words with meaning. She waved goodbye to her guests. Which are of Tanya's development is delayed?
579.e: Commando crawl (gross motor), picking up gems from cake- pincer grasp (fine motor), speaking 2 meaningful words (language), waving good bye (personal-social); all are achieved latest by 12 months. Hence, she has achieved all her milestones needed for her age. MILESTONES AT 12 MONTHS GROSS MOTOR Stand without support Walk with support FINE MOTOR Mature pincer grasp (holding like a pen) PERSONAL SOCIAL Plays a simple ball game LANGUAGE 1-2 meaningful words Tags : Topic : NORMAL DEVELOPMENT & ASSESSMENT Difficulty : MUST KNOW PYQ : FMGE JUNE 2022; NEET PG 2021 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 137

579.q: Which of the following is most suggestive for suspecting cerebral palsy in children?
o: Smiling for the first time at 8 weeks
579.e: Hand preference, or handedness, is the tendency to use one hand more naturally and efficiently than the other for fine motor tasks. This usually develops in early childhood, often becoming clear between the ages of 2 and 4 Hand preference or hand dominance before 12 months of age is a red flag sign and needs evaluation. All other development milestone mentioned are achieved at optimal age. KEY TAKEAWAYS: Identifying and supporting hand preference helps children develop motor skills effectively, which can aid in tasks like writing and drawing as they grow Tags: Topic: CEREBRAL PALSY Difficulty level: MAY KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2021 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 143

579.q: All of the following are true regarding development sequence in children, except?
o: Development occurs in spurts rather than being a continuous process
CNS maturity is a major determinant of development
Primitive reflexes must be lost for complex milestones to be attained
579.e: Six rules of development in a child 1 st : Development is a continuous process - Begins in utero. 2 nd : CNS maturity is the major determinant. 3 rd : Cephalo-caudal progression is shown. 4 th : Primitive reflexes must be lost. 5 th : Initially reflexes or milestones are general or crude. As age progresses, they become more complex 6 th : Similar sequence occurs in all children. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Ed, Page 22

579.q: What is the rate of increase in head circumference in infants during the first 3 months of age?
579.e: Explanation: Head circumference increases most rapidly during the first 3 months of life at a rate of 2 cm per month . (Option D ruled out) Head Circumference Growth Pattern: 0-3 months: 2 cm/month 3-6 months: 1 cm/month (Option B ruled out) 6-12 months: 5 cm/month (Option A ruled out) 1-3 years: 2 cm/month Developmental Milestones: Birth: HC = 33-35 cm (2.5 cm > chest circumference) 1 year: HC = Chest circumference After 1 year: HC Measurement Technique: Maximum head circumference measured from occipital protuberance to supraorbital ridge using cross-tape method.

579.q: Sigmoid-shaped growth curve is shown by which among the following tissues/organs?
579.e: Somatic growth shows a typical sigmoid/S-shaped growth curve. There is rapid growth initially in the first 4-5 years, then there is a relatively stable growth, followed by pick-up again occurring around peri-pubertal period. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 6-7.

579.q: 70% of the adult head size is attained by which age?
579.e: At birth, about 70% of the adult head size is attained, while it becomes approximately 90% of the adult head size by 2 years of age. Thus, first 2 years of life are critical for brain growth. Maturation of functions occurs later in life. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Ed, Pages 6-7

579.q: Which of the following is not seen in Down's syndrome?
579.e: Caudal Regression Syndrome (CRS), also called Sacral Agenesis, is rare in the general population, but more common in infants of diabetic mothers (specific for these babies). It has not been described in Down's syndrome. Option B: Linear growth is retarded in Down's syndrome. Option C: About 13-34% patients with Down's syndrome have hypothyroidism. Option D: 40-60% patients have conductive hearing loss and are prone to Serous Otitis Media-commonly during the first year. Reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 10th Edition, Page Number-667.

580.q: A neonate has not passed urine in the last 24 hours since birth. Next step in management is?
580.e: According to Cloherty & Stark, 90% neonates void urine within 24 hours and 99% do so by 48 hours. Neonates without any risk factor can pass urine anytime before 48 hours of life. Until then we need to observe and feed the child. If more than 48 hours have passed, the baby needs to be shifted to the ICU and evaluated for volume status & investigated. Reference: Cloherty and Starks manual of neonatal care, SA ed., pg. 128

580.q: Breastfeeding should be started within how much time after birth?
580.e: Points to remember regarding breastfeeding Breastfeeding should be started as soon as possible after birth. As per WHO, UNICEF it must be started within 1 hr of birth Exclusive BF till: 6 months of age. Then start complementary feed and continue to breastfeed till 18-24 months. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 142

580.q: Indication to use prednisolone in Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura is?
580.e: Treatment for mild and self-limited HSP is supportive, with an emphasis on ensuring adequate hydration, nutrition, and analgesia. Corticosteroids are most often used to treat significant GI involvement or other life-threatening manifestations. Glucocorticoids such as oral prednisone (1-2 mg/kg/day), or in severe cases, intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone for 1-2 wk, followed by taper, reduce abdominal and joint pain but do not alter overall prognosis. Corticosteroids are not routinely recommended for prevention of complications such as nephritis. Corticosteroids may also be needed in any orchitis, CNS involvement and pulmonary hemorrhage Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed, Chapter 192, OP Ghai 10 th Ed, Page 661

580.q: When is it recommended to introduce solid foods to an infant while continuing breastfeeding?
580.e: Explanation: According to current recommendations by World Health Organization (WHO) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), solid foods should be introduced to an infant while continuing breastfeeding at around 6 months of age. At 6 months, infants have typically developed the necessary oral motor skills to handle solid foods, including loss of the tongue-thrust reflex, ability to sit with support, and adequate head and neck control . Breast milk or formula remains the primary source of nutrition during the first year, with complementary foods gradually introduced to meet increasing nutritional demands, especially for iron and zinc. Breastfeeding can go up to 2 years of age or till the time the mother wants.

580.q: All are true about human colostrum; EXCEPT?
580.e: In human colostrum, sugar content, i.e., Lactose content is low. Types of breast milk Colostrum- Secreted in the first 72 hr of life. Small in quantity, yellow coloured, thick in consistency, contains IgA, Vit A, D, E and K. Contains good amino acids but has lower lactose content Transitional Milk- Secreted between 4 days to 14 days. Protein content falls while fat and lactose content increase Mature Milk- Secreted after 2 weeks. Has high lactose, low fat and very low protein. Watery in consistency but contains all nutrients needed for the growth and development of the child. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 144

580.q: Which of the following statement defines wasting?
580.e: UNDERWEIGHT WEIGHT FOR AGE IS An underweight child can be wasted or stunted or both STUNTING HEIGHT FOR AGE IS It indicates chronic malnutrition. WASTING WEIGHT FOR HEIGHT IS It indicates acute malnutrition Tags : Topic : ASSESSMENT OF NUTRITION Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : INICET NOV 2023 Reference : Ghai essential pediatrics, 8 th ed., pg. 93

580.q: In a child suffering from pneumonia, all the following are indications to admit the child, who was previously healthy, except
580.e: INDICATIONS FOR ADMISSION Poor oral intake Persistent vomiting Convulsions Stridor at rest Severe malnutrition Tags : Topic : PNEUMONIA & COMPLICATIONS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : FMGE JUNE 2022; AUG 2020; DEC 2021 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2266

581.q: While treating the child with severe acute malnutrition, which of the following factor is not one of the criteria for discharge of the child?
581.e: Discharge criteria for SAM child Child is alert and active , eating atleast 120-130 kcal/kg/day with consistent weight gain of atleast 5g/kg/day on exclusive oral feeding Child is receiving adequate micronutrients Child is free of infections Child has completed immunization appropriate for age The caretaker has been sensitized for home-based care . Tags : Topic : SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2021; FMGE JAN 2022; AIIMS JULY 2020; FMGE JUNE 2022 Reference : Ghai's essential pediatrics, 9 th ed., pg. 107

581.q: Hepatitis B subunit vaccine is derived from?
581.e: The current subunit Hepatitis B vaccine is derived from surface antigen, i.e., HBsAg. The vaccine is based upon DNA recombinant technology and uses Aluminium as an adjuvant. The hepatitis B vaccine is made by taking the part of the virus that makes surface protein ("surface protein gene") and putting it into yeast cells. The yeast cells then produce many copies of the protein that are subsequently used to make the vaccine. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 198

581.q: A 6-year-old female child presented with non-blanchable, palpable petechial rash on lower limbs and buttocks, along with 3+ urinary protein and joint pains in knee and ankle. There was a preceding sore throat 2 weeks back, which was conservatively managed. What is the therapy of choice?
581.e: The child was having a trigger factor in the form of sore throat & 2 weeks later, she presented with non-blanchable, palpable petechial rash on dependent parts, renal and joint involvement. This translates to a diagnosis of Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura, HSP- Also known as IgA Vasculitis. Management of HSP is Conservative- More than 90% improve in about 4 weeks. Steroids, e.g., Prednisolone are indicated in severe GIT involvement Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 661

581.q: All of the following are true regarding tubercular meningitis in a child, except?
o: Total duration of ATT is 12 months
Basal cistern exudates are the radiological hallmark
No role of steroids in the therapy
581.e: Let us evaluate the options sequentially Option A is True: Risk factors for tubercular meningitis include young age, household contact, recent measles and protein-energy malnutrition. Option B is True: As per IAP-NTEP Guidelines and OP Ghai 10 th Edition, ATT comprises 2 months of Intensive therapy + 10 months of Maintenance Therapy. Total Duration of ATT is 12 months Option C is True. Basal cistern exudates are the CT scan hallmark of the disease. Option D is False. Intravenous Dexamethasone is followed by oral steroids for 6-8 weeks to prevent sequelae in most children. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 586 - 587.

581.q: A 12-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus, is reviewed in the outpatient clinic. In spite of maintaining good control of his diabetes, his height has remained static for 9 months. He says his appetite is alright, but he has lost interest in sports. and he can't keep up with the other boys any more. He just stays at home and watches TV, but wants to be out playing football and getting back his energy. A full blood count and C-reactive protein are normal and his HbA1C is satisfactory. What is the most likely diagnosis?
581.e: Children with type 1 diabetes mellitus are at increased risk of thyroid disease and should be screened annually. His static height and his lethargy would support this diagnosis. He is also at increased risk of coeliac disease and this should also be considered but is less likely as his appetite is good and his weight is satisfactory. Eating disorders can co-exist with diabetes mellitus but he does not have the clinical features of anorexia nervosa. (Option a) GH deficiency is not an autoimmune problem. Would not explain his lethargy. (Option b) Blood and mucus in the stool would be expected with ulcerative colitis and anorexia and malaise and abnormal full blood count and C-reactive protein would be expected with Crohn's disease. (Option d) TAGS: Topic: DIABETES Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2022 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 3022

581.q: Which of the following symptoms is most suggestive of a diagnosis of IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy rather than non-IgE mediated?
581.e: IgE mediated cow's milk protein allergies have a rapid onset of up to 2 hours after ingestion, whereas non-IgE mediated are more delay and may not present until up to a week after ingestion. Both IgE and non-IgE mediated cow's milk protein allergy can cause pruritis, erythema, and lower respiratory tract infections including wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. Loose stools is more characteristic of non-IgE mediated allergies. Tags: Topic: MILK PROTEIN ALLERGY Difficulty level: MAY KNOW Reference: Nelson pediatric symptom-based diagnosis, pg no: 236

581.q: Which of the following is correct comparing breast milk with cow's milk?
o: Breast milk contains more Vitamin K
581.e: Absolute amount of calcium is less in breast milk than animal milk but since the calcium: phosphorous ratio is 2:1, the absorption is better. Key points to note: Vitamins deficient in breast milk: Vit K, Vit D, Vit B1. Mineral deficient in breast milk: Fluoride. Breast milk has more lactose but less fat, protein, and calcium than animal milk. Breast milk is rich in whey protein (better) compared to casein of animal milk. Breast milk also has more taurine and cysteine. Breast milk has more MUFA, PUFA and is especially rich in DHA, i.e. Docosahexaenoic Acid. Reference: Care of Newborn by Meharban Singh, 8 th Edition, Page Number-221.

581.q: A 6-year-old male child presented with a boil on the leg 2 weeks ago and is now presenting with cola coloured urine, 2+ urinary protein, facial edema and has BP of 120/80 mm of Hg. There is no other symptom or rash. What is the likely diagnosis?
581.e: A school-going-aged boy developing acute nephritic syndrome 2 weeks after a boil (pyoderma) indicates a likely diagnosis of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis. Kindly note that BP of 120/80 is Hypertension in a 6-year-old boy. Regarding other options Option A- Minimal Change Disease usually does not have gross hematuria & tends to have massive proteinuria (3+ or 4+) Option B- IgA Nephropathy presents with acute nephritic syndrome within 2-6 days of preceding sore throat or pyoderma, not 2 weeks after. Option D- HSP nephritis will also have palpable purpura, joint involvement with GIT manifestations and since these are not mentioned, unlikely to be the answer here. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition Pages 496-497

582.q: Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is associated with increased risk of thrombosis?
582.e: Deficiency in vitamin E is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis, particularly in neonates, due to its role in platelet aggregation. Vitamin K deficiency leads to hemorrhagic disorders , since vitamin K is essential in the production of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C and S. Increased bruising can be seen in vitamin C deficiency due to an inability to synthesize collagen. Vitamins A is not associated with either an increased bleeding or thrombosis risk. Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : FMGE JUNE 2022; DEC 2021 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 1846

582.q: What is absent in breast milk ?
582.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Vitamin K o Milks from the mother whose diet is sufficient and properly balanced will supply all the necessary nutrients except fluoride and Vitamin D. o The iron content of human milk is low, but most normal term infants have sufficient iron stores for the first 4-6 months. Human milk iron is well absorbed. Nonetheless, by 6 months the breast-fed infant's diet should be supplemented with iron fortified complementary foods. o The Vitamin K content of human milk is low and may cause hemorrhagic disease of newborn.

582.q: Vitamin K is given at birth to prevent the following?
582.e: Neonates have low Vitamin K levels due to Poor transplacental transfer Low Vitamin K in breast milk Lack of gut colonization with Vit K producing bacteria Thus, neonates are predisposed to Vitamin K deficiency, which can cause bleeding manifestations, called as Hemorrhagic Disease of newborn, also called as Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding (VKDB). To prevent this, Government of India recommends one intramuscular dose of Vitamin K at birth to all neonates. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 183

582.q: When suspecting early vitamin D deficiency in the patient, which of the following test is standard for determining the patient's vitamin D status?
