582.e: The initial laboratory tests in a child with rickets should include Serum calcium, Serum phosphorus Alkaline phosphatase Parathyroid hormone (PTH), 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25- D), Creatinine Electrolytes 25-hydroxy vitamin D is reduced in initial phase, while 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D levels are maintained. 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D levels fall in very severe condition only. Other lab tests help in confirmation of the type of rickets. Tags : Topic : RICKETS Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2021;2023 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 3746

582.q: Which mineral deficiency causes Keshan's disease?
582.e: Keshan's disease is due to deficiency of selenium. It causes Cardiomyopathy Its major sources are meat, seafood, whole grains and garlic Tags : Topic : MINERAL DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2021;2023 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 387

582.q: Which of the following vitamin is the most important for free radical scavenging action?
582.e: Out of all the options, Vitamin A, C and E have antioxidant property . Out of these, Vitamin E is the most important. It is mainly located within the cell membranes, preventing lipid peroxidation and formation of free radicals. Deficiency of vitamin E can cause, hemolysis and neurological symptoms especially in the posterior column. Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : INICET NOV 2022 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 385

582.q: A vegan patient with MCV of 110 fL and Hb of 10 g% is most likely to have?
582.e: Clues in the question include a low Hb with a high MCV suggesting macrocytic anemia. Furthermore, vegan diet indicates Vitamin B12 deficiency to be likely and thus the likely cause is Megaloblastic Anemia. Kindly note that MCV >100-120 fl indicates Macrocytic anemia. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 356

582.q: A child developed sudden-onset cardiac arrest. CPR was started and rhythm was checked. Since there was asystole, it was decided to give injection epinephrine to the child. However, intravenous access could not be obtained immediately. What alternative site can you inject epinephrine in such a patient?
582.e: In pediatric cardiac arrest, if the central or peripheral venous access is not immediately achieved, intraosseous (IO) access should be secured. The usual site for IO access is upper end of tibia, medial to the tibial tuberosity. Other sites include distal femur, lower end of tibia above medial malleolus and anterior superior iliac spine. All drugs and infusions which can be given via intravenous route, can also be administered via intraosseous route. Tracheal route is not a preferred site even in emergencies. However, if even IO access is not possible, it can be considered for lipid-soluble agents like epinephrine, lidocaine, atropine and naloxone, if indicated. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 766

583.q: Which of the following is not associated feature with zinc deficiency?
583.e: Symptoms associated with zinc deficiency are: Decreased growth Dermatitis of extremities and around orifices Impaired immunity Poor wound healing Hypogonadism Diarrhea Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : MAY KNOW PYQ : FMGE AUG 2020; NEET PG 2023 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 334

583.q: Choose the correct statement/s about Vitamin C and Scurvy A. It is a heat labile vitamin B. Exclusive breastfeeding can cause scurvy in infancy C. Therapeutic dose of vitamin C is 100-200mg/day D. Vitamin C is predominantly stored in Liver
583.e: Vitamin C supplements of 100-200 mg/day orally or parenterally ensure rapid and complete cure of Scurvy. The treatment should be continued for up to 3 months for complete recovery. Breastfeeding protects against vitamin C deficiency throughout infancy . In children consuming milk formula, fortification with vitamin C must be ensured. Children consuming heat-treated milk should consume adequate vitamin C-rich foods in infancy. Vitamin C is easily destroyed by prolonged storage, overcooking, and processing of foods. Vitamin C is not stored in the body but is taken up by all tissues; the highest levels are found in the pituitary and adrenal glands. Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : MAY KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2021:FMGE JAN 2023; INICET NOV 2021 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 372

583.q: Low glycemic index is classified as value less than:
583.e: Concept of glycemic index has utility in management of diabetes and obesity. GI range Classification Example Most fruits and vegetables except potatoes and water melon, Low GI 55 or less pasta beans, lentils Medium GI 56-69 Sucrose, brown rice, basmati rice 70 or High GI Corn flakes, white bread, candy bar more Ref: Park 22nd edition, page

583.q: When suspecting vitamin C deficiency in a child, which of the following test is the best indicator of Vitamin C levels?
583.e: Plasma ascorbate levels are convenient for diagnosis . Leukocyte ascorbate levels are better indicator of body stores but are difficult to perform. Urinary ascorbate levels can be measured after an oral load of vitamin. Plasma amino acid levels are normal in vitamin C-deficient individuals. Hence, out of all the methods, best for diagnosis is leukocyte ascorbate level and convenient and commonly used is plasma ascorbate level. Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : MAY KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2021:FMGE JAN 2023; INICET NOV 2021 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 373

583.q: Which vitamins need to be supplemented in CF patients?
583.e: Malabsorption is a known complication of cystic fibrosis causing decreased absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. A, D, E and K are fat soluble vitamins and need supplementation in CF . Tags : Topic : CYSTIC FIBROSIS Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2021;2023; INICET MAY 2023; 2024 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2286

584.q: Dosage of intravenous fluid for 2 month old child in diarrhoea with severe dehydration -
584.e: Answer- A. 100 ml/Kg in 6 hour So total fluid to be given 100 ml/Kg in 6 hour.

584.q: Rehydration therapy in a 2 year old severely dehydrated child is -
o: 30 ml/kg in 1 hour, 70 ml in 5 hours
30 ml/kg in 30 min, 70 ml/kg in 2'/2 hours
584.e: Answer- B. 30 ml/kg in 30 min, 70 ml/kg in 2'/2 hours 12 Month - 5 year 30 ml/Kg in 30 min 70 ml/Kg in 2.30 hour

584.q: An 8-month-old child has profuse diarrhea since last 3 days. The stool routine shows absence of blood and stool culture shows no growth. There is no fever and no dehydration. Child is growing fine otherwise. The perianal area shows skin excoriation. What is likely cause of this diarrheal illness?
584.e: The history is very much suggestive of post viral lactose malabsorption. After the viral enteritis, the mucosal brush border cells are lost and these causes lactose malabsorption. Also , perianal excoriation is favorable to diagnosis of lactose intolerance. Other bacterial enteritis might show growth in culture or may have changes in stool routine like pus cells, occult blood. Though, they cannot be ruled out completely, likelihood of lactose malabsorption is more than bacterial. Celiac disease is a cause of chronic diarrhea and failure to thrive. Tags: Topic: DIARRHOEAL ILLNESS Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2022; AIIMS JULY 2020; FMGE DEC 2020;AUG 2020 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed, pg no: 2035

584.q: A 9-month-old child is passing 10 to 12 loose stools per day for last 9 days. There is no blood or mucus in stools. There is no dehydration as well. Which is the therapy of choice in such a child?
584.e: This child has acute watery diarrhea and no dysentery. Hence needs only ORS with Zinc. Remember that oral zinc for 14 days is recommended in all childhood diarrheas in age Antibiotics are indicated only in dysentery. Probiotics are not routinely recommended in childhood diarrhea and quality of evidence for their routine usage is very low. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 313-314.

584.q: A term neonate is sick and cannot be immediately started on mother's milk. He is started on IV Fluids. What shall be the total amount to be given on day 1 in this baby?
584.e: Feeds/Fluids to be given in neonates Day 1 of life- For term babies, give 60 ml/kg/day and for preterm babies, give 80 ml/kg/day Increase daily at 10-15 ml/kg/day gradually Maximum fluid to be administered is about 150 to 160 ml/kg/day Maintenance Fluid used in 1 st 48 hr of life in neonates is generally sodium-free, e.g., 5% or 10% Dextrose Beyond 48 hours, Sodium-containing maintenance fluids can be safely used. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 151

584.q: A child presented to the clinic with complaints of malnutrition and severe dehydration. What would be the choice of IV fluid for this patient?
584.e: Explanation: Ringer's Lactate (RL) with 5% Dextrose is commonly used as the initial IV fluid in children with severe dehydration and malnutrition . It ensures rehydration, corrects electrolyte imbalance, and supplies energy through dextrose. Explanation of Other Options: ORS (Option A): Oral Rehydration Solution is the first choice for mild to moderate dehydration , but in severe dehydration, especially when the child is drowsy or unable to drink, ORS is not suitable. NS (Option B): Normal Saline is isotonic and can restore hydration, but it does not provide energy since it lacks dextrose. In malnourished children, the additional glucose is crucial. DNS (Option D): Dextrose Normal Saline contains glucose and helps in rehydration, but it does not offer the same balanced electrolytes as Ringer's Lactate, making it less ideal in severe cases.

584.q: Which of the following clinical feature is less likely in a condition of hypernatremia dehydration?
584.e: The following may be present in hypernatremia dehydration, whereby proportionally more water than sodium is lost from the body: Jittery movements Increased muscle tone Hyperreflexia Convulsions Drowsiness or coma. KEY TAKEAWAYS: Hypernatremic dehydration occurs when there is a greater water loss relative to sodium loss, resulting in an increased plasma sodium concentration (serum sodium >145 mEq/L) . It is most commonly observed in settings of inadequate water intake, excessive water loss, or high solute intake. Tags: Topic: ELECTROLYTE DISTURBANCES Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Manual of paediatric emergencies & critical care, 2 nd ed., pg. 341

584.q: While promoting oral fluids in a child with active diarrhea, which of the following fluids must be avoided completely?
584.e: While treating the child with dehydration, we must promote intake of clear liquids like water, ORS, Lemonade, coconut water We must continue breastfeeding, formula feeds. We must completely avoid fruit juices and carbonated drinks. Tags: Topic: DIARRHOEAL ILLNESS Difficulty level: MUST KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2022; AIIMS JULY 2020; FMGE DEC 2020;AUG 2020 Reference: Ghai essential pediatrics, 9 th ed, pg no: 291

585.q: Wolf Hirschhorn syndrome involves which among the following genetic abnormalities?
585.e: Wolf Hirschhorn syndrome. Also known as 4p- (deletion of4pl6), this syndrome is characterized by microcephaly and unusual development of the nose and orbits that produces an appearance suggesting an ancient Greek warrior's helmet. Other anomalies commonly seen include cleft lip and palate and cardiac and renal defects. Seizure disorders are common, and the majority of patients have severe intellectual disability. Reference: CDT Pediatrics 2020/Page 1097

585.q: Which among the following disorders is an example of polygenic inheritance?
585.e: Cleft lip/palate shows polygenic/multifactorial inheritance. Fragile X syndrome and G6PD deficiency show X linked recessive, whereas Cystic fibrosis shows Autosomal recessive inheritance. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed/Chapter 97

585.q: A male boy has a large head, large ears, large jaw and large testes. He also has features of autism and delayed development. Likely diagnosis is?
585.e: The findings of large head, large ears, large jaw and large testes (macro-orchidism) are suggestive of Fragile X Syndrome. More commonly seen in boys, it is considered to be a trinucleotide repeat disorder Involves >200 CGG repeats in FMR-1 gene on Chromosome Xq27.3 Other features include hyperextensible joints, increased risks of ADHD, Autism, Anxiety Disorders Most patients have low IQ, indicating intellectual disability and delayed development milestones during childhood. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed, Chapter 98.5

585.q: What type of chromosomal abnormality is associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia?
585.e: Childhood acute leukemias can be divided into myelocytic and lymphocytic. Acute myelocytic leukemias (AML) involve greater than 20% of myeloid blasts in either of these. Myeloid lines include erythrocytes, granulocytes, monocytes, and megakaryocytes. Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) involves the B and T cell lymphocyte lineage. There are different chromosomal rearrangements that can occur, including translocations, deletions, and inversions. Chromosomal translocation (15;17) has a specific association with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). This translocation involves the alpha retinoic acid receptor gene on chromosome 17, which is why the specific treatment for APL is all-trans retinoic acid. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th edition, pg. 2442

585.q: A child with Trisomy 21 developed Transient Leukemia. Such patients are likely to show which additional genetic abnormalities?
585.e: Upto 10% of Down Syndrome patients can develop Transient leukemia, previously called as Transient Myeloproliferative Disorder. Those developing Transient Leukemia in such patients are often found to have GATA-1 mutations in the transcription factors, producing proliferation of blast cells. 20-30% of these patients tend to develop AML-M7 leukemia by 3 years of age. Reference: Nelson 20 th Ed, Page 609, OP Ghai 10 th Ed, Page 667.

585.q: Which of the following is most common preventable cause of intellectual disability, previously called as mental retardation?
585.e: One-liners to remember regarding intellectual disability or mental retardation MC genetic cause: Down syndrome MC inherited cause: Fragile X syndrome MC preventable cause: Hypothyroidism MC treatable cause: Hypothyroidism Variable degree in the same family: Tuberous Sclerosis Mild MR in male with aneuploidy: Klinefelter Syndrome Reference: OP Ghai 9 th Edition, Various Pubmed Articles

585.q: Which genetic condition of the following is associated with an increased risk of leukemia?
585.e: Down syndrome has higher incidence of leukemia among the options. The most common is Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia The most specific sub type of AML is M7. Tags : Topic : DOWNS SYNDROME Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : FMGE JULY 2023 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 660

585.q: Down syndrome patients are found to have a reduced life expectancy compared to the general population. Which among the following is considered the chief cause of mortality especially in the first decade of life?
585.e: As per OP Ghai 10th Edition, the chief cause of early mortality in Down Syndrome patients is Congenital Heart Disease. Furthermore, Endocardial Cushion Defects (ECDs) are the most common congenital heart disease in patients with Down Syndrome. Extra-Edge Point: Nelson 21 st Ed says that the current average life expectancy in Down Syndrome is 50-55 years. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 668, Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 98.2

586.q: A neonate with hypoglycemia is being managed using IV Dextrose infusion. He needs a bolus or hiking in Dextrose rate every time tapering is tried and more than 7 days have passed with the child being on IV dextrose infusion. What shall be done next?
586.e: Recurrent/ resistant Hypoglycemia This condition should be considered when the infant fails to maintain normal BGL despite a GIR of 12 mg /kg/min or when stabilization is not achieved by 7 days of therapy. High levels of glucose infusion may be needed in these infants to achieve euglycemia. Hyperinsulinism must be excluded because it is the most common cause of persistent hypoglycemia. Hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia can be congenital [due to mutations affecting the regulation of insulin secretion from the pancreas] or acquired [neonates with maternal diabetes, birth asphyxia, polycythemia, Rh incompatibility, and severe intrauterine growth restriction, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. etc.] Many patients may have underlying metabolic disorders or hypocortisolism Hydrocortisone is often considered in such cases. Reference: AIIMS Protocols In Neonatology, 3 rd Edition, Volume 2, Page 305

586.q: Which of the following condition you do not expect risk of developing cerebral palsy?
o: A 2 year old child, born at 32 weeks gestation
A 4 year old child, born at term and had birth asphyxia due following obstructed labor
A 14 year old child had significant head injury at 13 years of age
A 12 year old child, who developed kernicterus at 10th day of life
586.e: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent neurological disorders affecting movement, posture, and muscle tone, resulting from brain damage that occurs before, during, or shortly after birth. Risk factors of developing cerebral palsy Prenatal insult Preterm birth Birth asphyxia CNS infections Toxin exposure like bilirubin (Kernicterus) CNS hemorrhage Metabolic disorders KEY TAKEAWAYS: Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive motor disorder that affects a growing brain. Hence, insult after brain growth is nearly complete, does not cause Cerebral palsy. Tags: Topic: CEREBRAL PALSY Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2021 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 3168

586.q: You are asked to see a 2-year-old child who has a 12-hour history of severe diarrhoea and vomiting. He is pale and lethargic with a HR 180/min, BP 80 mmHg systolic, and capillary refill time of 7 seconds. What type of shock are they likely to be in?
586.e: This child is likely to be dehydrated from losing fluid through vomiting and diarrhoea, and may not have adequate oral intake to replace losses. This has resulted in severe dehydration, evident from the increased HR (due to compensation for a low blood volume in attempt to increase BP), increased cap refill time and low BP (indicating uncompensated shock), and pale and clammy appearance. KEY TAKEAWAYS: Hypovolemic shock occurs due to a significant reduction in intravascular volume, leading to inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery. This can result in cellular hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, and multi-organ dysfunction if untreated. Tags: Topic: SHOCK Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Manual of paediatric emergencies & critical care, 2 nd ed., pg. 158

586.q: Thirty-six hours after initiation of treatment with insulin for DKA, a 4-year-old girl's serum glucose level is 240 mEq/L. Further laboratory work reveals a bicarbonate level of 16 mEq/L. She is currently receiving 0.1 units/kg/h of regular insulin as well as normal saline. What is the next step in treatment?
o: Continue intravenous insulin therapy and change IVF to D5 0.45% normal saline
Stop intravenous insulin therapy and allow the patient to begin subcutaneous insulin administration
Stop intravenous insulin therapy and administer bicarbonate
586.e: Although the patient's serum glucose is decreasing, her metabolic acidosis has not yet resolved and will require continued intravenous insulin therapy and IV Fluid for treatment. The patient should not be converted to subcutaneous insulin until her glucose has normalized, her bicarbonate level is greater than 18 mEq/L, and her serum pH is greater than 7.3. Because of the risk of causing hypoglycemia with continued insulin therapy, dextrose should be added to her fluids. Bicarbonate therapy has not been shown to be effective in the treatment of metabolic acidosis associated with DKA and can actually be harmful. Reference: AIIMS PICU Protocols 2022, Pages 411-419

586.q: Vitamin B6 administration is helpful in which among the following metabolic disorders?
586.e: Vitamin B6, i.e., Pyridoxine administration is helpful at 200 mg/day in many patients of Classic Homocystinuria. These patients are milder and have a better outcome than the non-responsive forms. However, methionine restriction to keep the plasma homocysteine levels low is the mainstay of therapy. Regarding other options Hydrocortisone is the therapy needed in CAH. Some forms may need additional drugs. Phenylketonuria needs dietary restriction of phenylalanine and a low-protein diet Alkaptonuria responds to Nitisinone to inhibit pigment production. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 684-685

586.q: After the delivery of an infant of diabetic mother, blood glucose of infant was 60mg/dl. Which other investigation does the sister expects that the physician would ask her to do?
586.e: Hypoglycemia and Hypocalcemia are the two major metabolic complications seen in infants of diabetic mothers. Hypoglycemia develops in approximately 25-50% of infants of mothers with pregestational diabetes and 15-25% of infants of mothers with gestational diabetes, but only a small percentage of these infants become symptomatic. Apart from hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia is another common metabolic complication seen in these babies and results from the diminished production of parathormone in the 1 st week of postnatal life. Now in this question, since Serum glucose is normal, next logical thing to check is serum calcium. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 182; Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 127

586.q: Recently approved drug indicated in Rett syndrome is?
586.e: Treatment of Rett Syndrome Trofinetide is a new drug, approved for use in 2023 in children aged 2 years and above with Rett Syndrome. The drug is commercially marketed as Daybue. It is a novel synthetic analogue of the amino terminal tripeptide of IGF-1 The drug acts by decreasing neuroinflammation and supporting synaptic function tripeptide GPE. L-Carnitine & Melatonin may be helpful in a few cases. Reference: NIH Publications 2023

586.q: A 35-year-old woman gives birth to a female infant who is growth restricted, microcephalic, and has a congenital heart defect. She has had 1 prior miscarriage and reports that she has a 3-year-old son who is abnormally fair, with mental impairment. She also recalls being on a special diet as a child which she subsequently discontinued. Which of the following maternal conditions is most consistent with this history?
586.e: Intrauterine exposure of an unborn child to elevated phenylalanine concentrations due to maternal PKU can disrupt embryo-fetal development. Effects include facial dysmorphism resembling fetal alcohol syndrome, microcephaly, mental impairment, and malformations especially of the heart. Hypopigmentation occurs owing to a lack of pigment formation. Musty or mousy urine odour is also produced. None of the other maternal conditions listed above would lead to the clinical features described in this vignette. Maternal diabetes leads to macrosomia not growth restriction. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 637

587.q: Which among the following conditions presents in infancy with cyclic cyanosis?
587.e: Infants with bilateral choanal atresia who have difficulty with mouth breathing make vigorous attempts to inspire, often suck in their lips, and develop cyanosis. Distressed children then cry (which relieves the cyanosis) and become calmer, with normal skin color, only to repeat the cycle after closing their mouths. This is called cyclic cyanosis. Also note that bilateral choanal atresia is often a part of CHARGE Syndrome. Reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 10 th Edition, Page Number-388.

587.q: A 6-month-old girl is brought to the ED for excessive fussiness and colicky behavior. On exam, she has repetitive clusters of stereotyped flexion movements of the trunk, associated with a cry. Her EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. A few flexion movements are captured and are associated with a generalized slow wave followed by an electro-decrement. She has several scattered hypo-pigmented spots on the trunk and extremities. What is the best treatment option?
587.e: The diagnosis is Tuberous sclerosis, with the child having Infantile Spasms. In such a case, Vigabatrin is more efficacious than ACTH. Vigabatrin (VGB) is a structural analogue of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and irreversibly inhibits the GABA degradative enzyme GABA-transaminase (GABA-T), thus increasing brain levels of GABA. VGB is very effective against infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), and it is the first-choice drug of in this case based on many reports. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SE edition, pg. 2879

587.q: What therapy would you recommend for the most effective treatment of the hematologic complications for Gaucher disease?
587.e: ERT has emerged as one of the most important advances in the treatment of sphingolipidoses. ERT with biweekly infusions of recombinant human glucocerebrosidase is invariably effective in reversing the hematologic and early skeletal complications of Gaucher disease. None of the other options listed above are valid treatment options for Gaucher disease. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 708

587.q: A 15-year-old presents with chronic fatigue and severe bone pain of 1 year's duration. He has hepatosplenomegaly and a normal retinal examination. Laboratory studies reveal normocytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Radiographs of the distal femur reveal Erlenmeyer flask deformities. The most likely diagnosis is?
587.e: Patients may have bruising from thrombocytopenia, chronic fatigue secondary to anemia, hepatomegaly with or without elevated liver function test results, splenomegaly, and bone pain. Most patients develop radiologic evidence of skeletal involvement, including an Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femur. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 709

587.q: A 20-day-old breastfed girl presents to the emergency department with jaundice, vomiting, lethargy, and rectal temperature of 102°F. Physical examination is significant for hepatomegaly. Catheterized urinalysis demonstrates reducing substances and white blood cells. Patient also got repeated cultures positive for E coli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
587.e: Galactosemia is a disorder of carbohydrate metabolism in which early ingestion of galactose, found in breast milk and cow's milk formula, leads to jaundice, lethargy, vomiting, acidosis, cataracts, failure to thrive, and bleeding; Lab abnormalities may include indirect hyperbilirubinemia and coagulopathy, and urinalysis with reducing substances present but negative glucose on dipstick. Infants with galactosemia commonly present with gram-negative rod UTI or urosepsis, especially with E coli, such as in this patient. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 726

587.q: The mucopolysaccharidosis (MPSs) are a group of inherited disorders caused by defects in the catabolism of glycosaminoglycans. Which of the following MPS disorders is inherited in an X-linked manner?
587.e: Hunter syndrome is inherited as an X-linked condition. All the other MPSs are autosomal recessive (like most IEM). Males with Hunter syndrome present fairly similar to patients with Hurler syndrome. Hunter syndrome is not associated with corneal clouding, which is part of Hurler. It is important to check for carrier status in mothers of affected males with Hunter syndrome to establish appropriate recurrence risks. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 739

587.q: A child was brought with mental retardation. He had a Cherry red spot with no organomegaly. What is the probable diagnosis?
587.e: Patients with the infantile form of Tay-Sachs disease have clinical manifestations in infancy including loss of motor skills, increased startle reaction, and macular pallor and retinal cherry-red spots. Affected infants usually develop normally until 4-5 months of age when decreased eye contact and an exaggerated startle response to noise (hyperacusis) are noted. Macrocephaly, not associated with hydrocephalus, may develop. In the 2nd year of life, seizures develop which may be refractory to anticonvulsant therapy. Neurodegeneration is relentless, with death occurring by the age of 4 or 5 years. The juvenile and later-onset forms initially present with ataxia and dysarthria and may not be associated with a macular cherry-red spot. Reference: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 708

588.q: A child with HIV presents with features of pneumonia. Which of the following organisms would be most commonly responsible?
588.e: P.jirovecii (previously P. carinii) pneumonia is the opportunistic infection that led to the initial description of AIDS. This is one of the commonest AIDS defining illnesses in children; most cases occur between 3rd and 6th months of life. Reference: Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 9 th ed., pg. 225

589.q: A 14 days-old neonate who had bilateral conjunctivitis, now has a cough with chest infiltrates. Which among the following could be the causative organism?
589.e: Chlamydia is the most common cause of neonatal pneumonia associated with neonatal conjunctivitis. Chlamydial genital infection is reported in 5-30% of pregnant women, with a risk for vertical transmission at parturition to Newborn infants of approximately 50%. The infant may become infected at 1 or more sites, including the conjunctiva, nasopharynx, rectum, and vagina. Most commonly these infections manifest as inclusion conjunctivitis and Pneumonia. Rectal and vaginal infections are also seen but most of them are asymptomatic. TLC in these patients is normal to high & CXR often shows interstitial infiltrates. Drug of choice is usually IV Azithromycin Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 1495

589.q: Which of the following is true about DiGeorge syndrome?
o: It results from a duplication of chromosome 22q11.
There is hypoplasia of the second pharyngeal pouch.
Apnea, jitteriness, and high-pitched cry may complicate the course of the disease
Cardiac defect may be a cause of death.
589.e: DiGeorge Syndrome DiGeorge syndrome is a congenital hypoplasia of organs derived from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. It results in hypoplasia or agenesis of the thymus and parathyroid glands, the auricle, and the external auditory canal; congenital cardiac anomalies; cleft palate; and short stature. It is associated with microdeletion of chromosome 22q11 . The main features are hypocalcemia, seizures, congenital heart disease, lymphocytopenia, and multiple minor anomalies. Hypocalcemia can manifest as apnea, jitteriness, crying episodes and tetany. Affected newborns may die from cardiac causes during the first month. Frequent infections due to a defect of cell-mediated immunity and failure to thrive may complicate the course of the surviving newborn. Reference: Nelson 20 th edition, pg-2650

589.q: A baby developed congenital toxoplasmosis. Presence of which among the following will predict a higher risk of severe infection?
589.e: HLA-DQ3+ predicts a more severe and fulminant course of congenital toxoplasma infection. According to Nelson, In monozygotic twins with congenital toxoplasmosis, the clinical pattern of involvement is most often similar, whereas in dizygotic twins the manifestations often differ. The major histocompatibility complex class II gene DQ3 appears to be common even among HIV-infected persons seropositive for T. gondii who develop toxoplasmic encephalitis, as well as in children with congenital toxoplasmosis who develop hydrocephalus. These findings suggest that the presence of HLA-DQ3 is a risk factor for severity of toxoplasmosis, in all patients including congenital toxoplasmosis. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 316

589.q: A 6-year-old boy presented to your clinic with recurrent subcutaneous abscesses, lymphadenitis, osteomyelitis, and family history of recurrent granulomatous infections, you suspected chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). The diagnosis is confirmed by which of the following methods?
589.e: CGD is an immune disorder where there is decreased NADPH dependent, free oxygen radicle production needed for killing catalase positive organisms. The diagnosis is most often made by performing flow cytometry using dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR) to measure oxidant production through its increased fluorescence when oxidized by H2O2. Tags : Topic : IMMUNE DISORDERS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1046

589.q: A child with hydrocephalus had undergone a V-P shunt. He developed fever and irritability. A dose of Acetaminophen for fever spikes was given. What is the next step?
o: Blood culture with CSF culture via LP
Blood culture with CSF culture via shunt
589.e: The child in the question has signs of CNS infection. Best method to confirm this is CSF culture. As the child already has a shunt in situ, it gives us an option to withdraw a sample of CSF via shunt and hence we can avoid an invasive LP procedure. Incorrect Options : Radionuclide scan and neuroimaging doesn't aid in the diagnosis of shunt infections Tags: Topic: CNS INFECTIONS Difficulty level: MUST KNOW PYQ: INICET NOV 2022 Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 3079

589.q: Regarding Urinary tract infections in children, true statement is?
o: Most commonly caused by Proteus mirabilis
Can be associated with constipation and bowel dysfunction
Prevention is best achieved by long-term amoxicillin
589.e: Let us evaluate each option individually Option A is False. VUR is usually a cause of UTI rather than a result. Option B is False. E coli is the commonest organism isolated from UTIs. Option C is True. Risk factors for UTI include female gender, underlying VUR, constipation, neurological problems involving the bladder and bowel (spina bifida, operated sacro-coocygeal teratoma, etc. Bladder-bowel dysfunction (BBD) can cause recurrent UTI in Children. Option D is False. Long-term agents like Cotrimoxazole, Cephalexin, Cefadroxil and Nitrofurantoin are usually used as prophylactic agents. Amoxicillin is useful in treating UTI, but not recommended in prevention of UTI. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 507-511; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2559

589.q: Choose the false statement regarding neonatal tetanus
o: Cephalosporins are the drug of choice
Antitoxin given in all suspected cases
589.e: It occurs in unimmunized mothers The contamination of umbilical stump during delivery is important cause. Usually presents in 3-12 days of life with feeding difficulties and excessive crying Treatment includes antibiotics- Penicillin G (Drug of choice), Metronidazole/erythromycin (alternative). Human tetanus immunoglobulin must be given in all cases. Tags : Topic : NEONATAL TETANUS Difficulty level : MUST KNOW Reference : Cloherty and starks manual of neonatal care, SA ed., pg. 731

589.q: Which of the following is not an important mechanism for maintaining vitamin B12 levels?
589.e: Intrinsic factors get bound to the cobalamin in the duodenum and gets transported to the ileum. From the distal ileum, under alkaline conditions , the cobalamin is internalized in to the enterocytes and transported through the Transcobalamin. Overgrowth of bacteria in the small bowel can reduce the B12 absorption as they consume the vitamin or they disintegrate the cobalamin from the intrinsic factor. Tags : Topic : VITAMIN DEFICIENCY & TOXICITY Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : FMGE JAN 2023; DEC 2021 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2520

590.q: What is the Most common clinical manifestation of mumps?
590.e: Epididymo-orchitis is the next most common manifestation of mumps (after parotid gland swelling), developing in 15-30% of cases in postpubertal males, with bilateral involvement in 10 - 30% of those cases Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 2st Ed, Ch:207 Pg: 1617

590.q: A mother with no prenatal care gives birth to a term infant with findings of IUGR, microcephaly and hepatosplenomegaly. His hemogram shows thrombocytopenia. BERA test reveals sensorineural hearing loss. Ophthalmic examination shows chorioretinitis. The most important diagnostic study for evaluation in this newborn is
590.e: The newborn in the question shows characteristics of congenital CMV infection. In addition to those findings mentioned above, these patients can have petechiae and purpura, ventriculomegaly, periventricular calcifications, cerebral atrophy, cortical dysplasia, and chorioretinitis. The most important diagnostic study in the evaluation of newborn CMV disease is viral culture, preferably done before 3 weeks of life to help exclude the possibility of perinatal CMV acquisition. Viral PCR is a useful adjunct to culture techniques but does not replace viral culture. Tissue biopsy, while sometimes used for diagnosis, is not standard and is more commonly used in the lung and liver than in the brain. CMV antibody titers are generally not helpful in diagnosis. Tags : Topic : CONGENITAL INFECTIONS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : INICET NOV 2022; JULY 2021; NEET PG 2023

590.q: A mother is very reluctant in giving breast feeding to her newborn. She is lactating well. But she has a fear that her milk is not good for her baby. While counselling the mother about the advantages of breast milk, she must be explained that breast milk protects against multiple types of infections. Which of the following infection is not prevented in exclusively breastfed child?
590.e: Breastfeeding has been suggested to have a possible protective effect in : Diarrhea Otitis media (option a) Urinary tract infections (option b) Necrotizing enterocolitis, Septicemia (option c) Infant botulism Celiac disease Childhood cancer Allergy Hospitalizations and infant mortality Tags : Topic : BREAST FEEDING & NUTRITION Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : INICET MAY 2022 Reference : Nutrition and child development, KE Elizabeth, 5 th ed., pg. 113

590.q: An infant had refractory hypocalcemia in first few weeks of life and was diagnosed with congenital hypoparathyroidism. The child was referred to a pediatric cardiologist for further evaluation and also evaluated for a microdeletion defect. Which other clinical manifestation will often be present in such a child?
590.e: An interesting question, similar to what many of you may encounter in clinical practice too. Let us go stepwise. Information given: Infant with refractory hypocalcemia due to congenital hypoparathyroidism Some cardiac disease A microdeletion defect. Now, the microdeletion defect with hypoparathyroidism and cardiac disease is DiGeorge Syndrome. It occurs due to microdeletions in 22q11.2. Most of these patients have thymic aplasia due to 3 rd and 4 th pharyngeal pouch hypoplasia. Thymic aplasia causes reduced T-lymphocytes and cellular type of primary immunodeficiency. Such patients predisposed to recurrent viral and fungal infections. Thus D is the likely manifestation to be found in such patients. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed, Chapter 151

590.q: An adolescent 16 year old boy has been having multiple attacks of rhinosinusitis since birth. At the age of 10 years, he had productive cough with hemoptysis and HRCT revealed cystic spaces with honeycombing which required antibiotics & chest physiotherapy. There was no situs inversus. The treating doctor advised a semen analysis to check for sperm counts. What syndrome the doctor is thinking about?
590.e: The patient has recurrent rhinosinusitis, history suggesting bronchiectasis, but there is no situs inversus. Since semen analysis has been advised to check for azoospermia, the doctor is likely thinking about Young Syndrome. Young's Syndrome is a rare condition that encompasses a combination of syndromes such as bronchiectasis, rhinosinusitis and reduced male fertility. In individuals with this syndrome the functioning of the lungs is usually normal but the mucus is abnormally viscous. The reduced fertility (obstructive azoospermia) is due to functional obstruction of sperm transport down the genital tract at the epididymis, where the sperm is found in viscous, lipid-rich fluid. Possible causes include genetics, helminthic infections and exposure to mercury during childhood, but the cause is unknown. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 417; Nelson 21 st Edition

590.q: A 2-year-old male child was admitted with recurrent bloody stools, atopic dermatitis like rash and petechiae. On CBC, his TLC was normal and platelet count 20000/mm3. What is the next best step to establish the diagnosis?
590.e: This is a male child presenting with a triad of Atopic dermatitis-like rash Recurrent bloody stools indicating recurrent infections Petechiae due to thrombocytopenia. This is the classic triad seen in patients with Wiskott Aldrich Syndrome. The disease occurs due to mutations in WASp gene mutations, present on Chromosome 11p22.23 Hence, patient needs to be screened for WASp gene expression. Regarding other options Anti platelet antibody should be checked in isolated thrombocytopenia where you suspect ITP. Bone marrow aspiration will be needed in bicytopenia or pancytopenia. LFT and RFT have no role in the evaluation of such a case. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 21st edition, Chapter 152, Page 1117

590.q: A 5-year-old child develops fever with rash. Rash is polymorphous, itchy and starts on trunk and disappears after few days. Most probable diagnosis is?
590.e: Clues here Fever with Itchy rash Starts from trunk Polymorphous nature of the rash All these findings are suggestive of Chicken pox/Varicella infection. Regarding other options Measles presents with a non-itchy maculopapular rash which first starts on the face, behind the ears and then goes to the trunk Fifth Disease presents with bilateral slapped cheek appearance RMSF presents with non-itchy rash & the child has toxicity, petechiae and transaminitis commonly associated. Reference: OP Ghai 9 th Ed, Pg 210-11, Nelson 21 st Ed

590.q: Identify the incorrect match for pediatric infection and characteristic feature on clinical examination?
o: Petechiae at junction of soft and hard palate- Pertussis
Dew drops on rose petal appearance- Varicella
590.e: Petechiae at the junction of soft and hard palate are often seen in patients of Epstein Barr Virus- EBV Infection. Also note that Nagayama spots are seen in 6 th disease, caused by HHV-6. Forchheimer Spots are seen in soft palate region in patients of Rubella, also called German Measles. Dew drops on rose petal appearance has been described for skin vesicular lesions seen in Varicella or Chicken Pox. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 232-234

591.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Rectal biopsy o Rectal suction biopsy is procedure of choice.

591.q: 24 day neonate with projectile vomiting & failure to gain weight .what is the diagnosis
591.e: Answer- A. CHPS Projectile vomiting in 4th week is quite suggestive of CHPS. In duodenal atresia the vomiting (usually bilious) is right from the 1st day of life. NEC and Hirschsprung's disease have different clinical presentation.

591.q: You are called to the nursery to assess a newborn girl. She was born at 39 weeks via normal spontaneous delivery to a mother who had no prenatal care. APGAR scores are 7 and 9. At four hours of life, the nurse noted respiratory distress. On physical examination, her heart rate is 150 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 70 cycles per minute, temperature is 37.1 C with barrel-shaped chest, a scaphoid-appearing abdomen, and absence of breath sounds on the left chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
591.e: The newborn girl has findings that are suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a developmental defect of the diaphragm that allows abdominal viscera to herniate into the chest. Although routine prenatal ultrasound screening may identify CDH at a mean gestational age of 24 weeks, there is a wide range of reported sensitivity in its detection. Physical findings include a barrel-shaped chest, a scaphoid-appearing abdomen (because of loss of the abdominal contents into the chest), and absence of breath sounds on the ipsilateral side. Reference: Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1 st SA ed., pg. 772

591.q: Intussusception was a known complication of which of the following vaccines?
591.e: Things to know and remember about Rotavirus Vaccine: Vaccine withdrawn due to intussusception risk: Rotashield (Oral) Vaccine part of National Immunization Schedule: Rotavac (Oral) How many doses are recommended in NIS: 3 doses, given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks of age. Catch-up vaccination upto: 1 year Other Rotavirus Vaccines: Rotateq, Rotarix, Rotasiil Reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 10 th Edition, Page Number 200-201.

591.q: An infant with a history of recurrent pneumonia is diagnosed with TEF at 8 months of age. Which of the following statements is correct?
o: The infant most likely has an H-type TEF
The infant most likely has proximal esophageal atresia with distal fistula
The infant likely has a previously undetected, associated finding of imperforate anus
The infant is unlikely to have gastroesophageal reflux
591.e: The key to making the diagnosis is age and features in this question. This infant likely has an H-type TEF, found later in infancy with recurrent pneumonias and/or feeding difficulty. Patients with esophageal atresia and distal fistula present in the first hours of life because of their inability to swallow oropharyngeal secretions. Infants with imperforate anus also present as neonates. All patients with TEF are at high risk for gastroesophageal reflux. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1783

591.q: All of the following are common complications in survivors of CDH, except?
591.e: Hepatic fibrosis is not mentioned as a complication in CDH survivors. Among other options: Option B- Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is reported in >50% of children with CDH. GERD is more common in children whose diaphragmatic defect involves the esophageal hiatus. Option C- Recurrent diaphragmatic hernia is reported in 5-20% in most series. Option D- Intestinal obstruction is reported in up to 20% of children and may result from a midgut volvulus, adhesions, or a recurrent hernia that became incarcerated. Children with patch repairs are at highest risk. Children with CDH typically have delayed growth in the 1st 2 yr of life. Neurocognitive defects are common and may result from the disease or the interventions. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 345.1

591.q: A >48-hour neonate has still not passed meconium after birth. What is the investigation of choice?
591.e: A water-soluble contrast enema is the investigation of choice in delayed passage of meconium since it is both diagnostic and therapeutic. It can diagnose Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus, atresias Can also remove meconium plug in meconium plug syndrome and have therapeutic action. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 358

591.q: Which among the following is associated with a good prognosis in congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
o: Symptoms develop beyond 48 hr of birth
CDH detected in the 1st trimester scan prenatally
591.e: Symptoms developing beyond 48 hr of birth usually indicates a milder variant of CDH and thus has a better outcome. Extra-Edge: Poor prognosis predictors in congenital diaphragmatic hernia Lung: Head Ratio Severe pulmonary hypoplasia An associated major anomaly Herniation to the contralateral lung Symptoms before 24 hr of age Liver herniation into thorax CDH detected in the 1 st trimester Need for ECMO Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 122.10

592.q: You are teaching a group of medical students the differential diagnosis of edema in children. You take them to the bedside of a patient who has edema associated with hypoproteinemia secondary to proteinuria. Of the following, the feature you are MOST likely to observe in this patient is?
o: Edema that improves throughout the day
592.e: Nephrotic syndrome usually presents with edema that is periorbital and more prominent early in the morning and with minimal systemic symptoms. Edema is the most easily identified clinical feature associated with hypoproteinemia. Impaired cardiac function leads to worsening peripheral edema as the day progresses and is associated with exertion and increased activity. Pitting edema is not pathognomonic for any specific underlying etiology. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2521

592.q: A 9-yr old boy passes hard infrequent stools for the last 2 years. Also, sometimes he soils his under wear. On examination, you found an anal fissure and his rectum is full of hard stools. All other examination is normal. Your most likely diagnosis is functional constipation. What is the most effective initial treatment?
o: Combination of Polyethylene glycol solution & enema
High fiber diet and follow up after 3 months
592.e: The child has now presented with severe constipation with rectal impaction. The 1st step in treatment of severe constipation is disimpaction which requires administration of Polyethylene glycol solution (movicol) (or mineral oil) ± rectal enema As per OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 301, any child with constipation who has hard stools felt on per rectal examination or has abdominal fecoliths or retentive encopresis should undergo immediate disimpaction as the first step in management. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 301; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1765

592.q: A child has been recently diagnosed as Celiac Disease. His parents ask you for foods which are safe to be consumed. You will suggest all of the following foods as safe to eat in this patient, except?
592.e: Since the child has been diagnosed with Celiac Disease, the child should avoid eating foods and grains which contain gluten in them. Among the options, Semolina is puffed wheat and thus should be avoided. Grains unsafe to eat in Celiac Disease- Contain gluten. Mnemonic is BROW Barley Rye Oats Wheat, including whole wheat & semolina (suji/rava) Grains safe to eat in Celiac Disease- Do not contain gluten. Includes Rice, including Puffed Rice like Poha Maize Quinoa Sorghum Chia Seeds Flax Seeds Tapioca Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 320; Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 364

593.q: What is the amount of milk given to a term baby in the first 24 hours after delivery?
593.e: Explanation: On the first day of life, a term newborn usually receives about 60 ml of milk per kilogram of body weight . This volume is tailored to match the limited stomach capacity of the infant and to support a gradual adaptation of the gastrointestinal system , allowing feeding tolerance to improve as digestion matures. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK326679/

593.q: Jaundice due to biliary atresia is suspected when it persists beyond?
593.e: Neonatal cholestasis tends to produce conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a neonate & usually produces prolonged jaundice. Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA) is one of the most common causes of neonatal cholestasis and should be suspected in a term neonate if jaundice fails to resolve and persists beyond 2 weeks of postnatal age. EHBA should also be suspected if the neonate has jaundice with dark-coloured urine & clay-coloured stools. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 345-349

593.q: Most common indication of liver transplantation in children is?
593.e: Biliary atresia is the most common indication for liver transplantation in children, followed by metabolic disorders. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed, Harrison 20 th Ed, page 2415

593.q: An infant presented with progressive jaundice and pale coloured stools. Liver biopsy revealed bile plugs and bile ductular proliferation. Likely diagnosis?
593.e: The clinical picture is suggestive of neonatal cholestasis. The most common cause of neonatal cholestasis is Extra hepatic biliary atresia (EHBA). Biliary atresia is characterized by bile ductular proliferation, the presence of bile plugs, and portal or perilobular edema and fibrosis, with the basic hepatic lobular architecture intact. In neonatal hepatitis, there is severe, diffuse hepatocellular disease, with distortion of lobular architecture, marked infiltration with inflammatory cells, and focal hepatocellular necrosis; the bile ductules show little alteration. Giant cell transformation is found in infants with either condition and has no diagnostic specificity. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 383

593.q: Identify the enzyme deficient in Von-Gierke Disease?
593.e: Glucose-6-Phosphatase deficiency produces GSD-1, also called as Von-Gierke's Disease. Deficiency of the enzyme leads to inadequate hepatic conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose through normal glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, resulting in fasting hypoglycemia and accumulation of normal structure glycogen in the liver. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 105.1

593.q: A 12-year-old boy seen in your clinic has a history of Wilson disease. Which of the following tissues may accumulate excessive copper if the disease is left inadequately treated?
593.e: Wilson disease is a metal metabolism disorder characterized by excessive copper deposition in the liver, brain, kidneys, and eyes. Features include hepatic failure or cirrhosis, hemolytic anemia, KF rings in the eyes, sunflower cataracts, neuropsychiatric manifestations and parkinsonism-like features In CNS, the excess copper gets deposited into basal ganglia. Patients with Wilson disease may suffer from arthralgias and osteoarthritis but do not typically develop copper deposition in the bones, pancreas, ovaries, or salivary glands. Also note that pancreas and ovaries show deposition with iron in hemochromatosis, but these are not much affected by copper deposits in Wilson Disease. Infants with neonatal iron storage disease typically have excessive iron deposition in the liver, heart, pancreas, and salivary glands. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1939

593.q: Dubin Johnson syndrome and Rotor Syndrome can be distinguished on the basis of all of the following except?
593.e: Degree of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is not a relevant distinguishing point between the two conditions. All others can be used to distinguish the two conditions. Also remember the following: Differences of Rotor Syndrome from DJS Unlike DJS, total urinary coproporphyrin excretion is elevated with a relative increase in the amount of the coproporphyrin I isomer. If liver biopsy is performed, there is no abnormal pigmentation in contrast to Dubin-Johnson. The gallbladder is normal on imaging in Rotor Syndrome, while it may be difficult to visualize in DJS Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 331-332; Nelson 21 st Ed, Harrison 20 th Ed, page 2345

594.q: Which of the following cells are deficient is a premature infant with RDS?
594.e: Hyaline membrane disease Also called as respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) Major cause of this disease is Deficiency of pulmonary surfactant produced by type II alveolar cells Commonly seen in. Premature infants Maternal diabetes (Gestational diabetes mellitus) delivery by cesarean section Reference: Ganong 25th edition page no.631

594.q: In children with respiratory distress, there is deficiency of which of the following lipids:
594.e: Surfactant lipids Account for approximately 90% of surfactant Major surfactant lipids is: Dipalmotoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC) - Lecithin- most abundant component of surfactant Reference: Ganong 25th edition page no.631

594.q: In preterm baby with respiratory distress syndrome which of the following lipid would be deficient?
594.e: Phospholipid Dipalmitoyl Phosphatidyl Choline acts as surfactant and Acts to reduce surface tension, which helps in proper expansion of Lungs. In preterm babies, it is deficient. So preterm babies are prone for respiratory distress syndrome

594.q: 3 month infants with abdominal palpable mass & non bilious vomiting -
594.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis Hypertophic pyloric stenosis Most common cause of nonbilious vomiting is Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Male > female. Vomiting starts with 3 week of age. Palpable mass is seen in epigastric region. Visible peristalsis is seen soon after feeding. Confirmed by USG abdomen. Contrast study shows : . Shoulder sign . Double tract sign. Treatment surgery = Ramstedt procedure.

594.q: A preterm infant admitted to the NICU shows reticulo-granular opacities on X-ray with white out appearance. The child had chest retractions, tachypnea, and nasal flaring. A diagnosis of Hyaline membrane disease was made. The following phospholipid is used as a test for diagnosis of fetal lung maturity.
594.e: The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of Hyaline membrane disease or Respiratory distress syndrome which is due to defective production of surfactant. The active component of surfactant is phosphatidylcholine(lecithin) Choline + PA→ phosphatidylcholine (PC) (lecithin) Ethanolamine + PA→ phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (cephalin) It is a component of cell membrane and plays a role in blood coagulation Serine + PA → phosphatidylserine (PS) (option c) It plays a role in programmed cell death Inositol + PA → phosphatidylinositol (PI)(option d) It plays a role as a secondary messenger Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition and LIPPINCOTT illustrated reviews 6 th edition biochemistry page 204-6.

594.q: A baby is born at 27 weeks of gestation required mechanical ventilation for next 4 weeks & 02 for next 1 week. He maintained at room temperature subsequently. As per new Bronchopulmonary dysplasia definition, he has which of the following ?
594.e: Mild Supplement O2 (for 28 days) and diagnostic criteria of mild BPD.

594.q: Most common presentation of wilm's tumor ?
594.e: Ans. is `b' i.e., Asymptomatic abdominal mass Wilm's tumor (Nephroblastoma) Most common malignant tumor of kidney. 80% of tumor present below 5 year of age. Presention :? Asymptomatic abdominal mass (M.C.). Haematuria (10-25%). Hypertension (25%). Abdominal pain (30%). Fever (20%).

594.q: Which among the following is the most common cause of abdominal mass in a neonate?
594.e: Multicystic dysplastic kidney- MCDK is the most common cause of an abdominal mass in the newborn, but the vast majority are nonpalpable at birth. In most cases, it is discovered incidentally during prenatal sonography. Contralateral hydronephrosis is present in 5-10% of patients. Sonography shows the characteristic appearance of a kidney replaced by multiple cysts of varying sizes that do not communicate, and no identifiable parenchyma is present. Serial USGs done at 3 month initially and then every 6 monthly post infancy show regression of the cysts. Most cysts resolve by 7 years of age. References: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 552; OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 528-529.

595.q: Which of the following is a known environmental risk factor for asthma?
595.e: RISK FACTORS FOR ASTHMA IN CHILDHOOD Parental asthma Allergy: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) Allergic rhinitis Food allergy Inhalant allergen sensitization Food allergen sensitization Severe lower respiratory tract infection: Pneumonia Bronchiolitis requiring hospitalization Wheezing apart from colds Male gender Low birthweight Environmental tobacco smoke exposure Reduced lung function at birth Out of all this, only Smoking exposure is environmental factor Tags : Topic : ASTHMA Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : INICET NOV 2022; AIIMS JULY 2020 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 1189

595.q: Which of the following is not a known risk factor for bronchiolitis in an infant?
o: Chronic lung condition due to prematurity
595.e: RISK FACTORS FOR BRONCHIOLITIS Parents who smoke Siblings attending day care or school (risk of transmitting viral infections) Chronic lung disease due to prematurity Breastfeeding given for Tags : Topic : BRONCHIOLITIS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW PYQ : FMGE AUG 2020 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2217

595.q: A 10-year-old boy has a history of recurrent sinusitis and multiple episodes of pneumonia. You suspect CF and order a sweat chloride test. The sweat electrolyte test result is within the normal range. What is your next step in management?
o: Perform DNA testing for CFTR gene mutations.
Perform a pH probe test for gastroesophageal reflux.
Reassure parents that he does not have CF.
Place him on a high-calorie, high-protein diet.
595.e: The child has recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract infections suggesting CF. The sweat chloride test can yield falsely low values, so the next step would be to perform DNA testing to identify any of the common CFTR mutations. Negative sweat chloride test results do not exclude CF. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2104

595.q: A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated lung infections. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the CFTR gene. Which test is considered the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis?
595.e: Explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a CFTR gene mutation leading to defective chloride transport across epithelial cells. The sweat chloride test is the gold standard diagnostic test , with chloride levels ≥60 mmol/L being diagnostic. It directly measures abnormal electrolyte transport and is the most reliable confirmatory tool despite genetic testing. Explanation of other options: Lung biopsy (Option B): Rarely used; invasive and not diagnostic for CF. Used mainly for histopathology in other lung diseases. Chest X-ray (Option C): May show bronchiectasis or hyperinflation, but findings are nonspecific and cannot confirm CF. Nasal swab culture (Option D): Identifies infections like Pseudomonas , but is not confirmatory for CF diagnosis.

595.q: Congenital absence of seminal vesicles and vas deferens is seen in?
595.e: More than 95% of males with cystic fibrosis are azoospermic because of failure of development of wolffian duct structures, but sexual function is generally unimpaired. Many male patients with Cystic Fibrosis have an abnormality called CAVD= Congenital Absence of Vas Deferens. This contributes to azoospermia and infertility in males Please note that female fertility may be reduced due to thick cervical mucus but there is no structural issues of reproductive tract in female patients with Cystic Fibrosis Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 2104

595.q: Which of the following amino acid position, amino acids and channel combination is defective in Cystic fibrosis?
595.e: Cystic fibrosis has defective CFTR gene on 7q31.2. It is autosomal recessive. Mutation most common is Del 508 phenylalanine for the Chloride channel. Previously it was called as Delta F 508 Mutation. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 2098

595.q: Which among the following is the most common cause of bronchiolitis obliterans in children?
595.e: Bronchiolitis obliterans (BO) is an uncommon form of obstructive lung disease that occurs as a result of a severe insult to the small airways and ultimately leads to fibrosis and obliteration of the bronchioles. Epidemiology studies suggest that BO occurs frequently in children of Asian and South American descent. In children, the leading cause of BO is infectious, with adenovirus being the most common offending agent. BO also occurs in patients with lung or bone marrow transplants (BMTs) and in those with autoimmune disorders. Other causes include toxic inhalation injury or aspiration, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug toxicity, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, SJS. Reference: Rudolph's Pediatrics 23 rd Ed/Chapter 508

595.q: A 7-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital in respiratory distress due to pneumonia. This is her third admission in the past 6 months. At this time, you are suspecting cystic fibrosis (CF) and order a sputum culture. Which organism would be most consistent with a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis?
595.e: This girl has recurrent pulmonary infections. The presence of P aeruginosa on a sputum sample strongly suggests the diagnosis of CF. Patients with CF have a high prevalence of colonization with P aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and Burkholderia cepacia. The innate defenses of the airway epithelium cells of CF patients may be compromised, making them unable to fight these organisms. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1414

596.q: A 15-year-old adolescent collapses while playing in a high school basketball game without any preceding trauma. He is unconscious and not breathing. Of the following, the BEST sequence of actions is to?
o: Administer a precordial thump and perform a jaw-thrust manoeuvre
Ask someone to retrieve an automatic external defibrillator and start chest compressions
Immobilize the cervical spine and attempt to palpate the carotid pulse
Perform rapid assessment of circulation/airway/breathing and call 108
596.e: As per PALS guidelines and OP Ghai 10 th Edition, if the victim/patient is unresponsive and not breathing, begin CPR immediately. Also call for an automatic external defibrillator (AED) to check for rhythm. If there is VF/pVT, give electric shock and continue CPR If there is Asystole or PEA (Pulseless Electrical Activity), give injection epinephrine and continue with CPR. Effective cardiopulmonary resuscitation includes pushing hard (to 1/3 of the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest), pushing fast (100 compressions per minute) with minimal interruptions, and rotating personnel performing compressions every 2 minutes. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 763, 765; PALS 2020 Guidelines

596.q: During the examination of the child at birth, you observe that the umbilical cord of the baby has single umbilical artery. While counselling the parents of the baby, you explain them the importance of USG abdomen in this child, due to the risk of which of the following defects?
596.e: Single umbilical artery has association with renal agenesis. Hence, all babies with single umbilical artery must be scanned with USG abdomen and KUB to diagnose or rule out the same. Tags: Topic: FETAL CIRCULATION Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2021 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 975

596.q: The MOST common cause of syncope in children is
596.e: Neurocardiogenic syncope, also known as vasovagal syncope, is a common type of fainting or temporary loss of consciousness that occurs due to a sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure. This decrease in circulation reduces blood flow to the brain, leading to fainting. Neurocardiogenic syncope can be triggered by several factors, such as: Prolonged standing Extreme emotional stress Pain Heat exposure Physical exertion KEY TAKEAWAYS: In otherwise healthy children, neurocardiogenic syncope is most common . This entity goes by a number of terms, including vasovagal syncope, neurally mediated syncope, and autonomic syncope. Tags: Topic: EPIDEMIOLOGY Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW Reference: Park’s Pediatric cardiology, 6 th ed., pg. 505

597.q: In children, CHF (congestion heart failure) is diagnosed by
597.e: Answer- C. Tender hepatomegaly Heart failure in infants & children results some degree of hepatemegaly which is usually tender & sometimes splenomegaly. Peripheral edema is age dependent : In infants, edema usually eye & over flank. Older childern & adolescent shows both periorbital edema & pedal edema and occurs late.

597.q: Which of the following features is not associated with patent ductus arteriosus?
597.e: PDA is associated with a collapsing pulse Patent ductus arteriosus Overview Acyanotic congenital heart defect Connection between the pulmonary trunk and descending aorta More common in premature babies, born at high altitude or maternal rubella infection in the first trimester Features Left subclavicular thrill Continuous 'machinery' murmur Large volume, bounding, collapsing pulse Wide pulse pressure Heaving apex beat Management Indomethacin closes the connection in the majority of cases If associated with another congenital heart defect amenable to surgery then prostaglandin E1 isuseful to keep the duct open until after surgical repair. Reference: Braunwald's heart disease 12 th edition, page no.1559

597.q: Medical closure of PDA is contraindicated in which of the following?
597.e: Contraindications for medical closure of PDA Platelet count 3 AKI or Sr. creatinine >1. 8mg/dl. NEC/Feed in tolerance Unexplained bleeding. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 122.5

597.q: A child is a known case of VSD with surgery planned after 3 months. He had 1 episode of severe bronchiolitis last year requiring hospitalization. Now, there is another outbreak of RSV infection in the community. What prophylactic agent you will consider in this child?
597.e: Administration of palivizumab (15 mg/kg IM once a month), a neutralizing humanized murine monoclonal antibody against F-protein of RSV, is recommended for protecting high-risk children against serious complications from RSV disease. Immunoprophylaxis reduces the frequency and total days of hospitalization for RSV infections in high-risk infants in about half of cases. Ribavirin is therapeutic, not prophylactic. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed/Chapter 418

597.q: A child with PDA will not have which among the following?
597.e: Children with PDA have pulmonary congestion due to increased pulmonary blood flow, which results in CO2 Retention, not CO2 Washout. Regarding other options Option A is True. Bounding pulses are seen in PDA due to wide pulse pressure found in most patients. In PDA, there is diastolic run-off of blood due to L -> R shunt. This causes a fall in Diastolic BP, producing a wide pulse pressure. Option B is True. Pulmonary hemorrhage has been described in some patients due to pulmonary congestion and increased pulmonary pressures. Option C is True. Necrotizing Enterocolitis can occur in preterm babies with NEC, since a large L -> R shunt reduces descending aorta blood flow. This produces vasoconstriction in the gut circulation and predisposes to NEC. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 122.5

597.q: Causes of congenital unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia may include all except?
597.e: Sepsis, Crigler Najar syndrome and Gilbert syndrome can all present with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in neonates and even in first 24 hr of life (the so-called congenital jaundice). Rotor syndrome produces conjugated jaundice and usually does not manifest in the neonatal period, hence the answer. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 171

597.q: Which of the following complication is not expected in babies of diabetic mother? A. Hypoglycemia B. Intrauterine growth retardation C. Hypocalcemia D. Ventricular septal defect E. Neural tube defect
597.e: Common presentations in an infant of diabetic mother are Hypoglycemia (selection A) Hypocalcemia (Selection C) Neural tube defects Macrosomia Other manifestations Respiratory distress syndrome Cardiomegaly Cardiac malformations (VSD, TGA, Truncus arteriosus, Double outlet right ventricle, tricuspid atresia, COA) (Selection D) Lumbosacral agenesis Neural tube defect (Selection E) Renal agenesis, hydronephrosis Anorectal atresia Small left colon syndrome Tags : Topic : INFANT OF DIABETIC MOTHER Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : FMGE DEC 2022 Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 983

597.q: Most common cardiac lesion in down's syndrome is?
597.e: Affected individuals with Down Syndrome are more prone to congenital heart defects (50%) such as atrioventricular septal defects, ventricular septal defects, isolated secundum atrial septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, and tetralogy of Fallot. MC congenital heart disease in down syndrome is endocardial cushion defect, also called as complete AV septal defect or atrioventricular canal defect. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 98.2 And Chapter 453.5

598.q: Which of the following is not true regarding Tetralogy of Fallot?
o: Squatting improve the cyanotic spells in children
Egg on side appearance in chest x-ray
Rastelli procedure is performed for surgical correction
598.e: Tetralogy of Fallot Most common cyanotic congenital heart disease Components: pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding of aorta, RV hypertrophy Characterised by cyanotic / tet spells during childhood while exertion Squatting increases peripheral vascular resistance thereby reducing the magnitude of right to left shunt across VSD Boot shaped heart or 'coeur en sabot' is the characteristic xray appearance Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20th edition, ch:264 pg:1833, 1834

598.q: The 'snowman' appearance of heart on chest xray is seen in which congenital heart disease:
598.e: Eponymous chest X ray appearances in congenital heart disease Snowman sign : Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection Egg on side appearance: Transposition of great arteries Boot shaped heart : Fallot's tetralogy Scimitar sign : Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection Figure of 3 sign : Coarctation of aorta Waterbottle sign : Ebstein anomaly (commonly described in pericardial effusion) Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:264 pg:1831,1832

598.q: Which congenital disease has equal saturation in all four chambers of the heart?
598.e: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connections (TAPVC) is a cyanotic congenital heart disease where all of the pulmonary veins drain directly or indirectly open into the right atrium. O2 saturation of blood in the pulmonary artery is often identical to that in aorta due to complete mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous returns in the right atrium.

598.q: Of the following patients, who is at highest risk for bacterial endocarditis?
o: A child with tetralogy of fallot with an aortopulmonary shunt
Toddler with transposition of the great arteries following arterial switch operation at age 1week
A child who had a cardiac transplant 4 years ago
An infant with unrepaired total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
598.e: Patients with prosthetic material used during palliative or corrective surgery are at the highest risk for bacterial endocarditis . In the current guidelines, patients with aorto-pulmonary shunts continue to be in the small subset of patients for whom antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended. Other Indications for prophylaxis of infective endocarditis Child with transposition and transplant for the first 6 months following the operation. (Option b, c) The child with unrepaired cardiac defects (option d) Tags: Topic: ACQUIRED CARDIAC DISEASE Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: INICET MAY 2021 Reference: Park’s Pediatric cardiology, 6 th ed., pg. 342

598.q: All of the following are common diseases in Turner Syndrome, except?
598.e: As per Nelson 21 st Ed, the most common heart defects in Turner syndrome patients are bicuspid aortic valves, coarctation of the aorta, aortic stenosis, and mitral valve prolapse. TOF is not described in most textbooks and is thus the answer by exclusion. Reference: Nelson 21 st Ed, Chapter 98.4, OP Ghai 10 th Ed, Page 669

598.q: Least risk of CCF is seen in which of the following heart diseases?
598.e: The VSD of TOF is always large enough to allow free exit to the right-to-left shunt into overriding aorta. Since the right ventricle is effectively decompressed by the VSD, CCF seldom occurs in TOF. The exceptions to this rule include Anemia Infective Endocarditis Systemic HTN RV Dysfunction from long-standing hypoxia AR or TR Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 445

598.q: Which of the following congenital heart disease would be expected to exhibit cyanosis?
o: A 2-year-old girl with tetralogy of Fallot with concomitant Hb of 4.5 g/dl
A term neonate having TGA with VSD
A preterm neonate with large PDA with distal aortic narrowing
598.e: TGA with VSD is the most common cause of cyanosis in the first week of life. About other options: Although TOF is a cyanotic disease, there must be atleast 5 g/dl of reduced Hb to produce clinical cyanosis. Hence despite having TOF, in the presence of severe anemia, child will not show cyanosis PDA and supracristal VSDs are acyanotic diseases. Ref: Perloff's Cardiology, Nelson 21 st Edition

598.q: Which one of these syndromes is associated with total anomalous pulmonary venous return?
598.e: Turner’s syndrome is associated with coarctation of the aorta. 49XXXXY and 49XXXXX are associated with patent ductus arteriosus. Holt-Oram syndrome is associated with ASD. Ellis-van Creveld syndrome is associated with ASD, PDA, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, TAPVD and TGA. Tags: Topic: EPIDEMIOLOGY Difficulty level: MUST KNOW PYQ: INICET NOV 2021 Reference: Park’s Pediatric cardiology, 6th ed., pg. 237

599.q: An 8-year-old child presented with periorbital edema and mild oliguria but no hypertension. On evaluation, he was found to have serum albumin <2.5 g/dL, serum creatinine 0.5 mg/dL, urine protein 3+, and no RBCs or RBC casts in the urine. What histopathological diagnosis will you suspect?
599.e: Explanation: The clinical features: significant proteinuria (3+), hypoalbuminemia, and edema; are characteristic of Nephrotic Syndrome . In children aged 2-8 years, the most common histopathological diagnosis is Minimal Change Disease (MCD) . Absence of hematuria and hypertension supports the diagnosis of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome. Light microscopy typically shows minimal or no changes. Electron microscopy reveals effacement of podocyte foot processes. Oliguria , although more typical of nephritic syndrome, may occur in nephrotic syndrome due to worsening edema and hypoalbuminemia. Explanation of Other Options: IgA nephropathy (Option B): Presents with hematuria, often post-infectious. Membranous nephropathy (Option C): More common in adults; shows thickened GBM on microscopy. FSGS (Option D): Presents with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and may show hematuria or hypertension.

599.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with swelling that has increased over the past week. The swelling is most noticeable around his eyes in the mornings but is most notable in his legs in the afternoon. On examination, he has pitting edema of the bilateral lower extremities. He is also mildly hypertensive. Labs are significant for hypoalbuminemia and 3+ proteinuria. What is the most likely etiology of the child's hypoalbuminemia?
599.e: The child's presentation is consistent with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome results from urinary protein losses, which lead to hypoalbuminemia. The hypoalbuminemia leads to dependent edema. As such, the edema may be most noticeable around the eyes in the mornings with a shift to the lower extremities as the day progresses. Hypertension may occasionally be present. Typical laboratory findings include serum hypoalbuminemia, proteinuria, and hyperlipidemia. Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in childhood. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 500-501; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2523
