599.q: A 10-year-old child presented with generalized edema. On investigation, his serum cholesterol level was 238 mg/dl, urine protein was 3+ and stool microscopy revealed oval fat bodies. What is the probable diagnosis?
599.e: Nephrotic range proteinuria is defined as proteinuria >3.5 g/24 hour or a urine protein : creatinine ratio >2. The triad of clinical findings associated with nephrotic syndrome arising from the large urinary losses of protein are hypoalbuminemia (≤2.5 g/dL), edema, and hyperlipidemia (cholesterol >200 mg/dL). Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed., pg. 2521

o: More common in girls than boys
599.e: Minimal Change Disease is a histopathological entity commonly seen in children with nephrotic syndrome. The disease is so-named because the light microscopy shows minimal to no change. However, electron microscopy shows effacement of foot process of podocytes. Let us evaluate each option Option A is False. Minimal change disease is more common in boys than girls Option B is False. It causes selective proteinuria Option C is True. MCD leads to excess albumin loss in urine, causing severe hypoalbuminemia and is thus the MC cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome. Option D is False. Most cases respond well to Oral Prednisolone as the first line therapy. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 500-501.

599.q: All are true regarding childhood nephrotic syndrome except?
o: Hypertension is relatively uncommon compared to nephritic syndrome
Minimal change disease is common in age <10 years
599.e: Presence of low complement level indicates complement-mediated injury, which is a feature of glomerulonephritis like PSGN, but is not seen in Nephrotic Syndrome. Regarding other options Option A is True. Hypertension can sometimes occur in Nephrotic syndrome, but is more commonly a feature of acute nephritic syndrome Option B is True. Minimal Change Disease tends to occur in age 2-8 years Option C is True. Massive proteinuria is a hallmark of nephrotic syndrome Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 500-501

599.q: A 10-year-old child presents with edema, anasarca and massive proteinuria. A diagnosis of minimal change disease was made. Which of the following statements is true about this condition?
o: Light microscopy shows effacement of podocyte
599.e: The child in the case has Nephrotic syndrome characterised by selective proteinuria of albumin. It is more common in the paediatric population. Minimal change disease is the most common type in children. Light microscopy is normal in minimal change disease. Electron microscopy will show effacements of podocytes. It shows excellent response to oral prednisolone. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 500-501; Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20 th ed, pg. 2521

599.q: A child with nephrotic syndrome on high dose steroids comes in contact with an active case of chicken pox in neighborhood. He is not vaccinated to varicella. Which of the following treatment is advised for this child?
o: Observe and treat only if symptomatic
599.e: Following close contact with varicella infection, give immunocompromised children on immunosuppressive agents varicella-zoster immune globulin if available ; immunize healthy household contacts with live vaccines to minimize the risk of transfer of infection to the immunosuppressed child, but avoid direct exposure of the child to gastrointestinal or respiratory secretions of vaccinated contacts for 3-6 weeks after vaccination. Live vaccines are contraindicated for this child. ( Option A) IV acyclovir is recommended by some literature. ( Option C) KEY TAKEAWAYS: Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients with nephrotic syndrome. Tags: Topic: NEPHROTIC SYNDROME Difficulty level: MUST KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2022; 2021; FMGE JAN 2023; DEC 2020 Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2753

599.q: All of the following can be used to distinguish bartter syndrome from gitelman syndrome, except?
599.e: Both Bartter Syndrome & Gitelman Syndrome have hypokalemia and thus serum potassium levels can't be used to distinguish between them. Regarding other options Option B- Bartter Syndrome shows hypercalciuria while Gitelman Syndrome shows Hypocalciuria Option C- Serum Mg is normal in Bartter and low in Gitelman Option D- Facial dysmorphism occurs in some forms of Bartter syndrome but not in Gitelman syndrome Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 525; Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 549

600.q: During his 1st physical examination following birth at home with the assistance of a midwife, a 5- week-old male is suspected to have congenital hypothyroidism. His parents refused all newborn screening at the time of his birth. Which of the following may be the earliest clinical sign of congenital hypothyroidism?
600.e: Prolongation of physiologic jaundice, due to delayed maturation of glucuronide conjugation, is often the 1st clinical finding in an infant with congenital hypothyroidism. Poor feeding, partly due to a large tongue, somnolence, and lack of interest are characteristic. Additional clinical findings may include a large protuberant abdomen; umbilical hernia; mottled, cool, and dry skin; extremity edema; and widely open fontanelles. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2668

600.q: A full term baby born to a mother with hypothyroidism, needs to be screened for congenital hypothyroidism ideally at what age?
600.e: A newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism must be done at 3-4 days of life coupled with newborn screening for inborn errors of metabolism. Screening test that are positive must be reassessed with a repeat venous sample and read according to cut-off values for the age. Tags : Topic : CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2022 Reference : AIIMS protocols in neonatology, 2019, pg. 236

600.q: What is the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism?
600.e: Causes of permanent congenital hypothyroidism are: Thyroid dysgenesis (most common) Thyroid agenesis TSH resistance Thyroid dyshormonogenesis (2 nd most common) Central hypothyroidism Tags : Topic : CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM Difficulty level : MUST KNOW PYQ : NEET PG 2022 Reference : Cloherty and Stark's manual of neonatal care, SA ed., pg. 933

600.q: Most common cause of hyperthyroidism in children is?
600.e: The most common cause of hyperthyroidism is Grave's disease . This is an autoimmune condition where antibodies (TSH receptor antibodies - TRAb ) mimic TSH and activate the TSH-R on the thyroid gland, producing excessive thyroid hormone. Other causes of hyperthyroidism include: Toxic multinodular goitre Toxic adenoma Thyroid carcinoma Neonatal hyperthyroidism - due to transplacental transfer of maternal TRAb to the fetus hCG-secreting tumors - hCG has a similar structure to TSH and so can mimic it Functioning pituitary adenoma leading to increased production of TSH KEY TAKEAWAYS: The most common cause of hyperthyroidism is Grave's disease . Tags: Topic: THYROID DISORDERS Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2929

601.q: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is due to deficiency of enzyme a. 3β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency b. 5a Reductase c. 17a-Hydroxylase deficiency d. 21-Hydroxylase deficiency
601.e: Enzymes deficiency causing Congenital adrenal hyperplasia are 21-Hydroxylase deficiency 11β-Hydroxylase deficiency 17-Hydroxylase/17, 20 lyase deficiency 3B-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency Lipoid adrenal Hyperplasia Reference: Ganong, 25th edition page no.366

601.q: An 8-day-old baby presents with vomiting, poor feeding and loose stools. On examination, his heart rate is 190 bpm, BP 50/30 mmHg and respiratory rate 72 breaths/min. Blood tests: Hb 15 g/dl (13-18), sodium 120 mmol/l (137-144), potassium 6.0 mmol/l (3.5-4.9), chloride 80 mmol/l (95-107), bicarbonate 15 mmol/l (21-28), urea 30 mg/dl and creatinine 0.6 mg/dl (both normal). What is the most likely diagnosis
601.e: The features and findings are highly suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia presenting as salt wasting crisis 21 hydroxylase is the most common enzyme deficiency in CAH and salt wasting crisis. Absence of jaundice and hepatomegaly make the diagnosis of Galactosaemia unlikely. Acute tubular necrosis is ruled out, as urea and creatinine levels are normal. In congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, hypokalemia is the presenting feature and constipation (not loose stools) is the chief complaint. Lactose intolerance would again present with diarrhea or vomiting, thus hypokalemia would be the characteristic finding. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2973

601.q: A 2-month-old infant is presented with failure to thrive, recurrent emesis, hepatosplenomegaly, and adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal calcification is noted radiologically. The most likely diagnosis is?
601.e: Vomiting, hepatosplenomegaly, adrenal insufficiency and adrenal calcification point to a diagnosis of Wolman Disease. Wolman Disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage diseases that results from deficiency of lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) and accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides in histiocytic foam cells of most visceral organs. The LAL gene is on chromosome 10 (10q24-q25). Clinical features become apparent in the 1st weeks of life and include failure to thrive, relentless vomiting, abdominal distention, steatorrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly. There usually is hyperlipidemia. Hepatic dysfunction and fibrosis may occur. Calcification of the adrenal glands occurs in about 50% of patients and is an important clue to the underlying diagnosis, when present. Death usually occurs within the 1st 6 months of life. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 104

601.q: Which of the following is not a classic feature of a salt-losing crisis in an infant with congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
601.e: In CAH, an enzyme deficiency in the steroid hormone synthesis pathway can lead to a combined cortisol and aldosterone insufficiency. Aldosterone promotes water and sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium by upregulating Na/K pump activity in the distal nephron . Its absence therefore results in a salt-losing crisis with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (and associated metabolic acidosis), and hypotension. At the same time, the lack of cortisol causes Tags: Topic: CONGENITAL ADRENAL HYPERPLASIA Difficulty level: MUST KNOW PYQ: NEET PG 2022 Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2960

601.q: A 18-day-old female infant, has congenital adrenal hypoplasia. She presents having vomited all her feeds today. She has become lethargic and will no longer feed. On examination she has tachycardia, with a heart rate of 160 beats/min and a capillary refill time of 3 seconds. A bedside blood test shows that she is hypoglycemic. What is the best immediate management?
o: Oral rehydration, sodium supplements and oral glucocorticoid
601.e: The child is having an adrenal crisis. This requires urgent treatment with intravenous saline, glucose and hydrocortisone. Long-term treatment is with glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement and oral sodium chloride may be needed during infancy. The dose of glucocorticoid needs to be increased at times of illness. The child is having a salt-losing crisis. Saline is needed along with glucose infusion. (option a) This child is seriously ill. IV is preferred over Oral due to sickness of child. (option c, d) TAGS: TOPIC: CONGENITAL ADRENAL HYPERPLASIA DIFFICULTY LEVEL: GOOD TO KNOW Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2975

601.q: Parents of a 3-month-old infant comes to you with complaint of blood in stool over last 15 days. He has been treated with oral antibiotic and probiotic but no improvement. The child is otherwise healthy, feeds and sleeps well. Which of the following condition is not considered in the differential diagnosis of the child?
601.e: An infant with painless lower GI bleedhas 3 differentials- Meckle's diverticula Lymphonodular hyperplasia Intestinal duplication. Other causes of lower GI bleed in infants like volvulus, intussusception, colitis, anal fissure, infantile colitis presents with other associated complaints and they are painful. Tags: Topic: MISCELLANEOUS Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Nelson pediatric symptom-based diagnosis, pg no: 235

602.q: A 10-year-old girl is 4 ft 10 in (147 cm) tall. Her father is 5 ft 10 in (178 cm) tall, and her mother is 5 ft 5 in (165 cm) tall. Over the past 3 years she has dropped from the 25th percentile for height to the 5th percentile. Her weight has remained stable. Radiographs show bone age is delayed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?
o: Send patient to the emergency department for CT evaluation of the brain
602.e: This child has evidence of possible growth hormone deficiency. Obtaining an IGF-1 level would be the most appropriate initial choice. Growth hormone deficiency is not an emergent condition but the earlier the diagnosis is made the sooner appropriate treatment can be initiated. Obtaining a growth hormone level would not be diagnostically helpful because its secretion is pulsatile. Referral to a pediatric endocrinologist would be warranted if initial screening tests confirm the suspected growth hormone deficiency. Reference: Nelson-Pediatric Symptom based diagnosis, pg. 791

603.q: The following are complications of Neurofibromatosis-1, EXCEPT?
603.e: Complications in NF-1 Learning disability affects approximately 30%. Seizures occur in approximately 8%. The cerebral vessels may develop aneurysms or stenosis resulting in moyamoya syndrome. Neurologic sequelae of these vascular abnormalities include transient cerebrovascular ischemic attacks, hemiparesis, and cognitive defects. Precocious puberty may become evident in the presence or absence of lesions of the optic pathway tumours. Malignant neoplasms affecting approximately 3% of patients. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20 th edition, pg. 2876

603.q: What is the recommended chest compression rate during CPR in a child according to PALS 2020 guidelines?
o: Rates not specified in the new guidelines
603.e: As per CPR guidelines for children in PALS 2020 In CPR, start chest compressions with rescue breaths in cardiac arrest. If unable to give rescue breaths, compressions alone to be given Chest compression rate: 100-120/min Allow adequate chest recoil between 2 compressions Depth of compression: At least 1/3 rd the AP diameter of the chest , approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm) in infants and 2 inches (5 cm) in children. Post puberty, use the adult compression depth 5-6 cm A rhythm check every 2 min , lasting 10 sec Ventilate with 100% O2 Reference: PALS Guidelines 2020; OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 763.

603.q: Which of the following complications is not expected in a child diagnosed with neurofibromatosis (type 1) NF-l
603.e: Complications in NF-1 Option A : Learning disability affecting approximately 30%. Option D : Seizures in approximately 8%. The cerebral vessels may develop aneurysms or stenosis resulting in moyamoya syndrome. Neurologic sequelae of these vascular abnormalities include transient cerebrovascular ischemic attacks, hemiparesis, and cognitive defects. Option C : Precocious puberty may become evident in the presence or absence of lesions of the optic pathway tumors. Malignant neoplasms affecting approximately 3% of patients. Tags: Topic: NEUROCUTANEOUS SYNDROME Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW PYQ: INICET NOV 2020 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 3141

604.q: Commonest tumor of face in chidren is-
604.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Rhabdomyosarcoma Rhabdomyosarcoma o The most common soft tissue sarcoma in children is rhabdomyosarcoma. o The common site of involvement are : - o Head & Neck (25%) 2"d most common Extremities Genitourinary (22%) —> 2nd most common Retroperitoneum

604.q: Which is MC genetic cause of mental retardation -
604.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Fragile-X-syndrome o Down's syndrome is the most common genetic cause of mental retardation, and fragile-X is second to Down's. Also know o Most common inherited cause of mental retardation is fragile-X- syndrome (because down's syndrome is congenital cause but not inherited).

604.q: Most common cerebellar tumor in children?
604.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Astrocytoma o The most common cerebellar tumor in adults is metastasis, whereas in children the most common tumor is an astrocytoma.

604.q: Dinutuximab has been recently approved for which among the following pediatric malignancy?
604.e: Dinutuximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets a diasialoganglioside, GD2, which has ubiquitous expression on neuroblastoma cells Incorporation of the mAb into consolidative therapy after autologous stem cell transplant improves the 2-yr event-free survival from 46.5% to 66.5%. Dinutuximab is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a standard of care for this subset of patients. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 525

604.q: Which among the following is contraindicated in childhood dysentery?
604.e: Antimotility agents (loperamide) are contraindicated in children with dysentery and probably have no role in the management of acute watery diarrhea in otherwise healthy children. Similarly, antiemetic agents, such as the phenothiazines, are of little value and are associated with potentially serious side effects (lethargy, dystonia, malignant hyperpyrexia). Incorrect Options: Option B- Ondansetron is safe and a useful adjunct in troublesome vomiting. Option C- Probiotics can be given but are not routinely indicated. Option D- Remember: Ciprofloxacin is the drug of choice in childhood dysentery. Reference: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 20th Edition, Page Number-1873; OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 10th Edition, Page Number-314.

604.q: A 4-year-old child is presented with abdominal lump. Bone scan is being done to rule out which of the following condition?
604.e: Among the given options, Neuroblastoma frequently produces bony metastasis. Bony metastases in Neuroblastoma often occurs to orbital bones, producing proptosis and/or Raccoon Eyes/Panda Eyes. Vertebral spread is also reported. As per Nelson 21 st Edition, Metastatic spread in Neuroblastoma, which is more common in children >1 yr old at diagnosis, occurs through local invasion or distant hematogenous or lymphatic routes. The most common sites of metastasis overall in Neuroblastoma are the regional or distant lymph nodes, long bones and skull, bone marrow, liver, and skin. Kindly note that bone scan is needed in Neuroblastoma as well as Clear cell sarcoma variant of Wilms tumour in children. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 525; OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 637-639

604.q: "I am a pediatric malignancy. I often afflict young children & can produce lung, lymph node and liver metastases. FNAC & Blind Biopsy is not recommended in me. I respond well to chemotherapy with Vincristine, Actinomycin-D and Doxorubicin. Who am I?"
604.e: Clues to the diagnosis of Wilms Tumour here. Clue 1- Pediatric malignancy in young children. Wilms tumour occurs in children aged 2-3 years. Clue 2- Metastases to lung, lymph nodes and liver is seen in Wilms tumour Clue 3- Blind biopsy is avoided since it can upstage the disease, as per Nelson 21 st Imaging studies include plain abdominal radiography, abdominal ultrasonography (US), and CT of the abdomen to define the intrarenal origin of the mass and differentiate it from adrenal masses (e.g., neuroblastoma) and other masses in the abdomen Clue 4- Responds to chemotherapy with Vincristine, Actinomycin-D and Doxorubicin- Seen in Wilms Tumour. After radical nephrectomy, most patients receive chemotherapy using the said agents. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 526; OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 636-638

604.q: Which statement about childhood brain tumors is true?
o: Most are located in the midline and/or below the tentorium cerebri.
Brain tumors are a rare type of cancer in childhood.
Signs of increased intracranial pressure are rare in midline tumours
Seizures are the presenting complaint in all cases.
604.e: Most brain tumours in children are infratentorial, hence option A is correct. About other options Brain tumours are relatively frequent in childhood among malignancies and comprise most common solid malignancy in childhood. Signs of raised ICP can develop commonly with midline brain tumours like medulloblastoma Seizures may or may not be present in all cases Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 642-643

605.q: Handedness is established in a child at what age?
605.e: Handedness: dominance of one hand over the other for performing tasks or activities. It is established in children at around 3 years. key takeaways : Bidextrous grasp -4 months Unidextrous grasp-6 months Palmar grasp-7 months Pincer grasp (immature)-9month Pincer grasp (mature)-12month Handedness-3 years Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatric

605.q: Ideal time gap between two live vaccines, if both can't be given together, should be?
605.e: If two live vaccines cannot be given together, there should be a gap of at least 1 month (or 4 weeks) to ensure that the antibodies developed from the first vaccine do not interfere with the effectiveness of the second vaccine. Key takeaways:- -There is no need to keep a gap of 1 month between a live vaccine and a killed (inactivated) vaccine. They can be given at the same time or at different intervals -All live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy & immunocompromised except During outbreaks &travel (YF,OPV,Cholera) & bite case (rabies) -If two live vaccines are given together, they should be administered at different injection sites. ref :Nelson textbook of paediatric

605.q: Which of the following is most common pulmonary tumor in children?
605.e: The most common tumor types are Carcinoid inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor pleuropulmonary blastoma Rare pediatric lung tumors include small cell carcinoma adenocarcinoma pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis KEY TAKEAWAYS: The most common pulmonary tumor in children is carcinoid tumor. Tags: Topic: SOLID TUMORS Difficulty level: MUST KNOW PYQ: FMGE JULY 2023 Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics, 21 st ed, page number: 2316

605.q: A child with Kawasaki Disease underwent echocardiography and was found to have a giant aneurysm on Right Coronary Artery, for which he was hospitalized and managed. Which among the following is a cut-off to define a giant coronary artery aneurysm in a Kawasaki Disease patient?
605.e: In KD Patients, large or giant coronary artery aneurysms are responsible for most of the morbidity and mortality. Large or giant aneurysms have been defined by the 2017 American Heart Association (AHA) as having a z score ≥10 or an absolute dimension of ≥8 mm. Japanese Classification of Aneurysms in KD Small: ≤4 mm internal diameter [ID]) Medium (>4 to ≤8 mm ID) Giant (>8 mm ID). Specifically, large or giant aneurysms are associated with the greatest risk of thrombosis or stenosis, angina, and myocardial infarction. Rupture of a giant aneurysm is a rare complication that generally occurs in the 1st months after illness onset and may present as hemopericardium with tamponade. Axillary, popliteal, iliac, or other arteries may also become aneurysmal, but always in the setting of giant coronary aneurysms. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 191

605.q: Which among the following pediatric condition is associated with mutations in ITPKC gene as well as anti-endothelial cell antibodies positivity?
605.e: The likely condition is Kawasaki Disease. Exact cause is unknown. Considered to be a T-cell mediated disease More common in Japanese population Young children more affected, with peak age of 18-24 months Males are more commonly affected than females Anti-Endothelial cell antibodies are positive in many patients, although they are not implicated directly in the disease pathogenesis Genes implicated in Kawasaki disease include ITPKC, CASP-3. Reference : Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 191

605.q: Which of the following is the most common complication associated with Kawasaki disease?
o: Congestive cardiac failure due to mitral regurgitation
605.e: Most common complication associated with KD is Myocarditis . It might be asymptomatic or present with congestive cardiac failure. Most common cause of death is Thrombosis of Coronary artery aneurysm (CAA). Other complications include: Kawasaki disease shock syndrome Mitral regurgitation Asymptomatic pericardial effusion KEY TAKEAWAYS: Myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, is a recognized complication of Kawasaki disease. It occurs due to the widespread inflammation in blood vessels and heart tissue that characterizes the disease. Myocarditis in Kawasaki disease can lead to symptoms such as rapid or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, fatigue, and in severe cases, heart failure. Tags: Topic: KAWASAKI DISEASE Difficulty level: MUST KNOW PYQ: INICET MAY 2024 Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 1510

605.q: All of the following features can present in Kawasaki's disease except?
605.e: Kawasaki Disease (KD) is an acute febrile mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome mainly affecting infants and young children. Cervical Lymph Nodes, NOT axillary LN are involved in Kawasaki Disease Cervical LNs are most commonly unilateral, with at least one node >1.5 cm. Other options are correct. Reference : OP Ghai 10 th Ed, Page 658

605.q: The following symptoms may be suggestive of rheumatic disease except?
o: Malar rash with chest pain: systemic lupus erythematosus
605.e: Arthralgia is pain in the joints when trying to use them in active or passive movement. This occurs in SLE, JRA and JD, as well as in other, non-rheumatic, conditions. Weakness is mainly associated with dermatomyositis, but not a feature of JIA Malar rashes are seen with SLE and photosensitive dermatitis. Chest pain from pericarditis is seen with SLE and JRA. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA edition, pg. 1204

606.q: Which of the following is the most common cause of shock in paediatric patient?
606.e: Dehydration (hypovolemic) shock is the most common type of shock in paediatric population. Common Causes in Paediatrics Gastrointestinal Losses: Diarrhea (e.g., rotavirus, cholera). Vomiting. Hemorrhage: Trauma (e.g., accidents). Post-surgical bleeding. Burns: Fluid loss through damaged skin. Other Causes: Inadequate fluid intake (e.g., neglect, illness). Third-spacing (e.g., sepsis, nephrotic syndrome). Septic shock is most common in neonates. Tags: Topic: SHOCK Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Manual of paediatric emergencies & critical care, 2 nd ed., pg. 158

606.q: Two weeks after a viral syndrome, a 2-year-old develops bruising and generalized petechiae that is more prominent over the legs. He has neither hepatosplenomegaly nor lymph node enlargement. Laboratory testing reveals a normal hemoglobin, hematocrit, and white blood cell count and differential. The platelet count is 15,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
606.e: Immune (or idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is common in children. In most cases, a preceding viral infection can be documented. The platelet count frequently is less than 20,000/mm3, but other laboratory test results are normal, including the bone marrow aspiration (which may show an increase in megakaryocytes). These patients have no hepatosplenomegaly or generalized lymphadenopathy. Treatment consists of observation or possibly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), intravenous anti-D (in Rh-positive patients), immunosuppressives, or steroids. The history must be reviewed for other possible causes of thrombocytopenia, including recent MMR vaccination, drug ingestion, and human immunodeficiency virus. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA edition, pg. 2402

606.q: Desmopressin is relatively contraindicated in which type of Von Willebrand disease?
606.e: Type 2B vWD results from gain-of-function mutations that increase the ability of vWF to bind platelets. This leads to increased clearance of both vWF and platelets from circulation and results in the loss of high-molecular-weight multimers and decreased vWF activity, similar to that seen in type 2A vWD. Desmopressin is relatively contraindicated in type 2B vWD as it may accelerate VWF-platelet binding and clearance. Please note that Desmopressin is highly effective in Type 1 vWD Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SE edition, pg. 2390

606.q: Cryoprecipitate will control bleeding due to deficiency of all of the following except?
606.e: In emergencies when factor IX is unavailable, only FFP is used as cryoprecipitate does not contain factor IX. Cryoprecipitate contains Fibrinogen, VWF, factor VIII, XIII & fibronectin, but no Factor IX. Hence it will not be useful in Factor IX deficiency, i.e., Hemophilia B Reference: OP Ghai 9 th Ed/Page 351

606.q: Which of the following is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis?
606.e: Prothrombin G20210A mutation occurs in approximately 3% of the general population and increases the risk for thrombosis mainly by causing excess prothrombin production. Regarding other options Factor V deficiency is associated with increased bleeding, not with increased thrombosis. (Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia and the mutation causes a resistance of factor V to inactivation by activated proteins C and S.) Patients with nephrotic syndrome, not nephritic syndrome, are at an increased risk of thrombosis due to loss of clotting factors in the urine. Hyperhomocysteinemia is a risk factor for thrombosis and stroke in children, but not Homocysteine Deficiency. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA edition, pg. 2393

606.q: Which of the following is the most common type of ectopic tissue found in Meckel's diverticulum?
606.e: Rule of 2's in Meckel's Diverticulum Seen in 2% population Two times common in F>M - 2:1 Presents before 2 years of age 2 inches length Present 2 feet proximal to ileocecal value, along the antimesenteric border Ectopic tissue common in meckel diverticulum : Gastric tissue(>50% cases)>Pancreatic tissue>jejunum Meckel's diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa secretes hydrochloric acid (HCl), which can lead to ulceration in the adjacent intestinal mucosa and result in gastrointestinal bleeding. Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

606.q: A 1-week-old presents to your office with bruising and coffee ground emesis. She was a term baby who was born at home and is now exclusively breastfed. Her PT is prolonged >100 seconds, and her aPTT is relatively normal. This patient has?
606.e: A Neonate delivered at home would not have likely got Vitamin K injection at birth. Now she is presenting with bleeding manifestations. Classical vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns presents in the first week of life. Typical symptoms include easy bruising, mucus membrane bleeding, and hematemesis. Risk factors include babies who have not been given vitamin K treatment, are breastfed, or are poor feeders. Such patients will have low levels of vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, and X. Prothrombin time will be prolonged Factor V and VIII levels are unaffected. Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1 st SA edition, pg. 2397

606.q: Which among the following is the procedure of choice in aspirated foreign bodies in lower airway in children?
606.e: Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic procedure in children who aspirate foreign body into the lower airway in children. Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy is sensitive to visualize but cannot be used to remove stuck FB. As per Nelson 21 st Ed, "The treatment of choice for airway foreign bodies is prompt endoscopic removal with rigid instruments by a specialist (otolaryngologist or pulmonologist)." Potential complications of rigid bronchoscopy include bronchospasm, desaturation, bleeding, and airway edema, in addition to the inherent risks of anesthesia. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 414.

607.q: Which of the following microorganism is the most common cause of aplastic crisis in Sickle Cell Anemia & Hereditary Spherocytosis?
607.e: Human Parvovirus B19, also written as B19V, is notorious for aplastic crisis in chronic hemolytic states. Individuals with chronic hemolytic anemia and increased red blood cell (RBC) turnover, including Sickle Cell Anemia & Hereditary Spherocytosis, are very sensitive to minor perturbations in erythropoiesis. Infection with B19V leads to a transient arrest in RBC production and a precipitous fall in serum hemoglobin, often requiring transfusion. The reticulocyte count drops to undetectable levels, reflecting the lysis of infected erythroid precursors. Humoral immunity is crucial in controlling infection. Specific immunoglobulin (Ig) M appears within 1-2 days of infection and is followed by anti-B19 IgG, which leads to control of the infection, restoration of reticulocytosis, and a rise in serum hemoglobin. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 278

607.q: Type of change seen in sickle cell anemia is?
607.e: Sickle cell hemoglobinopathy occurs due to mutation of beta-globin gene situated on short arm of chromosome 11, where adenine is replaced by thymine in base of DNA coding for the amino acid in the sixth position in beta-globin chain. This leads to an amino acid change in beta chain of Hb molecule, from glutamic acid to valine. The result is profound change in the molecular stability and solubility of Hb "S". Reference: IAP Textbook of Pediatrics 5 th Ed/Page 700, OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 364

607.q: A 5-year-old child is diagnosed with sickle cell anemia. He is more susceptible to all the following bacterial infections except
607.e: All patients with sickle cell anemia are at increased risk of infection and death from bacterial infection, particularly encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae Hemophilus influenzae type b Neisseria meningitidis Tags : Topic : BACTERIAL INFECTIONS Difficulty level : GOOD TO KNOW Reference : Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21 st ed., pg. 2542

607.q: Which among the following is not useful in the management of Sickle Cell Anemia?
607.e: Bebtelovimab : This is a monoclonal antibody used for COVID-19 treatment , not related to the management of sickle cell anemia. Disease-Modifying Drugs in ménagement of Sickle cell anemia (A): Hydroxyurea :It increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels, reducing sickling and vaso-occlusive crises. (C): L-Glutamine : Approved for sickle cell disease; reduces oxidative stress and decreases the frequency of pain crises. (B): Voxelotor : A hemoglobin modulator that stabilizes oxygenated hemoglobin, reducing hemoglobin polymerization and improving anemia Crizanlizumab :A monoclonal antibody targeting P-selectin to reduce adhesion of sickled cells to the endothelium. Decreases vaso-occlusive crises Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

608.q: A child was advised yearly vaccination with a vaccine, which is not a part of the national immunization schedule. Yearly vaccination is recommended against?
608.e: Annual vaccination is given against Influenza Vaccine in selected high-risk groups. The type of influenza vaccine currently marketed for use in India is an inactivated, quadrivalent vaccine. The vaccines are highly immunogenic and safe for use above 6 months of age. The vaccine is not part of the National Immunization Schedule, but recommended by IAP in selected high-risk groups like Chronic cardiac, pulmonary, renal, hepatic or hematological disease Asthma or wheezing in the past one year Chronic diseases like Sickle Cell Anemia, DM, SLE and Morbid Obesity Immunodeficiency Prolonged Aspirin Use Laboratory and Health-Care Workers Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 205-206

608.q: A 6-week-old child has just received Pentavalent vaccine today. Components of Pentavalent vaccine shall include?
608.e: Pentavalent vaccines are given according to the National immunization Program at 6-week, 10 week and 14 weeks. It provides protection against 5 vaccine preventable diseases including Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B and H. Influenzae type b. Pneumococcal vaccines and Fractional IPV are also administered along with this but are not part of pentavalent vaccine. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 189

608.q: Which one of the following murmur characteristics supports the diagnosis of an innocent murmur?
o: Maximum intensity at the left lower sternal border.
608.e: The characteristics of innocent murmur are Medium-pitched, vibratory or "musical," Relatively short systolic ejection murmur, Heard best along the left lower and midsternal border Has no significant radiation to the apex, base, or back. The intensity of the murmur often changes with respiration and position and may be attenuated in the sitting or prone position. It is heard most frequently in children between 3 and 7 years of age. Tags: Topic: BASICS OF CARDIOLOGY Difficulty level: MUST KNOW Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 2169

608.q: A school nurse called you to see a 6-year-old boy with school refusal, he is always crying after parental leaving, refuses to stay in the classroom, the school nurse informed you that she tried her best during the last 4 weeks; and she met with the parents frequently. Of the following, the BEST action is to?
o: Refer the child to a pediatrics psychologist
Start selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor treatment
608.e: Management of school refusal typically requires parent management training and family therapy, with school personnel is always indicated; anxious children often require special attention from teachers, counsellors, or school nurses. Parents who are coached to calmly sending child to school and to reward the child for each completed day of school are usually successful; in this scenario this option had been used. In cases of ongoing school refusal, referral to a child psychiatrist or psychologist is indicated. SSRI treatment may be helpful. Young children with affective symptoms have a good prognosis. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20 th edition, pg-146

608.q: Which of the following is NOT an essential medication for acute asthma exacerbations?
608.e: Montelukast is a leukotriene modifier that is used in the long-term control of asthma. The other medications are used in acute asthma exacerbations. Please note that Salbutamol is also called as Albuterol. Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1 st SA ed., pg. 1106

608.q: Which among the following is the drug of choice in patients with KD?
608.e: DOC in KD is Single-dose IVIG. Patients with acute KD should be treated with 2 g/kg of IVIG as a single infusion, usually administered over 10-12 hr within 10 days of disease onset, and ideally as soon as possible after diagnosis. In addition, moderate (30-50 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hr) to high-dose aspirin (80-100 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hr) should be administered until the patient is afebrile, then lowered to antiplatelet doses. Other NSAIDs should not be given during therapy with aspirin because they may block the action of aspirin. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 659, Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 191

608.q: Which among the following is the most common cause of infective endocarditis in children?
608.e: According To Nelson 21 st Edition, Viridans-type streptococci (α-hemolytic streptococci groups such as Streptococcus mitis, S. anginosus, S. mutans, S. salivarius, and S. bovis ) and Staphylococcus aureus remain the leading causative agents for endocarditis in pediatric patients. Other organisms cause endocarditis less frequently, and in approximately 6% of cases, blood cultures are negative for any organisms. According to OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Streptococcus viridans, followed by Staph aureus, Enterococci, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and some Gram negative bacilli are responsible for most episodes of infective endocarditis in children. Reference: Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapter 464; OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Page 467

608.q: A child with recurrent UTI is most likely to show?
608.e: VUR (Vesico-ureteric reflux) refers to the retrograde flow of urine from bladder to pelvis or ureters either during rest or during micturition. Recurrent UTIs occur in 30-50% children and major factors include female sex, age VUR is the most common cause of recurrent UTI in children, overall as well as in females PUV is a common cause of recurrent UTI only in males. Reference: OP Ghai 10 th Edition, Pages 507-511; Nelson 21 st Edition, Chapters 553 And 554

609.e: Oliver Wendel Holmes coined the term Anaesthesia . John snow- administered chloroform analgesia to Queen Victoria for the delivery of her eighth child. This was a success and led to medical and religious acceptance of obstetrical anesthesia. When cholera returned to London in 1853, John Snow undertook an epidemiological study and linked the outbreak in Golden Square to the water pump on Broad Street. WTG Morton is considered as father of Anaesthesia The concept of balanced anesthesia was introduced in 1926 by Lundy and others and evolved to include thiopental for induction, nitrous oxide for amnesia, an opioid for analgesia, and curare for muscle relaxation. The term "spinal anesthesia " was coined in 1885 by Leonard Corning, a neurologist,and Augest Bier used cocaine for spinal anesthesia Reference : Lundy Js . Balanced Anaesthesia .minn .med . 1926;9:399-404

609.q: World Anaesthesia Day is celebrated on ?
609.e: In the Bullfinch amphitheater of the Massachusetts General Hospital. On Friday 16 October 1846 , Morton administed volatile anesthetic Ether to Edward Gilbert Abbott when John Collins Warren was operating a vascular lesion at the left side of Abbott's neck Gilbert Abbott later reported that he was aware of the operation but had experienced no pain . At the moment that the procedure ended, Warren turned to his audience and allegedly announced, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug" To honor this humongous achievement, the day is celebrated as world anaesthesia day Reference : E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 1 Page No 4 Table 2

609.q: "Chloroform a lareine", a technique was invented by ?
609.e: John snow administered labour analgesia using Chloroform to Queen Victoria's 8 th delivery, to the birth of, Prince Leopard During the delivery, Snow administered analgesic doses of chloroform on a folded handkerchief, a technique that was soon termed ' chloroform a la reine ' Victoria abhorred the pain of labor and enjoyed the relief that chloroform provided; she wrote in her journal," Dr.Snow gave that blessed chloroform and the effect was soothing, quieting, and delightful beyond measure " Reference : E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 1 Page No 4 Table 2

609.q: For elective procedures, an anesthesia provider must obtain informed and preferably written consent
o: Just prior to transferring the patient to the operation room for surgery
At the same time that a surgeon obtains consent for the surgical procedure
Just prior to induction of anesthesia in the operating room
609.e: An anesthesia consent should be obtained during pre-anesthetic evaluation, whenever possible. This is one of the prime aims that need to be filled as a component of preoperative anesthetic evaluation. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 297.

609.q: First public demonstration of ether was given by ?
609.e: William Thomas Green Morton began experiments with inhaled ether at Boston and with Ether he started anesthetizing patients in his dental office. Because of his success, he received an invitation to give a public demonstration in the Bullfinch amphitheater of the Massachusetts General Hospital In the Bullfinch amphitheater of the Massachusetts General Hospital. On Friday 16 October 1846 , Morton administed volatile anesthetic Ether to Edward Gilbert Abbott when John Collins Warren was operating a vascular lesion at the left side of Abbott's neck Reference : E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 1 Page No 4 Table 2

609.q: On October 16, 1846, the first public demonstration of general anesthesia for surgery using ether was conducted at ether dome by
609.e: In Boston, Massachusetts, on October 16, 1846, William T.G. Morton conducted the first public demonstration of general anesthesia for surgical operation using ether The surgeon was John Warren and the operation was the removal of a vascular lesion from the left side neck of Edward Gilbert Abbott Wrong answers: Option A : Joseph Priestley produced nitrous oxide in 1772 Option B: August Bier is credited with administering the first spinal anesthetic in 1898 . He was also the first to describe intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier block) in 1908 Option D : Thiopental, synthesized in 1932 by Volwiler and Tabern, was first used clinically by John Lundy and Ralph Waters in 1934 Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology, 6th edition, Chapter 1, page 2

609.q: William Thomas Green Morton used to refer Ether as?
609.e: Morton called the component of the colored fluid, which he had used to put Abbott to sleep during the first public demonstration as " Letheon ," which was , chemically the drug diethyl ether Reference : E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 1 Page No 4 to 6

609.q: Levels of ether anesthesia were demonstrated by whom?
609.e: Ans. B. Guedel Guedel described four stages of ether anesthesia known as Guedel stages.

610.q: A 50-year-old patient is being planned for hernia repair. He is a known smoker with history of 20 pack years. His investigations are normal. How long should he be advised to stop smoking prior to surgery?
610.e: Stopping smoking is thought to be beneficial preoperatively, in order to minimize its acute adverse effects. Effects of carbon monoxide and nicotine are significantly reduced after 12-24 h abstinence; up to 6-8 weeks is thought to be necessary for restoration of ciliary and immunological activity. Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 530

610.q: A 38-year-old woman with a history of diverticulosis is scheduled for an exploratory laparotomy for lysis of adhesions. Which of the following is the best way of maintaining core body temperature during the initial hour of general endotracheal anesthetic?
o: Providing warm and humidified inspired gases
610.e: The initial reduction in core temperature during general anesthesia is caused by redistribution of heat from the core to the periphery, which can be attenuated by increasing ambient temperature to minimize the gradient Reference: lippincott's anesthesia review chapter 14.

610.q: You are planning an elective cesarean section for a patient with fetal breech. The patient falls under:
610.e: Explanation: ASA II: This classification is assigned to a patient with mild systemic disease . In this case, an uncomplicated pregnancy is considered a physiological state that alters the woman's baseline health but does not constitute a severe systemic disease. Pregnancy leads to changes such as increased cardiac output, altered respiratory mechanics, and changes in blood volume, which necessitate careful monitoring but generally does not increase the risk category beyond ASA II in the absence of other complications. Key Takeaways: ASA II reflects a healthy pregnan t patient with no significant comorbidities. Understanding the ASA classification helps assess the risk during anaesthesia and surgery. Reference : https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-practice-parameters/statement-on-asa-physical-status-classification-system

610.q: In preoperative assessment of patients, physical activity is graded in terms of metabolic equivalents (METs). The value that corresponds to oxygen consumption of 1 MET in an adult is
610.e: One metabolic equivalent is defined as the amount of oxygen consumed at rest, and is equal to 3.5 mL O2/kg/min. The energy cost of any activity can be determined by multiplying 3.5 to the oxygen consumption (mL O2/kg/min). METs can be assessed as follows: 1 MET-can take care of self (eating, dressing, toilet) 4 METs-can walk up a flight of steps or a hill 4 to 10 METs-can do heavy household work (scrubbing floors, lifting heavy furniture) >10 METs-can participate in strenuous sports (swimming, tennis, basketball, skiing) Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

610.q: A 68-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis undergoes pulmonary function evaluation before an elective abdominal surgery. Forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and FVC are within normal limits; however, the maximum voluntary ventilation (MVV) is only 40% of predicted. The next step in the pulmonary function evaluation of this patient should be to
o: Obtain a measurement of peak flow
610.e: Maximum voluntary ventilation (MVV) is a nonspecific pulmonary function test that measures the endurance of the ventilatory muscles and indirectly reflects the compliance of the lung and thorax as well as airway resistance. A decreased MVV may be caused by impairment to inspiration or expiration. In this patient, FEV1 is normal, which strongly suggests that the ventilatory impairment is during inspiration. A flow-volume loop would be a very useful confirmatory test. Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 1033-1034.

610.q: Each of the following is a predictor of difficulty with mask ventilation EXCEPT
610.e: Mask ventilation, one of the most basic anesthesia techniques, can be challenging in some patients. Use of mask ventilation in patients who are prone to airway obstruction can be more difficult because of extra airway tissue (i.e., obese patients with a BMI >26), patients without teeth (i.e., tongue is closer to the roof of the mouth, and face conformity may not fit the mask well), and patients who snore (i.e., already have reason for airway obstruction). Mask ventilation can also be more difficult in patients who have a beard (i.e., harder to get a good mask seal), patients whose age is older than 55 years, patients with facial tumors, and patients with facial trauma. Use of an oral airway may be needed in many of these patients. Reference: Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, p 227; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 1651.

610.q: One of the following is a primary risk factor for difficult mask ventilation
o: Inability to bring mandibular incisors anterior to the maxillary incisors
610.e: Mask ventilation can be made difficult by anything that prevents the face mask from forming an adequate seal with the patient's face (e.g., a beard) or increases the resistance to airflow between the mouth and larynx. Edentulousness, a history of snoring, history of neck radiation, male gender, obesity, and Mallampati status ≥3 are all factors associated with difficult mask ventilation. Options a, b, and c represent risk factors for difficult intubation. In general, factors that make it difficult to align the oral axis with the laryngeal axis result in difficult intubation. Difficult mask ventilation can be remembered by BONES Beard Obesity No teeth Elderly Snorer Reference: Airway management by Rashid Khan 6th edition.

610.q: Which of the following factors is the greatest predictor of sleep apneas in an adult?
610.e: Although many books suggest that obesity is the most common cause of OSA, more recent data suggest that a large neck circumference (>44 cm) reflects pharyngeal fat deposition and is more strongly correlated with OSA than obesity (BMI >30). Other risk factors include male gender, middle age, evening alcohol consumption, or sleep-inducing medications. Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, p 320; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 2203-2204; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, pp 435-436.

611.q: While monitoring a patient for return of neuromuscular function after using rocuronium, you notice the patient has regained four twitches using train of four stimulations. With four twitches on train of four stimulations, the patient may still have blockage of acetylcholine receptors of up to
611.e: At the point the fourth twitch reappears, still up to 75% to 80% of acetylcholine receptors may be blocked. Adequate reversal (neostigmine–glycopyrrolate) should be given, and clinical signs for return of neuromuscular function should be used to gauge readiness for extubation. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 134.

611.q: Identify the correct relationship between the cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), intracranial pressure (ICP) and central venous pressure (CVP) from the ones given below.
611.e: Cerebral perfusion pressure is the pressure gradient driving cerebral blood flow. CPP = MAP - (ICP + CVP) Where CPP is cerebral perfusion pressure, CVP is central venous pressure, MAP is the mean arterial pressure and ICP is the intracranial pressure. Reference: Physics, Pharmacology and Physiology for Anaesthetists, Matthew E. Cross, second edition, pg 313.

611.q: A 54-year-old male hypertensive patient underwent laparoscopic lower anterior resection. His blood pressure in the recovery was 190/80 mm Hg and heart rate was 91 beats per minute. He was maintaining saturation of 100% with oxygen mask of 4 liters. Given that, the reason is the pain, step of management will include the following:
611.e: Noxious stimulation from incisional pain, endotracheal intubation, full bladder, or preoperative discontinuation of anti-hypertensive medication, is usually responsible for increased blood pressure in the recovery area. Adequate analgesia preoperatively given with opioids. Mild to moderate elevations can be treated with intravenous labetalol; an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, such as enalapril; or a calcium channel blocker, such as nicardipine. The end point for treatment should be consistent with the patient’s own normal blood pressure. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology, page no 1300

611.q: Best skin disinfectant for central line insertion is:
611.e: Ans is 'd' i.e. Chlorhexidine "Chlorhexidine is now the disinfectant recommended for all catheter placement procedures and for routine site cleansing during dressing changes."- Comprehensive Hospital Medicine: An Evidence-Based And Systems Approach By Mark V. Williams, Scott A. Flanders, p320 "Use of antiseptic solution for skin disinfection at the catheter insertion site helps prevent catheter-related infection. Chlorhexidine- based solutions appear to be superior to both aqueous and alcohol- based povidone-iodine in reducing the risk for catheter colonization and catheter-related bloodstream infection. If there is a contraindication to chlorhexidine, tincture of iodine, an iodophor or 70 percent alcohol can be used as alternatives"-uptodate.com

611.q: Systemic blood pressure measurements at what minimum intervals are recommended by the ASA under anaesthesia?
611.e: During the delivery of anesthesia, the current standard of care is to measure systemic blood pressure and heart rate every 5 minutes as a minimum. The clinical scenario and phase of the operation may mandate more frequent monitoring, which is up to the judgment of the anesthesia provider. Reference: https://www.asahq.org/standards-and-guidelines/standards-for-basic-anesthetic-monitoring

611.q: Below what value of cerebral blood flow (CBF) will signs of cerebral ischemia first begin to appear on the electroencephalogram (EEG)?
611.e: The human brain is able to maintain neuronal function in the face of decreasing CBF below the normal level of 50 mL/100 g/min. Because O2 delivery is directly related to CBF, EEG evidence of cerebral ischemia will appear if CBF is diminished sufficiently. The CBF reserve, however, is substantial, and the first signs of cerebral ischemia do not appear on EEG until CBF has fallen to approximately 22 mL/100 g/min. When CBF has fallen to 15 mL/100 g/min, the EEG becomes isoelectric. Irreversible membrane damage and cellular death do not occur, however, until CBF falls to 6 mL/100 g/min. Areas of the brain in which CBF falls in the 6 to 15 mL/100 g/min range are referred to as zones of ischemic penumbra. Several hours may elapse in these areas of the brain before irreversible membrane damage occurs. Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 410

611.q: During cervical spine surgery for the resection of an intradural mass, the patient begins to cough. The concentration of isoflurane is subsequently increased. With respect to somatosensory-evoked potential (SSEP) monitoring, you would expect
o: Amplitude to decrease and latency to increase
Amplitude to increase and latency to decrease
611.e: Indications for intraoperative monitoring of evoked potentials (EPs) include surgical procedures associated with possible neurological injury: spinal fusion with instrumentation, spine and spinal cord tumor resection, brachial plexus repair, thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm repair, epilepsy surgery, and cerebral tumor resection. Volatile agents decrease the amplitude and increase the latency of evoked potentials. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 596.

611.q: During a complex mitral valve replacement, it is determined that the patient will benefit from brief protective hypothermia. Of the options listed below, core temperature is best measured via the
611.e: Numerous sites can be used to monitor temperature in the operating room. The tympanic membrane theoretically reflects brain temperature because the auditory canal ' s blood supply is the external carotid artery. Tympanic membrane temperatures reflect core body temperature. After tympanic membrane (perfused by carotid artery) and pulmonary artery measurements, the best reflector of core temperature is bladder temperature. Axillary and skin temperatures are highly prone to errors. Rectal temperature is a poor substitute and probe can induce trauma. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 132.

612.q: Which of the following is most likely to be associated with a falsely elevated Sao2 as measured by pulse oximetry (dual wave)?
612.e: Most pulse oximeters illuminate tissue with two wavelengths of light: 660-nm red light and 940-nm infrared light. Because carboxyhemoglobin has an absorbance at 660 nm, very similar to O2 hemoglobin, it produces a falsely elevated Sao2 when present in the blood. Hemoglobin F, bilirubin, and fluorescein dye have no effect on pulse oximetry. Methylene blue, as well as indigo carmine and indocyanine green, lowers the Sao2 as measured by pulse oximetry. Methemoglobin absorbs red and infrared light equally well and gives saturation readings of 85%. Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 702-703; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, p 327.

612.q: A 60-year-old patient undergoes a midline laparotomy for intestinal obstruction. All of the following respiratory effects can be seen in the post-operative period in this patient, except:
o: Increased tidal volume due to pain
612.e: Pain due to abdominal or thoracic incisions compromises pulmonary function because of guarding (splinting). Decreased movement of the chest wall reduces tidal volume and functional residual capacity, promoting atelectasis, intrapulmonary shunting, hypoxemia, and less commonly, hypoventilation. Reductions in vital capacity impair coughing and clearing of secretions. Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition pg 1062

612.q: Capnography can help detect all of the following promptly, except
612.e: It is important to remember that capnography will show a normal capnograph and end-tidal CO 2 immediately following endo-bronchial intubation. Anesthesia providers must be vigilant to always listen for bilateral breath sounds and observe bilateral chest rise to confirm tracheal intubation. Oesophagal intubation will show progressive decrease of etCO 2 with breaths. Bronchospasm will show steep upslope of the trace Sudden decrease in etCO 2 is seen in pulmonary embolism. Reference : dorsch and dorsch 5th edition pg 594.

612.q: Pulse oximetry illuminates tissue samples with two wavelengths of light in order to calculate oxygen saturation. These wavelengths are of the following nm:
612.e: Oximetry depends on the observation that oxygenated and reduced hemoglobin differ in their absorption of red and infrared light (Lambert–Beer law). Specifically, oxyhemoglobin (Hbo2) absorbs more infrared light (940nm), Whereas deoxyhemoglobin absorbs more red light (660nm) and thus appears blue, or cyanotic, to the naked eye. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 120.

612.q: A patient with methemoglobinemia will have a pulse oximetry reading that converges around a saturation of
612.e: Many different clinical situations will cause pulse oximetry to read in characteristic patterns. Methemoglobinemia absorbs both wavelengths of light and tends to converge around a saturation of 85% Carboxyhemoglobin only absorbs red light, but not infrared light, and can vary widely in saturation readings Methylene blue, a common dye used during surgery, tends to cause saturations to converge around 65%. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 121.

613.q: All are features of difficult airway except ?
613.e: Ans. D. Increased thyromental distance Decreased thyromental distance predicts difficult airway (not increased TM distance).

613.q: Airway adjust play a vital role in maintaining a patent airway. For selecting a oropharyngeal airway, measurement should be taken from
o: Angle of the mouth to angle of mandible
613.e: Explanation: Measurement for Size Selection: The appropriate size of the oropharyngeal airway (OPA) is determined by measuring the vertical distance from the patient's incisors to the angle of the mandible . This ensures that the OPA fits correctly, allowing for optimal airway patency without causing obstruction. Consequences of Incorrect Sizing: Too small: Can kink the tongue, leading to obstruction of airflow. Too large: May push the epiglottis backward, causing further obstruction or trauma to the larynx. Key Takeaways: Accurate sizing of the oropharyngeal airway is crucial for maintaining a patent airway. Proper measurements help prevent complications associated with incorrect airway adjunct sizing.

613.q: Laryngeal mask airway was discovered by
613.e: Brain demonstrated the first commercially made silicone model of LMA . First commercial devices were made available in the UK Reference : E Book of Baheti's Understanding Anesthetist Equipments and Procedures a Pratical Approach First Edition Chapter 16 Page No 197 to 204

613.q: You are using a Guedel airway for a patient to improve the upper airway patency. How will you estimate the size you will require for the same?
o: By placing the flange at the level of the incisors and the tip at the angle of the mandible
By placing the flange at the angle of mouth and tip at the angle of the mandible
By placing the flange at the level of the incisors and tip at the tragus of the ear
By placing the flange at the external nares and the tip at the tragus of the ear
613.e: A Guedel airway maintains upper airway patency by keeping the mouth open and preventing the tongue falling backwards. The airway is available in a range of sizes from neonate to adult. To determine the correct size, the airway is held up to the patient's face. The size that is most appropriate for the patient can be estimated in two ways: the 'hard-to-hard' method, where the flange is placed at the level of the incisors and the tip at the angle of the mandible, or the 'soft-to-soft' method, from the angle of the mouth to the tragus of the ear. Reference: Equipment in Anaesthesia and Critical Care, Daniel Aston, Angus Rivers, Asela Dharmadasa, pg 28

613.q: A 42 years old, 120 kg patient is posted for a laparoscopic umbilical hernia repair surgery. After insertion of a supraglottic device, it is observed that the peak airway pressure required to ventilate the patient is about 40 cmH2O. What will be the next best step in airway management of this patient?
o: Put a smaller size LMA and ventilate
Intubate with appropriate sized endotracheal tube and ventilate
Abort the procedure and wake up the patient
613.e: The mean pressure at which gastric insufflation occurs is 28cm H 2 O. When airway pressures with an LMA exceed this limit, there is a possibility of gastric insufflation because of raised pressure as the LMA doesn't form a watertight seal around the larynx and hence cannot be relied upon for protection against aspiration of gastric contents. Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch) 5th edition pg 488

613.q: Complications associated with the use of face mask ventilation are all except
o: Cervical spine movement in unstable injuries
613.e: Incidence of sore throat is minimal with face mask, as compared to supraglottic airway devices or intubation with an endotracheal tube, since there is no airway instrumentation in facemask ventilation. With face mask, when a positive pressure ventilation is provided, gases are likely to enter the stomach. So it is recommended that inspiratory pressure be kept below 20 cm H 2 O. Mask ventilation moves the cervical spine, sometimes even more than commonly used methods of tracheal intubation. This may be of significance in the patient with an unstable cervical spine injury. Face mask is associated with greater operating room pollution with anesthetic gases and vapors than with a tracheal tube or supraglottic airway device. Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch) 5th edition pg 450

613.q: A nasopharyngeal airway may be used as an airway adjunct in all of the following conditions except patients with:
613.e: The nasopharyngeal airway is a simple airway adjunct that can be used to facilitate ventilation and removal of secretions. A nasopharyngeal airway can be used in patients with an intact gag reflex, unstable fractures of the mandible, trismus (lockjaw), or oral trauma, complications include soft tissue damage of the nasal mucosa and bleeding. Reference: Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation, Fourth Edition by David W. Chang, page no 130

613.q: An esophageal-tracheal combitube (ETC) is inserted into the:
613.e: Esophageal-tracheal combitube (ETC): An airway that may be inserted into the esophagus or trachea. The ETC is inserted blindly either into the trachea or esophagus. Both lumens on the ETC can be used to provide ventilation. Lumen 1 is used when the tube enters the esophagus and lumen 2 is used when it is in the trachea. Reference: Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation, Fourth Edition by David W. Chang, page no 139

614.q: Pre oxygenation replaces the nitrogen in the functional residual volume with oxygen. This can achieved by
o: Tidal respiration for 3-5 mins with 100 percent o2
614.e: The optimal technique is uncertain; 3 min administration is thought to be as effective as 5 min administration, or even four vital capacity breaths. A tightly fitting face-mask (to prevent entrainment of room air) and adequate flow of O 2 are vital. Monitoring of end-expiratory O 2 concentration may be a useful guide during pre-oxygenation; washout of nitrogen from the lungs is indicated by an increase in expired O 2 concentration towards steady state (near 100% in ideal conditions with no gas leaks or mixing). Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 479

614.q: A patient suffering a stab wound to the abdomen arrives in the operating room for an emergency exploratory laparotomy. His BP is 70/40, and his HR is 118. Which of the following fluid regimens are appropriate for his fluid resuscitation?
o: Normal saline, at a ratio of 3 mL per estimated 1 mL of blood lost
Blood at a ratio of 3 mL blood administered to 1 mL of blood lost
Hetastarch (Hespan) in a ratio of 3 mL per estimated 1 mL of blood lost
D5W in a ratio of 3 mL of D5W to 1 mL of blood lost
614.e: Lactated Ringer's solution or Plasmalyte in approximately three times the volume of the blood lost, or colloid in a 1:1 ratio , until the transfusion trigger point is reached is used for fluid resuscitation of a patient. At that time, blood is replaced unit-for-unit as it is lost , with reconstituted packed red blood cells. Reference : Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition, pg. 1196.

614.q: A 54-year-old woman is undergoing a total thyroid ectomy under general anesthesia. The patient is awak ened in the OR, the mouth and pharynx are suctioned, and after intact laryngeal reflexes are demonstrated, the endotracheal tube is removed. Two days later, the anesthesiologist is consulted because the patient has severe stridor and upper airway obstruction. The most likely cause of airway obstruction in this patient is
o: Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve
614.e: The symptoms of hypocalcemia, which manifest as laryngospasm or laryngeal stridor, usually develop within the first 24 to 96 hours after total thyroidectomy. After the airway is established and secured, the patient should be treated with IV calcium in the form of either calcium gluconate or calcium chloride Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 352-353, 1330.

614.q: First year trainee in anaesthesia intubates a patient posted for an elective surgery. Which auscultator technique give the most reliable indication that the tracheal tube is in the trachea?
614.e: Auscultation should be performed high in each midaxillary area , not just the anterior chest region. The quality of the sounds is important. A gurgling sound (death rattle) suggests esophageal placement. This test is not always reliable. Auscultating the upper abdomen as well as the lungs may increase the reliability of auscultation. But these sounds may be confused with breath sounds that are often heard in the epigastric area in thin individuals and pediatric patients. Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch) 5th edition pg 590. 5th edition pg 601.

614.q: Pre oxygenation replaces the nitrogen in the functional residual volume with oxygen. This increases the apnea time upto
614.e: Pre-oxygenation. Administration of 100% O 2 before induction of anaesthesia. Increases the O 2 reserve in the lungs (by replacing N 2 O in the FRC) and thus the time to hypoxemia during subsequent apnea to 8-10 minutes, e.g. during tracheal intubation. Also increases arterial PO 2 , although O 2 content and saturation may not increase by much. Particularly useful when difficulties are anticipated, or in patients at risk from aspiration of gastric contents. Thus a vital part of 'rapid sequence induction'. Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 479

614.q: A junior trainee has been assigned the task to intubate a young female patient posted for a laparoscopic appendectomy. Which is the single best method among the following to rule out esophageal intubation in this patient?
o: Seeing the tube pass through the vocal cords
Observing chest wall movement during inspiration and exhalation.
Hearing breath sounds during controlled ventilation
614.e: The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring and the American Association of Nurse Anesthetists (AANA) require that when a tracheal tube is inserted, its correct positioning must be verified by identification of CO 2 in the expired gas. Observation of passage of tube through the vocal cords, chest wall movement or chest auscultation are subjective methods and are inferior to capnography. Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch) 5th edition pg 592

614.q: A 4-year-old child weighing 16 kg is scheduled for inguinal hernia repair. She is at the 55th percentile for height for her age. An appropriately sized uncuffed endotracheal tube for this patient will have an internal diameter of
614.e: Appropriate uncuffed endotracheal tube size may be determined by the following formula (age in years): (Age/3) + 3.5 Ie., (4/3)+3.5 = 4.8 Ie, 5, as per the given options (Subtract 0.5 for appropriate sized cuffed ETT.) Reference: Airway management (Rashid Khan) 7th edition, pg 52

614.q: A 25 year old female has presented with achalasia cardia and planned for Heller myotomy. During the induction of anesthesia, the patient aspirates. The immediate management includes all, except
614.e: Patients with esophageal disease have the risk of pulmonary aspiration. In such patients, a rapid-sequence induction should be used. Aspiration leads to Mendelson's syndrome. Steroid and prophylactic antibiotic administration is not indicated as part of management. Reference : Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesia, 6th edition, page no. 579

o: Increase tidal volume (Vt) and decrease respiratory rate
Increase Vt and increase respiratory rate
Decrease Vt and decrease respiratory rate
Decrease Vt and increase respiratory rate
615.e: At concentrations of 1 MAC or less, volatile anesthetics, as well as the inhaled anesthetic N 2 O, will produce dose-dependent increases in the respiratory rate in spontaneously breathing patients. This trend continues at concentrations greater than 1 MAC for all of the inhaled anesthetics except isoflurane. With the exception of N 2 O, the evidence suggests that this effect is caused by direct activation of the respiratory center in the CNS rather than by stimulation of pulmonary stretch receptors. Additionally, volatile anesthetics decrease Vt and significantly alter the breathing pattern from the normal awake pattern of intermittent deep breaths separated by varying time intervals to one of rapid, shallow, regular, and rhythmic breathing. Reference: Miller’s Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 691-692.

615.q: Anaesthetic breathing systems can be open or closed. To be a closed circuit, which of the following is a pre requisite
615.e: The components of a circle system include: a CO 2 absorber containing CO 2 absorbent; a fresh gas inlet; an inspiratory unidirectional valve and inspiratory breathing tube; a Y-connector; an expiratory unidirectional valve and expiratory breathing tube; an APL valve; and a reservoir. Reference: Morgan, edition 4, page no 40

615.q: Compared to the Mapleson A system, the circle system
o: Has a decreased risk of disconnection
Has decreased resistance to patient breathing
615.e: Advantages of the circle system include economy (low fresh gas flow rates, decreased use of volatile agents), conservation of heat and humidity, and decreased operating-room pollution. Disadvantages of circle system include greater size, decreased portability, increased risk of disconnection, and increased resistance to patient breathing. Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

615.q: What is the typical pressure setting for the valve in a Mapleson circuit?
615.e: Explanation: The adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) valve in a Mapleson breathing circuit is typically set at 30-40 cm H 2 O to allow appropriate control of airway pressure during manual ventilation. The Mapleson circuit is a semi-open anesthetic breathing system used in controlled and spontaneous ventilation. It consists of: Fresh gas flow inlet Corrugated tubing Reservoir bag Adjustable Pressure-Limiting (APL) valve The APL valve is crucial for: Controlling the maximum pressure delivered during manual ventilation Preventing barotrauma by allowing excess gas to escape once a set pressure is reached The typical pressure setting for the APL valve is 30-40 cm H₂O, which ensures: Adequate positive pressure during assisted breaths Protection against excessive airway pressure

615.q: Since fresh gas flow equal to minute ventilation is sufficient to prevent rebreathing, which of the following Mapleson circuit breathing/ventilation systems is the most efficient for spontaneous ventilation of the patient?
615.e: During spontaneous ventilation/breathing of the patient, the Mapleson circuit providing for the most efficacy ranges from A > D > C > B (in the order of decreasing efficiency). Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

615.q: Which of the following statements regarding the Mapleson D breathing circuit is FALSE?
o: It has a proximal fresh gas inflow and a distal overflow valve
With an inspiratory-to-expiratory (I:E) breathing ratio of 1:2, rebreathing is eliminated with sponta neous ventilation when the fresh gas flow is three times the minute ventilation
To eliminate rebreathing, higher fresh gas flows are needed with spontaneous ventilation than with controlled ventilation
The Mapleson D circuit is the most widely used of the Mapleson circuits for pediatric anesthesia
615.e: All of the statements are correct except for C. The Mapleson D system is a semiopen anesthetic system with a proximal fresh gas inflow and a distal overflow valve. To eliminate rebreathing, higher fresh gas flows are needed with spontaneous ventilation than with controlled ventilation. Note the Mapleson A system is a semiopen anesthetic system with a distal fresh gas flow and a proximal overflow valve. The Mapleson F circuit is most widely used for pediatric anesthesia. Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 294-297.

615.q: A 4-year-old child weighing 20 kg has a minute volume of 3 L/min. If using the Jackson Rees circuit for spontaneous ventilation, how much fresh gas flow should be used for such a patient to prevent rebreathe growth?
615.e: While using Jackson Rees circuit, Fresh gas flows of 2-3 times minute volume should be used to prevent rebreathing during spontaneous ventilation, (But plz note, whatever be the baby's weight, a minimum flow of 3 L/min should be kept) During controlled ventilation in children, normocapnia can be maintained with a fresh gas flow of 1L + 100 mL/kg/min E.g. a 4-year-old weighing 20 kg would need a total FGF of around 3 L/min. Reference: Objective anesthesia review (Atul Kulkarni) 3rd Ed Pg. 403

615.q: Mapleson A design is the most efficient Mapleson circuit for spontaneous ventilation because:
o: Fresh gas flow equal to minute ventilation
Fresh gas flow equal to tidal volume
Fresh gas flow less than minute ventilation
Fresh gas flow less than tidal volume
615.e: In Mapleson A, just a minimum Fresh gas flow (FGF) is enough to prevent normocapnia in the circuit, making it the most efficient circuit for spontaneous respiration Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anaesthesiology 6th Edition Chapter 3 Page No 80

616.q: When compared to a cylinder manifold, a vacuum-insulated evaporator (VIE) is the most economical way to store and supply oxygen in a large hospital. What is the single most important reason for this?
o: The critical temperature of liquid oxygen is ideal to store as a liquid
Liquid oxygen is easier to store.
VIE does not require rigorous maintenance.
When evaporated, liquid oxygen occupies a large volume as gas.
616.e: Liquid oxygen is stored in a vacuum-insulated evaporator (VIE) at a temperature of -150°C to -170°C and at a pressure of 5-10 atmospheres. In simple terms this works like a giant thermos flask. At 15°C, one volume of liquid oxygen occupies 842 times its volume as gas. Oxygen constantly evaporates from the top of the VIE.
