As this oxygen is very cold, it needs to be passed through a super heater. When the oxygen flows at a faster rate, the temperature of the liquid falls due to the latent heat of evaporation. To overcome this problem additional heat is provided by a pressure-raising vaporiser. Regular maintenance, monitoring of usage of oxygen and topping up the tank at regular intervals is necessary. Reference: Al-Shaikh B, Stacey S, Eds. Liquid oxygen. In: Essentials of anaesthetic equipment, 3rd ed. London, UK: Churchill Livingstone, Elsevier, 2007; Chapter 1: 9-10.

616.q: True statement about Volatility and vaporization?
o: The more volatile a liquid, the faster it vaporizes
Volatility and vaporization are not related
The more volatile a liquid, the slower it vaporizes
616.e: The more volatile a liquid, the faster it vaporizes and the greater the loss of latent heat of vaporization Liquid cools à rate of vaporization falls Reference : Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 44 Page No .423

The ideal vaporizer should be Lightweight, robust and durable Easy to transport Corrosion and solvent resistant Leak proof Economical and safe to use Require minimal servicing Accurate over a wide range of: Freah Gas Flow Liquid agent levels Ambient pressures Ambient temperatures Unaffected by: Heat loss due to vaporization Pressure changes downstream of the vaporizer Tilting or tipping Compatible with vaporizer interlock systems Reference :Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 44 Page No .423 to 428

616.q: Which test is performed on gas cylinders to check the quality of manufacturing?
616.e: The cylinders used in medical practice are either solid drawn or made from seamless steel tube, and never welded at the ends. After manufacturing, the cylinders are kept in a furnace at a temperature of 860-890 degree C and then carefully removed and cooled at atmospheric pressure . As the cylinders must withstand a high gas pressure and rough handling during transport, they are subjected to mechanical testing before marketing for use. The tensile test, flattening test, impact test and bend test are performed on one cylinder from a batch of every 100 finished cylinders. Reference: Anaesthesia Review: A Comprehensive Textbook by Atul, 5th Edition, Page Number 396-409.

Explanation: Pressure Conversions: 1 kPa = 10 cm H2O is a valid approximation, which is useful in clinical settings for measuring pressures in respiratory physiology and anaesthesia. To understand this, atmospheric pressure is often measured in various units, including mmHg, mbar, and psi. Atmospheric Pressure Reference: Atmospheric pressure is defined as the pressure exerted by the weight of air in the atmosphere, commonly measured using a barometer. 760 mmHg (Torr) is equivalent to 1 bar = 1000 mbar = 101.3 kPa . Conversions for Context: 1 kPa ≈ 7.5 mmHg (Option C) 1 bar = 14.5 psi , thus 1 kPa ≈ 0.145 psi (Option B) 1 kPa is equivalent to 10 mbar , not 100 mbar (Option D) Key Takeaways: 1 kPa is approximately 10 cm H2O, a key conversion for understanding pressures in clinical practice. Familiarity with pressure units is essential in anaesthesia and critical care settings.

616.q: Which of the following is NOT found in the low pressure circuit on an anesthesia machine?
616.e: The anesthesia machine, now more properly called the anesthesia workstation, has two main pressure circuits. The higher-pressure circuits consist of the gas supply from the pipelines and tanks, all piping, pressure gauges, pressure reduction regulators, check valves (which prevent backward gas flow), the oxygen pressure sensor shutoff valve (also called the oxygen failure cutoff or fail-safe valve), the oxygen supply failure alarm, and the oxygen flush valve-or, simplistically, everything up to the gas flow control valves and the machine common gas outlet. The low-pressure circuit starts with and includes the gas flow control valves, flowmeters, vaporizers, and vaporizer check valve and goes to the machine common gas outlet. See also figure for explanation to Question 12 Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 641-650; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, pp 198-204.

616.q: Which of the following prevents delivery of hypoxic gas mixture once the oxygen pressure falls below 25 psi?
616.e: The fail-safe valve automatically closes nitrous oxide (and other gases) to prevent delivery of hypoxic gas mixture to the patient. The fail-safe valve is designed to be activated when oxygen pressure falls below 25 psi. Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

616.q: The oxygen-flush valve provides which of the following oxygen flows (L/min) to the common gas outlet?
616.e: The oxygen-flush valve provides gas flow at pipeline pressures of about 45 to 55 psi at 35 to 75 L/min. The high flow of oxygen is provided directly to the common gas outlet, bypassing the flowmeters and vaporizers. One should be careful when using the oxygen-flush valve, as high gas flows at high pressures can cause lung barotrauma in the patient. Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

617.q: Which of the following are components of High-Quality CPR? 1: Chest compression at a rate of 100-120/min 2: Breathing at a rate of 20-25/min 3: Depth of compression should be 5-6 cm 4: Allow Chest Recoil
617.e: High-Quality CPR in adults includes: Effective compressions at least 100/min, no more than 120/min Minimal interruptions ( Allow for chest recoil, monitoring via capnography *less than 10 is ineffective Compression depth should be at least 5-6 cm Rotate q2mins/5cycles Chest Compression Fraction (CCF) at least 60%, goal of greater than 80%

617.q: Arrange Steps of CPR: A) Check pulse B) Check respiration C) Assess responsiveness D) Start chest compressions E) Start bag and mask
617.e: Assess responsiveness Check pulse Check respiration Start chest compressions Start bag and mask

618.q: Which of the following are methods of invasive ventilation
618.e: Invasive ventilation uses gadgets which pass beyond vocal cords and achieve a definitive airway. In mechanical ventilation, artificial airways provide a vital link between the ventilator and the patient. Two common artificial airways used in conjunction with mechanical ventilators are the endotracheal (ET) and tracheostomy tubes. Reference: Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation, Fourth Edition by David W. Chang, page no 151

618.q: Incorrect statement regarding the mechanisms of an Ambu bag is
o: It contains a nonrebreathing valve, same as the circle system
It is capable of delivery of nearly a 100% O2 concentration
Patient valve has low resistance to both inspiration and expiration
618.e: While resuscitation devices such as Ambu bags or bag-mask units have nonrebreathing valves, neither the Mapleson (only has adjustable pressure-limiting valve) nor the circle system (only has unidirectional valves and does allow rebreathing) has this component. Ambu resuscitation bags do allow for positive pressure ventilation as the intake valve closes during bag compression. The patient valve has low resistance, but can become obstructed by exhaled moisture. Ambu bags have a reservoir system to prevent room air entrapment and are able to deliver nearly 100% oxygen. Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

618.q: A 65-year-old patient with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and coronary artery disease (CAD) undergoes a laparoscopic nephrectomy uneventfully under general desflurane anesthesia. In the recovery room, ABGs are as follows: Pao2 60 mm Hg, Paco2 50 mm Hg, pH 7.35, and hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL. Which of the following steps would produce the greatest increase in O2 delivery to the myocardium?
o: Administration of 100% O2 with a close-fitting mask
Administration of 35% O2 with a Venturi mask
Transfuse with 2 units of packed red blood cells (RBCs)
618.e: One gram of hemoglobin can combine with 1.34 mL of O2. None of the other choices in this question will do as much to increase the O2-carrying capacity of this patient's blood as a transfusion Reference: Stoelting: Pharmacology and Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, ed 4, pg 787, 849.

618.q: All are true except High air flow oxygen enriched (HAFOE) devices
618.e: They are fixed performers HAFOE stands for 'high air flow oxygen enriched' devices. The Bernoulli principle is used with a venturi device to cause entrainment of air around an oxygen jet venturi. These devices are constant in performance and require masks with holes to enable high volumes of air to be entrained. Reference: Yentis S, Hirsch N, Smith G. Anaesthesia A to Z. Butterworth-Heinemann, 1995.

618.q: A patient on the high dependency unit has pneumonia and is hypoxic on room air. When deciding which method of oxygen administration is appropriate which of the following statements is FALSE?
o: Maximum inspiratory flow may exceed 30L/min during spontaneous breathing.
Nasal cannulae significantly improve oxygenation even if the patient breathes through the mouth.
A Venturi mask uses the Bernoulli principle.
A Hudson mask is a fixed performance device.
618.e: During spontaneous breathing the maximum inspiratory flow rate can exceed 30L/min for brief periods. A standard Hudson-type mask will therefore not supply a constant fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) unless the flow rate of oxygen through the connecting tubing exceeds 30L/min, since air will be entrained at a variable ratio throughout the respiratory cycle. Masks such as the Venturi and Hudson are loose fitting and have holes permitting ready elimination of waste gases; they do not significantly increase dead space. Anaesthetic face masks have a tight seal with the patient's face and may be bulky, increasing dead space, although this is not usually clinically significant in adult practice. Reference: Masks. In: Essentials of Anaesthetic Equipment, 2nd Ed. Al-Shaikh B, Stacey S. London: Churchill-Livingstone, 2002: 73-9.

618.q: Which of the following is the effect of Positive end -expiratory pressure (PEEP)
o: No change in functional residual capacity (FRC)
618.e: PEEP increases FRC and decreases the work of breathing. Compliance is increased, and the lung volume is increased. Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) increases the end-expiratory or baseline airway pressure to a value greater than atmospheric pressure. It is often used to improve the patient’s oxygenation status, especially in hypoxemia that is refractory to high level of FiO 2 . Reference: Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation, Fourth Edition by David W. Chang, page no 87

618.q: Clinical conditions that may require independent lung ventilation include all of the following except:
618.e: Double-lumen Endobronchial tube: A special airway for independent lung ventilation. It has two separate lumens, two cuffs, and two pilot balloons. Independent lung ventilation is done via a DLT to facilitate lung isolation, surgical procedure, and Broncho pleural/Broncho cutaneous fistulas. They are used to provide independent lung ventilation where isolation of the lungs is desirable in order to prevent lung-to-lung spillage of blood or pus. They are also used to provide one-lung ventilation so that the non-ventilated lung may undergo surgical procedure on the thoracic structures with minimal movement. Reference: Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation, Fourth Edition by David W. Chang, page no 141

618.q: About the Mechanical ventilation; Assertion: Mechanical ventilation works on principle opposite to that of physiological ventilation Reason: mechanical ventilation is a positive pressure ventilation
o: Both assertion and reason are correct
Both assertion and reason are wrong
Assertion is correct but reason is wrong
Assertion is wrong but reason is correct
618.e: The normal physiological respiration is a process of generation of negative pressures inside the thoracic cavity during inspiration and expiration is passive .In contrast mechanical ventilation involves positive pressure to inflate the lungs during inspiration. There are opposite mechanisms. During positive pressure ventilation, gas flow is delivered to the lungs under a positive pressure gradient (i.e., airway pressure is greater than alveolar pressure). When positive pressure is used for ventilation, the pressures in the airways, alveoli, and pleura are increased during inspiration. Under normal conditions, the pressure gradient and tidal volume are directly related. Reference: Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation, Fourth Edition by David W. Chang, page no 28

619.q: Reason for preferring Cis-Atracurium over atracurium is:
619.e: Cisatracurium This R-Cis, R-Cis enantiomer of atracurium is nearly 4 times more potent , slower in onset (Option A ruled out), but similar in duration of action .(Option C ruled out) Like atracurium it undergoes Hofmann elimination (Option D ruled out), but in contrast to the racemate, it is not hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase and hepatic metabolism is limited, so that less of the toxic metabolite is formed. Most importantly, it does not provoke histamine release and side effects are fewer. Currently, cisatracurium is one of the preferred muscle relaxants, especially for liver/kidney disease patients and for the elderly.

619.q: The atropine is added to neostigmine to?
o: Facilitate earlier recovery from neuromuscular blockade
619.e: Atropine, a tertiary amine, is an anticholinergic drug which is used along with anticholinesterases like neostigmine to minimize the muscarinic adverse effects of anticholinesterases ( Option C is CORRECT ) It has no effect on the reversal of neuromuscular blockade produced by the nicotinic effect of anticholinesterases (Option A, B & D) It counteracts the cardiovascular effects of anticholinesterases like bradycardia and other bradyarrhythmia Glycopyrrolate , a quaternary amine, is another anticholinergic which can be used with the anticholinesterases It has slower onset than atropine but does not cause central effects as it does not cross blood brain barrier unlike atropine Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

619.q: Dose of succinyl choline in infant?
619.e: Neonates, infants, and young children have relatively greater alveolar ventilation and reduced FRC compared with older children and adults This greater minute ventilation-to-FRC ratio with relatively greater blood flow to vessel-rich organs contributes to a rapid increase in alveolar anaesthetic concentration and speeds inhalation induction Furthermore, the blood/gas coefficients of volatile anaesthetics are reduced in neonates compared with adults, resulting in even faster induction times and potentially increasing the risk of accidental overdosage Reference: E Book Morgan and Mikhail’s 6th Edition Chapter 42 Page No 1532.

619.q: Not true about priming dose of neuromuscular blockers is?
o: Can produce significant muscle paralysis in healthy patient also
Used to shorten the onset of action
619.e: The introduction of short- and intermediate- acting agents has resulted in the greater use of priming doses Theoretically, giving 10% to 15% of the usual intubating dose (Option A) 5 min before induction will occupy enough receptors so that paralysis will quickly follow when the balance of relaxant is administered A priming dose does not usually lead to clinically significant paralysis, which requires that 75% to 80% of the receptors be blocked (a neuromuscular margin of safety) Priming can additionally cause measurable deterioration in respiratory function (e.g., decreased forced vital capacity) and may lead to oxygen desaturation in patients with marginal pulmonary reserve These negative side effects are more common in older, sicker patients Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

619.q: Which of the following is safe to use in patients with reactive airway disease?
619.e: The benzylisoquinolinium class of drugs comprises atracurium, 51W89, doxacurium, rocuronium, tubocurarine and vecuronium and mivacurium The administration of benzylisoquinolinium neuromuscular blocking drugs ( except for cisatracurium ) is associated with → histamine release, which may result in →increased airway resistance and bronchospasm in patients with hyperactive airway disease Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

619.q: A 40-year-old male had presented to the emergency department following road traffic accident. He had sustained major injuries and required airway to be relatively secured and protected. He was managed primarily. He comes back after 2 months for contracture release. Which of the following drugs is to be avoided?
619.e: In patients with significant burns (>20% TBSA), injury and disruption of neuromuscular end plates occurs, followed by up regulation of acetylcholine receptors. Beyond 15-48 h after significant burn injury, succinylcholine can produce lethal hyperkalemia. This risk for succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia persists for up to 2 years following burn injury. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 837.

Succinylcholine has been associated with severe hyperkalaemia in patients with Burn Severe abdominal infections Severe metabolic acidosis Closed head injury Conditions associated with upregulation of extra junctional acetylcholine receptors (e.g., hemiplegia or paraplegia, muscular dystrophies, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and burn) Because of the risk of massive rhabdomyolysis , hyperkalaemia, and death in children with undiagnosed muscle disease, succinylcholine is not recommended for use in children except for emergency tracheal intubation Patients with renal failure are no more susceptible to an exaggerated hyperkalaemia response to succinylcholine than are patients with normal renal function ( Option A ) Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

619.q: A 40-year-old male has presented to the emergency department following road traffic accident. He has sustained major injuries and requires airway to be relatively secured and protected. Any of the given muscle relaxant can be used in rapid sequence induction and intubation except
619.e: All the other given agents can provide for ideal intubation condition following induction rapidly. Atracurium besylate. Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking drug, first used in 1980. A bis-quaternary nitrogenous plant derivative. Initial dose: 0.3–0.6 mg/kg. Intubation is possible approximately 90 s after a dose of 0.5 mg/kg. Effects last 20–30 min. Supplementary dose: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg. May cause histamine release, usually mild, but severe reactions have been reported at body temperature and pH, undergoes spontaneous Hofmann elimination to laudanosine. Up to 50% ester hydrolysis also occurs. Often considered the drug of choice in renal or hepatic impairment. Its cardio stability, low risk of accumulation and spontaneous reversal are also advantages. Stored at 2–8°C; at room temperature. Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 56

620.q: A patient was admitted for surgery and halothane is being planned to be used as an anaesthetic agent. The patient was explained about the adverse effect of malignant hyperthermia with this drug. Which of the following drugs may also result in malignant hyperthermia?
620.e: Malignant hyperthermia produced by halothane and isoflurane in rare (genetically predisposed) individuals is more common in patients receiving SCh as well.

620.q: Which of the following inhalational anaesthetic agents is with highest respiratory irritation?
620.e: Desflurane It has minimum blood gas partition coefficient and therefore is the fastest inducing agent. It has very high vapour pressure . Its boiling point is 23°C; therefore it boils at room temperature. It requires special vaporizers due to this property. It produces cardiovascular effects similar to isoflurane except coronary steal phenomenon. Induction with desflurane is unpleasant. It causes maximum irritation to airways . As it can lead to coughing, breath holding and laryngospasm. It can also be used in day care surgery.

620.q: Ratio of 02: N20 in Entonox is ?
620.e: Ans. A. 50 : 50 Entonox contain equal amount (50/50) of N2O and O2.

620.q: Which is the critical temperature of N20 ?
620.e: Ans. D. -36.5°C Critical temperature of N2O - 36.5 Critical pressure of N2O - 214.7 atm

620.q: An air bubble is injected into the posterior chamber at the conclusion of retinal surgery (pneumatic retinopexy) to facilitate anatomically correct healing. The most appropriate anesthetic management, before the air bubble is injected, is
620.e: In the presence of N 2 O, air bubbles and air filed spaces will increase in size as N 2 O is 35 times more soluble compared to molecular nitrogen (the major component of air), allowing it to diffuse into an air bubble more rapidly than nitrogen is absorbed out of the bubble. If the bubble expands after the incision is closed, intraocular pressure will rise. This complication can be avoided by discontinuing N 2 O prior to the bubble injection. Option a, c and e: increasing the depth of anesthesia, hyperventilation and muscle relaxation have no role in this scenario. They do help in reduction in intraocular pressures in some scenarios. Reference: Drugs in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition pg 277.

620.q: Inhalational agent suitable for neurosurgery is?
620.e: Among the given options, isoflurane is best suited for neurosurgery All the inhalational anaesthetics are cerebral vasodilators The order of vasodilating potency is halothane →enflurane → desflurane → isoflurane → sevoflurane Though isoflurane increases cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure these effects are less pronounced than with halothane, nitrous oxide, and ether Though inhalational anaesthetics are used in neuro anaesthesia, if the intracranial pressure is persistently raised →they should be replaced with intravenous agents Earlier, it had been believed that isoflurane is cerebro-protective in the presence of ischemia, but now no such evidence of cerebral protection has been documented and there is no difference among the inhaled anaesthetics in this respect Reference : Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

620.q: A drug with lowest MAC would have the following characteristic?
620.e: Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of an inhaled anaesthetic is the lowest concentration which is required to prevent movement in response to a defined noxious stimulus in 50% of subjects It is a measure of potency of the inhalational anaesthetics So, lower the MAC value, lower is the concentration of anaesthetic drug required which would imply the drug is more potent. Example: Nitrous oxide with a MAC value of 104 is the →least potent inhaled anaesthetic Methoxy flurane - MAC- 0.2 →most potent Other drugs: Desflurane: 6.0 Sevoflurane- 2.05 Isoflurane- 1.28 Halothane - 0.75 (since methoxyflurane is no longer in use, among the commonly used inhalational agents, halothane is the most potent ) Reference : Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition; Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 3th edition

620.q: Meyer Overton rule relates to potency of an anaesthetic by explaining the mechanism of action via?
620.e: Meyer Overton Rule states that the potency of inhalation agents correlates directly with their lipid solubility - the fat/ water partition coefficient Anaesthesia results from dissolving of the drug molecules at specific lipophilic sites but not all lipid soluble molecules are anaesthetics Exception to Meyer Overton Rule: Non- immobilizers (Non- Anaesthetics) Nonimmobilizers are compounds whose properties are like that of inhaled anaesthetics but do not induce immobility at their expected concentrations Reference : Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 3th edition

621.q: Which can replace N20 as 02 carrier?
621.e: Ans. C. Helium Helium can be used to replace nitrogen, as the carrier gas for oxygen (Helium) to reduce the work of breathing.

621.q: Which of the following is a contraindication for the use of Inhalational agents
621.e: Malignant hyperthermia is a contraindication for the use of Inhalational agents and succinylcholine Pseudocholinesterase deficiency can cause prolongation of action of Succinylcholine leading to delayed recovery from the muscle relaxant and scoline apnea Reference: FRCA in a box, page no 188

Enflurane is the most epileptogenic inhalational anaesthetic especially in the presence of cerebral injury and hypocapnia So enflurane is contraindicated in patients with a Known history of seizures Cerebrovascular disease In head injuries as seizure activity can increase the cerebral metabolism manifold Besides enflurane increases cerebrospinal fluid secretion and decreases its absorption which is deleterious in those with poor intracranial compliance Seizures have been associated with the use of sevoflurane in high concentrations, especially in the paediatric population. Epileptogenic Potential : Enflurane >>> Sevoflurane Reference : Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

621.q: Which of the following is the correct sequence of potency of anesthetic agents?
621.e: Potency is inversely proportional to MAC i.e. agents with high MAC will have low MAC. N 2 O has the highest MAC, hence it is least potent. Methoxyflurane has the lowest MAC, hence it is the most potent. The potency of inhalational anesthetic agents is measured inversely by their Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) . Potency is inversely proportional to MAC (lower MAC = higher potency). Methoxyflurane has the lowest MAC among these agents, making it the most potent. Nitrous Oxide (N 2 O) has the highest MAC , making it the least potent. Sequence Explanation: Methoxyflurane: Most potent (lowest MAC). Halothane: Next most potent after Methoxyflurane. Isoflurane: Less potent than Halothane. N 2 O: Least potent (highest MAC). Key Takeaway: The potency of anesthetic agents follows the sequence Methoxyflurane > Halothane > Isoflurane > N 2 O , as determined by their MAC values.

621.q: Best uterine relaxation is seen with?
621.e: All fluorinated inhalational agents (including halothane ) can cause uterine relaxation Traditionally, Halothane is a as to possess maximum uterine relaxant property Reference : Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

621.q: The phenomenon by which the speed of onset of inhalational anaesthetic agents is increased when they are administered with N2O as a carrier gas is known as
621.e: The phenomenon by which the rise in the alveolar partial pressure of nitrous oxide is disproportionately rapid when it is administered in high concentrations is known as concentration effect. The phenomenon by which the speed of onset of inhalational anaesthetic agents is increased when they are administered along with N 2 O as a carrier gas. The combined action of two drugs is greater than would be expected from a purely additive, and thus called the second gas effect . Reference: Physics, Pharmacology and Physiology for Anesthetists, Matthew E. Cross, second edition, pg 149-150.

621.q: The Inhalational agents are influenced by a number of patient and environmental factors. The factors that increase the Minimum Alveolar Concentration or decreasing the potency of the agent are
621.e: MAC is reduced by: other depressant drugs (e.g., opioids, sedatives, other inhalational agents). CNS depletion of catecholamines, e.g., by α-methyldopa, reserpine. hypoxaemia/hypotension. pregnancy, possibly due to increased progesterone extremes of age. MAC is increased in: children. hyperthermia. hyperthyroidism. chronic alcoholism. chronic alcoholism. It is unaffected by duration of anesthesia, sex, acidemia/ alkalemia, hypercapnia or hypocapnia. Reference: FRCA A to Z, edition 5, page no 381

621.q: A cirrhotic patient is posted for surgery. Which would be the inhalational anaesthetic agent of choice?
621.e: Isoflurane is the agent of choice in cirrhosis The cirrhotic liver has compromised portal venous blood flow and hence it is essential to preserve hepatic arterial blood flow Though isoflurane may reduce hepatic blood flow, hepatic oxygen supply is better maintained Another alternative to isoflurane is Sevoflurane which decreases portal vein blood flow, but increases hepatic artery blood flow , so that the total hepatic blood flow and oxygen delivery are better maintained Reference : Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

622.q: What is the correct dose of thiopental?
622.e: The principal clinical uses of thiopental (3–5 mg/kg IV) or methohexital (1–5 mg/kg IV) is for induction of anaesthesia (unconsciousness), which usually occurs in less than 30 seconds. Patients may experience a garlic or onion taste after administration. Barbiturates such as methohexital (20–30 mg/kg) may be administered per rectum to facilitate induction of anaesthesia in mentally challenged and uncooperative paediatric patients. When a barbiturate is administered with the goal of neuroprotection, an isoelectric EEG indicating maximal reduction of CMR O 2 has traditionally been used as the end point. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 25- General Anaesthetics by Dr. Helge Eilers,MD & Dr. Spencer Yost,MD. Page no. 442

622.q: Benzodiazepines are usually used as premedication before general anaesthesia. Which are the desired effect of benzodiazepines useful in premedication?
622.e: Benzodiazepines commonly used in the perioperative period include midazolam, lorazepam, and less frequently, diazepam. Benzodiazepines are unique among the group of intravenous anaesthetics in that their action can readily be terminated by administration of their selective antagonist, flumazenil. Their most desired effects are anxiolysis and anterograde amnesia, which are extremely useful for premedication. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 25- General Anaesthetics by Dr. Helge Eilers,MD & Dr. Spencer Yost,MD. Page no. 442

622.q: During the course of a complicated cardiac case, the surgeon informs you that he is worried about damage to the right coronary artery in a patient with a right-dominant coronary system. During reperfusion, you are looking for signs of ischemia, and are most interested in leads
622.e: Ischemic changes in leads II, III and aVF suggest right coronary artery disease, leads I and aVL monitor the circumflex artery distribution and leads V3 to V5 look at the distribution of the left anterior descending artery . Reference: objective anaesthesia review 4th edition pg 18

622.q: The pain of labour arises from?
622.e: The pain of labour arises from Contraction of the myometrium against the resistance of the cervix and perineum , Progressive dilation of the cervix and lower uterine segment Stretching and compression of pelvic and perineal structures Pain during the first stage of labour is → primarily visceral pain resulting from uterine contractions and cervical dilation It is usually initially confined to the T11-T12 dermatomes during the → latent phase , but eventually involves the T10-L1 dermatomes as labour enters → the active phase . Reference: Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 12 Page No.110

622.q: Changes in the cardiovascular system that accompany aging include?
622.e: Cardiovascular diseases are more prevalent in the geriatric than general population Still, it is important to distinguish between changes in physiology that normally accompany aging and the pathophysiology of diseases common in the geriatric population Changes in the cardiovascular system that accompany aging include Decreased vascular compliance Decreased myocardial compliance Decreased autonomic responsiveness Myocardial fibrosis Myocardial calcification of the valves Reference: Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 24 Page No 214.

622.q: Elderly are more prone to hypothermia Intraoperatively because?
o: Hypothalamic temperature-regulating centres may reset at a lower level
622.e: Basal and maximal oxygen consumption declines with age After reaching peak weight at about age 60 years , most men and women begin losing weight ; the average elderly man and woman weigh less than their younger counterparts Heat production decreases , heat loss increases, and hypothalamic temperature-regulating centres may reset at a lower level. Reference: Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 24 Page No.217.

622.q: Measures to prevent perioperative hypoxia in elderly patients?
o: Decreased inspired oxygen concentrations during anaesthesia
622.e: Measures to prevent perioperative hypoxia in elderly patients include a Longer Preoxygenation period prior to induction Increased inspired oxygen concentrations during anaesthesia Positive end-expiratory pressure Pulmonary toilet Reference: Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 24 Page No 222.

622.q: Exaggerated drops in blood pressure during induction of general anesthesia in elderly is due to?
622.e: The elderly patient with diastolic dysfunction may poorly tolerate perioperative fluid administration, resulting in Elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure Pulmonary congestion. Diminished cardiac reserve in many elderly patients may be manifested as exaggerated drops in blood pressure during induction of general anesthesia Reference: Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 24 Page No. 214, 215 , 216.

623.q: Which of the following anaesthetic agent is not painful on intravenous administration
623.e: Ketamine is a strong analgesic drug and is water soluble. Its injection is not painful. Propofol and etomidate solutions have to be made in oil due to poor water solubility, so these injections are quite painful.(Option B,C) Methohexitone can cause hyperalgesia.(Option D)

623.q: Which of the following intravenous general anaesthetic agent has cardiovascular stability?
623.e: A characteristic and desired feature of induction of anaesthesia with Etomidate is cardiovascular stability after bolus injection. In this regard, decrease in systemic blood pressure is modest or absent and principally reflects a decrease in systemic vascular resistance. Therefore, the systemic blood pressure-lowering effects of Etomidate are probably exaggerated in the presence of hypovolemia, and optimization of the patient’s intravascular fluid volume status before induction of anesthesia should be achieved. Reference : LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 25- General Anaesthetics by Dr. Helge Eilers,MD & Dr. Spencer Yost,MD. Page no. 443

Dexmedetomidine markedly increases the range of temperatures not triggering thermoregulatory defences, Thus proving to be an effective treatment for nonthermally induced shivering Severe bradycardia may follow the administration of dexmedetomidine and cardiac arrest has been reported in a patient receiving a dexmedetomidine infusion as a supplement to general anaesthesia Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anaesthesiology 6th Edition Chapter 17 Page No 496 to 499

623.q: Clinical effects of Dexmedetomidine are all except?
623.e: Dexmedetomidine is a new generation highly selective α2-adrenergic receptor (α2-AR) agonist The Alpha 2-adrenergic receptor agonists effects - Sedative ( Option C ) Anxiolytic Hypnotic (Option B) Analgesic (Option D) Perioperative sympatholytic effects ( Option A is False) Cardiovascular stabiliser Reduced delirium and agitation Preservation of respiratory functions Reference : E Book of Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anaesthesiology 6th Edition Chapter 17 Page No 496 to 499

623.q: The drug for OPD analgesia is -
623.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Alfentanil Drugs useful for day care surgery o Propofol o Sevoflurane, desflurane & isoflurane o Midazolam o Mivacurium o Alfantanil

623.q: Intravenous induction agent with abuse liability is?
623.e: Propofol is an intravenous induction agent that can be addictive because of its hypnotic property and development of tolerance on prolonged use The abuse potential is common among health care workers with reports of self-administration Note : Ketamine also has the potential for abuse and addiction. Trivia : The death of music icon, Michael Jackson has been attributed to Propofol intoxication, administered by his personal physician. Though this powerful drug is one of the greatest boons to the field of anaesthesia, administering it without adequate justification, expertise and equipment (to manage airway) can lead to casualties Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anaesthesiology 6th Edition Chapter 9 Page No 321 to 324

623.q: 20-year-old burns patient with post burns contracture needs wound dressing. Which is the induction agent of choice for such a patient?
623.e: Due to its intense analgesic activity, ketamine has been used extensively for burn dressing changes, debridement’s, and skin grafting procedures. The excellent analgesia and ability to maintain spontaneous ventilation in an airway that might otherwise be altered by burn scar contractures are important advantages of ketamine in these patients. Reference: Stoelting’s pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition pg 189

623.q: Among the given intravenous induction agent, which is an imidazole compound?
623.e: Etomidate: IV anaesthetic agent, introduced in 1973. A carboxylated imidazole (five-membered ring containing three carbon atoms and two nitrogen atoms) compound presented in 35% propylene glycol; pH is 8.1. 75% bound to plasma proteins after injection. Midazolam hydrochloride. Benzodiazepine, used for sedation, premedication and induction of anaesthesia. Has also been used for status epilepticus. Water-soluble at pH Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 218 and 380

624.q: Which is the reference local anaesthetic agent against which all agents are compared?
624.e: Aside from the issue of a high incidence of TNS with spinal administration, lidocaine has had an excellent record as an intermediate duration anaesthetic, and remains the reference standard against which most anaesthetics are compared. Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 460

624.q: Local anaesthetic agents cause neural toxicity. Which of the following is TRUE? 1. Neural injury occurs from voltage gated sodium channels 2. Clinical effect and toxicity is tightly linked.
o: Sentence 1 and 2 both are True and 2 is correct reason for 1
Sentence 1 and 2 both are True but 2 is not the correct reason for 1
Sentence 1 is True but Sentence 2 is False
624.e: It is not clear what role these factors or others play in clinical injury. It is clear, however, that injury does not result from blockade of the voltage-gated sodium channel per se, and thus clinical effect and toxicity are not tightly linked. Reference LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 459

624.q: The manifestations of shellfish poisoning are due to the action of the poison on which channel?
624.e: Saxitoxin and Tetrodotoxin are two potent poisons whose mechanism of action is like that of local anaesthetics - blockade of Na channels. Saxitoxin is produced by certain dinoflagellates which are consumed by shellfish → When such shell fish are consumed by humans, fatal shell fish poisoning occurs with hypotension and respiratory paralysis → This is due to blockade of Na channels by the poison in excitable cells preventing action potential generation Treatment consists of Gastric lavage Vasopressors Mechanical ventilation if respiratory paralysis sets in Prognosis is good when the patient survives after 24 hours Tetrodotoxin is a poison found in some fish of the order Tetraodontiformes (puffer fish) and newts Mechanism of action and manifestations are like shellfish poisoning Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

624.q: While infiltration of local anesthetic, highest chance of increased systemic concentration depending on the site of injection is at
624.e: The rates of local anesthetic systemic absorption and rise of local anesthetic concentrations in blood are related to the vascularity of the site of injection and generally follow This rank order: intravenous (or intraarterial) > tracheal > intercostal > paracervical > epidural >brachial plexus > sciatic > subcutaneous. Reference: Morgan Anesthesia, edition 6, page no 267

624.q: While infiltrating local anesthetics, to prolong the duration of action adrenaline is added. This should be however avoided in
624.e: Addition of epinephrine-or less commonly phenylephrine-causes Vaso- constriction at the site of administration. The consequent decreased absorption reduces the peak local anesthetic concentration in blood, facilitates neuronal uptake, enhances the quality of analgesia, prolongs the duration of analgesia, and limits toxic side effects. However, they cannot be used in parts having end arterial supply, as it will cause distal necrosis. Reference: Morgan anesthesia, edition 6, page no 267

624.q: When asked to describe the symptoms of her allergy to a local anesthetic that a 26- year-old female had at the dentist's office, the patient describes a feeling of light- headedness, palpitations, and flushing. This reaction is most likely caused by
624.e: Dentists usually add epinephrine to the local anesthetic to decrease the bleeding associated with the dental procedure. If any epinephrine gets access to the vascular system, it can cause transient tachycardia and hypertension that patient may describe as palpitations, flushing, and dizziness. If labeled as an allergic reaction, it may limit anesthetic options for the patient in the future. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5586559/

624.q: Anesthetic agent with vasoconstrictor is contraindicated in:
624.e: Vasoconstrictor should not be added for ring block of hand, finger, toes, penis, pinna as all these organs are supplied by end arteries and ischemic damage may occur Adrenaline is most commonly used vasoconstrictor. Felypressin is preferred in cardiovascular disease patient. Reference: Morgan, clinical Anesthesiology, 4 th ed. pg. 34

624.q: Among the ester and amide group of local anesthetic agents, increased tendency to develop allergic reaction is with which of the following:
624.e: Esters of local anesthetics that produce metabolites related to para-aminobenzoic acid are more likely than amide local anesthetics, which are not metabolized to para-aminobenzoic acid, to evoke an allergic reaction. Of the given options, only procaine is the Ester LA, all others are amides. Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition pg 292

625.e: As previously discussed, this S (–) enantiomer of bupivacaine is somewhat less cardiotoxic than the racemic mixture. It is also less potent, and tends to have a longer duration of action, though the magnitude of these effects is too small to have any substantial clinical significance. Interestingly, recent work with lipid resuscitation suggests a potential advantage of levobupivacaine over ropivacaine, as the former is more effectively sequestered into a so-called lipid sink, implying greater ability to reverse toxic effects should they occur. Reference LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 460

625.q: What is the only drawback of lidocaine?
o: Higher incidence of TNS(transient neurogenic symptoms)
625.e: Aside from the issue of a high incidence of TNS with spinal administration, lidocaine has had an excellent record as an intermediate duration anaesthetic, and remains the reference standard against which most anaesthetics are compared. Reference LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 460

625.q: An anesthetist injected bupivacaine in a patient for axillary nerve block. Later, the patient developed restlessness, agitation and cardiovascular collapse. Next best step in the management would be?
625.e: Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anaesthetic At toxic doses, local anaesthetics can result in CNS (convulsions) or CVS (hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias) symptoms. Diazepam is used to treat convulsions. If not responding, thiopentone may be used. Arrhythmias should be promptly treated using bretylium, amiodarone, disopyramide, magnesium sulphate, esmolol or sotalol. Lignocaine should be avoided as antiarrhythmic because it canexacerbate the CNS toxicity. In refractory arrhythmias, intravenous lipid emulsion (like intralipid)has been found to be extremely useful. Bupivacaine induced cardiotoxicity is enhanced by acidosis, hypercarbia and hypoxemia.

625.q: Which is the TRUE for Ropivacaine?
o: Its low cardiac toxicity has led to use for high volume peripheral blocks
Its high cardiac toxicity has led to decrease use for high volume peripheral blocks
It is not used for epidural infusions for control of labour
625.e: Ropivacaine is an S (–) enantiomer in a homologous series that includes bupivacaine and mepivacaine, distinguished by its chirality, and the propyl group off the piperidine ring ( Table 26–1). Its perceived reduced cardiotoxicity has led to widespread use for high-volume peripheral blocks. It is also a popular choice for epidural infusions for control of labor and postoperative pain. Although there is some evidence to suggest that ropivacaine might produce a more favourable differential block than bupivacaine, the lack of equivalent clinical potency adds complexity to such comparisons. Reference LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 26- Local Anaesthetics by Dr. Kenneth Drasner,MD. Page no. 461

625.q: Hydrolysis by plasma cholinesterase is the primary elimination route of all the following drugs EXCEPT
625.e: Plasma cholinesterase (PChE), also known as pseudocholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase, or serum cholinesterase, is a serine hydrolase from the family of human cholinesterase’s. Anesthetic drugs metabolized by PChE include succinylcholine, mivacurium, and all ester local anesthetics (e.g., cocaine, procaine, and chloroprocaine). PChE is produced in the liver, and its plasma half-life is approximately 8 to 12 days. Advanced age, pregnancy, chronic kidney failure, or specific gene variations may result in reduced PChE activity. Reference: FRCA A TO Z , page no 136

625.q: Which medication is often recommended to decrease the likelihood of coughing and laryngospasm due to ketamine-induced salivary secretions?
625.e: Inclusion of an anti-sialagogue in the preoperative medication is often recommended to decrease the likelihood of coughing and laryngospasm due to ketamine-induced salivary secretions Glycopyrrolate may be preferable , as atropine or scopolamine can easily cross the blood-brain barrier and could theoretically increase the incidence of emergence delirium Reference : Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anesthetic practice 5th edition

625.q: Cardiac or central nervous system toxicity may result when standard lidocaine doses are administered to patients with circulatory failure. This may be due to the following reason:
o: Lidocaine is converted into a toxic metabolite due to its longer stay in liver
Lidocaine concentration are initially higher in relatively well perfused tissues such as brain and heart
There is a sudden out-burst of release of adrenaline, noradrenaline and dopamine in brain and heart
Histamine receptors in brain and heart gets suddenly activated in circulatory failure
625.e: CNS or CVS systemic toxicity may result when standard lidocaine dose is administered to patient with circulatory failure because its concentration is initially higher in relatively well perfused tissue such as brain & heart And reduced cardiac output (in CHF) slows delivery of lidocaine (amide LA) to liver reducing their metabolism (to MEGX=mono ethyl glycine xylidide) à prolonging Lidocaine's plasma half life Toxicity of Lidocaine is due to its own concentration in blood NOT due to its toxic metabolite MEGX can cause seizures in neonates Reference : Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

625.q: The advantage of ropivacaine over bupivacaine is?
625.e: Ropivacaine has a higher therapeutic index and lesser cardiotoxicity as compared to bupivacaine This is because ropivacaine is the S (-) enantiomer of bupivacaine The cardiotoxicity of bupivacaine is due to the R (+) isomer which blocks the cardiac Na channel s more avidly and dissociates more slowly Ropivacaine is less potent Epidural ropivacaine is 40 % less potent than bupivacaine Ropivacaine has a shorter duration of action and produces less motor block than bupivacaine Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

626.q: A 32-year-old man is apprehensive of general anesthesia and prefers a regional anesthetic. Decision is made to conduct spinal anesthesia for the repair of inguinal hernia along with midazolam and fentanyl to allay anxiety. During the procedure, he suddenly loses consciousness. There is profound hypotension with systolic blood pressure of 44 mm Hg and a heart rate of 28 bpm. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is started. The best appropriate intervention is administration of
626.e: In the clinical scenario described, atropine by itself, may not be able to correct the hemodynamics, and the situations call for initiation of measures required in advanced cardiac life support If there is no pulse → chest compressions along with → administration of epinephrine may be the best course of action Reference : ACLS guidelines AHA

626.q: The surgeon is performing a right total knee arthroplasty under a combined spinal-epidural anesthetic. The surgical team is providing you with information that within the next 15 minutes they plan to place bone cement to anchor the prosthesis. The most likely side effect that may occur is
626.e: The clinical manifestations of bone cement implantation syndrome include Hypoxia (increased pulmonary shunt) Hypotension Arrhythmias (including heart block and sinus arrest) Pulmonary hypertension (increased pulmonary vascular resistance) Decreased cardiac output Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg. 805.

626.q: You are giving caudal block for a lower limb surgery in a pediatric patient. The equilateral triangle is formed between the posterior superior iliac spines and _______
626.e: Caudal epidural anesthesia is a common regional technique in pediatric patients. Caudal anesthesia involves needle or catheter penetration of the sacrococcygeal ligament covering the sacral hiatus that is created by the unfused S4 and S5 laminae. The hiatus may be felt as a groove or notch above the coccyx and between two bony prominences, the sacral cornua. The posterior superior iliac spines and the sacral hiatus define an equilateral triangle Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 987.

626.q: A 75-year-old man is scheduled to undergo elective orchiectomy for prostate cancer. The patient has selected spinal anesthesia. What is the minimum dermatomal level that must be achieved to carry out this operation?
626.e: Testicular innervation can be traced up to the T10 dermatomal level. For this reason, any operation that involves manipulation or traction on the testicles must have adequate anesthesia to prevent pain. This can be achieved with spinal or epidural anesthesia, which is associated with a T10 level of blockade. Reference: Miller, ed 8, p 2219

626.q: The artery of Adamkiewicz MOST frequently arises from the aorta at which spinal level?
626.e: Blood supply to the spinal cord comes from several sources. The anterior spinal artery is derived from the vertebral arteries and runs the entire length of the spinal cord and supplies the anterior two thirds of the cord. There are segmental arteries from the aorta that join the anterior spinal artery to help supply the spinal cord. One of the larger arteries is called the artery of Adamkiewicz, which arises from the lower thoracic area (T9-T12). Damage to this artery can lead to ischemia for the lower two thirds of the spinal cord and can result in paraplegia. The posterior one third of the cord is supplied by two posterior spinal arteries that also arise from the vertebral arteries and receive some blood supply from the segmental arteries. Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 1131.

626.q: In epidural anesthesia, Which of the following layers is least likely to be punctured during the procedure?
626.e: Explanation: It is the least likely layer to be punctured during epidural anesthesia, as it is not meant to be breached during the procedure. Sequence of structures typically traversed in epidural anesthesia: Skin Subcutaneous tissue Supraspinous ligament (Option C ruled out) Interspinous ligament (Option D ruled out) Ligamentum flavum (Option B ruled out) The epidural space lies just after the ligamentum flavum, making deeper layers-like the dura mater- L ess likely to be punctured if the procedure is done correctly.

626.q: Spinal cord in adult terminates at what level of vertebrae?
626.e: Explanation: In adults , the spinal cord ends at the level of the: Lower border (inferior end) of L1 vertebra. Sometimes can extend to upper L2 , but most commonly lower L1. This terminal portion of the spinal cord is called the conus medullaris . Explanation for other options: Upper end of L1 (option A): Incorrect. The level is too high. The spinal cord usually extends a bit lower. Upper end of L3 (option B): Incorrect. This is too low; spinal cord ends well above this level in adults. Lower end of L3 (option D): Incorrect. This is true in neonates or infants , not adults.

626.q: An 18-year-old woman in the active stage of labor requests an epidural anesthetic. Immediately following injection of 2 mL and 5 mL test doses of 1.5% lidocaine with 1:200,000 epineph- rine through the epidural catheter, the patient complains of lip numbness and becomes very apprehensive. Her heart rate has increased from 85 to 105 beats/min. What is your presumptive diagnosis?
626.e: Circumoral numbness and apprehension immediately following administration of lidocaine suggest an intravascular injection of local anesthetic. Abrupt tachycardia strongly suggests intravascular injection of epinephrine. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition pg 272.

627.q: A 21-year-old patient reports tingling in her thumb during her cesarean section under epidural anesthesia. To which dermatomal level would this correspond?
627.e: The thumb corresponds to dermatome C6, the second and middle fingers correspond to dermatome C7, and the fourth and little fingers correspond to dermatome C8. Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, p 920

627.q: Transient neurologic syndrome (TNS) is MOST commonly seen after the spinal anesthetic injection of which local anesthetic?
627.e: Transient neurologic syndrome (TNS), formerly called transient radicular irritation (TRI), occurs most commonly after spinal anesthesia with lidocaine (Xylocaine). Symptoms include back pain that develops after the block resolves and radiates to the buttocks and legs. The pain is not associated with motor or sensory loss or electromyographic changes. It can be severe, requiring hospital admission of outpatients, and typically resolves within 1 to 4 days. It appears to occur more commonly when outpatients are operated on in the lithotomy position and appears to be less likely when patients are pregnant Reference: Chestnut: Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia, ed 5, p 756; Suresh: Shnider and Levinson's Anesthesia for Obstetrics, ed 5, pp 112-113.

627.q: During performance of lumbar epidural anesthesia for labor analgesia, you experience free-flowing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the advancing 17G Tuohy epidural needle. The epidural needle is removed and a second attempt is successfully performed with an epidural catheter placed at a different level. Which of the following you would not recommend for the patient to practice in the next 72 hours?
627.e: In patients who may experience a "wet tap" during placement of an epidural, conservative therapy should include bed rest and plenty of fluid intake, including caffeine; food diet low in fiber and stool softeners are encouraged to prevent straining. Leakage of CSF can lead to a reduction in intracranial pressure and post dural puncture headache chances are high since the epidural needle is an 16/18 G needle . Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 992.

628.q: A 30-year-old male underwent ACL reconstruction of the left knee under general anaesthesia and adductor canal block. After the surgery, the Inhalational agents were stopped and reversal was giving with Neostigmine (with glycopyrrolate). He did not regain consciousness or spontaneous efforts of breathing. Given that he received high dose of Morphine for premedication, next line of management will include the following,
628.e: When the patient fails to regain consciousness within an expected period of time after general anesthesia, the most frequent cause is residual drug effect. Delayed emergence may occur as a result of absolute or relative drug overdose. The effects of preoperative sleep deprivation or drug ingestion (alcohol, sedatives) can be additive to those of anesthetic agents in producing prolonged emergence. Intravenous naloxone and flumazenil will readily reverse the effects of an opioid and benzodiazepine, respectively. Intravenous physostigmine may partially reverse the effect of other agents. Reference : Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology, page 1289

628.q: A 30-year-old man presents for open reduction and internal fixation of a left radius fracture as an outpatient. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 12 years. The plan is general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation. Which one of the following agents is most appropriate for him?
628.e: Although all agents could be used, sevoflurane would be the preferred choice. Sevoflurane could be used in combination with nitrous oxide Wrong Answers: Option A : Isoflurane could also be used, but because of its high blood: gas solubility it may delay emergence, which is undesirable in outpatients Option B : Desflurane has a lower blood: gas solubility that would provide rapid awakening , but desflurane is irritating to inhale and can cause bronchoconstriction in smokers Reference : Drugs in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

628.q: Local infiltration of lignocaine and other local anesthetic agents are less reliable for ankle block of an infected diabetic foot. This is because
628.e: Since local anesthetics are weak bases, they exist largely in the ionic form, making it difficult for them to cross the cell membrane, thus delaying their local anesthetic action. Further they become ionized when the local tissue is infected and the local pH is acidic. Their action becomes unreliable. Addition of sodium bicarbonate promotes nonionized fraction of local anesthetic, promoting more rapid onset of its action. Reference: Stoeltings pharmacology and physiology in anesthetic practice 5th edition pg. 291

628.q: The drug that has been used most frequently for intravenous regional anesthesia is?
628.e: Lidocaine has been the drug used most frequently for intravenous regional anesthesia Prilocaine, mepivacaine, chloroprocaine, procaine and etidocaine have also been used successfully Intravenous regional anaesthesia or Bier’s block involves the intravenous administration of a local anesthetic into a tourniquet- occluded limb It is used to provide anesthesia for short surgical procedures ( ) on the limbs Note: Bupivacaine is not used for Biers block. It is the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic. Accidental early inflation of the tourniquet →can lead to massive systemic doses of bupivacaine resulting in → cardiac arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse Reference : Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

628.q: A 25-year-old, otherwise healthy patient, received a right sided interscalene block for a shoulder surgery. 3 hours after the surgery, you are called to the post anaesthesia care unit as patient is having drooping of the right eyelid, redness of the conjunctiva, and pupillary constriction. The most likely diagnosis is:
628.e: These signs described above are specific to Horner Syndrome. Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis, and anhydrosis) frequently results from proximal tracking of local anesthetic and blockade of sympathetic fibers to the cervicothoracic ganglion. Other site-specific risks include vertebral artery injection (suspect if immediate seizure activity is observed), spinal or epidural injection, and pneumothorax. In patients where a CVA may also be within the differential diagnosis, a thorough history and neural exam should always be included. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1007.

628.q: Anatomical location of the musculocutaneous nerve in the upper arm is most frequently found within which of the following muscles?
628.e: Although some anatomical variation can be found with the brachial plexus at the level of the axilla, the musculocutaneous nerve is most commonly positioned within the coracobrachialis muscle or between the bellies of the biceps and coracobrachialis muscles. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1019.

628.q: While performing a peripheral nerve block in an awake patient, access and/or use of all of the following should be considered mandatory, except
o: Access to resuscitation medications and equipment
Immediate access to a mechanical ventilator
628.e: Immediate access to a functioning anesthesia ventilator is not always necessary while administering regional anaesthesia. Regional anesthesia should be administered in a monitored location where standard ASA monitors. Supplemental oxygen along with resuscitative medications and equipment should be readily accessible and immediately available. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 999.

628.q: After administering which of the following nerve blocks would you expect the highest blood levels of local anaesthetic per local anaesthetic dose injected?
628.e: The intercostal block has one of the highest complication rates of any peripheral nerve block due to the close proximity of the intercostal artery and vein (intravascular local anesthetic injection), as well as underlying pleura (pneumothorax). Intercostal blocks result in the highest blood levels of local anesthetic per local anesthetic dose injected of any nerve block procedure, and if multiple blocks will be performed care must be taken to avoid toxic levels of local anesthetic. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1040.

629.q: A hyperthyroid patient presents to the casualty room following road traffic accident. He has sustained right leg crush injury that requires amputation. He is taken up for surgery under general anesthesia. Which of the following monitors is likely to indicate precipitation of a thyroid crisis intraoperatively
629.e: Thyroid storm can present during and post surgery with fever (>40°C), sweating, sinus tachycardia (>140bpm), coma, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea. Management involves rehydration with IV saline and glucose, administration of steroid, beta blockers, propylthiouracil and paracetamol. Reference : Oxford handbook of Anesthesia, edition 4, page no 577

629.q: A 37-year-old man with myasthenia gravis arrives in the emergency room confused and agitated after a 2-day history of weakness and increased difficulty breathing. ABGs on room air are Pao2 60 mm Hg, Paco2 51 mm Hg, HCO3 - 25 mEq/L, pH 7.3, Sao2 of 90%. His respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min and tidal volume (Vt) is 4 mL/kg. After administration of edrophonium 2 mg IV, his Vt declines to 2 mL/kg. What should be the most appropriate step in the management of this patient at this time?
o: Repeat the test dose of edrophonium
629.e: Cholinergic crisis can be differentiated from myasthenic crisis by administering small IV doses of anticholinesterases. With a cholinergic crisis, there are significant muscarinic effects (e.g., salivation, bradycardia, miosis) and an accentuated muscle weakness. Because this patient's Vt decreased with the administration of edrophonium, the diagnosis of cholinergic crisis is made. Although atropine may be needed to treat the cholinergic symptoms, muscle weakness will be worse and these patients need to be intubated until the muscle strength returns. Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, p 450

629.q: An end stage renal disease patient has been scheduled for renal transplant. He is on thrice weekly hemodialysis. His blood investigations revealed high potassium levels more than 6.0 mEq/L and he was dialyzed preoperatively, repeat potassium was 5.2 mEq/L. The drugs to be used in caution include all except
629.e: Succinylcholine, depolarizing muscle relaxant can cause an increase in the potassium concentration up to 0.5 mEq/L can be used to facilitate endotracheal intubation only in the absence of hyperkalemia. Meperidine (pethidine), opioid should be avoided because of accumulation of its metabolite normeperidine. Sevoflurane usage for long hours can cause accumulation of compound A, that has been found nephrotoxic. Reference : Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesia, 6th edition, page no. 689

629.q: An end stage renal disease patient has been scheduled for renal transplant. He is on thrice weekly hemodialysis. His blood investigations revealed high potassium levels more than 6.0 mEq/L and he was dialysed preoperatively, repeat potassium was 5.2 mEq/L .The drugs to be used in caution include all except
629.e: Succinylcholine, depolarizing muscle relaxant can cause an increase in the potassium concentration upto 0.5 mEq/L can be used to facilitate endotracheal intubation only in the absence of hyperkalemia. Meperidine(pethidine), opioid should be avoided because of accumulation of its metabolite normeperidine. Sevoflurane usage for long hours can cause accumulation of compound A, that has been found nephrotoxic in rats. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anaesthesia, 6th edition, page no . 689

629.q: A paediatric patient presents with an open globe injury. Which induction agent should be avoided?
629.e: Ketamine use may cause nystagmus and Blepharospasm. It is also known to increase intra-ocular pressure . Hence should be avoided in eye surgeries. Reference: Morgan and mikhail’s clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition pg 591.

629.q: Pheochromocytoma would be MOST likely to coexist with which of the following?
629.e: Pheochromocytoma is an endocrine tumor (with release of catecholamines) in which 90% of patients are hypertensive, 90% of the tumors originate in one adrenal medulla, and 90% of all pheochromocytomas are benign. This disease is rare ( Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 1339-1340; Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 392-395.

629.q: Hypoglycemia is more likely to occur in the diabetic surgical patient with which of the following diseases?
o: Chronic obstructive lung disease treated with a terbutaline inhaler and aminophylline
629.e: Insulin metabolism involves both the liver and kidneys. Renal dysfunction, however, has a greater impact on insulin metabolism than does hepatic dysfunction. In fact, unexpected prolonged effects of insulin sometimes are seen in patients with renal disease. Reference: Stoelting: Pharmacology and Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, ed 4, p 478

629.q: A 50 years old male patient was evaluated for refractory hypertension and was diagnosed as pheochromocytoma. He was planned for laparoscopic adrenalectomy. He was started on Phenoxybenzamine and propranolol preoperatively. While planning for anesthesia, it should be kept in mind that surges in blood pressure can occur during all the following except:
629.e: Surges in BP can occur at induction, formation of the pneumoperitoneum, and with tumor handling. The fluctuations in BP tend to be transient, and medication needs to respond in a similar fashion. hypertension can be treated in a number of ways: intermittent 2g boluses of Magnesium, boluses of remifentanil, phentolamine, sodium nitroprusside, or labetalol (if associated with a tachycardia). Reference : Oxford handbook of Anesthesia, edition 4, page no 582

630.q: A 7-week-old male infant is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (ICU) with a bowel obstruction. His laboratory values are sodium 120 mEq/L, chloride 85 mEq/L, glucose 85 mg/dL, and potassium 2.0 mEq/L. Respiratory rate is 20 breaths/min, and according to the patient's mother, urine output has been 0 for the last 4 hours. The most appropriate fluid for resuscitation of this patient would be
o: D2.5W with 0.45 sodium chloride and 20 mEq/L potassium chloride
0.9% sodium chloride with 30 mEq/L potassium chloride
630.e: The symptoms described in this patient are consistent with severe dehydration. Thus, the vascular volume should be expanded initially with an isotonic saline solution or a colloid solution until the patient voids. When the urine output increases, potassium can be added to the IV fluids. Although glucose administration for long procedures may prevent hypoglycemia, D5W alone or with a crystalloid solution should not be used to replace fluid deficits. Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 126-129.

630.q: A premature male neonate born at 34 weeks of gestation is scheduled to undergo emergency repair of a left-sided diaphragmatic hernia. Which of the following vessels could be cannulated for preductal arterial blood sampling?
630.e: Newborns with diaphragmatic hernia have significant respiratory difficulty. In addition to their hypoplastic lungs, persistent pulmonary hypertension is present, producing right-to-left shunting through the patent ductus arteriosus. To more appropriately administer the anesthetic, a preductal (ductus arteriosus) artery should be cannulated to monitor arterial blood gases and blood pressure. The right radial or temporal arteries arise from vessels that originate from the aorta proximal to the ductus arteriosus. The oxygen saturation monitors should be placed on the right arm as well. Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 595-596.

630.q: Main determinant of cardiac output in infants and children?
630.e: Cardiac stroke volume is relatively fixed by a noncompliant and immature left ventricle in neonates and infants The cardiac output is therefore very sensitive to changes in heart rate Although basal heart rate is greater than in adults Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail’s 6th Edition Chapter 42 1521, 1522.

630.q: True about paediatric respiratory system in comparison to adult?
o: Weaker intercostal muscles and weaker diaphragms
630.e: Compared with older children and adults, neonates and infants have Weaker intercostal muscles Weaker diaphragms (due to a paucity of type 1 fibres) Less efficient ventilation More horizontal and pliable ribs Protuberant abdomen Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail’s 6th Edition Chapter 42 Page No 1520, 1521 .

630.q: In the premature newborn, the glottis is at which level relative to the cervical spine?
630.e: The glottis of a premature newborn is at the level of C3, for the term newborn the level is C4, and in the adult the glottis is at the C5 level. The relatively high glottis makes intubation more difficult in the premature newborn (i.e., more tissue and less distance). Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, p 1185; Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, p 351; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 2757-2761.

630.q: Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate technique for induction of general anesthesia in a newborn for surgical repair of TEF?
o: Inhalation induction with spontaneous ventilation and tracheal intubation
Inhalation induction using positive-pressure bag and mask ventilation and tracheal intubation
Rapid-sequence IV induction and tracheal intubation
630.e: Anesthesia for patients with EA and TEF can be safely induced with either an intravenous or volatile anesthetic. However, positive-pressure bag and mask ventilation should be avoided because it will force gas into the stomach, potentially making ventilation of the lungs more difficult. A frequently used technique to facilitate correct placement of the endotracheal tube is to advance the tube into a bronchus. While listening over the stomach, slowly withdraw the tube until breath sounds are heard over the stomach. Advance the tube until these sounds become diminished. Bronchoscopy is used by some anesthesiologists to make sure only one fistula is present and to help position the endotracheal tube. Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 576-577; Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 597-598.

630.q: A healthy 2-year-old male is scheduled to undergo a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. His airway was managed uneventfully with mask ventilation, which was followed by direct laryngoscopy and intubation with a 4.5-mm uncuffed endotracheal tube (ETT). Manual ventilation produces an air leak in the oropharynx beginning at a peak pressure of 20 cm H2O. The best next step in the anesthetic management is to
o: Replace the ETT with a smaller-sized uncuffed tube
Replace the ETT with a larger-sized uncuffed tube
Replace the ETT with a 4.0-mm cuffed ETT
630.e: Correct tube size and appropriate cuff inflation is confirmed by easy passage into the larynx and the development of a gas leak at 15 to 25 cm H 2 O pressure.(which is acceptable as described in the case as leak above 20 cm of H20) No leak indicates an oversized tube or overinflated cuff that should be replaced or deflated to prevent postoperative edema, whereas an excessive leak may preclude adequate ventilation and contaminate the operating room with anesthetic gases. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition, pg 914.

630.q: At what maximum inspiratory pressure should an endotracheal tube leak in a child?
630.e: In infants and young children, there should be a small air leak around the endotracheal tube at peak inflation pressures of approximately 15 to 25 cm H2O. The leak test can be performed by slowly increasing the airway pressure and listening with a stethoscope over the larynx to hear when a leak develops. An air leak within this pressure range allows for adequate ventilation and reduces the incidence of postintubation croup. The most common cause of postintubation croup is a tight-fitting endotracheal tube without a leak at 30 to 40 cm H2O. Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 356-357, 389-390.

631.q: Which of the factors in adults listed below is the strongest independent predictor of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in most studies?
631.e: PONV is the second most common complaint from patients after surgery (postoperative pain is the number one complaint). Of the many independent predictors of PONV in adult prospective studies, female gender is the strongest predictor for PONV and the need for postoperative antiemetic rescue treatments. It is interesting to note that although patients often experience nausea when smoking their first cigarettes, smokers have a lower incidence of PONV compared to nonsmokers. Other predictors of PONV include nonsmokers, previous history of PONV, history of migraine headaches, use of post[1]operative narcotics, lengthy surgical procedures, use of nitrous oxide, and the use of volatile anesthetics Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 2947-2954.

631.q: A 40-year-old woman undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy has an oxygen saturation which rapidly decreases to 80% on 100% inspired oxygen, peak airway pressures increase to 38 cmH2O, and blood pressure reduces to 72/42 mmHg. Examination demonstrates absent breath sounds and a hyper-resonant percussion note on the left side of the chest. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
631.e: This patient is demonstrating clinical features of a tension pneumothorax with hypoxia, elevated airway pressures and hypotension. This is a recognized risk of laparoscopic surgery and requires immediate recognition and treatment with insertion of a cannula in the second intercostal space, midclavicular line on the affected side. An intercostal chest drain should then be inserted for this life-threatening emergency. Optimizing ventilator parameters would not treat the cause and may worsen any tension by increasing the size of the pneumothorax. Administration of intravenous fluid boluses would be of benefit but would not be addressing the underlying cause. Reference: Hayden P, Cowman S. Anaesthesia for laparoscopic surgery. Contin Educ Anaesth Crit Care Pain 2011; 11:177–180.

631.q: A 78-year-old woman is anesthetized for a right hemicolectomy for 3 hours. At the end of the operation the patient's blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg, heart rate is 84 beats/min, core body temperature is 35.4°C, and Peco2 on infrared spectrometer is 38 mm Hg. Which of the following would be the LEAST plausible reason for prolonged apnea in this patient?
o: Unrecognized obstructive pulmonary disease and high baseline Paco2
631.e: Hyperventilation to Paco2 of 20 mm Hg or higher for more than 2 hours will result in active transport of HCO3 - out of the CNS. This results in spontaneous breathing at a lower (not higher) Paco2. The other choices should be included in the differential diagnosis of apnea. Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 5, pp 359-361; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, pp 62-64, 340; Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 271-273.

631.q: 4 hours into a laparotomy surgery, the temperature probe reads a measurement of 28 degrees Celsius. Detrimental effects of hypothermia include all of the following except:
o: Increasing the duration of action of muscle relaxants
631.e: Cerebral oxygen consumption decreases by approximately 7% per degree Celsius decrease in temperature. Hypothermia is associated with delayed drug metabolism, increased blood glucose, Vasoconstriction Impaired coagulation postoperative shivering accompanied by tachycardia and hypertension, and Increased risk of surgical site infections. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 132.
