631.q: A 20-year-old male patient is admitted following a road traffic accident. He has sustained both bone fracture of the right leg and is planned for nailing of Tibia. He is a known asthmatic on regular use of asthalin metered dose inhaler. You have the patient nebulized prior to the surgery. What are the following drugs considered safe to use in this patient?
631.e: Anesthetic agents that release histamine directly include Atracurium, Mivacurium, Morphine and meperidine. They cause histamine release, mainly cutaneous when used in patients. Betablockers can increase airway reactivity and may interfere with the activity of beta agonists. Hence, they are avoided in asthmatic patients. Reference: FRCA A TO Z , page no 277

631.q: A 36-year-old woman with a history of hiatal hernia and acid reflux is undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia. She has family history of malignant hyperthermia of her distant relative. Which of the following agent is allowed to be used in anesthesia induction?
631.e: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a life-threatening hyper metabolic state of skeletal muscle that is triggered by the volatile inhaled anesthetics isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane and by the depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine. Malignant hyperthermia presents as an increase in carbon dioxide production, acidosis, cardiac arrhythmias, muscle rigidity, and hyperthermia. Death can occur if the MH crisis is not managed appropriately and early in the course of the episode. The mainstay of treatment is I.V. dantrolene. Reference: stoelting’s anaesthesia and coexisting diseases sixth edition pg 635

631.q: A 30-year-old woman presents for laparoscopic appendicectomy. She had a malignant hyperthermia crisis during a prior surgery. Which of the following inhaled anesthetics would be appropriate for this patient?
631.e: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a life-threatening hypermetabolic state of skeletal muscle that is triggered by the volatile inhaled anesthetics- Isoflurane Desflurane Sevoflurane Depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine Malignant hyperthermia presents as an increase in Carbon dioxide production Acidosis Cardiac arrhythmias Muscle rigidity Hyperthermia Death can occur if the MH crisis is not managed appropriately and early during the episode The mainstay of treatment is i.v . Dantrolene Of the inhaled anesthetics, only nitrous oxide is not contraindicated in malignant hyperthermia Reference: stoelting's anaesthesia and coexisting diseases sixth edition pg 635; Drugs in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition pg 278.

631.q: A patient was undergoing posterior fossa surgery in the sitting position. During recovery from anesthesia, the patient complained of a severe headache and was agitated. X-ray shows intracranial air. Which of the following anesthetics would have been responsible?
631.e: Pneumocephalus is a recognized complication of surgery in the sitting position. During surgery, various techniques may be used to reduce the volume of the brain which encourages air to enter the intracranial space and, when the cranial cavity is closed and the brain expands, the air is compressed causing a mass effect with elevated ICP. The condition is worsened with the use of nitrous oxide since it has increased solubility in blood, leading to expansion of air bubbles. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 606.

632.q: Common causes for lower back pain include all of the following, except
632.e: Chronic lower back pain is one of the top reasons for physician office visits and also one of the greatest reasons for work absence. Lumbosacral strain, degenerative disk disease, and myofascial syndromes are the most common causes, and fibromyalgia is not typically associated with a diagnosis of lower back pain. Reference: lippincott's anaesthesia review pg 212.

632.q: Hyperpathia is the simultaneous presence of which of the following?
632.e: Presence of hyperesthesia, allodynia, and hyperalgesia usually associated with overreaction, and persistence of the sensation after the stimulus is known as hyperpathia. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1050 table 47-1.

632.q: A trauma patient presenting with acute pain can be expected to have all of the following systemic responses to pain except:
632.e: Enhanced sympathetic tone increases sphincter tone and decreases intestinal and urinary bladder motility, promoting ileus and urinary retention and not increased peristalsis. Cardiovascular effects of acute pain often include hypertension, tachycardia, enhanced myocardial irritability, and increased systemic vascular resistance. An increase in total body oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production due to pain, necessitates a concomitant increase in minute ventilation which in turn increases the work of breathing. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1062.

632.q: An intradural mass lesion at the tip of a drug infusion catheter is LEAST likely to present as
o: Development of numbness in T8 dermatomal pattern
632.e: Overdose of intrathecal opiates would not be a sign of an intradural mass lesion. Granulomas at the tip of intrathecal catheters used with intrathecal drug delivery systems are gaining increased attention. Granulomas are more frequently associated with high concentrations and doses of either morphine (> 10 mg/day) or hydromorphone (> 10 mg/day). Most patients who will develop granulomas receive the intrathecal medications for more than 6 months. Presenting symptoms may include loss of drug effect, new pain or paresthesias, or neurologic deficits. Patients should be routinely screened for signs and symptoms of granuloma formation at scheduled intrathecal pump refill appointments. In suspicious cases, patients should undergo prompt diagnostic imaging, and neurosurgical consultation should be considered. Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 1911-1912

632.q: Regarding acute pain, all of the following statements are true except:
o: It is caused by noxious stimulation due to injury, a disease process, or the abnormal function of muscle or viscera
Four physiological processes are involved: transduction, transmission, modulation, and perception
It is associated with a systemic neuroendocrine stress response
632.e: Acute pain can be Nociceptive and Neuropathic Nociceptive pain is caused by activation or sensitization of peripheral nociceptors , specialized receptors that transduce noxious stimuli. Acute pain is almost always nociceptive. Nociceptive pain serves to detect, localize, and limit tissue damage. All other statements given above regarding acute pain are true. Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1050.

632.q: Regarding the treatment of neuropathic pain, the correct statement is
o: Narcotics is the most effective and "first-line" treatment option
It is most optimally treated with multimodal therapies
Sympathetic blockade will eliminate all neuropathic pain
Spinal cord stimulator is not an effective therapy
632.e: Neuropathic pain can be very difficult to treat effectively and often requires multiple therapeutic modalities for treatment. These include anticonvulsants, antidepressants, antiarrhythmic, α2-adrenergic agonists, topical agents, and analgesics (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and opioids). Sympathetic blocks as well as spinal cord stimulation work for certain patient's resistant to pharmacological interventions. Reference: lippincott's anaesthesia review pg 213.

632.q: At what time frame following the postsurgical period does persistent postsurgical pain become defined as being "Chronic pain"?
632.e: IASP definition of chronic postsurgical pain: Chronic postsurgical or posttraumatic pain is defined as chronic pain that develops or increases in intensity after a surgical procedure or a tissue injury and persists beyond the healing process, i.e., at least 3 months after the surgery or tissue trauma . Reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30586070/

632.q: Which of the following choices is NOT consistent with a limb affected by complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
632.e: CRPS is associated with trauma. The main feature is burning, with continuous pain that is exacerbated by normal movement, cutaneous stimulation, or stress, usually weeks after the injury. The pain is not anatomically distributed. Other associated features include cool, red, clammy skin and hair loss in the involved extremity. Chronic cases may be associated with atrophy and osteoporosis. Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, p 161

633.q: Which of the following is the correct order of layers of epidermis from deep to superficial?
o: S.basale, S. granulosum, S. spinosum, S. corneum
S. corneum, S. granulosum, S. spinosum, S. basale
S. basale, S. spinosum, S. granulosum, S. corneum
S. corneum, S. spinosum, S. granulosum, S. basale
633.e: Explanation: The correct order of epidermal layers from deepest to most superficial is: Stratum basale -single layer of mitotically active keratinocytes Stratum spinosum -cells with desmosomal "spines" Stratum granulosum- keratohyalin granules present Stratum corneum- outermost layer of dead, keratinized cells Epidermal layers (deep to superficial): S.basale : Stem cell layer, melanocytes, Merkel cells S.spinosum : Thickest living layer, Langerhans cells S.granulosum : Granular layer, barrier formation S.lucidum : Present only in thick skin (palms, soles) S.corneum : Anucleate keratinized layer providing protection

633.q: Which of the following is the most important enzyme in melanogenesis?
633.e: Tyrosinase is a copper dependent enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of L-tyrosine into L-DOPA, the rate-limiting stage in melanin synthesis. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 88, page 5

633.q: The Malpighian layer of the epidermis includes _______.
633.e: The basal layer is the mitotically active layer, divides to give rise to outer population of cells that constitutes the spinous layer. These two epidermal layers together are referred to as the Malpighian layer. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 5

633.q: Which layer of epidermis is underdeveloped at birth in the VLBW infants ?
633.e: During development of the epidermis, first layer to form is S. Basale and subsequently, layers form from below upwards. Thus, stratum corneum is the last layer to develop and is underdeveloped (only 2-3 layers) in preterm/ very low birth weight (VLBW) infants in initial one week. In these babies, stratum corneum is thin and permeable, leading to more fluid/heat losses. It becomes similar to the adult and full term infant after 2 to 3 weeks postnatal maturation. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 7

633.q: Odland bodies are present in the:
633.e: Odland bodies/lamellar bodies/membrane-coating granules, are present in the stratum granulosum. They contain lipids/sterols and discharge lipid components into the intercellular space that play the role of intercellular cement in the stratum corneum and perform the barrier function. Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page Number-7.

In palm and soles, stratum lucidum is sandwiched between the granulosum and corneum. These cells are nucleated and are referred to as 'transitional' cells. Eleidin granules are present in this layer. Their refractile nature gives this layer a translucent appearance, because of which it is also called as clear cell layer. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 7

Stratum corneum, outermost layer, consists of cells without the nucleus and hence it is dead layer This layer functions as a mechanical barrier and prevents the entry of microbes/allergens/irritants from the environment into the body as well as prevents loss of fluids/electrolytes from the body. As keratinocytes divide and move up to the stratum corneum from stratum basale, they undergo the following changes: Loss of nucleus and ability to divide Increase in size Flattening of cells Dehydration of cell Focussed metabolic activity Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 1

MelanoCytes originate from neural crest and are present in the stratum basale. They produce melanin and transfer to keratinocytes. Epidermal Melanin unit : Ratio of 1:36 (melanocyte : keratinocyte) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 1

634.q: The epidermis contains multiple specialized cell types with distinct functions, locations, and embryological origins. Understanding where each cell type resides is essential for dermatology and pathology. Which of the following statements about skin structure is NOT true?
o: Langerhans cells originate from bone marrow and are present in granular layer.
Melanocytes are present in stratum basale.
Stratified squamous epithelium with hallmark keratin intermediate filaments.
Merkel cells are present in stratum basale.
634.e: Explanation: Langerhans cells do originate from bone marrow, but they are primarily located in the stratum spinosum, not the granular layer. Key epidermal cell types and their locations: Langerhans cells: Antigen-presenting dendritic cells derived from bone marrow; mostly in stratum spinosum. Melanocytes: Neural crest-derived pigment cells; found in stratum basale. Merkel cells: Mechanoreceptors involved in touch sensation; located in stratum basale. Keratinocytes: Main epidermal cells with abundant keratin intermediate filaments, forming stratified squamous keratinized epithelium.

634.q: A patient presented with multiple hypo-aesthetic patches on limb and trunk with bilateral symmetrical nerve thickening. What is the diagnosis?
634.e: Multiple lesions on limb and trunk with B/L symmetric Nerve thickening are pointing towards lepromatous end of spectrum, which could be BL or LL. BL - hypoesthetic lesions LL - normoesthetic lesions and glove and stocking type anesthesia. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 28, page 10

Combination of giant hemangioma, thrombocytopenia, and consumption coagulopathy KMS is an infrequent but potentially fatal complication of rapidly growing vascular lesions in infants The low platelet count in Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is due to a combination of increased destruction and sequestration of platelets within the expanding vascular tumour. The tumor here is infantile haemangioma. MC vascular tumor in infants Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 101, Page 4

634.q: The mechanism of action of Psoralen is:
634.e: Combination of psoralens and ultraviolet light (UVA, 320- 400 nm) - PUVA Psoralen intercalates into the DNA double helix where it is ideally positioned to form adduct(s) with adjacent pyrimidine bases, preferentially thymine, upon excitation by an ultraviolet photon Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 35, page 26

634.q: Which of the following genetic mutation leads to Darier's disease?
634.e: Darier disease, previously known as keratosis follicularis, is a rare autosomal dominant genodermatosis characterized by keratotic papules and longitudinal eyrthronychia; it is caused by mutations in the ATP2A2 gene, encoding a calcium pump within the endoplasmic reticulum. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 66, Page 2

Desmosomes are the intra-epidermal inter-cellular adhesions that are helpful in connecting keratinocytes in the epidermis. Max concentration is in spinous cells. Desmosomes contain various proteins : Desmogleins, desmocollin and desmoplakin. Damage to the desmosomes leads to separation of keratinocytes leading to acantholysis. The cells separate from each other, become round with large nucleus and perinuclear halo called as acantholytic cells. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 18

634.q: Increase in the thickness of the prickle cell layer of the epidermis is called?
634.e: An increase in number of cells in the stratum spinosum / Prickle cell layer of the epidermis Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 37, page 14

Miliaria, or eccrine miliaria, - Blocked eccrine sweat glands and ducts. The obstruction leads to leakage of sweat into the epidermis or dermis, resulting in cellular overhydration, swelling, and further occlusion of the ducts. It is most common in warm, humid climates during the summer months. The 3 main types of miliaria are crystallina, rubra, and profunda. Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 94, Page 12

635.q: Which bedside tests helps to differentiate nevus anemicus and nevus depigmentosus ?
635.e: Pressing the lesion with glass slide - diascopy Helps differentiate between ND and NA. The margins of ND remain distinct from normal skin during diascopy. While margins of NA blend in with surrounding skin as normal skin also blanches on pressing with the slide

635.q: The cell seen in Tzanck smear in pemphigus is:
o: Cell with hyperchromatic nuclei and perinuclear halo
Cell with hypochromatic nuclei and perinuclear halo
635.e: Acantholytic cells appear as round cells with perinuclear halo in Tzanck smear: Characteristic of Pemphigus Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, page 3

635.q: A patient presented to the OPD with dome shaped papules with central umbilication, on face and cytology smear was made. What is the finding observed?
635.e: Dome shaped papules with central umbilication - diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum Tzanck smear can be made from the white pasty core of the molluscum lesion - Giemsa stain done. Tzanck smear reveals the presence of diagnostic intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies (Henderson-Patterson bodies), the largest known inclusion bodies (30-35 m) Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 12

635.q: Which of the following is a clear fluid filled blister, >1 cm in diameter?
635.e: Clear, fluid filled 1cm → bullae. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 4, page 3

635.q: Visible desquamation of the stratum corneum is known as:
635.e: Scale: Visible desquamation of corneocytes (SC) (keratinocytes) Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 4, page 13

635.q: Which of the following is a flat, non-palpable lesion of less than 1cm in diameter?
635.e: Flat, non-palpable, Change in color of skin 1cm → patch Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 4, page3

635.q: Break in continuity of epidermis is called:
635.e: Full thickness loss of epidermis BM: not intact Reaches dermis Heals with scarring Erosion - partial loss of epidermis. Excoriation - linear scratch marks Atrophy - loss of substance in skin Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 4, page 11

635.q: Application of pressure from side on an intact bulla is called as the elicitation of:
635.e: Nikolsky sign: Application of tangential pressure on intact skin leads to formation of erosion Bullae spread sign: Application of pressure from side on an intact bulla leads to extension of bullae Asboe Hansen sign: Application of pressure on the bullae from the top/centre Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, page 5

636.q: Eccrine glands are involved in which of the following:
636.e: Syringomas are benign, eccrine sweat duct tumours, typically found clustered on eyelids in a symmetric pattern. Syringomas are skin-coloured or yellowish, generally small, dermal papules. Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page Number-30.

Clinical Presentation of Acne Sites: Face, shoulders, upper trunk Polymorphic eruption: Comedones, papules, nodules, cysts Comedones: Pathognomonic lesions of acne vulgaris Open comedones (Black heads): Block on skin surface Closed comedones (White heads): Block below skin surface Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 90, Page 1

636.q: All of the following are Premalignant lesions except:
636.e: Rhinophyma is a disfiguring nasal deformity due to the proliferation of sebaceous glands and underlying connective tissue. The name itself is broken down into "rhis," derived from Greek meaning nose, and "phyma," also Greek, for skin tumor. Rosacea is the precursor condition to the later development of rhinophyma Rhinophyma has no malignant potential Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 142, page 142.1

636.q: Following does not form a part of follicular occlussion tetrad?
636.e: Acne inversa is another name for Hidradenitis Suppurativa HS can be associated with other follicular occlusion diseases such as pilonidal cysts (PCs) of the sacrum and buttocks, dissecting cellulitis (DC), and acne conglobata (AC), which usually involves the face, chest. PCs, DC, and/or AC - the follicular occlusion triad When HS occurs with PCs, DC, and/or AC it is referred to as the follicular occlusion tetrad. Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 92, Page 2

636.q: Among the following alternatives, which is not a feature of rosacea?
636.e: Rosacea is defined as a chronic disease that impacts fair skinned middle aged adults. This chronic disease is characterized as telangiectasia and flushing in early stage, pustules and papules in inflammatory stage, papules and induction and rhinophyma in chronic stage Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 91, Page 2

636.q: Differential diagnosis of Rosacea includes all of the following except:
636.e: Differential diagnosis of Rosacea includes Acne vulgaris, Seborrheic dermatitis, Perioral dermatitis, Carcinoid syndrome, Lupus erythematosus, Basal cell carcinoma Most common potential diagnostic confusion is between rosacea and acne vulgaris, owing to the presence of pustules and papules. Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 91, Page 10

636.q: Local side effects of topical corticosteroids among the following: 1. Blue discolouration of skin 2. Atrophy 3. Acneiform eruption 4. Hypertrichosis
636.e: Explanation: Blue discolouration of skin is not a side effect of corticosteroids Topical corticosteroids cause a variety of local adverse effects due to dermal atrophy and altered follicular activity. (Mneumonic - STEROID ) S - Skin thinning ( atrophy , striae) (Option 2 is true) T-; Telangiectasia E - Ecchymosis (easy bruising) R -; Rosacea-like dermatitis O - Opportunistic infections (folliculitis, tinea incognito) I - Induced acne ( steroid acne ), Increased hair growth ( hypertrichosis ) (Option 3 and 4 are true) D -; Decreased pigmentation and Delayed wound healing Key Takeaway: Bluish-Grey Discolouration of Skin (Ceruloderma) is caused by Antiarrhythmic: Amiodarone Antibiotics: Minocycline Antimalarials: Hydroxychloroquine, Chloroquine Silver compounds: Argyria Antipsychotic: Chlorpromazine

636.q: Which of the following drugs plays a role in chemoprevention of skin malignancies in albinism ?
636.e: Incidences of Squamous cell, carcinoma, Basal cell carcinoma, and Actinic keratosis are markedly increased in patients with Oculocutaneous albinism. Retinoids like isotretinoin are effective as chemopreventive agents in premalignant lesions of the skin. If retinoids are given at an early stage, they can cause regression of premalignant lesions of the skin. These can be recommended as they reduce the potential effects of carcinogenesis. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 70, page 8

637.q: Which of the following is present in both skin and hair?
637.e: Keratin is a protein produced by skin cells Outermost layer of skin cells contains keratin Hair and nails are also made of keratin Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 2.

637.q: Flag sign in hair is characteristic of:
637.e: Skin Manifestations of Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM) Crazy pavement 'like skin (parchment) Flag sign' in hair (alternate bands of light and dark colours) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 63, page 5

637.q: Stem cells of the hair follicle are present in?
637.e: The isthmus is the part of hair follicle between the opening of the sebaceous gland and the insertion of arrector pili muscle. Hair follicle stem cells are thought to reside in the bulge area on the isthmus close to the insertion of the arrector muscle. Bulge stem cells are multipotent, migrate in a downward direction, enter the hair bulb matrix and generate the new lower anagen hair follicle. They also migrate distally to form sebaceous glands and to proliferate in response to wounding Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 2, Page 45

637.q: Which of the following stages have longest duration in hair cycle?
637.e: Anagen is the active phase in which the hair follicle grows. Of the total hair on scalp, about 85% are in anagen and this phase can last for several years(average 3 years). The duration of catagen and telogen phase is 3 weeks and 3 years respectively. So the longest phase in anagen. Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 89, Page 7

637.q: Which is the primary target of androgen in hair follicle?
637.e: In Androgenetic Alopecia, familial tendency is seen and Genetic factors modify the magnitude of the hair follicle response to circulating androgens. Along with genetics, the 5 alpha reductase enzyme plays a central role through the intrafollicular conversion of testosterone to the more active metabolite DHT. DHT binds the androgen receptor with 5 times the avidity of testosterone and is more potent in its ability to cause downstream activation. It leads to Hair follicle miniaturization , which is the histological hallmark of androgenetic alopecia. Converts terminal hair to vellus hair which ultimately shed off. The androgens acts on the androgen receptors, located in the dermal papilla nuclei of the hair bulbs. The dermal papillae are thus, main target of androgens in AGA Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 89, Page 7

637.q: A 60-year-old patient of cervical carcinoma presents with excessive hair loss 2-3 weeks after starting chemotherapy. What is the diagnosis?
637.e: Anagen effluvium is a form of nonscarring alopecia commonly associated with chemotherapy. In this disorder, affected anagen hairs suffer a toxic or inflammatory insult, resulting in fracture of the hair shaft. Shedding usually takes place within 14 days of administration of the offending drug, however, in many instances it is reversible, with hair regrowth occurring upon discontinuation of the offending agent. Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 89, Page 48

637.q: Which of the following is the treatment of choice for patient for patchy alopecia areata?
637.e: Spontaneous remission occurs in up to 80% of patients with limited patchy hair loss of short duration (less than 1 year) Intralesional steroids are the most effective treatment in patchy alopecia areata. A depot steroid (triamcinolone acetonide 5-10 mg/mL), administered by fine needle injection into the upper subcutis. It will stimulate hair growth at the site of injection in some patients. Multiple injections are usually needed. Reference: Rook's Textbook Of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 89, Page 33

637.q: Canites subita is the characteristic feature of ____
637.e: An intriguing feature of alopecia areata is the sparing of white hairs. In patients with grey hair, which is an admixture of pigmented and non-pigmented hair, the disease process appears preferentially to affect pigmented hair, so that non-pigmented or white hair is spared. This may result in a dramatic change in hair colour if the alopecia progresses rapidly, and this phenomenon is called as 'going white overnight' syndrome or Canites Subita (Canites = white, subita = sudden). Reference: Rook's Textbook Of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 89, Page 31

638.q: Which of the following is not a NEVUS of melanocyte?
638.e: Ans. D. Becker nevus Becker nevus is appendageal nevi where as other three are melanocyitc nevi. Melanocytic nevi are :- Dysplastic nevus BIue nevus Nevus of ito & nevus of ota Spitz nevus Giant pigmented nevus Mongolian spot Intramucosal neyus

638.q: Inverted Champagne bottle appearance is seen in
638.e: Answer- C. Lipodermatosclerosis The most commonly recognized form of lipodermatosclerosis (LDS), chronic LDS presence with induration and hyperpigmentation of the skin involving the one or both of the lower legs in a characteristic "inverted champagne bottle" appearance. Associated with venous insufficiency, LDS is most common in middle-aged women.

638.q: Which of the following histological type is most sensitive in cold?
638.e: Melanocytes are very susceptible to thermal injury and may die at temperatures below -5 C. As compared to other cells in the skin, including epidermal keratinocytes, merkel cells, langerhans cells, mesissners corpuscles, contact cooling of the skin surface causes selective loss of epidermal melanocytes when the tissue temperature reaches −5 °C or cooler with an exposure time of 10 minutes or longer, leading to partial skin depigmentation Longer exposures combined with colder temperature exposure led to more complete depigmentation in the treated skin surface. This is a reason why cryosurgery procedures on skin - using liquid nitrogen at -196 degrees Celsius - causes depigmentation as a common side effect Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 17

638.q: Lichenification occurs in which layer of skin:
638.e: Lichenification is characterized by thickening of skin, increased skin markings and hyperpigmentation. Increase in thickness of Stratum Spinosum/Malpighi Seen in Chronic itchy dermatoses Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 4, page 13

638.q: Which of the following is not true about the lichenification?
638.e: Lichenification: Chronic, long term itching, HPE: Acanthosis Increase colour (dark) Increase thickness Increase lines Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 4, page 5

638.q: Which of the following is not used in treatment of melasma?
638.e: Hydroquinone is the gold standard of topical treatment. It exerts its effect by inhibiting tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin synthesis. HQ 2%-4% is prominently used as mono-therapy A triple combination of hydroquinone, retinoic acid, and corticosteroids (HQ 4%, tretinoin 0.05%, and fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) Kligman regimen is commonly used Other depigmenting drugs - azelaic acid, kojic acid, glycolic acid Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 88, page 13

638.q: Melanocytes are reduced in number in all of the following except :
638.e: Albinism - AR disorder, Tyrosinase absent Melanocytes are present in normal distribution but they fail to synthesize melanin adequately Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 70, page 7

638.q: Which of the following is not a poor prognostic factor for vitiligo?
638.e: Poor prognostic factors for vitiligo: Leucotrichia Lip tip variant Long standing disease Thyroid abnormalities Vitiligo on bony prominence Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 88, page 37

639.e: Profilaggrin is found in the keratohyalin granules present in the stratum granulosum. Profilaggrin breaks down to yield individual filaggrin monomers at the transition between the stratum granulosum and stratum corneum. Deficiency of filaggrin: Atopic dermatitis & Ichthyosis vulgaris Reference : Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page Number-7.

639.q: In which of the following conditions Parakeratosis most frequently occurs -
639.e: Normally, nuclei are absent in stratum corneum. Retention of nuclei within the cells of stratum corneum - Parakeratosis. Parakeratosis is seen in - Normally → Mucous membrane of mouth and vagina. Disorders → Benign (Psoriasis, Seborrheic dermatitis) Malignant (Actinic keratosis, Squamous cell carcinoma) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 3, page 34

639.q: Which of the following is characteristically associated with Acute eczema?
639.e: Spongiosis: Intraedpidermal intercellular edemaDermal inflammatory infiltrates around the dilated venules of the superficial plexus, edema, and spongiosis Fully developed spongiosis becomes organized in focal micro vesicles Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 39, page 39.3

639.q: A patient presents with an eczematous rash with yellow greasy scaling. The microorganism most intimately associated with causation is:
639.e: Seborrheic Dermatitis Site: areas rich in sebaceous glands, particularly the scalp, face, and body folds. Linked to the interplay of normal skin flora - Malassezia spp, the composition of lipids on the skin surface and individual susceptibility. C/F - folliculocentric erythematous papules and plaques with a fine white scale, and a yellowish crust often described as a greasy scale-crust. Treatment: Topical antifungals: Ketoconazole, Ciclopirox, Selenium sulphide Topical steroids Topical immunomodulators: Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 40, page 2

639.q: Which of the following statements about lichenification is NOT true?
639.e: Explanation: Lichenification is characterized by thickened, leathery skin, not atrophy. Atrophy refers to thinning of the epidermis or dermis, which is the opposite of what occurs in lichenification. Lichenification occurs due to chronic irritation or scratching, typically seen in: Chronic eczema Lichen simplex chronicus Atopic dermatitis Key features: Thickened skin Hyperpigmentation due to chronic inflammation Hyperlinearity, where skin markings become prominent Dryness and scaling may accompany it

639.q: MC plant implicated in the causation of phytodermatitis is:
639.e: This is the most common cause of plant induced dermatitis (phytodermatitis) in India Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 128, page 51

639.q: Nasolabial dyssebacea and neovascularisation of cornea are features seen in deficiency of ?
639.e: Riboflavin, vitamin B2, is a water-soluble and heat-stable vitamin that the body uses to metabolize fats, protein, and carbohydrates into glucose for energy. Clinical deficiency of riboflavin - sore throat, hyperemia and edema of the pharyngeal and oral mucous membranes, cheilosis, angular stomatitis, glossitis, seborrheic dermatitis (dyssebacea), and normochromic, normocytic anemia associated with pure red cell cytoplasia of the bone marrow. Severe riboflavin deficiency can also affect the conversion of vitamin B 6 to its coenzyme and even curtail conversion of tryptophan to niacin. Neovascularisation of cornea can also be seen. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 63, page 14

639.q: All of the following statements are true regarding Asteatotic eczema except
o: It usually affects legs, arms and hands with dry skin
It is also known as Eczema craquele
It is more common in winters
639.e: Asteatotic eczema, also known as eczema craquelé, is a common type of pruritic dermatitis. C/F - dry, cracked, and scaling skin that is typically inflamed. Can lead to fissures are a result of epidermal water loss. The fissured skin occurs in a polygonal or curvilinear pattern (crazing pavement sign). typically presents on the anterolateral aspects of the lower legs Asteatotic eczema occurs especially in winter months when the skin is more at risk for becoming dry. Asteatotic eczema is also more common in the elderly. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 39, page 10

640.q: Darier's sign is positive in the following :
640.e: Darier's Sign :The skin characteristically urticates within minutes of gentle rubbing in children causing localized pruritus, redness and wheal, which subside within an hour. It is not 100% specific for mastocytosis, since it has been described on rare occasions in juvenile xanthogranuloma and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia of neonates Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 46, page 4

640.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is seen in urticaria
640.e: Type I hypersensitivity is also known as an immediate reaction and involves immunoglobulin E (IgE) mediated release of antibodies against the soluble antigen. This results in mast cell degranulation and release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators. Manifestations - anaphylaxis, urticaria, angioedema, food, and drug allergies The allergens that result in a type I hypersensitivity - pollen, mites, or foods, drugs, etc Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 42, page 4
Acute urticaria resolves within 6 weeks . Urticaria longer than 6 weeks' duration is considered chronic. Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 42, page 5

640.q: A 17-year-old female with no previous medical history presented with swelling of her lips, face and mouth area. She claims that she had four previous episodes over the past two months, each lasting two days. No recent insect bites or stings. She denies any itching or pain but feels a warm sensation around the mouth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
640.e: Acquired angioedema occurs because of an acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency. It is usually characterized by recurrent episodes of asymmetric swelling of the face and oral area, without urticaria or pruritis. The disease is usually self limiting but laryngeal swelling can cause significant morbidity. Patients with this disorder either have a total quantitative deficiency or a qualitative deficiency. Although it is usually a clinical diagnosis, frequently along with a positive family history. Laboratory data to confirm diagnosis include serum C1INH, and C4. Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 43, page 4

640.q: A patient with recurrent lip edema underwent Laboratory evaluation which shows decreased C4 and C1 INH (quantity and function) with normal C1q. The diagnosis is
640.e: The 3 types of HAE can be differentiated with complement testing and, in the case of HAE with normal C1 inhibitor levels, genetic testing. Type I HAE is characterized by the following: Low C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) protein level Low C4 level Normal C1q level Type II HAE is characterized by the following: Normal or elevated, but dysfunctional, C1-INH level Low C4 level Normal C1q level HAE with normal C1 inhibitor levels is characterized by the following: Normal C1-INH level Normal C1-INH functional assay Normal C4 and C1q level Factor XII mutation may be present Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 43, page 4

640.q: Most common type of Cutaneous mastocytosis is?
640.e: Cutaneous Mastocytosis (CM) Most cases of Pediatric mastocytosis are sporadic and appear during the first 2 years of life, especially on the trunk Urticaria pigmentosa is the most frequent variant Three main forms of CM (defined by the WHO) Urticaria pigmentosa (UP - Maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis MPCM) Diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis (DCM) Mastocytoma of skin Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 46, page 4

641.q: A patient developed bullae without erythema on elbows, knee & sacral area fib crust formation, scarring & milia. He had no photo sensitivity and negative family history for bullous diseases. On DIF IgG deposition at DEJ with no blood vessel involvement is seen probable diagnosis is:
641.e: Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA) Epidermolysis bullosa - congenital, present from birth EBA is not inherited and usually presents in adult life EBA is a rare disease in which tense blisters appear at sites of trauma EBA blisters tend to be localized to areas that are easily injured such as the hands, feet, knees, elbows, and buttocks Sometimes there is mucosal involvement with blisters forming in mouth, nose and eyes EBA may mimic Bullous pemphigoid Salt split immunofluorescence used to differentiate between EBA and BP Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 45

641.q: What can patient with gluten sensitive hypersensitivity consume as food?
641.e: Gluten is found in grains such as wheat, barley, rye, oats, triticale A gluten-free diet is a diet that excludes the gluten Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 54

641.q: Immediately after eating peanut butter sandwich, a man develops swelling of face and lips, respiratory distress, intense pruritus, hypotension and feeling of impending doom. The most likely diagnosis is:
641.e: Intense pruritus and hypotension is characteristic of anaphylaxis Besides immediate onset, welling of face and respiratory distress is conclusive of Anaphylaxis Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 43, page 4

641.q: Gluten free diet is beneficial in:
641.e: Gluten-free diet is recommended in patients of Dermatitis herpetiformis Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 54

641.q: False regarding dermatitis herpetiformis is/are? 1. Associated with gluten sensitive enteropathy 2. Caused by herpes virus 3. Mucosal involvement is common 4. Deposition of IgG in dermis 5. Dapsone is used in the treatment
641.e: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a complex disease of the skin caused by the deposition of IgA in the papillary dermis which triggers an immunologic cascade. It has no association with viral or bacterial etiology. Dermatitis herpetiformis aka Duhring's disease is commonly a/w genetic predisposition for gluten sensitivity, l/t formation of IgA antibodies against gluten-tissue transglutaminase. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 53

641.q: A 17-year-old male presents to the clinic due to an intermittent pruritic rash. He has a past medical history of asthma. On physical examination, the rash can be reproduced by drawing on the skin with a blunt object. Which of the following is the phenomenon is elicited here?
641.e: The examination finding is s/o symptomatic dermographism which is seen in chronic urticaria Prevention and avoidance of precipitating factors such as physical stimuli and stressors are important in managing dermatographism. Choice therapy includes treatment with H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine or loratadine. Reference : Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 42, Page no 11

641.q: All the following are TRUE about erythema multiform EXCEPT :
o: Vesicle and bullae are not seen
Target lesion with bull's eye lesion seen over palms and soles
Associated with adverse reaction to drugs
641.e: Erythema multiforme - manifests as very characteristic 1-2 cm circular lesions consisting of 3 concentric zones - a pinkish raised periphery, pallor in middle and a dark violaceous centre thickened to the iris of the eye or the target of the shooting range. Such a lesions are therefore called iris lesions or target lesions Some case may develop tense blister at the centre of the target lesions Approximately 90% of cases of erythema multiforme minor follow outbreaks of herpes simplex (HSV 1 infection)

641.q: Body surface area percentage involved in Stevens-johnson syndrome is :
641.e: 10-30% - SJS-TEN complex > 30% - Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 119, page 10

642.q: Which of the following is the most common sexually transmitted pathogen?
642.e: Genital HPV remains the most common sexually transmitted pathogen in the United States, infecting 60% of a cohort of initially HPV-negative, sexually active Washington state college women within 5 years in a study conducted from 1990 to 2000-i.e., during the pre-HPV immunization era. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 136, Pg: 1079

642.q: What is the Most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis ?
642.e: Most common cause of urethritis in males is N. gonorrhoea. The most common cause of Non-Gonococcal urethritis in males is Chlamydia trachomatis. The most common cause of urethritis in females is Chlamydia. Hence chlamydia is the most appropriate answer. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:136 Pg: 1081, 1083

642.q: Ichy purple papule followed by hayperpigmentation on resolution, is seen in?
642.e: Ans. D. Lichen planus LP is characterized by shiny, violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules which retain the skin lines. White lines, known as Wickham's striae, may traverse the surface of the papules. Linear lesions often appear along scratch marks or in scars (Koebner phenomenon). In most cases, the papules eventually flatten after a 6 months to 2 yrs, often to be replaced by an area of hyperpigmentation.

642.q: The following are disorders of apocrine glands except:
642.e: Four disorders of apocrine glands need to be remembered Apocrine bromhidrosis - excessive foul smelling body odor Apocrine chromhidrosis - secretion of colored apocrine sweat Fox - Fordyce disease Hidradenitis suppurativa Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 94, Page 15

Oral Lesion of Lichen Planus White, reticulate lacy pattern on the buccal mucosa, tongue and gingival Asymptomatic - Reticular OLP complain of intolerance to spicy food - Erosive OLP Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 37, page 5

642.q: All of the following are included in 5'P's of lichen planus except
642.e: "Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar, Papules "are the traditional 5 "P's" of LP Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 37, page 3

642.q: Not a histological feature of lichen planus is -
642.e: Histopathology in Lichen planus The basic pathology in lichen planus is the damage to the basal cell layer of epidermis leading to degeneration of basal cells. Epidermal thickening especially of granular cell layer → Hypergranulosis. Hyperkeratosis (Thickening of stratum corneum) Acanthosis (Thickening of Stratum) malpighii. Subepidermal - lichenoid band due to deposition of lymphocytes & histiocytes in upper dermis. Dropping of melanin pigment from damaged keratinocytes of epidermis into dermis → pigment incontinence. This melanin is engulfed by macrophages which results information of cytoid bodies (civatte or colloid bodies). Max Joseph Histological cleft → Separation of epidermis in small clefts. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 37, page 14

642.q: 'Claw clutching a Ball' appearance is seen in histopathology of which disease?
642.e: The hallmark of lichen nitidus is a well-circumscribed granulomatous infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, Langerhans giant cells, and multinucleated epithelioid histiocytes in the papillary dermis bordered by extensions of epidermal ridges. This sharply circumscribed inflammatory infiltrate generally spans 4 to 5 dermal papillae within the dermis, giving a "ball-in-clutch" configuration Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 37, page 10

643.q: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of psoriasis?
o: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland
Defective T cell maturation in the thymus
643.e: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells: This describes Type 1 diabetes, not psoriasis. Hyperproliferation of keratinocytes: Psoriasis is characterized by the rapid turnover and proliferation of skin cells (keratinocytes), leading to thickened skin and scaling. Immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland: This is seen in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, not psoriasis. Defective T cell maturation in the thymus: This is related to autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, not psoriasis. Key Takeaway: Psoriasis is primarily due to the hyperproliferation of keratinocytes. Tags: Good to know Tag Line: Moderate Reference: Shastri, A., & Bhatt, S. (2023). Essential Microbiology . Chapter 17: Autoimmunity, pp. 203-207

643.q: A 19 years old male patient is on treatment for psoriasis. He came to OPD with the complaints of malaise, easy fatiguability, fever with chills. He was diagnosed as malaria fever upon laboratory investigation. Which of the following drug is contraindicated?
643.e: Chloroquine is contraindicated in patients with psoriasis or porphyria, in whom it may precipitate acute attacks of these diseases. It should generally not be used in those with retinal or visual field abnormalities or myopathy. Chloroquine should be used with caution in patients with a history of liver disease or neurologic or hematologic disorders. The antidiarrheal agent kaolin and calcium-and magnesium-containing antacids interfere with the absorption of chloroquine and should not be co-administered with the drug. Chloroquine is considered safe in pregnancy and for young children. Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12 th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal. Page no. 920

643.q: Which keratin pair is normally expressed in the stratum basale?
643.e: Explanation: The stratum basale expresses keratin 5 (K5) and keratin 14 (K14). These keratins provide structural support to the basal keratinocytes, which are mitotically active and attached to the basement membrane. Mutations in K5 or K14 lead to epidermolysis bullosa simplex. Keratin expression by epidermal layer: Stratum basale: K5/K14 Stratum spinosum & granulosum: K1/K10 Non-keratinizing epithelia (eg. esophagus): K4/K13 Hyperproliferative states (psoriasis, wound healing): K6/K16 Clinical relevance: Keratin profiling helps diagnose blistering disorders

643.q: Spongiform neutrophilic collections in stratum spinosum are seen in?
643.e: Pustule of Psoriasis (Clusters of neutrophils) Sponge-like array in the stratum spinosum - Spongiform pustule of Kogoj's In the stratum corneum - Microabscess of Munro Other features - parakeratosis, hypogranulosis, regular elongation of rete ridges, supra-papillary thinning, dilated tortuous dermal capillaries Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 35, page 7

643.q: Dyskeratosis refers to abnormal, premature keratinization of individual keratinocytes within the epidermis. This microscopic change is characteristic of certain dermatological disorders involving faulty keratinization. Which of the following conditions classically shows dyskeratosis?
643.e: Explanation: Darier's disease (keratosis follicularis) shows dyskeratosis with hallmark histological features: Corps ronds Grains These represent prematurely keratinized cells within the epidermis. It is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the ATP2A2 gene affecting calcium regulation in keratinocytes. Dyskeratosis: Abnormal keratinization occurring below the stratum granulosum Seen in conditions where integrity of epidermal adhesion or keratinization is altered Conditions associated with dyskeratosis: Darier's disease (most classic) Warty dyskeratoma Grover's disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis) Pemphigus vulgaris: Shows acantholysis (Option B) Psoriasis: Shows hyperproliferation with parakeratosis (Option C) Lichen planus: Shows hyper granulosis and saw-tooth rete ridges (Option D)

643.q: A patient presents with asymptomatic erythematous scaly lesions on extensor aspect of elbows and knee. A bedside test is useful in making the diagnosis :
643.e: Psoriasis Lesions Show positive auspitz sign - pin point bleeding on scratching with a glass slide (Grattage test ) Auspitz sign: Not diagnostic of psoriasis but when positive, helps in pointing to it. Skin biopsy is investigation of choice Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 35, page 8

643.q: Which of the following is a true association:
643.e: Psoriasis and metabolic syndrome> Vitiligo and metabolic syndrome

643.q: All are seen in Reactive arthritis except:
643.e: Arthritis + Conjunctivitis + NGU Iridocyclitis & conjunctivitis Mucocutaneous lesions: Rupioid psoriasis, /Keratoderma blennorrhagicum (crusted, exudative plaques on palms and soles) and Circinate balanitis Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 154, Page 2

644.q: SAPHO Syndrome components are all except:
644.e: Acronym for the combination of Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, and Osteitis Chronic disorder that involves the skin, bone, and joints Some researchers feel that the SAPHO syndrome is related to the group of arthritis conditions which typically affect the spine, called Spondyloarthropathies Treatment typically involves medications which reduce inflammation Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 90, Page 54

644.q: Loss of Intercellular cohesion between keratinocytes is called as ?
644.e: Ans. B. Acantholysis Separation of epidermal keratinocytes due to loss of intercellular bridge is referred to as acantholysis. Acantholysis is seen in the epidermis (especially in basal layer).

644.q: Tzanck smear in bullous pemphigoid shows:
644.e: Cytologic examination of Tzanck smear in bullous pemphigoid and pemphigoid gestationis shows numerous eosinophils without Tzanck cells (acantholytic cells). Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 18

644.q: Drug of choice for dermatitis herpetiformis is:
644.e: Dermatitis Herpetiformis: Sub-epidermal immunobullous disorder Association: Gluten sensitive enteropathy (GSE) Treatment: Gluten-free diet Dapsone (Drug of choice) Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 54

644.q: All are causes of papulosquamous lesions except:
644.e: Selected Causes of Papulosquamous Skin Lesions Primary cutaneous disorders Psoriasis Tinea Pityriasis rosea Lichen planus Parapsoriasis Bowen's disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) Drugs Systemic diseases Lupus erythematosus Cutaneous T cell lymphoma/ Mycosis fungoides Secondary syphilis Reiter's disease Sarcoidosis

644.q: Pemphigus vulgaris is a which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
644.e: The pathogenesis of pemphigus revolves around the formation of antibodies anti dsg1 and anti dsg3, and antibodies binding to the antigen dsg1 and dsg3 at their site. This mechanism is explained in type 2 hypersensitivity reaction. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, page 3

644.q: Which of the following is the correct pair?
644.e: Separation of epidermis - intra epidermal split Pemphigus vulgaris - intraepidermal split, suprabasal level, row of tombstones appearance Pemphigus vegetans (Subtype of PV) - suprabasal Pemphigus foliaceous - sub corneal Pemphigus erythematosus (Subtype of PF) - sub corneal Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50 page 3

644.q: Following is true about pemphigus erythematosus except:
o: It is the rarest type of pemphigus
It is considered as a variant of Pemphigus foliaceous
It is also called as Senear Usher Syndrome
It has features of Lupus erythematosus and pemphigus
644.e: Senear-Usher syndrome is a disorder which results from combination of lupus erythematosus (photosensitivity) and pemphigus foliaceus. Rarest variant of pemphigus: P. vegetans Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, page 6

645.q: Facies leprosa is characterised by all except:
645.e: Nodules on face are not a feature of facies leprosa. Facies leprosa - Seen in lepromatous leprosy Characterized by the resorption of the nasal bone, anterior nasal spine, supra-incisive alveolar region, and anterior alveolar process of the maxilla, with associated sensory or motor damage depending on the type of nerves involved. Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8 th Edition, pg. no 182 International Textbook Of Leprosy, Part I, Section II, Chapter 2.1, Page 16,17

645.q: Which form of leprosy is the Most common form of the disease encountered in India?
645.e: Tuberculoid leprosy(TT) leprosy is the most common form of the disease encountered in India and Africa but is virtually absent in Southeast Asia, where borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy is frequent. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 179, Pg: 1385

645.q: What is The Most commonly affected nerve trunk in leprosy?
645.e: The most commonly affected nerve trunk in leprosy is the ulnar nerve at the elbow, whose involvement results in clawing of the fourth and fifth fingers, loss of dorsal interosseous musculature in the affected hand, and loss of sensation in these distributions Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 179, Pg: 1387

Dermatophyte species which have the capabilities to infect keratin and keratinized tissue including the hair. the dermatophytes prefer a warm, moist environment for growth, and as a consequence, infections are common in tropical regions. Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 32, Page 18

645.q: Which among the following is the only recommended diagnostic test for chlamydia?
645.e: The gold standard for the diagnosis of urogenital chlamydia infections is nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT). This test is run on either the vaginal swabs for women or first-catch urine for men. Testing can also be performed on endocervical or urethral swabs. Swabs should have a wire or plastic shaft; the tip should be dacron or rayon or a cytobrush. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 30, page 13 CDC guidelines 2021

645.q: A 12 years old boy presented with gradually progressive annual plaque on his buttocks with central scarring. What is the most likely diagnosis?
645.e: Gradually progressive annular plaque with central scarring and active margins – lupus vulgaris. Tinea cruris: itchy erythematous annular plaque with central clearing Granuloma annulare: asymptomatic skin colored leion with annular beaded margins. Annular psoriasis: erythematous annular plaque with silvery white scaling Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 27, page 21

645.q: A 12 years old boy presented with gradually progressive annular plaque on his buttocks with central scarring. What is the most likely diagnosis?
645.e: Explanation: Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous tuberculosis in India. It is a chronic, progressive, paucibacillary form occurring in patients with a high degree of immunity to the bacillus. Lesions commonly appear on the legs and buttocks. The plaque enlarges peripherally with serpiginous or verrucous borders , often exceeding 10 cm in diameter, with central discoloration and atrophy . On diascopy, the lesion shows characteristic golden-yellow "apple jelly" nodules . Key Takeaways: Lupus vulgaris = chronic progressive plaque with apple-jelly nodules on diascopy; common on buttocks/legs in India.

645.q: In which of the following disease diascopy is not used?
645.e: Diascopy: pressing a glass slide or a stiff clear colorless piece or plastic onto the skin to cause blanching by compressing blood out of small vessels. This allows colors to be seen. Use of diascopy: Apple jelly nodules: yellow brown lesion seen in lupus vulgaris and sarcoidosis Spider naevi: compression of radiating arterioles Differentiation of erythema and purpura Differentiation of nevus anemicus from nevus achromicus Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 4, page 19

646.e: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome, also known as Ritter disease is a disease characterized by denudation of the skin caused by exotoxin producing strains of the Staphylococcus species, typically from a distant site. Also called as pemphigus neonatorum. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 50, page 27

646.q: Which of the following diseases is not caused by Staphylococcus?
646.e: Characterized by a painful bright red appearance of the involved skin, which forms a sharply demarcated plaque. Involve upper dermal lymphatics. Classic cause: group A streptococci.

646.q: What is the most common cause of follicular pyodermas
646.e: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen of folliculitis and furuncles. Gram-negative pathogens including Klebsiella , Enterobacter , and Proteus species may replace the gram-positive flora on facial skin, nasal mucous membranes, and neighbouring areas, causing gram-negative folliculitis and boils. 'Hot tub' folliculitis is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa contamination of undertreated water in saunas or whirlpools.

It has a non-fluorinated quinolone, antibiotic, showing potent antimicrobial activities against Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. Ozenoxacin inhibit the enzymes DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, involved in the DNA synthesis in bacteria. Approved in to treat non-bullous impetigo in adults and children aged ≥6 months. Also used in treatment of acne

646.q: All of the following are caused by streptococcus pyogenes except
646.e: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus ) is one of the most important bacterial causes of skin and soft tissue infections worldwide. Specifically, this organism causes infections in the superficial epidermis (Non-Bullous Impetigo), the dermal lymphatics (erysipelas), the subcutaneous tissue (cellulitis), the fascia (necrotizing fasciitis), or muscle (myositis and myonecrosis). It is also the etiologic agent of scarlet fever and Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome (StrepTSS). Bullous impetigo - caused by staphylococcus aureus

646.q: Most common skin infection in children is:
646.e: Impetigo is the most common bacterial skin infection in children and manifests as thin, superficial vesiculopustular which soon rupture to form a honey colored crusts.

Mupirocin belongs to the topical antibiotic class of medications and is utilized for managing and treating various skin and soft tissue infections Mupirocin is believed to exert its antimicrobial activity by inhibiting isoleucyl-transfer RNA, thereby obstructing bacterial protein and RNA synthesis, ultimately resulting in cell death. Mupirocin is recognized as the most widely used topical antibiotic globally for treating methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), particularly in cases of impetigo Mupirocin has consistently demonstrated its efficacy in eradicating intranasal MRSA colonization in healthcare settings

646.q: An 18-year-old female presents to the clinic complaining of foul smelling watery vaginal discharge for the past 7 days. A vaginal swab is taken, which shows a pH of 4.9. The discharge gives off a fishy odor when KOH is applied onto it. What is this test called?
646.e: This patient is probably suffering from bacterial vaginosis, as she has typical foul smelling watery discharge, pH greater 4.5, and positive whiff test. Wet mount/gram stain of discharge Bacterial vaginosis can be diagnosed in this case as she meets three out of four Amsel criteria. The first-line treatment for bacterial vaginosis is metronidazole. REFERENCE: IADVL textbook of dermatology, 4 th edition chapter 4

647.q: A 25-year-old female presents with red crusted lesions around the mouth and finger pulps, three months after having had small bowel resection for Crohn's disease. What is the most likely cause of her skin condition?
647.e: The features of this patient who had bowel resection suggest zinc deficiency . Zinc deficiency can lead to a condition called acrodermatitis enteropathica which presents with diarrhea, alopecia, muscle wasting, depression, irritability, and a rash involving the extremities, face (perioral), and perineum . The rash is characterized by vesicular and pustular crusting with scaling and erythema. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:333 Pg: 2532

647.q: In Tzanck smear, multinucleated giant cells are seen in:
647.e: A Tzanck smear is a cytologic technique commonly used in the diagnosis of herpes virus infections (simplex, genitalis, varicella-zoster). An early vesicle is deroofed, and the base of the lesion is scraped gently with a scalpel blade. The material is then placed on a glass slide, air-dried, and stained with Giemsa stain. Multinucleated giant cells suggest the presence of herpes. Another finding - presence of acantholytic cells Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 4, Page 22

647.q: Ballooning degeneration is a characteristic feature of:
647.e: Vesicles in herpetic infections (simplex, genitalis, varicella-zoster ) show degenerative changes characterized by ballooning, the presence of multinucleated giant cells, and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions. Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 27

647.q: Immunomodulator used in treatment of genital warts is
647.e: Imiquimod 5% cream is an immunomodulator Applied OD for 6-10 hours at bed time, 3 times/week X 16 weeks Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 25, page 58

647.q: Post herpetic neuralgia is defined as pain persisting after how many weeks?
647.e: Herpes zoster (Shingles) is caused by reactivation of a latent varicella zoster virus in sensory nerve ganglion. More common is elderly / immuno-suppression. Post herpetic neuralgia is defined as pain persisting beyond 4 weeks since the eruption of acute infection It is a type of allodynia Post herpetic neuralgia could last for 3 months or longer. Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 27

647.q: What is the causative agent of anogenital wart?
647.e: Anogenital warts caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). The most common strains of HPV that cause anogenital warts are 6 and 11. HPV is a double-stranded DNA virus primarily spread through sexual contact Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 55

647.q: All of the following are drugs used in the management of verruca vulgaris except ?
647.e: Salicylic acid is a first-line therapy used to treat warts. Others - Cantharidin, Trichloroacetic acid Oral - Retinoids Surgical - Cryosurgery (Liquid nitrogen (-196ºC)), Carbon dioxide lasers, electrodesiccation and curettage, Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 46

647.q: Verruca plana is caused by which of the following ?
647.e: HPV 3,10 - Plane warts HPV 6,11 - genital warts HPV 2, 4 - verruca vulgaris HPV 5,8 - Epidermodysplasia verruciformis Reference : Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 47

648.e: Answer- D. Hypergonadism LEOPARD syndrome Lentigines Electrocardiographic conduction abnormalities Ocular hypertelorism Pulmonary stenosis Abnormal genitalia Retarded growth Deafness

648.q: Pruritus is seen in all except:
648.e: Dermatological Causes of Pruritus: Autoimmune causes: Dermatitis herpetiformis Pemphigoid Sjogren's syndrome Infectious causes: Dermatophytosis Insect bites Pediculosis Scabies Neoplastic causes: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Mycosis fungoides) Leukemia cutis Genetic causes: Darter's disease Hailey-Hailey disease Inflammatory causes: Atopic dermatitis Contact dermatitis Drug reactions Lichen planus Mastocytosis Miliaria Keloid scar Urticaria Pregnancy causes: Pemphigoid gestationis Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 83, page 4

648.q: Besniers sign is a clinical test described in which of the following disease?
648.e: Besnier's sign: Also referred to as the scratch sign or coup d' ongle sign. In this, the indistinct scales of the macules in P.versicolor can be accentuated by scratching with nail . Psoriasis - Auspitz sign Pityriasis rosea - Hanging curtain sign Reference: Madke B, Nayak C. Eponymous signs in dermatology. Indian Dermatol Online J. 2012 Sep;3(3):159-65. doi: 10.4103/2229-5178.101810. Erratum in: Indian Dermatol Online J. 2013 Apr-Jun;4(2):164. PMID: 23189246; PMCID: PMC3505421.

648.q: Which of the following is not a risk factor for vaginal candidiasis?
648.e: Risk factors for vaginal candidiasis: Antibiotic use, which causes an imbalance in natural vaginal flora Pregnancy Uncontrolled diabetes An impaired immune system Taking oral contraceptives or hormone therapy that increase estrogen levels REFERENCE: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 31

648.q: Which of the following is known as Dhobi's itch?
648.e: Tinea cruris, also known as jock itch/Dhobi itch is an infection involving the genital, pubic, perineal, and perianal skin caused by pathogenic fungi known as dermatophytes. Intertriginous areas are hospitable environments for fungus due to moisture and sweating. Trichophyton rubrum has been isolated most commonly and remains the most frequent cause of tinea cruris worldwide Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 32, Page .46

648.q: The histopathology of Chromoblastomycosis is characterized by
648.e: Chromoblastomycosis histology - In the foreign-body granuloma ,- giant cells engulfed with groups of fungal cells may be seen. They are chestnut or golden brown, and therefore can be easily distinguished in the infiltrate. The cells characteristically divide into several planes of division by thick septa and are termed muriform or sclerotic cells/copper penny bodies Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 32, Page 76

648.q: Which of the following is not a form of leishmaniasis?
648.e: There are four main forms of the disease: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL, also known as kala-azar), Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL), and Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis. CL is the most common form of the disease; VL is the most serious and is almost always fatal if untreated. Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 33, Page 40

648.q: Which of the following fungi cause ectothrix type Tinea capitis?
648.e: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp hairs. It is caused primarily by the dermatophyte species Microsporum and Trichophyton - Dermatophyte species which have the capabilities to infect keratin and keratinized tissue including the hair. Epidermophyton does not cause tinea capitis. Hair will typically get infected in one of three principal ways: Endothrix: where the fungi affect the hair shaft - Trichophyton tonsurans Ectothrix: where the fungi affect the outer sheath root - Microsporum canis Favus: where there is an inflammatory reaction, crusting or scutula, and hair loss : Trichophyton schoenleinii Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 32, Page 38

649.q: True about the burrow of scabies is all except:
o: Burrow is present in stratum granulosum
Burrow appears yellow on woods lamp
Burrows are located in the distribution - hebra circle
Burrow is a classical sign of scabies
649.e: Burrow is present in stratum corneum Burrow appears yellow on woods lamp Burrows are located in the distribution - hebra circle Burrow is a classical sign of scabies Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 34, Page 30

650.q: All are true regarding secondary syphilis except :
650.e: Secondary syphilis presents with a variety of symptoms. The cutaneous manifestations are also varied A diffuse mucocutaneous rash (generally coppery red, non-pruritic and bilaterally symmetrical), coppery brown scaly macules on palms and soles are seen. Most often, the lesions are macular, discrete, reddish brown, and 5 mm or smaller in diameter; however, they can be pustular, annular, or scaling. Vesicular rash is typically absent. Generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy is typical, especially epitrochlear LN. Mucosal - condyloma lata, mucous patches, snail track ulcers - they contain a high load of spirochetes, these lesions are highly contagious. Hair - patchy non-scarring alopecia (Moth-eaten alopecia) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 12

Hutchinson's triad : Common pattern of presentation for congenital syphilis Triad: Interstitial keratitis, Hutchinson incisors, and Eighth nerve deafness Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 31

650.q: The lesions not containing Treponema are:
650.e: Late syphilis not infective are Gumma, neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 28

650.q: Button hole sign can be seen in
650.e: Buttonhole sign In type 1 neurofibromatosis (Von-Recklinghausen's disease), neurofibromas can be invaginated with the tip of index finger back into the subcutis and again reappear after release of pressure. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 80, page 3

650.q: All of the following statements are correct regarding jarisch-Herxheimer reaction except
o: It occurs within 24 hours of penicillin administration
It is a type 3 hypersensitivity reaction
Fever and increased prominence of skin lesions seen
All patients are given steroids to reduce symptoms
650.e: Jarisch Herxheimer reaction (JHR) is a transient clinical phenomenon that occurs in patients infected by spirochetes who undergo antibiotic treatment. It is a type 3 hypersensitivity reaction to breakdown products of the spirochete after the use of antibiotics The symptoms usually begin 2 hours from the administration of the antibiotic and resolve within 24 hours Along with systemic symptoms - body aches, fevers, nausea and vomiting, and flushing, exacerbation of skin lesions is seen Mild reactions are self-limiting and often resolve spontaneously within 24 hours. The patient should be treated for symptoms with antipyretics and kept under observation. More severe cases may need steroids Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 26

650.q: Which of the following statement is incorrect regarding syphilis?
o: The incubation period varies from 9-90 days
Serum from the chancre is infectious
650.e: Syphilis is a bacterial infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum . Due to its many protean clinical manifestations, it has been named the "great imitator and mimicker." T. pallidum is the only treponemal agent that causes venereal disease. Primary syphilis appears 10 to 90 days after exposure to the infection and comprises a painless, indurated ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation with the T. pallidum . Regional lymphadenopathy is common and consists of rubbery lymph nodes. The chancre oozes serum, which is teeming with treponema Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 8.

650.q: The pathology of positive Buschke-ollendorff sign in secondary syphilis is
650.e: First described by Abraham Buschke and Helene Ollendorff Curth, this sign was named after their observation of slight tenderness on applying pressure with a dull probe on papular lesions of palms in secondary syphilis and is due to cutaneous vasculitis. Necrotic keratinocytes are one of the characteristics of secondary syphilis along with plasma cell infiltrate and obliterative end-arteritis are seen. Further, treponema are also present in the dermis. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 13

650.q: All of the following are true about latent syphilis except
650.e: Latent syphilis is a stage at which the features of secondary syphilis have resolved, though patients remain seroreactive They are asymptomatic during the latent phase, and the disease is detected only by serologic tests Latent syphilis is divided into early latent and late latent. The distinction is important because treatment for each is different. The early latent period is the first year after the resolution of primary or secondary syphilis. Late latency syphilis is not infectious About one third of untreated latent syphilis patients go on to develop tertiary syphilis, whereas the rest remain asymptomatic Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 29, page 13

651.q: Correct about stages of LGV is :
651.e: Primary Stage: The patient characteristically develops a painless genital ulcer or papules which are about 1 to 6 mm in size. secondary stage presents with the development of unilateral or bilateral tender inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy (also called buboes), which occurs two to six weeks after the primary stage; this is called the inguinal syndrome. Late stage : necrosis of lymph node when left untreated. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 30, page 17

651.q: You are posted as MO on a rural PHC. A patient comes with painful genital ulcer. You issue a STI kit to him. Which of the following will be provided?
651.e: As a PHC MO, follow the guidelines of syndromic management NACO guidelines. According to it, a painful genital ulcer patient should be given red kit- kit no. 5 It contains tab acyclovir 400mg. Dose : Three tablets a day for 7 days (21 tablets total) Reference: NACO guidelines for Syndromic Management of STI

651.q: Which of the following statements is false about disseminated gonococcal infection?
o: It occurs as a result of direct spread by ascending infections
Classic presentations is with a dermatitis - arthritis syndrome
Skin lesions are small, tender and maculopapular
651.e: DGI occurs when the sexually transmitted pathogen Neisseria gonorrhoeae invades the bloodstream and spreads to distant sites in the body, leading to clinical findings such as septic arthritis, polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, petechial/pustular skin lesions, bacteremia, or, on rare occasions, endocarditis or meningitis. The classic triad of features consists of dermatitis, tenosynovitis and migratory polyarthritis DGI is uncommon and thought to occur in 0.5-3% of untreated gonorrhea cases. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 30, page 5

651.q: Recurrent genital ulcer is caused by:
651.e: Genital herpes MC ulcerative STI among adolescents, is a chronic, lifelong viral infection Two sexually transmitted HSV types have been identified, HSV-1 and HSV-2 Majority of cases of recurrent genital herpes are caused by HSV-2, which is also called HHV2 Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 25, page 20

Trachomatis isolates exist as 15 serovariants. Trachoma - ocular tropic strains (A, B, Ba, and C) Genitourinary tract tropic (D, E, F, G, H, I, J, and K) strains Invasive lymphogranuloma venereum (L1, L2, and L3) The causative agent of LGV is Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 30, page 16

651.q: Pseudo bubo formation is seen in :
651.e: Granuloma Inguinale Genital ulcerative disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacterium Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly known' as Calymmatobacterium granulomatis) Painless, slowly progressive ulcerative lesions on the genitals or perineum without regional lymphadenopathy, subcutaneous granulomas (Pseudo buboes) Lesions are highly vascular (beefy red appearance) and bleed on touch Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 30, page 25

651.q: Secondary stage of LGV is characterised by :
651.e: The secondary stage presents with the development of unilateral or bilateral tender inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy (also called buboes), which occurs two to six weeks after the primary stage; this is called the inguinal syndrome. An anorectal syndrome also presents which is characterized by proctitis or proctocolitis-like symptoms. Pain during urination, rectal bleeding, pain during passing stools, abdominal pain, anal pain, tenesmus. Generalized symptoms like body aches, headache, and fever can occur during this stage.
