This syndrome usually occurs when the transmission is via the anal route. An oral syndrome can occur in people get LGV through the oral route. Cervical lymphadenopathy can occur. There are also reports of systemic complications like pneumonia and hepatitis. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 30, page 18

651.q: Which of the following is not considered as a sexually transmitted infection?
651.e: Bacterial vaginosis is not considered as an STI. It is usually caused by imbalance between aerobic and anaerobic flora of the vagina. However it is mostly seen in sexually active women, with new partner or multiple partners. It is rare in virgins. REFERENCE: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 31

652.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Essential fatty acid In vitamin 'A' deficiency there is toad like skin also known as phrynoderma. o But this is due to associated deficiency of essential fatty acids.

652.q: In congenital dystrophic variety of epidermolysis bullosa, mutation is seen in the gene coding for:
652.e: There are two types of EB Acquired and Congenital The congenital has 3 types (Simple x, Junctional and Dystrophic) Keratin 14 : EB Simplex Laminin 4, Alpha 6 integrin : Junctional EB Collagen type 7: Dystrophic EB Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition Chapter 71, page 2

652.q: Which of the following is/are correct regarding Hailey-Hailey disease? 1. Steroid not ffective 2. ATP2Cl impairment 3. Autosomal recessive 4. Flexural distribution 5. Benign pemphigus
652.e: Hailey-Hailey Disease Synonym: Benign familial pemphigus Autosomal dominant inheritance ATP2Cl enzyme insufficiency Flexural distribution: Painful erosions, vesico-pustules and scaly erythematous plaques appear at sites of friction such as the sides of the neck, the axillae, the groins and the perineum. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 66, page 10

652.q: The etiology of congenital epidermolysis bullosa is:
652.e: Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of mechanobullous disorders in which the skin breaks down and blister forms due to minor trauma. It is a genetic disorder with mutations in skin proteins. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition Chapter 71, Page 2

652.q: A 8-day-old child with history of consanguinity in the parents, the mother reports blisters and peeling off of the skin at the site of handling and pressure. There was a similar history in the previous child, which proved to be fatal. The diagnosis is:
652.e: Diseases characterized under the general term epidermolysis bullosa are a heterogeneous group of hereditary blistering disorders. All of them are characterized by induction of blisters by trauma and exacerbation of blistering in warm weather. Disorders can be categorized in 3 main headings, viz. epidermolysis bullosa simplex, junctional epidermolysis bullosa and dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa. Affected infant is usually blistered at birth or develops lesions during the neonatal period. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition Chapter 71, page 11

652.q: Direct Immunofluorescence is negative in all except
652.e: DIF is positive only in the immunobullous group of disorders due to presence of auto-antibody-antigen complexes in the skin. So, it will be positive in EB acquisita as it is a subepidermal IB disorder DIF will be negative in diseases which have a genetic etiology like Congenital EB, hailey hailey disease, darriers disease and Transient acantholytic dermatoses (Grovers disease). Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 66, Page 1

652.q: In the congenital dystrophic form of epidermolysis bullosa, which gene is mutated?
652.e: Explanation: Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) has acquired and congenital Among congenital types: Simplex, Junctional, and Dystrophic, each is linked to a specific structural protein defect: EB Simplex: Mutation is seen in Keratin 14 Junctional EB: Mutations happen in Laminin 4 and α6 integrin Dystrophic EB: Caused by mutations in Collagen type VII , the main component of anchoring fibrils Collagen VII defect is characteristic of dystrophic EB .

652.q: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is a hereditary condition commonly associated with multiple café-au-lait spots on the skin. Which pattern of inheritance is seen in this?
652.e: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1) or Von Recklinghausen disease is an autosomal dominant disorder. It is the most common hamartoma neoplastic syndrome The gene for NF-1 is located on chromosome 17 and encodes a gene product called neurofibromin Neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein, normally inhibits the rat sarcoma (RAS) pathway. Mutations of the NF-1 gene result in a lack of expression of neurofibromin, thereby promoting tumorigenesis. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, Chapter 80, page 1

653.q: Which of the following is not nevus of melanocyte?
653.e: Epidermal naevi Keratinocytic/hyperkeratotic/verrucous epidermal naevus Inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal naevus (ILVEN) Sebaceous naevus Pigment cell naevi Congenital melanocytic naevus Congenital blue naevus Congenital naevus spilus Congenital Spitz naevus Mongolian blue spot (dermal melanocytosis) Connective tissue naevi - Shagreen patch Muscle naevi Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma Leiomyoma Fat naevi - Congenital lipoma unclassifiable naevi - Becker naevus Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 75, page 2

653.q: The most common site of morphea is:
653.e: Sites of morphea: Upper trunk (MC), buttocks & legs Linear lesions on extremities & fate (en coupe sabre) Reference: Rook's textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 57, Page 11

653.q: Which of the following is not seen in Dermatomyositis?
653.e: Clinical Features of Dermatomyositis Itchy lesion Facial lesion's: Heliotrope erythema, malar erythema, oedema Gottron's papule: Violaceous, atrophic papules over knuckles and pressure points Gottron's sign: Symmetrical, somewhat linear, lilac papulosquamous plaques Telangiectasia and ragged cuticles Poikiloderma: Hyperpigmentation, hypo pigmentation, telangiectasia and atrophy Mechanic's hand: Confluent symmetric hyperkeratosis along ulnar aspect of thumb and radial aspect of fingers Calcinosis cutis Shawl sign: Symmetrical confluent violaceous erythema extending from dorsolateral aspect of forearms and arms to deltoid region, shoulder and neck Reference: Rook's textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 53, Page 6

653.q: The most abundant form of collagen present in dermis is
653.e: Dermis forms a major part of the skin and is highly vascular, primarily consisting of the extracellular matrix of connective tissue. Type I collagen is the predominant type of collagen present in the dermis, approximately 80% of the total collagen Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 2, page 27

653.q: Identify the false statement regarding Discoid lupus erythematosus.
o: Topical steroids is the first line treatment for localized lesions
Hydroxychloroquine is effective in disseminated lesions
653.e: General measures, such as sun avoidance, avoidance of photosensitizing medications, and liberal application of sunscreen. Current first-line treatment for DLE consists of photoprotection in conjunction with topical or intralesional corticosteroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors. Antimalarials Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ)- are considered first-line systemic therapy for CLE. Reference: Rook's textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 51, Page 3

653.q: Which antibody is associated with subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus?
653.e: subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is a subtype of LE presenting as symmetric, non-scarring photosensitive erythematous rash usually over sun-exposed areas like face, neck, arms, upper back, and shoulders. The systemic lupus erythematosus lesions have a characteristic distribution with either papulosquamous lesions or annular lesions with central clearing. Patients with SCLE frequently have a mild illness with musculoskeletal complaints and serologic abnormalities. Laboratory studies 0 anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La Reference: Rook's textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 51, Page 11

653.q: Carpet tack sign is described in which of the following?
653.e: Carpet tack sign is a characteristic sign of DLE. It is also known as "cat's tongue sign" or "tin tack sign" It occurs due to the accumulation of scales in the hair follicles with resultant loss of hair. Later on, when scales are peeled off, typical keratotic spikes become visible producing characteristic "carpet-tack sign". Reference: Rook's textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 51, Page 3

653.q: A patient presents with difficulty in climbing stairs and combing hair. On examination, violaceous macular erythema is noted in the periorbital area. What is the diagnosis?
653.e: In the patient - violaceous macular erythema is noted in the periorbital area - Heliotrope rash difficulty in climbing stairs and combing hair - s/o proximal myopathy Together - diagnosis is Dermatomyositis Myositis (Weakness of proximal muscles), Difficulty in speech and swallowing, Cardiomyopathy, Reynaud's phenomenon, Arthralgia Reference: Rook's textbook of dermatology, 9 th Edition, Chapter 53, Page 6

654.q: A naevus present at birth which has predisposition to the development of malignant melanoma is-
654.e: Congenital melanocytic nevi are classified according to their estimated adult size as small (less than 1.5 cm), medium (1.5 to 20 cm), large (20 to 40 cm), and giant (>40 cm). This classification is essential as the size of nevi is one of the main risk factors of melanoma development and neurological involvement. CMNs frequently present with a garment appearance (in a bathing trunk, in coat sleeve, Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 143, page 143.2

654.q: Mycosis fungoides is a malignancy of -
654.e: This is the most common variant of primary CTCL; it is generally associated with an indolent clinical course Mycosis fungoides is characterized by polymorphic patches and plaques usually involving limb/girdle sites, the breast and especially the buttock area. The histological hallmark of the mycosis fungo ides is the presence of the Sezary-Lutzner cells. These are CD4 helper T cells. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 140, page 140.1

654.q: Mycosis fungoides which is not true-
o: It is the most common form of cutaneous lymphoma
Indolent course and good prognosis, easily amenable to treatment
Erythroderma seen and spreads to peripheral circulation
654.e: Mycosis fungoides is an indolent cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (indolent course. but is inevitably fatal (not easily amenable to treatment), except for patients in stage I. MF is the most common primary cutaneous lymphoma. Pautrier microabscess is characteristic of MF. Erythroderma can occur in MF (Sezary syndrome) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 140, page 140.10

Characteristic microscopic finding in sarcoidosis: Discrete, compact, non-caseating epithelioid cell granuloma' CD4+, CD8+ T lymphocytes and, to a lesser extent, B lymphocytes form a concentric rim around the epithelioid granuloma Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 98, page 3

654.q: Which of the following is associated with sun exposure?
654.e: Actinic keratosis or solar keratosis are a reflection of abnormal skin cell development due to exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 142, page 142.1

654.q: The most common premalignant tumour of skin is-
654.e: Actinic keratosis/Solar keratosis/ Keratosis senilis - Actinic keratoses are premalignant cutaneous lesions that may progress to squamous cell carcinoma. These lesions commonly appear on sun-exposed areas of the skin in individuals with a history of cumulative sun exposure. Common locations for actinic keratoses include the face, scalp (bald or thinning hair), back of the arms, and dorsal aspect of the hands. individuals with actinic keratosis may present with irregular, red, scaly papules or plaques on sun-exposed regions of the body The primary histopathologic feature of actinic keratosis is the presence of atypical keratinocytes(dyskeratotic cells)within sun-damaged skin that is limited to the lower third of the epidermis Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 142, page 142.2

654.q: Total Skin Electron Beam therapy is used for the treatment of -
654.e: Total Skin Electron Radiation is used primary in patients with Mycosis Fungoides. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 140, page 140.22

654.q: Which of the following skin malignancies are seen in Xeroderma pigmentosum patients ?
654.e: The median age for the development of their first non-melanoma skin cancer is about 9. The common skin cancers in XP patients include Basal cell carcinomas (BCC)Squamous cell carcinomas (SCC), keratoacanthoma-SCC type and malignant melanoma Given the wide variation of clinical presentation of various skin cancers, patients with xeroderma pigmentosum must be followed closely for regular total body skin exams by a dermatologist. The mainstay of management is the avoidance of UVR exposure from sunlight through the application of high-factor sunscreen

655.e: During development of the epidermis, first layer to form is S. Basale and subsequently, layers form from below upwards. The principal function of epidermis is constant replacement of the stratum corneum which is being continuously shed and replaced Total epidermal cell turnover time is 52-75 days. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 2

655.q: All of the following statements are true regarding the skin, except that ____.
o: Langerhans cells originate from bone marrow and are present in granular layer.
Melanocytes are present in stratum basale.
Stratified squamous epithelium with hallmark keratin intermediate filaments.
Merkel cells are present in stratum basale.
655.e: The epidermis is a keratinized, stratified, squamous epithelium and the hallmark filaments are the keratin intermediate filaments. Melanocytes originate from neural crest and are present in stratum basale. Merkel cells originate from ectoderm and are present in stratum basale. Langerhans cells are dendritic cells which originate from bone marrow and function as antigen presenting cells. They are present in stratum spinosum Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 1

655.q: Which of the following component in the skin give protection from UV radiation?
655.e: Present in Stratum Germinativum/ Basal Cell Layer Contains Melanocytes which produce melanin Sun exposure increase melanin production to prevent damage from UV rays (sun tanning) Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 2, page 17

655.q: An 18-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of a white spot on his back. You suspect nevus anemicus and perform skin biopsy. What will be the findings?
655.e: Skin biopsy of a nevus anemicus lesion will show normal findings, including an uninvolved epidermis with normal melanocyte number and distribution. Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9 th edition, chapter 70, page 5

655.q: What is the ratio of Type 1 to Type 3 collagen in the adult human skin?
655.e: Most collagen fibrils are comprised of several collagen types and are called heterotypic Collagen fibrils are made of collagens I and III in skin. Type 1 is most abundant collagen in skin (80%) and second most common is type 3 (10. Type 2 collagen is not found in skin and is unique to cartilage. The ratio between type I and Ill collagen is 8:1. The rating of Type 1 to Type 3 collagen in the adult human skin is 8:1 and increases with age Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 2, page 27

655.q: All of the following are true about skin except ?
o: Skin accounts for 15% of total body weight
Dermis is made up of type 1 and type 3 collagen
655.e: Epidermis, keratinocytes, merkel cells originate from ectoderm. Langerhans cells and dermis originates from mesoderm. Skin weight is 4-5 kg and makes 15% of total body weight. Most collagen fibrils are comprised of several collagen types and are called heterotypic. Collagen fibrils are made of collagens I and III in skin. Type 1 is most abundant collagen in skin (80%) and second most common is type 3 . Type 2 collagen is not found in skin and is unique to cartilage. The ratio between type I and Ill collagen is 8:1 and increased along with increase in age. Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 2, page 1

655.q: Pre-malignant condition of the skin include all of the following EXCEPT:
655.e: Acanthosis nigricans is not pre malignant: It is a paraneoplastic condition associated with gastric adenocarcinoma. Pre-malignant skin lesions: Cutaneous horns, Keratoacanthoma, 'Bowen's disease, Actinic keratoses, Arsenical keratoses, Leukoplakia Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 142, Chapter 142, page 1

655.q: Which of the following is/ are associated with Acanthosis nigricans? 1. Carcinoma stomach 2. Obesity 3. Insulin resistance 4. Hemochromatosis
655.e: Associated Features of Acanthosis Nigricans Obesity, Diabetes mellitus, Metabolic syndrome Hyperandrogenism, Cushing syndrome polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) HAIR -AN syndrome - HAIR-AN-a syndrome of hyperandrogenism(HA), insulin resistance (IR) and acanthosis nigricans (AN)-is a specific and rare subphenotype of the polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) characterised by the presence of severe insulin resistance. Drugs : Nicotinic acid,, Corticosteroids, Oral contraceptives Gastric adenocarcinoma Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9 th edition, chapter 89, page 3

656.q: All are true regarding Sunitinib except -
o: It is used for renal cell carcinoma
It is used for the treatment of GIST
It is excreted primarily in urine
656.e: Ans. is 'd' i.e., It is excreted primarily in urine Sunitinib inhibits multiple Tyrosine kinase receptors. It inhibits PDGF, VEGF and c-kit. o Sunitinib and sorafinib are used in renal cell carcinoma (in RCC there is overexpression of VEGF) and GIST (in GIST there is over expression of C-Kit & PDGF). o It is eliminated primarily by hepatic route with excretion in faeces.

656.q: Meningitis with rash is seen in -
656.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Neisseria meningitidis om

656.q: All of the following are features of juvenile CML except -
656.e: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Philadelphia chromosome is positive Juvenile CML is mostly seen in children below 2 years of age. Philadelphia chromosome is negative and leukocyte count is less than 100'000/mm3. Features Adult CML Juvenile CML Age 10-12 years 100'000 < 100'000 WBC type Granulocyte Monocyte Normoblastic Unusual Common HbF Normal Increased Immunoglobulins Normal Increased Muramidase levels Normal Increased Response to Busulphan Good Poor Survival 2.5-3 years 9 months
Answer- A. 5 gm/kg/day In malnourish child if there > 10 gm/kg/day = good weight gain 5-10 gm/kg/day = moderate weight gain < 5 gm/kg/day = poor weight gain

656.q: Hereditary angioneurotic edema is due to ?
656.e: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Deficiency of C1 inhibitor Hereditary angioneurotic edema is due to C1inhibitor (Ci esterase inhibitor) deficiency.

657.q: Most common bone for which nailing is done
657.e: Answer- C. Tibia Most common bones for which intramedullary nailing is done are Tibia and femur.

657.q: Most common organism causing infection after open fracture
657.e: Answer- A. Pseudomonas staphylococcus aureus was the most common organism causing infection in open fractures. More recent studies have shown that gram negative organisms such as pseudomonas aeruginosa and E.coli are becoming more common

657.q: Tension band wiring is indicated in fracture of which of the following ?
657.e: Tension band wiring is indicated in the treatment of two types of olecranon fracture. First type is a clean break with separation of the fragments, and second type is comminuted fracture of the olecranon with displced fragments. A crack in the olecranon without displacement is treated by immobilising the elbow in an above elbow plaster slab in 30 degrees of flexion.

657.q: An athlete who has been training constantly for 6 months for the upcoming national selections has pain over posteromedial aspect of right leg. He has point tenderness on the posteromedial aspect of mid tibia and the pain is aggravated by activity. What is the treatment plan?
657.e: From the history, patient has stress fracture. Stress fractures are generally managed conservatively with cast immobilization. Exception is stress fracture of neck of femur, which might require surgical fixation. Reference: Rockwood and green adult fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-668

657.q: All of the following is used for giving skeletal traction except:
657.e: Rush pin is used for pediatric diaphyseal fracture fixation. All other devices are used for giving traction. Reference- Rockwood and Green’s adult fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-214

657.q: Open fracture in a child of 2 ½ years is managed by?
657.e: In pediatric patients generally managed conservatively so option a, c, d are not true. And for open fracture debridement is more important. Reference- Rockwood and green's pediatric fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-124

657.q: Which of the following statement is false
o: All fractures heal with callus formation
All intra articular fracture requires anatomical reduction
Relative stability involves restoring length, rotation and alignment
Fracture healing requires combined activity of osteoblast and osteoclast cells
657.e: Fracture healing is of two types. Direct and indirect bone healing. Direct bone healing occurs without callus formation. Indirect healing occurs with callus formation. Reference- Rockwood and green’s adult fracture trauma 8ᵗʰ edition, page-198

657.q: 10 days old open grade-3A fracture shaft of tibia with pus discharge should be treated with?
o: Closed reduction and intramedullary reamed nail
657.e: Open fracture with improper soft tissue condition is an indication for external fixation. Infection is considered a contraindication for any kind of implant fixation Reference- AO trauma basic trauma manual- Principle of open fracture management and its complication

658.q: In a patient with compartment syndrome, which of the following signs would be the last to appear?
658.e: Whenever perfusion to an extremity is inadequate (e.g., trauma or poor perfusion), hypoxic edema develops, producing swelling. When this occurs in a compartment, tissue pressures rise, decreasing capillary perfusion. Symptoms of compartment syndrome include extreme pain unrelieved by analgesics, paresthesias, paralysis, and pallor. Extensive rhabdomyolysis may develop as well as permanent nerve and muscle injury in the compartment. Because the problem is at the tissue level, pulses and capillary refill may still be present. Treatment includes fasciotomy to relieve the elevated pressure Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, p 1514; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 2450.

658.q: Not a common cause of compartment syndrome
658.e: Compartment syndrome is defined as the elevation of pressure in a closed fascial compartment causing a decrease in perfusion to the limb leading to irreversible muscle and neurovascular damage. So in compartment syndrome, by definition there must be a closed fascial compartment for the pressure to build up and rise. In a gun shot injury, there will be bullet wounds, making the fascial compartments open, and hence making compartment syndrome unlikely. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 47

658.q: Which is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome?
658.e: The earliest sign of compartment syndrome pain on passive stretch. Compartment syndrome is defined as the elevation of pressure in a closed fascial compartment causing a decrease in perfusion to the limb leading to irreversible muscle and neurovascular damage. The clinical features of compartment syndrome are summarized as the 6 Ps of compartment syndrome, which are Pain Pallor Pulselessness Paresthesia Paralysis Pain on passive stretch (earliest and most important) Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 47

658.q: A 20-year-old man sustained a closed tibial fracture and is treated with a reamed intramedullary nail. What is the most common complication associated with this treatment?
658.e: The most common complication of reamed intramedullary nailing is anterior knee pain (57%). The knee pain is activity related (92%) and exacerbated by kneeling (83%). Although knee pain is the most common complication, most patients rate it as mild to moderate and only 10% are unable to return to previous employment. The incidence of the other complications is: infection 0% to 3%, nonunion 0% to 6%, and malunion 2% to 13%. Compartment syndrome is rare after nailing. Reference- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31315794/#:~:text=Introduction%3A%20The%20treatment%20of%20choice,47.4%25%20in%20meta%2Danalyses.

658.q: Most commonly fractured carpal bone is
658.e: Scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. These patients present with pain & swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist following fall on out stretched hand. The most important clinical sign is tenderness in the anatomical snuff box. Oblique view of the wrist is the best radiographic view to diagnose it. Scaphoid is most commonly fractured at its waist (at the junction of anterior & mid one thirds) in adults while the commonest site for fracture in a child is the distal pole. Very important point to note is that, the common complications of scaphoid fractures- nonunion and AVN usually occur most often in proximal pole fractures. Reference: Maheshwari, Orthopaedics, 5th ed page no 95

658.q: A 55-year-old woman is noted to have a traumatic injury to her right thigh. Which of the following is most sensitive for the diagnosis of compartment syndrome?
658.e: Pain typically severe and out of proportion to the injury, represents the first and most sensitive symptom of compartment syndrome. Pain, however, is extremely nonspecific . A better sign is pain on passive stretch, which by itself can be used as an indication to do fasciotomy. Pulselessness represents a very late finding, and therefore the finding of a palpable pulse should not exclude compartment syndrome in your differential diagnosis. Reference- Maheshwari Ortho 5th edition, page number 47.

658.q: The preferred treatment of cubitus varus is
658.e: Cubitus varus deformity can be treated with lateral closing wedge osteotomy or medial opening wedge osteotomy. A named lateral closing wedge osteotomy is French osteotomy. Cubitus valgus is treated with medial closing wedge osteotomy or lateral opening wedge osteotomy Closing wedge osteotomies are preferred as it avoids complications related to bone healing such as nonunion which is seen in open wedge osteotmies. Reference: Paediatric Orthopaedics: A System of Decision-Making, Second Edition By Benjamin Joseph, P141

658.q: Which fracture among the options has the highest risk of avascular necrosis?
658.e: Fracture of the scaphoid is notorious for AVN. Scaphoid fracture can occur at 3 sites – distal pole, waist and proximal pole. All complications of scaphoid fracture, be it non union or AVN occurs maximally in proximal pole fractures, followed by waist # and distal pole. This I so because of the abnormal blood supply of the scaphoid, where the blood vessel enters distally and goes proximally, thereby making the proximal pole the least vascular part of the scaphoid. If proximal pole of scaphoid was given in the options, it would have been the answer. But from the available options, the best choice would be waist of scaphoid #. Reference- Maheshwari ortho 5th edition, page no 115

659.q: A 67 year old woman has neck pains and occipital headaches for 2 years. She is referred to the neurology outpatients for assessment. Investigations showed a normal CT of the brain. Cervical X ray showed degenerative changes of narrowed disc spaces and loss of cervical lordosis. What is the likely diagnosis?
659.e: In cervical spondylosis, several overlapping syndromes are seen: neck and shoulder pain, suboccipital pain and headache, radicular symptoms, and cervical spondylotic myelopathy. Examination findings include neck pain, radicular signs, and myelopathic signs. Cervical spine films can demonstrate disk space narrowing, osteophytosis, loss of cervical lordosis, uncovertebral joint hypertrophy, apophyseal joint osteoarthritis, and vertebral canal diameter. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3452

659.q: Not true about congenital muscular torticollis
o: Can be associated with a mass
659.e: Congenital muscular torticollis occurs because of the contracture of sternocleidomastoid muscle and there is no fusion of vertebrae. Fusion of vertebrae is seen in Klippel Feil syndrome. Sometimes a mass can be palpable in the SCM which is the fibrotic muscle. Reference: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics 5th edition page no. 169

659.q: A 50 year old female presented with sudden onset pain, weakness and wasting of muscles of arm. She gives history of getting a TT injection in the deltoid 5 days back. What is the diagnosis?
659.e: Tetanus toxoid injections can rarely lead to brachial plexus neuritis. This presents as sudden onset pain, paresthesia and weakness of the affected arm. It can also lead to muscle wasting in the long run. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1513

660.q: Proximal humerus fracture which has maximum chances of avascular necrosis
660.e: Answer- D. Four part Neer's classified proximal humerus fracture into 4 types, based on these four segments :

660.q: 32 year old pregnant female with 2 months of amenorrhea comes with mid clavicle fracture. What is your treatment of choice?
660.e: Clavicle fracture is commonly managed conservatively but in young female for cosmetic reasons, some surgeons prefer to perform plate fixation. But in case of young pregnant female, it is an absolute contraindication to operate any fracture in first trimester of pregnancy. Reference- Campbell operative procedure 13ᵗʰ edition, page-3054

660.q: 17-year-old high school tennis player trips while returning a serve and sustains a right mid-shaft clavicle fracture. Which of the following increases the risk of nonunion in the nonoperative treatment of clavicle fractures?
660.e: Displacement and comminution have been shown to increase risk of non- union in nonoperative management. There are no significant differences between outcomes when using sling immobilization versus a figure-of-eight bandage. Reference- Fundamentals of Orthopaedics 1st edition, page no. 44

660.q: A 55 year old electrician fell down after sustaining an electric shock and injured his left shoulder. On examination the patient was unable to abduct or externally rotate the shoulder. What is the diagnosis?
660.e: Falls after an electric shock/ epileptic fit or Extreme trauma can cause posterior shoulder dislocation. These etiologies are together called the triple E syndrome. Injury mechanism in electrical injury is similar to epileptic seizures, where the shoulder is forced to internal rotation, flexion and adduction. Classical deformity in posterior shoulder dislocation is adduction and internal rotation. This means that the patient will be unable to abduct or externally rotate his shoulder. Luxation erecta is another name for inferior dislocation of shoulder. Reference- The Shoulder volume 1, Charles A Rockwood, P 151

660.q: An acute posterior shoulder dislocation should be suspected in a patient with pain and the shoulder locked in what position?
660.e: Patients with posterior shoulder dislocations are often overlooked as it is not associated with gross deformities or severe pain. Further posterior dislocation is also difficult to pick up on xrays. They usually present with a history of fall after electric shock, epileptic seizure or severe trauma. O/E, the shoulder would be locked in internal rotation and adduction and lack external rotation. Orthogonal radiographs (anterior-posterior and axillary lateral) are absolutely necessary for proper diagnosis. Posterior dislocation patients often have reverse Bankart and reverse Hill-Sachs lesions. Posterior dislocation is treated with closed reduction and immobilization Reference - Maheshwari Ortho 5 th edition page no 89

660.q: Which of the following shoulder positions presents the greatest risk for anterior dislocations of shoulder especially in a patient suffering from recurrent disloctions?
660.e: Abduction and external rotation is the position in which, most of the recurrent shoulder dislocations occur. For e.g. throwing a ball, playing a smash in badminton or volleyball, sleeping with hand under the head etc. Rarely a direct blow on the front of the shoulder can cause the head of the humerus to be pushed out posteriorly Reference - Essential Orthopaedics, Maheshwari, 5th ed. P 90

o: Supraspinatus tendon is most commonly involved
Mid range of abduction alone may be painful
Surgical decompression is the first line of treatment
660.e: Shoulder impingement is treated conservatively in majority of the case. Surgical decompression is rarely indicated. Shoulder impingement results from compression of the rotator cuff between the Acromion process and the Humeral head. Supraspinatus us the most commonly affected tendon. Impingement can present with painful arc syndrome, where the initial 60 degrees and the final 60 degrees of shoulder abduction will be pain free. However the mid abduction i.e, between 60 and 120 degrees will be painful. Prolonged impingement can cause rotator cuff tears. The tests for impingement are - Neer's test and Hawkin's test. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 833

660.q: A 55 year old lady who is a known case of diabetes, presents with severe pain and stiffness of the right shoulder for the last 3 months. O/E, there is global restriction of both active and passive movements of the right shoulder. X ray is normal. What is the diagnosis?
660.e: Global restriction of both active and passive movements of the shoulder is seen in post traumatic stiffness and adhesive capsulitis. In this patient the diagnosis is adhesive capsulitis because No history of trauma Normal x ray Presence of diabetes, which is the most important risk factor for adhesive capsulitis. Adhesive capsulitis is also called Periarthritis or Frozen shoulder It is an idiopathic condition characterized by global reduction in passive and active range of motion of shoulder due to fibrosis and adhesions in the capsule It is usually self limiting, but it takes a lot of time for that. It is usually treated conservatively with physiotherapy. Surgery is rarely indicated. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 858

661.q: True about supracondylar fracture of humerus
661.e: Answer- B. Extension type most common Supracondylar humeral fractures are the most common elbow fractures in children. Most common age group affected is 5-8 years. Boys are affected more than girls. Left side is more common than right. Extension type is most common

661.q: The malunion of supracondylar fracture of the humerus most commonly leads to:
661.e: B i.e. Cabitus Varus Malunion : - It is the commonest complication of supracondylar fracture and results in cubitus varus (Gun stock deformity). Cubitus valgus is rare and may occur occasionally in posterolateral displacement.

661.q: What is seen on x-ray with posterior elbow dislocation
661.e: Answer- A. Coronoid process posterior to humerus AP view : Greater superimposition of distal humerus with proximal ulna and olecranon (normally, only terminal part of humerus is superimposed).

661.q: Volkmanns contracture, which artery is involved
661.e: Answer- B. Brachial Injury to brachial artery may cause nerve and muscle ischemia (Volkmann's ischemia of flexor compartment) or may result in postischemic swelling due to edema or hemorrhage, thereby causing compartment syndrome, which can cause, if not treated immediatealy, Volkmann's ischaemic contracture later on.

661.q: The 'terrible triad' injury of the elbow consists of radial head fracture, elbow dislocation and which of the following fracture?
661.e: The terrible triad of the elbow is a severe elbow fracture-dislocation pattern with the following features: Posterior elbow dislocation Coronoid process fracture Radial head fracture Reference: Manish kumar varshney 1st edition page no 978

661.q: Which of the following injuries would require plating of the radius along with closed reduction and evaluation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ)?
661.e: A Galeazzi fracture is a fracture of the distal third of the radius with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint. It commonly results from a fall onto an outstretched hand with the forearm in pronation. A Galeazzi fracture is an injury that requires surgical treatment. The algorithm includes anatomic reduction and fixation of the radial shaft, and closed reduction of the DRUJ with assessment of stability. If the DRUJ remains unstable, supination of the wrist may reduce the DRUJ. Otherwise, either open or closed reduction with pinning can be undertaken to stabilize the joint. The closer the radius fracture is to the DRUJ, the more likely it is to be unstable. Acute intervention results in improved outcomes as compared to delayed reconstruction. Reference: Maheshwari ortho 5th edition page no 111

661.q: Which of the following statements best describe the terrible triad of Hodgkiss?
o: Flexion-type supracondylar fracture with radial head and elbow dislocation
Coronoid fracture, olecranon fracture and elbow dislocation
Coronoid fracture, radial head fracture and elbow dislocation
661.e: The combination of valgus, axial, and posterolateral rotatory forces (forearm supination) can result in a "terrible triad" injury of the elbow. The key features of a terrible triad injury include a radial head fracture, coronoid fracture, and dislocation of the elbow. Disruption of the lateral collateral ligament complex often concomitantly occurs. While restoration of the bony anatomy is important for static stability, the key primary stabilizer that needs to be addressed is the lateral collateral ligament complex. In acute injuries LCL repair may be possible. In chronic injury, LCL reconstruction would need to be considered. Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1 st edition, page number 979

661.q: Following dislocation of shoulder, patient developed weakness of flexion of elbow and sensory loss over the lateral aspect of forearm. Which nerve is injured ?
661.e: Weakness of flexion of elbow and sensory loss over the lateral aspect of forearm is seen in Musculocutaneous N injury. This occurs due to the palsy of Brachialis and Biceps which are supplied by the Musculocutaneous nerve. The Lateral cutaneous N of forearm is also a branch of Musculocutaneous N, hence the sensory loss. Musculocutaneous N is the second most commonly injured nerve in shoulder dislocation after the Axillary N. Reference: Koval's Handbook of fracture's 5th edition, page no. 173

662.q: A 60 year old postmenopausal woman came with reports of DEXA scan which showed a t score of -2.5. She had a history of colles fracture 6 months back which was fixed. She is not a smoker and does not consume alcohol. Which of the following is correct about her further management?
662.e: The patient is a post menopausal female with t score of -2.5, with a past history of Colles fracture, is an indication for anti resorptive treatment. The anti-resorptive agent in the given option is alendronate.

662.q: Most common complication of Colles fracture?
662.e: The complication rate is 55%, with the most common complication being some degree of residual finger and wrist stiffness (39%). Most common complication of Colles fracture → Finger stiffness, 2nd most common complication of Colles fracture → Malunion Complications of Colles fracture: Stiffness of fingers and joints Stiffness of finger; wrist and shoulder are the most common avoidable complication of collie's fracture. This occurs due to lack of exercise. Therefore, patient should be encouraged for active exercise of finger and shoulder. Malunion It is the second most common complication It results in dinner fork deformity Sudek's osteodystrophy (reflex sympathetic dystrophy) Carpal tunnel syndrome: Median nerve may get compressed in carpal tunnel Carpal instability Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus tendon TFCC injury Reference: Maheshwari 4th /e p. 110

662.q: An extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation is also known as a...
662.e: A Colles fracture consists of a fracture of the distal radius at the cortico cancellous junction with dorsal angulation and impaction, but without the involvement of the articular surface. Chauffeur’s fracture is an intraarticular fracture of radial styloid A die-punch fracture is a depressed intra-articular fracture of the lunate fossa of the distal radius Barton fracture is an intraarticular fracture involving the dorsal/ volar lip of the distal radius with subluxation of the carpus and hand bones. Reference: Maheshwari ortho 5th edition page no 111

662.q: All are complications of Colles fracture except
662.e: Malunited Colles fracture can cause Extensor pollicis longus tendon rupture. It will not produce FPL rupture. Complications of Colles fracture are Joint stiffness Malunion - causes dinner fork deformity Carpal tunnel syndrome Sudek's osteodystrophy EPL tendon rupture Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 114

The Piano-Key Sign Test is a test carried out for the clinical assessment of wrist instability. It is used as an indicator for distal radio-ulnar joint instability and tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex of the wrist. TECHNIQUE: In the Piano-key Sign Test, the wrist is supported in pronation and the hand is stabilized in the neutral position. Force is applied to the head of ulna. The test is positive if the ulnar head goes back to its anatomic position after the removal of the force applied to the ulnar head. This bears resemblance with when a piano key springs up after the force from a finger is removed from the key, hence, the name 'piano-key' sign. This instability and pain are judged relative to the contralateral wrist. No instability or movement observed on removal of pressure on the ulnar head. Reference: Manish kumar varshney 1st edition page no 1674

Radiological findings in RA Soft tissue shadow at the level of the joint because of joint effusion or synovial hypertrophy Reduced joint space Erosion of articular margins Subchondral cysts Juxta-articular osteopenia Deformities of the hand and fingers Reference- Manish Kumar Varshney 1st edition page no 405

663.q: A 50 year old male suffers an injury to the right upper limb, resulting in a fracture. He is also unable to dorsiflex his fingers and there is no sensory loss. Which fracture can cause this presentation?
o: Fracture of Humerus at Spiral Grove
Fracture of the Neck of Humerus
663.e: The patient presents with a fracture in the upper limb plus finger drop and no sensory loss. This means that the patient's fracture has caused a Posterior interosseous N (PIN) injury. PIN passes very close to the head and neck of radius and can be injured if there is a fracture or dislocation in this region. So, the answer is fracture of radial neck. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 2038

663.q: Which is the most common muscle involved in pseudotumor formation in hemophilia?
663.e: Sometimes, there is bleeding into a muscle in a patient with hemophilia resulting in the formation of an intramuscular hematoma. This may give the appearance of tumor, hence the name pseudotumor. The most common muscles involved are - Iliopsoas > Quadriceps The most common upper limb muscle involved is the deltoid Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 698

663.q: Content of anatomical snuff box includes?
663.e: The only content of the snuff box is Radial A. As the snuffbox is triangularly shaped, it has three borders, a floor, and a roof: Ulnar (medial) border : Tendon of the extensor pollicis longus. Radial (lateral) border : Tendons of the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus. Proximal border : Styloid process of the radius. Floor : Carpal bones; scaphoid and trapezium. Roof : Skin. Reference: Maheshwari 5th edition p. 156

663.q: Limbs elevated against gravity but not against force is which power grade?
663.e: Evaluation of Strength of Muscles The strength of a muscle is graded from 0 to 5 as follows: Zero-no contraction Trace-palpable contraction only Poor-moves joint but not against gravity Fair-moves joint against gravity Good-moves joint against gravity and resistance Normal-normal strength Reference: Campbell, 12th /ep. 3497.

663.q: In which of the following tumour of the extremity of limb is excision of regional lymph node done
663.e: In SYNOVIAL CELL SARCOMA Lymph node metastasis is relatively common(10% to 12%) and should be evaluated carefully on physical examination. This is a malignant tumour, histologically a combination of synovial cells and fibroblasts. It occurs most commonly around the knee. It may not necessarily originate from the synovial membrane. More often than not, it is extra-articular in origin. The tumour spreads via the blood vessels, lymphatics and along the soft tissue planes. Treatment is by amputation, as for other bone malignancies. Prognosis is poor. Reference: Maheshwari Essentials Ortho, 5 th edition, Page no. 246.

663.q: A 50 year old male suffers an injury to the right upper limb, resulting in a fracture. He is also unable to dorsiflex his wrist and there is sensory loss over the dorsum of the 1st web space. Which fracture can cause this presentation?
o: Fracture of humerus at spiral grove
Fracture of the neck of humerus
663.e: The patient presents with a fracture in the upper limb plus wrist drop and sensory loss. This means that the patient's fracture has caused a high Radial N injury. Out of all the options, only a fracture of the humerus at the spiral groove can cause a high Radial N injury. Reference: J. Maheshwari's Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 94

664.q: Why fracture shaft femur is early stabilised
664.e: Answer- A. To prevent blood loss Fracture shaft femur can cause upto 2L of blood loss and severe hypotension, if not immoblized early. the fracture shaft femur should be immoblized early. This can be temporary immobilization by TT splint followed by surgery or can be by immediate surgery.

664.q: The MOST common type of dislocation of elbow joint is:
664.e: In adults, the elbow is the second most frequently dislocated major joint, after the shoulder. It is the most commonly dislocated joint in children. More than 90% of all elbow dislocations are posterior dislocations. This injury entails disengagement of the coronoid process of the ulna from the trochlea of the humerus with movement posteriorly. The mechanism of injury is typically a fall onto an outstretched hand with the elbow in extension upon impact.

664.q: Most common complication of inter trochanteric femur fracture is
664.e: Most common complication of extracapsular inter trochanteric femur fracture is MALUNION. Most common complication of intracapsular neck of femur fracture is nonunion followed by AVN. Reference- Maheshwari ortho 5 th edition page no 139

664.q: In patient with femoral head fracture associated with femur neck fracture. What is the grading according to Pipkin classification?
664.e: Pipkin classification for femur head fracture (#)- Type I - Femoral head # caudal to fovea capitis Type II - Femoral head # cephalad to fovea capitis Type III - Femoral head # associated with femoral neck # Type IV - Any of the above with acetabular # Reference- Maheshwari Essential Ortho 5 th edition, page no 133

664.q: The investigation of choice for identifying occult fracture neck of femur is.
664.e: MRI is investigation of choice for all occult fractures. Reference- Maheshwari Essential Ortho 5 th edition, page no 134

664.q: What is not required in an emergency management of an open femur fracture?
664.e: Open reduction and internal fixation is not done on emergency basis in cases of open fractures. First fracture should be stabilized with external fixator and wound should be debrided. Once wound gets healed and infection is cleared thereafter open reduction and internal fixation is done. For open fractures gustilo and Anderson classification is used for grading. For open fractures like 3B - antibiotics coated intramedullary nails are preferred over K wires. With the evolution of available nails like antibiotic impregnated nails, intramedullary nailing is now performed even in 3B fractures. Although there was initial phobia for the use of intramedullary nails, their usage has become widespread not only in grade 1 and 2 but even in grade 3 injuries. Reference:Anderson JT, Gustilo RB. Orthopedics clinics of North America, 1980; 11:56

664.q: What is the Treatment for Open fracture of femur?
664.e: In cases of open fracture first fracture should be stabilized with external fixator and wound should be debrided. Once wound gets healed and infection is cleared thereafter open reduction and internal fixation is done. For open fractures Gustilo and Anderson classification is used for grading. For open fractures like 3B antibiotics coated intramedullary nails are preferred over K wires. With the evolution of available nails like antibiotic impregnated nails, intramedullary nailing is now performed even in 3B fractures. Although there was initial phobia for the use of intramedullary nails, their usage has become widespread not only in grade 1 and 2 but even in grade 3 injuries. Reference: Anderson JT, Gustilo RB. Orthopedics clinics of North America, 1980; 11:56

665.q: Which of the following describes grade 2 fracture neck femur?
o: Moderate displacement of neck, vascularity damaged
665.e: Answer- B. Complete fracture with undisplaced neck Garden stage I: undisplaced incomplete, including valgus impacted fractures medial group of femoral neck trabeculae may demonstrate a greenstick fracture Garden stage II: undisplaced complete no disturbance of the medial trabeculae

665.q: Most common complication of fracture neck of femur
665.e: Answer- B. AVN AVN is the most common complication of femoral neck fracture. Non-union is the second most common complication of femoral neck fracture.

665.q: Which is NOT true about fractured neck of femurs?
o: The leg is shortened and externally rotated in most fractured neck of femurs
The main source of blood to the femoral head is via the vessels running within cancellous bone from the diaphysis
Subcapital fracture cuts off all the blood to the head of the femur resulting in avascular necrosis
The blood supply to the head is increased by vessels in the capsular retinacula and it is this which prevents avascular necrosis of the head after an intertrochanteric fracture the ligamentum teres.
665.e: The leg is shortened and externally rotated in most fractured neck of femurs. The main source of blood to the femoral head is via the vessels running within cancellous bone from the diaphysis. The blood supply to the head is increased by vessels in the capsular retinacula and it is this which prevents avascular necrosis of the head after an intertrochanteric fracture the ligamentum teres. Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Lower Limb, Page number - 554

665.q: An 80-year-old male, immobilised following an intertrochanteric fracture, develops pain and swelling in the right calf. What is the most likely diagnosis?
665.e: Explanation: Immobilisation and calf swelling with pain suggest DVT , caused by thrombus formation in the deep veins. Risk factors include stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability (Virchow's triad) . Features: calf pain, tenderness, swelling, erythema, and warmth. Explanation of other options: Chronic osteomyelitis (Option A): Involves chronic bone infection with sequestrum and sinus, not acute calf swelling. Compartment syndrome (Option C): Severe pain, numbness, tense compartment, usually within 48 hrs of trauma/surgery. Pulses preserved but foot cold. Arterial claudication (Option D): Intermittent exertional calf pain from PAD; not acute, not linked to immobilisation.

665.q: Vascular sign of Narath is not seen in
665.e: Vascular sign of Narath: inability to feel femoral pulse against femoral head in the inguinal region. It is positive in all conditions where the femoral head is not present in its normal position. Eg. Traumatic hip dislocation, DDH, Tom Smith arthritis and Girdlestone arthroplasty Useful signs in orthopedics VIC: Volkmann’s sign Piano key sign: Distal radio ulnar joint instability (e.g., Madelung deformity, Malunited colles fracture etc.) De Quervain’s syonvitis: Finkelstein test Flexor tenosynovitis: Kanavel’s signs AVN hip: Sectoral sign Iliopsoas tendonitis: Ludloff sign Reference- Fundamentals of Orthopedics Mohindra and Jain 1 st edition, page no 100

665.q: What is the treatment of Anderson Gustillo classification grade 3B?
665.e: Type 3B fractures are usually treated with external fixation. However if the wound is not very contaminated and patient presents early to the orthopedic center, then antibiotic coated nailing can be performed. Reference- Anderson JT, Gustilo RB. Orthopedics clinics of North America, 1980; 11:56

665.q: A 12-years-old boy presents with a symmetric, expansile cystic lesion in the proximal humerus. All of the following can be done for his treatment except:
665.e: Solitary bone cyst is the diagnosis of a 12 years old boy, who presents with a symmetric, expansile cystic lesion in the proximal humerus. Solitary Bone Cyst: Common in first two decades, primarily between 5-15 years More common in males MC site: Proximal humerus(50-60%) >Femur(25-30%) Cyst appears as centrally radioluscent lesions, on the metaphyseal side of the growth plate of a long bone Treatment: Curettage Methylprednisolone acetate injection into lesion Radiographic contrast injection into lesion Intralesional injection of sclerosing agents Reference: Chapman's Orthopedic Surgery, 3rd edition, Pg: 3392-3394.

666.q: An army recruit has pain over both of his feet for the last 3 months since he started training. He has point tenderness and pain in the forefoot which is aggravated by activity. However, his x rays are normal. What is the next line of investigation?
o: No further investigations are required as his x-rays are normal
666.e: From the history, the person has stress fractures. Stress fracture is sometimes not seen on x-ray in early stages. Hence we need further investigations to confirm our diagnosis. For suspected stress fracture in one site, the investigation of choice is MRI. But for B/L stress fractures or multiple stress fractures, bone scan is recommended over MRI as it is easy, effective and economical. Reference- Rockwood and green adult fracture 8ᵗʰ edition, page-653

666.q: An army recruit with smoking addiction has pain in his right foot for the last 3 months after he started training. He has point tenderness and pain in the forefoot which is aggravated by activity. What would be the clinical diagnosis?
666.e: Stress fracture occurs due to abnormal loading of a normal bone. This is classically seen in individuals who perform repetitive, strenuous activities that he/she is not accustomed to. The most common site of stress fracture is Tibia followed by 2 nd metatarsal (March Fracture) Reference- Rockwood and green adult fracture 8 th edition, page-652

666.q: Pigmented villo-nodular synovitis most commonly occurs at
666.e: Pigmented villonodular synovitis: Pigmented villonodular synovitis(PVNS) is a rare benign disease of the synovial membrane which is characterised by hypervascular neoplastic proliferation of the synovium with deposition of macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and hemosiderin. Knee joint is most commonly involved joint. On arthroscopy typical brownish pigmentation of synovium is seen due to deposition of hemosiderin pigment. Two varieties have been described: Diffuse variety and localized nodular variety. Chances of recurrence are higher in diffuse variety. Low dose external beam radiotherapy and arthroscopic/open synovectomy have been tried with varying success for the treatment. Malignant transformation has been reported but very rare. Reference: Fundamentals of Ortho Mohindra and Jain, Page no. 268.

666.q: Patient sustains twisting type of injury followed by locking of knee. Most likely structure to be injured is?
666.e: Locking is the phenomenon in which the patient is unable to fully extend the knee due to intra articular block by a torn meniscus. Hence, when the patient has locking of knee, it means he/ she has sustained a meniscus injury. Locking is most common in bucket-handle type of longitudinal tears of meniscus, where the inner segment of the meniscus is caught in the intercondylar notch and cannot return to its former position. Reference - Manish Kumar Varshney 1 st edition page no 901.

666.q: Which of the following structure is intracapsular and extrasynovial?
666.e: Both the anterior and posterior cruciate ligamnets are intracapsular but extrasynovial. In the knee, the extra capsular structures are the MCL and LCL The Intracapsular structures are Intrasynovial - Menisci Extrasynovial - ACL, PCL Reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy-Volume 1, Edition 6th, page no. 144.

666.q: Clergyman's knee involves which of the following bursa?
666.e: Given below are the common named bursitis of the body. Prepatellar bursitis -Housemaid’s knee Infrapatellar bursitis- Clergyman’s knee Olecranon bursitis -Student’s elbow Ischial bursitis -Weaver’s bottom On lateral malleolus -Tailor’s ankle On great toe –Bunion Reference - Maheshwari 4th /e p. 292

Given below are the common named bursitis of the body. Prepatellar bursitis- Housemaid's knee Infrapatellar bursitis- Clergyman’s knee Olecranon bursitis -Student’s elbow Ischial bursitis- Weaver’s bottom On lateral malleolus -Tailor’s ankle On great toe- Bunion Reference - Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics 4th /e p. 292

666.q: Most common mechanism of PCL injury is
o: Blow on the front of upper tibia while knee is flexed and foot is plantar flexed
Blow on the back of upper tibia while knee is flexed and foot is plantar flexed
666.e: PCL tears are typically produced by external trauma such as the classic “dashboard injury” resulting from a posteriorly directed force on the anterior aspect of the proximal tibia with the knee flexed and foot plantar flexed. In athletics, the typical mechanism of isolated PCL tears is a direct blow to the anterior tibia or a fall onto the knee with the foot in a plantar flexed position. Football, soccer, rugby and skiing are among the sports with the highest incidence of PCL tears. Non-contact mechanisms, such as hyperflexion, are less common. Reference - Manish Kumar Varshney 1 st edition page no 888

667.q: Osteonerosis is seen in all except
667.e: Answer- D. Paget's disease Storage disorders : - Gaucher's disease Caisson disease : - Dysbaric osteonecrosis Hemoglobinopathy & Coagulation disorder: - Sickel cell disease, Familial thrombophilia, Hypofibrinolysis, Hypolipoproteinemia. Congenital disorders : - Perthe's disease, Slipped capital femoral epiphysis. Hematological malignancies : - Leukemia, lymphoma, Polycythemia. Hyperlipedemia : - Nephrotic syndrome

667.q: After chronic use of steroids severe pain in right hip with immobility is due to
667.e: Answer- A. Avascular necrosis Pain in hip and limitatation of movement (immobility) ofter chronic use of steroids suggest the diagnosis of AVN of femoral head.

667.q: A 50 year old male on walker support presents with back pain and weakness of both lower limbs for 1 month. MRI reveals TB spine with abscess compressing the spinal cord. Next line of action is?
o: Emergency surgery and drainage of the abscess
Elective surgery with ALD + fixation of spine
667.e: In, India we follow the middle path regime for treatment of TB paraplegia. All patients with TB paraplegia are first started on ATT and advised bed rest and given a spine brace. These patients are the monitored for improvement. Patients who improve on ATT are continued with it. Those who are not improving are treated with surgery. Indications of surgery in middle path regime are Bowel and bladder involvement Worsening of paraplegia while on ATT Appearance of a new neurological deficit while on treatment No improvement in paraplegia even after 3-4 weeks of ATT In this question, the patient does not have any bowel or bladder symptoms, so he is started on ATT and monitored. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 193

667.q: Anterolateral tibial bowing is associated with which of the following lower extremity conditions in children?
667.e: Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia: A birth defect in the lower third of the tibia in children, whereby a fracture in this region fails to unite. "It is a congenital condition characterized by bowing of tibia (mostly anterolateral bowing). Neurofibromatosis type 1 is found in 50–55 % of patients with congenital pseudoarthrosis (while 10% of patients with neurofibromatosis have pseudoarthrosis). It is equally distributed in boys and girls and is almost always unilateral. There is little tendency for the lesion to regress, and the bone eventually fractures through the weakened area. Treatment: Before a fracture occurs, a total contact orthosis is prescribed as prophylaxis. But once a fracture occurs. surgery is indicated. Reference- Maheshwari 5 th /ep. PG NO 225

668.q: What is the management in case of a stable cervical spine injury with no neurological changes?
668.e: In a stable cervical spine injuries with no neurological deficit, a rigid cervical brace or halo for 8-12 weeks is usually sufficient. Stable compression fractures of vertebral bodies and undisplaced fracture of laminae, lateral masses or spinous process may also be treated conservatively. Reference: Ebnezar, 5 th edition, Page no. 304.

668.q: Which of the following is not a known complication of TB spine?
668.e: TB produces fibrous ankylosis in all joints except the spine, where it produces bony ankylosis. Complications of TB spine include Kyphotic deformity Neurological deficit Paraplegia Bowel and bladder involvement Bony ankylosis of vertebra Abscess Psoas abscess Paravertebral abscess Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1757

668.q: Indicators of poor prognosis in the pott's spine is/are:
668.e: Factors leading to poor prognosis in potts spine: Inactive disease with poor mechanical compression Complete paralysis/Complete cord involvement Paralysis for more than 1year Presence of severe kyphosis(>60 degree) Older age and poor nutrition Healed vertebral lesion Presence of myelomalacia and syringomyel ia on magnetic resonance imaging(MRI). Good prognosis is associated with: Inflammatory cause of cord involvement Incomplete involvement Short duration of deficit Minimal kyphotic deformity Younger age Good nutritional status. Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 17, Pg: 257.

668.q: In the lumbar spine, 90% of the disc herniations occur at which of the following level:
668.e: Most common site of spinal disc herniation: Lumbar region(95% in L4-L5 or L5-S1). The second most common site is the cervical region(C5-C6, C6-C7). Thoracic region accounts for only 0.15% to 4.0% of cases. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th ed., Pg: 253.

668.q: Medulloblastoma most common metastasis is to ?
668.e: Ans. is 'b' i.e., CNS o Medullablastoma spread through CSF and frequently metastasizes to different locations in the brain and spine. o Extraneural metastasis to the rest of the body is rare.

668.q: Pott's spine spine commonly affects all of the following parts of vertebrae except
668.e: Facet joint > Spinous process are least involved structures in Posterior type of vertebral TB. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Ortho, 7 th edition, Page no. 184.

668.q: The earliest neurological sign in a patient with TB spine is
668.e: ORDER OF NEUROLOGICAL INVOLVEMENT IN TB: Rarely is paraplegia the presenting symptom. Motor system is almost always affected before the sensory system because diseased area in spine(i.e., vertebral body) lies anterior to the cord near the motor tracts. The first neurological sign is ankle clonus followed by plantar extensor. Thereafter the patient develops mild spastic motor weakness manifesting as clumsiness or incoordination of gait which ends in severe weakness to the extent where patient is unable to stand and is bed ridden. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7 th edition, Page no. 190.

668.q: All of the following are used in the treatment of TB spine except
668.e: The surgery used for treating spine TB in India is Left anterolateral decompression. Anterolateral decompression should not be done through the right side as there is high risk of injuring the inferior vena cava, which if it occurs can be fatal. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 194

669.q: In scoliosis degree of deformity is calculated by
669.e: Answer- A. Cobbs method Cobb angle is a measurement of the degree of side-to-side spinal curvature, which is a deformity you may know as scoliosis.

670.q: An adult patient with a grade I isthmic spondylolisthesis at L5-S1 is most likely to have weakness of which of the following?
670.e: The clinical findings for fifth lumbar root involvement include: Weakness of EHL, extensor digitorum longus(EDL), knee flexion(hamstrings), tensor fasciae lata(TFL), gluteus medius(hip abduction) Sensory loss over lateral and anterolateral leg and dorsum of foot(typically in the first web space-deep peroneal nerve territory) Weakness or mute posterior tibialis reflex and medial hamstring reflex Positive trendelenburg sign(variable) Trendelenburg gait(variable). Reference: Manish Kumar Varshney, 1 st edition, Page no. 1389.

670.q: Condition in which there is anterior or posterior displacement of a vertebra in relation to the vertebrae below:
670.e: Spondylosis - Degenerative osteoarthritis of the joints of the spinal column. Spondylitis - is an inflammation of the vertebra. It is usually seen in inflammatory conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis. Spondylolysis - it is a defect or break in the pars interarticularis of the vertebra. Pars interarticularis is an important structure that links a vertebra to its adjacent vertebrae. Any defect in it can predispose the slipping of one vertebra over its lower vertebra resulting in spondylolisthesis. So, spondylolysis is the precursor of spondylolisthesis. Spondylolisthesis - The anterior or posterior displacement of a vertebra or the vertebral column in relation to the vertebrae below it. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th ed, Pg: 283-284.

671.q: Which of the following drugs can be used in the treatment of GCT of pelvis?
671.e: Denosumab can be used in the treatment of GCT, especially in those tumors that arise in difficult to access areas such as the pelvis and the sacrum. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that blocks RANK ligands. The tumor cells in GCT acts via the RANK ligands to stimulate the osteoclasts. And its this activated osteoclasts that destroy the bone in GCT. Therefore, Denosumab can stop activation of osteoclasts, thereby causing shrinkage of the tumor. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 1895

672.e: Answer- B. Joint aspiration Quickest and best method of diagnosis of septic arthritis is aspiration of joint.

672.q: Which of the following is an orthopedic emergency?
672.e: Septic arthritis is an absolute orthopedic emergency as delaying arthrotomy can cause serious joint damage. The pus in septic arthritis contains collagenases and metalloproteinases that start destroying articular cartilage within a period of 8 hours. So arthrotomy and lavage should be done as early as possible. Reference: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics 5th edition page no. 1055

GARRE'S OSTEOMYELITIS Sclerosing non suppurative chronic osteomyelitis Fusiform osseous enlargement. Cortical thickening No discharging sinus There is tenderness on deep palpation Shafts of the femur or tibia are most common site Treatment is guarded. Acute symptoms subside with rest and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Sometimes, making a gutter or holes in the bone bring relief in pain. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7 th edition, Page no. 173.

672.q: True about GARRE'S OSTEOMYELITIS include the following EXCEPT
o: Local pain and fever may be present
Usually there is no discharging sinus
672.e: Most common site is mandible GARRE'S OSTEOMYELITIS: Sclerosing non suppurative chronic osteomyelitis Fusiform osseous enlargement. Cortical thickening present. No discharging sinus There is tenderness on deep palpation Overall mandible is most common site. Shafts of the femur or tibia are other most common site Treatment is guarded. Acute symptoms subside with rest and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Sometimes, making a gutter or holes in the bone bring relief in pain. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7 th edition, Page no. 173.

Note that responsible pathogens may be isolated in only 35-40% of infections. Bacterial causes of acute hematogenous and direct osteomyelitis include the following: Most common organism causing acute osteomyelitis: Staph. Aureus MCC of osteomyelitis in sickle cell anemia patient: SALMONELLA MCC of osteomyelitis in IV drug abuser: PSEUDOMONAS MC organism causing osteomyelitis in open foot injury: PSEUDOMONAS MC organism causing osteomyelitis in HIV patient: Staph. Aureus MC organism causing osteomyelitis in case of animal bite: Pasteurella Multiocida MC organism causing osteomyelitis in case of human bite: Eikenella Corrodens Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5th ed, Pg: 168.

672.q: Cells involved in bone remodelling are
672.e: Remodeling is the process by which bone gets reshaped according to external forces. This a slow, continuous and dynamic process. Here, some bone is removed form certain areas and some bone gets deposited in other areas, so both osteoblasts and osteoclasts are needed for remodeling. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 11 Reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics 14th edition page no. 1186

672.q: Which bone cell produces osteonectin and osteocalcin?
672.e: Osteoblast is the bone building cell. It produces all the proteins needed to make up bone tissue, which includes type I collagen, osteocalcin, osteonectin etc It also produces an important enzyme, Alkaline phosphatase, which can be used as a marker for bone formation. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 18.

672.q: A 12 year old boy presented with a lytic lesion in proximal humerus. Which is the least likely cause?
672.e: When a child comes with a lytic lesion in the proximal humerus there are 3 possibilities Simple bone cyst - It will appear as a cyst in the metaphysis. Chondroblastoma - It will appear as a lytic lesion in the epiphysis. Metastasis - Even though rare, mets can occur in the proximal humerus in a child e.g. neuroblastoma Plasmacytoma is a solitary myeloma and is always seen in elderly patients and never in this age group Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 245

673.q: Chronic fluorosis is caused by drinking water with fluoride content of
673.e: Chronic fluorosis is seen in localities where the water supply contains > 10 ppm fluoride (Davidson). Fluorosis It is characterized by excessive deposition of calcium in bone & soft tissues due to increased intake of fluorides through drinking water. Clinical features: Dental fluorosis— earliest sign of fluorosis (mottling of enamel) – MC involve the incisors of upper jaw. Skeletal fluorosis— pain in back & joints, stiff spine, paranesthesia, spastic paraparesis & anemia. Radiological findings: Spine: Calcification of posterior longitudinal ligament. Pelvis: Calcification of ischio pubic & sacroiliac ligaments Forearm & leg: calcification of interosseous membrane. Treatment: Defluridation of water (Nalgonda technique) Reference: Maheswari, 55th ed, p. 314

673.q: Triple deformity of knee includes all EXCEPT:
673.e: Tuberculosis of the knee is classical cause of triple deformity. It includes: Flexion Lateral(external) rotation of tibia Posterior subluxation of tibia Better treatment results are seen with ATT and arthrodesis This condition can also be seen in Rheumatoid arthritis. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5 th edition, Page no. 201.

673.q: Not a part of triple deformity in TB knee
673.e: Triple deformity is seen in advanced TB knee. It has 3 components Posterior subluxation of tibia External rotation of tibia Flexion of knee Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 200

673.q: Triple deformity of knee is classically seen in
673.e: Tuberculosis of the knee is classical cause of triple deformity. It includes: Flexion Lateral(external) rotation of tibia Posterior subluxation of tibia Better treatment results are seen with ATT and arthrodesis This condition can also be seen in Rheumatoid arthritis. Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 5 th edition, Page no. 201.

673.q: Commonest site for tuberculous spondylitis is?
673.e: Majority of cases reported in dorsolumbar region(lower thoracic and upper lumbar) due to: Greater extent of movement - stress zone due to transition of kyphosis to lordosis Degree of weight bearing Large surface area of spongy cancellous bone Proximity to cisterna chyli and kidney. In order of involvement lumbar → upper dorsal → cervical → sacral → atlantoaxial Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7 th edition, Page no. 182.

o: Inherited as an autosomal dominant trait
Caused by FGFR 3 mutation on Chr 4
The problem is defective enchondral ossification of long bones
673.e: In achondroplasia, the IQ and sexual development are absolutely normal. Achondroplasia MC skeletal dysplasia MC cause of disproportionate dwarfism Autosomal dominant Caused due to FGFR 3 mutation on Chr 4 The basic problem is defective enchondral ossification of long bones Proximal bones are most affected - Rhizomelic shortening Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 675

674.q: What is the most common complication after successful treatment of a distal femoral physeal fracture?
674.e: Following are some facts about fractures in children Fractures in children heal faster. Fractures close to the joint heal faster. Sideways displacement will remodel. Angulation in the plane of the adjacent joint is acceptable. Rotational malalignment will never remodel. Physis subjected to compressive forces inhibits growth Reference- Maheshwari 5th /ep. PG NO 59

674.q: Radial head excision is avoided in all except
674.e: The treatment of radial head fractures depend on the amount of comminution and the age of the patient. Comminuted fractures in adults is treated by excising the broken fragments. However the radial head excision is contraindicated in Essex Lopresti fracture - Combination of radial head fracture with interosseous membrane rupture and DRUJ subluxation. Displaced fracture in children - Excision of radial head in children will cause cubitus valgus Undisplaced fractures in adults - These can be treated with POP cast. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 107

674.q: Which tumor is responsible for the most incidence of metastasis in a child?
674.e: Neuroblastoma is responsible for the most incidence of metastasis in children. Important points: Most common malignancy of bone: Metastasis MC primaries for bone mets: Breast > Prostate> Lung MC primaries for mets in children: Neuroblastoma MC bone involved: Spine> proximal femur MC part of spine involved: Thoracic > Lumbar Reference: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics 5th edition page no. 89

674.q: Type 1 collagen are found in all except
674.e: Type I collagen is seen in the following skeletal tissues Annulus fibrosus of intervertebral disc Bone Menisci Articular cartilage contain type II collagen Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 98. Reference: Rockwood and Wilkin's Fractures in Children's 8th edition, page no. 609.

674.q: A 45 year old man presents with back pain, stooped posture and reduced chest expansion. Which of the following tests will you do to arrive at your diagnosis?
674.e: The clinical picture points towards ankylosing spondylosis, so the best test to be done in HLA B 27 which will be positive in 80% of cases of ankylosing spondylosis. Reference: J. Maheshwari's 5th Edition of Essential Orthopaedics page no. 291

674.q: Poor prognostic factors in Pott's paraplegia?
674.e: Prognosis of Pott's paraplegia depends upon the following factors: Age: Children respond to treatment better than adults. Onset: Gradual onset paraplegia has a better prognosis. Duration: Long standing paraplegia has a worse prognosis. Severity: Motor paralysis alone has a good prognosis. Sphincter involvement i.e., urinary or bowel incontinence are bad prognostic indicators. Progress: Sudden progress of the paraplegia has a bad prognosis. Poor prognostic factors in Pott's paraplegia are acute onset, sudden progression and long-standing paraplegia Reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopedics, 7 th edition, Page no. 192.

674.q: Anorexic female presented with bleeding gums, loose teeth and subperiosteal hemorrhages. What is the defect?
674.e: The clinical features are consistent with scurvy. Scurvy occurs due to deficiency of vitamin C Vitamin C is a coenzyme in the hydroxylation of proline and lysine. Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine are the precursors of collagen synthesis. In scurvy, due to vitamin C deficiency, there is reduction in collagen synthesis. So, wherever collagen is required to provide structural integrity, problems occur. E.g. there is weakening of the capillary basement membrane leading to bleeding at sites through out the body. Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 91

674.q: Which is the biochemical finding seen in renal osteodystrophy?
674.e: The most important biochemical change in renal osteodystrophy is elevated phosphate levels. This is due to the inability of the failing kidney to excrete phosphate, leading to phosphate retention. The biochemical changes in renal osteodystrophy are: Calcium - ↓↓ PTH - ↑ ↑ Serum PO 4 - ↑ ↑ Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) - ↑ Serum 1, 25 OH Vit D - ↓ Reference: Miler's 8th Edition of Review of Orthopaedics, page no. 75

675.q: In neglected cases of CTEV, joint fused are
675.e: Answer- A. Calcaneocuboid, talonavicular and talocalcaneal Joints fused in triple arthrodesis for CTEVare i) Subtalar (tolocalcaneal) joint, ii) Calcaneocuboid joint, iii) Tolonavicular joint.

675.q: All are causes of clubfoot at birth except
675.e: Poliomyelitis cause acquired club foot deformity. It is not seen at birth.
