694.q: In a 72-year-old diabetic patient having chronic renal failure, functionally dependent for daily activities on others, and also having moderate hearing impairment, which of the following characteristics carries the highest risk of predisposing the patient to an episode of delirium?
694.e: Advanced age is a major risk factor for the development of delirium. Approximately 30 to 40% of hospitalized patients older than age 65 years have an episode of delirium. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Textbook of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 21.2 Delirium, Page number 698.

694.q: A 70-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by the police due to complaints from her neighbours for wandering around the neighbourhood without clothes and poor self-care since last 5 days. When found by the police, she was dirty, foul-smelling, in a half-naked state, with garbage and rotting food all over her house. When interviewed, she appeared confused, disoriented, not able to recognise where she was and was unresponsive. Which of the following neurotransmitter and neuroanatomical area could majorly be implicated for her present confused condition?
694.e: The major neurotransmitter hypothesized to be involved in delirium is acetylcholine and the major neuroanatomical area is the reticular formation. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Textbook of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 21.2 Delirium, Page number 699.

694.q: A 66-year-old woman recently operated for fracture of femur around two days' back presents with episodes of getting disoriented, behaving as if she is at her native village, remaining sleepy, stuporous and giving sluggish responses. Which of the following types of acute confusional state describes her condition?
694.e: In hypoactive delirium, the individual has a hypoactive level of psychomotor activity that may be accompanied by sluggishness and lethargy that approaches stupor. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Textbook of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 21.2 Delirium, Page number 700.

694.q: Which of the following mechanism is implicated in cerebral insufficiency caused by head trauma?
694.e: Pathophysiological mechanisms involved in delirium: Neurotransmitter mechanism- Decrease in levels of acetylcholine Increase in levels of dopamine (reciprocal acetylcholine-dopamine balance) Increase in glutamate levels (Excitatory neurotoxicity causing neuronal damage) Increase in GABA levels (implicated in hepatic encephalopathy, delirium secondary to benzodiazepine and alcohol withdrawal) Other neurotransmitters like norepinephrine and serotonin may also have a role Inflammation (Delirium as a CNS response to systemic inflammation)- Cytokines (IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-a, interferon) may contribute to delirium by increasing permeability of blood-brain-barrier and altering neurotransmission. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 10 th edition, Chapter 10.2 Delirium, Page number 3052.

694.q: A 46-year-old chronic alcoholic (heavy prolonged drinking) presents with altered sensorium, frequent disorientation, and stuporous state. Laboratory investigations show highly deranged liver enzymes. Which of the following mechanism is responsible for encephalopathy stage in this patient?
694.e: Hepatic encephalopathy (following prolonged heavy use of alcohol) has been associated with increased GABA and serum ammonia levels. Ammonia and several other factors are known to induce and aggravate astrocyte swelling that initiates a cascade of events leading to delirium. In addition, elevated ammonia levels can contribute to increased glutamate and glutamine levels, which are precursors to GABA. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 10 th edition, Chapter 10.2 Delirium, Page number 3052.

694.q: In a patient having parkinsonian features presenting in a delirious state, all of the following statements hold true except;
o: Antiparkinsonian agents are protective in delirium
Clozapine is the safe antipsychotic in this condition
Use of haloperidol is associated with worsening of parkinsonian features
694.e: In Parkinson’s disease, the antiparkinsonian agents are frequently implicated in causing delirium. If delirium persists after attenuation of antiparkinsonian agents, clozapine is recommended. Use of other antipsychotics like haloperidol or risperidone is associated with worsening of parkinsonian features in such patient. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Textbook of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 21.2 Delirium, Page number 703.

694.q: Sometimes patient of dementia may develop superimposed delirium. This is called as:
694.e: Dementia with Delirium. It is called as beclouded dementia. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 21, Page No.: 701

695.q: Subcortical dementia is seen in all except ?
695.e: Ans.B. Alzheimer's disease Subcortical dementia is seen in parkinsonism, Huntington's disease, wilson's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, idiopathic basal ganglion calcification (Fahr's disease), thalamic lesions, multiple sclerosis, HIV associated dementia and multisYstem atroPhY. Alzheimer's disease causes cortical dementia.

695.q: True statements regarding Marchiafava-Bignami disease are all except?
o: Usual symptoms are personality change or psychomotor impairment
695.e: Marchiafava-Bignami Disease should be considered in patients with chronic alcohol abuse or malnutrition who present with certain neurological symptoms. These symptoms include Dementia Altered mental status Personality change Spasticity Dysarthria Ataxia Gait abnormalities Seizures Other reported clinical findings include desynchronization of bilateral symmetric movements and unilateral signs of agraphia, apraxia, dyspraxia and anomia. Marchiafava-Bignami disease(MBD) is a very rare disorder of demyelination/necrosis of the corpus callosum and the near subcortical white matter that is especially predominant in ill-fed alcoholics. Vitamin supplementation is usually helpful. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526007/

695.q: Which nutrient deficiency is responsible for cognitive decline in elderly individuals?
695.e: Explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a common cause of cognitive impairment in the elderly. It can result in memory loss, confusion, and even dementia if left untreated. The deficiency disrupts myelin synthesis, leading to demyelination and neuronal dysfunction. Explanation for other options: Vitamin C (Option A): Deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by symptoms like bleeding gums and weakness, but it is not associated with cognitive decline. Vitamin B6 (Option C): Deficiency may cause irritability, depression, and confusion but is less frequently linked to significant cognitive impairment in older adults. Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) (Option D): Deficiency leads to Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's syndrome, which are less common causes of cognitive impairment in the general elderly population compared to vitamin B12 deficiency.

695.q: What is a characteristic of Sundowner Syndrome?
o: Confusion and ataxia in the evening
695.e: Explanation: Sundowner syndrome is characterised by drowsiness, confusion, ataxia, and accidental falls. It occurs in older people who are overly sedated and in patients with dementia who react adversely to even a small dose of a psychoactive drug. The syndrome also occurs in demented patients when external stimuli, such as light and interpersonal orienting cues, are diminished.

695.q: Who was responsible for translating 'demence precoce' into 'dementia praecox'?
695.e: Kraepelin translated the term 'démence précoce' into dementia praecox. (OPTION D) Kraepelin coined the term ' dementia praecox' . He distinguished between manic depression and dementia praecox, which was later named schizophrenia. Adolf Meyer was the founder of psychobiology . (OPTION A) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 7, page no. 301

695.q: Which of the following medications is associated with a risk of hepatotoxicity and is rarely used in treating Alzheimer's disease?
695.e: Explanation: Tacrine is an older acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that's rarely used now. The main reason for the decline in its usage is the significant risk of hepatotoxicity it poses.

695.q: An elderly patient with Alzheimer's disease is not able to tolerate medication orally. Which of the following acetylcholinesterase inhibitors can be used?
695.e: Rivastigmine is the correct choice because it is available as both an oral medication and a transdermal patch. The patch is particularly useful in elderly patients who have difficulty swallowing. Incorrect options: (A): Donepezil is only available in an oral form and would not be appropriate for a patient who cannot tolerate oral medications. (B): Memantine is not an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It is an NMDA receptor antagonist used in Alzheimer's disease, but it is not suitable for this question. (C): Galantamine is another acetylcholinesterase inhibitor but is also only available in oral form. Key Takeaways: Rivastigmine can be used in patients who cannot tolerate oral medications, as it comes in a transdermal patch form. Donepezil and Galantamine are available only in oral form. Memantine works differently from acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and is not used in this context.

695.q: Who was the first person to use the terms 'mania' and 'melancholia' to describe mental illness?
695.e: In 1984, Jules Falret described the condition associated with alternating moods of depression and mania. He called it ' folie circulaire' . ( OPTION B ) It was Hippocrates who used the terms such as ' mania' and ' melancholia' to describe mental illness. ( OPTION A ) Kahlbaum used the term ' cyclothymia' . ( OPTION C ) Kraepelin coined the term ' dementia praecox' . ( OPTION D ) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 8, page no. 347

696.q: When exposed to positive events, like going on a holiday or receiving a compliment, transient upliftment of mood is seen in depressed patients. This is termed as ____________.
696.e: Reactivity of mood is the term used to describe the fluctuations in mood that occur in parallel with changes to one's environment Mood will improve on going on holiday or when the stressful situation alters An example, when difficulties with a workmate resolve when that person resigns, but recur when the subject is re-exposed to the stressful situation Reference : Fish's Clinical Psychopathology, third edition, Chapter 5 Disorders of emotion, Page no. 74

696.q: In a patient with Melancholic depression, the mood is characteristically described as _______________.
696.e: A distinct quality of depressed mood characterized by profound despondency, despair, and/or moroseness or by ; so-called empty mood is a characteristic feature of Melancholic depression Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 8, Mood Disorders, Page 362

696.q: How long after a stroke is a patient at a higher risk for developing a depressive disorder?
696.e: Studies of the course and prognosis of post stroke depression indicate that the high-risk period can last up to 2 years. The presence of depression is associated with an eightfold increase in mortality risk. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh Edition, Chapter 21st, Neurocognitive Disorders, Page no. 738.

696.q: After experiencing a road traffic accident in which she lost her brother, an 11-year-old girl presented with difficulty in sleep due to frightening and terrifying dreams involving the accident, which are prolonged and awaken her. On waking up, she remembers the dreams and finds herself sweating, panting and her heart racing. Due to such frequent fearful dreams, she often has fear of sleeping. Which of the following would best describe her condition?
696.e: Nightmares are frightening or terrifying dreams , also called dream anxiety attacks, they produce sympathetic activation and ultimately awaken the dreamer. Nightmares occur in REM sleep and usually evolve from a long, complicated dream that becomes increasingly frightening. Nightmares have a strong association with traumatic events. Sympathetic over activity → sweating, palpitations, tachypnoea is seen in nightmares. Usually, patients can recollect the contents of the frightening dreams , which is how it can be differentiated from parasomnias of NREM/sleep like night terrors. Hypnagogic hallucinations are visual/auditory perceptions occurring while going to sleep. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 16, Normal Sleep and Sleep-wake Disorders, Page no. 556.

696.q: Laughing or crying occurring spontaneously after seemingly minor provocation is observed in several patients who have suffered cerebrovascular stroke. This condition is known by all of the following terms except:
696.e: Pathological laughter/ crying is defined as laughing and/or crying occurring spontaneously or after some seemingly minor provocation. Indicative of underlying depression. It is seen in post-stroke period. Other names: Emotional incontinence, emotional lability, pseudobulbar effect, pathological emotionalism, involuntary emotional expression disorder. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 10 th edition, Chapter 2.2 Neuropsychiatric aspects of cerebrovascular disorders, Page number 1283 .

696.q: A bibliophilic person, while reading a newspaper, may misread the word '-ook' as 'book' even though the faded letter is a 'l'. This kind of illusion is known as ___________.
696.e: Completion illusion: It depends on inattention such as misreading words in newspapers or missing misprints because we read the word as if it were complete Alternatively, if we see faded letters, we may misread the word on the basis of our previous experience , our interests, etc. For example, to the person with an interest in reading, the word '-ook' might be misread as 'book' even though the faded letter was an 'l' Reference: Fish's Clinical Psychopathology, third edition, Chapter 3 Disorders of Perception, Page no. 26

697.q: What percentage of new mothers is believed to develop postpartum depression?
697.e: Postpartum depression is relatively common, occurring in about 10% to 15% of new mothers. Symptoms are indistinguishable from those characteristics of nonpsychotic major depression and usually develop insidiously over the 6 months following delivery. Some women , however, experience an acute onset of symptoms immediately after delivery and occasionally depression starts during pregnancy. Ambivalence toward the child and doubts about the mother's own parenting abilities are common, but the rate of suicide is low. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh Edition, Chapter 27th, Psychiatry and Reproductive Medicine, Page no. 839.

697.q: What is the feature of atypical depression?
o: The individual shows psychotic symptoms that align with depressive themes
There is a marked decrease in sleep and a high level of energy
Mood brightens in response to positive events, with symptoms like weight gain and hypersomnia
The presence of severe agitation and distinct despair
697.e: Explanation: Atypical depression is defined by mood reactivity (mood improves with positive events) along with features like increased appetite/weight gain, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, and rejection sensitivity.

697.q: All of the following symptoms are a common overlap in grief and Major Depressive Disorder, except:
697.e: Symptoms like sadness, sleep impairment, appetite impairment and weight loss can be similar symptoms in both grief and MDD. (Option A, B & D) However, symptoms like worthlessness, hopelessness and suicidal ideation are infrequent in grief and if present, may be only in context of the bereaved person. Self-esteem (self-worth) is usually preserved in grief. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Chapter 34 End of life issues, Page number 1356.

697.q: A 38 year old female, presents to OPD with complaints of persistent sadness, sleeping problems, loss of interest in activities and poor appetite for past few months. As per her condition, she is diagnosed with major depressive disorder. Which drug is the most appropriate for initial treatment?
697.e: SSRI is the first line management for depression Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Clinical Practice Guideline for Depression, Chapter 8, Page No.: 375

697.q: What happens to the time between depressive episodes as a patient experience more episodes?
697.e: Explanation: As a patient experiences more depressive episodes, the time between episodes generally decreases and episodes become more frequent over time.

697.q: A young boy feels that dirt has hung onto him whenever he passes through the dirty street. He knows that there is actually no such thing after he has cleaned once but he is not satisfied and compelled to think so. Although he knows that this is completely irrational but he can't control his thoughts. It gives him anxiety and depressive mood. Which of the following is wrong about his condition?
o: Exposure therapy and response prevention can be supportive
697.e: This is a case of OCD. OCD patients can easily slip into depression as it is ego dystonic. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 10, Page No.: 418

697.q: A junior resident of general surgery department is washing his hands for 45 minutes before he gets ready for any procedure in OT. Many a times he got scolded by his seniors for wasting so much time. He complains that he doesn't get satisfied after washing his hands for one time. Although he knows that this is completely irrational but he can't control his thoughts. It gives him anxiety and depressive mood. Which of the following is wrong about his condition?
697.e: Clinical scenario depicts OCD. It's a neurotic condition and patient is intact with the reality. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 10, Page No.: 421

697.q: All of the following delusional themes are mood congruent in a patient of Major Depressive Disorder, except:
697.e: In depression , delusions of guilt, poverty, nihilism, reference are commonly seen to be mood-congruent However, grandiose delusions in which a person believes himself to be of supreme importance is commonly seen as a feature of mania and not depression Reference: Fish's Clinical Psychopathology, third edition, Chapter 4 Disorders of Thought and Speech, Page no. 51

698.q: A 30 year old female presented to psychiatry OPD with symptoms of hypomania. She has a past history of mania and wants to conceive. Which of the following drugs is most teratogenic?
698.e: Drugs like Oxcarbazepine, Lamotrigine are safe in pregnancy. Both Lithium and Valproate are teratogenic, but with respect to the risk vs benefit ratio, Lithium is comparatively safer in pregnancy. Adverse effects of Valproate Anorexia, vomiting, loose motions and heartburn are common but mild. Drowsiness, ataxia and tremor occur at high doses. Alopecia, curling of hair, weight gain and increased bleeding tendency have been observed. Rashes and thrombocytopenia are infrequent hypersensitivity phenomena. Administered during pregnancy, it has produced spina bifida and other neural tube defects in the offspring; should be avoided.

698.q: A female came to the psychiatry OPD with a past history of hypomania, now planning to conceive. Which of the following drugs should be avoided?
698.e: Drugs like Oxcarbazepine, Lamotrigine are safe in pregnancy. Both Lithium and Valproate are teratogenic, but with respect to the risk vs benefit ratio, Lithium is comparatively safer in pregnancy. Adverse effects of Valproate Anorexia, vomiting, loose motions and heartburn are common but mild. Drowsiness, ataxia and tremor occur at high doses. Alopecia, curling of hair, weight gain and increased bleeding tendency have been observed. Rashes and thrombocytopenia are infrequent hypersensitivity phenomena. Administered during pregnancy, it has produced spina bifida and other neural tube defects in the offspring; should be avoided.

698.q: A pregnant female presented to OPD in 3rd trimester. She is known case of bipolar disorder with history of 3-4 exacerbation episodes. She's maintained well on lithium from last year. What is next appropriate management?
698.e: Fetal exposure to lithium causes: fetal and neonatal cardiac arrhythmia, hypoglycemia, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, polyhydramnios, reversible changes in thyroid function, premature delivery, floppy infant syndrome. Small increase in congenital cardiac malformation (ebstein's anomaly). Physiological alteration in pregnancy may affect absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination of lithium. Women with bipolar disorder who are treated with lithium and plan to conceive: Mild and frequent episodes: treatment with lithium should be gradually tapered More severe episodes with moderate risk of relapse: taper dose of lithium and again reinstituted after organogenesis Severe and frequent episodes: continue same dose throughout pregnancy Fetal assessment with fetal echo considered in female who exposed with lithium in first trimester.

698.q: Since there is increasing interest in the potential utility of cannabis for a variety of medical conditions, FDA has approved all of the following cannabinoids for medical use except:
698.e: FDA has approved various cannabinoids for medical use, for example: Epidiolex approved for → Lennox-Gestaut syndrome Dronabinol and Nabilone → approved for nausea in patients receiving chemotherapy. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Chapter 20.4, Cannabis-related disorders, Page number 647.

698.q: A 44 year old male with a past history of a manic episode presents with an illness of 1 month duration characterized by depressed mood, anhedonia and profound psychomotor retardation. The most appropriate management strategy is prescribing a combination of:
698.e: Patient is presented with depression with h/o mania. So better treatment option is antidepressants with mood stabilizers. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition; Clinical Practice Guideline for Bipolar mood Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder, Chapter 8, Page No.: 357

698.q: A female patient of bipolar disorder is on lithium for the last 1 year. Which of the following side effects is least likely to occur?
698.e: Explanation: Tardive dyskinesia is an extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) associated with antipsychotic drugs , not lithium. Thus, among the given options, tardive dyskinesia is least likely with lithium therapy. Explanation of Other Options: Option A - Hypothyroidism: Recognized adverse effect of lithium. Option B - Tremors: Common neurological side effect of lithium. Option D - Diabetes insipidus: Lithium interferes with renal concentrating ability, leading to nephrogenic DI.

698.q: The current agent of choice for treatment of bipolar affective (manic- depressive) disorder is:
698.e: Lithium carbonate is the current agent of choice, particularly during the manic phase. Because the onset of action is slow, concurrent use of antipsychotic agents such as chlorpromazine or haloperidol may be necessary to control mania. Concurrent use of tricyclic antidepressants may be necessary in the depressive phase. Monitoring of lithium levels is necessary because of the serious nature of the adverse effects (neurologic, renal, cardiac). Ref: Ropper A.H., Samuels M.A. (2009). Chapter 57. Depression and Bipolar Disease. In A.H. Ropper, M.A. Samuels (Eds), Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology, 9e.

698.q: A 32-year-old woman with cyclothymia presents to the obstetrician at 22 weeks pregnant for a routine prenatal visit. She has continued her prescription of valproate during pregnancy. Which of the following is the most likely abnormality that might be found on an ultrasound examination due to the effects of the mood stabilizer?
698.e: Maternal use of valproate is associated with an increased risk of foetal neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Increasing folic acid supplements(1-4 mg daily) can help reduce the risk of birth defects. For women in the reproductive age, ensure appropriate contraception if prescribing a medication associated with teratogenicity. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh Edition, Chapter 29th, Psychopharmacological treatment, Page no. 1047.

699.q: When deprived of food for more than 6 hours, a group of participants in an experiment would be more likely to interpret ambiguous pictures presented to them as something to do with food. This concept is the basis for:
699.e: Apperception means awareness of meaning of a stimulus as modified by one’s own experiences , thoughts and emotions . For example, when hungry, people would more likely interpret ambiguous stimuli as something related to food. This is the basis for projective personality tests like Rorschach inkblot test Thematic Apperception test Children Apperception test. Reference : Morgan and King's Introduction to Psychology, 7th edition, Chapter 13 Psychological Assessment and Testing, Page number 550.

699.q: Identify the hallucinogens whether they are natural or synthetic: 1-Psilocybin 2-Phencyclidine 3-LSD 4-Mescaline 5-Salvia Divinorum
699.e: Hallucinogens derived from natural source are psilocybin mescaline, harmine, harmaline, ayahuasca, salvia divinorum. While synthetic hallucinogens are ketamine, phencyclidine, LSD. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 20.5, Hallucinogen-related disorders, Page number 648.

699.q: Which of the following opioid receptors is responsible for drug dependence?
699.e: The μ-opioid receptors are involved in the Regulation and mediation of analgesia Respiratory depression Constipation Drug dependence The K-opioid receptors with Analgesia Diuresis Sedation The Δ-opioid receptors, with analgesia . Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter number 20, Stimulant-related disorders, Page number 677.

699.q: A 40-year-old man with alcohol dependence saw his wife talking to her boss at work. Since then he believes that she was having an affair with her boss that involved a sexual relationship, despite a lack of evidence. Which of the following is most likely to describe his belief?
699.e: Othello’s syndrome is also known as morbid jealousy in which an individual believes that his or her spouse or partner is unfaithful. De Clerambault syndrome, also known as erotomania, is a condition in which that patient believes that an exalted or well-known person is in love with him or her. (Option C) In Cotard’s syndrome, the person believes that he or she is dead or some part of his or her body is rotten or doesn’t exist. (Option B) In Capgras’ syndrome, the patient believes that a person who is close has been replaced by an exact double. (Option A) Reference: PGNIP2, Cijo Alex, 2 nd Edition, Chapter 3, page no. 27

699.q: On asking the name of the city that he lives in, an elderly patient having right hemispheric stroke replied, 'Jodhpur'. Next, on asking him the current year, he replied the same answer 'Jodhpur'. In fact, on asking any further question, he kept on giving the same reply. Such a formal thought disorder is known as ___________.
699.e: Perseveration is a formal thought disorder in which there is repetition of a particular response , such as a word, phrase, or gesture , despite the absence or cessation of a stimulus , usually caused by brain injury or other organic disorder rather than a psychopathology It is clear that this is not a problem of volition, which helps differentiate it from verbal stereotypy, which is a frequent spontaneous repetition of a word or phrase that is not in any way related to the current situation In verbal stereotypy , the same word or phrase is used regardless of the situation, whereas in perseveration a word, phrase or idea persists beyond the point at which it is relevant Echolalia refers to meaningless repetition of another person's spoken words Reference: Fish's Clinical Psychopathology, third edition, Chapter 4 Disorders of Thought and Speech, Page no. 45

699.q: A 30-year-old man comes to the psychiatrist for the evaluation of a depressed mood. He states that at least since his mid-20s he has felt depressed. He notes poor self-esteem and low energy and feels hopeless about his situation, though he denies suicidal ideation. He states he does not use drugs or alcohol and has no medical problems. His last physical examination by his physician 1 month ago was entirely normal. Which of the following treatment options should be tried first?
699.e: This patient has a dysthymic disorder. There are a number of studies that show positive responses to antidepressants with these patients. Venlafaxine and bupropion are generally believed to be the treatments of choice for dysthymic disorder , though there is a subgroup of patients that will respond to the MAOIs as well. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh Edition, Chapter 8th, Mood disorders, Page no. 381.

699.q: A 48-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department. She is unresponsive to questions, stumbles around the room and is agitated. On physical examination, you notice that she smells of alcohol and she is not cooperative during the remainder of the examination. Administration of what medicine would be the most appropriate initial treatment?
699.e: The most appropriate treatment is the immediate administration of thiamine. This patient presents with Wernicke encephalopathy, characterized by the triad of delirium, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia Thiamine must be given prior to glucose in patients suspected of having this disorder. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 20.2, Alcohol-related disorders, Page no. 637.

699.q: A 23 year old man has presented with increased alcohol consumption & sexual indulgence, irritability, lack of sleep & not feeling fatigued even on prolonged periods of activity. All these changes have been seen for last 3 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
699.e: Hyperactivity, over sexual and drug indulgence, decreased need for sleep. All signs and symptoms are relevant to mania. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 8, Page No.: 358

700.q: A 45-year-old man with a history of depression presents with difficulties in ejaculation, particularly during intercourse. He has been taking an SSRI for the past six months. He reports that he feels physically capable of sexual activity but has trouble ejaculating. What is the most appropriate diagnosis for this patient?
700.e: Explanation: The patient has difficulty ejaculating during partnered sexual encounters, which has developed after the initiation of SSRI treatment, suggesting a medication-related issue. Delayed Ejaculation: Duration: Symptoms must persist for at least 6 months. Symptoms: Difficulty with ejaculations: Delayed ejaculation. Absent or reduced frequency of ejaculation. Marked delay or absence of orgasm. Symptoms Needed: At least one symptom must occur. Exclusions: Symptoms should not be attributed to: Relationship problems. Substance use (including prescribed medications). Another medical condition. Another psychiatric condition. Severity Specifiers: Mild: Causes mild distress. Moderate: Causes moderate distress. Severe: Causes severe distress.

700.q: A 30-year-old homeless woman with an 18-year history of daily intravenous heroin use comes into the community rehabilitation clinic asking to be "detoxed" in order to "kick my heroin habit" once and for all. While she is motivated for treatment, she currently is shivering, with rhinorrhoea, tearing, gagging and grabbing her abdomen in pain due to cramps. When questioned about her last use, she claims she used shortly before arriving, but that a peer gave her "something different to shoot up". Which of the following substances would be most likely to cause her current symptoms?
700.e: This patient is suffering from classic symptoms of opioid withdrawal. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist which, when given to a patient actively using another opiate, will precipitate withdrawal. Alprazolam and cocaine would not present with this clinical picture.( OPTION A & C ) Methadone and morphine are opioids which would cause further intoxication, not withdrawal.( OPTION D ) Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 29, Psychopharmacological treatment, Page no. 1002.

700.q: All of the following receptors are involved in chocoholics except:
700.e: Anandamide , an ingredient in chocolate, stimulates the same receptors as marijuana. Other compounds in chocolate include tryptophan , the precursor of serotonin and phenylalanine , an amphetamine-like substance, both of which improve mood. So-called chocoholics may be self-medicating because of a depressive diathesis. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 20.12, Other Substance Use and Addictive Disorders, Page number 690.

700.q: All of the following are high risk factors for suicide except:
700.e: Family history of suicide ( OPTION A ), previous suicidal attempts (OPTION B) , substance abuse , and chaotic family background are all high risk factors for suicide . Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 23.1 Suicide, Page number 763

700.q: All of the following substance are capable of causing Anxiety Disorder except?
700.e: The following substances are prone to cause Anxiety Disorder: Alcohol Caffeine Cannabis Cocaine Phencyclidine Hallucinogen(LSD) Opioid Amphetamines Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 9, Anxiety Disorders, Page no. 413.

700.q: A diagnosis of polysubstance addiction is appropriate for all of the following substances of abuse except:
700.e: A diagnosis of polysubstance dependence is appropriate if, for a period of at least 12 months, a person has repeatedly used substances from at least three categories, NOT including nicotine and caffeine . Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 20.12, Other Substance Use and Addictive Disorders, Page number 690.

700.q: Which of the following medication is a recognized panicogen?
700.e: Panic-inducing substances (sometimes called panicogens) induce panic attacks in most patients with panic disorder . Respiratory Panicogens: Carbon Dioxide (5-35% mixtures) Sodium lactate Sodium bicarbonate Neurochemical Panicogens (act through specific neurotransmitter systems): Yohimbine mCPP and m-caroline drugs GABA-b receptor inverse agonists: Flumazenil Cholecystokinin Caffeine Isoproterenol is also a panicogen, however, its mechanism of action is poorly understood. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th Edition, Page Number-392.

700.q: A 26-year-old man comes to the physician with the chief complaint of a depressed mood for the past 5 weeks. He has been feeling down, with decreased concentration, energy and interest in his usual hobbies. Six weeks prior to this office visit, he had been to the emergency room for an acute asthma attack and was started on prednisone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Mood disorder secondary to a general medical condition
700.e: According to DSM-V criteria, patients developing a mood disorder after using a substance(either illicit or prescribed) are diagnosed with a substance-induced mood disorder. The diagnosis of major depression cannot be made in the presence of either substance use or a general medical condition that might be the cause of the mood disorder. Prednisone is a common culprit in causing mood disorders ranging from depression to mania to psychosis. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 8th, Mood disorders, Page no. 371.

o: Fear that escape might be difficult in specific situations
Fear that panic-like symptoms or embarrassing symptoms may occur in specific situations
No clinically significant distress is present despite the symptoms
701.e: In Agoraphobia, the individual fears or avoids specific situations because of thoughts that escape might be difficult or help might not be available in the event of developing panic-like symptoms or other incapacitating or embarrassing symptoms (e.g., fear of falling in elderly adults; fear of incontinence). The fear, anxiety or avoidance causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational or other important areas of functioning. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 9.3, Agoraphobia, Page 399.

701.q: Which of the following is a common symptom of Agoraphobia?
o: Fear of being in crowded places
701.e: Explanation: Agarophobia refers to the fear of being in crowded places Individuals with Agoraphobia often avoid situations where escape might be difficult. Duration: Symptoms last for ≥6 months. Key Symptoms: Fear/anxiety in specific situations (e.g., public transport, open spaces). Avoidance of situations due to fear of panic attacks. Fear and avoidance are disproportionate to potential threat. Exclusions: Not due to another medical or mental disorder.

701.q: Which is true for blood-injection-injury type of specific phobia?
o: One of the Most common type of specific phobia
Bradycardia and Hypotension are characteristically seen as compared to tachycardia seen in other phobias
All of the above are true
701.e: The blood-injection-injury type is the most common type of phobia found (Option A) . It is differentiated from the others in that bradycardia and hypotension often follow the initial tachycardia that is common to all phobias (Option B) . The blood-injection-injury type of specific phobia is particularly likely to affect many members and generations of a family (Option C) . In the special situation of blood-injection-injury phobia, some therapists recommend that patients tense their bodies and remain seated during the exposure to help avoid the possibility of fainting from a vasovagal reaction to the phobic stimulation. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 9.4, Specific Phobia, Page 402.

701.q: DSM-V includes all of these types of specific phobia based on the phobic stimulus except:
701.e: The DSM-5 includes distinctive types of specific phobia: Animal type (Option B) . Natural environment type(e.g., storms) (Option C) . Blood-injection injury type(e.g., needles) (Option A) . Situational type(e.g., cars, elevators, planes) Other type(for specific phobias that do not fit into the previous four types). Phobia for social situations is termed as Social phobia , which is separate entity from Specific Phobia Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 9.4, Specific Phobia, Page 402.

701.q: A person was found wandering on the streets after one month of running away from his home. His family members saw him and brought him for psychiatric consultation. Wandering behavior is seen in psychiatric patients in all of the following conditions, except:
701.e: Wandering behavior is seen during a variety of conditions like dissociative fugue , substance intoxication, delirium, dementia, manic phase of bipolar disorder, schizophrenia. (Option A, C & D) It is less likely during panic attack. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 457.

701.q: Which of the following drugs is a dopamine-2(D2) antagonist?
701.e: Buspirone is an anxiolytic medication with 5-hydroxytryptamine(5-HT1A) partial agonist activity. It is a potent D2-receptor antagonist (OPTION B IS CORRECT) . It is mainly used for treatment of generalised anxiety disorder and other anxiety disorders. Even though it is an antianxiety medication, it is not related to benzodiazepines or barbiturates. It is not helpful for treating benzodiazepine withdrawal symptoms. These patients will need benzodiazepines to relieve their symptoms before starting buspirone. Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 29th, Page no. 957.

701.q: When starting an SSRI, such as fluoxetine, in an adolescent patient with separation anxiety disorder, the Food and Drug Administration(FDA) recommends the clinician monitor closely for which of the following?
701.e: The FDA recently placed a black box warning for the use of antidepressants in children and adolescents. This warning reminds clinicians of some evidence indicating a possible increased incidence of suicidal thoughts among adolescents using antidepressants-particularly SSRIs. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 31.13, Anxiety Disorders of Infancy, Childhood and Adolescence, Page no. 1254.

701.q: A 32-year-old woman with agoraphobia was assessed for behavior therapy. Which of the following is she fearful of?
701.e: Agoraphobia is anxiety associated with places or situations either from which escape may be difficult or in which help may not be available in the event of a panic attack. It means literally fear of the crowded place . It is strongly associated with panic. ( OPTION B ) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 9, page no. 395

702.q: A 29-year-old male CT3 psychiatric trainee was put down badly by his consultant in a ward round. He couldn't say anything to the consultant when the consultant shouted at him. When he returned home, he became verbally abusive and aggressive towards his wife. What is the most likely phenomenon?
702.e: Anna Freud described 10 defence mechanisms in her work. Reaction formation projection and regression are three of them. In displacement, emotions or wishes are transferred from the original object or person to a more suitable substitute. ( Option A is CORRECT ) Reaction formation is seen in patients with obsessive–compulsive disorder . ( Option D ) Here the attitude is opposed to the oppressed wish and constitutes the opposite reaction Projection : unacceptable thoughts, emotions and feelings are projected on to some other person ( Option C ) Identification : a person takes the attributes of others to him or herself ( Option B ) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 4, page no. 161

702.q: Regarding the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder, which of the following is most correct?
o: Cognitive and behavioural strategies are more effective than serotonergic antidepressants
Group therapy is less effective than individual therapy
More frequent therapy sessions are associated with improved outcomes
Treatment of any kind is more successful if compulsions are present
702.e: Treatment is more effective if compulsions are present . Cognitive and behavioural therapies have similar effectiveness to SSRIs. (Option A) Likewise, group and individual therapies have similar success rates. (Option B) Patients with more bizarre obsessional thoughts are less likely to resist carrying out compulsive acts. The frequency of psychotherapy sessions has not been shown to influence outcome although duration of each session and the therapy overall is associated with better outcomes. (Option C) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 10, page no. 423

702.q: Suicidal tendencies are most commonly seen in: March 2003
702.e: Ans. C i.e. Severe depression 1458. Repetitive irresesistable thought to do something a) Phobia b) Obsession c) Compulsion d) Anxiety Correct Answer - B Ans. is 'b' i.e., Obsession Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) OCD is an anxiety disorder which is characterized by recurrent, unwanted thoughts (Obsessions) and repettive behaviors (compulsions). An obsession has following characteristic : -

702.q: A 33-year-old woman with an obsessive-compulsive disorder gets intrusive thoughts about the safety of her husband. To cope with these thoughts, she prays three times, buys things in multiples of three and washes her hands three times on each occasion that she experiences these thoughts. Which of the following is most appropriate to describe her behaviour?
702.e: Obsessions are repetitive, intrusive thoughts that are recognised as irrational thoughts by the sufferer. Several unsuccessful attempts have been made to resist these thoughts. The content of the thought can be related to aggression, dirt, contamination, fear of causing harm, and religious or sexual thoughts. In order to reduce the associated anxiety symptoms patients, carry out repetitive acts such as counting, cleaning repeatedly, or touching or arranging things in symmetry; These acts are termed ' compulsions' . Reference: PGNIP2, Cijo Alex, 2 nd Edition, Chapter 3, page no. 28

702.q: Which of the following disorders typically has the oldest age at onset?
702.e: The mean age of onset for OCD is 20 years . Social phobia typically begins to develop after puberty. Features of Asperger’s syndrome are commonly noted from the age of three or earlier. The majority of females with anorexia nervosa have on set within five years of menarche. Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 10, page no. 419

702.q: In considering obsessive compulsive disorder, which of the following statements is least true?
o: A bimodal age of onset with peaks occurs at ages 12-14 years and 20-22 years
Brain imaging shows morphological changes in basal ganglia structure
First-degree relatives have a higher-than-normal incidence of psychiatric disorders
Predominance of phobic ruminative ideas and absence of compulsions is a poor prognostic factor
702.e: Predominance of phobic ruminative ideas and absence of compulsions is favourable prognostic factor . ( Options A, B & C are all true ) Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 10, page no. 420

702.q: What is the most common pattern of obsession?
702.e: Explanation: Contamination/Cleansing is the most commonly seen pattern of obsession Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) A disorder characterized by intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours (compulsions). Symptoms: Obsessions: Unwanted thoughts or urges causing anxiety (e.g., contamination fears, doubts). Compulsions: Behaviours performed to alleviate anxiety (e.g., excessive washing, checking). Common Patterns: Contamination/Cleansing: Fear of germs leading to compulsive washing. Pathologic Doubt/Checking: Doubts about safety (e.g., turning off appliances). Intrusive/Forbidden Thoughts: Distressing thoughts about aggressive or sexual acts. Symmetry/Ordering: Compulsion for order or symmetry. Insight: Most patients recognize their beliefs are irrational, but some have poor or no insight.

702.q: Identify the OCD related disorders as per ICD-11: 1. Hoarding disorder 2. Trichotillomania 3. Hypochondriasis 4. Olfactory reference syndrome
702.e: OCD related disorders: UPDATES: ICD-11 & DSM-5 Hoarding disorder Body dysmorphic disorder (Dysmorphophobia) Olfactory reference syndrome Body focused repetitive behavior disorder: Trichotillomania Excoriation (skin-picking) disorder Hypochondriasis (as per ICD-11)DSM-5 : It is Somatic (a/c Illness anxiety disorder) Reference: ICD-11, Obsessive Compulsive and related disorder, BlockL1-6B20, Page No.: 43-47

703.q: Which among these symptoms must be present to fulfil the criteria for PTSD according to DSM-V?
703.e: The 5th edition of DSM-V criteria for PTSD specify that the following symptoms must have lasted >1 month: Intrusion Avoidance Alterations of mood and cognition Hyperarousal Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th Edition, Page Number-349.

703.q: A 40-year-old man was recently rescued by the fire department from his building which caught fire. He presented with flashbacks, repeated distressing memories and disturbed dreams of the event for about 20 days after the traumatic incident. Which of the following characteristics differentiate acute stress disorder from PTSD in his case?
703.e: According to DSM-5, acute stress disorder (ASD) and PTSD are differentiated by time duration If symptoms are present up to one month of exposure to traumatic event, it fulfils the criteria for ASD However, if symptoms occur more than a month, the criteria of PTSD is fulfilled In this question, the person developed symptoms of flashbacks, distressing memories, disturbed dreams for 20 days after experiencing the fire accident Hence, the diagnosis of ASD would be more appropriate Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 11, Trauma and stressor related disorders, Page 439-441

703.q: In the context of Acute Stress Disorder, which of the following symptoms is not typically included?
703.e: Explanation: Emotional blunting is more commonly associated with PTSD, not typically listed as a symptom of Acute Stress Disorder. Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) Diagnostic Criteria (DSM-5) Symptoms occur 3 days to following exposure to trauma. Symptoms arise transiently in response to stress and usually resolve quickly. Required Symptoms: Presence of symptoms from intrusion, negative mood/cognition, dissociation, avoidance, or arousal categories. Nine symptoms needed from these categories. Symptoms Include: Cognitive "daze," narrowed attention, disorientation. Autonomic panic symptoms. May include partial or complete amnesia related to the event. Exclusions: Not due to substance use or other psychiatric disorders.

703.q: Which pharmacologic treatment is recommended for nightmares associated with PTSD?
703.e: Explanation: Prazosin is noted for its effectiveness in treating nightmares related to PTSD. Pharmacotherapy: Effective Medications: Sertraline and paroxetine are the most supported. Venlafaxine (SNRI), risperidone (atypical antipsychotic), and topiramate (anticonvulsant). Prazosin (for nightmares), while benzodiazepines lack supportive evidence and are often discouraged. Low-dose trazodone and the orexin antagonist suvorexant are used for insomnia

703.q: All of the following conditions are included in 'depressive disorders' section of DSM-5 except:
703.e: Acute stress disorder is classified under trauma-and stressor related disorders in DSM-5. While other conditions like Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and dysthymia are classified under depressive disorder spectrum. Reference: Diagnostic and Statistical manual, 5 th edition.

703.q: A young boy has suffered road traffic accident on NH-16, 2 months back, presents with complaints of horrible dreams about the accident. He is afraid of going to that highway again. He has visualization of same accident again and again. What is the diagnosis?
703.e: Flashback and nightmare, avoidance are the features of PTSD Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 11, Page No.: 440

703.q: In a patient of PTSD, a psychotherapeutic technique is practiced in which the patient focuses on the lateral movement of the clinician's finger while maintaining a mental image of the trauma experience. The general belief is that symptoms can be relieved as patients work through the traumatic event while in a state of deep relaxation. What is this technique called?
703.e: A variant of trauma-focused CBT for PTSD is called eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) , in which an exposure and cognitive reprocessing interventions are paired with directed eye movements In this, the patient focuses on the lateral movement of the clinician's finger while maintaining a mental image of the trauma experience The general belief is that symptoms can be relieved as patients work through the traumatic event while in a state of deep relaxation Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 11, Trauma and stressor related disorders, Page 445

703.q: Out of a 20-year-old girl having recently suffered sexual assault, a 25-year-old female fired from her job for her incompetence, a 30-year-old male whose father recently underwent a surgical procedure, and a 17-year-old boy having recently witnessed a car accident that killed his mother, which one of them are more prone to develop PTSD in terms of the stressor they went through?
o: Those who faced stalking and job loss
Those who suffered sexual assault and witnessed car accident
Those who suffered sexual assault and witnessed surgical procedure
Those who suffered job loss and witnessed surgical procedure
703.e: PTSD occurs following exposure to a violent, accidental, traumatic event The stressor should be severe enough so as to endanger one’s or close one’s life or should be sufficiently overwhelming to affect almost everyone , e.g., sexual assault, directly experiencing or witnessing an accidental death, etc. Stressors such as job loss or a regular surgical procedure are not severe enough to cause PTSD Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 11, Trauma and stressor related disorders, Page 437

704.q: The concept of inferiority complex and birth order in relation to personality were given by:
704.e: Alfred Adler’s individual psychology gives the concept of inferiority complex. And he also gave the concept of importance of birth order in personality structure . Reference : Morgan and King’s Introduction to Psychology, 7 th edition, Chapter 14 Personality, Page number 572.

704.q: A 30 year male is over enthusiastic and sensation seeking. He loves to explore new places and dishes of different cities. He makes big list of trying bungee jumping and sky diving and planning to organize camping in a deep forest. His personality trait is considered as:
704.e: Openness to experience (High means adventurous) Conscientiousness Extraversion Agreeableness Neuroticism Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 22, Page No.: 761

704.q: Mr Mark, who was flying on spicejet. Suddenly he got up and started giving instruction to air hostesses to do pole dance. He instructed everyone in a melodramatic manner to clap for these ladies. He started behaving like a boss. One old man shouted on him and asked him to shut up and sit down. Mr Mark felt insulted and became very anxious. Which type of personality Mr Mark has?
704.e: Excessive sense of self-importance and fragile emotion at the same time: Narcissistic PD. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 22, Page No.: 753

704.q: An 18-year-old girl is brought by her parents with history of frequent episodes of irritability, suicidal threats and excessive emotionality on trivial issues. On asking the patient, she denies of having any symptoms and blames her parents for not raising her properly. She reports of feeling chronically empty from inside. All of the following defence mechanisms explain her symptoms except:
704.e: The above case scenario depicts Cluster B personality disorder , Borderline Personality Disorder . In this disorder, defence mechanisms like denial, acting out, projection are frequently used. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 22 Personality Disorders, Page number 750

704.q: Gestaut Geschwind syndrome refers to a group of personality traits developing in a patient with epilepsy. These traits include all of the following except:
704.e: Gestaut Geschwind syndrome: Group of traits in some patients with focal dyscognitive seizures Temporal Lobe focus Heightened significance of things Serious, humourless, over inclusive & circumstantial speech – viscous Increased philosophical interest Hypergraphia Hypo sexuality Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 10 th edition, Chapter 2.4 Neuropsychiatric aspects of epilepsy, Page number 1366.

704.q: All of the following tools can be used to assess personality except:
704.e: Rorschach and TAT test → projective personality tests Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory → pencil-and-paper method of assessing personality . Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSE) → used to assess cognition and not personality . Reference : Morgan and King's Introduction to Psychology, 7th edition, Chapter 13 Psychological Assessment and testing, Page number 546.

704.q: A 20-year-old male presents with long-standing pattern of suspiciousness and mistrust on persons in general. In this case scenario, Paranoid personality disorder can be differentiated from Schizophrenia by:
o: Absence of hallucinations or formal thought disorder
Using projection as primary defence mechanism
704.e: Unlike in paranoid schizophrenia , patients with paranoid personality disorder do not have hallucinations or any formal thought disorder or disorganized speech However, in both Paranoid personality disorder and Schizophrenia, persons may appear socially withdrawn , lack friends and confidants , are unemotional and do not express emotions (restricted affect) In both, paranoid ideations are common , that is they interpret the world as threatening and believe intentions of others as malevolent , exploiting or deceiving In such paranoid ideations, defence mechanism of projection is often used in which unacknowledged feelings of self are attributed and projected onto others Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 22, Personality Disorders, Page 744

704.q: Which of the following terms describe personality changes occurring after traumatic brain injury?
704.e: Two subsets of personality changes seen after traumatic brain injury: Pseudo-depressed personality: characterised by apathy and blunted affect Pseudo-psychopathic personality: characterised by disinhibition, egocentricity, and sexual inappropriateness. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 10 th edition, Chapter 2.5 Neuropsychiatric consequences of Traumatic Brain injury, Page number 1400.

705.q: Conversion disorder was earlier, termed as 'Hysteria' by Hippocrates due to the belief that:
o: Uterus wanders in the body and presses on different organs thus causing symptoms
Emotionally charged behaviour is seen which seems out of control
Physical symptoms were found to have a psychological cause
Physical symptoms were attributed to demonic possession
705.e: In 1900 BC, Hippocrates coined the term hysteria to describe an illness in which the uterus (hystera) dries up and wanders the body in search of moisture Symptoms would then be caused by the uterus pressing on different organs Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.4, Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder), Page 473

705.q: Terminology for which of the disorders has been modified in DSM-V?
705.e: Term for Conversion disorder was modified to Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (FNSD ) in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition (DSM-5) The term ' Factitious Disorder' has not been modified in DSM-V (Option A) Chronic Fatigue Syndrome is not an entity included in DSM-V (Option C) Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.5, Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder), Page 473

705.q: Abnormal prion protein (PrPSc) is seen in all of the following conditions except:
705.e: Prion diseases: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Kuru Gerstman-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome Fatal familial insomnia Prions are infective agents composed of protein. Prion are made of proteins called PrP. PrP exists in a normal form (PrPc) and an abnormal form (PrPSc). PrPSc is resistant to protease and therefore cannot be broken down in the body. PrPSc can change adjacent PrPc into PrPSc (this is how the 'infection' spreads). Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive textbook of Psychiatry, 10 th edition, Chapter 2.10 Neuropsychiatric Aspects of Prion disease, Page number 1599.

705.q: What outcome may result from a failure to resolve the conflict between initiative and guilt in children?
o: Development of a strong sense of justice
705.e: Explanation: Erikson notes that unresolved conflict between initiative and guilt can lead to psychological issues such as conversion disorders or phobias . This is because the internalized guilt can stifle the child's initiative and lead to anxiety. Explanation for the other options: Development of a strong sense of justice: A healthy resolution leads to a sense of justice, but failure results in negative outcomes. Enhanced curiosity and exploration: These traits would likely diminish due to the guilt and anxiety that result from unresolved conflicts. Establishment of healthy relationships: Poor resolution of guilt typically leads to challenges in forming healthy relationships. Key Takeaways: Unresolved conflict between initiative and guilt can lead to psychological issues such as conversion disorders or phobias .

705.q: Which of the following is false about Conversion disorder?
o: Symptoms result due to repression of unconscious intrapsychic conflict and conversion of anxiety into a physical symptom
Conversion and repression are common defence mechanisms used
Results due to fixation in second stage (anal phase) of psychosexual development
Results due to non-resolution of Oedipal/ Electra complex
705.e: THEORIES OF CONVERSION DISORDER: Caused by repression of unconscious intrapsychic conflict and conversion of anxiety into a physical symptom Conversion, repression and regression are common defence mechanisms used Fixation in third stage (phallic stage) of psychosexual development and non-resolution of Oedipal or Electra complex Childhood physical/ sexual abuse Learning theory states that conversion symptom can be seen as piece of classically conditioned learned behavior Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.4, Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder), Page 474

706.q: Factitious disorder is the faking of physical or psychological signs and symptoms in order to maintain a sick role. All of the following clues should trigger suspicion of Factitious disorder except:
o: Unusual dramatic presentation of symptoms that defy conventional medical or psychiatric understanding
Emergence of new and unusual symptoms when other symptoms resolve
Resistance to undergo procedures or testing
706.e: CLUES THAT SHOULD TRIGGER SUSPICION OF FACTITIOUS DISORDER: Unusual, dramatic presentation of symptoms that defy conventional medical or psychiatric understanding (Option A) Symptoms do not respond appropriately to usual treatment or medications Emergence of new, unusual symptoms when other symptoms resolve (Option B) Eagerness to undergo procedures or testing or to recount symptoms (Option C) Reluctance to give access to collateral sources of information (i.e., refusing to sign releases of information or to give contact information for family and friends) Extensive medical history or evidence of multiple surgeries Multiple drug allergies Medical profession (Option D) Few visitors Ability to forecast unusual progression of symptoms or unusual response to treatment Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.6, Factitious Disorder, Page 490

706.q: In a case of Factitious disorder, all of the following methods can be used to detect possibly simulated fever except?
o: Simultaneous recording of temperature from two sites i.e., oral and rectal
Recording temperature of freshly voided urine
Relying on temperature readings given by patients
706.e: METHODS OF SIMULATION OF FEVER IN FACTITIOUS DISORDER: Warming thermometer against a lightbulb or other heat source Drinking hot fluids Friction from mouth or anal sphincter False recordings Injection of pyrogens such as faeces, vaccines, thyroid hormone, or tetanus toxoid POSSIBLE METHODS OF DETECTION OF FALSIFIED HISTORY OF FEVER GIVEN IN FACTITIOUS DISORDER: Simultaneous taking of temperature from two different locals (orally and rectally )- (Option A) Recording the temperature of freshly voided urine (Option B) The appearance of cool skin despite high thermometer readings Normal white blood cell count (Option D) Unusually high or inconsistent temperatures Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 13.6, Factitious Disorder, Page 494

707.q: A 45-year-old divorced male bus driver was referred for psychiatric consultation for complaints of memory loss for the previous 12 years, behaving and responding to the environment as if it were 12 years previously, e.g., he didn't recognize his 8-year-old son, and denied recollection of current events like name of current president. On mental status examination, the patient displayed intact intellectual function and brain imaging was normal. The patient's mother described a family history of brutal beatings and physical discipline subjected towards the patient. Pick the correct diagnosis.
707.e: The above case scenario is suggestive of dissociative amnesia. The main feature of dissociative amnesia is an inability to recall important autobiographical information , usually of a traumatic or stressful nature, that is inconsistent with ordinary forgetting. Dissociative amnesia can occur in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) , however other symptoms should be present as well to fulfil the criteria for the same. (Option B) In malingering, there is usually a secondary gain. (Option C) Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 452.

707.q: All of the following are non-pathological forms of amnesia, except:
707.e: Ordinary forgetfulness, infantile and childhood amnesia, amnesia for sleep and dreaming and hypnotic amnesia are non-pathological forms of amnesia. (Option A, C & D) Dissociative amnesia is pathological. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 452.

707.q: Psychotherapeutic technique proven to be effective in dissociative identity disorder?
707.e: Treatment option out of these, in dissociative disorders is hypnosis. Hypnosis can be useful for accessing specific alter personality states and their sequestered affects and memories. Hypnosis is also used to create relaxed mental states in which negative life events can be examined without overwhelming anxiety. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 461.

707.q: A 21-year-old lady presented with history of episodes where she would behave as if possessed by some spirit. She would display extraordinary strength and become aggressive towards her family members, speak in foreign language and display bizarre behavior. She would always claim amnesia for the event. Pick the correct diagnosis for her condition.
707.e: Possession trance , involves single or episodic alternations in the state of consciousness , characterized by the exchange of the person's customary identity with a new identity usually attributed to a spirit, divine power, deity, or another person. In this possessed state, the individual exhibits stereotypical and culturally determined behaviors or experiences being controlled by the possessing entity. There must be partial or full amnesia of the event. The trance or possession state must not be a normally accepted part of a cultural or religious practice and must cause significant distress or functional impairment in one or more of the usual domains. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page number 463.

707.q: All of the following conditions may produce feelings of being 'detached from oneself or from environment,' except:
707.e: Depersonalization can result from a Medical condition Neurological condition Intoxication Withdrawal from illicit drugs Side effect of medications Panic attacks Phobias PTSD Acute stress disorder Schizophrenia Dissociative disorder Drug related depersonalization is typically transient, but persistent depersonalization can follow an episode of intoxication with a variety of substances, including marijuana, cocaine, and other psychostimulants However, it is rarely seen with caffeine use disorder Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 12, Dissociative disorders, Page 456

708.q: Counter-transference is commonly encountered in all of the following conditions, except:
708.e: Countertransference is the process where the physician unconsciously displaces onto the patient patterns of behaviors or emotional reactions as if he or she were a significant figure from earlier in the physician's life Signs of countertransference: Missed appointment by the psychiatrist Boredom Sleepiness in a session Counter transference by physicians is commonly encountered in disorders in which frequent complaints, non-remitting symptoms are seen: Psychosomatic diseases (Somatic Symptom disorder, Factitious disorder) Personality disorders (Cluster B personality disorders) Impulse Control disorders Reference : Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 5, Examination and Diagnosis of the psychiatric patient, Page 194

708.q: A 75 year old man flown to america from Siberia (war zone), to stay with his son. He is having nightmares and flashback. He was brought to hospital by his son. It was informed that he is getting irritated, insomnia and easily forgetting incidences. What is the most probable diagnosis?
708.e: Its old age related disease and patient is forgetting the incidences. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 21

708.q: A 54-year-old man sees a physician complaining of a depressed mood and inability to sleep for the past 3 weeks. He tells the physician that in the past when he has had similar episodes, he was placed on a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, which proved effective. The physician diagnoses the patient with major depression and agrees to use an MAOI. Which of the following foods must be completely avoided by this patient while on this medication?
708.e: There is a list of foods that should be avoided due to small amounts of tyramine and rare association with hypertensive episodes while a patient is taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor , but only a few that must be completely avoided. To be completely avoided: Aged cheese Red wine Cured meats To be consumed in small quantities: Anchovies Beets Caviar Chocolate Coffee Colas Curry powder Figs Liquorice Mushrooms Rhubarb Snails Soy sauce Worcestershire sauce Reference : Jacobson, Pg no. 121-22.

708.q: Which statement regarding serotonin(5-HT2A) Agonism is correct?
o: 5-HT2A-receptors have no role in sleep regulation
708.e: 5-Hydroxytryptamine (5-HT2A ) receptors excite cortical pyramidal neurons, increase glutamate and decrease dopamine release .( OPTION D IS CORRECT & OPTION C IS WRONG) These receptors are involved in the mechanism of sleep and hallucinations. Blockade of 5-HT2A receptors leads to release of dopamine. 5-HT2A antagonism decreases extrapyramidal side effects. Reference: Stahls Essential Psychopharmacology, Fourth edition, Chapter 7th, Page no. 294.

708.q: Narcolepsy is due to abnormality in ?
708.e: Ans. A. Hypothalamus Narcolepsy is unique in that those who suffer from it tyPicaly fall almost instantaneously into REM sleep. It is thought that narcolepsy is caused by a malfunctioning of the hypothalamus in brain.

708.q: Which of the following is a key feature of Paradoxical Insomnia?
o: Sleep disturbance with no subjective complaint
Inability to sleep despite having a sleep-deprived body
Perception of insomnia despite objective evidence of normal sleep patterns
708.e: Explanation: A hallmark feature of Paradoxical Insomnia is that individuals perceive insomnia (difficulty falling or staying asleep) even though objective sleep studies (like polysomnography) show that their sleep is actually normal. This creates a dissociation between the subjective experience of sleeplessness and objective evidence of sleep.

709.q: A 19-year-old girl referred for evaluation of menstrual disturbances. She weighs only 38 kg and is 1.78 m tall. She is emaciated, her skin is dry and she has excessive growth of lanugo hair. She has been amenorrhoeic for 9 months. Her cortisol level is elevated, her Free T4 is normal. She has anemia and associated reduced white cell and platelet count. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to fit with this clinical picture?
709.e: Anorexia nervosa has a female to male preponderance of 9:1. It is estimated that around 0.5-1% of women between 15 and 30 years of age have anorexia. The aetiology of anorexia is unknown, but it is likely to be an interaction between environmental and genetic factors, Patient may also have bradycardia and low / low-normal BP Typical laboratory tests include decreased FSH, LH, estrogens and 17-OH steroids. Free T4 and TSH levels are usually normal. Anemia with decreased white and platelet cell count may also occur. There may be metabolic alkalosis, hypocalcaemia, hypokalemia and hypomagnesaemia. Treatment may involve complex psychotherapy for a number of years, and referral to a specialist in the field is recommended. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:444 Page number: 3274

709.q: A 17-year-old adolescent suffers from Bulimia nervosa and is very depressed. She is also suffering from insomnia and apathy. Which of the following medications should be avoided?
709.e: Bupropion is a NDRI (norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor). Seizure disorders and eating disorders are contraindications for bupropion because of its possible lowering of the seizure threshold and its anorectic effects. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11th Edition, Chapter 29, Page Number-955.

709.q: A 15 year old female is brought to OPD by her mother for evaluation as she has been eating very less and becoming very thin. O/E: her BMI <17.5, russel's sign was seen. Mother is reporting that she is indulged into rigorous exercises and over gymming. During interview, girl is irritated and saying that she is doing good and eating fine. On further enquiry, it was found that she didn't had menses for last 3 months. What is the diagnosis?
709.e: She is image conscious and has BMI Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 22, Page No.: 511

709.q: A 21 year old female is presented to OPD with complaints of nutritional deficiencies and weight loss. She avoids eating food as she doesn't like the smell of food. On further evaluation, it is found that she is not image conscious. She is suffering from:
709.e: In avoidant restrictive food intake disorder: A person avoids eating food because he/she doesn't like taste or smell of food. Person is not image conscious. Reference: ICD-11, Feeding or Eating Disorders, BlockL1-6B8, Page No.: 59

709.q: A 23-year-old college student comes to the physician because her roommates are worried about her eating. She tells the physician that she regularly eats large amounts of food(more than 10,000 calories on occasion) and then has to 'punish herself' and 'get rid of it'. She explains that she does this by sticking her finger down her throat, which causes her to vomit. She tried to hide this activity from her roommates, but on more than one occasion they have heard her retching in the bathroom. The patient is 5'5" tall and weighs 132 lb. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
709.e: This college student has the classic symptoms of bulimia, in which she eats huge amounts of food (binging) and then feels the need to "get rid of it" (purging) Her body mass index (BMI) is within a normal range and therefore anorexia is ruled out. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder is more commonly found in children, and at any rate, this woman's food intake is anything but restrictive (OPTION B). Likewise, while she does binge, she also purges, making binge-eating disorder less of a good fit than bulimia (OPTION D). Pica is the eating of non-nutritional objects that are not meant to be consumed (e.g., lead paint chips). There is no history of this given in the vignette. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, Eleventh edition, Chapter 15.2, Bulimia Nervosa, Page no. 517.

709.q: Hospitalized management of anorexia nervosa is done on priority in patients with:
o: Weight for height less than 75% of normal
709.e: Weight for height less than 80% of expected is an indication for admission. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 15, Page No.: 514

709.q: Differentiating feature of avoidant restrictive food intake disorder and restrictive type of anorexia nervosa is:
709.e: In avoidant restrictive food intake disorder: A person avoids eating food because he/she doesn't like taste or smell of food. Person is not image conscious. Reference: Kaplan and Saddocks Synopsis of Psychiaitry, 11th Edition, Chapter 22, Page No.: 514

710.q: A 35-year-old patient reports experiencing sudden, uncontrollable urges to act. This is characteristic of which symptom?
710.e: Explanation: Impulse is a sudden and irresistible urge to take a specific action. Impulse is a strong and often uncontrollable desire to act without much forethought or consideration of the consequences. Explanations of other options: Hallucination (Option B): A hallucination is the experience of sensing something that does not actually exist in the external environment. Delusion (Option C): A delusion is a firmly held false belief that persists despite logical reasoning or evidence proving otherwise. Pseudohallucination (Option D): A pseudohallucination resembles a hallucination but is acknowledged by the individual as originating from their own mind rather than the external world.

710.q: A 38-year-old divorced female professor, belonging to high socio-economic class, was reprimanded many times for charges of shop-lifting, which she had started at the age of 22. She would steal only on impulse, not from pre mediation, and experienced tension prior to, and satisfaction after shoplifting. The stolen items included crayons, spoons, candles, coloured papers, earrings, etc. which she hoarded in her cupboard. In the above case, which of the following statements is false?
o: This disorder is categorised under Disruptive and Impulse Control disorders in DSM-5
The object stolen is usually the goal of stealing
Antisocial personality disorder should be ruled out
SSRI and CBT are usually helpful
710.e: In Kleptomania, the act of stealing is the objective and not the object stolen. It is characterized by mounting tension before the act, followed by gratification and lessening of tension with or without guilt, remorse, or depression after the act. Kleptomania is categorised under Disruptive and Impulse Control disorders in DSM-5 SSRI and CBT are usually considered in management of Kleptomania. In patients with habit of stealing, antisocial personality disorder is an important differential diagnosis; however, in them, the object stolen and violation of norms is the objective. Reference : Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, 11 th edition, Chapter 19 Disruptive, Impulse control, and Conduct disorders, Page number 611.
